en: A Brief Account of the Śākya Clan, Compiled and Revised by the Bhikṣu Śramaṇa Jue’an of Baoci Monastery in Zhili, Wucheng; and Baozhou. [Section on] the Three Sovereigns.
The Three Sovereigns.
Taohao Baoxi was of the Feng clan.
He ruled by the virtue of Wood.
His capital was Wancheng (present-day Chen Prefecture, Huaiyang Commandery, within the territory of Bianliang).
This was the domain of Yuzhou as recorded in the "Yugong" (Tribute of Yu).
In ancient times, people hunted wild animals;
they ate meat and wore skins, making it difficult to provide for them through conventional means.
Taohao taught the people how to make nets and traps for hunting and fishing,
and to raise the six domestic animals;
furthermore, he offered sacrificial victims to the spirits and deities.
He was called Pao-xi;
later generations called him Fu-xi.
He first drew the eight trigrams and created writing and tally marks.
From this, written records were produced.
He took the dragon as the basis for his official titles and reigned for one hundred and sixteen years.
The *Yi* says:
"Fuxi hollowed out wood to make boats and sharpened wood to make oars."
The *Qincao* says:
"Fuxi fashioned the *qin* to cultivate the person and refine the nature,
returning to one's original truth."
The Tongli states:
"Fuxi fashioned a twenty-five-stringed se to establish the rites of marriage."
The *Tujing* states:
"Paoxi was born in Chengji County of Qinzhou, Gongchang Road, Shaanxi.
His mother was named Huaxu."
It lies within the domain of Yongzhou as described in the *Yugong*.
In Huozhou of Hezhong Prefecture, under the Jining Road, there is Mount Funiu (伏牛臺).
This is the place where Fuxi lay upon his ox and mounted his horse.
The tomb of Nüwa is located there within the domain of Jizhou; furthermore, there is an ancient temple of Nüwa in Luzhou, west of the Huai River. [The successive sovereigns were:

the Clan of Nüwa, the Clan of Gonggong, the Clan of Datingshi, the Clan of Bohuangshi, the Clan of Zhonghuangshi, the Clan of Lilushi, the Clan of Lilianshi, the Clan of Hexushishi, the Clan of Zunlushi, the Clan of Hunchunshi, the Clan of Haoyingshi, the Clan of Zhuxiangshi, the Clan of Getianshi, the Clan of Yin Kangshi, and the Clan of Wuhuaishi. In the second month of the fifth year of the Yuanyou era of Emperor Zhezong of the Song dynasty...
Zhuge Shen’s *Shaoyun tu* states:
"The above fifteen dynasties together total seventeen thousand seven hundred and eighty-seven years."
Regarding the deity of the Altar of Soil and Grain (*sheji*), the *Fengsu tong* states:
"The son of the Lord of Gonggong was named Xiu;
he delighted in traveling far and wide."
Wherever boats and carriages could reach,
and wherever human footsteps could extend,
there was nothing he did not exhaustively explore.
Therefore, he was sacrificed to as the deity of the She altar.
The *Zuozhuan* states:
"Gonggong’s clan had a son named Goulong."
Because he leveled the lands and regulated the waters, he was worshipped with the sacrifice of She (the Earth Altar).
The *Liji* states:
"When the Lord of Gong divided the Nine Provinces..."
His son was Hou-tu.
He was able to level the Nine Provinces;
therefore, he was sacrificed to as the God of the Soil (She).
Furthermore, when the Lord of Lishan possessed the world,
his son Zhu was able to cultivate the five grains; therefore,
he was enshrined as the Sacrificial Official of the Grains (Ji).
Cai Yong’s *Duduan* states:
"In the Zhou dynasty, Qi cultivated and planted the hundred grains;
thus Ji was established as the chief of the hundred grains."
He was named Ji because of this;
his spirit is Qi, the Lord Houji of Zhou.
Yan Di, the lineage of Shen Nong, was of the Jiang clan.
Succeeding the Lord Fu Xi,
he ruled with the virtue of Fire and established his capital at Lu.
The present-day region of Dongping Road corresponds to the territory of Yanzhou as described in the *Yugong*.
At that time, the people ate herbs and drank water,
and subsisted on the fruits of trees and the flesh of birds and beasts.
There were many diseases.
Yan Di sought edible things and taught people to cook their food with fire.
At that time, heaven rained down grain.
He then taught the people to sow the five grains and to fashion pottery,
axes, hoes, plows, and weeding tools.
Because he cleared away the weeds and brush so that the five grains could flourish, he was called the Lord of Divine Agriculture (Shennong).
Furthermore, he tasted the hundred herbs.
In one day, one encounters seventy poisons;
yet, as one person alone is insufficient for sustenance,
markets are established at midday to facilitate the exchange of what is available for what is not.
He took fire as the basis for his official calendar.
He occupied the throne for one hundred and twenty years.
*Huantan Xinlun* states:
Shennong fashioned paulownia wood into a *qin* lute and used twisted silk as strings,
in order to communicate with the virtue of the divine and the intelligent.
The Guangya states:
"The qin of the Lord of Shenong was three feet six inches long and had five strings."
It is said that these are gong, shang, jiao, zhi,
and yu. King Wen of Zhou added two strings,
called shao-gong and shao-shang.
Di Cheng, Di Lin, Di Ming, Di Xuan, Di Li, Di Ai, Di Yu, and Di Gang—these eight emperors all belonged to the lineage of Shennong.
The total duration was five hundred and ten years.
Toward the end of this period, the feudal lords fought one another and submitted to the Yellow Emperor.
The Yellow Emperor, Lord of Youxiong: The Yellow Emperor, Lord of Youxiong, was of the Gong-sun clan;
his name was Xuanyuan.
He was the son of Shao Dian, the ruler of the state of Youxiong.
When Shennong was the Son of Heaven,
the feudal lords attacked one another;
Shennong was unable to punish them.
Among the feudal lords who committed aggression and oppression,
the most powerful and violent was Chiyou.
Xuanyuan cultivated virtue and disciplined his army.
He fought against the Lord of Flame (Yandi) and defeated him;
he captured Chiyou at Zhuolu and killed him. The present-day administrative seat of Zhuozhou in Daidu Road is located within the jurisdiction of Fanyang in the region of Yu.
Thereupon, the feudal lords all turned their allegiance to Xuanyuan.
They enthroned Xuanyuan as the Son of Heaven, succeeding the lineage of Shennong.
In the first year of the Yellow Emperor’s reign, the year Dinghai, he began to establish the fundamental institutions of government.
He followed and campaigned against all those in the world who were not compliant with him.
His territory extended to the sea in the east and to Mount Kongtong—
located in present-day Suzhou Prefecture of Gansu Province, within the domain of Yongzhou— in the west.
To the south he reached the sea;
to the north he pursued the Xunyu tribes and established his capital on the slopes of Zhuolu.
They migrated without constancy,
using their military forces as guards and taking the clouds as the basis for their official titles.
There were auspicious omens of the virtue of the Earth.
He appointed Fenghou, Limu, Kuanshanji, Changxian, and Dahong, thereby obtaining the Six Ministers;
thus heaven and earth were brought to order and the divine intelligences arrived.
The Emperor received the *Hetu* (River Chart) and beheld therein the images of the sun, moon, and stars; thus,
the treatises on the stellar officials first came into being.
He commanded Dainao to investigate the essence of the five elements and observe the position of the celestial polestar; thus,
he first established the cycle of Jiazi.
He charged Rongcheng to create the calendar;
he charged Lishou to devise arithmetic;
and he charged Linglun to fashion the pitch-pipes and musical scales.
He ordered Ji to observe the stars and atmospheric vapors,
while Rongcheng concurrently oversaw them both;
he composed writings to distinguish between the noble and the humble.
He constructed boats and carts to facilitate passage where it was obstructed;
he demarcated the fields and divided the territories, establishing ten thousand districts of states each spanning one hundred *li*,
and organized eight households into a *jing* (well-field).
One well constitutes a neighborhood;
three neighborhoods constitute a village;
three villages constitute a ward.
Five *li* make one *yi*;
ten *yi* make one *du*;
ten *du* make one *shi*.
The Master [Yao] divided the state into ten provinces and established the Left and Right Grand Supervisors to oversee the myriad nations.
He instituted the rites of feng and shan and performed the music of Xianchi;
thus, even the most distant barbarian nations sent tribute.
Huangdi had twenty-five sons.
There were fourteen individuals who obtained surnames,
forming twelve clans:
Ji, You, Qi, Yi, Teng, Zhen, Ren, Xun, Xi, Ji, Huan, and Xiu.
The two sons of the primary consort were the first named Xuāoxiāo and the second named Chángyì;
both became feudal lords. When the Yellow Emperor passed away, [the succession proceeded].
People believed he had ascended as an immortal.
According to the *Shiji*, the Emperor reigned for one hundred and ten years.
Huangfu Mi stated:
The Yellow Emperor was born at Shouchiu in Qinzhou, Gongchang Road, Shaanxi.
His tomb is located at Mount Qiaoshan in Ningzhou, within the domain of Yongzhou.
The place where the Yellow Emperor ascended, Dinghu, is currently within the domain of the southern region of Xiandushan in Chuzhou Road, Zhexi Province.
The tomb of Chiyou is now located in Kǎnxiāng on the East Ping Road; it is seventy feet high.
The people regularly worship it in the tenth month, at which time a crimson vapor issues forth.
It was like a roll of vermilion silk;
the people named it the "Banner of Chiyou.
The *Qian Zuodu* says:
In antiquity, the Lord Sui-ren looked up at the Dipper and the Pole Star to determine the names of the directions;
Fuxi followed this by drawing the Eight Trigrams;
and the Yellow Emperor received the Mandate.
He commissioned Daonao to create the sexagenary cycle beginning with Jiazi and appointed Rongcheng to arrange the calendrical calculations;
from this point on, the theories of the Five Elements and the Nine Palaces flourished.
Therefore, the *Explanation of the Hexagrams* says:
"The yang number is nine.
To establish the Way of Heaven, one speaks of yin and yang.
Two yangs and one yin constitute the three aspects of Heaven.
The Way of establishing the Earth is said to consist of the supple and the firm;
with two yins and one yang, the Earth likewise possesses these three aspects.
The Way of establishing humanity is said to consist of benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*).
Since there are two aspects of righteousness and one of benevolence, humanity likewise possesses three [qualities].
Three times three makes nine.
Yin and yang embrace one another to bring all things into being.
The South-Pointing Chariot: When the Yellow Emperor and Chiyou were at war, Chiyou created a great mist.
The soldiers were all disoriented;
therefore, the Yellow Emperor fashioned the south-pointing chariot to show them the four directions.
He subsequently captured Chiyou and killed him. The State of Youxiong is present-day Xinzhou in Henan, according to the *Shiji*.
The Five Emperors: The first was Shao Hao Jintian Shi. Shao Hao Jintian Shi was of the Yi clan;
he was a son of the Yellow Emperor, styled Qingyang.
During the reign of King Jinde,
at Qongsang (present-day Qufu, Yanzhou, Jinning Prefecture),
there was the auspicious omen of a phoenix.
Thereafter, he used birds to record his officials.
He occupied the throne for eighty-four years and reached the age of one hundred at his death.
Zhuanxu of the Gaoyang clan was the son of Changyi and the grandson of the Yellow Emperor.
He ruled according to the virtue of Water.
The capital was Dujing; it is now the region of Puzhou in Dongchang Road and Yanzhou.
He fathered eight men of talent, known as the Eight Kai.
During the decline of the Lord of Shaohao,
the people became intermingled and confused;
the populace grew irreverent toward the ancestral sacrifices.
Sacrificial offerings were conducted without restraint.
When the Emperor quelled the rebellion of the Jiuli,
spirits and humans were no longer intermingled.
There was no mutual encroachment or violation;
he established the calendar with the first month of spring as its starting point.
Thus, the Emperor was the progenitor of the calendar.
Its territory extended to Mount Pan in the east,
to the Flowing Sands in the west,
and to Jiaozhi in the south.
To the north it reached Youling, which is present-day Yanjing; he reigned for seventy-eight years.
The *Haowai jing* states:
"In the midst of the Eastern Sea there is a mountain named Duaso."
Above there is a great peach tree,
coiled and winding for three thousand li.
The *Dili zhi* states:
The Flowing Sands (Liu Sha) are located in Ganzhou Road, Gansu Province;
the name of the commandery is Zhangye.
Emperor Gaosun of the Di Ku clan was the son of Qiao Ji.
He was the great-grandson of the Yellow Emperor.
He ruled according to the virtue of Wood.
His capital was at Xihao, located in present-day Yan Shi County of the Henan Fu region.
In the ancient region of Luozhou,
the Emperor was born with divine sageliness;
he spoke his own name at birth.
He accords with the righteousness of Heaven,
knows the urgent needs of the people,
and is both benevolent and majestic.
Be benevolent and trustworthy.
Take the wealth of heaven and earth and use it with moderation.
Care for and instruct the myriad people, benefiting and teaching them.
They calculated the movements of the sun and moon to welcome and bid them farewell;
they understood the spirits and ghosts and served them with reverence.
Wherever the sun and moon shone, [they extended their influence].
Wherever his winds and rains reached,
all submitted without exception;
he fathered eight men of talent, known as the Eight Xuans.
He reigned for seventy years and lived to the age of one hundred and five.
He passed away and was buried in the region of Mount Qiushan in Kaizhou, within the territories of the two prefectures of Yuan and Ji, in today’s Daming Road.
Zi Zhi (the son of Zhuanxu) ascended the throne and ruled for nine years;
his governance was not good,
so he abdicated to Yao, the Marquis of Tang.
Emperor Yao of the Tàodáng clan was the younger brother of Zhì, the son of Emperor Kù.
When Zhì ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Yao as the Marquis of Táo.
He was subsequently enfeoffed as the Lord of Tang, hence called the Clan of Tao-tang.
His surname was Qí.
After Yao had received the abdication from Zhì, [he ascended the throne].
By virtue of the Fire Mandate,
he established his capital at Pingyang— present-day Jinning Road, within the domain of Jizhou—
where the thatched roofs remained untrimmed.
The earthen steps were three feet high, and *míngjiè* plants grew in the courtyard—these are *míng* grasses.
One leaflet sprouts each day;
by the fifteenth day, fifteen leaflets have formed.
On the sixteenth day, one pod falls;
by the thirtieth day, they have fallen until the month is exhausted. If the month is short, two pods fall consecutively;
as they are produced again, they fall again.
The Emperor’s own sustenance was extremely meager, and his levies and corvée labor were very few.
At that time, there arose great winds, along with *yà* (pronounced kǔ-bā-fǎn), *yū* (sound yóu-fēng), *hǔi* (hú-guǐ-fǎn), wild boars, and long serpents.
All were harbingers of harm to the people.
The Emperor then sent Yi to entangle Dafeng in the marshes of Qingqiu—an eastern marsh—where he slew the Yakwu;
and he cut the Long Serpent at Dongting.
He captured Fengxi at Sanglin,
and the people were thus delighted. Yet,
the floodwaters became a calamity.
The Four Mountains (Si Yue) recommended Gun, the father of Yu;
however, after nine years of managing the floodwaters, he did not succeed.
The Son of Heaven’s son, Dan Zhu, was unworthy, so [the ministers] sought a man of virtuous excellence with whom the throne could be abdicated.
The ministers recommended Shun.
The Emperor gave his two daughters in marriage to Shun and subjected him to a series of difficult trials.
He was led to the great mountain pass— present-day Shunde Road—
where, amidst fierce winds, thunder, and rain, he did not lose his way. Thereupon,
he was appointed to act as regent.
Furthermore, in the twenty-eighth year, the Emperor passed away.
From Yao’s accession to the throne through Shun’s regency, a total of ninety-eight years elapsed.
His lifespan was one hundred and ninety-eight years.
Yao composed the music known as "The Great Chapter.
Shun withdrew from Yao’s son Danzhu to the south of the River, at the present site of Bianliang.
Those in the world who came for audiences or to settle lawsuits did not go to Danzhu, but went to Shun.
Shun then ascended the throne as the Son of Heaven. The *Shujing* (Book of Documents), in the "Annals of Yao" (*Yaodian*), refers to him as Fangxun.
Cai Shengshen comments:
"Fangxun is a general term for the virtue and achievements of Yao."
Di Shun of the Youyu clan— Di Shun of the Youyu clan was called Chonghua.
He was titled Duke of Du and was the eighth-generation descendant of the Yellow Emperor.
The Yellow Emperor fathered Changyi;
Changyi fathered Zhuanxu;
Zhuanxu fathered Qiongchan.
Qiong Chan gave birth to Kang Jing;
Kang Jing gave birth to Ju Mang;
Ju Mang gave birth to Jiao Niu.
Jiao Niu gave birth to Gu Sou;
Gu Sou gave birth to Shun.
Their surname was Yao.
Shun’s mother died.
His stepmother gave birth to Xiang.
[There were thus] his father, his mother, and Xiang.
He constantly sought to kill Shun;
yet Shun practiced the way of filial piety and fraternal duty in serving his parents,
treating his younger brother with even greater reverence.
He plowed at Mount Li in the east of the River;
he fished at Leize in Yanzhou;
and he practiced pottery-making on the banks of the River at Tiaochou Village, southwest of Dingtao in present-day Jiyin.
Where they dwelt, a village was formed;
in two years, it became a town;
in three years, it became a city.
He became renowned for his filial piety at the age of twenty.
At thirty, Yao gave him his two daughters in marriage and was about to abdicate the throne to him.
Shun raised the eight Kaies and the eight Yuans, the sons of the lords of Gaoyang and Gaoxin.
The Kaies presided over the earth,
while the Yuans disseminated the five teachings throughout the four quarters.
Thereupon Yao appointed Shun to act as regent.
The Lord of Dihong had an unworthy son,
known as Hunchun.
Huan Dou. Under the Xiaohao clan,
there was an unworthy son of Heaven,
known as Qiongqi.
The Gonggong clan and the Zhuanxu clan had unworthy sons.
They were styled Taohui; he was Gun.
The Lord of Jin-yun had an unworthy son,
known as Tao-tie;
he was of the San-miao clan.
These are called the Four Tyrants.
They served under Yao,
yet Yao was unable to dismiss them.
Shun banished them all to the four remote frontiers and appointed Yu to manage the floodwaters.
Shun acted as regent for Yao for twenty-eight years.
When Yao passed away, Shun ascended to the throne as Son of Heaven.
He ruled as a sovereign based on the virtue of Earth.
His capital was at Puan, which is the present-day city of Hezhong Fu in Jinning Lu.
He played the five-stringed zither and sang the "Nan-feng" (South Wind).
He aligned the seven celestial offices with the *xuánjī* and *yùhéng*.
He rectified the calendar and intercalary days to complete the year.
The music performed was called the Jiushao.
When the people of Miao rebelled against the mandate,
he displayed his virtue by performing the dance with shields and feathers at both steps for seventy days.
The people of Miao came to submit.
But his son Shangjun was unworthy;
thus Shun recommended Yu to Heaven.
He caused [his son] to succeed him on the throne.
He reigned for fifty years.
During a southern tour of inspection, he passed away in the wilds of Cangwu. The present-day administrative seat of Wuzhou in Guangxi Province is named Cangwu; it belongs to the domain of Jingzhou.
He lived for one hundred and ten years.
Yu withdrew from Shangjun, the son of Shun, at Yangcheng;
the people of the world did not turn to Shangjun but turned to Yu.
Yu subsequently ascended the throne as the Son of Heaven;
the state was named Xia. When Shun wished to have lacquerware vessels made, he desisted upon receiving remonstrance.
This is also seen in the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong of Tang.
Auspicious Birth: A great star, like a rainbow, descended and flowed [into the water].
At the Flower Marsh (Huazhu), the female ruler was moved by this and gave birth to Shaohao (*Shiji*).
A star, like a rainbow, moved the female ruler Qushu and she gave birth to Emperor Zhuan (*Shushu*).
According to the *Shidiwang Shiji*, Shun’s mother conceived him after being moved by a great rainbow.
Before the era of Shao Hao,
the titles bestowed upon rulers throughout the world were modeled upon their virtues.
Since the time of Zhuanxu,
the titles used for the rulers of the world have been derived from their personal names,
such as Gaoyang and Gaoxin.
All are sites where [the Dharma] was established.
In the third year of the Yuanfeng era of Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty,
Liu Shu, styled Daoyuan, Director of the Bureau of Secretaries, authored the *Waiji* (External Annals), stating:

Among the Six Classics, only the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, the *Hexagram Texts* (*Xiang*), the *Words on the Hexagrams* (*Wenyan*), the *Explanations of the Sequence of Hexagrams* (*Shuo Gua*), and the *Miscellaneous Hexagrams* (*Za Gua*) of the *Book of Changes* were composed by Zhongni (Confucius).
The *Book of Poetry* and the *Book of Documents* were edited and finalized by Zhongni.
None of these refer to the Three Augusts, the Five Emperors, or the Three Kings.
The *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes* says:
"In ancient times, when Bao-xi ruled the world..."
After the disappearance of Bao Xi, Shen Nong arose.
After the disappearance of Shen Nong, the lineages of Huang Di, Yao, and Shun arose.
They succeeded one another as kings without being restricted by the numerical limit of three or five.
Some take Fuxi through Shun as the Five Emperors; however,
Confucius never spoke of this,
and scholars must not indulge in forced interpretations or speculative theories.
The Guanzi states:
"He who clarifies the One is a Sovereign (Huang);
he who examines the Dao is a Lord (Di)."
"One who possesses universal virtue becomes a king;
one who wins through strategic planning achieves military victory.
Kong Yingda said:
The *Guanzi* texts may have been compiled by later generations and are not the original works themselves.
Both the *Zhuangzi* and the *Liezi* consist entirely of parables and extravagant fabrications.
The scholars of the Qin and Han dynasties took their literary compositions and discourses as their models;
consequently, they vied with one another in extolling the Three Augusts and Five Emperors,
unaware that such figures never existed in antiquity.
Zhongni (Confucius) never spoke of this.
Emperor Wu of Liang took Fuxi, Shennong, and Suirén as the Three Sovereigns (Sanhuang),
and Huangdi, Shaohao, Di Ku, Dizi, and Yao as the Five Emperors (Wudi).
Shun was neither of the Three Kings nor of the Five Emperors;
to include him with the Three Kings as forming four dynasties is a misinterpretation of their significance.
Through the ages, opinions have been manifold, and no definitive conclusion has been reached.
The Grand Historian said:
"Among scholars, many praise the Five Emperors as being of ancient antiquity."
However, the *Shangshu* alone records [the accounts] from the time of Yao onward,
whereas the various schools of thought speak of the Yellow Emperor;
their texts are neither elegant nor authentic.
The gentry and scholars find it difficult to speak of this.
It is what Confucius transmitted when Zai Yu questioned him regarding the "Virtues of the Five Emperors" and the "Lineage of the Emperors."
Confucian scholars may not have transmitted this.
I once traveled west to Kongtong and north past Zhuolu.
It spread eastward to the sea and floated southward across the Yangtze and Huai rivers.
Even among the elders, there were many who would frequently point out the sites where the Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun had dwelt.
The customs and teachings are indeed distinct;
in sum, that which does not depart from the ancient texts is close to being correct.
*Soyin* says:
The "Gǔwén" refers to the two books, "Dìdé" (Virtues of the Emperors) and "Dìxì" (Lineage of the Emperors), which are close to this [truth].
You, my son, observe the "Chūnqiū" and "Guóyǔ," and you will see therein the elucidation of the chapters on the "Virtues of the Five Emperors" and the "Lineages of the Emperors."
Although I have not investigated them in great depth,
what they manifest and reveal is entirely without falsehood.
There has been a long interval since the books were lost.
Its transcendence appears from time to time in what others have said.
Unless one studies with diligence and reflects deeply until knowing its meaning in one's heart,
it is truly difficult to explain to those of shallow insight and meager learning.
I have further arranged these accounts in sequence and selected those whose language is particularly elegant;
thus, I have composed them as the "Basic Annals" (*benji*) at the beginning of this book.

The Xia dynasty: Emperor Yu (the Great Yu), King Qi, Taikang, Zhongkang, Wangxiang, Shaokang, King Zhu, King Huai, King Mang, King Xie, Budiang, King Jiong, King Jin, King Kongjia, King Gao, King Fa, and Liui (Jie). Emperor Yu: Emperor Yu’s surname was Si.
The grandson of the Yellow Emperor was Zhuanxu;
Zhuanxu fathered Gun;
Gun fathered Yu.
In the time of Yao, the floodwaters overflowed the heavens.
Yao appointed Gun to manage the waters, but he was unsuccessful and was executed for it.
When Shun assumed the regency, he raised up Yu to continue his father’s work.
He toiled his body and exhausted his thoughts;
dwelling abroad for thirteen years,
he passed by the gate of his home but did not enter.
For traveling on land, one uses a carriage;
for traveling on water, one uses a boat;
for traveling through mud, one uses a sled (pronounced qiū).
When traveling through the mountains, he rode in a sedan chair (jù, pronounced jū).
He examined the terrain to determine what resources were available for tribute, as well as the advantages of the rivers and mountains.
Consequently, all water-related disasters were brought to rest.
The nine provinces were unified,
and the four remote frontiers became habitable.
Thereupon, Yao conferred upon Yu a dark-colored jade tablet.
He announced his success,
and Shun ascended to the throne,
appointing Yu as Minister of Works.
He presided over the hundred officials;
Heaven bestowed upon him the Great Plan of the Nine Categories,
whereby the constant patterns of human relations were brought into order.
When Yao and Yu were [ruling], a book emerged from the Luo River.
A divine tortoise bore markings arrayed upon its back;
these contained numbers reaching up to nine.
Yu subsequently categorized them accordingly, completing the nine classes.
Shun’s son, Shangjun, was unworthy;
thus Shun recommended Yu to Heaven so that he might succeed him on the throne.
When Shun passed away,
the people of the world did not turn to Shangjun but turned to Yu.
Yu then ascended the throne as the Son of Heaven.
The state name was Xia.
Ruling by the virtue of Metal,
it was headquartered in Han, which is present-day Yangdi in Junzhou, Bianliang Road.
The Yu domain still followed the Yu people in taking the month of Yin as the beginning of the year.
Ten cun constituted one chi.
Black was the favored color.
The sacrificial victim is black;
black is used as the emblematic color.
The music performed is called "Daxia."
"Xia" means "great.
It signifies the ability to magnify the virtue of Yao and Shun.
He suspended bells, drums, chimes, gongs, and rattles, and with their sounds resonating, awaited the scholars from the four quarters.
He said: "Those who instruct me in the Way shall strike the drum;
those who admonish me with righteousness shall strike the bell;
those who inform me of affairs shall shake the rattle."
For those speaking of sorrow, they struck the *qing* stone.
For those with legal disputes, they shook the *dao* rattle.
Initially, Shun divided the world into twelve provinces.
Yu re-established the nine provinces.
He collected the finest copper from all under heaven and cast it into nine tripods (ding) to represent the nine provinces.
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor fashioned the chariot;
Shao Hao added oxen to it,
and Xi Zhong added horses.
Yu commanded Xi Zhong to oversee the manufacture of chariots;

The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the country of Tāla.
His secular surname was Śūdra.
His father was Shan-yi.
At the age of seventeen he left the household life;
at twenty, he realized the fruit of enlightenment.
As he traveled through various regions to transform sentient beings,
the palace of Māra shook;
Māra Pāpīyas waited for the Venerable One to enter meditative absorption.
He secretly took a necklace and fastened it around the Patriarch’s neck.
The Patriarch emerged from his meditative absorption and recognized this as the work of a demon;
he then transformed the three corpses—a human, a dog, and a snake—into a flower garland.
He offered it to Pāpīyān, who was as foul-smelling as a corpse infested with maggots;
Pāpīyān loathed it and,
though he exerted all his supernatural powers, could not remove it.
He then hastened to the Brahma King to request that he remove the corpse's filth.
The Brahma King said,
"This is the work of a disciple of the One of Ten Powers."
"I cannot release you.
You must take refuge in the Venerable One.
Then he spoke this verse:
If one falls to the ground,
one must rise from the ground;
to seek to rise apart from the ground is impossible.
Ultimately, there was no such principle [in that].
Pāpīyān then wept and offered a sincere confession.
The Venerable One said to him:
"You may personally recite the words of taking refuge in the Three Jewels.
The Māra joined his palms and thrice proclaimed: "I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Saṃgha.
All of his flower garlands were then completely removed.
Pāpīyān was greatly delighted; he paid homage and spoke this verse:
"I bow my head to the Honored One of Samādhi, the noble disciple endowed with the ten powers."
I now dedicate this merit;
may there be no weakness or deficiency.
Having paid homage, he departed.
Whenever the Venerable One ordained a disciple,
he would place a tally-stick in a stone chamber;
that chamber was eighteen cubits in length.
It was twelve cubits wide and filled the space between them.
He entrusted the Dharma to Diṭṭhaka with this verse:
The mind is the mind from the very beginning;
the original mind is not a dharma that exists.
If there were dharmas that exist, then there would be an original mind.
"It is neither mind nor the fundamental dharma.
Having transmitted the Dharma, he leaped into the void and performed eighteen miraculous transformations,
then returned to his original seat.
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Kṛṣṇadīpa used counting sticks from within the room to cremate his teacher’s body;

Initially, the disciples of the Incense Assembly sought ordination from the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra.
Kātyāyanīputra questioned them, saying:
"Have you gone forth with your body, or have you gone forth with your mind?
Ghoṣila replied,
"I have come to go forth not for the sake of body or mind."
Kumārajīva said:
"If it is not for the sake of body and mind,
then for whom else would one leave the household life?"
He said:
"Now, those who have left the household life possess neither self nor what belongs to a self.
Because they possess neither self nor what belongs to a self, their minds are neither born nor extinguished."
The mind is neither born nor extinguished;
this is the eternal Way, and the Buddhas are likewise eternal.
The mind has no form or characteristics.
The nature of its substance is likewise so.
Kumāralāta said,

The Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Micchaka, was a native of Central India.
His clan name and surname are unknown.
One day, he arrived at a kingdom in Northern India.
In the marketplace, a man holding a wine vessel met him and said:
"Venerable sir, from where have you come?
Where do you intend to go?
The Patriarch replied:
"Coming from one's own mind, it seeks to go nowhere.
[The Buddha] asked: 'Do you recognize the object in my hand?'"
The Patriarch said,
"This is a vessel for contact yet carries purity.
[Nanquan] asked, "Venerable One, do you recognize me?"
The Patriarch said:
"I am not that which is known;
that which is known is not I."
The Patriarch spoke to him again, saying,
"You may state your own surname and name.
The man then spoke this verse:
I was born in this country in my present life;
furthermore, I recall that in former times,
my original clan name was Bharadvāja and my personal name was Vāsulimitra.
The Patriarch received him, ordained him,
and perfected his virtue through the full precepts;
he then addressed him, saying:
I am now old and about to enter parinirvāṇa.
I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s treasury of the true Dharma-eye;
you should transmit it so that it never comes to an end.
Listen to my verse:
"Where there is no mind, nothing can be attained;
what is spoken cannot be called a dharma."
Once he had realized that the mind is no-mind and had thus understood the verse on the mind and mental factors,
the Venerable One immediately entered the Lion’s Unfurled Prowess Samādhi.
He leaped into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees,
then returned to his original seat and transformed into fire to cremate himself.
Vāsulimitra collected his sacred relics and *śarīra*.
It was enshrined within a casket made of the seven precious gems and placed upon the upper story of a stupa for veneration.

"Houren" (The Watchman), "Jianqiu" (The Little Kite), and "Xiaquan" (The Spring Underneath) from the *Chen Feng* (Air of Chen); two pieces concerning Duke Ling:
"Zhulin" (The Mulberry Grove) and "Zebei" (The Marsh).
King Kuang succeeded King Kuangban;
Prince Qing was his heir.
He reigned for twenty-one years.
King Dingwang (定王) and King Dingwangyu (定王瑜).
They were both sons of King Kuang (匡王).
Each reigned for twenty-one years.
Laozi’s surname was Li;
his given name was Dan;
his courtesy name was Boyang.
"Dan" is his posthumous title.
He was born on the fourteenth day of the ninth month of the third year of King Ding (the Ding-si year) in the village of Quren, in Lai Township, Ku County, Chen Prefecture, the state of Chu.
This was the birth of Dan.
Three hundred and forty-six years had passed since the Parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Buddha.
It was the fourth year of King Jian, the Jia-mao year;
Boyang was twenty-three years old.
He served in the Zhou dynasty as a Keeper of the Archives.
In the thirteenth year of the reign, he was promoted to Archivist beneath the Pillars.
From that time until fifty-four years later, he was not transferred; his contemporaries characterized him as a "hidden official."
In the first year of King Jing’s reign,
the *renwu* year, Laozi was eighty-six years old.
He departed from Zhou for San Pass, which is now Fengzhou in the Xingyuan Road of Shaanxi.
The Grand Chancellor Yin Xi traveled westward to the shifting sands and died in Fufeng Commandery;
he was buried in Huaili, which is present-day Xingping County in the western region of Shaanxi Province.
The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, was a native of Northern India.
His secular surname was Bharadvāja.
He encountered Mitraka and left the household life to receive the Dharma.
While traveling to teach and transform others, he arrived at the kingdom of Kāmarūpa.
Suddenly, a man named Buddhudana came forward and addressed him by name.
Now I shall debate the principles with the Venerable One.
Sumati said: "If you, O worthy one, debate according to [mere] logic, it will not accord with the Dharma."
As for the meaning, it need not be discussed;
yet if one intends to discuss the meaning, it ultimately will not be a discussion of the meaning.
Nandika, because his understanding of the meaning was superior, subsequently sought ordination.
Śumati summoned four noble ones who had attained the fruits of the path and conferred the precepts upon them.
After a short while, he then addressed them, saying:
The Tathāgata now entrusts to you the treasury of the true Dharma eye;
you must transmit it,
taking care that it never be severed.
Listen to my verse:
"The mind is identical to the realm of empty space;
it manifests dharmas equal to empty space."
When he realized the state of space,
there was neither existence nor non-existence.
Thereupon, Subhūti rose from his seat and performed the eighteen transformations.
He then entered the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-samādhi*).
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas all came together to pay their respects and spoke these verses:
Among the noble ancestors of this Bhadrakalpa,
you shall occupy the seventh position;
O Venerable One, have compassion for me.
"Please proclaim the Buddha-ground.
Susīma arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Dharma I have attained is not existent;
if one realizes the Buddha-ground, it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Having spoken thus, he returned to samādhi.
Manifesting the signs of nirvana,
Nandi immediately erected a stupa of the seven treasures upon his original seat and enshrined his entire remains within it.
During the reign of King Ding of Zhou, according to the *Zongzheng ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage),
this was the beginning of the practice of interring the entire body of the imperial ancestors.
King Jian was the younger brother of King Ding.
He reigned for fourteen years.
King Ling (Ling-wang), whose personal name was Xie (Xie-xin),
was the son of King Jian (Jian-wang).
He reigned for twenty-seven years.
Confucius was born on the *gengzi* day of the eleventh month in the twenty-first year of King Ling’s reign, the *gengxu* year,
in the village of Zou, Pingxiang, in the state of Lu.
His mother, Lady Yan, prayed at Mount Niqu while giving birth to him; therefore, he was named Qiu.
His courtesy name was Zhongni.
Such was the birth of Confucius.
Four hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Buddha,
in the forty-first year of King Jing’s reign, the year of Renxu,
Confucius passed away at the age of seventy-three.
He was buried at Qufu in Lu, which is now part of Yanzhou in the region of Jining; this was one of the nine provinces according to the *Yugong*.
Mount Nichu is subordinate to Sishui County in Yanzhou.
King Jing—King Jing was noble.
Prince Ling reigned for twenty-five years.
In the eighteenth year of his reign, the Crown Prince Sheng passed away.
The King’s youngest son went to court to seek the throne,
but before his aim was realized, the King passed away.
The Zhou Chancellor Dan Qi and Liu Di installed the King’s second son, Meng, as king.
Zi Chao took advantage of the former officials and the artisans who had lost their offices and ranks to pursue Liu Zi;
Liu Zi fled to Yang.
Dan Zi escorted Zi Meng to the Zhuang Palace.
That night, the followers of Zi Chao sent men to seize Meng and bring him back.
Dan Zi fled into exile.
The followers of Zichao escorted Wang Meng to pursue Danzi.
The people of Jin led their army to restore Wang Meng to the royal city.
Meng soon passed away.
This was called King Dao.
The various high officials enthroned Wang Meng’s younger uterine brother, Qi, as king;
this was called King Jing.
Zi Chao also saw King Jing descend.
The eighth patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi, was a native of the kingdom of Kāmarūpa.
His secular surname was Gautama.
He has a fleshly protuberance on his crown;
his eloquence is swift and unimpeded.
He first encountered Vasumitra, left the household life, and attained the Way.
He traveled to the kingdom of Tiṅga to transform beings.
There he ordained the disciple Puṇyamitra and entrusted the Dharma to him with this verse:
Space has neither interior nor exterior;
the nature of mind is likewise.
If one thoroughly understands space, [one understands the nature of mind].
This is the realization of the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
At that moment, the Venerable One immediately manifested supernatural transformations and returned once more to his original seat.
He remained solemnly in a state of quiescent extinction;
the multitude erected a precious stupa and interred his entire body therein.
This was during the reign of King Jing of Zhou; the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage) states:
"King Jing, styled Gai, was the son of King Jing."
He reigned for forty-three years.
In the first year of his reign, the Grand Officer Yin of the Zhou state installed Zichao as king and entered the royal city;
the king then went to Liu.
In the winter of the fourth year of King Jing’s reign, he conquered Gong and expelled Prince Zhao.
The King entered Chengzhou;
from that time on, the royal city was called the Western Zhou.
The establishment of Chengzhou was in the sixteenth year of King Ping of the Eastern Zhou.
The followers of Zichao incited a rebellion,
and the King fled to Jin.
In the seventeenth year, the Marquis of Jin led an army to restore the King.
The King entered the royal city. The years and months mentioned above are recorded in the *Chunqiu*.
The Venerable Jiaozu Fotudeng was a native of the country of Tiegua.
His surname was Viśāla.
When the Eight Patriarchs were traveling to convert beings, they arrived at the house of Viśāla.
His father, the elder, paid his respects and asked what they required.
The Patriarch said,
"I am seeking an attendant.
The Elder said:
I have a son named Bhadramitra.
He is already fifty years old;
he has never spoken with his mouth nor ever stepped with his feet.
The Patriarch said,
"One such as you have spoken is truly my disciple.
When Vovada heard this, he was moved.
He rose immediately to prostrate and spoke these verses: "Parents are not my kin;
who is the most intimate kinsman?
The Buddhas are not my path."
"Who is the one most in accord with the Way?
The Patriarch replied,
"The one whose speech accords with the mind."
Parents cannot be compared [to this].
Your practice accords with the Way;
it is identical to the mind of all Buddhas.
Seeking an external Buddha with attributes is not like you;
if you wish to recognize your own original mind, [look within].
"Neither joined nor separated.
Having heard this verse,
Vatsa immediately took seven steps.
The Patriarch said,
"This son’s compassionate vow is vast and great;
it is only because he considers that his parents’ affection would be difficult to relinquish that he neither speaks nor walks."
The elder then relinquished him, allowing him to leave the household life;
the patriarch conferred upon him full ordination and entrusted him with the eye of the Dharma.
Having received the Dharma,
he traveled to Central India to propagate it.
He transmitted the Verse Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to his disciple, the Venerable Pārśva, saying:
Ultimate truth is originally nameless;
it is through names that ultimate truth is revealed.
Thus one receives and attains the true Dharma.
He was neither real nor false.
Having completed his teaching, he entered the samādhi of cessation and attained parinirvāṇa.
The assembly cremated him with fragrant oils and sandalwood.
The śarīra relics were collected and a stūpa was erected at Nālandā Monastery during the reign of King Jing of the Zhou dynasty.
According to the *Zhengzong ji*, this was the era of King Yuan of the Yuan dynasty;
[the name] Yuan Wang means "benevolent king."
King Gyeong (敬王子) reigned for eight years.
King Jeongding (貞定王), whose personal name was Gye (介).
Yuan was the Prince Wendi.
He reigned for twenty-eight years before he passed away.

His son Quji ascended the throne as King Ai; after three months, his younger brother Shu attacked and killed King Ai, establishing himself as King Si. After five months, the youngest brother Wei attacked and killed King Si, establishing himself as king.
According to the *Shiji*,
the nineteenth year, the Xinmao year,
was five hundred years after the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa.
In the land of India, the Bodhisattva Asanga and his younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu,
initially adhered to the Hīnayāna and composed five hundred treatises.
Later, he attained realization of the Mahāyāna and further composed five hundred Mahāyāna treatises,
whereby he was titled the "Master of a Thousand Treatises."
The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Pārśva, was a native of Central India.
His original surname was Nansheng; he remained in his mother’s womb for sixty years before his father, the elder Sugandhacchattra, relinquished him so that he might leave the household life.
He attended the nine patriarchs without ever sleeping;
because his side never touched his mat, he was called the Venerable Pārśva.
Carrying on the transformation [of the Dharma], he arrived at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
Resting beneath a tree, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"This ground shall turn the color of gold;
a sage is about to enter this gathering."
As soon as these words were spoken, the earth turned the color of gold.
There was a son of a householder named Pūrṇa-yaśas,
who stood before him with palms joined and spoke this verse:
The Master sits upon the golden ground,
constantly expounding the meaning of ultimate reality;
he turns his light back to illuminate me.
He caused him to enter samādhi.
Once he had received the full precepts,
the Master transmitted to him the Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury, speaking this verse:
The true essence is spontaneous; the true cause and the true teaching possess their underlying principle.
Having realized the truly true Dharma, there is neither practice nor cessation.
Having entrusted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and entered *nirvāṇa*.
He transformed into fire to cremate himself.
The fourfold assembly each took a fold of their robes to collect his *śarīra* relics.
Stūpas were erected in various places and offerings were made.
This was during the reign of King Zhouding of the Zhou dynasty. According to the *Zengzongji* (Record of the Successive Patriarchs), he was King Kāo, whose personal name was Wéi.
Zhen Ding was the Prince of Zi.
He reigned for fifteen years before passing away.
King Kao enfeoffed his younger brother at Henan; he was known as Duke Huan.
He continued the official duties established by the Duke of Zhou.
When Duke Huan died,
his son Duke Wei succeeded him.
Duke Wei passed away.
His son, Duke Hui, succeeded him.
He then enfeoffed his younger son at Gong; Xu Guang says: [the text continues].
He was the son of Duke Hui and served as the King's attendant;
he was titled Duke Hui of Eastern Zhou.
This continued until the time of King Nian.
The Eastern and Western Zhou were divided in governance.
King Nian moved the capital to the Western Zhou.
Regarding the Duke Wu of the Western Zhou, Xu Guang says: [text omitted].
The eldest son of Duke Hui was Gongshi.
King Weilie (King Wu).
The son of Duke Kao.
He reigned for twenty-four years.
In the twenty-third year of the King’s reign, the Nine Cauldrons shook.
He then appointed the Jin ministers Wei Si, Zhao Ji, and Han Qian as feudal lords, according to the *Shiji*.
The Wei were the descendants of Duke Gao of Bi;
they shared the same surname as the Zhou.
Bi Wan served Duke Xian of Jin, who, upon the destruction of Bi, enfeoffed Wan with the territory of Wei, making him the Grand Master of Wei.
When Huanzi, together with Zhao and Han, destroyed Zhibo,
they divided his territory among themselves.
This continued until Wenhou Si.
He took Bo Qixia and Tian Zifang as his teachers.
He resided in Anyi, under the jurisdiction of Hedong in Shanxi Province, during the reign of King Xian.
In the twenty-ninth year of King Xian’s reign, the state of Qin defeated the Wei army and captured the Wei nobleman Yin.
King Hui of Wei was appeased.
He dispatched an envoy to present the territory west of the River to Qin in order to establish peace.
He abandoned An-yi and moved the capital to Da-liang (present-day Xiaoliang).

The twenty-third year of King Weilie of Zhou; the twenty-second year of Wenhou Si; the sixteenth year of King An; the first year of King Wuji; the sixth year of King Lie; the first year of King Hui Ying; the thirty-fifth year of King Xian; the first year of King Hui’s reigned title of "Hou"; the third year of King Shenjing; the first year of King Xiang; the twentieth year of King Nan; the first year of King Zhao; the thirty-ninth year of King Nan; the first year of King Anli; the fifth year of the First Emperor of Qin; the first year of King Jingmin Zeng; the twentieth year of the First Emperor; the first year of King Wangjia; the twenty-first year of the First Emperor; and the fifty-second year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, when the state was extinguished.
The state of Wei submitted entirely to the commands of Qin.
In the twenty-first year of the First Emperor of Qin, Qin extinguished Wei.
The eight rulers together reigned for one hundred and seventy-nine years.
The Zhao and the Qin shared a common ancestor.
Feilian’s son was E-lai; his younger brother was Ji-sheng, whose fifth-generation descendant, Zao-fu, served King Mu.
This continued until the time of King You.
Shu Dai, the son of Zhao Yanfu, a Great Officer of Zhou, left Zhou for Jin.
He served Duke Wen and was the first to establish the Zhao clan in Jin.
Furthermore, five generations later was Zhao Su.
Seven generations later, Jianzi Yang fathered Xiangzi Wuxu,
who, together with Wei and Han, destroyed Zhibo.
Xiangzi died, and his grandson Huan succeeded him.
Huan’s son was Ji.

Having received the mandate from the King to become a feudal lord, he took the present-day Zhao Prefecture as his domain; it belongs to the southern part of Yan, the northern route of Hebei, and the Zhenning Circuit.
In the territory of Jizhou, during the eighth year of King Nan,
King Wu-ling of Zhao changed his attire to that of the Hu people and practiced mounted archery to prepare for the hardships on the four borders.
In the sixteenth year of King Nan,
the King of Zhao styled himself Zhufu.
In the seventeenth year of King Nan.
In the first year of King Huiwen of Zhao,
his younger brother Sheng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Pingyuan.
In the thirty-second year of King Nan of Zhou.
The King of Zhao obtained the Buzhou He Shi jade from Chu.
There were eleven rulers of Zhao over a period of one hundred and eighty-two years.
In the twenty-fifth year of the First Emperor of Qin, Qin extinguished Zhao.
Zhao Daiyu Jia was the eldest son of King Daorxiang and the elder brother of King Youmu.
After the Qin had captured the Lord of Zhao,
Jia established himself as ruler in Dai at Weizhou.
It is now part of the interior of the Capital Region (Shangdu Lu) under the jurisdiction of the Li dynasty;
it corresponds to the territory of Jizhou as described in the "Yugong" (Tribute of Yu), and was subsequently conquered by Qin.

The twenty-third year of King Weilie of Zhou (the third year of King An; the first year of Marquis Wu): the first year of Marquis Lie Hou Ji. The sixtieth year of King An (the second year of King Lie; the first year of Marquis Cheng Hou Zhong): the first year of Marquis Su Hou. The twentieth year of King Xian (the first year of King Wuling): the first year of King Huaiwen Xiang. The fiftieth year of King Nian (the first year of King Xiaocheng Dan): the first year of the First Emperor of Qin. The first year of King Daoliang: the twelfth year of the First Emperor. The first year of King Youmu Qian: the twentieth year of the First Emperor. The first year of King Dai Wang Jia: the twenty-fifth year of the First Emperor. In the twenty-fifth year of the First Emperor, Qin extinguished Han. Han shared the same surname as Zhou.
The younger brother of Zhuangbo of Quwo was named Han Wan.
His grandson Jian became Dingbo,
who begot Ziyu.
He served the Jin state and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Han (Han Wuzi).
In the third generation, Han Xianzi (Jue) first adopted the surname Han and became a high minister of Jin.
From his sixth generation descendant down to Kangzi, he and Zhao and Wei destroyed Zhibo.
From Kangzi’s second generation descendant down to Qian,
he first received the royal mandate to become a feudal lord.
The state was Yingchangfu.
In the first year of King Lie of Zhou, Han annexed Zheng and moved its capital there; it is now Zhengzhou in the present-day Beiliang Road. This was in the forty-sixth year of King Xian of Zhou.
The state of Han claimed it was the first year of King Nao’s reign; at that time, Han held its crown prince as a hostage in Qin.
In the fourteenth year of the First Emperor of Qin, the King of Han surrendered his territory to Qin.
He requested to serve as a vassal.
The Prince of Han, known as Han Fei, was then on a mission to Qin.
By the seventeenth year of the First Emperor’s reign, Qin had extinguished the state of Han.
The eleven rulers together reigned for one hundred and seventy-four years.

In the twenty-third year of King Weilie of Zhou (the first year of Lord Jian, the third year of King An, and the first year of King Lie): Lord Wen. In the sixteenth year of King An (the first year of Lord Ai, the sixth year of King Lie, and the eleventh year of King Xian): Lord Zhao. In the twenty-sixth year of King An (the first year of Lord Hui, the thirty-seventh year of King Xian, and the forty-sixth year of King Xian): Lord Huan. In the ninth year of Emperor Qin Shi Huang (the fourth year of King Nan, the first year of King Xiang, and the twentieth year of King She): King Xi. In the forty-third year of King She (the first year of King Huanhui, and the first year of King An): King An. In the seventeenth year of Emperor Qin Shi Huang (the first year of King An): the state perished. King An was arrogant.
Prince Weile (Weilie) reigned for twenty-six years.
The eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Punyayasas, was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra.
His secular surname was Gautama.
After his father, Ratnagotra, had received the Dharma from the Venerable Pārśva,
he arrived in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
There, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa took refuge in him and sought ordination.
The Patriarch said to the assembly:
"This Great Being was formerly the King of Vaiśālī."
In that country, there was a class of people who were as naked as horses.
The King, exercising his supernatural powers, divided his body into silkworms.
He then obtained the robe.
Later, he was reborn in Central India;
the horse-man, moved by longing and affection, neighed piteously.
For this reason, he was called Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigh).
At that time, the Great Being comforted the assembly with a verse, saying:
"I see you are without clothing."
The mind gives rise to the protection of goodness;
it manifests transformation within the nest-like enclosure,
whereby one shall attain all deliverances.
Shortly thereafter, Zu said to the Great Master,
"The Tathāgata’s prophecy states that six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa,
there shall be a worthy one named Aśvaghoṣa."
In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, he subdued the heterodox teachers and delivered immeasurable people;
he shall succeed me in transmitting the transformation of the Dharma.
"Now is precisely the right time.
He then addressed him, saying:
"The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata."
I now entrust this to you.
Listen to my verse:
"Delusion and enlightenment are like concealment and manifestation."
Brightness and darkness are not separate from one another;
now I entrust to you this Dharma of concealment and manifestation.
It is neither one nor two.
Having transmitted the Dharma,
he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and entered profound, perfect nirvana.
The multitude erected a precious stupa to enshrine his entire body;
this was during the reign of King An of the Zhou dynasty, according to the *Zhengzong ji*.
King Lie was a fierce king; he took pleasure in it.
Prince An succeeded him and reigned for seven years.
King Xian, posthumously titled King Bianlie, was the son of King Wang.
He reigned for forty-eight years.

During his seventh year, the six powerful states east of Mount Heshan and the dozen or so smaller states between the Huai and Si rivers—among which Chu and Wei bordered Qin—were such that Wei constructed a long wall.
From the banks of the Luo River in Zheng to the north lies Shangjun;
Chu has Hanzhong, and to the south are Ba and Qian (pronounced *chénzhōng*).
All of these are treated as if they were the Yi and Di barbarians.
The state of Qin expelled him,
so that he was not permitted to participate in the assemblies and alliances of the Central States.
When the man of Zou, Mencius, had an audience with King Hui of Wei— Wei having subsequently moved its capital to Liang— he consequently referred to it as Liang.
The king said,
"Elder, you have come from no less than a thousand li away;
do you also have some means to benefit my kingdom?"
Mencius said:
"Why must a ruler speak of 'benefit'?
Let him simply speak of benevolence and righteousness."
Initially, Mencius studied under Zi Si, the grandson of Confucius.
He once asked, "In the way of governing the people, what should come first?
Zi Si replied:
"First benefit them.
Mencius said,
"This is how the gentleman instructs the people."
"It is simply benevolence and righteousness;
why must there be profit? Zisi said:
Benevolence and righteousness are indeed the means by which the people are benefited.
If those above are not benevolent, those below will find no place of rest;
if those above are not righteous, those below will take pleasure in practicing deceit.
This constitutes a great disadvantage; therefore, the *Yi* says:
"Advantage is the harmony of righteousness.
It further says:
"Utilizing security to honor virtue—
this is all the greatness of benefit. Thus spoke Sima Guang,
Duke Wen of the State of Song and Minister of the Imperial Chancellery, in the *Kong Cong Zi*.
The words of Zisi and Mencius are one and the same.
Only those who possess benevolence understand the benefit inherent in benevolence and righteousness;
those who lack benevolence do not understand them.
Therefore, when Mencius responded to the King of Liang,
he spoke directly in terms of benevolence and righteousness without mentioning profit;
this was because the person with whom he was conversing was different [from others].— *Tongjian*.
In the thirty-second year of King Xian, Mencius served as a high minister of Wei;

in the forty-third year, he served as the Chief Minister of Qi. In Qufu, Yanzhou, there is the tomb of Mencius. In the fourth month of the summer of the forty-fourth year of King Xian, the state of Qin first assumed the title of "King."
In the forty-sixth year, both Korea and Yan all styled themselves kings.
Only King Wu-ling of Zhao said, "How can I dare assume the title when I lack the substance?
I order my people to address me as 'Lord' (Jun)."
In the forty-eighth year, Qi enfeoffed Tian Ying at Xue,
bestowing upon him the title of Lord Jingguo.
The lord had more than forty sons.
The son of his concubine was named Wen.
Wen was unconventional and possessed abundant wisdom and strategic insight.
Guests requested that Jingguo Jun appoint Wen as his successor; subsequently, Jingguo Jun passed away.
Wen-si was Lord Xue,
also known as Lord Mengchang.
The twelfth patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
It is also called "Superior Merit" (*guṇavara*).

This is because it possesses merit from long ago, and furthermore, because its various merits—both conditioned (*sābhisaṃskāra*) and unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*)—are most preeminent; for these reasons, it is so named.
Having received the Dharma,
he propagated it in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
There was a Māra named Kambala.
With three thousand followers,
he performed various supernatural transformations before the Patriarch.
The Patriarch said:
"Can you exhaust your supernatural powers to transform this Sea of Nature?
Māra asked.
"What do you mean by 'Sea of Nature'?"
The Patriarch said:
"As for the ocean of nature,
the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it as samādhi."
The six supernormal powers manifested from this. When Kāpila heard these words,
he pressed his inquiries even more,
but he recognized that the Master’s principles were superior.
He then gave rise to the mind of faith and,
together with three thousand followers, sought ordination.
The Patriarch thereupon summoned five hundred arhats.
He conferred the full precepts upon him.
Thereupon, the Mahāsattva extensively composed treatises and discussions,
and subsequently addressed him, saying:
The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury shall now be entrusted to you.
Listen to these verses.
Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma;
light and darkness are originally non-dual.
Now I entrust this Dharma of realized awakening.
"Neither grasping nor abandoning.
Having thus entrusted [the teaching],
he immediately entered the Dragon’s Impetuous Stride Samādhi.
He rose into the air,
appearing like the orb of the sun,
and then returned to his original seat to pass into nirvana.
The fourfold assembly concealed the true body in a dragon cave during the reign of King Xian of the Zhou dynasty; this is recorded in the *Zhengzong ji*.
[King] Shenling was the son of King Ding.
Prince Xian reigned for seven years.
[The reign of] King Nan extended [the dynasty].
During the reign of King Shenjing,
fifty-nine years passed. At that time,
the Zhou realm was divided into eastern and western territories.
He was invaded by the feudal lords.
This was the fifty-ninth year of King Nan,
which was also the fifty-first year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin.
General Jiao of Qin attacked Han and attacked Zhao. King Nan,
fearing this, then turned against Qin and entered into a confederacy with the various feudal lords.
He shall dispatch the sharp troops of the empire through Yi Que to attack Qin,
ordering that no one be allowed to pass through Yangcheng.
Qin will then send General Jiu to attack the Western Zhou.
King Nan entered Qin and prostrated himself;
he offered up all thirty-six of his commanderies.
Qin accepted his offerings.
The throne was returned to King Nan of Zhou.
In this year, King Nan passed away; the preceding years and months are recorded according to the *Chunqiu*.
Thus, the thirty-six kings of Zhou together ruled for eight hundred and sixty-seven years before the mandate of Heaven was transferred to Qin.
The Thirteenth Patriarch, Mahāsattva Kāpimāra, was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
His clan name is unknown.
Initially, he was a follower of non-Buddhist paths.
He possessed great illusory arts and had a retinue of three thousand followers;
having mastered various heterodox doctrines, he subsequently received the Dharma from the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa.
He traveled to West India to propagate the teachings.
There, a prince named Meghasvabhāva invited him to receive offerings within the palace.
The Patriarch did not grant permission.
The Crown Prince said,
"In a great mountain to the north of the city, there is a stone cave."
"You may stay here in meditative stillness.
The Patriarch agreed.
After traveling several li, he encountered a large python.
The Patriarch granted him the three refuges.
The python cast off its skin and went to a stone cave.
Furthermore, ten li to the north, there was a great tree providing shade for five hundred great nāgas.
The king of trees was named Nāga-vṛkṣa (Dragon Tree), where he constantly preached the Dharma for the assembly of nāgas.
He welcomed the Patriarch, saying,
"This deep mountain is solitary and desolate."
This is the dwelling place of dragons and pythons;
O Virtuous and Most Honorable One,
why do you deign to exert your divine power here?
The Patriarch said,
"I am not one who holds supreme authority;
I have come to visit a man of virtue."
Nāgārjuna thought silently to himself:
"Has this master attained the definitive nature and the eye of clear insight?
Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle?"
The Patriarch said, "Although you spoke with your mind, I have already known it by my own intent. The tree heard you and repented; seek ordination. The Patriarch then ordained him.
Not long after, he addressed him, saying:
I now entrust the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata to you.
Listen to my verse:
"The Dharma is neither hidden nor manifest."
This is called the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
To awaken to this dharma of concealment and manifestation is neither folly nor wisdom.
Having transmitted the Dharma,
he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and burned his body with fire.
Nāgārjuna collected the five-colored śarīra relics and erected a stūpa there.

During the reign of King Nanwang of the Zhou dynasty, the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage) states that the three refuges consist of taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Sangha.
"Qin" refers to the state of Qin, whose clan name was Ying.
The Water Virtue King.
His capital was Xianyang, located on the western road.
He established his state and originated his reign within the domain of Yongzhou, Jiaozhou.
Continuing from the section on King Zhou Xuan: Among the descendants of Qin Zhuanxu was a grandson named Nüxiu.
While Nüxiu was weaving, a dark bird dropped an egg;
she swallowed it and gave birth to Daye.
Great undertakings entail great expenditures.
Yu leveled the waters and the land;
Shun bestowed the surname Ying upon him.
The two sons of King Zhaoxiang, King Xiaowen, and King Zhuangxiang were the First Emperor; the second son was Ying, who was also called Xiang. He was the younger brother of King Wu of Qin.
He was the son of King Huïwen.
He reigned for fifty-one years and moved the Nine Cauldrons from the state of Zhou.
He reigned for fifty-six years.
King Xiaowen (King Wu), whose personal name was Wu, was the son of King Zhaoxiang;
he died after reigning for three months.
Zhuangxiang Wang (King Zhuangxiang) was of the state of Chu.
He was the son of King Xiaowen.
He reigned for four years.
In the first year, the ruler of Eastern Zhou conspired with the feudal lords to attack Qin.
Qin dispatched the Chancellor Lü Buwei to lead the army to suppress them.
Eastern Zhou was extinguished, and the Chancellor was enfeoffed as the Marquis Wenxin.
The First Emperor, Shi Huangdi.
Son of Zhuang Xiang Wang.
He succeeded to the throne at the age of thirteen.
All affairs of state were entrusted to Lord Wenxin, who was styled Zhongfu.
In the second year of the First Emperor’s reign, there were seven states in the world wearing caps and sashes, three of which bordered upon the Rong and Di tribes.
To the west of Long in Qin, there were the Mian-zhu, Kun, Rong, Di, and Min Rong.
To the north of Qi, Liang, Jing, and Qi, there were the Yi-qu, Da-ru, Wu-shi, Ju-qiu, and Yan Rong.
To the north of Zhao were the Linhu and Loufan Rong;
to the north of Yan were the Donghu and Shanrong.
Each of these peoples lived scattered throughout the mountain valleys.
When the Qin extinguished the Yiqu, they began from Longxi, Beidi, and Shangjun.
They built a long wall to resist the Hu.
King Wu-ling of Zhao defeated the Linhu and Loufan to the north.
He built the Great Wall from Dai along the Yin Mountains as far as Gaoque to serve as a defensive barrier.
He established the commanderies of Yunzhong, Yanmen, and Dai.
After Yan defeated the Eastern Hu, they were driven back more than a thousand li.
He built the Great Wall from Zao Yang to Xiangping,
establishing the commanderies of Shanggu, Yuyang, Youbeiping, and Liaodong to resist the Hu.
It was toward the end of the Warring States period that the Xiongnu first became a major power.
In the twenty-sixth year of the First Emperor, he first unified all under heaven.
He considered himself to possess the virtues of the Three Sovereigns and the achievements of the Five Emperors.
He then further styled himself Emperor (*huangdi*).
He abolished the system of posthumous titles (*shi-fa*), deeming it inappropriate for subordinates to deliberate upon their superiors.
He mandated that his edicts be termed *zhi* (ordinances) and his proclamations be termed *zhao* (imperial decrees).
He styled himself "Zhen.
Furthermore, he said:
"I am the First Emperor."
In later generations, they calculated by cycles;
from two generations and three generations up to ten thousand generations,
they inherited the Mandate through the Virtue of Water.
Originally, during the reigns of Kings Wei and Xuan of Qi,
Zou Yan composed treatises on the "Beginning and End" and the cyclical movement of the five virtues.
The people of Qi presented them to the throne.
The First Emperor adopted his proposal.

He first changed the year and the New Year’s salutations, both of which were held on the first day of the tenth month; furthermore, clothing, banners, standards, and ceremonial flags all took black as their primary color.
He changed the numerical cycle from six to twelve, altered the name of the *laxia* festival to *Jiaping*,
and divided the empire into thirty-six commanderies,
saying:

San-chuan, He-dong, Nan-yang, Nan-jun, Jiu-jiang, Zhang-jun, Hui-ji, Ying-chuan, Dang-jun, Si-shui, Xue-jun, Dong-jun, Lang-ya, Qi-jun, Shang-gu, Yu-yang, You-bei, Ping-liao, Xi-liao, Dong-dai-jun, Ju-lu, Han-dan, Shang-dang, Tai-yuan, Yun-chung, Jiu-yuan, Yan-men, Shang-jun, Long-xi, Bei-di, Han-zhong, Ba-jun, Shu-jun, Qian-chung, and Chang-sha.
In total there were thirty-five;
together with the Interior History (Neishi), they constituted thirty-six commanderies.
Each commandery was established with a Governor (Shou), a Commandant (Wei), and a Supervisor (Jian).
He collected the weapons of the empire and assembled them at Xianyang;
he melted them down to cast bells and ritual vessels, as well as twelve golden men.
This was the thirty-fourth year of the Emperor’s reign.
The Chancellor Li Si submitted a memorial stating that all records by historians other than those of the Qin should be burned; furthermore,
anyone who speaks in verse or discusses the Odes and the Books shall be punished.
Those who condemn the present by citing antiquity shall be executed in the marketplace;
yet even among those whose clans are not spared,
there are the books on medicine, divination, and arboriculture.
"If you wish for those in training to take officials as their teachers," he said.
The decree was "So be it.
Thereupon, the masters Hou Sheng and Lu Sheng fled together.
The First Emperor was enraged and sent officials to investigate.
The students informed one another,
leading to the arrest of more than four hundred and sixty people for violating the prohibitions.
In the tenth month of winter in the thirty-sixth year, the First Emperor went on a tour,
followed by his Left Chancellor, Li Si; his younger son, Hu Hai, requested to accompany him.
Traveling westward, he fell ill at Pingyuanjin.
On the Bingyin day of the seventh month,
the First Emperor passed away at the Sand邱 Terrace.
He reigned for thirty-seven years and reached the age of fifty.
While Zhongche Fuling was carrying out his duties,
Zhao Gao then hatched a fraudulent plot with Chancellor Si.
Having received the imperial decree to establish Hu Hai as the Crown Prince,
he returned to Xianyang,
where the funeral rites were finally commenced.
He succeeded to the throne.
In the ninth month, he buried the First Emperor at Mount Li.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, the Great Being Nāgārjuna, was a native of the kingdom of Aparāntaka in Western India.
He was also named Nāgasena.
After attaining the Dharma, he went to South India,
where the people of that country were largely devoted to meritorious deeds.
The Patriarch preached the Dharma for them.
They said to one another,
"There is a person whose meritorious karma is foremost in the world."
"Vainly one speaks of Buddha-nature;
who is able to behold it?
The Patriarch said:
"If you wish to see the Buddha-nature,
you must first eliminate your pride.
He replied:
"Is Buddha-nature large or small?
The Patriarch said,
"It is neither large nor small."
Neither broad nor narrow;
without merit and without retribution;
neither dying nor being born.
Having heard that this principle was superior,
they all returned to their original resolve.
Among that assembly was the son of an elder named Kanadeva.
The entire assembly likewise wished to leave the household life;
the Patriarch shaved their heads,
and he commanded the various sages to bestow upon them the full precepts.
In that country, there were previously more than five thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths who practiced great magical arts;
all the people revered and followed them.
The Patriarch transformed them all, leading them to take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Consequently, he composed the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, the Madhyamaka-śāstra, and the Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra,
which he bequeathed to the world.
Not merely tens of millions of verses,
all of which employ skillful means to expound and elucidate the True Dharma.
In accordance with their respective capacities,
he later commanded Kāṇadeva, saying:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the Great Dharma-eye to Kāśyapa."
"Even unto me.
I now entrust this to you.
Listen to my verse:"
To clarify the principles of concealment and manifestation,
one then explains the logic of liberation;
yet regarding these dharmas, the mind does not realize them.
Free from both anger and joy,
having entrusted the Dharma, he entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi and extensively manifested miraculous transformations.
He returned once more to his original seat and remained in profound meditative stillness.
Kanadeva, together with the fourfold assembly, constructed a precious stupa to enshrine him.
This was during the reign of the First Emperor of Qin.
The *Zengong ji* records that the Second Emperor, Hu Hai,
was the youngest son of the First Emperor.
In the autumn of the first year, Chen Sheng, styled She,
a man of Yangcheng, and Wu Guang, a man of Yangxia,
raised an army at Huaixi.
Xiang Liang, a native of Xixiang in Qizhou,
raised an army at Wu;
Tian Dang, a man of Di, raised an army at Qi.
Sheng and Guang falsely claimed the title of "Great Chu.
Sheng appointed himself General, while Guang served as Commandant;
they entered and took possession of Chen.
The elders of Chenzhong petitioned to establish Sheng as the King of Chu.
In the ninth month, Liu Ji raised troops at Pei;
he was called the Duke of Pei.
The heroes and eminent men of the world all rose up to contend for the establishment of the successor states of the six kingdoms.
Xiang Liang was the son of Xiang Yan, a general of Chu.
Xiang Ji, whose courtesy name was Yu, was the son of Liang’s elder brother.
In the second year, Zhao Gao killed Li Si, who died.
The Second Emperor appointed Gao as Chancellor.
The Duke of Pei returned to attack Feng and captured it.
Xiang Liang summoned the various separate commanders to Xue to deliberate on affairs.
Fan Zeng, a man from Junchao who was seventy years old,
advised Liang to establish a successor to the state of Chu.
He sought out and found the grandson of King Huai of Chu, named Xin.
In the sixth month of summer, he established Xin as the King of Chu,
following the aspirations of the people.
After three years, all of Guandong rebelled.
Fearing that the Second Emperor would be enraged and execute him for his own person,
Zhao Gao then pleaded illness and ceased attending court.
Yin, together with his son-in-law Yan Yue, the Magistrate of Xianyang,
conspired to depose the Emperor and install Prince Ying in his stead. Yue then led over a thousand officials and soldiers into the Wangyi Palace.
The Second Prince said,
"I wish to have one commandery as my kingdom," but [the King] did not grant it.
He spoke again, saying:
He wished to be a marquis over ten thousand households, but this was not granted.
He said, "I wish only that my wife and children and I may be commoners like other gentlemen. Yan Yue said:
"I, your servant, have received the mandate from the Chancellor to execute you for the sake of the empire.
Raise your banners and advance!"
The second generation then committed suicide.
Zhao Gao then summoned all the high ministers and the princes, saying,
"Qin was formerly a royal kingdom."
The First Emperor ruled over all under heaven, and therefore he was titled "Emperor.
Now that the six states have re-established themselves,
the territory of Qin has become increasingly diminished.
He then enthroned the one named Qing as Emperor;
it was not appropriate for him to remain King as before.
He subsequently established Ying, the son of the former Crown Prince Fusu, as the King of Qin.
He ordered Ziying to fast and receive the jade seal during a temple visit.
Ziying plotted with his two sons, saying:
The Chancellor Gao killed the Second Emperor.
Fearing that the ministers would execute him, he feigned the intention of establishing me on the throne; however, I claimed illness and did not go.
"The Chancellor will certainly come.
When he comes, kill him.
Shortly thereafter, he indeed came in person.
Ziying then had Gao assassinated at the Sacrificial Hall and exterminated his family to the third generation.
Ziying then ascended the throne.
He reigned for forty-six days.
In the tenth month,
the Lord of Pei arrived at Bashi.

Ziying surrendered. In the first year of the Second Emperor (Renchen), the first year of King Jiu of Wei; the first year of King Wuchen of Zhao; the first year of King Tian Dan of Qi; the first year of the Hidden King Chen Sheng of Chu; and the first year of King Han Guang of Yan. In the fifth year of the Han, the Han dynasty was established. In the second year (Guisi), the first year of King Bao of Wei—the Han destroyed him in the ninth month of the second year. The first year of King Xie of Zhao—the Han destroyed him in the third year. The first year of King Tian Zu of Qi—the Han destroyed him in the fourth year. In the sixth month of summer, Xiang Liang installed Xin, the grandson of King Huai of Chu, as the King of Chu. The first year of King Cheng of Han corresponds to the third year of the Second Emperor (Jiamu), which is the first year of the Han. The first year of King Zheng Chang of Han—the Han destroyed him in the third year. Ziying was the son of Fu Su, the Crown Prince of the First Emperor.
He remained enthroned for forty-six days.
In the tenth month,
the Duke of Pei arrived at Basha.
Ziying appeared in a plain carriage drawn by white horses, with a silken cord tied around his neck;
he presented the imperial seal, credentials, and insignia,
and surrendered by the side of the Zhidao road.
The Duke of Pei entered Xianyang from the west.
[This concludes] the history of Qin, from King Zhaoxiang to Ziying,
totaling fifty years.
The world turned to Han.

The Western Han consisted of the following rulers of the Liu clan: Gaozu, Emperor Hui, Empress Lü, Emperor Wen, Emperor Jing, Emperor Wu, Emperor Zhao, King of Changyi, Emperor Xuan, Emperor Yuan, Emperor Cheng, Emperor Ai, Emperor Ping, and Ruzi Ying.
He reigned as a King of Fire Virtue.
His capital was Chang'an, which is now Jingzhao in the western region of present-day Shaanxi; it is the site of Xianyang during the Qin dynasty and lies within the domain of Yongzhou.
The High Ancestor changed the name to Chang’an.
At the beginning of the Han dynasty, they used the calendar of Qin,
