taking the tenth month as the first month.
It was not until the first year of the Taichu era of Emperor Wu that the Xia calendar was first adopted, establishing the month of Yin as the first month.
This was after the empire had been pacified in the fifth year of the Han dynasty.
Lou Jing, while on guard duty in Longxi, passed through Luoyang.
He introduced himself to General Yu and presented himself to the Emperor, saying:
"The territory of Qin is protected by mountains and girded by rivers; its four borders are fortified as a natural bulwark."
He was about to recommend Yingdu.
The Emperor questioned his ministers,
and Zhang Liang said:
Lou Jing was right in his argument.
On that very day, the imperial carriage proceeded west to establish the capital at Chang'an,
and Lou Jing was appointed as a Langzhong.
He was granted the surname Liu.
His High Ancestor’s name was Bang, with the courtesy name Ji;
he was a native of Zhongyang Village in Fengyi.
In the state of Qin, he served as a *ting-chang* (village head) in Yanzhou;
he was escorting convicts to Mount Li when many of them escaped along the way.
He released his prisoners and went into hiding in Pei.
In the first year of the reign of the Second Emperor of Qin,
the elders of Pei enthroned Ji as the Duke of Pei.
Xiao He, Cao Can, and others recruited three thousand men from among the sons and younger brothers of Pei to respond to his call.
In the tenth month of the third year of the reign of the Second Emperor of Qin,
[the army] first entered the Passes and reached Baisang. There,
the Qin general Ziying surrendered and took up residence.
After several days, Xiang Yu slaughtered those of Xianyang,
killed the surrendered Qin prince Ziying,
and set fire to the Qin palaces.
The people of Qin were greatly disappointed.
Xiang Yu outwardly honored the King of Chu, Huai Wang Xin, as the Emperor of Righteousness (Yi Di),
establishing his capital at Chen, which is now the seat of Guiyang Prefecture.
The territory of Jingzhou was divided among the various generals who were made kings.
Liu Bei established himself as the King of Xichu,
with his capital at Pengcheng in the administrative region of Henan, present-day Xuzhou.
He established the Duke of Pei as the King of Han,
with his capital at Nanzheng— present-day Xingyuan Prefecture in Shaanxi, known by the commandery name of Hanzhong—
and divided the region of Guanzhong between two kings.
The three surrendered Qin generals, including Zhang Han,
were obstructing the Han routes;
the King of Han was enraged and wished to attack Xiang Yu.
Zhou Bo, Guan Ying, and Fan Zeng all urged him [to accept the title],
while Xiao He remonstrated against it.
Consequently, he proceeded to his fief and styled the first year of the Han.
He appointed someone as Chancellor and next invested Han Xin as Grand General,
leading his troops out to launch a surprise attack on Yong.
The Prince of Yong, Zhang Han, was defeated in battle and fled.
The Prince of Sai, Xin, and the Prince of Zhizhe, Yi, both surrendered.
Their territories were established as the commanderies of Wei-nan, He-shang, and Shang-jun.
In the tenth month of winter, the second year of the Han era,
the King of Xiang secretly dispatched Lüan Bu, King of Jiuyang, and others to attack the Emperor of Righteousness (Yìdì) and kill him in the Yangtze River.
The Han King then crossed southward at the Píngyīn Ferry and arrived at Luoyang.
Dong Gong, the Elder of Sancheng, intercepted King Xiang and exhorted him, saying:
"Those who follow virtue shall prosper;
those who oppose virtue shall perish."
An expedition launched without a just cause will not achieve its objective; Xiang Yu is devoid of the Way and has treacherously murdered his lord.
Your Majesty ought to lead the multitudes of your three armies, wearing plain mourning garments, to announce this to the feudal lords and strike him down.
Thereupon, King Han held a funeral for the Emperor of Righteousness to inform the feudal lords.
Lord Chen Yu of Zhao dispatched troops to assist Han.
Although Xiang Wang heard that Han was moving eastward, he intended to first defeat Qi and only then strike at Han.
The Han King was thus able to lead the armies of the various feudal lords, totaling five hundred and sixty thousand men, to strike at Chu.
He subsequently entered Pengcheng.
When Xiang Wang heard of this, he [was alarmed].
Leading twenty thousand elite troops himself, he arrived at Pengcheng and decisively defeated the Han army,
surrounding the Han Emperor in three concentric rings. At that moment,
a great wind arose, snapping trees and blowing away roofs.
In the profound darkness, it was as if day had turned to night.
The Chu army fell into great chaos and broke apart.
King Han was thus able to escape with several dozen riders; Shen Shiqi followed him, as did the Grandfather of King Han (Liu Ji). Empress Lü traveled by secret paths in search of King Han.
Unexpectedly, he encountered the army of Chu.
Xiang Yu had previously kept him in his camp as a hostage.
In the fourth year of the Han era, the Han dispatched Hou Gong to persuade Xiang Yu to release the Grandfather (Tai Gong).
Yu then made a pact with Han to divide the world in half:
they demarcated the Hong Gou— present-day Zhengzhou— as the boundary, with the area to the west belonging to Han and the area to the east belonging to Chu.
In the ninth month, Chu returned the Grand Duke and Empress Lü.
Thereupon, he led his troops eastward to return home.
The King of Han wished to return west.
Zhang Liang and Chen Ping said,
"Han possesses more than half of the empire,
while the Chu troops' provisions are exhausted."
"This is the time for this deity to perish.
If we now release him without striking,
it is what is called 'raising a tiger only to invite calamity upon oneself.'"
The Han King followed his advice.

In the winter of the fifth year, on the tenth month, the Han King pursued the Xiang King as far as Gu-ling—present-day Guoshi in Guangzhou, Runing Prefecture, along the route of present-day Bianliang. On the twelfth month, [he arrived there].
When the Heir Apparent of the Xiang clan arrived at Heng (in present-day Pei Prefecture), he heard the songs of Chu resounding from all four sides of the Han army during the night.
Consequently, his forces broke through the encirclement and fled southward, galloping to Wujiang (the territory of modern-day Hezhou in Huaixi).
When the ferryman at Wu Jiang moored his boat to await Xiang Wang, the latter laughed and said,
"Heaven has destroyed me;
why should I cross?"
Moreover, when I crossed the river with eight thousand youths from Jiangdong to go west, not a single one returned;
even if the fathers and elder brothers of Jiangdong were to pity me and grant me the title of King, what would it avail?
"What face would I have to see them?
Even if they did not speak of it,
how could I alone not feel ashamed in my own heart?"
She then took her own life by cutting her throat.
The Han Prince immediately ascended the imperial throne at Fankuan, on the southern bank of the river where the sword was turned back into water; he now crossed the boundary of the Han.
He further changed the title of the King’s Consort to Empress.
The Crown Prince said, "The Imperial Crown Prince.
In the summer of the sixth year, he honored his grandfather as the Retired Emperor (Taishanghuang).
Once the empire was settled, [he ascended the throne].
He charged Xiao He with the task of codifying the laws and edicts;
Han Xin was appointed to promulgate the military codes;
and Zhang Cang was tasked with determining the standards and regulations—wherein "zhang" refers to the calendrical calculations and methods of the *zhengce*.
"Measurements" (*cheng*) refer to the balance, scale, fathoms, feet, bushels, and pecks.
In the calendrical systems, when the new moon falls on the same day [as a specific solar term], it is called a "cycle" (*zhang*).
Seventeen years with seven intercalary months constitute one cycle.
Cheng Ru-cheng’s *Shi-cheng shu* states that "laws, measures, weights, and balances" (*lü-dù-liàng-héng*) refer to the standards for regulation.

Wén-zhōng-zǐ remarked that Emperor Xiān-zhān used "statutes and regulations" (*zhāng-chéng*) to refine names and realities, meaning the formal patterns and models of enacted laws. Shǔ-sūn Tōng established the ritual protocols.
Lu Jia composed the *Xinyu*.
The meritorious ministers were enfeoffed as marquises;
they were divided by the tally of office and bound by oath.
The red-scriptured tablets and iron seals were stored in the ancestral temple within golden caskets and stone chambers.
The oath was sworn thus:
"May the Yellow River remain as narrow as a sash and Mount Tai as small as a whetstone."
The state shall endure forever,
extending even to its descendants.
The Emperor reigned for twelve years.
He passed away at the age of fifty-three.
Emperor Hui, whose personal name was Ying,
was the Crown Prince of the High Ancestor.
He reigned for seven years.
His lifespan was twenty-four years.
Empress Lü (Lǚ Hòu): her courtesy name was Zhì, and her surname was Lǔ.
The Empress Dowager was the mother of Emperor Hui.
When Emperor Hui passed away,
the Empress Dowager took the son of a beautiful woman from the inner palace and established him as the Crown Prince.
The Empress Dowager presided over the court and exercised sovereign authority.
In the fourth year, the young Emperor learned of this and spoke of it;
consequently, the Empress Dowager confined the young Emperor within the Yongxiang Palace.
He established the principle of "the King who abides eternally in the Mean" as his imperial title;
he changed the reign name to Hong (Great) and did not designate a first year,
because the Empress Dowager governed all affairs of state.
When Emperor Wen came to the throne,
he had them all executed at their residences.
In the seventh month of the autumn of the eighth year, the Empress Dowager passed away.

He lived to the age of seventy-two and reigned for eight years. When Lü Lu and Lü Chan attempted to incite a rebellion, the Grand Commandant Zhou Bo and others executed the various members of the Lü clan.
Thereupon, the high ministers entered into a secret conspiracy.
The Emperor sent messengers to summon the Prince of Dai.
When the Prince of Dai received the imperial seal and credentials from Heaven,
he declined the succession five times.
He then ascended the throne as Emperor Wen.
Emperor Wen’s personal name was Heng;
he was the third son of the High Ancestor.
He was enfeoffed as the King of Dai.

After Chen Ping and Zhou Bo had executed the various members of the Lü clan, they dispatched an envoy to welcome the King to Chang'an, where he immediately ascended the throne; he reigned for sixteen years.
Furthermore, he reigned for another seven years of the Yuan era.
His total reign was twenty-three years, and he passed away at the age of forty-six.
The Emperor abolished corporal punishments involving dismemberment.
He was diligent in practicing broadminded generosity.
He wore plain dyed silk for his robes,
and his curtains and canopies were devoid of embroidery or brocade.
The burial sites at Baling were furnished exclusively with earthenware;
no ornaments of gold, silver, copper, or iron were permitted.

Taking advantage of the natural terrain, no mounds were raised for the tombs. The Emperor devoted himself solely to transforming the people through virtue, so that the realm became prosperous and wealthy.
The number of criminal cases adjudicated throughout the realm was several hundred;
it nearly reached the point where punishments were no longer required.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, the Great Being Kanadeva, was a native of South India.
His surname was Viśāla.
He went to visit Nāgārjuna; Nāgārjuna had previously filled a bowl with water and placed it before his seat.
Deva cast a single needle into it.
They joyfully reached a mutual understanding.
Having received the Dharma, he arrived at the kingdom of Kapilavastu,
where there was an elder named Brahmāyu.
Mushrooms grew upon the trees in the grove like fungi;
they would pluck them and eat them,
yet as soon as they were plucked, they grew back again.
When the Patriarch arrived at his home,
the elder asked where the mushrooms had come from.
The Patriarch replied:
In your family, you once supported a bhikṣu whose path-vision was not clear;
having vainly consumed the offerings of the faithful,
his karmic retribution has become this wooden fungus.
Then he spoke in verse:
"One who enters the Path but does not penetrate its principle returns in body to consume the offerings of the faithful."
"You are eighty-one years old;
that tree simply does not grow [fruit]. When the elder was eighty-one, the tree did not produce fruit, nor did mushrooms grow upon it.
The elder gave up his second son, Rāhula-bhadra, who followed his grandfather into the monastic life.
His grandfather ordained him,
and they proceeded to the city of Pāṭaliputra.
There were various non-Buddhists who suppressed the Buddha-dharma;
the Patriarch went to convert them,
but some did not comply.
He posed hundreds of thousands of difficult questions,
but the Patriarch allowed him to exercise his unimpeded eloquence,
refuting them all.
From this, extensive treatises and discourses were composed;
those such as the *Śata-śāstra* (The Treatise in One Hundred Verses) are examples of this.
Once these superior matters had been gathered together, [the work was completed].
He entrusted the Dharma to Rāhulabhadra.
A verse says:
"Originally for the sake of the one who transmits the Dharma."
For them, he explains the principle of liberation:
in reality, there is no realization of dharmas;
it has neither end nor beginning.
Thereupon, he entered the Samādhi of Vigorous Activity;
from his body, he emitted eight rays of light and proceeded toward nirvāṇa.
The assembly then erected a stupa for his interment.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty, this was recorded in the *Zhengzong ji*.
Emperor Jing succeeded Emperor Wen;
he was the Crown Prince of Emperor Wen.
He occupied the imperial throne for seven years;
furthermore, there were seven years of the Zhongyuan era and three years of the Houyuan era, totaling seventeen years.
His reign lasted forty-eight years.
The Emperor, finding the punishments of five hundred or three hundred lashes too severe,
abolished the law of flogging and followed the legacy of Emperor Wen.
Customs were transformed and social mores altered;
the common people became pure and sincere.
This was what the Zhou called the eras of Cheng and Kang.
The Han dynasty is praised for its Emperors Wen and Jing.
Emperor Wu was named Chè;
he was the son of Emperor Jing.
He reigned for fifty-four years and lived to the age of seventy-one.

He suppressed the Hundred Schools and championed the Six Classics; he established the Imperial Academy, renovated the suburban sacrifices, standardized musical tones, composed poetry and music, instituted the Feng and Shan rites, and worshipped the hundred spirits. He succeeded the Zhou dynasty, and his edicts and literary works were resplendent.
The Emperor was by nature fond of the Confucian arts; so too were the Chancellor Dou Ying,
the Grand Commandant Tian Fen,
and the Grandee Secretary Zhao Wan.
He requested that a Mingtang be established to receive the feudal lords and presented his teacher, Shen Gong,
who was then over eighty years of age.
He was appointed as Grand Master of the Central Palace (Taizhong Dafu).
Residing in the guest house of Lu, he deliberated upon the construction of the Mingtang, the imperial tours of inspection, the reform of the calendar, and the colors of ceremonial robes.
The Emperor summoned men of talent and virtue from all quarters.
Zhuang Zhu was the first to be promoted; he was originally Yan Zhu, who changed his name to avoid the taboo character of Emperor Ming.
Later, the state of Wu provided Zhu Maichen, and the state of Zhao provided Wuqiu Shouwang.
Sima Xiangru of Shu;
Dongfang Shuo of Pingyuan;
and Mugao of Wu.
Ji Nan and Zhong Jun were both in attendance at his side.
On the first day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Taichu era, under the *jiazi* stem, it was the winter solstice.
He commanded Sima Qian to create the Han Taichu calendar.
He took the month of Yin as the first month of the year and adopted yellow as the imperial color.
The number five is employed;
yet, in deploying troops and wielding martial force,
one opens up the way for the four barbarian tribes abroad.
As for the monopolies on liquor and brewing, the management of salt and iron,
the casting of white gold, and the production of leather currency,
it was during the Emperor's reign that these first began; he was also the first to establish an era name.
There has never been such a thing since the beginning of emperors and kings.

From the commencement of his reign, he designated the first year as Jianyuan 1; Jianyuan 6; Yuanguang 6; Yuanshuo 6; Yuanshou 6; Yuanding 6; Yuanfeng 6; Taichu 4; Tianhan 4; Taishi 4; Zhenghe 4; and Houyuan 2.
The sixteenth patriarch, the Great Master Rāhulabhadra, was a native of Kapilavastu.
While traveling to Śrāvastī to propagate the Dharma,
he addressed his disciples, saying:
There was a noble one who was destined to succeed to the ancestral throne.
Upon reaching the Golden Water River,
he saw Saṃghanandin seated in a stone cave, absorbed in meditative concentration.
After observing him for twenty-one days,
he finally arose from his meditative concentration.
The Patriarch asked:
"Is your body concentrated, or is your mind concentrated?
Ti replied,
"Both my body and my mind are concentrated."
The Patriarch said,
"When body and mind are both settled, how can there be entering or exiting?
Daitetsu replied:
Although there was coming and going, he did not lose the characteristic of meditative concentration;
he knew that the gold remained in the well, its essence eternally tranquil.
The Patriarch said:
Whether the gold is in the well or the gold has emerged from the well, the gold itself has neither motion nor stillness; what object could there be that enters or exits?
Daiti said:
[The student] asked, "Regarding gold, what things enter and exit its movement and stillness?
[The Master] replied, "Regarding the entry and exit of gold, the gold itself is neither moving nor still.
The Patriarch said:
"If the gold is in the well, what is it that has emerged?
If the gold has emerged from the well, what remains inside?
Thus he interrogated him back and forth.
Nandi was suddenly enlightened and immediately sought liberation.
The Patriarch took the golden bowl in his right hand and lifted it up to the Brahma Heaven.
He took that fragrant food,
yet the great assembly remained hesitant;
he then commanded Nanda to share his seat and eat together with him.
The assembly again harbored doubts,
thinking that the master and disciples were intermingled without distinction.
The Patriarch, knowing this, said:
"That you were unable to eat was entirely due to this reason.
The one who now shares his seat with me is none other than the Tathāgata Sālarāja of the past."
He merely manifested his traces in response to sentient beings.
When Nandika perceived that the assembly harbored arrogance, he said:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, people lack ultimate faith;
their right mindfulness is slight, and they do not believe in *tathatā* (suchness),
but only cherish supernatural powers.
Having finished speaking, he gradually extended his right hand into the earth until it reached the limit of the vajra-circle,
where he took up the dew.
He carried a vessel of lapis lazuli to the assembly hall.
When the great multitude saw it, they immediately conceived a sense of admiration, repented their transgressions, and prostrated themselves.
Thereupon, the Patriarch charged Saṃghanandi with the transmission of the Dharma-eye.
The verse says:
Regarding phenomena, there is truly nothing to be realized;
neither grasping nor abandoning occurs.
The Dharma has no characteristics of existence or non-existence;
how could it arise internally or externally?
Having entrusted the Dharma, he sat peacefully and returned to stillness.
The fourfold assembly erected a stupa to enshrine his entire body;
this was during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Former Han, according to the *Zhengzong ji*.
Emperor Zhao (Zhāo Dì), whose personal name was Fúlíng,
was the son of Emperor Wǔ.
He reigned for thirteen years.
He lived to the age of twenty-two.
The Grand Marshal and Grand General Huo Guang,
and the Cavalry General and Chief of the Imperial Stables Jin Midi.
General of the Left Shangguan Jie received the Emperor Wu’s final charge and testament regarding the administration of government.
The common people became prosperous and well-supplied; he promoted men of virtue and literary talent, and proposed the abolition of the state monopoly on brewing and liquor sales.
In the first year of Shiyuan,
Wang Ping was dispatched with full powers to tour the commanderies and kingdoms,
inquiring after the people's hardships and grievances. This occurred in the sixth year of Shiyuan, the sixth year of Yuanfeng, and the first year of Yuanying.
The Seventeenth Patriarch, the Great Being Saṃghanandin, was the son of King Ratnavyūha of Śrāvastī.
From birth he was able to speak and constantly praised the Buddha’s deeds.
At the age of seven, he addressed his parents with a verse, saying:
"I bow my head to my greatly compassionate father; I pay homage to my mother, who gave me flesh and blood.
I now wish to leave the home-life."
He earnestly entreated them with compassion,
and so his parents permitted him to leave the household life and become a renunciant.
They further appointed the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin as his teacher.
In his nineteenth year, he departed the royal palace and entered a great rocky cave by the Nairañjanā River to enter meditative concentration.
After another ten years, having attained the Dharma, he traveled to the kingdom of Magadha to propagate his teachings.
Arriving at the foot of the mountain peak,
he saw a youth holding a round mirror who walked straight toward the Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked:
"How old are you?
He replied, "One hundred years.
The Patriarch said:
"You are still young;
why do you say you are a hundred years old?
He replied, "I do not understand the principle; I am simply exactly one hundred years old."
The Patriarch said, "Are you skilled in the pivotal point?

He replied, "The Buddha said that even if a person lives for a hundred years, if they do not understand the pivotal point of the Buddhas, it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining decisive realization. The Patriarch said: [He was accepted.]
"What does that which is in your hand signify?
He replied, "It signifies the great perfect mirror of all Buddhas,
without flaw or obscuration within or without."
Both saw it together;
their eyes and minds were alike.
When the parents heard their son’s words, they were moved.
He immediately released him to allow him to leave the household life.
His grandfather ordained him and conferred upon him the full precepts, naming him Gayāśata.
At another time, when the wind blew and the bells of the hall chimed,
the Patriarch asked,
"Are the bells ringing, or is the wind ringing?"
Shexia said, "It is not the wind-bells that ring; it is my own heart that rings.
The Patriarch said:
"Whose mind is it? Śāradvatīputra replied,
"Because both are utterly tranquil."
The Patriarch said,
"Excellent, excellent!
Who else but you could continue my Way?"
He then transmitted the Dharma-eye,
saying in verse:
"The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth."
The ground arises from conditions;
the conditions and the seeds do not obstruct one another.
It is likewise with the flowers and the fruits.
After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma,
he passed away while grasping a tree with his right hand.
The assembly deliberated and decided to enshrine his entire body in a stupa on a high plateau.
The multitude was unable to lift it.
He was then cremated beneath the tree;
his relics were collected and a stupa was erected.
During the reign of Emperor Zhao of the Han dynasty, the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage) states:
"The Prince of Changyi, He,
was the son of King Ai."
In the fourth month of the first year of Yuanshi of Emperor Wu’s grandson, Emperor Zhao passed away without an heir.
The Grand General Huo Guang consulted with the ministers regarding the establishment of a king.
This king had long been known for his profligacy and recklessness.
In the sixth month, he received the imperial seal and ribbon from the Emperor.
He honored the Empress as the Empress Dowager.
The Emperor frequently refused to accept admonitions.
He reigned for twenty-seven days.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict to depose him and send him to the residence of Changyi.
She then invited Bingyi, a great-grandson of Emperor Wu, from among the common people to ascend the throne.
He was renamed Xun to serve as the successor to Emperor Zhao; this is recorded in the Basic Annals.
As for Emperor Xuan, his name was Xun;
he was originally named Bingyi.
Emperor Wu’s Crown Prince Lì gave birth to Shǐ Huángsūn;
Shǐ Huángsūn begot Xún, who was the great-grandson of Emperor Wu.
He ascended the throne at the age of eighteen.
He reigned for twenty-five years and passed away at forty-three.
The Emperor rose from among the common people.
He understood the hardships and sufferings of the people.
After the death of the Grand General Huo Guang,
he began to personally attend to the affairs of government.
Wei Xiang and Bing Ji served as Grand Ministers;
Huang Qiu, Gong Sui, and Dong were appointed as Commandery Governors.
Rewards were granted with sincerity and punishments were invariably meted out.
The officials fulfilled their duties,
and the people were secure in their occupations.
In the third year of the Diji era.
The Chancellor Wei Xian retired from office due to old age and illness and returned to his private residence.
It was from Wei Xian that the practice of retiring from office began for a Chancellor.
In the fourth year of the Wufeng era, Geng Shouchang, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat for Agriculture, petitioned for the establishment of the Changping Granary.
When grain is cheap,
increase the price to encourage farmers to sell;
when grain is expensive, decrease the price.
The people found the sale of grain convenient.
Shouchang was granted the rank of Guannei Hou.
This was in the third year of the Ganlu era.
The Emperor, because the Rong and Di tribes had submitted as guests,
contemplated the excellence of his ministers who were like his own limbs. He therefore depicted them upon the Qilin Terrace,
modeling their physical features and inscribing their official titles and names.
Only Huo Guang was not addressed by name;
he was simply referred to as "the Grand Commandant, the Great General, the Marquis of Bolu, surnamed Huo.
Following him were eleven others: Zhang Anshi, Han Zeng, Zhao Chongguo, Wei Xiang, Bing Ji, Du Yan'ian, Liu De, Liangqiu He, Xiao Wangzhi, and Su Wu.
All possessed meritorious virtues and were renowned in their time; therefore,
I have set them forth and extolled them.
He clearly highlighted the ministers who assisted in the restoration,
placing Fang Shu, Zhao Hu, and Zhong Shanfu among them;
he then commanded the various scholars to lecture on the similarities and differences of the Five Classics.
Xiao Wangzhi and others submitted their deliberations in a formal memorial.
The Emperor personally presided over the decision by issuing an imperial decree.
Thereupon, he established the doctoral positions for the Liangqiu Yi and the Da and Xiao Xiahou Shangshu, as well as for the Guliang Chunqiu.

He passed away in the first year of Huanglong. [The reigns included] four years of Benshi, five years of Dije, four years of Yuankang, five years of Shanjue, four years of Wufeng, four years of Ganglu, and four years of Huanglong.
[This corresponds to] the nineteenth year of Jianwu during the Eastern Han dynasty under Emperor Guangwu.
Emperor Xuan was posthumously honored as Zhongzong.
Emperor Yuan, whose personal name was Yan Shi,
was the son of Emperor Xuan.
He reigned for sixteen years and lived to the age of forty-three.
Ban Biao praised him, saying:
"My maternal grandfather’s brothers served as Attendants-in-Ordinary (*shizhong*) to Emperor Yuan.
They told me that Emperor Yuan was possessed of many arts and skills and was proficient in calligraphy and history."
From his youth, he was fond of Confucianism;
upon ascending the throne, he summoned and employed Confucian scholars,
entrusting them with the administration of government.
The Emperor’s governance restrained the interpretation of texts and meanings,
remaining leisurely and unimpeded;
his majesty was broad and magnanimous, while his subordinates were characterized by utmost reverence and frugality.
His edicts were mild and elegant, possessing the spirit of antiquity.
He passed away in the fifth month of the first year of Jingning. [The reigns were: five years of Chuyuan, five of Yongguang, five of Jianzhao, and one of Jingning.
Emperor Cheng (Chéng Dì) was arrogant.
He was the crown prince of Emperor Yuán.
He occupied the throne for twenty-six years.
His lifespan was forty-five years.
In the first year of the Jiānshǐ era, he enfeoffed his maternal uncle Wáng Chóng as Marquis of Ānchéng;
he also conferred the rank of Guānnèihóu upon Tán, Shāng, Lì, Gēn, and Fénghuí.
The Wang family monopolized the administration.
The Five Marquises were arrogant and extravagant, concurrently wielding authority and fortune.
In the first year of the Yongshi era, Wang Mang was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xindu.
In the eleventh month of the first year of the Shuihe era, the Grand Marshal Wang Gen recommended Maṅ to succeed him;
Maṅ was then twenty-eight years old. He became the Grand Marshal.
Mang changed his ways, distributing his wealth to cultivate friendships with scholars in order to establish a reputation for himself.
In the third month of the second year of Suihé, the Emperor passed away. [The reigns included] four years each of Jiānsì, Hé píng, Yángshuò, Hóngjiā, Yǒngshǐ, Yuányán, and Suīhé.
The eighteenth patriarch, the Great Being Gayāśata, was a native of the country of Mathurā.
His clan name was Udraka;
his father was Deva-āvaraṇa.
The mother conceived through sacred means.
After seven days, she gave birth.
During her childhood, she went out for a stroll while holding a mirror.
Encountering Nandika, he attained deliverance.
Continuing his ministry, he arrived at the kingdom of the Great Yuezhi and came to the house of a Brahmin.
The master of the house was Kumāralāta, thirty years of age, who had studied as a Brahmacharin.
Just then, he saw Nanyue Huizhu, who asked,
"Whose disciples are these?
Nanyue replied:
These are disciples of the Buddha.
Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, their hearts were struck with awe,
and they immediately closed their doors.
The Patriarch stood knocking on the door for a long time.
Lalita replied, "There is no one in this house.
The Patriarch said, "If you say there is no one, who is it that answers?"
Upon hearing these words, Rāta realized he was an extraordinary person;
he opened the door and welcomed him.
The Master pointed to the spot beneath the eaves where his dog used to sleep and said to Rāta:
"Your father buried gold here, which a dog now guards.
He then dug the earth and indeed found the gold;
thereupon, he attained the knowledge of his past lives (*pūrvajātismara*).
He surrendered himself to become a monk.
After the Patriarch had ordained him and conferred the full precepts upon him,
he entrusted the Dharma-eye to him.
The verse says:
When there are seeds and the ground of mind,
causes and conditions give rise to sprouts.
Regarding conditions, they do not obstruct one another;
thus, that which is about to arise does not arise.
Having thus transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch passed it on.
He leaped into the void and manifested eighteen transformations, then consumed himself by fire.
The multitude enshrined his relics and erected a stupa to make offerings to them;
this was during the reign of Emperor Cheng of the Former Han dynasty, according to the *Zhengzong ji*.
Emperor Ai (Ai Di) was named Xin.
He was the grandson of Emperor Yuan and the younger brother of Emperor Cheng.
He was the son of King Gong of Dingtao.
He reigned for six years and died at the age of twenty-five.
The Emperor repeatedly executed high ministers,
desiring to strengthen his sovereign authority;
Wang Mang declined the appointment on the pretext of illness and was excused from office.
The Emperor passed away without an heir.
The Empress Dowager summoned Wang Mang to serve as Grand Marshal and welcomed Prince Kan of Zhongshan to establish him on the throne.
This was in the fourth year of Jianping and the second year of Yuanshou.
Emperor Ping (Pingdi). His personal name was Kuan.
He was the grandson of Emperor Yuan and the son of Prince Ji of Zhongshan.
He reigned for five years;
he ascended the throne at the age of nine,
during which time the Empress Dowager governed from the throne.
The Grand Marshal Wang Mang held the administration of the government.
In the first year of Yuanshi, he was granted the title Duke Anhan.
In the summer of the fourth year, the title of Duke Anhan was augmented to that of Zhaiheng.
In the fifth year, the summer, the fifth month, the Marquis of Anhan, Wang Mang, was invested with the mandate;
by means of the nine emoluments, he assumed the duties of the Son of Heaven.
In the tenth year, the winter, the second month.
On the first day of the month of Mangyin, [Mang] offered *jiao* wine;
he had placed poison within the wine,
and the Emperor fell ill.
Mang Zha composed a memorial to request life for Tai,
vowing to sacrifice himself in exchange; he placed the petition in a golden casket and set it before the hall,
commanding all the dukes that none should dare speak against it.
On the Bingwu day, the Emperor passed away. His age was fourteen. This was the fifth year of Yuanshi.

He was granted the Nine Enfeoffments: first, chariots and horses; second, robes and garments; third, musical instruments; fourth, vermilion doors; fifth, steps with handrails; sixth, the *huben* (tiger-guarded) attendants; seventh, battle-axes and halberds; eighth, bows and arrows; ninth, the fragrant millet libation (*juchang*). The infant ruler Ying was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Xuan.
When he was two years old, he was installed [as heir apparent].
An official submitted a memorial,
stating that Meng Tong, a clerk of Wugong, had obtained a white stone while dredging a well.
It was circular at the top and square at the bottom;
there was a vermilion inscription carved upon it that read:
"Announcement to the Duke of Anhan, Mang: You shall become Emperor."
The emergence of the "mandates of authority" (fuming) began from this point.
The Empress Dowager was enraged, but she lacked the power to thwart Wang Mang.
Following the precedent of the Duke of Zhou, Wang Mang styled himself the "Regent Emperor" (she huangdi).
The officials and the people all addressed him as "Your Servant.
All ceremonial rites were conducted exactly as for the Son of Heaven.
In the fifth month of the first year, an edict was issued declaring that Wang Mang would assume the title of "Provisional Emperor" (Jia Huangdi).
In the third year of his regency,
he established the first year of the Initial Era and ascended to the true throne of the Son of Heaven.
It was settled that the empire shall have the title "Xin" (New).
The twelfth month of winter shall be designated as the first month of Mingyī;
this is the calendar of Shang.
At that time, the child-king had not yet ascended the imperial throne,
and the seal was stored in the Changle Palace.
When Wang Mang ascended the throne, he requested the seal.
The Empress Dowager refused to hand over [the seal] to Wang Mang.
Wang Mang dispatched An-yang Hou Shun to convey his instructions and intimidate the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager took the Han imperial seal from her person and threw it to the ground.
Cai appointed the infant Ying as Duke Ding’an. In the first year of the Initial Beginning (Wucheng), Wang Mang usurped the throne.
Thus, the Western Han comprised fourteen rulers for a total of two hundred and fourteen years.
The Xinshi: Wang Mang of the Xinshi period.
His courtesy name was Jujing.
He was a native of Yuancheng.
He was the son of Wang Man, the younger brother of Empress Dowager Xiaoyuan.
Once he had transferred the mandate of the Han,
he conferred upon the Lady of the Wang clan, the Grand Empress Dowager, the title "Cultured Mother of the New Realm."
Having discarded the Han title, Wang Mang relied upon his deceit and wickedness, exhausting the people and indulging in military exercises until his crimes were full and his resentment accumulated.
The world grew incensed against him and rose in arms to execute him.
The Han forces then enthroned Liu Xian as Emperor.
The heroes of the Three Commanderies (Sānfǔ) together killed Wang Mang.
Mang had usurped the throne for fourteen years.
The Three Commanderies consisted of Jìngzhào, Zuǒféngyì, and Tóngzhōu; Yòufúfēng was Fèngxiáng Fǔ. He established five celestial eras: Tiānfēng, Dìhuáng, and Sān.
Gengshi Gengshi was surnamed Liu;
his courtesy name was Xuanchong,
and his style name was Shengong.
The grandson of Dai Hou of Chongling ascended the throne and appointed Liu Xiu,
Guangwu, as the Commandant of the Imperial Attendants.
He was subsequently established as King Xiao.
When the Red Eyebrows entered the Passes and installed Liu Benzi, Gengshi fell.
Gengshi reigned for two years.
In the first year of Jianwu of Emperor Guangwu of the Later Han,
an imperial edict was issued enfeoffing Xuan as the Prince of Huaiyang.
Liu Pensi was a descendant of Liu Zhang, the Marquis of Chengyang during the Western Han.
Toward the end of Wang Mang’s reign,
Fan Chong raised an army at Ju.
Chonglu’s followers became entangled with the army of Wang Mang;
they all painted their eyebrows red to identify one another and thus defeated Wang Mang’s forces.
In the second year of Gengshi, Pensi was enthroned as the Son of Heaven.
In the third year of Jianwu of the Later Han, he surrendered to Emperor Guangwu, who appointed him as the Langzhong (Court Attendant) of Zhao Wang.
He subsequently lost his sight due to illness. Thus, the New Chamber (Xinshi) and Gengshi combined lasted for a total of sixteen years.

Furthermore, it was the Eastern Han. Guiwei, the first year of Gengshi. ○ Wang Mang having been extinguished, Liu Yong, the Prince of Liang, seized Suyang and proclaimed himself Emperor; Year One. Li Xian, the Prince of Huainan, seized nine cities and proclaimed himself Emperor; Year One. Jiashen, the second year of Gengshi; the second year of Liu Yong; the second year of Li Xian; Cheng Gongsun Mi seized Chengdu and proclaimed himself Emperor; Year One of Longxing. Ningshuo Wang Wei Xiao seized Qinzhou. Yiyou, the first year of Guangwu of the Eastern Han; the third year of Liu Yong; the third year of Li Xian; Cheng [Longxing] Year Two; Wei Xiao; Liu Yong; Liu Yong, the Prince of Liang, Liu Yong.
Claiming the imperial title in Suiyang,
Liu Xun established his first year in the fourth year of the Jianwu era of Emperor Guangwu of the Eastern Han, which was the Wuzi year.
The following year, the Jichou year, the Han dynasty extinguished him.
Li Xian— Li Xian, Prince of Huainan—
held nine cities and proclaimed himself emperor.
This continued until the gengyin year, the sixth year of Guangwu’s Jianwu era.
The Han dynasty extinguished it.
Gongsun Shu occupied Chengdu and proclaimed himself Emperor.
He began in the year Jiashen and ended in the year Bingshen.
In the twelfth year of Jianwu, the Han dynasty extinguished them.
Wei Xiao, the Ningshuo Wang (Prince of Pacifying the North), and Gongsun Shu established themselves and occupied Qinzhou.
This period began in the first year of Jiashen and ended in the first year of Jiamu.
The tenth year of the Jianwu era of the Han dynasty was the first year of Wei Chun.
Emperor Guangwu extinguished him.
Lu Fang occupied Anding (present-day Jingzhou in Dianyuan Prefecture) and, styling himself Emperor of Han, proclaimed his reign.
The first year was designated as the first year of the [reign] beginning in the year Yiyou (109 CE).
In the sixteenth year of Jianwu of the Eastern Han, he surrendered to Emperor Guangwu.
Peng Chong was the Governor of Yuyang.
According to the records of Tan and Ji states, he was titled King of Yan.
He began his reign in the tenth year of Jianwu (Ji-hai) and ended it in the fifth year of Jianwu (Ji-chou).
Emperor Guangwu extinguished his state.
Zhang Bu was the King of Qi.
In the third year of the Jianwu era of the Eastern Han (the Dinghai year),
Liu Yong installed him as king.
In the fifth year of Jianwu, the year Jichou (529 CE),
Emperor Guangwu extinguished it.
The nineteenth patriarch, the Great Being Kumārajīva, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi.
Having attained the Dharma-eye,
he traveled to the kingdom of Central India,
where there was a great being named Jayata.
Question:
My parents have long been faithful believers in the Triple Gem,
yet they are constantly afflicted by chronic illness.
Whatever I undertake never turns out as I wish;
yet my neighbor, who has long followed the occupation of a *caṇḍāla*,
remains constantly vigorous and healthy, and his undertakings always succeed.
"How fortunate they are, and what fault is mine?
Zu said, "What is there to doubt?"
Furthermore, there are three temporal dimensions to the retribution of good and evil.
Ordinary people, seeing only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious meet with fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune,
then claim that cause and effect do not exist and that merit and blame are empty.
Little do they realize that influences are interconnected;
there is not even the slightest discrepancy,
and even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, it shall never perish.
When the Buddha says that karma extends through the three periods of time,
it is because the retribution for wholesome karma performed in previous lives manifests in this present life;
yet if one acts unwholesomely in this life, [the consequences will follow].
It must therefore be experienced in a future life. Thus,
when a person undergoes this present existence and performs good deeds yet fails to obtain their reward,

In the sixth month of Wei, [the era] was changed. Jingyuan Year 1; Shu—Jingyao Year 3; Wu—Yong’an Year 3. Xinsi: Jingyuan Year 2; Jingyao Year 4; Yong’an Year 4. Renwu: Jingyuan Year 3; Jingyao Year 5; Yong’an Year 5. At this time, Xi Kang of Qiao Commandery [died].
His prose was magnificent and grand;
he delighted in speaking of Zhuangzi and Laozi,

Together with Chen Liu’s fellow courtier Ji, Ji’s nephew Xian, Shan Tao of Henei, Xiang Xiu of Henan, Wang Rong of Langya, and Liu Ling of Pei.

In the *guīwèi* year, the Wei dynasty divided Yizhou into Liangzhou. Six Western Region śramaṇas arrived in Wei to translate Buddhist scriptures.

They produced twelve divisions of the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras.
In the third month of the first year of the Xianxi era of the Wei dynasty,
the title of Prince Wen was conferred upon the Duke of Jin,
Zhao. In the fifth month, Sima Yi, the Marquis of Wuyang Wenxuan, was posthumously honored with the title of Prince Xuan of Jin.

In the eighth month, King Wen Sima Zhao died.

*Yi-yu* (Year of the Rooster). Jin Dynasty. The first year of Tai-shi. Ten emperors revered Buddhist affairs and extensively constructed monasteries. He went so far as to destroy shrines to the spirits and extend his ravages even to Buddhist monasteries.

the crimson crow soars and the star of the old man (Kṛttikā) appears by name."
When benevolence and virtue nourish the myriad things,
sweet springs flow clear and auspicious grain flourishes; thus,
goodness inevitably brings its own response.

when one commits evil in public, humans obtain and punish them.
The *I Ching* proclaims that accumulated goodness brings forth blessings;

Though these are the orthodox maxims of the Confucian classics, they are likewise true.
"This is precisely the clear instruction of Buddhism.

All of these are matters of goodness.

*Chongshi sita fayuan zhulin* (A Forest of Pearls from the Dharma Garden on the Veneration and Adornment of Temples and Stupas).

Recorded on the Bingxu day. Compiled by the Dunhuang Bodhisattva, the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanmoluocha of the Yuezhi Kingdom, during the second year of Taishi (the first year of the Baoding era of the Wu dynasty).
Dharmarakṣa, whose name means "Dharma Protection" in the language of Jin,
arrived in Luoyang.
Dharmarakṣa studied and mastered the arts and techniques of thirty-six countries, becoming thoroughly proficient in their respective matters.
He traveled from India himself, bringing a great many Sanskrit manuscripts of the Brahmanical scriptures to the Jade Gate.
He subsequently resided in Dunhuang, where he was popularly known as the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva. There, he first translated the Lotus Sūtra.
It is said that this is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Later, he traveled to Luoyang and then to the region east of the Yangtze River.
During the Yongjia era of Emperor Huai of the Jin dynasty, he translated scriptures wherever he stayed.
He never paused for a moment.
At that time, the lay devotee Nie Chengyuan held the pen to assist in the translation,
resulting in approximately four hundred fascicles.
Upon the death of Daochengyuan,
his son Daozhen received his instructions and consulted him regarding the oral transmission and the transcription of the texts.
Daozhen himself also translated over sixty fascicles of scriptures.
At that time, the Śramaṇas of Jin, Shi Faju, Falì, Zhi Mindu, along with the upāsaka Wei Shidu and others, translated various scriptures.
Faju, Falì, and the others frequently consulted and compared their respective versions.
Regarding the differences between the extensive and abbreviated versions,
they have been compiled and categorized into a total of more than one hundred and forty fascicles.
Furthermore, there were the śramaṇas Kāṅ-liáng-lóu-zhì, Ān-fǎ-qīn, Zhú Shū-lán, Bái Fǎ-zǔ, Zhī Fǎ-dù, and others, each of whom translated various sūtras.
Thus, from the Western Jin dynasty onwards, the translation and propagation of the teachings flourished;
that these scriptural systems spread so widely throughout this land was due to the extraordinary merit of Dharmarakṣa.
Dharmarakṣa translated a total of one hundred and seventy-five scriptures.
His work ceased with his final brushstroke in the first year of the Jianxing era of Emperor Min of the Jin dynasty.
Dharmarakṣa once resided in Dunhuang, now the Sha-zhou Prefecture of Gansu Province.
The ancient land of Liusha was part of the domain of Yongzhou as recorded in the *Yugong*. A monastery was established there, where practitioners cultivated the Path with diligent application.
When the Qin constructed the Great Wall, it did not extend westward beyond Lintao; thus, this place did not yet exist. During the Han dynasty, it became Dunhuang Commandery.
The Yangguan and Yumen Passes are located where the Guashui (Sinking Water) flows.

The relics of the World-Honored One appeared this year in Mingzhou—present-day Qingyuan Prefecture in the Zhejiang East Circuit—at what is now Ayuwangshan Guangli Chan Temple. They were first seen during the reign of King Gonghe of the Zhou dynasty.
The fourth year, Gui-mao; the fifth year, Jia-chen; the sixth year, Yi-si; the seventh year, Bing-wu; the eighth year, Ding-wei; the ninth year, Wu-shen. Regarding Zhu Shiheng:
initially, during the second year of the Ganlu era of Emperor Gaoguixiang of the Wei dynasty, he lectured on the *Daoxing jing*.
Having doubts and difficulties, he went directly to the Western Regions to seek the Sanskrit manuscripts for verification.

he obtained the Sanskrit texts in the kingdom of Khotan.
As they were about to set out on their return journey,
the followers of the Hinayana in Khotan said to their king:

The King said, "If you do not forbid this, the land of Han will become blind and deaf.

the king piled up firewood and set them ablaze,

leaving the royal assembly in awe and submission.

his courtesy name was Zhengdu,

on the eleventh month, the Emperor consumed poisoned cakes and passed away.

He regularly provided sustenance for a thousand monks during the first year of Yongxi, the ninth year of Yongkang, the first year of Yongning, the second year of Dajian, the second year of Yongxing, and the first year of Xianxi.

Empress Jia was treacherous,
fierce, and full of guile.

several thousand people were killed.

The regent, Xi Jiguan, detested Wei Jun Jiangjun, Prince Chu Wang Wei, the Emperor’s younger brother, who was headstrong, obstinate, and fond of killing.
Jiguan dismissed his army and sent him to his fief; Wei was filled with resentment.
In the sixth month, the Emperor issued a hand-written edict granting Wei amnesty for Liang and Juan and stripping them of their official ranks.
Wei then mobilized his own troops, forged the imperial decree, seized Liang and Juan, and put them to death.
Zhang Hua, the Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince, dispatched Dong Meng to persuade Empress Jia that Jia Hui should be executed on the grounds of his crime of usurping the power to kill.

Hua Bai dispatched the Palace Guard General Wang Gong to carry a *zouyu* (unicorn) banner and signal the multitude, saying:
"The King of Chu has issued a forged edict; do not obey it!

in the sixth year of Yuankang, the year of Bingchen,
the Śramaṇa from Western India, Ji Yu, arrived.

having reached Xiangyang,

Fayu, knowing that the world was about to fall into chaos,
took his leave and returned to India.

Foeryu summoned the assembly; when the multitude had gathered, he spoke.

be careful not to commit any evils."

Each was delighted by his arrival.
When he departed from Luonan and traveled slowly on foot,
those who pursued him could not catch up.
Huiri drew a line on the ground with his staff and said,

joined Faxian for lodging in Liusha; this is recorded in Faxian’s original biography.
In the year Jǐwèi, the ninth year of Yuánkāng (299 CE),
Empress Jia plotted to depose Crown Prince Yù and appointed her brother-in-law,
Emperor’s younger brother Chengdū Wáng Yǐng, to govern Yè.
With Yuan Hejianwang Ying— the grandson of Emperor Xuan’s younger brother— governing Guanzhong,
on the gengshen day of the first month of the first year of Yongkang (290 CE),
Empress Jia murdered Crown Prince Yu at Xuchang.
In the fourth month, Zhao Wang Lun— the ninth son of Emperor Xuan— acting on the scheme of Sun Xiu, attacked Empress Jia;
she was deposed as a commoner,
and Jia Mi was executed.
Lun Yin conspired with Sun Xiu to usurp the throne.
First eliminating those who were highly regarded by the court, he also sought to avenge old grudges;
he arrested Zhang Hua, Pei Wei, Jie Xi, and others, and executed them.
Lun forged an imperial decree to execute Empress Jia and posthumously conferred the title "Minghuai" (Pitiable and Held) upon the former Crown Prince Yü.
In the eighth month of autumn,
Sun Xiu took revenge for old grievances by murdering Shi Chong.
An imperial decree was issued bestowing the Nine Emoluments upon the Chancellor Lün.
On the day of Xin-you, in the first month of the first year of Yongning,
the Chancellor Lün dispatched the Attendant-in-Ordinary Prince of Yiyang to intimidate and seize the Emperor’s seals and ribbons.
He caused his brother Lun to abdicate the throne.
Lun prepared the imperial carriage and entered the palace,
where he immediately ascended the imperial throne.

The Emperor went to reside at Jīnyōng City.
[There was] the Prince of Qí, Huìdì’s younger brother, Jiǒng.
In the fourth month, Chengdu Wang Ying,
Hejian Wang Yong, Changshan Wang You,
and others raised troops to campaign against Lun.

He welcomed the Emperor from Jinyong City and restored him to the throne.
He granted death to Sun Lun and arrested his sons, Sun Fu and Sun Fang, putting them to death as well.
In the sixth month, an edict appointed Prince Qi, Jiong, as Grand Marshal and conferred upon him the nine emoluments (the details of the nine emoluments are found in the section on Wang Mang).
The Prince of Changshan was transferred to the fief of Changsha.
Renxu: the first year of Dà'ān.
Once Qi’s Prince Wumin, Xiao Jing, had attained his ambitions, he became increasingly arrogant, extravagant, and autocratic.

Yong then raised troops and,
leading Zhang Fang and others, marched toward [the capital].
In Luoyang,
an envoy was dispatched to invite Yao Ying.

He then led more than a hundred attendants into the palace, closed all the gates,
and escorted the Son of Heaven to attack the Grand Marshal’s residence.

Liu Jiong’s forces were utterly defeated.

Jiong was brought before the palace hall.

however, Yao Yi shouted at him to be led out and executed outside the Changhe Gate.

Although Prince Xiaoyi of Changsha remained at the court,

Tong appointed Sun Hui as Counselor and Lu Yun as Right Commandant. In this same year, the Prince of Chenliu passed away;

Yóng appointed Zhāng Fāng as Grand Commander and led his troops from Hánggu Pass eastward toward Luoyang.
He appointed Lu Ji, the Interior Historian of Pingyuan, as General of the Front,
commanding the forces of Shi Chao and others to head south toward Luoyang and station at the Heqiao Bridge.

Shi Chao fled, but Wang Ying captured him and killed him along with his younger brother Yun.
Meanwhile, the troops of Zhang Fang pressed upon the capital.

Hu was succeeded by Tuoba [Shi] for ten years; [the reign of] Prince Lì of Changsha, Xi.
He fought repeatedly with the Great General Wang Ying.
In the first month, Donghai Prince Yue— the grandson of Emperor Xuan’s younger brother— fearing that the matter would not succeed,
secretly conspired with several generals of the inner palace at night to arrest Xi and send him to the separate palace (Biesheng), where they presented a petition to the Emperor.
An imperial edict was issued to exempt Xi from office and place him under guard at Jinyong City.
Yue wished to kill Xi to sever the loyalties of the masses,
so he secretly sent a messenger to inform Zhang Fang.
Dongfang Xue then went to the camp and killed him.
Grand General Yu Ying entered the capital and subsequently returned to his command post at Ye.
The Emperor appointed Ying as Chancellor (Chengxiang) and promoted Donghai Prince Yue to the position of Acting Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shangshu Ling).
Ying submitted a memorial appointing Lu Zhi as Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhongshu Jian) to participate in the administrative affairs of the Chancellor’s office.
In the second month, after Hejian Wang Yong returned to his command post at Chang’an,
Chancellor Sima Ying submitted a memorial deposing Empress Yang and confining her in Jinyong City,
and deposing the Crown Prince Tan as Prince of Qinghe.
The Emperor issued an edict appointing Ying as the Crown Prince of the Second Rank.
The imperial carriage, robes, and regalia were all transferred to Ye.
Ying’s arrogance and extravagance increased day by day.
Favored favorites were employed in office,
which greatly disappointed public expectations.
The Minister of Works, Prince Yue of Donghai, conspired with Xi’s former general, Right卫 (Wei) General Chen Zhen, and others to suppress him.
King Yong of Hejian dispatched Zhang Fang to garrison Luoyang, while Liu Ying resisted him;
consequently, a rift opened between Yong and Ying.
On the wuxu day of the seventh month, Empress Yang and Crown Prince Tan were restored to their former positions.
In the year Jihai, Yue and others received the Emperor’s command to campaign against Ying.
Ying dispatched Shi Chao to lead fifty thousand troops to resist the battle;
the imperial carriage suffered defeat at Dangyin.
The hundred officials and attendants all dispersed;
the Palace Attendant Xi Shao, wearing his court robes, dismounted from his horse and ascended the palanquin,
shielding the Emperor with his own body.
Ying’s soldiers struck Shao,
and blood splattered onto the Emperor’s robes;
the Emperor fell into the grass and lost six seals.
The Emperor followed [the army] to Ye and proceeded to Ying; Sima Yue, the Minister of Works, fled to Xiapi.
In the eighth month, he again deposed Crown Prince Jia and Lady Yang.
Sima Teng, Duke of Dongying and younger brother of Sima Yue, and Wang Jun combined their forces to attack Wang Bin, a general of Liu Ying, and utterly defeated him.
Yecheng was struck with great terror;
the hundred officials fled in haste,
and the soldiers dispersed.
Lü Zhi urged Liu Ying to escort the Emperor back to Luoyang. However,
as Liu Yong led Zhang Fang’s troops to monopolize the administration of the court,
Liu Ying was no longer permitted to participate in state affairs.
Having resided in Luoyang for a long time,
Zhang Fang’s soldiers engaged in plundering, causing public unrest.
In the eleventh month, Zhang Fang coerced the Emperor to relocate the capital to Chang’an.
The soldiers fought over the imperial treasury,
and since the Wei and Jin dynasties, accumulated stores had been swept away without a trace remaining.
When the Emperor entered Chang’an, he restored Empress Yang to her position.
The Emperor issued a decree that the Second Prince, Ying, should return his residence to Chengdu,
and further established the Prince of Yuzhang, Chi, as the Crown Prince.
The Emperor had twenty-five brothers.
At that time, only Sengying and Sengchi remained, along with Prince Yan of Wu.
Prince Yan was of mediocre character and lowly disposition,
whereas Sengchi was humble, pure, and fond of learning.
Therefore, Grand Chancellor Ying established this in the Imperial Annals.

Yichou (2nd year of Yongxing of the Jin; 2nd year of Yuanshi of the Han; 2nd year of Jianxing of the Cheng; Former Liang Zhang Gui; Murong Huai of the Dai; Liu Qia, General of the Household of Donghai).
Because Zhang Fang had forcibly abducted the imperial carriage,
[Wang] Yue, the Minister of Works (Sikong), was urged to raise an army to punish him.
In the seventh month, Yue issued a manifesto to the provinces east of the mountains, proclaiming his campaign.
Desiring to rally a righteous army to welcome the Son of Heaven back to the ancient capital,
Fan Yang Wang Xie (pronounced with the *qie* rhyme of *xǔ*) and Wang Jun and others together elected Yu as their盟主 (*méngzhǔ*, confederate leader).
Xun dispatched his general Qi Hong,
leading cavalry and Xianbei and Wuhuan tribesmen as the vanguard.
Grand Chancellor Yong was greatly terrified.
The head of Zhang Fang was severed and sent to Yue.

Bingyin (the 1st day of the 5th month). Jin: Guangxi Year 1; Han: Yuanxi Year 3. Da Chengxiong ascended the throne as Emperor. Yanping Year 1. Former Liang: Zhang Gui; Former Yan: Murong Huai; Dai Xia: [vacant]. The fifth month.
Qi Hong and his followers entered the Pass from the west.
Grand Chancellor Yong escaped alone on horseback into the Taibai Mountains.
Hong and his party entered Chang’an and escorted the Emperor back east to Luoyang.
Si Kong Yue was appointed as Grand Preceptor (Taifu) and Director of the Secretariat (Lu Shangshu Shi).
Prince of Fanyang, Xiao Xiu, was stationed at Ye,

Wang Jun was the Governor of Youzhou.
Ying was killed by Liu Yu;
Yong was killed by Nan-yang Wang Mo. In the eleventh month, the Emperor passed away.
Emperor Huai’s personal name was Chi;
his courtesy name was Fengdu.
He was the twenty-fifth son of Emperor Wu.
In the first year of Yongxing, he was established as the Imperial Second Brother (Huang Taidi).
In the eleventh month of the first year of Guangxi, Emperor Hui passed away.
The Imperial Second Brother then ascended the imperial throne.
In the fifth year of Yongjia, he was captured by the Han forces.
The Emperor and the six imperial seals were taken to Pingyang—the territory of Jizhou in the present-day Jinning Prefecture.
The Han ruler Chong enfeoffed the Emperor with the title of Tejin Zuoguanglu Dafu Ping'a Gong.
In the year of Ren-shen, he was further enfeoffed as Duke of Kuaiji Commandery.
In the second month of the year of Gui-you, the Emperor was assassinated.
He was thirty years of age. This was the sixth year of Yongjia.

Emperor Huai was murdered.
In the fourth month, the news of this calamity reached Chang’an.

In the ninth month of the fourth year,
Liu Yao, the Grand Marshal of Han, pressed upon Chang’an.
In the eleventh month, the Emperor said to his ministers:
"The calamity is now such as this;
we ought to endure shame and surrender to save our soldiers and the people."
The ministers wailed and wept as they clung to the carriage and grasped the Emperor’s hand.
Liu Yao dispatched Zong Chang to escort the Emperor back to the palace.
On the day Dingyou, he transferred the Emperor, along with the high officials and those below them, to his own camp.

Emperor Cong of the Han appointed him as Palace Grandee of the Department of Sacrificial Worship and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Huai’an.
On the day of Dingchou, in the twelfth month of that year, he was put to death.
Age eighteen. Emperor [Wu] of the Jin dynasty commissioned the Tongling and Baima temples in Chang’an.
The Hongming ji (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism) was compiled in the fourth year of Jianxing.

Guiyou. Jin Jianxing Year 1; Han Jiaping Year 3; Dacheng Yuhean Year 3. Former Liang, Zhang clan; Murong Hu, Duke of Dai. In the third month, two stone Buddha images floated across the sea and entered the Wusong River at Huguduo.
The officials and the common people alike gazed upon him as he drifted across the water;
shamans, priests, and commoners vied with one another to go out and welcome him,
even as the wind and waves surged and roiled.

When he went to welcome the image and lift it onto his boat,
it was as light as a feather.
The names inscribed on the backs of the Buddhas are:
the first is Vipaśyin;

Enshrined at Tongxuan Temple—which is today’s Kaiyuan Temple on Pingjiang Road—is the temple record inscription composed by Emperor Jianwen of the Liang dynasty, including its preface, eulogy, and main text.

Jiaxu (313): The second year of Jianxing of the Jin; the fourth year of Jiaping; the fourth year of Yuheng. Former Liang, Duke Dai. The above covers the combined fifty-two years of the four emperors of the Western Jin dynasty, during which the capital was moved to Jiankang—originally called Jianye, later renamed Jiankang to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Min.

Emperor Yuan, Emperor Ming, Emperor Cheng, Emperor Kang, Emperor Mu, Emperor Ai, Emperor Haixi, Emperor Jianwen, Emperor Wu, Emperor An, and Emperor Gong. [The first] Zhongzong, Emperor Yuan, whose personal name was Rui. [Note: The text repeats "Zhongzong Emperor Yuan" twice.]
He was the son of Wang Jin of Langya and the great-grandson of Emperor Xuan.
At the age of fifteen, he succeeded to the title of Prince of Langya.
In the first year of Emperor Huai’s Yongjia era, he served as General Who Pacifies the East (Andong Jiangjun) and was stationed at Jianye.
In the fourth year of Emperor Min’s Jianxing era, Chang’an fell,
and the Emperor went into exile.
The King then dispatched his armies on a northern campaign.
In the second month of the year Dingchou, he ascended the throne as Prince of Jin in Jiankang.
He then formally established the various offices of state, instituted the ancestral temple, and erected the altars of the land and grain.
A general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the era name was changed to Jianwu.
In the twelfth month, Emperor Min was assassinated.
In the third month of the Wuyin year, the news of the Emperor’s passing arrived in Jiankang.
The Prince donned the hempen sackcloth and dwelt in the mourning shed;
shortly thereafter, he ascended the throne as Emperor.
A general amnesty was proclaimed.
The era name was changed to Dàxīng.
The Crown Prince Shào was established as the Heir Apparent.
At that time, following the period of war and disorder,
Jiangdong was in its infancy.
Diao Xie had long served in the central court and was thoroughly versed in established precedents.
He Xun was a preeminent master of Confucianism in his time and was profoundly learned in the rites and music.
Whenever there were matters of doubt or dispute, all sought his decision.
The Emperor occupied the throne for six years.
At the age of forty-seven,

the Emperor established the Waguan and Longxing monasteries in Jiankang and convened a thousand monks from Danyang and Jianye to compile the Hongming ji (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism) during the first year of Wuchengjian, the fourth year of Taixing, and the first year of Yongchang.

Dingchou: The first year of Jianwu of the Jin; the second year of Linjia of the Liu House of Han; the seventh year of Dayi Cheng of the Li House; the seventh year of Yuhen of Former Liang under Zhang Shí; the first year of Wenyu Lü of the Murong Dai. Wuyin: The first year of Daxing; Cóng died, and Liu Yào was established as ruler; the first year of Guanchū; the eighth year of Yuhen; the second year of Kang, Liang, and Dai. The Han ruler was Liu Cóng.
He passed away in this year, the Wuyin (57th) year.
Crown Prince Can ascended the throne but was subsequently killed by Jin Zhun.
The Chancellor Liu Yao ascended the throne as Emperor.
He changed the era name to Guangchu and returned to the capital at Chang’an.
The national name was changed to Zhao.
Shi Le was promoted to the rank of King of Zhao. From the *Lü Shichun’s Records of Liu Cong* (Liu Cong Carji), dated Jīmōu.

the first year of Yongchang of the Jin dynasty; the seventh year [of the reign]; the Emperor passed away; the fifth year of Guangchu; the twelfth year of Yuheng; the fourth year; the second year of the Former Liang, Former Yan, and Dai dynasties;
the *Peacock Sūtra*.

The Indian Venerable Śrīmitra, translated here as Jiyou (吉祥友), abdicated his royal throne to enter the monastic order—much like Taibo of the Wu state—and arrived in China during the Yongjia era of Emperor Huai of the Western Jin dynasty.
Upon arriving at Jiankang, he stayed at Jianchu Monastery.
When the Chancellor Wang Dao saw him, he said,
"A person such as I..."
The Grand Marshal Yu Liang, the Court Director Zhou Ji, and the Minister of Justice Huan Yi—
all eminent statesmen of the time— visited his door to form friendships with him.
His reputation became renowned among the ranks of officials.
He was skilled in expounding the essential teachings of the Dharma;
people of the time called him the High Seat Dharma Master.
Furthermore, he was adept at reciting incantations and performing Buddhist chants (*brahmaghoṣa*).
His pure resonance soared above the clouds.
He translated various sūtras such as the *Mayūra* (Peacock) Sūtra, along with their original biographies.
Emperor Suzong and Emperor Mingdi succeeded [the throne].
He was the eldest son of Emperor Yuan.
From his youth, he was intelligent and sagacious.
When he was several years old, an envoy from Chang'an arrived.
The Emperor then asked, "Which do you consider to be closer: the sun or Chang'an?
He replied:
Chang'an is near;
we only hear of people coming from Chang'an,
but we do not hear of anyone coming from the side of the sun.
Emperor Yuan was struck by this.
The next day, at a banquet for his officials,
he questioned him again.
He replied,
"The sun is near.
Emperor Yuan turned pale and said:
"How is it that this differs from what others have said?
He replied,
"Lift your eyes and you will immediately see the sun."
He did not see Chang'an;
for this reason, [the Emperor] considered him all the more extraordinary and established him as the Crown Prince.
By nature he was profoundly filial and possessed both civil and martial talents.
He revered the worthy and loved his guests,
and he was refinedly fond of literature and composition.
At that time, renowned ministers such as Wang Dao, Yu Liang, Wen Qiao, Huan Yi, and Ruan Fang all held him in high esteem and treated him with great favor.
He practiced martial arts and was skilled at rallying and consoling his generals and soldiers.
At that time, the court in the East was in full assembly, and those far and near turned their hearts toward it.
In the first month of spring in the first year of the Yongchang era,
Wang Dun submitted a memorial from Wuchang.
The charges were laid against Xiao Xie and Liu Wei.
Emperor Yuan urged Xie and Wei to avoid the impending disaster;
however, Xie was subsequently killed by others.
Songshou went to Dunhuang;
Kuai fled to Shi of Later Zhao.
His official rank reached that of Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince before he passed away.
Cao Dun advanced his troops to occupy Shitou.
Emperor Yuan appointed Cao Dun as Chancellor.
Cao Dun plotted to depose the Crown Prince but did not succeed.
He consequently failed to attend court before the Son of Heaven and returned to Wuchang.
In the eleventh month, Emperor Yuan died of illness brought on by grief and indignation.
The Crown Prince ascended the throne.
The reign title was changed to Taíning.
In the third month, Wang Dun plotted to usurp the throne and raised troops once more.
The Emperor dispatched his army to campaign against Dun.
In the fifth month of the second year, [Sima] Dun’s illness became severe.
Wang Han was defeated in battle,
and Dun subsequently passed away.
Dun’s faction kept the matter secret and did not announce the death.
They wrapped the corpse in mats and coated the exterior with wax.
He was buried within the administrative offices of Jiangning Commandery.
Once the Dun faction had been suppressed,
the local authorities exhumed his burial site.
The corpse was removed and its robes and cap were burned; he was executed while kneeling.
The Emperor reigned for three years.
He lived to the age of twenty-seven. The Emperor held the fasts in high esteem and promoted the cultivation of merit.

His divine realization was transcendent and his profound discernment surpassed that of others;
he studied under Dharmarakṣa.
Hu Shi greatly praised him.

That the Great Transformation flourished in the West was due to the power of his [the Buddha’s] vehicle.
*Biographies of Eminent Monks*. The twenty-fifth patriarch, Venerable Bodhidharma, was a native of the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
He was of the Brahmin caste;
his father was named Śāntacārin and his mother was named Nityasukhā.
Jinagupta followed the Venerable Siṃha to leave the household life;
having received full ordination and attained the Dharma,
he wished to travel to South India.
When he first arrived in the kingdom of Central India,
its king, named Kaśyapa,
welcomed him with ritual prostrations.
At that moment, a strange fragrance suddenly filled the royal palace.
The Venerable One, with solemn gravity, said,
"My teacher has passed away."
He then turned toward the north and performed a prostration.
He immediately took his leave of the king, who said:
"Venerable sir, please stay a short while so that we may ask a question.
There is a spring in this grove that is too hot to touch;
we pray that you will resolve this for us."
The Patriarch said,
"This is a hot spring,
caused by three conditions."
The first is the karma of spirits;
the second is the karma of ghosts;
the third is the hot stones.
The hot stones are golden in color because their nature is perpetually inflamed;
the springs that emerge from them are like surging waves.
Regarding the karma of ghosts: it refers to those ghosts who have recently emerged from their place of retribution and wander among human beings;
by the power of their residual karma, they scorch this spring to repay their long-standing debts.
Regarding "divine karma": it refers to spirits who do not maintain their proper Way, yet arbitrarily create calamities and blessings in order to receive offerings and sacrifices;
when their evil deeds have reached full measure, they are subjected to the punishments and labors of the unseen realm.
"Furthermore, let this spring be boiled dry to atone for the excessive sacrifices.
The King said,
"I would be fortunate if the Venerable One would verify these three conditions."
"What kind of action has brought about this fruit?
The Venerable One replied,
"It was brought about by the karma of this deity."
He immediately ordered incense to be burned at the water's edge and performed repentance rites for him.
In a short while, a tall man appeared by the water.
He prostrated before the Venerable One and said,
"By my slight merit, I have been able to encounter you, Venerable One;
since I have now been born among humans, I have come to take my leave."
Thereafter, he withdrew into seclusion.
Seven days later, the water of that spring became as cool and clear as an ordinary spring.
The Venerable One then took his leave of the king.
The king personally led his retinue to escort him.
Upon reaching South India,
its king was named Devaśakti (Tian De).
He went against the grain to pay him honor.
The King had two sons;
one was named De-sheng (Virtuous Victory).
The second was named Bhumimitra.
Later, his son Guṇasena succeeded him to the throne.
Believing in non-Buddhist paths, he caused difficulties for his grandfather.
He immediately asked the Patriarch,
"I have heard that the Bhikṣu Siṃha could not escape execution; how, then,
was he able to transmit the Dharma?"
The Patriarch said,
"When my teacher’s time of trial had not yet arisen, he bestowed upon me the robe of faith and the dharma verses to manifest the lineage of transmission.
The King asked:
"Where is that robe?
The Patriarch reached into his bag, took out the robe, and showed it to the King.
The King ordered it to be burned.
The five colors remained vivid and the firewood was as it had been before.
The King immediately paid his respects and said,
"Siddhārtha is truly a worthy successor."
The king’s younger brother, Amṛtodana, subsequently requested to leave the household life.
He served his grandfather for six years and received full ordination within the royal palace.
At the moment of the *karmavācanā*, the great earth shook violently.
The Patriarch addressed him, saying,
"I have already grown old and infirm."
How could you remain here for long?
You must well protect the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma to universally deliver all sentient beings.
Listen to my verse:
The Sage speaks of knowledge and vision;
whatever is before the sense-fields is none other than this.
Now I have awakened to true nature.
"There is neither principle nor reason [in this].
After hearing these verses from Miṇḍhaka,
he addressed his grandfather, saying:
"Should this Dharma robe be transmitted?
The Patriarch said,
"Because this robe is difficult to encounter, it is used as a provisional token of certification."
Your body is free from hardship;
why rely upon that robe?
Let your transformative influence reach the people of the ten directions so that they may believe and turn toward you with confidence.
The Patriarch then manifested a supernatural transformation;
he conjured the fire of samādhi to spontaneously consume his own body,
leaving śarīra relics on level ground approximately one chi in height.
King Deśeṇa (德勝王) founded a stūpa and kept it secret;

this was during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Jin dynasty. According to the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage), the Emperor who manifested the lineage was Chengdi (成帝); Chengdi’s personal name was Yan (衍).
He was the eldest son of Emperor Ming.
In the eighth month of the third year of the Taíning era,
he ascended the throne at the age of five.
Empress Dowager Yu was presiding over the court.
In the second year of the Xianhe era, Su Jun, the General of the Crown, defied his mandate and plotted rebellion.
In the fourth month of the third year, Su Jun seized the Emperor and took him to Shitou.
The palaces and residences of the capital were all reduced to ashes and charred remains;
only the murals depicting Buddhist images painted by Emperor Ming’s own hand on the walls of Taiping Hall remained standing, undamaged.
All people marveled at them, praising their divine and miraculous nature.
Tao Kan and Wen Qiao attacked Shitou.
Xu Jun fell from his horse during the battle;
they cut off his head, minced his flesh, and burned his bones.
After Xu Jun’s death, his followers installed his younger brother, Xu Yi, as king.
They closed the gates and held their position.
In the second month of the fourth year, various armies attacked Shitou.
Teng Han, the Assistant Director of the Jianwei Command, attacked Su Yi and crushed his forces.
The western army captured Yi and executed him.
Teng Han’s subordinate general, Cao Ju, took up the Emperor in his arms and fled to the ship of Wen Qiao.
The ministers, seeing the Emperor, wept aloud and begged for his forgiveness.
At that time, the palace buildings had been reduced to ashes;
they therefore used Jianping Garden as the new palace.
Wen Qiao wished to relocate the capital to Yuzhang,
while the elites of the Three Wu regions desired to move it to Kuaiji;
these two arguments were so conflicting that no decision could be reached.
The Minister of Education, Wang Dao, deliberated on the matter and decided not to relocate the capital.
On the first day of the first month of the first year of Xiankang (the gengwu day), the Emperor donned his ceremonial cap;
a general amnesty was proclaimed and the reign title was changed.
In the fifth month of the eighth year, the Emperor fell ill.
His two sons, Pi and Yi, were both still in swaddling clothes.
Yu Bing, the Director of the Central Secretariat, considered that he and his brothers had long held the reins of power.
Fearing that there might be an interval between generations,
he repeatedly urged the Emperor that the state had powerful enemies and that a long-reigning ruler was necessary;
he requested that the Emperor’s uterine younger brother, Prince Yue of Langya, be appointed as his successor.
The Emperor granted his request.
In the sixth month, the Emperor passed away at the age of twenty-two.
He reigned for seventeen years.

The Emperor established the two monasteries of Zhongxing and Luyuan, where he convened a thousand monks—scholars specializing in the translation of scriptures—in six sections. This occurred during the ninth year of Xianhe and the eighth year of Xiankang.

Bingxu (1st year of Xianhe, Jin; 9th year of Guangchu, Zhao; 16th year of Yuheng, Cheng; 8th year of the Shi clan of Later Zhao; 2nd year of Dai, Former Liang and Former Yan). At Feilai Peak: Dharma Master Hui-ri from the Kingdom of West India.
This year, while traveling through China,
he arrived at Hangzhou in western Zhejiang and,
seeing the exquisite beauty of the mountain crags, said:
This is a small ridge on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in our country of Central India.
It is unknown in what year it flew here.
During the Buddha's lifetime, it was frequently inhabited by immortals and spirits.
Is this case also like that?
There was an old cave where a white monkey had lived for a long time, so he called out to it.
The white monkey emerged at the sound of his voice.
People first saw something fly there,
from which it derived its name.
The Master then established two monasteries on that very site.
First at Vulture Peak and later at Lingyin,
the Master sat in meditation upon a cliff known as Master Li’s Cliff;
his burial stupa remains there today, as recorded in the temple chronicles and inscribed upon stone monuments.
