*Dinghai* (Year of the Earth Pig): The second year of the Xianhe era of the Jin; the tenth year of the Guangchu era of the Zhao under the Liu clan; the seventeenth year of the Yuheng era of the Cheng under the Li clan; the ninth year of Shi Le of the Later Zhao; the third year of the Dai era of Zhang of the Former Liang; and the third year of the Tai era of the Former Yan. *Wuzi* (Year of the Earth Rat): The third year of the Xianhe era of the Jin. Liu Yao was destroyed by Shi Le; this totals twenty-six years. The eighteenth year of the Yuheng era; Shi [Le] occupied the Central Plains. The first year of the Taihe era of the Former Liang; the fourth year of the Former Yan. The Han Zhao, the Han Zhao, and the Han under Liu Yuan.
His courtesy name was Yuanhai.
He was a Xinxing Xiongnu.
The Han dynasty gave him a princess of the imperial clan as a wife for Modun.
Therefore, his descendants have taken the surname Liu.
In the first year of the Yongxing era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin, the year Jiazi, Sima Ying, Prince of Chengdu, was established as the Crown Prince (Yuandi).
Yingbiao appointed Liu Yuan, the Left Righteous King of the Xiongnu, as General of Supreme Victory (*Guānjuàn Jūnjiāng*) and Supervisor of Military Affairs for the Five Divisions.

He led troops stationed at Ye (the present-day administrative seat of Zhangde Road, known as Ye Commandery, within the region of Ji). Yuan’s son, Cong, was exceptionally brave and valiant beyond compare.
He was extensively versed in the classics and histories,
skilled at composing literature,
and capable of drawing a bow weighing three hundred jin.
In his early twenties, he traveled to the capital,
where no renowned scholar failed to form a friendship with him.
Xing Ying appointed Cong as General of Accumulated Bows.
Yuan’s great-uncle, Liu Xuan, the Right Commandant of the Right Virtuous Prince,
said to his kinsmen:
"Since the fall of the Han dynasty..."
I, the Chanyu, possess only a hollow title and no longer have even a foot of territory.
Although my people have declined, they still number no fewer than twenty thousand.
How can I fold my hands and submit to servitude for another hundred years?
The Left Wise King’s heroic prowess transcends the world.
If Heaven did not intend for the Xiongnu to flourish,
it would certainly not have brought such a man into existence in vain.
Now that the Sima clan has engaged in fratricidal strife and the four seas are boiling like a cauldron,
this is the time to restore the legacy of Huhanxie.
They then conspired together to appoint Yuan as the Grand Shanyu.
They sent their partisan Huyan You to Ye to inform Yuan,
who petitioned Liu Ying to request leave to return for the funeral.
Ying did not consent.
When Wang Jun, Prince Dongyin, and Cheng Teng set out to suppress Ying,
Yuan advised Ying, saying:
"Please speak on behalf of His Highness to the five tribes to mobilize them against the national crisis.
Ying was delighted and bowed, appointing Yuan as the General-in-Chief for the Northern Xiongnu, with authority over military affairs.
Yuan arrived at the city of Zuoguo.
Liu Xuan and others conferred the title of Great Shanyu upon him.
Within twenty days, his host numbered fifty thousand;
he established his capital at the city of Zuoguo.
He said to his ministers,
"In the past, when the House of Han possessed the empire, its benevolence was deeply rooted among the people;
I am a nephew of the Han dynasty."
He then established the national designation as "Han" and ascended the throne as the King of Han,
naming the era Yuanxi.
Xuan, the Right Noble Prince (Youxian Wang), was appointed as Chancellor.
In the second year of the Yongjia era of Emperor Huai of Jin,
the Han Prince Yuan captured the region west of the mountains.
Pingyang is the present-day Jinning Prefecture; it was formerly the city of Jinzhou. The Governor, Song Chou, abandoned the commandery and fled to Yuan.
Yuan then moved his capital to Pingyang, at Puzi, and ascended the throne in Shangjun.
The era name was changed to Yongfeng.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, Shi Yao fell ill;
he appointed Chuwang Chong as Grand Marshal and Grand Shanyu.
Prince Cheng of Anchang, Prince Qin of Anyi, and Prince Jun of Xiyang all concurrently held the rank of Commander of the Imperial Guard.
They were divided to command the palace troops.
Yuan died.
The Crown Prince He immediately ascended the imperial throne.
Prince Rui of Xichang was ashamed that he had not been included in the final testamentary instructions;
he then conspired with others and persuaded He, saying:
The late Emperor failed to consider the balance of power;
he allowed the three princes to maintain strong forces within the capital,
while the Grand Marshal stationed a host of one hundred thousand at the New Suburb.
"Your Majesty ought to devise a plan for this early.
He summoned Fu Sheng and informed him of the matter.
Sheng said:
Your Majesty, believing the words of a slanderer, harbored suspicion toward your brother;
you sharpened your wrath and commanded your attendants to strike him down with blades.
You then led troops to attack Chu Wang Cóng at the Shanyu Terrace—this is the present-day route to the Western Capital, namely the Datong Road.
The commandery was named Yunzhong,
the very place where Emperor Gao of Han was besieged at Bai Deng.
Cong of Ji attacked and captured Ximing Gate.
He executed He at the Western Hall of Guangji and beheaded Shou Rui in the marketplace;
Cong then ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the reign title to Guangxing and appointed the Prince of Beihai, Xi, as the Imperial Second Brother.
He enfeoffed his son Can as the King of Henei.
Shi Le was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Bingzhou, which is present-day Taiyuan.
This was the first year of the Jiaping era of the Han dynasty, the Xinwei year [249 CE].
At that time, Liu Cong dispatched the Former Army General-in-Chief Huyan Yan, Prince Shian Wang Liu Yao, Wang Mi, and Shi Le.
They attacked Luoyang and captured the Xuanyang Gate.
Emperor Huai of Jin attempted to flee to Chang’an,
but the Han troops pursued and captured him.
He transferred the Emperor and the six imperial seals to Pingyang.
Lü Cun appointed the Emperor as the Special Advancement, Left Grand Master for Record-keeping,
and enfeoffed him as the Duke of Ping’a.
In the second year of the Jiaping era of Emperor Chong, the cyclical year being Renshen,
the future Emperor Huai was enfeoffed as the Duke of Kuaiji.
In the second month of the following year, Emperor Huai was assassinated.
In the fourth month, the tragic news of the Emperor’s demise reached Chang’an.
The Jin Emperor Min ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jianxing.
In the ninth month of the fourth year of Jianxing, Liu Yao, the Grand Marshal of Han, attacked Chang’an.
In the eleventh month, the Emperor of Jin said, "I must endure this shame and surrender so as to save the soldiers and the people."
Liu Yao escorted the Jin Emperor to Pingyang.
The Han ruler, Liu Cong, appointed the Jin Emperor as Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Huai’an.
In the twelfth month of the year Dingchou, Emperor Min was assassinated.
In the year Wuyin, the Han ruler Chong died;
his crown prince, Can, ascended the throne.
He was killed by Jin Feng.
Chancellor Liu Yao then ascended the throne as Emperor;
the era name was Guangchu.
He returned to the capital Chang'an and changed the state's title to Zhao,
taking the Chanyu as his ancestor.
Shi Le was promoted to the rank of Prince of Zhao.
By this time, in the third year of the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng of the Eastern Jin, Yao, the ruler of Zhao, had laid siege to Luoyang.
In the eleventh month, Shi Le led his army to the rescue of Luoyang.
In battle, he captured Emperor Yao of Zhao and transported him in a horse-drawn carriage to Xiangguo, where he was executed.
On the first day of the first month of the year Jichou, Zhao’s Crown Prince Xi heard that Yao had been taken captive.

He then led his hundred officials and fled toward Guān (modern-day Gāngchāng County, Gansu Province), an ancient garrison site located west of Jiá and south of Gǒngchāng. The region of Guānzhōng was in great chaos;
General Jiǎng Yīng and Xīn Shù occupied Cháng’ān.
He dispatched an envoy to submit to Shi Le.
In the ninth month, Shi Hu, the Duke of Zhongshan of the Later Zhao, inflicted a great defeat upon the Zhao forces at Yiqu.

Taking advantage of his victory, he pursued and captured Liu Xi, the Prince of Zhao, along with more than three thousand of his generals, including Wang, Gong, Qing, and Xiao, all of whom were executed.
Qin and Long were entirely pacified.
The Liu clan of Han and Zhao originated during the Jiazi year of the Daxing era of Emperor Hui of Jin.
In the end, it was completed in the Jichou year of Emperor Xianhe’s twenty-sixth year.
Jichou.
In the fourth year of the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty (329 CE),
Cheng Yu was nineteen years old; this was during the Later Zhao period.
In the second year of Taihe, during the reigns of Former Liang and Former Yan, in the first year of Daiyi Huai, he was posthumously honored as Emperor Lie.
On the day of Gengyin, in the fifth year of Xianhe (the twentieth year of Yuheng), Shi Le ascended the imperial throne;
this was the first and second year of Jianping. On the day of Xinmao, the third year.
The sixth year of Xiánhé (the twenty-first year of Yùhéng); the second and third years of Jiānpíng; the *rénchén* year [of the sexagenary cycle];

the seventh year of Xiánhé (the twenty-second year of Yùhéng); the third and fourth years of Jiānpíng; the *guīsī* year [of the sexagenary cycle]; the eighth year of Xiánhé (the twenty-third year of Yùhéng);
the fourth year of Lèjìānpíng, in the seventh month he died; the first year of Dài established by Mùróng Wǎo of Yàn; the fifth year of Dài; the *jiǎwǔ* year [of the sexagenary cycle].
In the ninth year of Xiánhé, the twenty-fourth year of Yùhéng, Fúxióng died;
Wáng Hóng, Prince of Hǎiyáng, ascended the throne.
In the first year of Yánxī, the sixth year, the *yǐwèi* year, the first year of Xiānkāng, Hàn Gēng changed the name to Hànqī. In the first year of Yùhéng, Shíhǔ ascended the throne.
The first year of Jianwu (the seventh year, Bingshen);
the second year of Xiankang; the second year of Yuheng; the second year of Jianwu (the eighth year, Dingyou);
the third year of Xiankang; the third year of Yuhuan; the third year prior to Jianwu. Previously, Wang Rhuang of Former Yan proclaimed himself king of Dai.
The first year of the Later Yuan era (Wu-xu), the fourth year of Xian-kang (338 CE):

Li Shou established the Han dynasty, the first year of its reign (Jian-wu, 340 CE). In the first year of the Jian-guo era of Tuoba Shi-yu Jian (338 CE), he was posthumously honored as Emperor Cheng. *Xue-zhen* (Admonition on Learning).
Wang Dao, the Minister of Education of the Jin dynasty, appointed Li Chong as an assistant to the Chancellor.
Because the customs of the time venerated superficiality and emptiness,
Li Chong composed the "Admonition on Learning" (Xuezhen).
It is said that Laozi remarked,
"When benevolence is severed and righteousness abandoned, the people return to filial piety and kindness.
Does this mean that the Way of benevolence and righteousness is actually severed?
Only then can filial piety and compassion truly arise.
This is because there is concern that those who feel genuine affection for benevolence and righteousness are few, while those who pursue benevolence and righteousness for their own profit are many;
thus, one must entrust the responsibility to the Sage and cast off the burden of lingering traces.
Among ordinary people who perceive only outward forms,
those who attain the Way are rare;
yet they pursue mere traces with ever-increasing intensity.
As they drift further and further from the source,
I have therefore composed this "Admonition for Students" to dispel their delusions, saying:
When names are prominently displayed,
the Way is neglected; thus,
one must diminish that which is exalted.
Thus, what is honored replaces what has fallen into disuse.
Without benevolence, there is no means to nurture all things;
without righteousness, there is no means to rectify shame.
"Benevolence and righteousness truly must not be distanced;
one need only remove that which harms benevolence and righteousness. (From the *Book of Jin*, Biography of Li Chong).
Yan Han, the Grand Master for Ceremonial of the Jin Dynasty, resigned from his post on account of old age.
He retired from official service more than twenty years ago.
On the tenth month of this year, he passed away at the age of ninety-three.
Guo Pu once visited Yin Hao and wished to perform a divination for him.
Yin Hao said,
"The years are determined by Heaven, while the positions are determined by man."
To cultivate oneself yet Heaven does not grant one's desires is destiny (ming).
To uphold the Way yet others do not recognize it is nature (xing).
One possesses both nature and destiny inherently.
Do not weary yourself consulting the tortoise-shell.

Jihai (己亥). Jin: the fifth year of Xiankang; Han Li Shi: the second year of Hanxing; Hou Zhao Shi: the fifth year of Jianwu; Qianliang Zhang Shi; Qianyan Dai: the second year of Jianguo. The Jin Minister of Education Wang Dao died.
Daoyou had a younger brother named Daobao,
who renounced worldly glory to become a monk;
he was renowned for his learning and conduct and is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

Gengzi (1st year): The 6th year of Xiankang; the 3rd year of Hanxing; the 6th year of Jianwu. (2nd year): The 4th year of Hanxing; the 7th year of Jianwu. Bingyin (3rd year): The 8th year of Xiankang; in the sixth month, Emperor Kang ascended the throne; the 5th year of Hanxing; the 8th year of Jianwu. Dingmao (4th year): The 5th year of Hanxing; the 5th year of [Emperor] Kang. Emperor Kang, surnamed Yue.
He was the younger uterine brother of Emperor Cheng.
Having ascended the throne from his status as Prince of Langya,
he reigned for two years.
He died at the age of twenty-three.
During the period of mourning, he observed silence and did not speak;
he entrusted the administration to Yu Bing for enshrinement.
The son of Emperor Cheng was Prince Cheng of Langya. Yi was the Prince of Donghai.
In the second year of Jianyuan, on the day of Guimao.

In the first year of Jianyuan (the sixth year of the Han dynasty’s founding), in the ninth year of Jianwu, in the sixth year, on the day of Jiachen. In the second year of Jianyuan, in the ninth month, the Emperor passed away. In the first year of Tahe, before the tenth year of Jianwu. Former Liang, Former Yan, and Dai. In the seventh year, [reigned] Emperor Xiaozong Mudi, the grandson of Emperor Xiaozong Mudi.
The Crown Prince of Emperor Kang ascended the throne at the age of two;
Empress Dowager Chu ruled as regent.
Both within and without the realm were free from disturbances.
On the first day of the first month of the first year of the Shengping era, the Emperor donned his ceremonial cap of adulthood,
and the Empress Dowager returned the administration of state affairs to him.
Lifespan: Nineteen years. Reign: From the twelfth year of Yonghe to the fifth year of Shengping.

Biyi (1357): He occupied the throne for seventeen years. Yonghe Year 1: Li Zhi. Taixiao Year 2: Jianwu Year 11: Former Liang proclaimed itself king; Former Yan’s Wang Rhuang succeeded him. Bingwu (1358): Yonghe Year 2; Jianning Year 1: Jianwu Year 12: Zhonghua was established and succeeded him. Dingwei (1359): Yonghe Year 3: Huan Tang destroyed it. Total: Forty-five years. Jianwu Year 13: The dynasty was changed from Dachen to Han. Li Chi was a native of Baxi.
In his youth, he served the Jin dynasty.
In the second year of the Taian era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin (257 CE), he took control of Yizhou—the Sichuan region, the western route of the Four Provinces, and the territory of Liangzhou;
its commandery was named Jincheng, and its state title was Cheng.
The year was designated Jianchu.
Te died, and his son Xiong succeeded him.
In the tenth month of the first year of Yongyuan during the reign of Emperor Hui of Jin:
Xiong immediately ascended the throne as the Prince of Chengdu.
He changed the era name to Jianxing and appointed his uncle Xiang as Grand Preceptor.
His father was posthumously honored as King Jing of Chengdu.
In the first year of the Xih era of Emperor Hui of Jin,
Chengdu Wang Xiong ascended the imperial throne.
The era name was Yanyanping;
the state was titled Dacheng;
and he was specially honored as Emperor Jing.
In the ninth year of the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng of the Eastern Jin, Lǐ Xióng passed away.
His eldest son, Lǐ Bān, ascended the throne.
His younger brother, Lǐ Qī, General of the Pacification of the East, plotted to incite a rebellion.
Taking advantage of the mourning vigil at night, he assassinated him in the funerary hall.
He ascended the imperial throne after one year;
his posthumous title was Xiong, and he was styled Emperor Wu.
His temple name was Taizong.
In the first year of the Xiankang era of Emperor Cheng of the Jin dynasty,
Lord Qi of You changed the era name to Yuheng and altered the dynastic title to Han.
In the fourth year of the Xiankang era of the Jin dynasty,
Li Shou, the Prince Muwen of Hanzhong, assassinated his elder brother Li Qi and established himself as ruler.
He changed the reign title to Hanxing.
In the seventh year of the Xiankang era of the Jin dynasty,
Liu Shou, the ruler of Han, appointed his son Liu Zhi as Grand General and Director of the Secretariat.
In the second year of the Jianyuan era of Emperor Kang of the Jin, Liu Zhi ascended the throne.
The reign title was Tahe (Great Harmony).
This was the second year of the Yonghe era of the Jin dynasty;
it was the eleventh month of the Jianning era of Han.
In the third month of the third year of the Yonghe era of the Jin dynasty, General Huan Wen of the Western Command of the Jin attacked Han.
Wen’s troops reached Chengdu.
He set fire to the city gates.
The Han people were terrified and lost all will to fight;
Li Zhi, who called himself a native of Luoyang, surrendered at the gates of the various armies.
Wen sent envoys to escort him and more than ten members of his clan.
At that time, the state of Fonguihou (Lord of Submission) in Jiankang was abolished.
Cheng rose to power from the second year of the Tai’an era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin, which was the year of Guihai.
Finally, in the third year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Eastern Jin, the year Dingwei, five rulers had reigned for a total of forty-five years.

In the fourth year of Yonghe, the year Wushen: in the fourth year of Yonghe of the Jin; the fourteenth year of Jianwu of Shi [Hou Zhao]; and the year of the death of Murong Huang of Zhang [Qian Liang] and Murong Jun of Tuoba [Qian Yan], who succeeded him. At that time, the monk Fotucheng was invited; he was a native of the country of India. He replaced [the previous master].
In the fourth year of the Yongjia era of Emperor Huai of the Western Jin, he arrived in Luoyang.
He claimed to be over one hundred years old and sustained himself by ingesting qi.
He did not eat for many days.
He was skilled at reciting mantras and commanding ghosts and spirits.
There was a hole by his side, which he plugged with cotton.
At night, it would pull out its cotton-like wool to emit light for self-illumination.
Whenever it approached a stream, it would extrude its intestines and stomach through its pores to wash them;
it would then retract them back into its belly.
During the rebellion in Luoyang,
he went into hiding among the grasses and wilds.
At that time, Shi Le was stationed at Gepo and was committing many acts of slaughter.
Fotucheng, carrying his staff and alms bowl, went to pay his respects to Shi Le.
Shi Le ordered him to demonstrate his spiritual arts;
Fotucheng took a bowl full of water and recited incantations over it.
Suddenly, a blue lotus flower grew within the bowl.
Fu Le, filled with reverence for it, invited it into his army.
In the third year of the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng of the Eastern Jin, Liu Yao besieged Luoyang.
Shi Le tried to save himself by knocking on Fo Tucheng’s door.
Tucheng said,
"The Buddhist stupa has no wind."
A single bell rang out alone, saying:
"Xiū zhī tì lì gāng pú gǔ qú tú dāng. This is the language of the Qiang.
The army marched out and captured Liu Yao.
Shi Le fought the battle and captured Shi Yao,
transporting him to Xiangguo.
In the fifth year of the Xianhe era, Shi Le proclaimed himself the Heavenly King of the Great Zhao.
Acting as the Emperor,
he served Fotudeng with ever-deepening devotion and respect,
bestowing upon him the title "Dàhéxiàng" (Great Harmonious Advisor).
When Shi Le’s beloved son Bin died and was about to be encoffined,
Shi Le sighed and said,
"I have heard that the Crown Prince of Guo died."
"Bian Que was able to restore life.
Can this be demonstrated now?
He then ordered that [the situation] be reported to Sengcheng.
Tancheng took a willow branch, moistened it with water, and sprinkled it [over him].
Grasping Bin’s hand, he said, "You may rise.
Bin then revived and rose.
From then on, Shi Le raised most of his sons within the temple of Fotudeng.
In the seventh month of the eighth year of the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty, Shi Le passed away.
His younger brother Hu, styled Jilong, succeeded him to the throne.
The capital was moved to Ye, which is within the domain of present-day Zhangde Road and Jizhou; [the people] there were especially devoted to Shi Cheng.
By this time, in the fourth year of the Yonghe era of the Jin dynasty, as Cheng was about to pass away, he went to take leave of Shi Jilong.
The king asked in alarm,
"Has a great calamity suddenly befallen my kingdom?
Sengtong replied:
To emerge from life and enter into death is the constant way of things.
Longevity or brevity are determined by destiny and cannot be increased or diminished.
It is only that the Way prizes the completion of practice, and virtue prizes the absence of indolence.
If one's moral character is without blemish,
then even in death it is as if one were alive;
since this is entirely absent, what benefit would there be even in living for a thousand years?
However, what is regrettable is that although our state sets its heart upon Buddhist principles,
and the construction of temples and the ordination of monks ought to bring about blessings, [this is not yet the case].
Yet, the administration of government was violent and cruel,
and rewards and punishments were both indiscriminate,
specifically contravening the sacred scriptures.
This resulted in the state’s fortunes not being prolonged.
Shi Jilong wailed and sobbed with grief.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, Fotudeng passed away while sitting peacefully.
He lived to the age of one hundred and seventy.
He entered the Way for one hundred and nine years and ordained over seven thousand disciples, including the Dharma Master Dao’an.
From the time the Great Teaching first came to the East until its flourishing under [Dao]cheng, the *Monk Biographies* (Sengzhuan) records:

In the year Jǐyǒu—the fifth year of Yǒnghé of the Jìn dynasty and the first year of Dàníng of the Later Zhào—Shí Hǔ passed away and the state fell into chaos. Former Liáng and Former Yán followed; Mùróng Juàn of the Former Yán took over from the Later Zhào. Shí Lè of the Later Zhào was a native of Shàngdǎng (the modern name for Lùzhōu Prefecture in Jīn’íng Road). He was originally from the Ji region; at first, he returned to serve the House of Liu with eight horsemen.
In the fourth year of the Yongjia era of Emperor Huai of the Western Jin, Liu Cong, the ruler of Han, ascended the throne as Emperor.
He appointed Shi Le as the Inspector of Bingzhou; Bingzhou refers to Taiyuan.
Now it is said that in the territory of Jizhou, within Jinjing Road, he slew the Han general Wang Mi.
Shi Le was greatly incensed, yet he still appointed [Wang Mi] as the Great General Who Pacifies the East.
In the first year of the Daxing era of Emperor Yuan of Eastern Jin, the Han ruler Shi Le passed away.
The Chancellor Liu Yao ascended the throne as Emperor.
Shi Le was promoted to the rank of Prince of Zhao.
In the second year of the Daxing era, Shi Le occupied Yanji, proclaimed Xiangguo as his capital, and designated it the first year of his reign.
In the third year of Xiankang of Emperor Cheng of Jin, the [Huan]xi year, the [Shi]le era was renamed Taixuo.
The Zhao ruler Liu Yao besieged and defended Luoyang;
in the eleventh month, Shi Le came to the rescue of Luoyang.
Yao was captured by Shi Kan, a general of Shi Le,
and carried away in a litter to Xiangguo, where he was executed.
This occurred in the fifth year of the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty.
Shi Le styled himself the Heavenly King of the Great Zhao and acted in the capacity of Emperor;
in the ninth month, he ascended the imperial throne.
The era name was changed to Jiāngpíng.
In the fourth month of the second year of Jiāngpíng, Shi Le went to Yè to oversee the construction of a new palace.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Jiāngpíng, Shi Le passed away.
The Crown Prince Hong ascended the throne;
he was the King of Haiyang.
He changed the era name to Yanxi.
At night, Lei escorted the remains and secretly buried them in a mountain valley, so that no one knew their location.
Preparations for ceremonial guards were made, and he was given a hollow burial at Gaoping Ling,
posthumously titled Emperor Ming.
His temple name was Gaozu.
In the eighth month, Zhao’s ruler Hong conferred upon Zhongshan Wang Hu— the Chancellor and Prince of Wei— the nine emoluments of investiture,
entrusting him with the governance of all state affairs.
Wei Hong held the throne for one year.
In the ninth month of the following year, Zhao Wei Wang Hu ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jianwu.
The capital was at Ye.
By this time, in the first month of the fifth year of the Yonghe era of the Jin Emperor, the Zhao ruler Hu changed the era name to Taining.
Shortly thereafter, he died of illness.
Prince Shi was the younger son of Hu and ascended the throne.
Prince Zhen of Pengcheng was the eldest son of Hu; he deposed Shi, making him the Prince of Qiao, and subsequently killed him.
Zhen then ascended the throne.
Yi Yangwang Jian was appointed as Palace Attendant (Shizhong).
Duke Wuxing Min was appointed as Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs both within and without the realm.
Initially, Zhao’s ruler Zun had promised that Duke Wuxing Min would be his heir apparent.
In the tenth month, as Emperor Zun established Prince Yan as the crown prince, Mi grew increasingly resentful and envious.
In the eleventh month, Mi led armored troops,
seized Zun at the Southern Terrace, and killed him.
He established Prince Jian as King Yang and appointed Min as Grand General,
enfeoffing him as the King of Wude.
In the first month of the sixth year of the Yonghe era of the Jin dynasty, Ran Min, the Prince of Wude, ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the era name to Yongxing and established the state title as Da Wei (Great Wei).

The Later Zhao began in the second year of the Daxing era of Emperor Yuan of the Eastern Jin, the Jimao year (343 CE), and ended in the seventh year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu, the Xinhai year (351 CE).
Under six rulers, it lasted for thirty-three years; this is recorded in the *Shilei Carji*.
Min Da was a native of Neihuang County in Huazhou, Daming Commandery.
His original surname was Ran.
He was captured by Shi Le, the ruler of Zhao.
He ordered his younger brother, Hu, to raise him as his own son.
Upon reaching adulthood, Min restored his surname to Ran.
In the third month of the gengxu year, Shi Ji of the Later Zhao heard that Ran Min had usurped the throne at Ye.
He then ascended the imperial throne at Xiangguo and changed the era name to Yongning.
In the tenth month, Ran Min attacked Xiangguo.
The following year, in the *xinhai* year, Shi Ji’s general Liu Xian killed Ji and established himself as emperor.
In the *renzi* year, Ran Min attacked and killed Liu Xian.
Min reigned for three years.
Former Yan’s慕容俊 advanced his troops to attack and capture Min, whereby the state was extinguished.
Ran Min was not included among the sixteen kingdoms that occupied the territories; this is recorded in the *Ranmin Jì* (Annals of Ran Min).

Gengxu (the 29th day of the second month): In the sixth year of the Yonghe era of the Jin dynasty, Fu Hong of Qin—a general of Zhao—held Chang’an; while Ran Min of Wei was in power during the first year of the Yongxing era, the Former Liang Zhang clan and the Former Yan Murong clan were also ruling. In the second month, a golden image of the Buddha appeared in Jingzhou.
When Sima Huanwen went to welcome him, he remained unmoved.
At that time, Teng Jun of Jiangling had donated his residence to become a monastery and appointed Dharma Master Tanyi to preside over it.

Yì led his followers to prostrate and entreat him to accept [the scriptures]. He ascended lightly and floated away, and they enshrined them in their own temple. The *Account of Miraculous Responses* and the Illustrated Scripture [were thus established]. Xīnhài (1351st year of the sexagenary cycle): The seventh year of Yǒnghé of the Jìn dynasty.

Hóng died; his son Jiàn styled himself Heavenly King. The first year of Huángshǐ: The second year of Yǒngxīng of the Former Liáng. The first year of Dàrénzǐ: The eighth year of Yǒnghé of the Jìn dynasty. Jiàn ascended the imperial throne. The first year of Huángshǐ: The third year of Yǒngxīng. In the Former Liáng and Former Yán, Juàn ascended the imperial throne. The first year of Yuánxǐ: The first year of Dàfāngwàijiāo. [He] associated with the Dharma Master Zhī Dùn.
His courtesy name was Daolin.
He was refined in his mastery of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Xie An, the Grand Tutor, and Wang Xizhi, the Right General, were on intimate terms with him.
When Xie An was serving as Governor of Wuxing,
he wrote a letter to Zhi Dun,
which read in brief:
My longing for you grows with each passing day, even more so than at dawn.
Knowing that you intend to return to Shan to manage your own affairs, I am deeply moved by sadness.
Human life is but a temporary lodging.
Lately, matters of elegance and refined pleasure have almost entirely vanished.
I am left with nothing but constant sorrow all day long,
waiting for you to come once so that we may converse and dispel these feelings.
A single day is like a thousand years.
In the tenth month of the second year of the Xingning era of Emperor Ai of the Eastern Jin,
the śramaṇa Zhu Quan took his leave of the imperial court and returned to Mount Shan.
By imperial decree, Huiyun was commissioned to continue the Dharma lectures within the palace.
At that time, renowned scholars such as Yin Hao, Xi Chao, Sun Chuo, Huan Yanbiao, Wang Jingren, He Chong, Wang Tanzhi, and Yuan Yanbo all formed "square friendships" with him.
The world yearned to behold his majestic bearing.
In the second year of the Taihe era of Emperor Fei of the Jin dynasty,
Huidun submitted a memorial to decline the imperial summons and returned to the mountains.
An imperial edict was issued to provide him with provisions.
Hui Dun sent various officials to see him off at Zenglu Pavilion.
Thereupon, he set out for Mount Shan in Yue.
He established a monastery on a small hill in Wozhou to practice the Way,
where the assembly of monks received his instruction.
At that time, there was one among them who was indolent.
Huida composed an inscription to exhort him, saying:
"Be diligent, be diligent!
The Ultimate Way is not far off."
Vast and boundless are the three realms;
far-reaching and endless is the long night.
I reverently observe the clear prohibitions.
He set his will upon non-action,
and so forth.
Someone once left him his horse.
He kept it, saying,
"I cherish its magnificent form. Then,
someone presented him with a crane.
He released it, saying:
"A creature that soars toward the heavens—
how could it be a mere plaything for the ears and eyes?"
The gentleman was highly esteemed for his broad understanding.
Later, he went to Mount Yin to lecture on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra,
with Xu Xun serving as the presiding lecturer (*dōngjiǎng*).
Nanyi (Nan-yi) repeatedly refuted [heretical arguments];
his listeners revered and submitted to him. He passed away at the age of fifty-three.
Dai Kui visited his stupa and sighed, saying:
The virtuous reputation has not yet faded,
yet the trees for his funeral shrine have already grown thick;
one must reckon that the subtle principle of the spirit is continuous and does not perish along with the movement of the vital breaths, as recorded in his original biography.

Gui-chou (10th year of the sexagenary cycle): Jin, the ninth year of Yonghe; Yue-lan-ting Preface; Former Qin, the fourth year of Huangshi of the Fu clan; Former Liang, the first year of the reign of Heping; Former Yan, the third year of Yuanshi; Dai, the third year of the era. [Recorded by] the Śramaṇa Bo Faqiao. Jia-yin (1st year of the sexagenary cycle): Jin, the tenth year of Yonghe; Former Qin, the fourth year of Huangshi of the Fu clan; Former Liang, the second year of the reign of Heping; Former Yan, the third year of Yuanshi; Dai, the third year of the era. [Recorded by] the Śramaṇa Bo Faqiao.
His voice grew faint while reciting the sutras, so he performed repentance for seven days and nights,
praying to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to seek a manifest response.
On the seventh day, his throat suddenly cleared.
From then on, he recited the scriptures day and night, his voice carrying for nearly a *li*.
He lived to over ninety years of age;
his voice was elegant and resonant, as recorded in his original biography.
Yimao (the second day of the second month), the eleventh year of Yonghe: Juqu Jian died.
Shengli ascended the throne in the first year of Shouguang. Juqu Jing ascended the throne.
The first year of Jianxing (the fourth year of Yuanzhi,
the *bingchen* year), the twelfth year of Yonghe, the second year of Shouguang, the second year of Jianxing, the fifth year of Yuanzhi, the *dingyi* year,
and the first year of Shengping.
The Emperor further strengthened his resolve;
he was born in the first year of Yongxing and passed away in the third year of Jianxing. The capital was moved to Ye in the first year of Guangshou.
In the wu-wei year of the sexagenary cycle, he succeeded [to the throne].
In the second year of Shengping, the second year of Yongxing, the fourth year of Jianxing, and the second year of Guangshou;
in the *jǐwèi* year, the third year of Shengping, the first year of Ganglu, the fifth year of Jianxing, and the third year of Guangshou;
in the *gēngshēn* year, the fourth year of Shengping, the second year of Ganglu, and the sixth year of Jianxing—Jùn passed away. His courtesy name was Lì.
In the first year of Jianxi (the Xinyou year), it was the fifth month of the fifth year of Shengping when the Emperor passed away.
In the third year of Ganlu, Xuanjing received the calendar of the Jin dynasty. In the second year of Jianxi, Emperor Ai—Emperor Ai Pi.
He was the eldest son of Emperor Cheng and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Langya.
Emperor Mu had no heir.
The Empress Dowager, because the King had ascended the throne to uphold the great succession,
took elixirs for longevity;
when the effects of the medicine manifested, she was unable to attend to the administration of government in person.
Empress Dowager Chu presided over the court.
[His] age was twenty-five. Lohé (隆和) year 1; Xingning (興寧) year 3. *Renxu* (壬戌).

The Emperor occupied the throne for four years. Lohé year 1; Ganlu (甘露) year 4; Jianxi (建熙) year 3. *Guihai* (癸亥). Xingning year 1; Ganlu year 5; Tiansi (天錫) Jianxi year 4. *Jiazi* (甲子). Xingning year 2; Ganlu year 6; Jianxi year 5. *Yichou* (乙丑). Xingning year 3. In the second month, the Emperor passed away. Jianyuan (建元) year 1; Jianxi year 6. During this period, Wang Tanzhi (王坦之) of Jin donated his gardens and residences to establish Anle Temple (安樂寺).
Shi Hui received his transformation [of faith] through the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism) and the temple records.
As for Emperor Fei, his personal name was Yi;
he was the younger brother of Emperor Ai.
Emperor Ai had no sons.
The Empress Dowager appointed him as the successor, and he ascended the throne.
Later, Huan Wen harbored ambitions of insubordination and incited Empress Dowager Chu.
The deposed emperor was made Prince of Donghai,
and Haixi Gong was also enfeoffed.
He lived to the age of forty-five, in the fifth year of Taixu.

Bingyin (546): The Emperor had been on the throne for six years. Year 1 of Tahe (Northern Qin); Year 2 of Jianyuan (Former Liang); Year 7 of Jianshi (Former Yan). Daosheng translated three versions of the *Śāriputra-dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃgraha* (Ji ben shou jie ben). The Vinaya-piṭaka was translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Dharmahṛti (translated as Fǎhǎi) of the Qin dynasty; this is recorded in his own biography.

Dingmao (47th year of the sexagenary cycle): During the second year of Taihé of the Jin dynasty, the third year of Jiànyuán of the Former Qin Fú clan, and the eighth year of Jiānxī of the Former Liáng Zhāng clan and the Former Yàn Mùróng clan; [this entry] replaces the śramaṇa Zhúdàoyóu.
This was Bo Daoyou.
He had initially resided at Mount Shicheng in Shan,
and that year he moved again to Taizhou.
At the Stone Meditation Chamber on Mount Chicheng in Shifeng— now Mount Tiantai in Taizhou—
there was a pack of tigers crouching before him as Huiyou recited the sutras.
A tiger was sleeping alone;
Sengyou struck its head with his *ruyi* (willow-sprout staff) and said,
"Why do you not listen to the sutras?"
When Qingshi and Bi had both departed,
a large snake ten spans in girth suddenly appeared,
coiled itself around [the tree] and raised its head toward Huiyou.
After half a day, he departed.
One day, a man came before him and said,
"I am the son of Emperor Xia."
Having dwelt here for more than two thousand years,
I am now departing for Mount Han-shi;
I hereby offer this chamber to you.
He then sounded his *bherī* drum, changed the musical mode to *gāndhāra*, and ascended into the clouds to depart.
Sengyou entered nirvana in the eighth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin, according to his original biography.

On the wuchen day—the third year of Taixu, the fourth year of Jianyuan, the ninth year of Jianxi of Former Liang and Former Yan—he, together with Shi Huichang, translated the *Biqiuni zhuan* (Biographies of Bhikṣuṇīs) in six fascicles. Prince Huan Wen, General of the West for the Jin dynasty, and his younger brother Wang Min, the Secretariat Director, donated their residence to establish this monastery.
This is Lùqiū Mountain in Píngjiāng; according to the *Tújīng* (Illustrated Gazetteer) and temple records,
the śramaṇa Yìshù Yú Fǎkāi entered nirvana this year.
He was a disciple of Master Kāilán.
He was skilled in the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* of the Radiant Light and was especially proficient in medical arts.
Emperor Mu once summoned him.
Upon examining his pulse, [the physician] knew he would not recover and therefore did not treat him.
Someone asked him why.
The Master was lofty, brilliant, firm, and simple.
Why did he take medical arts to heart?
Daokai said:
To clarify the six perfections in order to eliminate the maladies of the four māras,
and to regulate the nine pulses in order to treat the ailments of wind and cold—
is this not a means of benefiting both oneself and others? (From the *Benzhuan*).

Jisi (1059): The fourth year of Taihe; the fifth year of Jianyuan; the tenth year of Jianshi of Former Liang. Gengwu (1070): The fifth year of Taihe of Jin; the sixth year of Jianyuan of Former Qin; the eleventh year of Jianshi of Former Liang; [the reign of] Shiwei of Former Yan. In the eleventh month of the Xinwei year (1071), the state was extinguished, succeeding Jin.
Huan Wen traveled from Guangling to Jiankang and, through persuasion,
urged Empress Dowager Chu to petition for the abdication of the Emperor in favor of the Chancellor, Prince Yu of Kuaiji.
An imperial decree was issued promoting Wen to the rank of Chancellor and Grand Marshal, with instructions to remain in the capital to assist in the administration.
Wen then took his leave, requesting to return to his command at Gushu.
Regarding the history of Former Yan: Murong Hu (Hù Huǎi Fǎn) was a person of the Xianbei of Chari (Cháolī), who had inherited the titles granted by the Jin dynasty for generations.
In the second year of the Daxing era of Emperor Yuan of the Eastern Jin, Huai established his staff as he served as the Inspector of the Eastern Barbarians.
In the eighth year of the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng of the Jin, Murong Huang was established after Hu Guang rebelled.
In the year of Dingyou, Gao Rang proclaimed himself king.
Rang was naturally fond of literature and personally presided over the schools of learning.
Regarding instruction and examination:
in the eleventh month of the fourth year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Jin dynasty, Tuoba Rhuang passed away.
His eldest son, Tuoba Jun, ascended the throne.
He dispatched an envoy to Jiankang to announce his death.
The Jin Emperor issued an edict ordering the courtier Chen Guang to invest Liu Jun with the title of King of Yan.
In the year Wushen, Liu Jun proclaimed the first year of his reign.
In the year of Renzi, Yao Jun destroyed the Shi Zhao state.
In the eleventh month, Jun ascended the throne as Emperor;
he styled his era the first year of Xishi.
In the year of Ding-si, Shi Zhun moved the capital to Ye in Zhangde Lu (the ancient region of Xiangzhou) within the territory of Ji; this was the former capital of Shi Hu.
He changed the era name to Guangshou.
In the first month of the year of Geng-shen, Emperor Zhao Zhun passed away.
The Grand Marshal Murong Ke received the final testament and assisted Crown Prince Wei in ascending the throne;
he changed the era name to Jianxi.
Wei said, "This refers to Emperor You.
In the year Jisi, the tenth year of Jianxi, Murong Ping, the Grand Tutor and Duke of Shangrong of Yan, resented the prestige and fame of Murong Chui, the Prince of Wu."
Furthermore, he engaged in disputes and feuded with Ping.
Empress Dowager Zu-hun secretly conspired with Ping to assassinate Chi;
consequently, Chi fled to Qin together with his sons, younger brothers, and nephews.
King Fu Jian of the Qin was greatly delighted and went out to welcome him at the outskirts of the capital.
He then appointed Shui as General of Supreme Martial Valor and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Bingcong.
Previously, when the Jin had attacked Yan...
Yan sought military assistance from Qin.
Yan promised to cede the territory west of Hulao as a bribe to Qin.
Once the Jin troops had withdrawn, [the agreement was fulfilled].
The people of Yan regretted this.
Qin’s ruler, Jian, was greatly incensed and led his troops to invade Yan.
In the twelfth month, they launched an attack on Luoyang.
In the first month of the eleventh year of the Jianxi era,
the Prince of Wuwei, the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Jingzhou of Yan, constructed [the fortress].
He surrendered Luoyang to Qin.
In the sixth month, he launched a second expedition against Yan;
Yan was defeated.
In the eleventh month, Qin Lord Jian entered Ye;
Yan Lord Wei went out to surrender.
In the twelfth month, Qin Lord Jian transferred Murong Wei, along with the royal consorts, princesses, dukes, and high officials of Yan, to Chang’an.
Feng Wei was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xinxing;
the remaining appointments and grants were distributed according to their respective ranks.
Fu Huai’s rise began in the second year of the Taian era of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, the Guihai year.
It ended in the fifth year of the Taihe era of Emperor Fei of the Eastern Jin, the gengwu year.
Four emperors reigned for a total of sixty-eight years.
[The fourth was] Emperor Jianwen, Taizong, whose personal name was Yu.
He was the youngest son of Emperor Yuan.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Kuaiji.
When Emperor Kang passed away, [he succeeded him].
The Empress Dowager issued an edict appointing Wang as the one who would manage the myriad affairs of state;
he was promoted to the rank of Minister of Education (Situ), Chancellor (Chengxiang), and Director of the Secretariat (Lu Shangshu Shi).
When Huan Wen deposed Emperor Haixi, he did so by the Empress Dowager’s command.
When the Emperor ascended the throne as the successor to the imperial line,
Huan Wen usurped power;
the Emperor dealt with him through benevolence and forbearance.
He lived to the age of fifty-three. The Emperor commissioned the creation of Buddha images, established monasteries, held vegetarian feasts, and ordained monks.
At Changgan Monastery in Jiankang, he constructed a magnificent Buddha stupa. (Recorded in the Hongming ji, Year 2 of Xian’an).

Xinwei (the 10th year of the Tianjian era): In the eleventh month of the Jin dynasty, the Emperor ascended the throne and changed the era name to Xian’an Year 1. During the seventh year of Jianyuan, the Former Qin Fu clan occupied the Central Plains, and the Former Liang Zhang clan supplanted the Jin; the śramaṇa Zhu Fatai [served under them].
He resided at Waguan Temple in Jiankang.
The Emperor held him in deep reverence and requested that he lecture on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The Emperor personally visited the site;
the high officials and nobles assembled in full,
and both the clergy and the laity paid their respects with deep reverence.
In the twelfth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu,
Fatai entered nirvana at the age of sixty-eight.
Emperor Wu issued an edict stating:
Dharma Master Tai’s Way spread throughout the eight directions;
he has suddenly passed away.
Ten thousand coins may be provided as funeral expenses.
The funeral rites were entirely managed by the relevant officials, as detailed in the original biography.

On the *renshen* day, the seventh month of the second year of Xian’an, the Emperor passed away. This was the eighth year of Jianyuan of the Former Qin; the Former Liang had succeeded the Jin, and Xu Xun [was active] at that time.
His courtesy name was Xuandu.
The Emperor held him in great esteem and respect,
and they frequently engaged in pure conversation together.
Inquiries reveal that his later incarnation was a monk named Tanyan, who constructed a stupa at Shaoling Temple in Shaoxing, Zhejiang.
Tanyan lived to the age of one hundred and twenty; this is recorded in his own biography and the inscription on the stupa.
Emperor Xiaowu of the Liezong era was Emperor Yao,
the third son of Emperor Jianwen.
He ascended the throne at the age of eleven.
On the first day of the first month of the first year of the Taiyuan era,
the Emperor donned his ceremonial cap of adulthood,
and the Empress Dowager returned the administration of government to him.
He reigned for twenty-four years.
His life span was thirty-five years.

In the third year of Ningkang (337) and the twenty-first year of Taiyuan (385), in the year Guiyou, during the first year of Ningkang of the Jin dynasty and the ninth year of Jianyuan of the Qin, in the seventh month of the Northern Liang era, Duke Xuanwu of Nanjun, Huan Wen, fell gravely ill.
His younger brother, Chong, led his followers until he passed away.
Chong, honoring Wen’s final testament,
appointed his youngest son, Xuan, as his successor.
At that time, he was five years old.
He inherited the title of Duke of Nanjun.
In his youth, he took over the duties previously held by his father Wên, serving the royal house with complete loyalty.
In the eighth month, the Empress Dowager again presided over the court and assumed the regency.

On the *jiashu* day, in the second year of Ningkang—the first year of the reign era—ten years prior [to the present], the Dharma Master Zhu Fashen, a śramaṇa from the former Liang dynasty, was granted imperial permission for his burial.
In the second year of the Xingning era of Emperor Ai, an imperial decree was issued to lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* within the palace precincts.
Huiqian arrived at the hall wearing wooden clogs;
the assembled crowd gazed upon him and sighed in admiration at the height of his virtue and the excellence of his lofty character.
The Emperor once tried to compel him to wear official robes,
but Qian declined with reluctance and returned to Mount Shan.
Later, Zhi Dun sent a letter requesting to purchase a small ridge at Wozhou to retire there in seclusion.
Qian replied:
"If you wish to come, I shall provide for you;
I have never heard that Chao Fu and Yu You bought mountains to hide away in."
In this year, he entered nirvana.
Emperor Wu issued an edict stating:
"The Dharma Master’s realization of principle was profound and far-reaching."
Possessing a refined and lofty character according to physiognomy,
he renounced the glory of being a high minister and donned the simple white robes of a monk.
Dwelling in the mountains beyond the world,
he was steadfast and diligent without slackening;
it was precisely through his propagation of the Way that he could bring salvation to the masses.
He has suddenly passed away;
this causes deep sorrow in my heart.
I hereby grant him one hundred thousand strings of cash as a funeral gift.
[He] assisted in the construction of a funerary pagoda.
Generally, the imperial enshrinement of *śramaṇas* in China began with [Dao]qian. According to the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*):

In the year Yihai (397 CE), prior to the Ningkang era of the Jin dynasty and the Jianyuan era (11th year) of Former Qin, during the reign of Former Liang; in the year Bingzi (406 CE), on the first day of the first month of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, the Emperor donned his adult headdress. During the twelfth year of the Jianyuan era of Former Qin under the Fu clan, Former Liang was ruled by the Zhang clan. Former Qin extinguished it after seventy-four generations. Under Tuoba Gui, cities and towns were built in this year. Former Liang was founded by Zhang Gui.
His courtesy name was Shiyuan.
A native of Anding (in present-day Jingzhou, Yongzhou, within the Zhuanglang Road of Shaanxi), he served the Jin dynasty as an Attendant-at-Large.
In the first month of the first year of the Yongning era of Emperor Hui, he was appointed as the Governor of Liangzhou.
As the times were fraught with many difficulties,
Guǐ secretly harbored the ambition to secure and hold Hexi; therefore,
he requested the governorship of Liangzhou.
He took control in the year Guihai.
In the second year of Emperor Min’s Jianxing era, Juigui was titled Protector of Liangzhou and Duke of Xiping.
In the fourth year of Jianxing, Zhang Shi succeeded to the throne.
In the fourth year of the Daxing era of Emperor Yuan of the Eastern Jin, his younger brother Mao succeeded to the throne.
In the second year of the Taining era of Emperor Ming of the Jin, his son Jun succeeded to the throne.
In the first year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Jin, he assumed the title of King.
In the fifth month of the second year of the Yonghe era, Zhang Jun, Prince Zhongcheng of Xiping, passed away.
His officials petitioned for his eldest son, Zhonghua, to be appointed as the Governor of Liangzhou, Duke of Xiping, and Acting King of Liang.
In the eleventh month of the ninth year of Yonghe, Zhang Hua, Duke Jinglie of Xiping, passed away.
His eldest son, Yao-ling, was only ten years old.
Zhao Chang and others, the Right Chief Scribes, proposed that Zuo, the Marquis of Changning, be established as the successor.
Chonghua was the elder brother of Shu.
He demoted Yao Ling to the rank of Marquis of Liangning and appointed Fu as the Governor of Liangzhou.
The era name was changed to Heping.
In the first month of the tenth year of the Yonghe era of the Jin dynasty, Zhang Zu proclaimed himself King of Liang.
He established the various offices of state and performed sacrifices to Heaven and Earth using the rituals and music of the Son of Heaven.
In the eleventh year of the Yonghe era, [the monk] Chonggong Qing established it;
the era name was Jianxing.
This continued until the first year of the Xingning era of Emperor Ai of the Jin dynasty.
Liangchuo Gong Zhang Tianxi killed Fu Jing and established himself as ruler.
This lasted until the first year of Emperor Wu’s Taoyuan era, when the Fu Qin dynasty extinguished him.
Altogether, this state endured for seventy-four years.
Liangzhou is subordinate to present-day Gansu Province;
it is part of the domain of Yongzhou.

Dingchou (377 CE): Jin Taiyuan 2nd year, Former Qin Jianyuan 13th year. The *Book of Jin* states that by this time, of the nine provinces, Qin possessed eight, while the Jin occupied only a single corner in the southeast. [This was] Dailu Mountain, Xilin Monastery, where the Jin monk Shi Huiying resided.
Originally, he and Master Yuan had both relied upon Master Dao’an.
By this time, Master Yong had already arrived in Xunyang;
the Regional Inspector, Tao Fan, invited him to stay and rest at Mount Lu.
He donated his residence as a place of retreat and founded a temple called Xilin (Western Grove). On the ridge,
he built a single chamber called Xianggu (Fragrant Valley), as recorded in the *Benzhuan* (Original Biography).

Wu-yin (the year 386 CE): Jin Dynasty, prior to the Taiyuan era; Former Qin, fourteenth year of Jianyuan. The *Dūvīna* (Administrative Director) was the Śramaṇa Zhu Daoyi, who studied under Zhu Fatai. Emperor Wen of the Jin deeply revered him. Later, Daoyi resided at Mount Huqiu in Pingjiang and subsequently traveled to Yuezhou’s Ruoye Creek. Shortly thereafter, the regional governor Wang Hui established Jiaxiang Temple and invited him to serve as its head monk; he was then titled the "Dūvīna of the Nine Provinces. Sun Chuo composed a eulogy for his biography. The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* (毘奈耶律), ten fascicles, was translated and completed this year by the Dharma Master Zhu Fannian.

Ji-mao (Year 4 of Taiyuan, Jin; Year 14 of Jianyuan, Former Qin): Qin took Xiangyang from Jin and captured Dharma Master Dao’an along with Xi Zuochi. Dai-geng-chen (Year 5 of Taiyuan, Jin; Year 16 of Jianyuan, Former Qin): Replaced the śramaṇa Zhu Fayi.
The Way of the King was widely spread;
[the people] received its influence and reverently befriended one another.
The Emperor once dispatched an envoy to summon him to the inner court.
He lectured on the sutras,
and Emperor Wu frequently attended his teachings.
That year, he entered nirvana.
The Emperor granted him one hundred thousand coins to construct a stupa for his burial on Xinting Gāng;
this is the present-day Tian'an Temple, according to his original biography.

Xinsi (the year Wuchen): In the first month of the sixth year of Taiyuan, the Emperor established a vihāra within the palace and invited various śramaṇas to lecture on the Way. Jianyuan 17th year. Renwu (the year Gengwu): Jin, seventh year of Taiyuan; eighteenth year of Jianyuan. Lü Guang occupied Guzang—that is, Liangzhou. He was dispatched by Fu Jian, the ruler of Former Qin, as Left General to campaign against Kucha.
He welcomed the Dharma Master Kumārajīva.
Lü Guang subsequently took control of Guzang— which is Liangzhou—
and established the state known as Later Liang.

Guiwei (10th day of the 10th month): The eighth year of Taiyuan of the Jin; the nineteenth year of Jianyuan of Former Qin. Lü Guang deposed Tuoba Gui. Jia Shen (1st day of the 1st month): The ninth year of Taiyuan; the twentieth year of Jianyuan; the first year of Baique of Later Qin (Yao Chang). Qi Fu Guoren of Xiqin occupied Jincheng. Lü Guang [established] Later Yan; Murong Chui succeeded him. Yuan Gong, the Dharma Master, departed for Yanyuan.
In this year, he arrived at Mount Lu in Jiangzhou.
In the tenth year of Taiyuan, the year of Yiyou, Yao Xian was assassinated; his son Pi ascended the throne. In the first year of Taiping, the second year of Baique, Western Qin [began].
In the first year of Jianyi, Lü Guang nearly seized Zhongshan. In the first year of Jianxing, [Yao] Gui [was succeeded].
On the Bingxu day, the eleventh year of Taiyuan, Pi passed away; Deng ascended the throne.

In the first year of Taichu of Longdong, Chang entered Chang’an and ascended the throne. In the first year of Jianchu (the second year of Jianyi), the Three Rivers King Lü Guang [ascended the throne]. In the first year of Tai’an, the second year of Jianxing, Gui was invested as the Prince of Wei.
The first year of Dengguo (Dinghai),
the twelfth year of Taiyuan, the second year of Taichu, the second year of Jianchu, the third year of Jianyi, the first year of Linjia, the third year of Jianxing,
and the second year of Dengguo under King Gui of Wei (Wuzi).

In the thirteenth year of Taiyuan, the third year of Taichu, the third year of Jianchu, the fourth year of Jianyi, the third year of Linjia, the fourth year of Jianxing, and the third year of Dengguo—
these twenty-six patriarchs include Venerable Ratnamitra, the second son of King Tiande of South India.
Having received the ordination and the Dharma, he traveled to Eastern India.
There, the king was named Sthira;
he venerated the non-Buddhist teacher, the brahmin Dīrghanakha.
The King beheld a white vapor penetrating from the top to the bottom.
The King asked,
"What auspicious omen is this?"
The brahmin said,
"This is an omen that Māra is coming.
He immediately gathered his disciples and said:
"As Upagupta is about to enter the capital city,
who could possibly defeat him?
His disciple said:
Each of us possesses incantations and arts by which we can move heaven and earth and enter fire and water;
what cause for concern could there be?
When the Patriarch arrived,
the King asked,
"Master, why have you come?"
The Patriarch said,
"I am about to deliver sentient beings.
The King said:
"By what dharma do they deliver them?
The Patriarch replied,
"Each is delivered by means of that which corresponds to its own kind."
At that time, the brahmin immediately used his illusory powers to conjure a great mountain above the patriarch.
The patriarch pointed at it, and it returned to crush the brahmin's followers.
Terrified, the brahmin threw himself upon the patriarch for refuge.
The Patriarch took pity on him and pointed again toward Mount Hua;
the mountain vanished as he pointed.
The Patriarch then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the King.
To cause them to proceed toward the True Vehicle.
At that time, there was a son of a Brahmin, about twenty years of age,
whose name and lineage were unknown.
Or he would call himself "The Necklace.
Because of this, people called him the Necklace Boy.
When the King went out in the same carriage as his grandfather, they saw the Necklace.
The Patriarch pointed and said to the King,
"This youth is the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
After this holy one, another person shall emerge."
One person transformed [the Dharma] in South India;
one person’s karmic conditions lay in China.
Because of past causes, he was named Prajñātāra.
I now entrust to you the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma.
A verse says:
The true nature is the treasury of the mind-ground.
Without head and without tail,
it transforms beings in accordance with conditions;
for the sake of skillful means, it is called "wisdom."
Having entrusted the Dharma, he took leave of the king, saying:
"I shall return to nirvana.
I pray that Your Majesty will not forget to provide external protection for the Supreme Vehicle."
He immediately passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
A transformative fire spontaneously consumed his body.
The king collected the relics and erected a stupa to enshrine them.
This was during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin. *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage). Jichou year. The fourteenth year of Taiyuan of the Jin;

the fourth year of Taichu of Fu Shi of Former Qin; the fourth year of Jianchu of Yao Shi of Later Qin; the first year of Taichu of Gan Gui of Western Qin; the third year of Linjia of Lü Shi; the fifth year of Jianxing of Chui of Later Yan; and the fourth year of Dengguo of the Wei King. Dharma Master Shi Dao’an, a native of the Wei clan from Fuli in Changshan.
His family had followed the scholarly tradition for generations.
Having lost his parents at an early age, he relied upon his cousin.
At the age of eleven, he left the household life and took Fotudeng as his teacher.
He could read ten thousand words a day;
his talent and eloquence were unrivaled.
He was intelligent by nature, yet his appearance was unattractive.
At that time, Yu said, "The lacquer-clad Daoist has startled his neighbors.
When Fotudeng passed away, [Tancheng] led his disciples across the river to rely on Mount Luhun,
where he lived on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams.
At this time, in the first year of the Ningkang era of Emperor Wu, the temple of Tanchi was established at Xiangyang.
A stupa was constructed and a bronze Buddha image was cast.
Upon hearing Hui'an's name, Emperor Wu issued an edict, saying:
The Dharma Master, by means of his virtue and wisdom, illuminates both devas and humans;
causing the Great Dharma to circulate and serving as a reliance for all living beings,
he ought to receive a daily stipend from the King and the high officials.
The relevant authorities provided him with provisions at the appropriate times,
but Dao’an firmly declined and would not accept them.
Jǐmǎo (the 10th day of the intercalary month), the second month of the fourth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty.
The Qin ruler Jian attacked and captured Xiangyang.
Upon capturing Han An,
he was delighted and said to his attendants:
"I dispatched a hundred thousand troops to take Xiangyang,
yet I gained not even one and a half men.
His attendants asked, "Who were they?"
It is said: "Master Dao’an alone is a complete person;
Xi Zuochi is but half a person.
When Dao’an arrived in Chang’an...
The śramaṇas numbered in the tens of thousands, each following his own teacher’s clan name.
Dao’an said, "No teacher can be compared to the World-Honored Buddha.
Śramaṇas should appropriately take 'Śākya' as their surname."
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Just as the four rivers enter the sea and no longer have distinct names,
so too do those who renounce the world from the four castes equally bear the name Śākya."
This accords with the sutras;
the world increasingly revered him.
On the final day of the first month in the year of Jichou (1069), he instructed his disciples to prepare for his bath.
Suddenly, a strange monk appeared and disappeared through a crack in the wall.
Dao’an asked him about his place of origin,
and the monk pointed toward the northwest.
The clouds immediately parted, revealing a multi-storied pavilion appearing as if produced by illusion;
it was said to be the Tuṣita Heaven.
That evening, several hundred small children all came to bathe there and then departed.
Those who understood him considered him a companion to the Arhats.
On the eighth day of the second month, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Whenever Dao’an annotated the meanings of the sutras, he invariably sought scriptural corroboration from the sacred texts.
On the left arm of his shoulder, there was a square inch of flesh that protruded like a seal;
he was thus known at the time as the Bodhisattva "Seal-Hand" (Inshu).
He composed twenty-four articles concerning the monastic rules for monks and nuns, as well as the regulations for the Dharma-gate.
The Fundamental Tradition of the World’s Adherence and Practice: Xiuzizhi’s Annalistic Discourse states:
"The flourishing of Buddhism was secured through Fotudeng, who in turn secured it through Dao’an;
and from Dao’an, it was secured by Master Huiyuan."
The transformative activities of these three Great Beings were entirely magnificent.

Gengyin: the fifteenth year of Taiyuan of the Jin; the fifth year of Taichu of the Former Qin Fu clan; the fifth year of Jianchu of the Later Qin Yao clan; the second year of Taichu of the Western Qin Qifu clan; the fourth year of Linjia of the Lü clan; the sixth year of Jianxing of the Later Yan; and the fifth year of Dengguo of the Wei. It was from this year that the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha in the Pure Land on Mount Lu first began; details are found below under Dharma Master Huiyuan.

Xinmao (19th year of Taiyuan): 16th year of Taichu, 6th year of Jianchu, 3rd year of Taichu, 5th year of Linjia, 7th year of Jianxing, 6th year of Dengguo. Rencheng (20th year of Taiyuan): 17th year of Taichu, 7th year of Jianchu, 4th year of Taichu, 6th year of Linjia, 8th year of Jianxing, 7th year of Dengguo. Guisi (21st year of Taiyuan): 18th year of Taichu, 8th year of Jianchu; [the previous] Prince Xing ascends the throne as Emperor Taichu, 5th year of Linjia, 9th year of Jianxing, 8th year of Dengguo. Jiawu (22nd year of Taiyuan): 19th year of Taiyuan; Fu Chong is extinguished; 1st year of Yanhe; Later Qin is established; 1st year of Huangchu; 6th year of Taichu, 8th year of Linjia, 10th year of Jianxing, 9th year of Dengguo. Former Qin: Former Qin Fu Jian.
The Di people of Liangyang:
his father, Hong, served as a military commander under the Later Zhao and,
taking advantage of the chaos caused by the Shi clan, came to control the region of Guanzhong.
In the sixth year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Eastern Jin, Hong passed away.
In the third month of the eleventh lunar month, his third son, Jian, entered Chang’an;
the people of both the Han and the barbarians throughout Qin and Yong then submitted to him.
In the first month of the following year, Jian ascended the throne as Heavenly King.
He changed the state name to Da Qin and styled himself the Great Shanyu.
In the Jianyuan and Huangshi eras,
he dispatched envoys in various directions to inquire about the hardships of the people and to seek out men of outstanding talent and extraordinary ability.
He lightened and reduced taxes and abolished useless implements;
all the oppressive policies of Zhao that were inconvenient for the people were eliminated.
In the first month of the Renzi year, Jian ascended the imperial throne.
In the Jiatyin year, Donghai Wang Xiong passed away;
his son Jian succeeded him to the title.
Jian was profoundly filial, widely learned, and possessed many talents.
In the sixth month of the year of Yimao, Jian passed away.
He was posthumously titled Emperor Jingming.
His temple name was Gaozu.
Upon the birth of the Crown Prince,
he ascended the throne and changed the era name to Shouguang.
He was born violent and drank wine day and night;
intoxicated, he attended to affairs and committed many killings.
His ministers were able to preserve their lives for a single day as if it were ten years.
In the sixth month of the year Wending-si (757 CE), Kang Quan, the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy, said to the Emperor:
"Last night, three comets appeared simultaneously;
the planet Pei entered the Taiwei mansion and extended toward Dongjing."
There was the impending calamity of subordinates plotting against their superiors;
taking his anger to be the result of demonic incitement,
he had Kang Quan beaten to death.
At night, he said to his attendant maidservant,
"The brothers Ārya and Dharmā are also untrustworthy;
they must be eliminated tomorrow."
The maidservant informed Shi Jian and his elder brother, Prince Fa of Qinghe.
Fa, together with the Grand Marshal Liang Pinglao and the Grand Marshal Qiang Wang, led several hundred brave warriors.
They secretly entered the Yunlong Gate.
Fu Jian and the Minister of State Lü Bolou led three hundred of their subordinates, advancing with a tumultuous roar.
The guards and soldiers all abandoned their weapons and defected to join Jian.
Jianbing led Sheng away and placed him in a separate chamber;
while Sheng was still intoxicated and asleep,
Fei Sheng usurped the throne as King of Yue and subsequently put him to death.
He was posthumously titled King Li.
Jian offered the throne to his elder brother Fa, who said:
Your direct heir is both worthy and capable;
he should be established [as ruler]. Jian then removed the title of Emperor and styled himself the Heavenly King (Tianwang) of the Great Qin.
He changed the era name to Yongxing.
He posthumously honored his father, Xiong, as Emperor Wenhuang,
and his mother, Lady Gou, as Empress Dowager.
The Heir Apparent Hong was made Crown Prince.
His elder brother, Prince of Qinghe Fadu, was appointed General-in-Chief of All Military Affairs Both Within and Without, while the Chancellor and Director of the Secretariat were abolished;
all other princes were demoted to the rank of Duke.
His younger brother Rong was made Duke of Yangping;
his son Pi was made Duke of Dangle.
They promoted men of exceptional talent and restored neglected offices.
He encouraged agriculture and sericulture, showed compassion for the destitute,
performed rituals for the hundred deities, established schools,
honored those of integrity and righteousness, and restored lineages that had been severed.
The people of Qin were greatly delighted.
In the year Jiwu, the era name was changed to Ganlu;
in the year Jichou, it was changed to Jianyuan.
In the *guiwei* year— the eighth year of the Taoyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin, which was the nineteenth year of the Jianyuan era of the Qin—
[Fu] Jian launched a major campaign to attack the Jin.
He suffered a great defeat and returned home.
In the fifth month of the year Wuyou, the Western Yan ruler Murong Chong attacked Chang’an.
Fu Jian personally supervised the battle;
arrows struck his body from all sides until blood flowed profusely down him.
Chong unleashed his troops to commit violent plunder throughout Guanzhong;
roads were cut off and for a thousand li there was no smoke.
Jian fled to Mount Wujiang.
Later, Yao Chang of the Later Qin dispatched the General of the Light Cavalry, Wu Zhong, to capture Fu Jian.
He was posthumously honored with a title at a Buddhist temple in Xinping, Binzhou.
Fu Jian’s son, Fu Pi, fled from Ye to Chang’an and subsequently reached Jinyang.
Only then did he learn that Chang’an was no longer held and that Jian had died.
He then initiated the funeral rites, ascended the throne as Emperor,
and changed the era name to Taiping.
He was posthumously titled Emperor Xuanshao,
with the temple name Shizu.
In the ninth month of the year Bingxu, Murong Yong of Yan dispatched an envoy to Shi Pi to request passage through his territory on his way back to the east.
Bo did not grant permission.
Bo fought a long campaign at Xiangling.
Having been defeated, he plotted to raid Luoyang.
At that time, Yangwei General Peng Gai intercepted and killed Cao Pi at Shan.
In the eleventh month, Fu Deng, Prince of Nan'an of Qin,
performed the funeral rites for Pi and ascended the throne as Emperor.
The era name was changed to Taichu.
Emperor Pi was posthumously titled Emperor Aiping.
This Jiamu year was actually the nineteenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty.
In the seventh month, Yao Xing, the ruler of Later Qin, traveled from Jingzhou in Shaanxi to Jingyang.
He engaged Deng in battle on the southern side of the mountain,
captured him, and put him to death.
Crown Prince Deng Chong ascended to Huangzhong and immediately assumed the imperial throne,
changing the era name to Yanhe.
He was posthumously titled Emperor Gao.
His state was eventually destroyed by the Later Qin Yao clan.
In total, he reigned for forty-five years.

Biyi (1st year): Jin Taiyuan 20th year; Later Qin Yao clan Huangchu 2nd year; Western Qin Qifu Taichu 7th year; Three Rivers King Lü Guang Linjia 9th year; Later Yan Murong Jianxing 11th year; Wei Dengguo 10th year. Bingshen (2nd year): Jin Taiyuan 21st year, June—the Emperor was assassinated; Later Qin Huangchu 3rd year; Western Qin Qifu assumes the title of Great King, Longfei 1st year; Murong Bao Yongkang 1st year; Wei raises the banners and flags of the Son of Heaven, Huangshi 1st year. Emperor An: his personal name was Dezong.
The Crown Prince of Emperor Wu ascended the throne in the ninth month of the twenty-first year of the Dàyuán era.
He reigned for twenty-two years.
He lived for thirty-seven years: from the fifth year of Long’an, the third year of Yuanxing, to the fourteenth year of Yixi.

*Dingyou* (Year of the Earth-Hen): First year of Long’an of the Jin; first year of Emperor De of the Southern Yan (Moyuk De); fourth year of Huangchu of the Later Qin (Yao clan); fourth year of Guicui of the Western Qin (Qifu clan); [year of] Gao of the Western Liang (Li clan); second year of Longfei of the Later Liang (Lü Guang); second year of Yongkang of the Later Yan; first year of Shenzhi of the Northern Liang (Zuqu clan); second year of Huangshi of the Wei. *Wuxu* (Year of the Earth-Dog): Second year of Long’an of the Jin; first year of Emperor Wu (De) of the Southern Yan; he occupied Guangwu; first year of Taichu; fifth year of Huangchu of the Later Qin; [year of] Zhen of the Western Liang; third year of Longfei of the Later Liang (Lü clan); third year of Sheng (Jianping) of the Later Yan; third year of Shenzhi of the Northern Liang; first year of Tianxing of the Wei, when the Wei Taizu issued an edict, saying:
The rise of the Buddha-dharma has come from afar.
Its merit in bringing salvation and benefit reaches both the living and the deceased.
The divine traces and the bequeathed Dharma can indeed be relied upon as a refuge.
The Emperor decreed that the relevant authorities construct and adorn the sacred images and repair the monasteries within the capital city,
so that those with faith might have a place of refuge. According to the Wei History,
the Taizu established a fifteen-story stupa on the site of the former state of Yu.
Furthermore, he constructed the two monasteries of Kaithai and Dingguo,
transcribed Buddhist sutras and treatises,
and fashioned a golden image worth a thousand pieces of gold.
Each day, three hundred monks gathered for the Dharma assembly. The *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism) records that in the third year of Long’an (499),
during the Jihai year, [the capital] was based at Guanggu in the Southern Liang dynasty.
The second year of Taichu (Later Qin); the first year of Longdi’s reign, titled Hongshi (Later Qin);
the first year of Xigufu’s reign, titled Yongchu (Western Qin); the first year of Xiliang’s reign, titled Jianxing (Later Liang);
the first year of the usurpation of Xianning (Later Liang); the first year of Changle (Later Yan); and the [first year of] Beiliang.
The first year of Tiānxǐ (the second year of Tiānxīng of the Wèi dynasty, the gēnzǐ year), the fourth year of Lóng'ān;
[the year] when [Shēndào] ascended the throne as Emperor of Nányuán; the first year of Jiànpíng (the first year of Lìlùgū’s Jiànhé era of Nánliáng); and the [first] year of Hòuqín.
The second year of Hongshi (Western Qin); the first year of Qifu Gao (Xiliang); the second year of Xianning (Later Liang);
the second year of Changle (Later Yan);
and [the reign of] Northern Liang.
The second year of Tianxi (the third year of Tianxing of the Wei dynasty, the *xinchou* year of the Jin dynasty).
The fifth year of Long’an; the second year of Jianping of the Southern Yan; the second year of Jianhe of the Southern Liang;
the third year of Hongshi of the Later Qin Yao clan; the second year of Gaohuang of the Western Qin Qifu; and the [second] year of Long of the Later Liang.
The first year of Shending (神鼎) was the first year of Xiguang (熙光) of Later Yan;
the first year of Yong’an (永安) of Mengsun of Northern Liang; the fourth year of Tianxing (天興) of Tuoba of Wei;
and the [first] year of Later Liang, under Lü Guang of Later Liang.
A person of the Di people from Liangyang,
he served under the Fu Qin as Left General.
In the eleventh year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin, there was a general named Wang Mu.
He occupied Suzhou and Jiuquan,
styling himself Protector of Liangzhou;
Gao Guang then attacked Jiuquan and captured it.
Guang immediately ascended to the throne as King of the Three Rivers.
He established the Taian era and occupied Ganzu in Liangzhou, within the region of Yong in present-day Gansu Province.
The year was changed to Linqia.
In the sixth month of the twenty-first year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty,
Guang, the King of Sanhe, ascended the throne as Heavenly King.
This was Emperor Wu;
the state name was Daliang,
and he changed the era name to Longfei.
He appointed his heir apparent, Shao, as the Crown Prince.
When the third month of the twelfth lunar month of the third year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty arrived, Emperor Guang passed away.
Crown Prince Shao ascended the throne.
Da Yuan Gong Zuan killed him.
Zuan then ascended the throne as the Heavenly King;
he was Emperor Ling.
The era name was changed to Xianning.
Fanzhu纂 was fond of wine and hunting;
in the fifth year of Long’an, Lü Chao assassinated him and established Lü Lóng on the throne.
The reign title was changed to Shending.
The following year, [the dynasty] fell to the Later Qin.
The Yao clan ruled for three sovereigns over a total of seventeen years.
Dharma Master Kumārajīva was a native of Kucha. Initially,
in the seventh year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin dynasty,
Fu Jian, the ruler of Former Qin, dispatched the General of the Light Cavalry Lü Guang to invade the kingdom of Kucha to capture the Master.
Guanghui heard of the chaos in the Qin state and subsequently took control of Guzang; now,
upon the arrival of this time, Yao Xing, the ruler of Later Qin, had extinguished Lü Long and sent an envoy to invite the Master.
In his youth, the Master could recite thirty-two thousand words daily.
He followed his mother into the monastic life and traveled extensively throughout the Western Regions.
Having mastered a vast array of scriptures, he was particularly proficient in the Mahāyāna teachings.
During his time in Kucha,
the kings of neighboring countries assembled together and repeatedly requested the Master to preach the Dharma.
He must prostrate himself before the seat;
then, he commands the master to step upon his shoulders to ascend the seat.
During the Later Qin period, he extensively propagated the sutras and śāstras.
The ruler of Qin appointed the Master as National Teacher and revered him like a deity;
he personally led his ministers and śramaṇas [to attend upon him].
He listened to the Master’s lectures on the sutras and further requested the Master to translate the sutras and treatises from the Western Regions.
In total, three hundred and eighty fascicles translated by the Master were disseminated throughout China.
They constructed great monasteries and stupas;
those who practiced seated meditation were constantly numbered in the thousands.
From the high officials down to the commoners, all followed and honored the Buddha.
The prefectures and commanderies were transformed by him.
On the day of Gui-chou, the ninth year of the Yongxi era of Emperor Yixi of the Jin dynasty— which was also the fifteenth year of the Hongshi era of the Qin—
the Master entered nirvana on the thirteenth day of the fourth month.
He lived to the age of seventy.
His disciples were Seng, Zhao, Rong, and Rui;
they are known as the Four Sages of Kumārajīva’s school.
Jia Tanying, Huiyan, Huiguan, Sengqie, Daochang, and Daobiao were known as the "Ten Disciples of Kumārajīva.
There were also Sengdao and Sengyin.
All were renowned masters of their time.
