On the day the Master entered *parinirvāṇa*, he said to the assembly:
"Of my translations, only the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* remains; I have not yet had the opportunity to edit away its redundancies."
"If my meaning accords with the Buddha’s mind,
may my tongue not be scorched or destroyed on the day I burn my body.
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Upon cremation, his tongue remained unburnt and was the color of a red lotus.
His master’s name was Kumārajīva, which is translated as "Child-Life" (Tóngshòu). *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gāosēngzhuàn).
The Mountain God Invites the Precepts by Shi Tanyong.
Initially, he served under Fu Qin as General of the Guard.
After [Fu] Jian’s defeat in the south, [Tanyong]...
He subsequently left the household life under the Venerable Dao’an.
Next, he served Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu.
Later, to the west of Mount Lu, he constructed a thatched hut.
While he was contemplating the gates of dhyāna together with his disciple Tanguo,
a man of refined and elegant appearance, accompanied by twenty followers,
suddenly appeared and requested the five precepts.
Tanyong realized this was a mountain deity;
he then held the incense burner for him and conferred upon him the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts,
and expounded the essentials of the Dharma for him.
The deity presented Yong with seven foreign chopsticks, paid his respects, and took his leave;
in an instant, he vanished.
The Three Refuges are: taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Sangha.
The Five Precepts consist of not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not drinking intoxicants, and not speaking falsely. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*,
Year Wenyin of the Jin Dynasty.)
The first year of Yuánxīng (Southern Yán Jiānpíng 3rd year;
Southern Liáng Nùtán Hóngchāng 1st year; Later Qín).
The fourth year of Hongshi (Western Qin); the third year of Gaoyang of Qi (Xiliang); the second year of Guangshi of Later Yan;
the second year of Yong’an of Northern Liang;
and the [same] year of Wei.
The fifth year of Tianxing, the Gui-mao year (403 CE),
the second year of Yuanxing of the Jin dynasty, and the [first] year of Nan-yen.
The fourth year of Jianping (Southern Liang);
the second year of Hongchang (Southern Liang);
the fifth year of Hongshi (Later Qin); the fourth year of Qifu (Western Qin); the fourth year of Xiliang; and the [reign of] Later Yan.
The third year of Guangshi (397 CE),
the third year of Yong’an of the Northern Liang (397 CE),
and the sixth year of Tianxing of the Wei dynasty, the Jiachen year.
The third year of the Yuanxing era of the Jin dynasty; the fifth year of the Jianping era of the Southern Yan;
the [fifth] year of the Southern Liang.
The third year of Hongchang (Western Qin);
the sixth year of Hongshi (Western Qin, Qifu); the fifth year of [the reign of] Xiliang; the fourth year of Guangshi (Later Yan);
the [first] year of Northern Liang.
In the fourth year of Yong’an (the first year of Tiāncí of the Wèi dynasty, the third year of Lóng’ān of the Jìn dynasty),
Húan Xuán, Duke of Nánjùn and son of the Grand Minister Wēn, having already conquered Jīng and Yōng through his tyranny.
Xiao [Huan] requested to take charge of the two provinces of Jingzhou and Jiangzhou;
the court could not refuse him.
In the first year of the Yuanxing era, the court appointed Yuan Xian as Minister of the Secretariat, Liu Laozhi as General Who Guards the North, and Xiao Sanzhang as [General].
He led troops to attack Xuan at Jiangling.
Xuan was greatly alarmed.
Bian Fanzhi, the Chief Secretary, formulated a plan for Xuan.
He marshaled his troops and arrived at Xinting.
Yuan Xian’s forces were routed.
Xuán entered the capital.
He presided over the hundred officials and executed Yuan Xian and others.
In the second year, in the second month, he appointed Xuan as Grand General.
In the ninth month, the Palace Attendant Yin Zhongwen and the Cavalier Attendant Bian Fanzhi secretly drafted the text for the Nine Bestowals and the imperial decree of investiture.
He appointed Xuan as Chancellor of State to oversee the hundred affairs, enfeoffed him as King of Chu over ten commanderies,
and conferred upon him the nine emoluments.
In the eleventh month, he issued an edict that King Xuan of Chu should perform the rites and music of the Son of Heaven.
Bian Fanzhi composed the edict for the abdication and had Prince Baoliang of Linchuan compel the Emperor to write it. Wang Mi,
the Minister over the Masses, presented the imperial seal and robes to transfer the throne to the Emperor of Chu.
He retired to reside at Yong’an Palace.
The hundred officials traveled to the city of Yangzhou on the Taiping Road of the Jiangdong Circuit in Gushu to urge him to ascend the throne.
In the twelfth month, Xuán ascended to the imperial position as Emperor.
The state was named Chu.
He established the Yongshi era and enfeoffed the Emperor as the King of Pinggu.

When Daoxuan entered the palace in Jiankang and ascended the imperial throne, the seat suddenly sank. The Palace Attendant Yin Zhongwen said, "This must be because the Emperor's virtue is so profound that the earth cannot support it.
Daoxuan was greatly pleased.
In the third month of the second year of the Yuanxing era,
Liu Yu, Governor of Xiapi, along with He Wujì, Liu Yì, and Meng Chǎng, the Secretary of the Qingzhou Office,
restored the Jin dynasty and deposed Emperor Xuān at Jiangzhou in Xúnyáng.
As the troops advanced toward Luoliao Bridge,
Xuan Qian dispatched Yin Zhongwen to prepare boats at Shitou;
they floated south across the Yangtze River and fled.
Yu entered Jiankang,
leading the hundred officials to welcome the imperial carriage and executing the members of Emperor Xuanzong’s clan residing in Jiankang.
Xuan reached Xunyang and urged the Emperor to proceed westward.
In the fourth month, Liu Yi and He Wuji attacked and captured the city of Xunyang.
Xuan, taking the Emperor with him, fled alone in a small boat toward Jiangling, intending to seek refuge in Hanzhong.
Chaos broke out within the city.
Xuán managed to reach the boat alone.
Wáng Kāngyàn, the Regional Aide (Biéjià) of Jingzhou, escorted the Emperor into the residence of the Nanjun Prefecture.
The Regional Inspector Wang Tengzhi led his civil and military officials as an escort.
When Xuancheng entered Shu and reached Meihui Island,
he encountered the funeral procession of Mao Fan, the Regional Inspector of Ningzhou, who had come out to meet Xuancheng in battle.
Arrows fell like rain.
Bing Qian, the Protector of Yizhou, drew his sword and struck Xuan, beheading him.
In the second month of the first year of the Yixi era, the Retained Court prepared the ceremonial carriage.
He welcomed the Emperor from Jiangling to Jiankang.
He appointed Liu Yu as General-in-Chief of the Central Military Affairs and Liu Yi as Left General.
He was appointed Governor of Yuzhou,
while Liu Daogui became Governor of Jingzhou.
In the fourth month, Yu returned to his command at Jingkou.
In the twelfth month of the twelfth year of the Yixi era, an imperial edict appointed Liu Yu as Chancellor (xiàngguó),
presiding over the hundred affairs of state; he was named Governor of Yangzhou and enfeoffed as Duke of Song over ten commanderies,
being invested with the nine emblems of regality.

Yu did not accept [the invitation]. *Yi-xi* Year 1 of the Jin Dynasty (Bing-si); *Chao* Year 1 of the Taishang era of Southern Yan; *Hong-chang* Year 4 of Southern Liang; *Hong-shi* Year 7 of Later Qin; *Jian-chu* Year 1 of Xi-qifu of Western Qin; *Jian-chu* Year 1 of Li Tao of Xiliang; *Guang-shi* Year 5 of Later Yan; *Yong-an* Year 5 of Northern Liang; *Tian-ci* Year 2 of the Wei Dynasty. The *Sengzheng* (Corrector of the Sangha) and *Yuezhong* (Registrar of the Sangha) was the Dharma Master Daoqie of Later Qin, a disciple of Kumārajīva.
He was devoted to the Vinaya and practiced with rigorous austerity;
the ruler of Qin held him in high esteem.
Since Master Shi entered Guanzhong, the number of monks and nuns had reached ten thousand.
He then established the position of Sangzheng (Chief Overseer of Monks) and issued an edict stating:
"The Great Dharma has flowed eastward and now flourishes more than ever.
The number of monks and nuns has steadily increased."
It is appropriate to establish a governing framework and proclaim far-reaching regulations to rescue these declining traditions.
Dharma Master Yue had long been renowned for his learning,
and in his later years, he was celebrated for his virtue.
He may serve as State Sangheśvara (National Monastic Head).
He shall be granted official laborers and the rank of Zishizhong (Attendant-in-Ordinary).
Two chariots for transmission and two sheep-drawn carts, each with two attendants, shall also be provided.
Furthermore, Sengqian was appointed as the *yuèzhòng* (director of communal affairs) for his meditative wisdom,
while Faching and Huibin were appointed as *sēnglù* (superintendents of monks);
their official ranks were thus differentiated.
The Emperor increasingly favored him, providing thirty personal bodyguards and thirty white-robed attendants (*Sengshilüe*). *Bingwu* (the year 406 AD):

the second year of Yixi, the second year of Taishang, the fifth year of Hongchang, the eighth year of Hongshi, the second year of Qifu Jianchu of Western Qin, the first year of Longsheng of Hexian, the sixth year of Guangshi of Later Yan, the sixth year of Yong’an of Northern Liang, and the third year of Tianshi of Wei. It was during this time that the Venerable Buddhabhadra—translated as Juexian—of Kaśmīra in North India arrived to travel within the Middle Kingdom.
Upon arriving in Chang’an during this Bingwu year,
Kumārajīva hurriedly stepped out from his seat to welcome him,
regretting that they had met so late in life.
Prince Yao Hong of Qin was invited to the Eastern Palace,
where he engaged in a discussion on the Dharma with Master Kumārajīva.
Master Shi asked,
"In what way is the dharma empty?
He replied:
The various atoms compose form;
since form has no intrinsic nature,
form is itself emptiness.
He asked again:
"Since you have already refuted the existence of form by means of the atom (*paramāṇu*),
how do you further refute the single atom?"
The answer is:
because of the single atom, the collection of atoms is empty;
because of the collection of atoms, the single atom is empty.
The śramaṇa Baoyun translated these words but did not comprehend their meaning;
everyone assumed that what Vasubandhu had calculated—the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*)—were permanent.
He therefore requested further clarification.
Bhadra said:
"Phenomena do not arise of themselves;
they arise through the convergence of conditions."
Because of one atom, there are many atoms.
Since an atom lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty.
How could one say that a single atom is not destroyed?
They did not reach an agreement.
After Buddhabhadra had crossed the river and entered Mount Kuang, he met Master Huiyuan;
impressed by Yuan’s lofty discourse, he requested that he translate various sūtras on dhyāna and abhidharma.
In the year Wuma (468 CE), the fourteenth year of the Yixi era,
he traveled to Jiangling;
there, Liu Yu, the Prince of Song, invited him to return to the capital to reside at the Daochang Temple of Xie Sijun.

In the third month, Meng Yi, the Interior Historian of Wu Commandery, and others invited the Venerable [Kumārajīva] to the monastery to translate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, completing it in sixty fascicles.
It was finished in the sixth month of the first year of Yongchu (Gengshen) of Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty.
At the time of translating the scriptures,
he was moved by two youths dressed in green who would regularly emerge from the pond in the courtyard to offer incense and replenish the water in his vases, never leaving his side.
At dusk, he would secretly enter the pond.
Having completed the translation of the sutra, he vanished without a trace. (From the *Xiuzi Zhi Bianian Huayan Ganying Ji*).
Regarding the *Lotus Sutra*: in the fifth month of this year.
Dharma Master Kumārajīva translated [the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*] into seven fascicles.
Kumārajīva also translated the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* in three fascicles and the *Puṣpakūṭa-sūtra* (*Huashou jing*) in thirteen fascicles.
Furthermore, he translated and transmitted the two-fascicle *Brahmajāla Sūtra* at Cudaparama Monastery (Caotang Si).

Dingwei year: The third year of Yixi of the Jin; The third year of Taishang of the Southern Yan; The sixth year of Hongchang of the Southern Liang; The ninth year of Hongshi of the Later Qin; The third year of Jianchu of Xiqifu of the Western Qin; The second year of Longsheng of Xia Bo-bo; The first year of Zhengshi of Yun of the Later Yan; The seventh year of Yong’an of the Northern Liang; The fourth year of Tianshi of the Wei; The [repeated] Later Yan of慕容垂 (Murong Chui).
He was the fifth son of Murong Huang, the ruler of Former Yan.
During the Yan dynasty, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wu.
He was quick-witted, intelligent, and courageous.
His prestige and reputation grew daily.
The Grand Tutor Murong Ping and Yao Chui were locked in bitter enmity over court disputes.
Empress Dowager and Ping conspired in secret to assassinate Chui.
In the fourth year of the Taixu era of Emperor Fei of the Eastern Jin, Yao Chui fled to the Qin together with his sons, younger brothers, and nephews.
The Qin ruler Fu Jian received him with great joy, welcoming him from the outskirts of the capital,
and appointed him as General of the Supreme Crown.
He enfeoffed the attendants of the Marquis of Bin.
In the eighth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin,
Qin Lord Jian, having been defeated by the Jin forces, returned to Mianchi.
He spoke to Jian, saying:
"The people of the northern frontier, hearing that the royal army has met with misfortune,
have been easily incited to unrest."
I, your servant, request to receive the imperial decree to pacify, comfort, and settle them.
When it drew near to Anyang— Yejun, formerly known as Xiangzhou—
he secretly conspired with former ministers of Yan to restore the legacy of Yan.
In the year of Dingling, Dui Bin rebelled against the Qin.
In the first month of the following year, Bin and his associates enthroned Shi Chui as their盟主 (overlord).
In the year of Yiyou, King Wu Chui first established his capital at Zhending, the Zhongshan Prefecture of the ancient Dingzhou region within the territory of Ji.
He ascended the imperial throne and established the era name Jianxing.
At that time, the Tuoba Wei rebelled against Yan and invaded the various tribes dwelling along the border.
In the Bingshen year, the twenty-first year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty,
in the third month, Yan Lord Chui personally launched an expedition against Wei;
in the fourth month, he passed away at Zuyang in Shanggu.
Upon returning to Zhongshan, he then announced the mourning for the deceased.
The Crown Prince Bao ascended the throne and was titled Emperor Min.
The era name was changed to Yongkang.
In the wu-xu year, Emperor Wu,慕容盛 (Murong Sheng), ascended the throne;
the year was named Jianping.
The following year, it was renamed Changle.
In the *xinchou* year, the first year of Emperor Zhao’s reign known as Xiguangshi,
up until this *dingwei* year of Emperor Yi Gaoyun.
The era was named Zhengshi.
The state fell into chaos due to the usurpation and destruction by Pingba,
lasting a total of twenty-four years.
Bao Ba styled himself King of Beiyin.
The Indian Buddhayaśas—here translated as the Venerable Jue Ming—arrived at Guzang, which is now within the domain of Yongzhou on the route of Suzhou.
In the ninth year of the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty, an envoy was dispatched to invite him to Chang’an.
The ruler of Qin went out to meet him at the suburban altar and provided him with a separate monastery for his residence,
where he was supplied with provisions befitting a king.
The Venerable One accepted nothing at all.
When the time came for almsround, he would eat only a single meal, begging for his food himself. He was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā* treatises and had a red beard.
At that time, he was known as "Red-Bearded Vibhāṣā.
Later, he traveled to Mount Kuang during the Jin dynasty and was held in high esteem by Master Huiyuan.
In the year Jiayin, the tenth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty,
the Venerable One personally carried iron to the summit of Mount Zixiao to cast a stupa,
in which he enshrined the true-body śarīra of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Venerable Buddhabhadra also constructed a stupa for five grains of the Buddha’s relics at Shangfang, to the north of Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu;
these remain intact to this day, as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Record of Mount Lu*.

Wu-shen (12th day of the 5th month). Jin: Year 4 of Yixi. Nanyan: Year 4 of Taishang. Nanliang: Year 1 of Jiaping. Hou Qin: Year 10 of Hongshi. Xiqin and Xiliang: Year 4 of Jianchu. Xia: Year 3 of Longsheng under the Helian. Beiyuan and Beiliang: Year 8 of Yong’an under Ju Changli. Wei: Year 5 of Tianshi. The Vinaya Master, an Indian Venerable named Vimarakṣa, which translates as "Stainless Eye."
After several years in the Qin state,
he has now traveled to the left of the Passes,
where he extensively expounds upon the Vinaya.
The fact that Kumārajīva’s translation of the *Śāriputra-prakīrṇaka-śīla-sūtra* (Ten-Recitation Precept Manual) and the Vinaya-piṭaka were widely practiced was due to the efforts of Daoyi.
The two volumes of internal and external prohibitions on light and heavy offenses composed by him are still in circulation today.
Chā was a man with blue eyes; he was thus known as the Vinaya Master Blue-Eye (Qingyan Lishi). According to his *Benzhuan* (Biography): Jǐyǒu (10th day of the 8th month, Year of Jǐyǒu):

The fifth year of Yìxī of the Jìn dynasty. The year of Jiāpíng (2) of Nányàn. The eleventh year of Hóngshǐ of Hòuqín. The first year of Gèngshǐ of Xīqífú (Xīqín). The fifth year of Jiàncū of Xīliáng. The fourth year of Lóngshēng of Xià Hèlián. The first year of Tàipíng of Běiyàn Píngbá. The ninth year of Yǒng’ān of Běilíáng. The first year of Sìyǒngxīng of Wèi. Regarding the year Dīngyǒu of Nányàn: it is the first year of Lóng’ān of Emperor Āndì of the Jìn dynasty. At that time, Mùchóng Dé ruled over Nányàn.
He was the youngest son of Ruo, the former ruler of Former Yan.
He occupied Guanggu (the ancient Bian, now Qingzhou).
In the wu-xu year, he proclaimed the first year of his reign.
In the year of Gengzi, De renamed himself Beide and ascended the imperial throne as Emperor Wu;
the era was called Jianping.
The year of Yisi was the first year of Emperor Chao’s reign as the Sovereign of the Southern Yan; it was the fifth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty.
Liu Yu, the Regional Inspector of Xuzhou under the Jin, submitted a memorial to launch a military campaign against the Southern Yan.
In the first month of the following year, Yan Shangshu Yue-shou persuaded Chao to surrender.
Chao did not comply;
Yue-shou then opened the gates to admit the Jin army.
Chao Zou pursued and captured him, sending him to Jiankang.
The Southern Yan was thus pacified;
in total, it had lasted thirteen years.
The Wei founder, Emperor Taizu Daowu Di Gui,
was assassinated by his younger son Shao.
Emperor Taizong Mingyuan Di succeeded him.

The imperial decree ordered the establishment of Buddha statues in the four directions of the capital city, and furthermore commanded the śramaṇas to instruct and guide the common people; this is recorded in the Wei History.

Gengxu (1st year): the 6th year of Yixi; the 3rd year of Jiaping; the 12th year of Hongshi; the 12th year of Gengshi; the 6th year of Jianchu; the 5th year of Longsheng; the 2nd year of Taiping; the 10th year of Yong’an; the 2nd year of Yongxing. Xinhai (2nd year): the 7th year of Yixi; the 4th year of Jiaping; the 13th year of Hongshi; the 13th year of Gengshi; the 7th year of Jianchu; the 6th year of Longsheng; the 3rd year of Taiping; the 11th year of Yong’an; the 3rd year of Yongxing. Renzi (3rd year): the 8th year of Yixi; the 5th year of Jiaping; the 14th year of Hongshi; the 1st year of Chipan (Yongkang); the 8th year of Jianchu; the 7th year of Longsheng; the 4th year of Taiping; the 1st year of Yuanshi (following the relocation of the capital); the 4th year of Yongxing; the years of Gusu and Chanding. Śramaṇa Huichi.
He was the younger brother of Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu.
In the second year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty,
he took leave of Master Huiyuan and entered Shu.
He resided at Longyuan Temple in Jiazhou;
both monastics and laypeople paid him profound respect,
and all who ascended his lecture hall were hailed as having "climbed the Dragon Gate."
In the eighth year of the Yixi era (the Renzi year),
he issued a final admonition to his disciples and subsequently entered meditative absorption within the Dragon Abyss Grotto tree.
In the third year of the Zhenghe era of the Song dynasty, a wind broke the tree.
Chih then emerged from meditative absorption.
Emperor Huizong composed three eulogies in verse for him,
which are found in the *Monastic Biographies of the Zhenghe Era* and the *Chronological Records*.

Gui-chou (10th day of the 12th month): Jin Dynasty, 9th year of Yixi; Nan-yun Dynasty, 6th year of Jiaping; Later Qin Dynasty, 15th year of Hongshi; Xiqi Dynasty, 2nd year of Yongkang; Xi-liang Dynasty, 9th year of Jianchu; Xia Dynasty, 1st year of Fengxiang; Bei-yun Dynasty, 5th year of Taiping; Bei-liang Dynasty, 2nd year of Yuanshi; Wei Dynasty, 3rd year of Yongxing. The stone pillar was erected to commemorate the lecture by the Dharma Master Sengluo’s disciple, Daosheng.
Before the final chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* had arrived,
he read it aloud repeatedly for a long time and said:
"An icchantika shall naturally attain Buddhahood."
This scripture has not yet reached its full extent;
at that time, the masters of letters attacked it in unison,
falsely accusing it of being heterodox doctrine.
According to the Vinaya, he should have been expelled;
yet, with his hands tucked into his sleeves, he came to Jin and entered Mount Huqiu in Pingjiang,
where he erected a stone as a pulpit to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for his disciples.
When he reached the place where the icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature, he asked,
"Does the meaning of what I have spoken accord with the Buddha’s mind?
All the stones nodded their heads in affirmation.
Later, he traveled to Kuangshan and resided at Xiaojing Rock.
Hearing that Tanmen was in Northern Liang revising the later chapters of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
he went to the Southern Capital.
If it is said that icchantikas all possess Buddha-nature, the joy and consolation one feels would be beyond compare with the original transmission.

[The years are as follows: Jiǎyīn (10th year of Yìxī), the year of the extinction of Nánliáng; Hóngshǐ 16th year; Yǒngkāng 3rd year; Jiàncū 10th year; Fèngxiáng 2nd year; Tàipíng 6th year; Yuánsǐ 3rd year; Shénruì 1st year. As for Nánliáng, there was Tùfǎ Wūgū of Nánliáng.
He was a Xianbei from Hexi. By this time,
the first year of the Long’an era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, he occupied Guangwu— present-day Lanzhou in the Gansu Corridor (Gongchang Road) of Shaanxi—
which is the ancient territory of Yongzhou.
He was styled the Southern Liang.
In the year Wuxu, Wu Gu established the era name Taichu;
in the first month of the first year of Heshi, established by Lilugu in the year Gengzi, he intended to assume the title of Emperor.
The General Who Pacifies the State, Tufan Yu, said:
"Since the remote antiquity of our nation, we have worn our hair loose and our robes fastened on the left, lacking the adornment of crowns and sashes;
we have wandered from place to place, following the water and grass."
Having no walled cities or houses,
they were thus able to gaze majestically upon the desert and rival the Central Plains;
Lilukuo followed this example.
He then further assumed the title of King of Hexi and changed the era name to Jiànhé.
He appointed Guǎwǔgōng Nùtán as the Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs at Home and Abroad and Governor of Liangzhou.
In the year of Renyin, King Nur-tan ascended the throne and changed the era name to Hongchang.
In the fourth month of the year of Wushen, Yao Xing, the Later Qin Emperor, desired to seize Nur-tan.
He sent Wei Zong, a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat, to visit Xian.
Their discussions on the great principles of the age were boundless and versatile.
After retiring, Wei Zong sighed and said:
Men of extraordinary talent and refined capacity need not necessarily come from China;
those of clear wisdom and keen insight need not necessarily have studied the classics.
Only now do I realize that there are worthy people beyond the Nine Provinces and outside the Five Classics.
Furthermore, there was another person who returned and said to Xing,
"Liangzhou cannot yet be plotted against."
Xing did not permit the dispatch of troops to raid Murong Nutan.
Consequently, the Later Qin army suffered a great defeat.
In the eleventh month, Nutan proclaimed himself King of Liang.
A general amnesty was proclaimed and the reign title was changed to Jiaping.
Offices for the hundred ministers were established.
This was the tenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, falling on a Jia-yin day.
Tuoba Nutan was killed by Qi Fu Chipan of Xiqin,
and Southern Liang perished.
It had three rulers and lasted for eighteen years.

Yimao (Year of the Rabbit): Jin Dynasty, 11th year of Yixi; Later Qin, 17th year of Hongshi; Western Qin, 4th year of Yongkang; Western Liang, 11th year of Jianchu; Xia, 2nd year of Fengxiang; Northern Yan, 7th year of Taiping; Northern Liang, 4th year of Yuanshi; Wei, 2nd year of Shenrui. Master Yuan of Mount Lu: his name was Huiyuan.
Having departed from Yanmen, he now travels the same road as Jia Shi.
In his youth, he was a Confucian scholar who had extensively mastered the multitude of books.
He was particularly profound in his mastery of the *Zhouyi*, the *Zhuangzi*,
and the *Laozi*. He once visited Dharma Master Dao’an with his younger brother Huichi and heard the teachings on the supramundane Dharma.
Delighted by this, he sighed and said,
"The nine schools of Confucianism and Daoism are but mere chaff.
Thereupon, he left the household life.
Dao’an had several thousand disciples,
and Huiyuan occupied the foremost seat among them.
Dao’an once said:
If the Way is to flow to the eastern lands, will it not be far off?
This was the ninth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, the Jia-shen year.
At that time, the state of Former Qin was in turmoil, and he came to travel in the Jin.
Arriving in Jiangxi, he beheld Mount Lu and took a liking to it;
he then stayed at Longquan Vihāra in Jiangzhou and subsequently resided at Xilin Temple of Huiyong.
Furthermore, he established Donglin Temple on the eastern side of the mountain.
During its construction, a mountain deity descended in spirit and vowed to provide assistance;
however, for two nights, wind and thunder arose in the night, and all was shrouded in darkness.
The heavy rain cleared at dawn.
He went there to observe the fine timber and extraordinary materials arranged in profusion.
At that time, the Jin General Huan Yi was present.
Upon first arriving at this pasture, he was struck by its divine and extraordinary nature and memorialized the throne to establish a monastery there; the temple was completed in the Bingxu year.
At that time, many men of extraordinary talent throughout the Jin empire were living in seclusion and refusing office.
Having heard of Master Yuan of Mount Lu’s Way,
they all came to follow him.
In the year Gengyin, the Master said to Liu Chengzhi and the others:
"Gentlemen, if you have the aspiration to journey to the Pure Land,
you should exert yourselves with diligence.
Thereupon, they together resolved their wills before Amitābha Buddha.
They established a fast and made a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land;
thus, one hundred and twenty-three people, both monastics and laypeople,
admired the Way and formed an alliance.
With their minds dwelling beyond the mundane world,
Xie Lingyun excavated two ponds at Donglin to plant lotus flowers,
while Master Huiyuan never crossed Tiger Creek when escorting guests.
In the gengxu year, the sixth year of the Yixi era,
the Daoist Lu Xiujing accompanied Tao Yuanming into the mountains to visit the Master;
as they saw him off, they held hands and conversed so intently that they did not realize they had passed beyond Tiger Creek.
The three men looked at one another and laughed aloud;
people today depict this scene as the "Three Laughs" (Sānxiào tú).
Tányíng was fond of wine and had been living in the mountains for a long time.
Because the mountain had no wine, he knit his brows in distress and departed from it.
On the sixth day of the eighth month in the year of Yimao (416 CE),
Master Huiyuan joined his palms, faced west, and passed away.
He lived to the age of eighty-four.
Xie Lingyun composed his stele inscription.
The community of followers numbered several thousand.
Among those whose names and achievements were particularly renowned, there were eighteen; as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).
Regarding the "Lotus Water-Clock": within the community of Master Huiyuan, there was a monk named Huiyao who suffered from the lack of a water clock in the mountains.
He then established twelve-petaled lotuses upon the water,
which rotated with the waves to mark the twelve periods of the day.
The shadow of the sun’s course does not err. What is called the "Lotus Water-Clock" (Lianhua lou) by Master Huiyuan today is this very thing.

Wuzi (2nd year): The 25th year of Yuanjia; the 9th year of Taiping Zhenjun.
Jichou (3rd year): The 26th year of Yuanjia; the 10th year of Taiping Zhenjun.
Gengyin: The 27th year of Yuanjia; the 11th year of Taiping Zhenjun. [The Emperor] exterminated the Minister of Education, Cui Hao, and others.
Xingmao: The 28th year of Yuanjia; the first year of Zhengping. In the second month of the second year of Zhengping, Emperor Taizu was assassinated.
The "White-footed Śramaṇa" was named Tanshi.
The first was Huishi.
The "Buddhism and Daoism" chapter of the *Weishu* states:
"The śramaṇa Huishi was the son of Zhang [family] from Qinghe."
Initially, Master Kumārajīva was taken by Liu Yu of the Jin dynasty after he extinguished the Later Qin; subsequently,
he was pursued and seized at Chang’an by Helian Chucai of the Xia state.
While both monastics and laypeople were being slaughtered in the pit,
Shi received the first blows of the blade without injury.
Gaoque was greatly enraged and summoned Shi before him.
He struck himself with his dagger,
yet was still unable to harm himself;
he then became terrified and apologized for his offense.
The common people relied on the compassionate power of Shi to escape all forms of cruelty and poison.
When Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty subdued Helian Chang, [Shi was captured].
Bai Zu returned to the Wei dynasty.
Initially, in the sixth year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of the Wei,
Emperor Taiwu went to Chang’an to suppress the rebellion of He Rong.
Seeing weapons and armor within the monasteries,
he became enraged;
consequently, the Minister of Education Cui Hao urged Emperor Taizu accordingly.
He ordered the total execution of the śramaṇas and the destruction of all scriptures and images.
In the eleventh year of the Taiping Zhenjun era,
Cui Hao, relying on his own talent and strategy, compiled the national history.
The records of Wei’s ancestral deeds were inscribed along the public thoroughfares,
and stone monuments were erected at the suburban altars;
there was no one among the northerners who did not feel resentment and indignation.
Emperor Taiwu was greatly incensed by Hao’s public exposure of the state's evils.
He ordered the relevant authorities to investigate the crimes of Hao, the Secretariat clerks, and other officials;
in total, one hundred and twenty-eight people were executed, their clans all exterminated.
At that time, Baimuzi went to pay his respects to Emperor Taiwu.
The Emperor grew angry and ordered him to be executed, but the executioner could not wound him.
Taiwu himself drew his girdle-knife and struck at him.
Furthermore, they could not harm him;
when he was cast into a tiger's cage,
the tigers all became submissive and compliant.
Wu was startled; he invited Shi to ascend the hall, where he repented, apologized, and returned his reverence.
Previously, Crown Prince Jingmu had been precise and discerning in his administration.
The Chief Eunuch Zong Ai, by nature sycophantic and wicked, committed many illegal acts and instigated discord against the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince passed away from grief;
it was only later that Da Wu came to know of this,
and he mourned him incessantly.
Zong’ai feared execution.
In the second month of the second year of the Zhengping era, he assassinated Emperor Taowu.
Yuan He and Lu Lü, the Ministers of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, raised troops and executed Zong’ai.
He served the Imperial Grandson Jun, who ascended the throne as Emperor. He changed the era name [to Xing'an].
According to the *Wei Shu*, he walked barefoot with his feet untouched by mud or filth;

thus he was named in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. Renchen year: the twenty-ninth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty; the first year of Xing'an of the Wei Dynasty, under Emperor Wencheng, son of Crown Prince Jingmu. The first year of Xing'an of the Wei Dynasty.
Many of the ministers petitioned to restore the teachings of the Śākya clan.
The Imperial Edict stated:
"Now, those who act as emperors and kings..."
One must surely revere the clear statutes and manifest the Way of Benevolence.
Those who are able to bestow kindness upon the people and provide benefit to all living beings—
though they lived in antiquity, their heroic deeds are still recorded in succession.
Therefore, in the Spring and Autumn Annals, there is joy in the rites that clarify and honor [virtue];
in the sacrificial canons, the lineages of those who have bestowed merit are recorded.
How much more so for the Tathāgata of the Śākya teaching, whose merit rescues the great trichiliocosm.
His grace flows throughout the realms of dust;
those who investigate birth and death marvel at his profound insight,
while those who examine the meaning of the texts prize his wondrous gateway.
It assists the prohibitions and laws of royal governance,
augments the virtuous nature of benevolence and wisdom,
and sweeps away the multitude of heterodoxies.
He expounded the Perfect Enlightenment;
therefore, from ancient times until the present, there has been no one who has not held it in high esteem,
and it remains that which our nation has always revered and served.
The current decree states that in all provinces, commanderies, and counties where people reside in communities,
each is permitted to establish Buddhist monasteries (bifu).
Furthermore, those who take pleasure in the Buddha-dharma and wish to become śramaṇas are permitted to leave the household life.
Fifty persons were assigned to the large prefectures and forty to the small prefectures.
Thereupon, the Buddhist temples that had previously been destroyed were for the most part restored.
(The *Wei Shu*, the *Sengshi Lue*, and an imperial edict to the relevant authorities likewise record this.)
At the Five-Tiered Great Temple, he cast bronze Buddha statues,
each sixteen feet in height,
for the five emperors beginning with his own great-uncle. The Emperor personally shaved the heads of five śramaṇas, including Master Shixian and others.
Because his teacher was virtuous, he served as the Superintendent of Monks (Dàotǒng) for the Way;

this is recorded in the *Wèishū Sēngshǐ* (History of Buddhism in the Wèi Dynasty). Guǐsī: In the second month of the thirtieth year of Yuánjiā, Prince Shào plotted rebellion and the Emperor passed away; the Prince of Wǔlíng campaigned against Shào and executed him. Wèi: The second year of Xìng’ān, during the reign of Shìzǔ Xiàowǔ Dì, whose personal name was Jùn.
He was the third son of Emperor Wen,
enfeoffed as Prince of Wuling,
and appointed as the Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou.
In the third month, the Prince assembled his forces to punish the chief offender, Shao.
In the fourth month, the Prince ascended the imperial throne at Xinting.
He reigned for eleven years.
He lived to the age of thirty-five.
The Emperor was widely learned;
he could read seven lines of a text at once while dictating his memorials. (From the *Song Shu*, "Emperor's Annals," under the third year of Xiaojian and the eighth year of Daming).

Jiawu (1st year of Xiaojian): In the first month, the Yuan era was changed to Xingguang, Year 1, by the Wei; the Song divided the five commanderies of eastern Zhejiang from the Yangzhou province and established Dongyang Province, headquartered at Kuaiji.
The eight commanderies of Jingzhou, Xiangzhou, and Yuzhou were divided [to form] Yingzhou, with its administration established at Jiangxia (Songshu).

On the day of Yimou, the second year of the Xiaojian era, an imperial edict appointed the śramaṇa Daoyou as the Dharma Master of Anzhen Temple (Sengzhuan). On the day of Bingjia, the first year of the Tai’an era, the third year of Xiaojian (the second year of Tai’an), [there was] the *Huayan jing shi shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) by Shi Yuanchang.
When the Wei dynasty suppressed the teachings,
he returned to the Song and came to Yangzhou,
where he resided at Mingyin Temple.
The commentary and sub-commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* have been transmitted and lectured upon until the present day.
To elucidate its origins, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* records:
In the year Dingyou, the first year of the Daming era (the third year of Taian of the Wei dynasty), the twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of Eastern India.
Having attained the Dharma, he traveled to South India to propagate his teachings.
There, a king named Gandhāra reigned,
who held the Buddha-vehicle in high esteem.
He welcomed his ancestors with great respect and made offerings to them,
bestowing precious jewels upon them.
The king had three sons.
They are named Candravimalatārā, Guṇavatītārā, and Bodhitārā.
The Patriarch asked the three princes about the bestowed pearl:
"Is there anyone who can equal this pearl in its perfect brightness?
The first and second princes both replied:
"This jewel is the most honored among the seven treasures; indeed, nothing surpasses it.
The third prince, Bodhitara, said, "This is but a worldly treasure;
it is not sufficient to be considered supreme."
Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme;
this worldly light is not sufficient to be considered supreme.
Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This worldly illumination is not yet supreme.
Among all forms of illumination, mental illumination is supreme.
This light of the jewel cannot illuminate itself.
One must rely on the light of wisdom to discern this through eloquent analysis.
Once this has been analyzed, one immediately knows it to be a pearl;
once it is known to be a pearl, one immediately knows it to be a treasure.
If one clarifies that it is a treasure, the treasure does not treasure itself;
if one discerns that it is a pearl, the pearl does not pearl itself.
That a pearl does not pearl itself means it must rely upon the wisdom-pearl.
As for the argument that worldly jewels are not themselves treasures, it is because they must rely upon the jewel of wisdom to illuminate the jewel of the Dharma.
Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, his treasure immediately manifests; when sentient beings possess it, their treasure likewise appears.
The Jewel of the Mind is likewise so.
The Patriarch praised his eloquence and wisdom,
and then asked him again:
"Among all things, what is signless?
He replied, "Among all things, that which does not arise is signless.
Again he asked, "Among all things, what is the highest?"
He said, "Among all things, the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) is the highest.
He asked again, "Among all things, what is the greatest?
He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the greatest."
Just as Gandhāra’s father, the King, passed away,
the multitude all wailed and fainted.
Then Bodhitara entered meditative absorption before the coffin for seven days and emerged.
He then requested to leave the household life.
Once he had received full ordination,
his master told him:
The Tathāgata entrusted the True Dharma-eye to Mahākāśyapa;
thus it was passed down in succession until it reached me.
I now entrust this precept to you.
Listen to my verse:
"The mind-ground gives rise to all seeds;
from conditions they arise, and by conditions they are sustained."
The fruit is fulfilled and Bodhi is perfected;
the flower blooms and the world arises.
Having transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch departs.
Immediately, he rose from his seat and extended his left and right hands, each emitting twenty-seven rays of light.
The three colors shone brilliantly as they surged upward into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees.
He manifested fire to cremate himself;
śarīras fell from the sky like rain,
which were collected to construct a stūpa.

During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage) notes that the Venerable One once accepted an invitation for a vegetarian feast from the King of Eastern India.
The King asked:
"All these people are reciting the sutras;
why do you, Master, not recite them?
The Venerable One replied:
This poor monk exhales without following external conditions,
and inhales without dwelling within the aggregates or realms;
he constantly recites this sutra in this manner hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of times.
Not merely one or two scrolls.
Jihai (Year of the Pig). The third year of the Daming era, the fifth year of Tai’an, gengzi (Year of the Rat).
The fourth year of the Daming era. Empress Dowager Luzhao commissioned this image of Samantabhadra, which was completed in the first year of the Heping era.
Xin-chou (the year of the Metal Ox): The fifth year of Daming; the second year of Heping.
Ren-yin (the year of the Water Tiger): The sixth year of Daming; the third year of Heping.
Gui-mao (the year of the Water Rabbit): The seventh year of Daming; the fourth year of Heping.
Jiachen (the year of the metal dragon): On the gengshen day of the fifth month in the eighth year of Daming, the Emperor passed away; the Crown Prince ascended the throne.
In the fifth year of Heping, the Emperor was deposed. The posthumous title of the deposed Emperor of Song was Ziyè.
He ascended the imperial throne at the age of sixteen.
He changed the era name to Jinghe,
and subsequently changed it again to Yongguang.
In the eleventh month of the year Yi-si,
the chamberlains Ruan Tianfu, Jiang Chanzhi, and others assassinated the Emperor, the Former Abolished Emperor (Faidi).
He had occupied the throne for one year.
Prince Xiangdong Yu ascended the throne.
Emperor Taizong Mingdi, Yu,
was the eleventh son of Emperor Wen.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiangdong.
After Shou Jizhi and others had assassinated and deposed the Emperor,
they escorted the Prince to the throne.
He reigned for seven years. His life span was thirty-four years. *Taishi* 7 and *Taiyu* 1. *Yisi*. *Song*: In the eleventh month of the first year of *Taishi*, the era name was changed;

this was the same as the *Yongguang* era of the deposed Emperor [Jianwen]. *Wei*: In the fifth month of the sixth year of *Heping*, the Emperor passed away. The Emperor ordained over thirty thousand monks and nuns, promoted Buddhism, and restored old temples. *Beishi*: *Bingwu*. In the second year of *Taishi*, Xianzu Emperor Wenxuan, the eldest son of Gaozong, ascended the throne at the age of twelve and ruled with the Empress Dowager as regent. In the sixth month of the first year of *Tian'an*, the prohibition on wine was lifted. Once the Prince of Xiangdong had ascended the imperial throne...
Yuan Yi submitted a memorial urging Prince Xun of Jin’an to ascend the Great Throne;
he then established his military headquarters at Sangwei and issued a manifesto to Jiankang.
At this point, Liu Wan led his generals and aides to offer him the imperial title.
Prince Zixun of Jin’an ascended the throne as Emperor at Xunyang in Jiangzhou,
changing the era name to Yijia.
Tributes from all four directions were all being sent to Xunyang.
The court retained control over only a few prefectures, such as Danyang and Huainan.
Consequently, the court appointed Prince Jian’an, Xu Huiren, as the Commander-in-Chief of all military operations for the campaign.
Shen Youzhi served as the Governor of Xunyang and led troops to campaign against Zixun. Subsequently,
Liu Wan became the Senior Secretary of the Front Army of Jingzhou.
Zhang Yue treacherously killed him.
When the various armies reached Xunyang,
they executed Prince Zixun of Jin'an.
The head was sent to Jiankang.
Zixun was eleven years old.
The Great Being Bao Gong’s name was Baozhi.
The world calls him Master Bao,
honoring him for his hands and feet, which were like eagle talons.
Formerly, the wife of a man surnamed Zhu from Dongyang in Jiankang heard the chirping of a chick within an eagle's nest;
she climbed the tree and retrieved it.
He was adopted as his son.
At the age of seven, he entered the monastic life under Sengjian at Mount Zhong,
where he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of dhyāna and contemplation.
At this point, he manifested his traces,
hanging a pair of scissors, a comb, a fly-whisk, and a fan from the tip of his staff,
and carried them upon it as he traveled through the villages.
Once, when he encountered someone eating minced fish,
he followed him and asked for some;
the eater cast it aside and treated him with contempt.
Zhi immediately spat them into the water, and they all became living fish;
these are the "turning-back" fish found in the river today.
They abound in divine wonders.
He entered nirvana on the sixth day of the twelfth month in the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.
He was ninety-three years of age.
Emperor Wu of the Liang purchased Dulonggang on Mount Zhong in Jiankang for two hundred thousand taels of gold and interred him there.
A five-storied stupa was erected upon it;
Emperor Wǎn-jūn was commanded to compose the inscription for the stele.
On the day of the burial, the imperial carriage personally arrived to offer sacrifices and commemorate him.
Monastics and laypeople alike venerated him,
and his marvelous and auspicious responses were preeminent in the world.
As for all the verses composed by this Great Being:
He was deeply devoted to the *Nanshi*.

For the sake of scholars, he composed ten chapters of "Hymns in Praise of Mahāyāna" (*Dacheng zan*), fourteen sections of "Verses in Prose and Verse" (*ke song*), and the "Songs of the Twelve Hours" (*Shier shi ge*).
These works were widely circulated throughout the world.
In the seventh year of the Taiping Xingguo era of Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty,
the Emperor dispatched an envoy to Zhongshan to perform a ritual fast,
personally inscribing a composed text in praise and reverence.
The Imperial Edict stated:
"From now on, he should be publicly honored and distinguished;
let him be granted the title 'Dharma Forest True Awakening Bodhisattva' and a commemorative stele be erected."
When the Dharma Master Tanzong was approaching his passing,
Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty addressed him on the first day of the New Year in the second year of the Daming era, saying:
"What sin have I committed that troubles you so much that you seek repentance?"
Zong said:
"Shun called his sons 'those who oppose their ministers,' and Yu said,
'If the myriad regions have transgressions, they lie with me alone.'"
How could Your Majesty possibly have any difference [of opinion]?
The Emperor was greatly pleased and established the regulations.
Dingwei, the third year of Taishi (the first year of Huangxing), the Dingwei year of the Wei dynasty.
Relying on the Empress Dowager’s restoration of power to him,
the Wei ruler finally attended to state affairs in person;
he changed the era name and applied himself diligently to governance.
Rewards and punishments were strict and clear;
those of pure integrity were promoted while the corrupt were dismissed,
and the state of Wei was praised for its good governance.
To the north of Chang’an, he established Yongning Temple on the Northern Terrace;
its seven-story pagoda was thirty *zhang* in height.
Furthermore, he commissioned a Buddha image forty-three chi in height at Tianguan Temple,
using seventy thousand jin of copper and six hundred jin of gold (Beishi, Basic Annals).

Wu-shen: The fourth year of Taishi; the Emperor completed the construction of Xianggong Temple. Ji-you, the second year of Huangxing: The fifth year of Taishi; the third year of Huangxing. Geng-xu: Song, the sixth year of Taishi; Wei, the fourth year of Huangxing. Xin-hai: Taishi, the seventh year; Wei, the first year of Yanxing (the year of Yanxing being the Xin-hai year), the sixth month. During this Xin-hai year, the High Ancestor, Emperor Xiaowen Hong of Wei—the eldest son of Emperor Changwen—received the abdicated throne at the age of five.
The founding ancestor, Emperor Xianwen Hong,
possessed vast wisdom that was fully realized from an early age; he was steadfast,
resolute, and possessed the power of decisive judgment.
He had a refined fondness for the studies of Huang-Lao and Buddhism,
and often harbored a desire to transcend the mundane world.
He wished to abdicate the throne in favor of his uncle, Prince Zongdui of Jingzhao, who held the office of Grand Official of the Central Capital.
Rencheng Wang Yunzi was the younger brother of [Prince] Tui.
He replied,
"The transmission from father to son has existed for a long time."
If the succession were granted to a collateral branch,
it would likely not have been the intention of the late Emperor;
therefore, [he] presented the imperial seal and ribbon to the Emperor.
He abdicated the throne to his crown prince, Hong.
When the crown prince was five years old,
he changed the era name to Yanxing.
The ministers submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, when the Han Gaozu ascended as Emperor,
he honored his father by bestowing upon him the title of Taishang Huang (Supreme August)."
This clarifies that Ming does not govern the empire.
Now that the Emperor is still young and impressionable,
the myriad affairs of state and great administration should still be presided over by Your Majesty.
I respectfully submit that his honorific title be proclaimed as the Supreme August Emperor (Taishang Huangdi).
He shall relocate to Chongguang Palace,
which is situated within the Northern Garden.
He constructed the Ruru Stūpa on the western mountain within the park.
While residing with the monks, he discussed the principles of Chan. *Weishu*, "Basic Annals of the Emperor":

Renzi, the first year of Taiyu (the fourth month), the Emperor passed away; the Crown Prince was installed at the age of ten. The second year of Yanxing: the Retired Emperor campaigned against the Rouran and defeated them. [This refers to] Song Mingdi.
He once commissioned a sixteen-foot golden image of the Buddha.
He maintained a fast at his morning meal and recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* daily.
Thereupon, moved by the appearance of śarīra relics,
he constructed the six sections of Hongpu Monastery.
[This was during the reign of] Emperor Cangwu, named Yu.
The Crown Prince of Emperor Ming ascended the throne at the age of ten and reigned for five years.
He frequently went out on excursions;
whenever there was even the slightest offense against his will,
he would immediately subject [the victim] to slaughter and dismemberment.
If for a single day they did not kill, they would feel distressed and unhappy;
the palace officials were filled with anxiety and dread, unable to find peace even in eating or breathing.
On the night of the wuzi day, in the seventh month of the ding-si year.
The Emperor commanded his attendants to watch for the Jade Husband as he waited for the Weaver Woman to cross the river;
"If you see him, report it to me.
If you do not, I shall have you executed."
That evening, Yu Fu waited until the Emperor was fast asleep;
together with Yang Wannian, he assassinated him.
The Emperor was fifteen years old.
The Right卫将军 (General of the Right Guard) Xiao Daocheng, by imperial decree issued by the Empress Dowager,
posthumously conferred the title of King of Cangwu upon Yu and welcomed Prince Zhun of Ancheng to ascend the throne as Emperor.
At that time, he was nine years old. In the fifth year of the Yuanhui era, the *gengzi* year;

in the first year of Yuanhui, the *guichou* year; in the third year of the Yanxing era of the Northern Wei, the *jiayin* year; and in the fourth year of Yanxing, the second year of Yuanhui. Prisoners in the Northern Wei jails were sometimes held for many years.
The ministers spoke of this at some length.
The Retired Emperor said,
"To allow prisoners to remain incarcerated is truly not a virtuous form of governance."
Is this not better than the indiscriminate excesses that occur in times of haste?
For when people suffer from grief and pain, they contemplate the good;
thus, the wise regard the prison as a hall of blessings.
I find this particularly distressing.
I wish for him to repent and reform, and thus I have shown him compassion and leniency.

(Beishi) Yimao: The third year of Yuanhui; the fifth year of Yanxing. Bingchen: The fourth year of Yuanhui; the first year of Chengming. In the second month, the Retired Emperor passed away, and Empress Dowager Feng again assumed the regency. This was during the reign of Emperor Xianwen of the Northern Wei.
He constructed Ming Temple within the clouds [of the mountains].
There were more than one thousand monasteries in the four directions, and seventy-seven thousand monks and nuns were ordained. (Northern History and the Hongming ji).
Shundi (Emperor Shun) succeeded the throne;
his courtesy name was Zhongmou.
He was the third son of Emperor Ming.
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Ancheng.
At the age of nine,
he ascended the throne and appointed Xiao Daocheng as Minister of Works and Director of the Secretariat.
Reigned for three years;
his age was twelve. The third year of Shengming, Wu-wu (478).
The second year of Shengming and the second year of Taihe.
In the second year of the Shengming era,
Wang Jian, the Right Chief Secretary, understood the intentions of Xiao Daocheng;
he then proposed that Yu Zheng, a Secretariat Drafter, compose an imperial edict.

He was promoted to General of the Pacification of the South (Jindao Cheng), Acting Commander-in-Chief of the Yellow Halberd (Jiahuang Yue), Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Within and Without (Da Zhongwai Zhumunshi), Grand Tutor (Taifu), and Concurrent Governor of Yangzhou.
In the third month of the Jiyi year,
Xiao Daocheng was appointed as Chancellor (Xiangguo) with the title of Grand Tutor.
He was appointed as the Chancellor over the hundred officials and enfeoffed as Duke of Qi over ten commanderies.
He was granted the nine emoluments,
and after four households had been added to his fief, his rank was advanced to King.
The Emperor issued an edict to abdicate the throne to the Prince of Qi,
but the Emperor refused to leave the palace.
Wang Jingze marshaled his troops in the court courtyard.
He entered to welcome the Emperor in a palanquin;
the Emperor wept as he abdicated,
swearing an oath, saying:
"I vow that in future lives and in every generation, I shall never again be born into the family of a Heavenly King.
Within the palace, there was great wailing.
The Emperor mounted a painted wheel-chariot and departed for the Eastern Residence.
The Minister of Works, Chu Yuan, and others presented the imperial seal and ribbon at the prayer-chamber and petitioned the Prince of Qi to ascend the throne as Emperor at the Southern Suburb,
while elevating the late Emperor Shun of Song to the status of Prince of Ruyin.
A palace was built in Danyang and stationed with troops for its defense.
The guards murdered the king and reported that he had died of illness.
Thus ended the eight sovereigns of the Song dynasty, totaling fifty-nine years, as they abdicated to the Qi.

The Qi dynasty, surnamed Xiao, had its capital at Jiankang. There were seven sovereigns—Emperor Taizu Gao Huangdi, Emperor Wudi, Prince Yulin, Prince Hailing, Emperor Mingdi, Prince Donghun, and Emperor Hedì—whose combined reign lasted twenty-three years. Emperor Taizu Gao Huangdi’s personal name was Daocheng.
His courtesy name was Shaobo.
He was a native of Lanling and a twenty-fourth-generation descendant of Xiao He of the Han dynasty.
He succeeded to the Song dynasty.
He reigned for four years.
His age was fifty-six. [His reign] lasted four Jianyuan years.
Gengshen (17th day of the month): The second year of Jianyuan; the fourth year of Taihe.
Xinyou (2nd day of the month): The third year of Jianyuan; the fifth year of Taihe.
Renxu (3rd day of the month): The fourth year of Jianyuan; on the third day of the third month, the Emperor passed away; the sixth year of Taihe.
The Emperor of Qi recited and upheld the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra;
on the eighth day of the fourth month, he cast a golden image of the Buddha.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he made offerings to the monks at all the monasteries and compiled the gazetteers of Zhiqu and Zhengguan Monasteries, as well as the Hongming ji (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification [of Buddhism]).
Regarding Emperor Shizu Wudi: his posthumous title was Shizu Wudi, and his personal name was Ze.
His courtesy name was Xuanyuan.
He was the eldest son of Emperor Gao.
He ascended the throne in the third month of the year Renwu.
He reigned for eleven years and lived to the age of fifty-four. The eleventh year of Yongming, the *gēnhài* year;

the first year of Yongming corresponds to the seventh year of Taihe, the *jiǎzǐ* year. In the second year of Yongming, the eighth year of Taihe, the Qi dynasty appointed Prince Ziliang of Jingling as General of National Protection (*hùguó jūn*) concurrently serving as Minister of Education (*sītú*).
He led troops and appointed assistants to govern the Western Regions.
Ziliang was pure and refined in his character, devoting himself to hosting guests who were men of talent and brilliance;
he held the followers of the Buddha in profound esteem.
He frequently invited monks to discourse on the Buddha-dharma;
the flourishing of the veneration for the Dharma was unprecedented in the region south of the Yangtze River.
The parents provided food for the assembly of monks and served water; according to the *Ji shu fang zhi* (Records of Local Geography in the Qi Dynasty):
Bingyin (the third year of the reign period): the fourth year of Yongming; the tenth year of Taihe.
Dingmao (the fourth year of the reign period): the fifth year of Yongming; the eleventh year of Taihe.
Wuchen (10th year): The 6th year of Yongming; the 12th year of Taixi. Jisi (11th year):
The 7th year of Yongming; the 13th year of Taixi. Gengwu (12th year):
The 8th year of Yongming; the 14th year of Taixi.

Xinwei (the 10th day of the 10th month): In the ninth year of Yongming and the fifteenth year of Taihe, Empress Dowager Feng Wenming passed away; the Emperor observed the three-year mourning period according to ancient rites.

Renshen (the 10th day of the 10th month): In the tenth year of Yongming and the sixteenth year of Taihe, the Wei Emperor commanded his ministers to deliberate on the order of precedence for the funeral procession.
High Jian, the Director of the Secretariat, deliberated and proposed that among emperors and kings,
none have ever regarded the Central Plains as the orthodox lineage based on the number of generations;
rather, they have determined right and wrong based on merit and demerit.
Thus, although Jie and Zhou were extremely tyrannical, they did not abolish the dynastic lineages of Xia and Shang;
and although Li and Hui were exceedingly corrupt, they did not harm the fortunes of Zhou and Jin.
Jin succeeded Wei as the Metal [Dynasty].
Zhao succeeds Jin as Water;
Yan succeeds Zhao as Wood;
Qin succeeds Yan as Fire.
After the fall of Qin,
the Wei dynasty then assumed sovereign authority over the remote north;
furthermore, the origin of the Wei clan name traces back to Xuanyuan.
Your humble servant considers that Xuan represents the virtue of Earth.
Li Biu, Director of the Imperial Library, Cui Guang, Lang of the Court of Historical Records,
and others submitted a memorial arguing that Shen-yuan had established friendly relations with Emperor Wu of Jin.
As for Huan and Mu,
their ambition was to assist the House of Jin;
thus, the mandate of the Simas came to an end at Guiguo (Jiagu).
Yet the Tuoba received their mandate in Yun and Dai.
In the past, when the Qin unified the world,
the Han still compared them to Gonggong.
The Zhou dynasty finally succeeded as the Fire Virtue (*huo-de*).
Now, consider that the Liu, Shi, and Fu houses were narrow in territory and brief in duration; Wei inherited their decline.
How could it possibly abandon Jin and adopt Earth as its virtue?
The Minister of Works Mu Liang and others all requested that the proposal of Liu Biao and his colleagues be followed.
Thereupon, a decree was issued establishing the Jin as the Water Virtue (Shuidé), beginning in the year Bingzi, the twentieth year of the Taihe era of the Wei dynasty.
The Emperor issued an edict stating that among the northern peoples, "tu" (earth) is called *tuo* and "shi" (clan) is called *ba*.
Since the ancestors of Wei descended from the Yellow Emperor and ruled by the virtue of earth (*tude*), they were therefore named the *Tuoba* clan.
Now, earth is the color of yellow,
the source of all things;
Xuan therefore changed his surname to Yuan.
The surnames of various meritorious ministers and ancient clans who had come from the Northern Dynasties were sometimes duplicated;
these were all changed.
Thereupon, the Babei (拔拔) clan was first changed to the Changsun (長孫) clan.
The Xi clan became the Xi clan;
the Yizhan clan became the Shusun clan;
and the Qiumuling clan became the Mu clan.
The Bupuguj clan became the Lu clan;
the Helai clan became the He clan;
and the Dugu clan became the Liu clan.
The He Lou clan became the Lou clan;
the Wu niu yu clan became the Yu clan;
and the Wei chi clan became the Wei clan.
The other changes he implemented were too numerous to record.
Upon reaching the reign of Emperor Kuang of the Western Wei,
he abolished the imperial era name and referred only to the "first year."
He further restored the family name to Tuoba.
Of the ninety-nine surnames that had been reduced to single characters, all were restored to their original forms.
In the year Jiashu, the Emperor of Wei traveled south past the tomb of Bi Gan.
He sacrificed with the "Grand Victim" (tai-lao).
He composed the inscription himself, saying:
"Alas! Great Hu, why do you not become my subject?"

Guiyou (the tenth day of the tenth month): In the seventh month of the eleventh year of Yongming of the Qi dynasty, the Emperor passed away. In the seventeenth year of Taihe of the Wei dynasty, the Emperor—because the land of Pingcheng was cold and snow fell there in the sixth month—proceeded to Ye in the tenth month to deliberate on the relocation of the capital to Luoyang. Pingcheng is the present-day site of the Western Capital road. This was the Qi Emperor Yulin, who was the Crown Grandson.
His taboo name was Zhāoyè.
He was the eldest son of Crown Prince Wénhuì and was enthroned in the seventh month of the year of Gēiyǒu.
In the first month of the Jiashu year, the reign title was changed to Longchang.
He did not attend to the affairs of government and acted with reckless abandon.
When the Marquis of Xichang, Liu Luan, remonstrated with him, he would not listen.
He then intended to execute Liu Luan.
In the seventh month, Luan led his troops into the Yunlong Gate and assassinated the Emperor in the western corridor.
By imperial decree of the Empress Dowager, he was posthumously deposed as King Yulin.
The second son of Emperor Wenhui, Prince Shao-wen of Xin’an, was invited to ascend the throne;
at that time, he was fifteen years of age.
The reign title was changed to Yanying.
Luan was enfeoffed as Duke of Xuancheng Commandery and promoted to the rank of Grand Tutor (Taifu) and Prince of Xuancheng.
In the tenth month, the Empress Dowager issued an edict stating:
"The Grand Tutor, Prince of Xuancheng, should enter to inherit the precious mandate.
The Emperor may be demoted and enfeoffed as the Prince of Hailing. In the eleventh month, the Prince of Hailing passed away.
Emperors Gao and Ming— Emperor Gao and Emperor Ming were the sons of Luan,
the son of the Prince of Shixian, the elder brother of Taizu. From their youth,
they were orphaned and noble-minded.
The Emperor nurtured him as his own son and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Xichang.
He held office for five years.
Age forty. The fourth year of Jianwu, the first year of Yongtai. Jiaxu.

In the tenth month of the first year of Jianwu, the era name was changed to Taixi. In the eleventh month of the eighteenth year [of Taixi], the Emperor arrived at Luoyang. Yihai. In the second year of Jianwu, the nineteenth year of Taixi, the Wei Emperor went to Lu to sacrifice to Confucius.
He selected one of the principal descendants of the Kong clan and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Chongsheng.
He visited the White Pagoda Temple in Xuzhou,
where Dharma Master Daodeng had entered nirvana.
An edict was issued expressing grief and lamentation;
one thousand rolls of silk were bestowed, and all the monks were invited to perform a seven-day ritual service in the capital. (From the *Wei Shu*).

Bingzi (14th year of Jianwu, 20th year of Taihe): During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty—who had changed his family name to Yuan—the Qi monk Huiji received two imperial edicts but did not rise to comply.
He established the Baolin Monastery on Mount Gui in the capital city.
He once composed a commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra* for Prince Wenxuan.
On the eleventh month, he entered nirvana.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* records that he lived to the age of eighty-five.

In the fourth year of Jianwu (the Dingchou year), the twenty-first year of Taihe, Emperor [Wu] established his son Ke as the Crown Prince. At that time, the Indian Buddhist Dhyāna Master Buddhatara from Central India—translated into Chinese as Jue-shou—resided at Mount Song, where he was devotedly fond of the mountain.
The Emperor issued an edict for [Bodhidharma] to establish Shaolin Monastery on Mount Shaoshi to reside there.
The master ordained the disciples Sengchou and Huiguang; this is recorded in the *Sengzhuan* and the *Sijiji*.
Xuyin. The first year of Yongtai (July), the Emperor passed away. During the twenty-second year of Taihe, the Qi Emperor was on the throne.
He observed the fast and cultivated the ten wholesome deeds;
he recited the two sutras of the Lotus and the Prajñāpāramitā,
and established a temple for taking refuge.
He commissioned a golden statue weighing one thousand *jin* and transcribed Buddhist scriptures and geographical treatises.
[This was done during the reign of] Emperor Donghun, Baojuan.
He was the third son of Emperor Ming.
In the eleventh month of the first year of the Jianwu era, he was established as the Crown Prince.
Upon ascending the throne, however, he lost his virtue.
He was assassinated after two years on the throne at the age of nineteen, in the second year of Yongyuan (the Jīmō year).

In the fourth month of the twenty-third year of Taihe, the first year of Yongyuan, Emperor Xiaowen of the Wei dynasty passed away; the Emperor then established monasteries and offered vegetarian feasts, founding Anxiang Monastery in Ye.
The palace ladies who observed the six fasts, diligently recited the scriptures, and aspired to the Way were permitted to leave the household life.
Emperor [Wenxuan] ordained fourteen thousand monks and nuns; this is recorded in the *Beishi* (History of the Northern Dynasties), "Biànzhèng" (Discriminating the Correct).

Gengchen: In the twelfth month of the second year of the Yongyuan era of the Qi dynasty, the Emperor was assassinated. Wei Shizong Xuanwu Di Ke, the second son of Xiaowen, ascended the throne. This was the first year of Jingming; at that time, Cui Huijing rebelled, seizing Guangling.
Xiao Yi, the Regional Inspector of Jingzhou, raised an army to come to the rescue.
He attacked and slew Huijing,
and was subsequently appointed Minister of the Secretariat.
The favored ministers, Ru Fazhen and others, fearing Emperor Yi’s authority and power, slandered him.
In the tenth month, they were granted death. Yi said:
My younger brother was in Yongzhou,
which caused deep concern for him from the imperial court.
Xiao Yan was serving as the Governor of Yongzhou at Xiangyang.
Upon hearing that his elder brother Yi had died, he raised his military banner that very day and assembled his forces.
The Emperor sent Xiao Yingwei to suppress him,
but Yingwei instead joined forces with Liu Yan.
In the third month of the following year, the Xin-si year, he received the Southern Prince of Kang at Jiangling and ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the era name to Zhongxing and appointed Xiao Yan as General of the Pacification of the East, with overall command of all military affairs for the campaign.
Empowered with the yellow battle-axe, he marched directly to Jiankang.
In the twelfth month, the Emperor was killed.
Xiao Yan, acting on the command of Empress Dowager Xuande, deposed him and demoted him to the rank of Prince Donghun.
Emperor He: His posthumous name was Baorong.
He was the eighth son of Emperor Ming and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nankang.
He departed from Sili and entered Jingzhou.
In the third month of spring in the year of Xinsi, he ascended the throne as Emperor.
In the first month of spring in the year of Renwu, he issued an edict promoting Xiao Yan, the Grand Marshal, to the rank of Chancellor (Xiangguo) with authority over all state affairs.
The Governor of Yangzhou was enfeoffed as Duke of Liang over ten commanderies and granted the nine emblems of investiture.
Within one month, his rank was advanced to that of King.
When the Emperor returned eastward, he reached Gushu, the present-day city of Taiping in Jiangdong.
He issued an edict to abdicate the throne in favor of the Prince of Liang, who then ascended the imperial throne.
[The former ruler] subsequently deposed the Emperor as the Prince of Baling and killed him.
He reigned for one year.
His reign lasted sixteen years.

In the first year of Zhongxing (the *xin-si* year), the Emperor ascended the throne in the third month; the following year, in the second month, he abdicated to the Liang. In the second year of Jingming, the Right Qi had seven rulers for a total of twenty-three years before it was ceded to the Liang.

The Liang dynasty was founded at Jiankang by those surnamed Xiao. There were four sovereigns: Gaozu Wudi, Dazong Jianwen Di, Shizu Yuan Di, and Jing Di. Regarding Gaozu Wudi: his posthumous title was Gaozu Wudi, and his personal name was Yan.
His courtesy name was Shuda.
A native of Lanling,
he served the Qi dynasty and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Liang.
He succeeded to the imperial succession.
He occupied the throne for forty-eight years and lived to the age of eighty-six.

[The years of his reign were: the eighteenth of Tianjian, the seventh of Putong, the second of Datong, the sixth of Zhongdatong, the eleventh of Dading, the first of Zhongdading, and the third of Tianqing.

Renwu (壬午): The first year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty. In the second month, the era name was changed. An imperial edict [stated that] the Great Being Bao Gong (寶公) was traveling to transform beings outside the palace precincts and forbade him from being obstructed. His original biography [records]: Jingming Year 3 (癸未), the second year of Tianjian; Jingming Year 4, Dharma Master Yun Guang (雲光法師) of Fayun Temple in Jiankang.
Whenever he preached the sutras, heavenly flowers fell like snowflakes.
At the Hanguang Hall, the Emperor burned a memorial petition for the preaching of Master Yun Guang Zhigong.
The following day, when the vegetarian feast was prepared, Zhigong arrived there.
The Emperor issued an edict stating: "The Great Being Baozhi confines his traces within the defilements of the mundane world,
yet his spirit wanders in profound stillness."
Water and fire cannot scorch or moisten them;
snakes and tigers cannot invade or frighten them.
In terms of their understanding of Buddhist principles, they are at the level of the *śrāvaka* and above.
Regarding their reclusion, those who have attained the heights of transcendence—how can they be subjected to empty suspicion and avoidance based on worldly laws and common sentiments?

From now on, let them be appointed to official duties within and outside the court to propagate the transformative teachings; this is further recorded in the *Shenggan zhuan* (Biographies of Sacred Responses) of the *Nanshi*.
The Compassionate Method of Repentance: When the Emperor of the Liang Dynasty was first serving as the Regional Inspector of Yongzhou, his consort, Lady Xi, was by nature cruel and jealous;
she had already passed away by this time.
He transformed into a giant python and entered the inner palace,
appearing in the Emperor's dreams to seek deliverance.
The Emperor consulted Buddhist scriptures and composed the *Cibei Daochang Chanfa* (The Ritual of Repentance for the Compassionate Way) in ten fascicles.
He requested the monks to perform a ritual of repentance and prostration.
The lady transformed into a celestial being and departed through the air, offering thanks to the Emperor.
The ritual for this repentance was practiced in the world and is known as the "Repentance of the Liang Emperor.

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Tianjian era (the first year of the Zhengshi era of the Wei dynasty), in the year Jiashen, the Emperor of Liang led the clergy and laity to ascend the Chongyun Hall.
He revealed his repentance and personally composed a vow,
offering it to the Buddha and the Triple Gem.
In the beginning, he established Guangzhai Temple.
He cast a large golden-bronze Buddha image and enshrined it for worship. [This is recorded in] the *Hongming ji*.

In the year Yiyou, the fourth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty (the second year of the Zhengshi era of the Wei), at the Great Water and Land Offering at Mount Jin, the Emperor of Liang first dreamed that a monk told him: [...text continues...]
"Beings in the six realms and four modes of birth are undergoing great suffering and affliction.
Why do you not perform the Great Water and Land Feast for them to rescue and deliver them?
The Emperor questioned the various śramaṇas.
Master Baizhi said,
"Seeking the sutras must surely have its own causes and conditions.
The Emperor then took the Buddhist scriptures and personally read through them.
He composed the ritual text for the rite of creation;
it was completed after three years.
One night, holding the text and extinguishing his lamp, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
If this textual principle accords with the noble path,
may this lamp illuminate itself when I bow and rise;
otherwise, the ritual remains incomplete.
The lamps remained as dim as before.
Having finished speaking, he prostrated himself on the ground once;
immediately, all the lamps and candles were brightly lit.
On the fifteenth day of the second month of this year, the ritual was performed according to the prescribed rites at Jinshan Temple in present-day Zhenjiang.
The Emperor attended the ceremony in person and issued an edict for Vinaya Master You to proclaim the text.
His benefits permeated both the hidden and the manifest worlds, and his teachings are followed to this day; see the *Weijiang Wencji* (Collected Works of Wei Jiang).

In the fifth year of the Tianjian era, the year Bingxu (506 CE), the Prince of Liang, Xiao Tong, was born; at five years of age, he was able to recite the Five Classics entirely. In the fourth year of the Zhengshi era, the sixth year of the Tianjian era (507 CE), the Emperor of Liang, relying on the supernatural power of Master Bao, beheld the suffering aspects of the hells.
Question: "How can one bring it to rest?
Master Bao replied:
"Only when the sound of the bell is heard does his suffering momentarily cease."
Thereupon, an edict was issued to all monasteries throughout the realm to strike the bells, prolonging their resonance. The Basic Annals record:

Wuzi (the 5th day of the 10th month), the seventh year of the Tianjian era, the first year of the Yongping era. Jichou (the 29th day of the 10th month), the eighth year of the Tianjian era, the second year of the Yongping era. At that time, the Indian Śramaṇa Bodhiruci arrived from the Western Regions during the Wei dynasty.
He was known as Jue Xi.
By imperial decree, he resided at Ziji Hall to translate treatises.
Emperor Wei lectured on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra at Shiqian Hall.
At that time, the Wei court exclusively venerated the teachings of Śākyamuni.
In Luoyang, in addition to the Chinese śramaṇas, there were more than three thousand people who had come from the Western Regions.
The Emperor separately established Yongming Temple for them.
He resided there in more than a thousand rooms.
During the Yanchang era,
there were approximately thirteen thousand Buddhist temples throughout the various prefectures and commanderies.
The number of monks reached two million (*Beishi*).

Gengyin, the ninth year of the Tianjian era: the Emperor issued an edict to the śramaṇa Baochang to compile the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* in eighty-one fascicles. In the third year of the Yongping era of the Wei dynasty, the Liang Emperor established the Great Aijing Temple on Mount Zhong for his ancestor, Emperor Wen.
He provided alms for a thousand monks and presented offerings to the Empress Dowager. On the western bank of Qingxi, he established the Dazhidu Monastery,
where various nuns lectured and recited the Hongming ji four times every season.

Xinmao (the 10th day of the 10th month): In the tenth year of Tianjian, the fourth year of Yongping, the Emperor of Liang dispatched Hao Qian and others to the kingdom of India to invite a sandalwood image of the Buddha.
Its king carved a replica of the image and entrusted it to Qian.
In this year, he arrived in Jiankang.
The Emperor welcomed him to the Taiji Hall to perform a *zhai* ceremony and ordain monks;
a general amnesty was proclaimed and the killing of living beings was prohibited.
From this point on, the Emperor followed a vegetarian diet and renounced desire (*Gantong lu*).

*Renchen* (the year 512): the eleventh year of the Tianjian era and the first year of the Yan'chang era. The Great Master Fu was born on the eighth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Jianwu era of Emperor Ming of the Qi dynasty at the home of Fu Xuanci in Shuanglin Township, Yiwu County, Wuzhou.
His name was Xi;
his courtesy name was Xuánfēng;
his style name was Shànhuì.
In this year, the sixteenth year, Renchen,
he married Lady Liu and had two sons:
Po-jian and Po-cheng.
