In the first year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, at the age of twenty-four,
while traveling upstream at Jiating Pond,
the Śramaṇa from the Western Regions, Sengtoutuo, led him to the water’s edge to observe his reflection.
The Dharma of the Circular Halo and the Jewel Canopy was flourishing most intensely;
his heart was moved by it,
and he consequently went to the summit of Mount Song.
He built a hermitage to dwell in between two *śāla* trees,
which he named "The Twin Forest" (*Śālavana*).
He styled himself the "Future Mahāsattva of Liberation and Good Wisdom Under the Twin Forest Trees."
They cultivate fruits and vegetables;
they work as laborers for others,
returning home at night after working during the day.
Together with his wife Miaoguang, he expounded the Buddha-dharma and practiced asceticism for seven years.
This continued until the second year of the Datong era.
As his disciples increased in number and the Great Being (Mahāsattva) desired to guide the multitudes of sentient beings,
he transformed his wife and children and sold himself to initiate the first great assembly.
In the sixth year of the Zhongdatong era, the Great Being dispatched his disciple Fu Yang to the imperial court to present a letter.
An imperial edict was issued for him to proceed to the capital.
He arrived in Jiankang in the intercalary twelfth month.
When the Emperor heard of the Great Master’s divine and extraordinary nature, he was deeply impressed.
The gates had all been pre-locked;
however, the Great Being struck one gate with a wooden mallet, and all the gates opened.
He entered directly into the Hall of Kind Words.
The Emperor asked, "From whom did you receive the teachings?
He replied,
"From no one."
The Master had no teacher;
there was nothing for him to attend to.
When the Emperor had finished providing him with food, [he departed].
He ascended Mount Zhong to Dinglin Temple;
by imperial decree, he was provided with all necessary provisions.
In the fifth year of the Datong era, the Great Being entered the capital once again.
In the third month, the Emperor summoned him to the Shouguang Hall for an audience.
They discussed the ultimate truth together,
and the Mahāsattva said:
The sound ceased but did not die away.
The Emperor again requested that he lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The Great Being struck the table once with his hand and rose.
The Emperor did not understand and requested him to lecture again.
The Great Being then called for the wooden clapper, ascended the seat,
recited forty-nine verses, and immediately departed.
Even today, this verse is still recited in the world.
One day, when the Great Being (the Bodhisattva) was wearing a crown, a monastic robe, and sandals,
the Emperor asked, "Is this a monk?"
The scholar pointed his finger at his crown;
the Emperor asked, "Is this the Way?
The scholar then pointed his finger at his straw sandals.
The Emperor asked, "Is this the secular way?
The Master pointed to his patched robe and, taking leave of the palace, returned home.
In the tenth year of the Datong era, the Great Being established a great Dharma assembly.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he universally repents for and extinguishes their karmic afflictions and sufferings,
so that they may swiftly attain liberation.
Since the titles of the Buddha’s scriptures are numerous and extensive, some people may be unable to read them all.
He then constructed a multi-storied niche;
in its center he erected a pillar,
opened eight sides, and filled them with various scriptures.
It is called the Wheel Treasury (Cakrakaraṇḍa).
He established a vow, saying:
"Whoever enters the gate of my treasury..."
May one never lose the human body throughout all successive lifetimes.
One who has resolved to attain Bodhicitta is able to push the wheel-treasury.
This is no different from the merit of reciting various sutras.
The installation of the Wheel Repository (Lunzang) featuring an image of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) originated from this.
In the fourth month of the first year of the Dajian era of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty, the Great Being addressed the two Dharma Masters Pujian and Pucheng, saying:
"I have come from the fourth heaven.
To deliver sentient beings,
you all must carefully guard the three karmas."
Diligently practice the six perfections and perform the rite of repentance to avoid falling into the three miserable realms.
On the twenty-fourth day, he entered nirvana at the age of seventy-three;
his remains were cremated and the relics were collected.
The cranial bone was enshrined at the Twin Śāla Trees,
which has now become a great site of practice (mahā-maṇḍala).
The verses of the Great Being circulate throughout the world.
He once composed the "Inscription on the Mind-King" (*Cittarāja-gāthā*). Its words say:
"Contemplate the mind as the empty king."
Profound and subtle, it is difficult to fathom;
it is without name and without form,
yet possesses great supernormal power.
It can extinguish a thousand calamities and accomplish ten thousand virtues;
though its essential nature is empty, it remains so.
It can bestow the principles of the Dharma;
when observed, it has no form;
when called upon, it has sound.
Acting as a great general of the Dharma,
he transmitted the sutras through the precepts of the mind;
like the flavor of salt in water.
The blue pigment within the lacquer is certainly present,
yet its form is not seen.
The mind-king is likewise:
it dwells within the body and enters and exits through the gate of the face.
Responding to things according to their dispositions,
one acts with sovereign mastery and unimpededness;
all that is undertaken is accomplished.
Having realized the fundamental consciousness-mind,
one perceives the Buddha through that consciousness-mind;
this mind is the Buddha.
This Buddha is this mind;
in every thought-moment, the Buddha-mind is present.
The Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha.
If you wish to achieve success early,
restrain yourself with the mind of precepts;
purify your discipline and purify your mind.
The mind is itself the Buddha.
Apart from this sovereign mind,
there is no other Buddha.
If you seek to attain Buddhahood,
do not defile yourself with a single thing;
though the nature of the mind is empty.
The essence of greed and hatred is real;
by entering this Dharma-gate,
one attains Buddhahood while sitting upright.
Having reached the other shore,
they attain the pāramitās;
these are the true practitioners who yearn for the Way.
Observe your own mind;
know that the Buddha is within,
and do not seek him outwardly.
Mind is Buddha; Buddha is mind.
When the mind is enlightened, it recognizes Buddha.
Clearly understand that consciousness is mind;
apart from mind there is no Buddha,
and apart from Buddha there is no mind.
None but a Buddha can fathom this;
it is beyond all capacity.
To cling to emptiness and stagnate in quiescence is a delusion.
Sinking and floating within this [samsara],
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas thoroughly understand it and thereby find peace of mind.
The Great Being Mingxin realized this profound resonance;
his body and mind became wondrous in their fundamental nature.
Since nothing can alter it,
the wise therefore allow the mind to rest in its natural freedom.
Do not say that the mind-king is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature,
for it is capable of animating the physical body.
It manifests as both the false and the true;
it is neither existent nor non-existent;
its concealment and manifestation are indeterminate.
Although the nature of the mind is empty,
it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely; therefore, I exhort you.
Be diligent in guarding against evil.
Even if you act for but a single moment,
you will once again drift and sink.
The pure mind-intelligence is like the gold of the world;
it is the Dharma-treasury of Prajñā.
It is entirely within body and mind;
it is the unconditioned treasure of the Dharma,
neither shallow nor deep.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have fully realized this fundamental mind; should anyone encounter it through the conditions of affinity, [they shall likewise realize it].

Neither past, future, nor present. Gui-si (10th day): Liang Tianjian 12th year; Wei Yanchang 2nd year. Jia-wu (11th day): Tianjian 13th year; Yanchang 3rd year. Yi-wei (12th day): Liang Tianjian 14th year; Wei Yanchang 4th year. In the first month, the Emperor passed away. Crown Prince Xu ascended the throne at the age of six. His mother, Empress Dowager Hu, assumed the regency and recited the *Yanshou Jing* (Sūtra on Prolonging Life). [Biography of] Dharma Master Shi Zhizang of the Liang dynasty.
When he first traveled to Jiankang,
the Emperor summoned him for an audience and paid him profound respect.
The Emperor established a pagoda and temple for the Great Being Baozhi, naming it Kaishan.
He was commanded to reside in a hidden place.
There he encountered a strange man who said,
"The Master's lifespan shall end at thirty-one years of age."
Zang exhausted his essence in practicing the Way,
specializing in the recitation of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
When he reached the year of his destined misfortune, suddenly a voice spoke from the air:
"By virtue of the power of Prajñā, you shall obtain double your lifespan.
Indeed, his life ended at sixty-two years of age.
By imperial decree, he was buried on the left side of Baogong Temple on Dulong Mountain.
Consequently, both monastics and laity throughout the region south of the Yangtze River all recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, resulting in accounts of spiritual responses.

In the year Bingshen, the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era, Emperor Xiaoming (r. 516–528), the second son of Emperor Xuanwu of the Northern Wei dynasty, commissioned Yaoguang Temple in the first year of the Xiping era (516); however, its construction was not yet complete.
In this year, Empress Dowager Hu established Yongning Temple;
all [these temples] were situated beside the palace.
She also constructed Shiku Temple at the mouth of the Yi Pass.
There was one golden image sixteen feet (one zhang liu chi) in height,
ten images of medium human size,
and two jade images.
He constructed a nine-storied stupa ninety zhang in height,
with its pinnacle further rising ten zhang.
On quiet nights, the sound of the bells could be heard for ten *li*.
Since the Buddha-dharma entered China,
there has never been such a flourishing state of stūpas and temples (*Beishi*).
Stone Image: The ten-jian stone Buddha image at Yinyue Temple in Yuezhou during the Liang dynasty.
Originally, during the Jianwu era of Emperor Ming of the Qi dynasty, the monk Senghu completed its construction, but he passed away while the face remained unfinished.
Subsequently, Sengshu succeeded him and continued the unfinished work.
Upon reaching this point, Prince Jian'an donated gold and entrusted it to Sengyou to complete it;
this is recorded in the "Stone Buddha Inscription."

Dingyou (1st year): The sixteenth year of Tianjian and the second year of Xiping; the names of the Buddhas. By imperial decree of the Liang Emperor, Dharma Master Sengshao compiled the *Catalogue of the Various Scriptures* in four fascicles.
An imperial decree ordered the śramaṇa Baochang to compile the *Biqiuni zhuan* (Biographies of Bhikṣuṇīs) in four fascicles.
He also compiled the *Zhongjing foming* (Names of Buddhas in Various Scriptures) in three fascicles.
In the third month of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor issued an edict to the weaving officials.
Brocade and embroidery must not depict the forms of immortals, birds, or beasts.
If the cutting and tailoring deviate from benevolence and forbearance, it violates the imperial records. Regarding the vegetarian feast:
in the fourth month, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty issued an edict stating that the use of sacrificial animals in the ancestral temples was an impediment to the Way of the幽冥 (the unseen realm).
It was deemed appropriate that these should all be made of flour.
The Eight Ministers of State, in their court deliberation, proposed substituting large dried meat for the "one great beast.
In the tenth month, an imperial edict stated that since the ancestral temple still used dried meat and cured meat, they were to be further discussed and replaced.
Thereupon, large cakes were substituted for large dried meats,
and all other items were entirely composed of fruits and vegetables according to the Imperial Records.
The practice of those who now prepare vegetarian meals is fundamentally derived from this.

Wu-xu (the year 518 CE): The *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism), compiled by the Śramaṇa and Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang Dynasty during the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era and the first year of the Shenguī era.
From the beginning of the Qi dynasty, he extensively propagated the Vinaya teachings.
Upon this, the Emperor showed him profound reverence and respect.
As Sengyou’s age advanced and he suffered from foot ailments,
the Emperor issued an imperial decree for him to enter the inner palace in a sedan chair to bestow the precepts upon the six palaces.
He entered nirvana on the twenty-sixth day of the fifth month at the age of seventy-four.
The Master’s works include the *Sanzang ji*, the *Fayuan ji*, the *Shijie ji*, the *Shijia pu*, and the *Hongming ji*.
This was compiled alongside the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

In the year Jihai—the eighteenth year of the Tianjian era and the second year of the Shenguī era—Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty bestowed upon Dharma Master Huìyuè the honorary title: [The Emperor said: "..."
The Way relies on people for its propagation;
principles are not bestowed in vain,
and practice depends on personal engagement.
When the people have faith, then [the Way] is established.
Dharma Master Huiyao’s virtue surpassed that of the world.
The Way spread even to the dark realms.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he invited the Master to the Dengjue Hall to receive the Bodhisattva precepts and further established a Great Unrestricted Assembly.
After the Emperor himself received the precepts,
he ate only one meal per day, consisting solely of vegetables.
While residing in the palace quarters,
he maintained himself as pure as a śramaṇa.
In the fourth year of the Putong era, an imperial decree was issued that the title "Dharma Master" (fashi) should not be used to address the monk Huiyue within or outside the court.
His posthumous title was Zhìzhě (Wise One).
The practice of monks adopting posthumous titles began with Dharma Master [Hui]ji.
On the sixth day of the ninth month in the first year of Emperor Wendi’s Datong era, the National Preceptor Zhìzhě Huìyuē entered nirvana.
He was eighty-four years old;
his monastic seniority was sixty-three summers.
The Emperor, wearing plain mourning dress, attended his funeral.
The court suspended its affairs for seven days to mourn him.
On the twenty-ninth day of that month, an imperial decree was issued to bury him at Dulongsan, to the left of Master Ji’s tomb.
Forty-eight thousand people who had received the precepts from the Master donned the *sīmā* (three-month) mourning dress and wept as they escorted his remains to the burial site.

In the second year of the Datong era of Emperor Wu, an imperial edict changed the name of Zhushan Li, where the Master resided, to Zhizhe Li. This is recorded in the *Beiji* (Basic Annals) of the Liang Dynasty, as well as in the *Master’s Stele Inscription* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
Furthermore, the *Biographies of Famous Monks* in twenty fascicles was compiled by Imperial Censor Pei Ziyě under the command of the Liang Emperor.
Shi Huijiao of Kuaiji compiled the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) in fourteen fascicles.
Spanning from the Yongping era of the Han dynasty to this year, it covers a period of approximately four hundred and fifty years and records the lives of two hundred and fifty-seven individuals.
More than two hundred individuals are included as supplementary entries;
[this work] was incorporated into the Tripitaka and circulated under the title *Weijiang ji*.
Empress Dowager Hu of the Wei dynasty ordered that a five-story pagoda be constructed in each prefecture.
Various kings and high-ranking officials each established monasteries in Luoyang.
The Empress Dowager frequently provided vegetarian feasts and alms (Beishi). Gengzi:
the first year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty; the first year of the Zhengguang era, when the Wei Emperor donned the ceremonial cap of adulthood.

The *Beishi* (History of the Northern Dynasties) and the *Bianzheng lu* (Record of the Rectification of Orthodoxy) record that the śramaṇa Tanwujie and the Daoist Jiang Bin were commissioned to lecture on the Way within the imperial palace.
Regarding the Venerable Bodhidharma, the First Patriarch of this land and twenty-eighth patriarch of the Western Heaven: he was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India.
He was of the Kṣatriya caste;
his original name was Bodhitāra.
When the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, arrived in that country...
He accepted the offerings from his father,
the king, and received the pearl bestowed upon him to test his words.
His grandfather said to him:
"You have already attained direct realization of all dharmas.
Now, 'Dharma' carries the meaning of 'penetration.
You should therefore be named Bodhidharma."
He consulted Maṃjuśrī, saying:
"Now that I have attained the Dharma,
to which country should I go to perform the Buddha-work?"
The Patriarch said,
"Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not travel far yet.
Stay in the Southern Heaven and wait for sixty-seven years after my passing."
When he was born in the eastern land of China, he established the great music of the Dharma.
Those who protected bodhi were beyond counting;
Ma, therefore, reverently received and followed these teachings and principles.
He served in attendance for nearly forty years;
until shortly before his master passed away,
he propagated the teachings in his native land.
At that time, there were two masters:
one named Buddhajīva and the other named Buddhasānta.
Both had studied together under Buddhabhadra in the meditative contemplations of the Hīnayāna;
however, after Buddhabhadra encountered the Venerable Prajñātāra,
he abandoned the Lesser Vehicle and turned toward the Mahāyāna.
Together with Dharmatrāta, they transformed beings in tandem,
being called the "Two Gates of Ambrosia.
Yet, because the Buddha was vastly superior, his followers were further divided into six schools.
The first is called the School of Characteristics;
the second, the School of Non-characteristics;
and the third, the School of Samādhi and Prajñā.
The fourth is the school of Precept Practice;
the fifth is the school of Non-Attainment;
the sixth is the school of Quiescence.
Each sealed their own understanding and separately unfolded their sources of transformation.
Bodhidharma lamented that those six schools were entangled in false views.
He went to each of them in turn to transform and instruct them.
The group of six were awakened;
they all vowed to take refuge.
At that time, there was a king named Vijaya,
the nephew of Māra;
he had initially placed his faith in non-Buddhist paths.
Bodhidharma converted him and led him back to the orthodox path.
Subsequently, reflecting that the conditions in China were ripe and the time for his mission had arrived,
he took leave of the King of Ceylon.
The King prepared for him a great ship,
laden with precious treasures, which he launched upon the vast ocean;
after three cycles of winter and summer, it reached the South Sea.
This was the twenty-first day of the ninth month in the first year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty;
the *Chuandeng lu* states it was the seventh year, but here we follow the *Zhengzong ji*.
Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, welcomed him with ceremonial rites and submitted a memorial to announce the event.
Upon reviewing the memorial, Emperor Wu dispatched an envoy to welcome and invite him.
On the first day of the tenth month of the following year, he arrived in Jiankang.
The Emperor asked:
"Since my accession to the throne, the temples I have built, the scriptures I have transcribed, and the monks I have ordained are beyond counting. What merit do these bring?
The Patriarch replied: "The merit lies in the mind that gives rise to them."
These are merely the minor fruits of humans and devas;
like a shadow following a form,
they exist but are not real.
The Emperor asked,
"What constitutes true merit?
The Patriarch replied:
"Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect, its essence being inherently empty and quiescent.
The Emperor asked:
"What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?"
The Patriarch said,
"Vast and open, there is no sage.
The Emperor said:
"Who is it facing me?
The Patriarch replied,
"I do not know."
The Emperor did not understand; the Patriarch, knowing that his timing was not yet harmonious with the ruler's,
departed secretly for the north of the Yangtze River on the nineteenth day of that month.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived in Luoyang;
this was the second year of the Zhengguang era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty.
He took up residence at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song.
He sat facing a wall.
Although Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty issued three edicts summoning him,
Sengzhu never rose to leave.
The Emperor then presented him with a *mohana* (ground-grinding) *kāṣāya* robe.
The Patriarch likewise would not accept it, even after three refusals.
When the Emperor insisted on bestowing it, there was a monk named Shenguang.
He had read extensively across many books and was skilled at discussing the profound principles of the mysteries.
Upon hearing that his grandfather was residing there, he went to pay his respects and seek instruction.
On the ninth night of the twelfth month of that year, it snowed heavily throughout the day.
Tanyouguang stood upright in the courtyard until dawn; by then, the accumulated snow had reached above his knees.
His grandfather took pity on him and asked:
"You have stood in the snow for a long time;
what do you seek? Guang wept and said:
"I pray that the Upādhyāya, out of compassion, will open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all classes of beings.
Thus he spoke with such earnestness that he even severed his own arm.
The Patriarch therefore changed his name to Huike.
Huike then asked,
"May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas?"
The Patriarch said:
"The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.
One may say:
"My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to bring peace to my mind.
The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind and I will pacify it for you."
After a long silence, he said,
"I have sought the mind, but it is utterly unattainable.
The Patriarch said:
"I have finished settling your mind for you.
After a long time, the Patriarch briefly expounded upon the four practices for entering the Way according to the Mahāyāna for Huìkě and the others.
The words were as follows:
Now, there are many paths for entering the Way;
to summarize them, they do not exceed two kinds:
first, entry through principle (li-rù).
Second, entering the principle through practice.
"Entering" means awakening to the fundamental tenet by relying on the teachings.
It refers to having deep faith that all living beings share the same true nature.
It is merely obscured by adventitious delusive thoughts and thus cannot manifest clearly;
if one abandons the delusive and returns to the true, it will become evident.
Abiding in contemplation as if fixed upon a wall, there is neither self nor other;
ordinary beings and sages are equal, remaining firm and unshakable,
no longer following the teachings of words and texts.
This is precisely in accord with the principle;
it is free from discrimination,
tranquil, and unconditioned— this is called "entry into the principle."

There are four types of practice for entering [the path]: first, the practice of requiting grievances; second, the practice of following conditions; third, the practice of seeking nothing; and fourth, the practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the practitioner who requites grievances:
when a person practicing the Way undergoes suffering, they should reflect as follows.
Throughout countless kalpas since the distant past, I have abandoned the fundamental for the peripheral,
wandering through the various realms and giving rise to resentment and hatred in infinite instances;
though I commit no offense now, [the consequences of those past acts remain].
"This is the ripening of the fruit of my past misfortunes and evil karma;
it cannot be seen or bestowed by gods or humans.
I accept and endure it with a willing heart."
There is no resentment whatsoever.
When one contemplates in this way, it accords with principle.
Because one takes the offender as the basis for advancing on the Path, it is called the "Practice of Repaying Offenses."
Regarding those who act in accordance with conditions:
sentient beings lack a self and are driven by the turning of conditions and karma;
they experience both suffering and pleasure equally, all arising from conditions.
If one obtains superior rewards such as honor and fame,
these are all the result of past causes from former lives;
when the conditions are exhausted, they vanish back into nothingness— what cause for joy is there?
Gain and loss follow conditions, yet the mind neither increases nor decreases;
unmoved by the wind of joy, one silently accords with the Way.
This is called the practitioner who acts in accordance with conditions and seeks nothing.
The people of the world are long lost in delusion, greedily attached to everything they encounter.
The wise awaken to the truth and find peace in non-action;
seeing that all phenomena are empty, they harbor no expectations.
Dwelling long in the three realms is like being in a burning house;
having a body entails suffering—whom can it ever bring peace?
To thoroughly understand this state is to cease discursive thought and seek nothing more.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All seeking is suffering;
non-seeking is bliss.
This means that non-seeking and the pursuit of truth constitute the practice of the Way.
Therefore it is called "the practice of seeking nothing," which is termed "practice in accordance with the Dharma.
The principle of inherent purity is what constitutes the Dharma.
According to this principle, all characteristics are empty;
there is no defilement and no attachment, neither "this" nor "that.
As the Sūtra says: "In phenomena, there is no self."
Because they are free from the stain of self,
the wise believe and understand this principle;
they should act in accordance with the Dharma.
The essence of the Dharma is free from stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth;
practicing the giving of dāna with a mind devoid of parsimony,
one thoroughly understands the three kinds of emptiness.
Neither leaning nor clinging,
he merely manifests as Vimalakīrti to transform sentient beings without grasping at signs;
this constitutes his own practice.
Furthermore, it benefits others and adorns the path to Bodhi.
As it is with the practice of giving,
so it is with the remaining five perfections.
To eliminate deluded thoughts, one practices the six perfections while remaining without any practice;
this is called "Dharma-practice.
Later, the Patriarch wished to return to India.
The Master addressed his disciples, saying:
"The time has nearly come.
You should each speak of what you have attained."
At that time, each of the attendants presented their own insights.
Finally, Huike stepped forward, performed three prostrations,
and stood in his place.
The Patriarch then turned toward Huìkě and said to him:
"In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to the Great Being Kāśyapa;
it was passed down through successive entrustments until it reached me."
I now entrust this to you;
you should protect and uphold it.
Furthermore, I bestow upon you this kāṣāya as a token of the Dharma.
Each has its own symbolic meaning, which should be understood accordingly. One may say:
"I request that the Master point these out for me."
The Patriarch said:
"Internally, the Dharma-seal is transmitted to accord with and verify the mind;
externally, the kashaya robe is bestowed to establish the fundamental tenet."
Anticipating the doubts and disputes of future generations,
he pointed to those from the Western Heaven as "I" and spoke of you as "the sons of this land."
By what means was the Dharma obtained? By what was it realized?
You shall now receive this dharma of the robe.
In the future, it will be difficult for people to believe;
simply produce this robe along with my verse of the Dharma to serve as clear evidence.
His transformations were unimpeded.
Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa,
the transmission of his robe will cease.
The Dharma pervades the *sāhasra* world-system;
those who understand the Way are many,
but those who practice the Way are few.
Those who discourse on principle are many;
those who penetrate principle are few.
Yet there are more than ten million who secretly accord with it and silently realize it.
You should propagate this teaching and not disparage those who have not yet awakened.
A single thought that turns back toward the source is identical to original attainment.
Listen to my verse:
I originally came to this land to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings;
one flower opens into five petals.
The result is spontaneously accomplished.
As for the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*,
it is indeed the Tathāgata’s ultimate discourse on the essentials of the Dharma.
It may also be used to instruct, inspire, awaken, and lead others in this world.
I now entrust it to you entirely.
It was for this purpose that I originally departed from South India to come here to this Eastern Land.
Seeking people for the sake of the Dharma,
our meeting has not yet been harmonized;
I am as if ignorant and as if mute.
"Now that I have received your transmission,
my purpose is fulfilled.
He then went with his disciples to Qiansheng Temple at Yumen and stayed for three days.
There was Yang Xuanzhi, the Governor of Qicheng,
who asked Sengzu:
"In the Five Indias of the Western Heaven, the lineage of masters is considered the ancestral source."
"What is that Way like?
The Patriarch replied,
"It is to clarify the mind-source of the Buddha."
"One whose practice and understanding correspond is called a patriarch.
He asked again,
"What is it like beyond this?"
The Patriarch said:
"One must clarify the minds of others and know their past and present;
one should not weary of existence or non-existence, nor take anything from the Dharma."
Neither virtuous nor foolish, without delusion and without enlightenment.
One who can understand this is called an Ancestor.
It is also said:
I, your disciple, have turned my heart toward the Triple Gem for many years.
Having just heard your words, I am at a loss as to what to do.
I pray that you, out of compassion, will reveal the essential principles of our school.
The Patriarch, knowing his sincerity,
immediately spoke a verse, saying:
"One does not see evil and give rise to aversion."
Nor do they observe what is good and strive to practice it;
nor do they abandon wisdom to associate with the foolish;
nor do they cast aside delusion to pursue enlightenment.
Reaching the Great Way, they transcend all measure;
penetrating the Buddha-mind, they manifest deliverance.
They do not share the same orbit as ordinary beings or sages.
Chaoxuan named him "The Patriarch.
Upon hearing the gāthā, Xuanzhi was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy, saying:
"I pray that you, Master, will long remain in this world to transform and guide all sentient beings."
The Patriarch said, "I shall depart immediately; I cannot remain for long.
Xuanzhi took his leave with formal courtesy and departed.
The Patriarch then suddenly passed away.

This occurred on the fifth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, coinciding with the period when the young Wei Emperor Zhao and Emperor Xiaozhuang were engaged in the affairs of deposition and enthronement.
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month of that year, he was buried at Mount Xiong’er in Songzhou, Luoyang.
A stupa was erected at Dinglin Temple.
The Wei dynasty subsequently informed the Liang of his passing.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty immediately bestowed precious silks upon him;
he then issued an imperial decree to all the imperial kinsmen and princes to provide offerings for his worship according to the sacrificial rites.
The Crown Prince composed a preface for it,
the gist of which states:
"We reverently contemplate the Great Master, a scion of the holy lineage."
Sealing with the wisdom-seal of the Ten Powers,
he sails the ocean by means of the six supernormal knowledges;
he directs compassion and wisdom toward the Brahma realm.
He rescued those in perilous straits within the land of China.
Three years later,
he encountered the Wei envoy Song Yun, who was returning from a mission to the Western Regions.
At the Pamir Mountains, the Patriarch took a single shoe in his hand and departed alone with graceful ease.
When Yung questioned him,
he replied:
He departed for the Western Heaven.
Yungui recounted these events in detail.
His disciples then prepared his burial mound.
An empty coffin and a single shoe remained there.
An imperial edict was issued to take the left-over shoe to be enshrined for veneration at Shaolin Monastery.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty heard of the Master’s transformative deeds.
His parents composed the inscription for his stele.
During the reign of Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty,
he was posthumously honored with the title Great Master Yuanjue (Perfect Enlightenment).
The stupa is titled *Kongguan Zhengzong Ji* (Record of the True Lineage of the Contemplation of Emptiness).

Xinchou (1526): The second year of the Putong era, the ninth month; the Emperor established Tongtai Temple. Zhengguang era (520–523): The third year of the Zhengguang era, the Emperor constructed Dajue Temple at the capital of Ye. Renyin (1522): The third year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty; the third year of the Zhengguang era of the Wei dynasty; the Zhengguang calendar was implemented by Empress Hu of the Wei.

In the first year of the Xiping era, the Bingshen year, Song Yun was dispatched together with the bhikṣu Huisheng to travel to the Western Regions to seek out Buddhist scriptures not yet available in China.
Traveling four thousand li west from Luoyang, they reached Mount Chiling, at which point they exited the borders of the Wei dynasty.
Furthermore, traveling west for two years, he reached the country of Kāṇauj and returned.
He obtained one hundred and seventy sections of Buddhist scriptures.
Arriving here in the second month, he returned safely to Luoyang.

The Wei Dynasty possessed a total of four hundred and fifteen Buddhist scriptures, comprising one thousand nine hundred and nineteen fascicles; these are recorded in the "Buddhism and Daoism" (Fo Lao Zhi) section of the *Wei Shu* (History of Wei), along with their catalog.

Gui Mao (Year 4 of Putong, Year 4 of Zhengguang) Jia Chen (Year 5 of Putong, Year 5 of Zhengguang) Yi Si (Year 6 of Putong, Year 1 of Xiaochang) Bing Wu (Year 7 of Putong, Year 2 of Xiaochang) Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty, Tong.
He established Huìyì Hall in the Eastern Palace and summoned renowned monks from all over the world to reside there.
The Emperor bestowed [this honor] upon Dharma Master Huìchāo.
For the sake of the Court Scholar (Xuanguxue shi) Liang Ji Sengzhuan. Dingwei: The first year of Datong of the Liang dynasty;

the Emperor completed the construction of Tongtai Temple. Weyi: The third year of Xiaochang of the Wei dynasty. In the third month of the fourth year of Xiaochang, the Emperor met his assassination; the era name was changed to Yong’an. Wushen: The second year of Datong of the Liang; the son of Emperor Jingzong of Wei, Xiaozhuangdi, [ascended]. The first year of Yong’an of the Wei; the first month of the Wushen year of the Wei.
The Emperor detested Zheng Yan and Xu Ge;
he secretly issued an edict to Er Zhu Rong to mobilize his troops and move toward the capital.
Er Zhu Rong appointed Gao Huan as the vanguard.
When he reached Shangdang,
the Emperor again stopped him with a private edict.
Zheng Yan and Xu He, fearing that disaster would befall them, plotted to poison the Emperor.
In the third month, the Emperor passed away suddenly.
The Empress Dowager established the imperial daughter as Emperor.
She further issued an edict declaring that she was indeed the imperial daughter.
He deposed the former Prince of Lintao, Baohui, and installed his son, Zhao,
who was only three years old.
When Er Zhu Rong heard of this, he was greatly incensed.
He said to Yuantian Mu:
"The Sovereign has passed away at the age of nineteen;
even throughout the realm, he is still regarded as a young ruler."
How much more so when one governs the world with an infant who has not yet spoken—
can one truly seek peace and order?
In the third month, Erzhu Rong and Yuan Tianmu welcomed Changle Wang Ziyou, the son of Prince Xuanwu of Pengcheng, to the River Bridge to ascend the throne as Emperor.
This was called "Honoring the Ancestral Line.
He changed the era name to Yong'an.
Rong dispatched cavalry to murder the Empress Dowager and the young Emperor at Heyin (North History).
Erzhu was a compound surname;
his ancestors were the elders of the Qiehu (Qiehu) tribal confederation,
who served as chieftains for generations.
He resided by the Erzhu River, and thus it became his surname. Jǐyǒu (the year Jǐyǒu):

the first year of Zhōngdàtōng of the Liáng dynasty, the second year of Yǒng'ān of the Wèi dynasty, the seventh month; the Emperor first entered the palace on the twenty-seventh day of the third month of the Liáng calendar.
Dharma Master Fayun passed away at the age of sixty-three;
both the imperial palaces were stricken with profound grief.
An imperial edict granted him the secret funerary vessels from the Eastern Garden;
all matters pertaining to the funeral were to be conducted according to the protocols of the Prince’s household.
He was buried by imperial decree beside Dinglin Temple.
An inscription was established for this in his original biography.
In the ninth month of the Liang dynasty,
the Emperor visited Tongtai Temple and convened a fourfold *amogha* (unrestricted) assembly of the four classes of followers.
He practiced pure and great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).
The ministers offered prayers to the Triple Gem and submitted a memorial requesting the Emperor to return to the palace. (From the *Biography of the Liang Emperors*).

Gengxu: In the second year of Zhongdatong (529), in the tenth month of the Wei calendar, Changguang Wang was established as emperor, marking the first year of Jianming. In the twelfth month, Erzhu Zhao assassinated Emperor Zhuang of the Wei, known as Xiaozhuangdi.
Already feeling constant resentment due to the external pressure from Erzhu Rong,
and further traumatized by the disaster at Heyin,
he secretly harbored the intention to plot against Rong.
In the eighth month, Rong and Yuantianmu entered the court;
the Emperor slew them both with his own hand,
and they died together.
Inside and out, the clamor of joy filled Luoyang.
The hundred officials entered to offer their congratulations.
In the tenth month, Er Zhu Zhao, the Regional Inspector of Fenzhou, heard that his elder brother Rong had died.
From his headquarters at Fenzhou, the commander rode to occupy Jinyang.
Thereupon, Er Zhu Shizong and others together enthroned Yuan Ye, the Prince of Changguang and Governor of Taiyuan, as Emperor.
He changed the era name to Jianming.
In the twelfth month, the omens were auspicious; light troops marched with double speed and reached the palace gates.
They seized Emperor Zhuang and moved him to Jinyang, where they strangled him to death. *Beishi*.

On the day of Xinhai, the fourth month of the third year of Zhongdatong, Crown Prince Tong passed away. [In the north], it was the first year of Putai of Emperor Gong, the Jie-min Di of Wei; and the first year of Zhongxing of Prince Lang of Anding. In the second month of Wei.
Prince Gong of Guangling was fond of learning and possessed noble aspirations.
Xue Xiaotong, the Grand Chancellor of Guanshi,
persuaded Erzhu Shilong to install him [as emperor].
At that time, Shi Long was stationed in Luoyang;
he then, by the command of Prince Changguang, abdicated the throne in favor of Prince Guangling Gong,
the grandson of Emperor Xianwen.
This was known as Emperor Jiemin.
He changed the era name to Putai and enfeoffed Wang Ye,
the Prince of Changguang, as the King of Donghai.
Gao Huan raised an army to punish Er Zhu Zhao for the murder of Emperor Xiaozhuang.
Sun Teng said to Huan:
Now the imperial court is cut off;
there is no authority to receive commands,
nor is there anyone to whom we can turn for provisional leadership.
Consequently, the masses were demoralized and dispersed.
Yuan Huan then established Wang Yuanlang of Anding, the Governor of Bohai, as Emperor.
He took the throne at Xindu (present-day Jizhou in the region of Zhending).
It was the birthplace of Gao Huan.
He changed the era name to Zhongxing and appointed Huan as Grand Marshal (Shizhong Chengxiang).
He was appointed General-in-Chief of All Military Affairs Within and Without the Passes.
Because Yuan Lang, the Prince of Anding, was distant from the capital,
he dispatched the Vice President of the Secretariat Wei Lan-gen to comfort and reassure those in Luoyang.
Observing the character of Emperor Jiemindì,
[Lan Gen] wished to serve him once more; however,
he feared that because the Emperor’s spirit was so lofty and brilliant, he would be difficult to control in the future.
Consequently, together with Gao Qian’s brothers and Cui Ling, he joyfully deposed the emperor.
He then confined Emperor Jieming at Chongxun Monastery and established Xiu,
Prince of Pingyang— the son of Guangping Prince [Tuoba] Guangping, a descendant of Emperor Xiaozhuang— as the new ruler.
This was Emperor Xiaowu.
He commissioned Prince Yuanlang of Anding to compose the imperial edict for the abdication of the throne.
He then administered a lethal dose of bezoar to Emperor Jieming at the Gatekeeper’s Office.
The funeral rites were conducted with exceptional honors.
Both Yuan Lang and Gao Huan were renowned figures from Xindu and Jizhou.
Initially, in the third year of the Xiaochang era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty, Liu Bei recommended him to Er Zhu Rong, the Grand Commander for the Suppression of Rebels.
Rong then promoted and employed him.
Previously, more than two hundred thousand followers from Ge Rong’s faction had fled into the Bing and Ying regions.
Because they were subjected to Hu barbarian oppression and violence, none of them could bear their lives; they plotted rebellion without ceasing.
Er Zhu Zhao grew weary of this.
He consulted Gao Huan regarding the matter.
Huan said, "It would be appropriate to select a loyal confidant of the King to command them.
Thereupon, Zhao entrusted his troops to Huan.
Huan feared that his words of intoxication might lead to regret upon sobering up;
he therefore issued a public proclamation stating that he had been entrusted with the command of the garrison troops and that they should assemble east of the Fen River to receive his orders.
He then established his military headquarters at Yangsichuan; the soldiers there had long detested Zhao and delighted in joining with Yuan Huangmo, so they all arrived without exception.
It was in the second year of the Yongxi era that Huangmo went to suppress Zhao.
Zhaobin fled toward Hanling Mountain on the road to Zhangde and threw himself into the woods.
He killed the white horse he was riding and hanged himself from a tree.
Gao Huan personally visited the site and provided him with a lavish burial (*Weishu*).

Renzi: The fourth year of the Zhongdatong era of the Liang dynasty; the Wei Emperor Xiaowu, who was styled Emperor Chudi, compiled the history. On the first day of the fourth month of the first year of Yongxi, the era name was changed. Guichou: The fifth year of Zhongdatong; the second year of Yongxi. On the twenty-sixth day of the second month of the Liang dynasty.
The Emperor visited Tongtai Temple and lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for twenty-one days,
convening an unrestricted great assembly (*amogha-mahāpariṣad*) of both monastics and laypeople.
319,642 people. *Yichu Liutie* (Six Categories of Meaning by Yi Chu). Jia-yin year. The sixth year of Zhongdatong;

the third year of Yongxi of the Western Wei. The Emperor fled to Chang’an. The first year of Tianping of Emperor Xiaojing of Eastern Wei; the first month of the third year of Yongxi of Emperor Xiaowu of the Northern Wei.
General of the Central Army Wang Sizheng addressed Emperor Wu, saying:
"The intentions of Gao Huan are clearly discernible;
Luoyang is not a place for the employment of military force."
"It would be appropriate to join Yuan Wei in Chang'an.
The Emperor deeply agreed with this and subsequently issued a general summons for troops from the various provinces and commanderies.
Pei Xie, the Governor of Dongjun, led his subordinates to Luoyang.
Wang Sijing asked him,
"Now that powerful ministers usurp authority and issue commands at will."
"How can the royal house continue to decline like this? Xia said,
"Yu Wentai has been elected by the three armies."
Occupying a position of one hundred and two [degrees of power], it is as if one has already grasped the halberd and spear; how could one be willing to hand the handle over to another?
Even if one wished to surrender it, it would likely be no different from fleeing from boiling water only to enter a fire.
Zixing asked, "How can this be managed?
Xia replied,
"Tu Huang faces the imminent danger of being overthrown."
Regarding the western expedition, there were concerns for the future;
furthermore, it was decided to first reach the region west of the Passes to deliberate carefully on what was appropriate.
In the seventh month, Fu Jian perceived the signs of impending change.
He led his troops across the river.
Emperor Xiaowu then personally led the Prince of Nanyang, Baoju, the Prince of Qinghe, Dan, and the Prince of Guangyang, Zhan, in a direct retreat toward Shen,
fleeing westward with five thousand cavalry.
Yu Wentai, having arrayed his ceremonial guards, welcomed the Emperor,
who subsequently entered Chang’an;
Gao Huan then entered Luoyang.
He resided at Yongning Temple.
In the tenth month, the Wei Chancellor, Yuan Hong, again presented a memorial to Emperor Xiaowu, saying:
"If Your Majesty would deign to grant a decree permitting his return to the capitals of Luoyang and Chang'an..."
I, your servant, shall serve as a model for both civil and military affairs to purify the imperial palace.
If there is no day when the rightful succession is restored, the Seven Temples must not remain without a presiding lord,
and the myriad states must have a place to which they may turn.
"I would rather betray Your Majesty than betray the state.
The Emperor did not answer.
Tanyuanchu then assembled the officials and the elders.
He established Shanjian, the crown prince of Prince Duanzhi of Qinghe, as emperor.
He was the great-grandson of Emperor Xiaowen;
at the age of eleven, he ascended the throne to the northeast of the city.
The era name was changed to Tenpyō.
The capital was moved to Ye.
Emperor Xiaowu resided in Chang’an.
He had a feud with the Vice President of the Secretariat, Yuwen Tai.
In the twelfth month, while drinking wine, he encountered poisoned liquor and passed away at the age of twenty-five.
Tai Feng served as Grand Chancellor to Emperor Baoru of Nanyang, who then ascended the throne as Emperor.
According to the *Wei Shu* (Book of Wei), the Yuan-Wei dynasty was surnamed Tuoba.
Their ancestors were originally Northern Di people from the Xianbei mountains, who were of Hu ethnicity.
Prior to the Qin and Han dynasties,
they had never communicated with China.
During the Jingchu era of Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty, [they first made contact].
At first, they established peaceful relations with them.
At the beginning of the Jin dynasty, there was Tuoba Yilu,
who moved his residence to Loufan.
The second year of the Taian era of Emperor Hui was the ninth year of Tuoba Lukuan’s reign.
The Tuoba resided in Dai Commandery and had previously assisted Liu Kun in resisting Shi Le.
The Jin dynasty enfeoffed him as the King of Dai.
For over sixty years, his descendants held power in the north of Dai until the tribes dispersed.
This continued until the time of the Eastern Jin.
The Qin ruler Fu Jian campaigned against the Dai, attacking Shi Yi Jian.
Jian was assassinated by his son Shi Shi;
Shi Shi also subsequently died.
His grandson, Gui, fled to rely upon the Dugu clan;
he was called Lusun.
This was the first year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Lu Sun collected the wings [of his followers] and crossed over to Gui; the *Weishu* states that Gui was none other than Emperor Taizu Daowu.
He went forth to occupy Shuozhou and, three hundred li to the east, built a city-state named Heng’an.
Because he served as the Protector of Qin, he remained under the jurisdiction of the Fu Qin dynasty.
In the eleventh month of the eighth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin, Fu Jian was defeated by the Jin forces.
In the first month of spring in the eleventh year of the Taiyuan era:
Guī then convened a great assembly of his tribal clans at Niu-chuan and immediately ascended the throne as King;
the year was designated as the first year of Dengguo.
He moved his residence to Shengle in Dingxiang; Dingxiang was the name of a commandery under Xinzhou in Jining Road.
This region of Ji was dedicated to agriculture and the rest of the people.
The people of the state were delighted with him.
Gui subsequently changed his title to King of Wei.
This was the twenty-first year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, the Bingshen year.
Gui first established the ceremonial banners of the Son of Heaven, with the imperial procession sounding the alarm upon departure and the halting of travel upon arrival.
He changed the year name to Huangshi (August Beginning).
In the wu-xu year, he moved the capital to Pingcheng, which is present-day Datong in the Xijing region.
The commandery is named Yunzhong.
The Shanyu Terrace and the Baideng Hill are located there;
it belongs to the region of Ji.
He first established the palace chambers,
constructed the ancestral temple, and set up the altars of the land and grain.
He performed five seasonal sacrifices to the ancestral temple each year.
He employed the system of solar terms and the *lā* (winter solstice) festival.
In the twelfth month, Gui ascended the imperial throne and changed the year name to Tianxing.
He mandated that both the court and the common people must bind their hair and wear caps.
He posthumously honored twenty-seven ancestors, from Mao downwards, all as Emperors.
For the first time, he modeled himself after ancient institutions to establish the rites and music for the suburban sacrifices, the ancestral temple services, and the court offerings.
In the tenth month of the Jiyou year,
the positions of Five Classics Professors were established, and the enrollment of students at the Guozijian was increased to a total of three thousand.
Tuoba Gui was the son born to Lady Helan; he was assassinated by Prince Shao of Qinghe.
Gui held office for twenty-four years and reached the age of thirty-nine.
Gui’s eldest son succeeded him and killed Shao to ascend the throne;
he was Emperor Mingyuan.
In the eighth year of Taichang, he captured Luoyang, and the provinces of Qun and Yu were all pacified.
At that time, there were only two states under heaven,
known as the Northern and Southern Dynasties.
The Rouran incited raids upon the borders of Wei.
The Wei dynasty constructed the Great Wall,
extending from the Red City (Chicheng) in the east to Wuyuan in the west for a distance of two thousand li.
Garrisons of soldiers were established throughout its length to defend against the Rouran.
In the fifth month of Mingyuan, he returned to Pingcheng.
He passed away in the eleventh month.
He had occupied the throne for fifteen years.
His reign lasted thirty-two years.
His son, the Crown Prince and Emperor Shizu Taowu (r. 424–451), ascended the throne;
he destroyed and defiled the Buddhist teachings during his twenty-nine-year reign.
He lived for thirty-five years.
His grandson, Emperor Gaozong Wencheng (r.
452–465), ascended the throne and issued an edict to restore the teachings of Śākyamuni, honoring them with reverence.
He reigned for thirteen years.
His life span was twenty-six years.
His eldest son, Hyeongjo (later Emperor Seonmun), succeeded him as King Hong.
He reigned for five years and abdicated the throne to his son, Hong.
The assembled ministers conferred upon him the honorific title of Taishang Huangdi (Supreme Sovereign Emperor).
He presided over all matters of state and military affairs.
Emperor Gaozu Xiaowen Di Hong ascended the throne at the age of five.
He reigned for twenty-nine years.
He moved the capital to Luoyang and discarded the Hu-style clothing and headgear.
He completely eliminated the speech of the barbarians and honored the refined customs of the Middle Kingdom;
he first donned the *gǔnmian* robes for court audiences and sacrificial feasts.
He established the household registration system,
instituted the five grades of official robes,
and commenced the construction of the Mingtang and Biyong.
In the fifteenth year of the Taihe era, Empress Dowager Feng passed away.
Emperor Xiaowen observed the three-year mourning period in accordance with ancient rites.
In the sixteenth year of Taihe, he commanded his ministers to deliberate on the order of succession.
Succeeding Jin, it was established as the Water Virtue.
In the twentieth year of the Taihe era, an imperial edict stated: "As for earth, it is the color of the center."
As the origin of all things,
he changed his surname to Yuan (Origin).
His lifespan was thirty-three years.
His second son, Shizong Xuanwu Di Ke,
ascended the throne and reigned for sixteen years;
his life span was thirty-three years.
Xuanwu’s second son, Xiao Mingdi Xu, was enthroned as Emperor Suzong.
He reigned for twelve years and died at the age of nineteen.
Jingzong, Emperor Xiaozhuang, was enthroned.
He reigned for three years and died at the age of twenty-four.
Emperor Jiemindì Gōngpíng Āndìng Wáng Yuànlǎng was established;
both were subsequently killed.
Emperor Xiaowŭ fled west to Chāng’ān to avoid Gāo Huān.
From this point on, the territories were divided between the west and the east. To the right [the western line]:

the Twelve Sovereigns of the Northern Wei ruled for one hundred and forty-nine years, which was divided into three periods; the Three Western Kings ruled for twenty-two years before they abdicated to the Zhou. The Eastern [line] consisted of one king who ruled for seventeen years before abdicating to the Northern Qi.
Nineteen masters translated Buddhist scriptures during the Wei dynasty,
producing four hundred and nineteen works comprising approximately one thousand nine hundred fascicles across the sutras, vinayas, and śāstras.
The number of monks reached two million.
There were forty-seven state-sponsored great monasteries,
eight hundred and forty monasteries of the Three Dukes and other officials,
and thirty-one thousand monasteries built by the common people (according to the *Weishu* and the *Bianzhenglu*).
The Rouran was the name of a state among the Yi-di (barbarians).
Their clan was the Yujüqian.
It first appeared at the end of the Shenyuan era of the Northern Wei.
A raiding party captured a slave whose hair had just reached his eyebrows and who had forgotten his original name and surname.
His master gave him the name Mugulur.
*Mugukryeo* means "bald-headed.
*Mugukryeo* and *Yukgwan* are phonetically close;
thus, they were adopted as a clan name (*se*).
Mugu Lü was in the state of Dai during the time of Yi Lu; he had been late for an appointment and was due to be executed.
He fled and hid in the mountain valleys of Guanghan, where he gathered a following of more than a hundred men.
When his son, Lùhuì (鹿會), became powerful and valiant,
he first began to have followers and called himself Rouran.
Because Emperor Taowu of the Northern Wei,
Tuoba Tao, considered their lack of knowledge to be similar to that of insects,
he changed their name to *Rourou* (Crawlers) in the *Beishi*.

Yimao (1st year of Datong) of the Liang dynasty; the 1st year of Baoru’s reign as Emperor Wen of Western Wei; the 2nd year of Tiānpíng of Eastern Wei. In this year, Emperor Wen of Western Wei established Bānruó Monastery.
The Emperor constantly exercised compassion and always practiced the giving of alms;
he rescued those drowning and supported the elderly.
Providing for sick monks,
reciting the Lotus Sūtra with their mouths,
and maintaining pure precepts with their bodies.
The Chancellor, Yuwen Tai, promoted the Buddhist scriptures and lectured on the Mahāyāna.
He commissioned the monk Tanxian to compile the *Essentials of the Various Scriptures* in twenty-two fascicles.
And the *Bianzheng lu* (Record of the Rectification of Orthodoxy) in one hundred and twenty fascicles.
During the Western Wei, the Chancellor Tai was promoted to the Duke of Anding.

Bingchen, the second year of Datong [537 CE]: Liu Xie, a palace attendant of the Liang dynasty, submitted a memorial requesting ordination; the Emperor commended him for this and bestowed upon the monk Hong the name Mudi (Huidi). According to the *Nanshi*, this was the second year of Dazhong [546 CE], the third year of Tianping [534 CE], the third month of the Liang dynasty.
Tao Hongjing of Danyang passed away.
Hongjing had once visited the Buddha-relic stupa at Yuyang in Mingzhou and vowed to receive the five precepts, which he subsequently transmitted.

The Eastern Wei appointed Hou Jing, Governor of Dingzhou, as Acting Right Vice-Director of the Secretariat and Commissioner of the Southern Circuit Commandery to oversee various generals in their invasion of Jiankang (*Beishi*). Ding-si:
The third year of Datong, the third year of Dazhong, and the fourth year of Tianping. The *Guan Shi Yin Jing* of King Gao. There was a man named Sun Jingde, a resident of Dingzhou in the Eastern Wei.
He served Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva with great devotion.
Later, he was falsely accused by bandits and compelled to confess to a crime he did not commit.
One night, he dreamed of a monk who instructed him to recite the *Dharani of Avalokiteśvara for Deliverance from Suffering*.
Jingde recited it as the executioner carried out the sentence;
the blade struck three times, yet the blade broke three times.
The Regional Inspector submitted a formal petition to the Chancellor Gao Huan.
Huan carefully inquired into the circumstances and submitted a memorial on his behalf requesting that he be spared from death.
When Sun returned home, he found three knife scars on the neck of the Avalokiteśvara image he had enshrined;
because of this, it came to be called the *Gāowáng jīng* (Sūtra of King Gao).

The *Gǎnyìng zhuàn* (Biographies of Miraculous Responses) records that in the fourth year of Dàtóng, the wùwǔ year [528 CE], the Emperor renovated Chánggān Temple and visited the temple to establish a Great Unobstructed Feast (*wú'ài dàzái*). According to the Liáng Annals, in the fourth year of Dàtǒng [538 CE], there were over thirty thousand Buddhist monasteries and two million monks and nuns. The *Běishǐ* (History of the Northern Dynasties) records that in the first year of Xīnghé [539 CE], the fifth year of Dàtóng, the fifth year of Dàtǒng under the Western Wèi, and the first year of Xīnghé under the Eastern Wèi, the Śramaṇa Dào Zhēn of the Western Wèi [was active].
He was extensively versed in the meanings of the scriptures.
Emperor Wen honored him as a Master (Shifu).
When Dazhongxing Temple was established in Chang’an, he resided there.
He served as the Grand Steward of the Wei State and established a comprehensive system of regulations;
consequently, Buddhism flourished once again.
The Emperor further established the Dacheng (Mahāyāna) and Zhihu (Climbing the Hill) monasteries.
When [Da]zhen entered nirvana,
the Emperor mourned him and suspended court proceedings.
All resources required for funeral rites were provided from the Northern Treasury (Beitianfu).

Gengshen (17th day of the seventh month): The sixth year of Datong, the sixth year of Dazhong, and the second year of Xinghe. An imperial edict established the former palace at Ye City as Tianping Monastery. Xinyou (28th day of the seventh month): The seventh year of Datong, the seventh year of Dazhong, and the third year of Xinghe. Vimokṣasena translated scriptures at Ye Commandery. Renxu (9th day of the eighth month): The eighth year of Datong, the eighth year of Dazhong, and the fourth year of Xinghe. Guihai (30th day of the eighth month): The ninth year of Datong, the ninth year of Dazhong, and the fifth year of Xinghe. Jiazi (11th day of the ninth month): The tenth year of Datong, the tenth year of Dazhong, and the second year of Wuding. Yichai (22nd day of the ninth month): The eleventh year of Datong under the Liang; the eleventh year of Dazhong under the Western Wei; and the third year of Wuding under the Eastern Wei. During this time, Yuwen Tai, the Chancellor of the Western Wei, [held office].
In Chang’an, he established six monasteries— Zhuoyuan, Zhiqu, Dacheng, Weiguo, Anding, and Zhongxing—
and ordained one thousand monks.
He also constructed Tianbao Monastery to provide offerings for Dharma Master Wei.
In Anzhou, he founded the two monasteries of Shoushan and Fanyun;
he also established Dafutian Monastery to provide offerings for National Preceptor Sigu.
In the third month of the first year of Zhongdatong (the Bingyin year),
Daoshi composed the *Futian Monastery Record* and the *Tujue Monastery Bianzheng Lu* for the sake of the Great Khan Dayunini.
The Emperor visited Tongtai Temple to lecture on the *Tri-sarvajñatā-sūtra*.

In the fourth month of summer, he issued a general amnesty and changed the era name. This was the eleventh year of Dàtǒng (the fourth year of Wǔdì). Since the Tiānjiān era, the Liáng Emperor had personally served the Buddha.
He maintained a long-term fast and refrained from listening to music.
He established five monasteries, including Guangzhai and Tongtai,
and regularly provided sustenance for a thousand monks.
The Emperor composed the "Fu on Pure Deeds" (*Jingye Fu*).
Its preface states:
"I, the Sovereign, do not consume fish or meat."
He has not lived in the company of palace ladies or attendants for over forty years. Furthermore,
he does not eat sentient beings.
There is no longer any obstacle of killing;
since one no longer indulges in internal [pleasures],
there is no longer any obstacle of lustful evil.
Once these two obstacles were removed and his consciousness was somewhat clarified,
he composed the "Rhapsody on Pure Deeds.
Now, its words are summarized as follows:
Contemplating the innate nature of human beings:
they embrace the wondrous vital energy (qì) and are pure and tranquil;
yet, moved by external things, their desires are stirred.
The mind clings to objects and thus forms a cataract;
faults constantly arise from external phenomena,
and afflictions must stem from preceding sensory realms.
Conceiving a greedy mind without weariness,
one lets the internal thoughts run wild;
the ears linger upon the sounds of strings and pipes.
The eye shifts toward the five colors;
fragrances waft forth, striking the nose and giving rise to consciousness;
the tongue experiences sweetness as it chews and eats food.
Her body experiences touch with self-comfort and delight;
her waist is slender, her hands delicate, her bones supple, and her flesh full.
Her body is fragrant and pure, and its touch is like that of fat.
With a deranged mind, deluded and inverted, they deceive themselves.
Thus, the six sense-objects equally obstruct the path of goodness;
they eclipse the purple with the violet, like grass bending before the wind.
Clinging to delusions, one is born and grows old together with them;
following after ignorance, there is nothing but affliction.
Therefore, purify the objects of the eyes externally and cleanse the dust of the mind internally.
Accompanied by virtue and dwelling as neighbors with the Way,
one beholds the loveliness of pure karma,
taking non-killing as its cause.
Having distanced oneself from desire and evil while cultivating one's own practice,
the spirit and mind are free from obstruction;
once afflictions and entanglements are eliminated, hindrances are likewise purified.
Like water long settled or a mirror newly polished, it reflects outwardly while images appear within;
one thus perceives the various maladies within.
Once the adventitious dust is removed, one returns to one's own original nature.
The mind is as clear as ice and the will is as pure as snow.
Once fetters are severed, sorrow and fear are extinguished;
one is forever parted from those held dear.
Reflecting upon life and death, I bid eternal farewell—*Bianzheng lu*.

Year Dingmao, the first year of Taiching (the thirteenth year of Datong of the Western Wei; the fifth year of Wuding of the Eastern Wei). In the first month, Gao Huan, the Prince of Bohai and Martial Victor of the Eastern Wei, passed away.
The heir apparent Cheng succeeded to the throne.
Hou Jing, having a feud with the Gao family,
rebelled and defected to the Western Wei.
The Western Wei appointed Jing as Grand Tutor.
Jing then dispatched Ding He to present a memorial of allegiance to the Liang court.
The Emperor of Liang received Jing.
He appointed Jing as Grand General and enfeoffed him as the King of Henan.
This was the second month of the second year of the Taicheng era, the wuchen year.
At that time, Gao Cheng, the Grand General of the Eastern Wei, sought to establish friendly relations with the Liang dynasty.
Consequently, Hou Jing became suspicious and rebelled.
The Emperor of Liang appointed Prince Zhengde of Linhe as General Who Pacifies the North and Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in the capital,
stationing him in Danyang Commandery.
Jeong-deok secretly ferried King Gyeong across the river using several dozen large ships.
Jeong-deok then guarded Seonyang Gate and led his troops to welcome King Gyeong to the foot of the palace.
He ascended the throne as Emperor Zhengde.
He changed the era name to Zhengping and issued a general amnesty.
This was the first month of the third year of Taicheng, the Jisi year.
The capital city fell.
Hou Jing entered the presence of Emperor Wu and unleashed his troops to plunder the imperial carriage and regalia.
Furthermore, Zhengde, Prince of Linhe, was appointed as Grand Guardian and Great Marshal.
On the *bingchen* day of the fifth month, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty passed away at the age of eighty-six.
Hou Jing kept the death secret and did not announce the mourning;
none of the civil or military officials outside the palace were aware of it until the day of Xin-si,
when the funeral rites finally commenced.
The imperial coffin was ascended to the Taiji Hall.
On this day, Hou Jing welcomed Crown Prince Gang and had him ascend the throne as Emperor.
In the sixth month, Prince Zhengde of Linhe resented that Hou Jing had betrayed him.
A secret letter was sent summoning Prince Fan of Poyang to enter with his troops.
Jing intercepted and obtained the letter;
he then strangled Zhengde to death.
In the eighth month, Gao Cheng, Prince Wenxiang of Bohai of the Eastern Wei, was assassinated by his cook Lan Jing.
His younger brother, Gao Yang, Duke of Taiyuan, punished the rebel and put him to death.
In the twelfth month, Chen Ji, the Governor of Shixing, first conspired with the local heroes of the commandery to revolt against Hou Jing.
Local figures such as Hou Andu and Zhang Cai each led more than a thousand men to join him.
He dispatched an envoy by a secret route to Jiangling to receive instructions from Prince Xiangdong, Xiao Yi. **The Liang Annals:** Wuchen (17 May):

In the second year of Taqing of the Liang (the fourteenth year of Datong of the Western Wei; the sixth year of Wuding of the Eastern Wei), on the fifth month of the third year of Taqing, the Emperor passed away. [This corresponds to] the fifteenth year of Datong and the seventh year of Wuding. **Emperor Taizong Jianwen:** Emperor Taizong Jianwen’s personal name was Gang.
The third son of Emperor Gaozu Wudi.
He reigned for two years.
His age at death was forty-nine. [His reign lasted] two years of the Dabao era.

Gengwu. The first year of Dàbǎo, the sixteenth year of Dàtǒng. The Gāo clan of Northern Qí received the abdication [of the throne]. The first year of Tiānbǎo, Northern Qí. In the first month of Northern Qí, Gāo Yáng, Duke of Tàiyuán of the Eastern Wèi, was promoted to the position of Chancellor and Prince of Qíjùn.
In the fifth month, he was promoted to the rank of Prince of Qi, Chancellor, and Director of the Hundred Officials, and invested with the nine emblems of imperial authority.
The Attendant-in-Ordinary Zhang Liang and others incited the Emperor to abdicate the throne to the Prince of Qi, Yang.
The Emperor then departed from the Yunlong Gate.
He dispatched the Grand Marshal, Prince Xiao Shao of Pengcheng, and others to present the imperial seal and ribbon.
The Prince of Qi immediately ascended the throne at the Southern Suburb and changed the era name to Tianbao.
He enfeoffed the Wei Emperor as the Prince of Zhongshan.
In the twelfth month, he poisoned him to death.
His posthumous title was Emperor Xiaojing of Wei, and he was buried west of Ye, north of the barrier.
The Eastern Wei lasted for seventeen years under one sovereign before its extinction.
His father, Wang Huan, was posthumously honored with the title Emperor Shenwu, the Gaozu; Huan’s surname was Gao, and he was a native of Jizhou. Initially, Huan served Er Zhu Rong.
Rongdi Zhao entrusted the military affairs to Huan;
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Bohai.
He passed away at the age of fifty-one.
His elder brother, Cheng, was posthumously titled Emperor Shenzu Wenxiang;
his son, Xianzu Wenxuan, was the second son of Shenzu.
It was at this time that he received the abdication from the Eastern Wei.
The state was established as Qi.
The era name was changed to Tianbao.
The capital was at Ye, in the Changde Prefecture of the ancient Xiangzhou.
He reigned for ten years.
His life span was thirty-one years.
His son, Yin, ascended the throne.
He was the deposed emperor.
He was seventeen years old.
He was the sixth son of Emperor Xuanzong (Xiaozhao) Yan, who possessed divine martial prowess.
In the first year of the Qianming era of the deposed emperor, the reign name was changed to Huangjian.
In the second year of Huangjian, while out hunting, he fell from his horse and suffered a broken rib;
he passed away at the age of twenty-seven.
Shizu Wuchengdi (Emperor Wucheng), named Tan, was the ninth son of Shenwu.
Upon his accession, he changed the era name to Taiping in the tenth month of the second year of Huangjian.
He reigned for four years.
He abdicated the throne to the Crown Prince and styled himself the Retired Emperor (Taishanghuang). He passed away in the fourth year of the Dàtǒng era at the age of forty-two.
His successor, the Later Ruler Wěi, was his eldest son; he reigned for thirteen years.
He fled to Qingzhou,
where he was captured by the Zhou forces.
Both the Empress Dowager and the young Emperor Heng were sent to Chang'an.
Feng Wei, Duke Wen. Five emperors for a total of twenty-eight years. *Xinwei* (the year 561), the second year of Dàbǎo:

one thousand five hundred years had passed since the World-Honored One entered *parinirvāṇa*. The seventeenth year of Dàtǒng, the third month: the Emperor passed away; Crown Prince Qīn ascended the throne. The second year of Tiānbǎo of the Northern Qi, the third month of Liáng: the Marquis of Jǐng pressured the Emperor to abdicate the throne to the Prince of Yùzhāng, Dòng.
The era name was changed to Tenjō.
The retired emperor was demoted to the rank of Prince Seian.
In the ninth month, he was assassinated at the age of forty-nine.
Dong Ga bestowed the nine emblems of enfeoffment upon Jing.
The state of Han established offices from the Chancellor downwards.
Dong then abdicated the throne to Jing.
Jing ascended the imperial throne at the Southern Suburb.
Upon his return, he ascended the Taiji Hall and changed the year name to Taishi, marking the beginning of the Liang era.
In the first month of the year Wenshen (572 CE),
Xiao Yi, Prince Xiangdong of the Liang dynasty, commanded Wang Sengbian and others to advance eastward against Hou Jing.
In the second month, the various armies set out from Xunyang.
Chen Baxian led one hundred thousand armored cavalry and two thousand warships out from the Nang River to Pénkǒu,
where he met Sēngbiàn at Báimáowān;
there they built an altar and swore an oath by blood.
Jing dispatched Hou Zijian with troops to resist the western forces.
They engaged in battle at Zhongjiang,
where Zijian suffered a great defeat.
He escaped with his life alone;
gathering his scattered troops, he fled back to Jiankang.
Liu Ying was struck with great terror, his tears falling so profusely that they covered his face.
Sengbian supervised the various armies as they entered the Huai River on the incoming tide.
They advanced their troops to the north of Zhaoti Temple,
while Hou Jing led his forces and drew up his battle lines to the west of Xizhou.
Chen Shou, Xian Wang Lin, Du Kan, and others attacked them with cavalry.
Sengbian followed with his main army,
and Jing’s forces were utterly defeated.
Accompanied by over a hundred cavalrymen, he fled eastward.
Sengbian and others welcomed the imperial coffin of Emperor Jianwen to the Hall of Audience and led the officials to wail and leap according to the ritual.
He ordered Hou Tian (also read as Tu Dian) and others to pursue Jing, catching up with him at the Songjiang River.
Tian advanced and defeated him;
Jing fled on a single boat.
He was killed by his younger wife’s brother, Yang Kun,
who stuffed salt into Jing’s abdomen and sent the corpse to Jiankang.
Sengbian’s head was taken to Jiangling and displayed on a pole in the marketplace for three days;
it was then boiled, lacquered,
and placed in the Armory.
In the eleventh month, the Emperor ascended the throne; this is the record of the Liang dynasty.
[The reign of] Emperor Shizu Xiaoyuan Huangdi, named Yi, was the seventh son of Emperor Wu.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiangdong and appointed as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Jingzhou.
He once abandoned his palace upon the passing of the High Ancestor to construct Tiangong Temple.
He invited Dhyāna Master Fachong to reside there to perform Buddhist rites.
In the eleventh month of the year Wenshen (572), he ascended the imperial throne at Jiangling.
He reigned for three years; his lifespan was forty-seven years. In the third year of Chengsheng, the *Ren-shen* year:

in the first year of Chengsheng (the first year of Emperor Qin of the Western Wei), and the third year of Tianbao of the Northern Qi, in the third month, Prince Ji of Wuling, the Governor of Yizhou, was in Shu.
In the seventeenth year, hearing that Hou Jing had captured the Tai City,
Prince Xiangdong Yi set out to suppress him and said to his officials and subordinates:
How could these seven officials and scholars be capable of providing effective counsel or salvation?
Recently, at the inner palace, flowers grew from the joints of the columns in the Cypress Hall;
this was taken as an auspicious omen.
In the fourth month, he ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the era name to Tenjō and appointed his son Enshō as Crown Prince.
In the third month of the second year of the Chengsheng era,
Emperor Yuan, hearing that Ji had arrived,
sent a letter requesting the Wei to invade Shu.
According to the *Jiwen*, there were Wei troops.
He dispatched Qiao Yan, the former Governor of Liangzhou, to return with his army to rescue Shu.
In the seventh month, Ji was unable to retreat from the mouth of the Gorges.
They then followed the current downstream toward the east.
Fan Meng, the General of the Cavalry of the Liang dynasty, pursued and slew Ji, along with his younger sons,
Yuanman, Yuanzhao, and Yuanzheng, who were subsequently imprisoned in the Court of Judicial Review and executed.
In the eighth month, Yuan Su surrendered Chengdu to the Wei dynasty (according to the *Liang shu*).
Emperor Wen of Northern Qi issued an edict summoning Meditation Master Sengchou to the capital; the Prince of Yang went out to the suburbs to welcome him and escorted him into the palace.
At the age of over seventy,
his spirit was clear and expansive;
the ruler of Qi bowed before him and received the Way of Seclusion.
From the time one receives the Bodhisattva precepts,
one shall abstain from alcohol, refrain from eating meat,
and release hawks and falcons.
He resigned his official post to engage in farming and fishing.
Furthermore, he issued an edict to all under heaven that on the sixth day of the third month, the people were to cease all slaughter.
He exhorted him to observe the fast and precepts;
all pungent vegetables from both public and private gardens were removed,
and the Master was retained within the palace for over forty days.
By imperial decree, Yunmen Temple was established in Ye City for the Master to reside in;
he was also appointed as the chief abbot of the Great Cave Temple.
Daoyang devoted himself exclusively to the study of Chan.
An imperial edict was issued to establish separate meditation halls in each province,
ordering that those who had attained mastery in concentration and wisdom should reside therein to transmit and instruct others.
Stupas and monasteries were extensively constructed,
and monks and nuns filled every province;
thus did the Buddha-dharma flourish as it flowed eastward— so records the History of the Sangha.

Guiyou (10th day of the tenth month): The second year of the Chengsheng era of the Liang; the second year of the Qian era of the abdicated Emperor of the Western Wei; the fourth year of the Tianbao era of the Northern Qi. Jiashu (1st day of the eleventh month): The third year of the Chengsheng era of the Liang; in the twelfth month, the Emperor surrendered to the Wei. The first year of the Kuang era of the Gongdi of the Western Wei; the fifth year of the Tianbao era of the Northern Qi. The Western Wei did not establish its own era name.
He plotted to assassinate Grand Preceptor Tai;
when the plot was revealed, Tai deposed him and sent him to Yongzhou,
establishing his younger brother, Prince Qi Kuo, on the throne.
Emperor Gong was the fourth son of Emperor Wen.
He also abolished the reign title and restored the Tuoba clan name;
according to the *Beishi*, all those whose surnames had been reduced to single characters from among the ninety-nine clans were restored to their original names.
In the eleventh month, the troops of the Western Wei pressed upon Jiangling.
The Emperor, along with the Crown Prince, Wang Bao, Xie Darein, and Zhu Maichen, retreated to Jincheng for protection.
The Emperor entered the Bamboo Courtyard at the Eastern Gate.
