He commanded his attendant Gao Shanbao to incinerate one hundred and forty thousand scrolls of books and maps from both ancient and modern times;
he also used a precious sword to strike a pillar, causing it to break.
He sighed and said,
"The way of the civil and military arts ends tonight.
Depart, O ceremonial regalia and cultural refinements!"
He emerged in surrender with white horses and a plain chariot.
In the twelfth month, the Emperor was killed by the Wei people.
The Prince of Liang, Chao, was established as the Sovereign of Liang.
Zi Cha took possession of the territory of Jingzhou;
this is known as the Later Liang. The Liang Annals:
Emperor Jing, whose personal name was Fangzhi.
He was the ninth son of Emperor Wu and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jin'an.
When Emperor Yuan was assassinated, [he ascended the throne].
In the second month of the year Yihai, King Sengbian presented Chen Baoshen as a subordinate to the Prince of Liang;
the Prince of Liang then arrived from Xunyang and ascended the throne.
At that time, he was thirteen years old.
With the Grand Marshal Wang Sengbian serving as the Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs both within and without the capital,
Chen Baxian was additionally appointed General of the West for the First Expedition.
The ruler of Northern Qi sent a letter to Wang Sengbian,
stating that the new sovereign was young and inexperienced, and that Prince Zhengyang, by virtue of both his age and reputation, was capable of safeguarding Jinling.
In the fifth month, Sengbian dispatched an envoy.
A formal announcement was made to Prince Yuanming of Zhengyang to establish the rites between sovereign and subject. On the day of Gengzi,
the imperial dragon boat and ceremonial carriage were dispatched to welcome him.
On the day of Gui-mao, Yuanming entered Jiankang;
on the day of Bing-wu, he ascended the imperial throne and changed the era name to Tiancheng.
The Prince of Liang was appointed Crown Prince;
Wang Sengbian was appointed Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ);
and Chen Zhixian was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
Originally, Sengbian had first joined forces with Xiao Mo to destroy Hou Jing,
and their personal friendship was very deep.
However, when Sengbian received the Prince of Zhenyang [as a hostage],...
The Emperor first dispatched an envoy to plead earnestly for him,
returning several times;
yet Sengbian would not comply.
Xian first raised troops to ambush Sengbian,
captured him, and strangled him to death.
Prince Zhenyang then abdicated his position and departed for his residence.
The hundred officials presented a memorial to Prince Jin’an, urging him to ascend the throne.
In the tenth month, Prince Jin’an ascended to the imperial position and changed the era name to Shaotai.
He reigned for three years.
Yuanming, the Marquis of Zhenyang, was appointed Minister of Education (Situ).

*The Annals of Liang* Shaothai Year 1; Taiping Year 2. Biyi (479): Liang Shaothai Year 1; Later Liang Emperor Xuan Chao, First Year of Dading; Western Wei Gongdi Year 2; Northern Qi Tianbao Year 6. In the first month of the Later Liang, the Lord of Liang, Chao, ascended the imperial throne at Jiangling.
This was Emperor Xuan.
He was the third son of Emperor Xiaowen and was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Yueyang.
Feeling dissatisfied with Emperor Yuan,
he subsequently sought the status of a vassal state under the Western Wei;
by this time, his state was known as Liang.
The year was named Dading.
He posthumously honored his father, the Crown Prince, as Emperor Shaoming,
with the temple name Gaozong.
Tuo reigned for seven years.
In his memorial to the Wei court, he styled himself a subject and followed the Wei calendar.
Emperor Ming Qi reigned for twenty-four years.
His son, Tai Zi Zong, ascended the throne;
he was the Duke of Ju.
He reigned for two years,
after which the kingdom was returned to the Sui.
In the eighth month, the ruler of Northern Qi traveled from Jinyang back to Ye.
Because the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism were different,
and wishing to eliminate one of them,
he gathered scholars from both schools.
Having been defeated in debate as previously described,
he then issued an edict that all Daoist practitioners must shave their heads and become śramaṇas.
The imperial edict stated:
"Those who have attained the state of an immortal may soar and fly far away.

Those who cannot do so should all reform their practices, return to the orthodox path, and go to the Chief Administrator of the Office of Monastic Affairs (Zhaoxuan Shangtong) to receive tonsure and enter the monastic order."
There was one who would not comply; only after four people had been killed did he obey the command.

Consequently, throughout the borders of Qi, there were no more Daoist practitioners. This is recorded in the *Beiqi ji* (Annals of Northern Qi) and the *Nanshan Xuanlüshi lunheng* (Treatise on the Balance of Vinaya Master Xuan of the Southern Mountains).

Bingzi year: First year of Taiping of the Liang; second year of Dading of the Later Liang; third year of the Western Wei. In the twelfth month, the mandate was ceded to the Zhou. Seventh year of Tianbao of the Northern Qi. Forty-two translators of scriptures for the Liang dynasty.
The *Bianzheng lu* (Record of the Rectification of Orthodoxy) states that seven hundred and eighty fascicles of sutras and treatises were translated,
two thousand eight hundred and forty-six monasteries were established,
and there were eighty-three thousand monks and nuns.
Thus, the four rulers of the Liang dynasty, totaling fifty-five years, were subsumed under the Chen.

The Chen dynasty was founded by those surnamed Chen, with its capital at Jiankang; its six rulers—the High Ancestor (Emperor Wu), the Worldly Ancestor (Emperor Wen), the Deposed Emperor, the High Sovereign (Emperor Xuan), and the Later Sovereign—totalled thirty-three years.
Emperor Wu, the Gaozu: His taboo name was Xian, and his courtesy name was Xingguo.
He was a native of Changxing in Huzhou.
Serving the Liang dynasty, he merited high honors for his role in defeating Hou Jing.

In the eighth month of the dingchou year, he was promoted to the rank of Chancellor (xiàngguó), granted overall authority over the hundred officials, enfeoffed as the Duke of Chen, and invested with the nine emblems of imperial regalia.
The state of Chen was then established with its full complement of government offices.
In the tenth month, he was advanced in rank to King and received the abdication of the throne.
He enfeoffed Emperor Jing of Liang as the Prince of Jiangyin.
The Emperor reigned for three years.
Age fifty-seven: Yongding 3. Dingchou year:

The first year of Chen Yongding, October; the third year of the reigned era Dading. First year of Zhou Wenyu Jue, August; Jue was deposed and Yu was enthroned. Tianbao 8 of Northern Qi. The Zhou dynasty had the surname Wenyu.
He was a native of Wuchuan in Daixu Commandery.
His father, Tai, served the Wei dynasty and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhou.
The third son, Jue, succeeded him in the title.
In the twelfth month of the Bingzi year, he received the abdication from the Wei dynasty;
by the first month of this year, he ascended the throne as Heavenly King,
and the state was named Zhou.
He posthumously honored his father, Tai, as Emperor Wen Taizu.
He established his capital at Chang’an and,
rather than instituting a formal era name, designated the first year of his reign as the "First Year."
He enfeoffed Emperor Gong of Wei as the Duke of Song,
succeeding the Wei dynasty based on the virtue of wood to inherit the water element,
and adopted the calendar of the Xia dynasty.
The color of his court attire was black.
Having realized that the nature of Yuwen Hu, Duke of Jin and Grand Marshal, was tyrannical and that he monopolized power,
in the eighth month he plotted to assassinate him.
When the matter was exposed,
Hu deposed the king and made him the Duke of Lueyang.
Within a month, he assassinated him.
He reigned for eight months.
At the age of sixteen,
he invited Yu, the Duke of Ningdu and Governor of Qizhou, to ascend the throne.
He immediately ascended the throne as Emperor Wen’s eldest son;
he was known as Emperor Ming, the "Enlightened Ancestor."
He reigned for four years.
For the first two years, he did not establish an era name.

In the first month of the Jīmō year, the Grand Preceptor and Second Duke, Yuwen Hu, submitted a memorial to return the administration to him; only then did Yù personally attend to the myriad affairs of state.
In all military affairs, the Protector shall still exercise general supervision;
the title of "Inspector General of State Military Affairs" (Dudu Zhoushen) is changed to "General Commander" (Zongguan).
In the eighth month, Cui You, Grand Master of the Palace Administration, submitted a proposal,
suggesting that the sages followed precedents and altered practices according to the times and circumstances.
He argued that the current Son of Heaven’s title of “King” was insufficient to awe the world.
Please follow the ancient precedents of the Qin and Han dynasties by assuming the title of Emperor and establishing an era name; thus,
the King of Zhou shall be titled Emperor.
The Emperor changed the era name to Wucheng; he was intelligent and possessed keen insight.
Duke Hu of Jin feared him.
In the fourth month of the second year of Wucheng:
Poison was placed in a sugar mallet;
the Emperor ate it and passed away.
His age was twenty-seven.
Emperor Wu (Yong) ascended the throne.
He was the fourth son of Emperor Wen.
He reigned for eighteen years.
He abolished the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism.
His life spanned thirty-six years.
Emperor Xuan (Bīn) was the eldest son of Emperor Wu.
Having reigned for two years,
he abdicated the throne to the Crown Prince Chǎn and styled himself Emperor Tiānyuán.
He lived to the age of twenty-two.
Emperor Jing later changed his name to Yan.
Yang Jian, the Duke of Sui, served as Chancellor.
He further interpreted the two teachings of Daoism and Buddhism.
Having reigned for one year,
he abdicated the throne in favor of the Sui Prince Jian.

Wuyi (5th day of the 5th month): Chen, second year of Yongding; Later Liang, fourth year of Dading; Emperor Ming of the Zhou Dynasty, second year of Yuzheng; Northern Qi, ninth year of Tianbao; Chen, fifth month.
The Emperor visited Da-zhuangyan Temple to practice the rite of "giving up the body.
The ministers submitted a memorial requesting his return to the palace,
where he established a Great Unrestricted Assembly (mochadai) to provide offerings and alms to the Sangha.
He practiced the release of living beings and the pardon of criminals.
In Yangzhou, he established Dong'an Temple,
as well as four other temples, including Xinghuang and Tiangong.
Emperor Zhou honored the Buddha-vehicle and personally attended to his kinsmen;
for the sake of the late Emperor, he commissioned woven images of Vairocana and two Bodhisattvas,
each twenty-six feet in height.
He commissioned twelve life-sized sandalwood statues, each accompanied by two bodhisattvas and a golden lion, all exquisitely crafted as if by nature;
this was recorded in the *Bianzheng lu*.

In the sixth month of the third year of Yongding (558), the Emperor passed away. In the eighth month of the fifth year of Dading (561), he was posthumously titled Emperor [of the Northern Qi]. In the tenth month of the first year of Wucheng (562), the tenth year of Tianbao, the Emperor died. The Chen Emperor had twelve sets of the Buddhist scriptures transcribed.
He commissioned one million statues made of gold and copper,
restored thirty-two old temples,
ordained seven thousand monks and nuns, and compiled the *Bianzheng lu* (Records for Distinguishing Orthodoxy).
Xianzu Xuan Di Yang of the Northern Qi reigned for ten years.
During his reign, the Buddha-dharma flourished greatly;
eight thousand monks and nuns were ordained, as recorded in the *Lüshi lunheng*.
Regarding Emperor Wenzu, Shizu Wendi: his personal name was Qiàn, and his courtesy name was Zihuá.
He was the eldest son of Prince Zhāoliè, the elder brother of Emperor Wǔzōng.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Linchuan.
The Empress Dowager established him on the throne according to her final testament.
He reigned for seven years.
Age forty-five. The sixth year of Tianjia (555), the first year of Tiankang (560). Gengchen.

The first year of Tianjia, the sixth year of Dading, the second year of the Zhou Wucheng era—on the fourth month, the Emperor passed away. The first year of Qianming of the Northern Qi, the first year of Huangjian—on the eleventh month, the second month of the Northern Qi.
The Crown Prince was established as Emperor Yin;
he changed the era name to Qianning.
In the eighth month, the Empress Dowager deposed him and made him the Prince of Jinan.
Changshan Wang Yan ascended the throne.
In the eleventh month, he changed the era name to Huangjian Year 1.
In the tenth month of Huangjian Year 2, the Emperor fell from his horse while hunting; his ribs were severed, and he passed away.
In his final testament, he commanded his younger brother, Zhan, to succeed to the imperial succession.
The second year of Huangjian was changed to the first year of Taining.
Both Yan and Zhan were younger brothers of Emperor Xuan.
The Second Patriarch, the Venerable Master Huike, was the son of Lady Ji of Wulao in Luojing;
his original name was Shenguang.
He had extensively studied the Odes and the Books.
He was particularly adept at the profound principles of the Dharma.
In his youth, he traveled to Longmen Xiangshan in Luoyang and took ordination under Chan Master Baojing.
He received full ordination at Yongmu Temple.
His master pointed him out,
and he subsequently beheld Bodhidharma on Mount Shaoshi at Shaolin Temple.
The circumstances regarding the attainment of the Dharma are listed below in the chapter on Bodhidharma.
As the Patriarch continued to propagate the profound wind of the Dharma, he extensively sought a Dharma heir.
During the Northern Qi dynasty, there was a lay practitioner.
He was over forty years of age and did not mention his name or lineage.
When he arrived to perform the rites, he asked about his ancestors, saying:
"Your disciple’s body is afflicted by a chronic wind-ailment."
"Please repent for your transgressions, Upādhyāya," he said. The Patriarch replied, "Bring forth your transgressions and I shall repent for them with you.
After a long while, the practitioner said:
When he searched for his offense, it could not be found.
The Master said,
"I have finished repenting for your offense on your behalf."
"You should dwell in reliance upon the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Sangha. The man said,
"Now that I have seen the Upādhyāya, I already know what the Sangha is."
"May I inquire what is called the 'Buddha-dharma'?
The Master replied, "This very mind is the Buddha;
this very mind is the Dharma."
The Dharma-Buddha is non-dual;
the Jewel of the Sangha is likewise so.
The scholar said:
Today I have finally come to know that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-dharma— there is no duality between them.
The Patriarch held him in high esteem, saying,
"He is my treasure.
He immediately ordained him as a monk and named him Sengcan.
He received full ordination at Guangfu Temple and served as an attendant for two years,
whereupon his master addressed him, saying:
Bodhidharma came from afar from Central India;
he secretly entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma along with the robe of faith to me.
I now transmit them to you.
"You should protect it so that it is not severed.
Listen to my verse:
'Originally, there is the ground of conditions.'"
Flowers grow from seeds in the ground;
yet fundamentally, there have been no seeds,
nor have flowers ever been produced.
The method for entrusting the robe is concluded.
Furthermore, he said:
"You must receive my teaching."
It is appropriate to dwell in the deep mountains;
you should not yet go forth to transform others through teaching,
for I fear you may encounter worldly calamities.
"However, I too have karmic debts from past lives that I must now repay. Thereupon,
Sengzu went to the capital city of Ye.
He preached the Dharma as was appropriate for each occasion.
After thirty-four years had passed,
he later expounded upon the Unsurpassed Way beneath the mountain gate of Kuangjiu Temple in Guancheng County.
At that time, there was a Dharma Master named Bianhe who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* within the monastery;
his disciples gradually drifted away.
Hui was resentful that his grandfather had been slandered by the district magistrate, Zhai Zhongkan.
When Zhai was punished for his crime against the grandfather,
Hui then submitted himself to the natural course of events.
At that time, he was one hundred and seven years old.
This was on the sixteenth day of the third month in the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
He was buried seventy li northeast of Fuyang County in Cizhou.

The Tang Emperor Dezong’s posthumous title was Taizu Chanshi (Ancestral Founder Chan Master). Xinsi (1st year): Chen Tianjia Year 2; Later Liang Dading Year 7; Northern Zhou Emperor Wendi Yong’s Baoding Year 1;

Northern Qi Huangjian Year 2; November, changed to Danning Year 1. Renwu (2nd year): Chen Tianjia Year 3; Qiao died; his son Kui ascended the throne and, receiving the mandate from the Zhou, styled himself Emperor. Tianbao Year 1; Baoding Year 2; Heqing Year 1. Guiwei (3rd year): Chen Tianjia Year 4; the Emperor held a Great Unobstructed Assembly in the Taiji Hall. Mingdi Kui; Tianbao Year 2; Baoding Year 3; Heqing Year 2; Dharma Master Fashang; Northern Qi Shizhu Chengdi Zhan.
An altar was constructed within;
he invited the Senior Dharma Master to bestow the precepts of taking refuge.
The Emperor spread his hair upon the ground.
He commanded the Dharma Master to step upon his hair and ascend the seat.
Once the Emperor had completed receiving the precepts,
he next conferred the Bodhisattva Precepts upon the eight high-ranking ministers, the empress, and their kinsmen.
He founded Bode Temple (Bōdé sì) to house the Dharma Master.
A popular saying states:
"The Sangha’s aspiration for the four seas; the Dharma site of the Fashang Temple Record Stele Inscription."
On one day, Master Sengshi, a minister of the Zhou Emperor who had fully exhausted himself in ritual reverence,
said to the assembly of monks:
"Quickly perform the dharma rites and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara."
He saved the lecture hall in Jiangnan from the calamity of its collapse.
At that time, the lecture hall in Yangdu was filled with a great assembly of people gathered to hear the Dharma,
both monastics and laypeople alike.
Suddenly, they heard an extraordinary fragrance from the northwest and the sound of music in the air.
The entire assembly emerged in astonishment to look,
and the hall instantly collapsed.
The great assembly suffered no harm.
[The matter] was reported to the Prince of Liang,
who then passed the report on to the Zhou.
Thus one knows the protection afforded by the Zen Master.
On the eighteenth day of the seventh month of that year, the Zen Master entered nirvana at the age of eighty-eight.

The Emperor mourned for him with great grief. He issued an imperial decree to have his portrait painted at Dàfútián Temple for veneration; this is recorded in the *Gǎnyìngzhuàn* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance). Jiǎshēn (Year 1):

The fifth year of Tiānjiā, the third year of Tiānbão, and the beginning of the Zhou dynasty’s regulations requiring the hundred officials to carry ceremonial tablets. Dìngchóu Sì (Year 4): The third year of Héquing during the Northern Qi. Yǐyōu (Year 2): The sixth year of Tiānjiā, the fourth year of Tiānbão, and the fifth year of Bǎodìng. The Emperor abdicated the throne to the Crown Prince Wěi. Dàtǒng Yī (Year 1): In the fourth month, it was changed to Bǐngxū. Tiānkāng Yī (Year 1): In the fourth month, the Emperor passed away. Tiānbão Wǔ (Year 5): Bǎodìng Liù (Year 6), Dàtǒng Èr (Year 2). Emperor Wén of the Chen dynasty repaired and restored sixty old temples.
He transcribed fifty *piṭaka* of Buddhist scriptures and ordained twenty thousand monks and nuns. Regarding Yi Chu’s *Liu tie*:
King Linhai, whose personal name was Bozong.
The History states: Emperor Fei was the eldest son of Emperor Wen;
he reigned for two years.
Emperor Ancheng Xu, acting on the command of Empress Dowager Zhang,
deposed the Emperor and made him the Prince of Linhai at the age of nineteen.
Xu ascended the imperial throne. Guangda 2. Dinghai.

Guangda 1. Tianhe 6. Tianhe 2. Bei Qi. Datong 3. Shi Wangming. By imperial decree of Emperor Wu of the Zhou, [Wang]ming—whose name was pronounced "Wu" (meaning "none")—was appointed as the Tripiṭaka Master of Xiazhou.
He was soon about to be appointed to an official post.
In the fifth month of the second year of the Tianhe era,
the Chancellor Yuwen Hu exhorted him with a letter.
He replied that his name was Da (Answer), and that his original aspiration was to withdraw his traces into the mountain crags and collect his mind beyond the dust of the world.
Consequently, he composed the "Admonition on the Golden Man" and the "Inscription for Quieting the Mind," which read as follows: [The texts of the Admonition and Inscription follow.]
In the Dharma-realm, there was a man who was like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
He concealed his person and inscribed [his resolve] upon his breast; the text of it ran briefly as follows:
"Much knowledge and many affairs are not as good as stilling the mind."
Excessive deliberation leads to many errors; it is better to maintain single-mindedness.
Excessive deliberation scatters one's resolve, and excessive knowledge agitates the mind.
An agitated mind gives rise to affliction, and a scattered resolve obstructs the Path.
"Excellence in talent and artistry is considered a foolish affliction;
a single skill or ability is like a solitary lamp in the falling dusk,
or a mosquito in mid-air," as recorded in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
The Great Chan Master Sengzhi of Nanyue, whose name was Huisi,
was the son of the Li family of Wujin.
Originally, he was a disciple of Chan Master Huiren of the Northern Qi.
Once, while perusing the Tripiṭaka, he obtained the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

He attained a profound realization of its essential meaning and immediately paid homage from afar to the Great Being Nāgārjuna— the fourteenth patriarch of India and author of the treatise— as his teacher.
He expounded upon the treatise on the three contemplations of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle,
the original text of which states:
"All phenomena produced by causes and conditions."
I say that this very thing is emptiness;
it is also called a provisional name, and it is also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
The Great Dhyāna Master Zhiyi, a master of wisdom, subsequently codified its teachings and contemplations.
In the third year of the Chengsheng era of Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty,
he sought to rely upon Huiren to awaken to and enter the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra and the Dvāra of the Revolving Dhāraṇī,
and he reverently received the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts.
He did not wear silk or cotton;
when it was cold, he would spread ripe mugwort beneath his seat.
His reputation for practicing the Way spread far and wide.
At that time, the Great Master Chengsi was once ill; he contemplated it and said:
"Illness arises from karma."
Karma arises from the mind;
when the mind does not arise through conditions,
what form do external objects take?
He observed that his karmic ailments and his body were both like clouds and shadows;
having made this contemplation, his body became light and at ease.
Later, as he led his disciples southward, he encountered the chaos of the Liang dynasty.
He stayed briefly at Taishu Mountain.
In the first year of the Guangda era of Emperor Chen Feidi,
he came to Nanyue and said to his disciples:
"I once lived in this place in a previous life.
Pointing to the groves and springs, he said, "This was an ancient temple.
Upon digging the earth, they discovered the foundations of the halls and the utensils used by the monks.
The remains were recovered from beneath two stones,
whereupon a stupa was erected called the "Stupa of Three Lives.
At the heart of the mountain, the Prajñā Monastery was established.
A spring emerged from the ground at Hupao to provide for his disciples.
In the first year of the Dajian era of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty,
a Daoist priest at the mountain shrine secretly informed the Emperor, falsely accusing the Master.
A monk from the north received a decree from the Qi state;
he gouged out the heart of the mountain, drove nails into the rock, and raised a demonic disturbance.
The Emperor of Chen dispatched an envoy to pursue the Master.
The Master arrived, his staff flying through the air;
the Emperor, marveling at this, welcomed him to provide for his needs and settled him at Qixuan Temple.
When the debate on Buddhist principles concluded,
the Emperor condemned the Daoist for his deception and intended to execute him;
the Master submitted a memorial on his behalf to secure his release.
The Emperor then issued an edict for all Daoist practitioners to provide service to the Master.
The Master submitted a memorial requesting to return to Mount Nanyue.
The Emperor saw him off with exceptional honors.
After a long time, the Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"The source of the Way is not far;
the ocean of nature is not remote."
Seek only within yourself;
do not seek from others.
If you seek, you shall not find it.
His attainment was likewise not ultimate.
He entered nirvana on the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty.
He was sixty-four years of age.
The Master’s writings are all extant in the world.
This is the *Xingzhuang benzhuan* (Biography) of the Third Patriarch of the Fahua [Lotus] School.

In the year Wuzi, the second month of the eleventh lunar month of Guangda 2 of Emperor Chen Wenxuan, the Later Liang was abolished. In the seventh year of Tianbao of the Northern Zhou, the third year of Tianghe, and the eleventh month of the fourth year of Datong of the Northern Qi, the Retired Sovereign passed away. [This was] the High Ancestor Xuan Di, Xu.
The second son of King So-ryeol.
He was enfeoffed as Prince Anseong and,
following the testamentary decree, assisted in the governance of the state.
In the eleventh month of this year, the minor emperor was deposed and the [new] emperor ascended the throne.
He reigned for fourteen years;
his age at death was fifty-two.
The Emperor constructed fifty Buddhist temples;
in Yangzhou, he built Taihuang Temple,
in which a seven-story great stupa was erected.
He cast twenty thousand statues of the Buddha in gold and copper,
established Chonghuang Monastery,
and restored one million three hundred thousand ancient images.
In the fourteenth year of the Dajian era, he transcribed the twelve *piṭaka* of the Buddha’s scriptures,
ordained ten thousand monks and nuns,
and compiled the *Bianzheng lu*.

Jichou (491): In the fourth month of the first year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty; in the eighth year of Tianbao; in the fourth year of Tianghe; in the fifth year of Datong—these correspond to the same period. The Venerable Master Sengcan, the Third Patriarch, was a person of unknown origins.
Initially, as a retired scholar (*chushi*), he met the Second Patriarch, Venerable Huikē, during the Northern Qi dynasty.
The Patriarch recognized his potential;
he was tonsured, received full ordination, and attained the Dharma.
In that year, he came from Beiqi to Mount Sikong and subsequently went into seclusion on Mount Wangong in Shuzhou;
this is the present-day Valley Mountain Monastery (Shan谷山寺).
For thirty years his traces remained obscure;
it was only during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty that scholars came to know of him and sought his Way.
Then there was a śrāmaṇera named Daoxin,
who bowed with merit and said:
"I beg the Great Master to reveal to me the Dharma-gate of liberation."
The Patriarch said,
"Who has bound you?
He replied, "No one has bound me."
The Patriarch said,
"Since no one binds you, you are already liberated;
why must you further seek liberation?"
Daoxin immediately attained enlightenment and wished to become his disciple.
After a long time, Daoxin went to Jizhou in Jiangxi to receive the precepts; having returned, [he approached the Master].
The Patriarch said,
"Now that you have received the precepts,
the Way is complete."
I shall go to him at once.
The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury is now entrusted to you;
take both his robe and bowl with you.
Listen to my verse:
"Although the seeds of flowers depend upon the earth,
it is from the earth that the flowers grow from the seeds."
"If no one sows the seeds,
the flower fields will entirely fail to grow.
He spoke again:
"You must transmit this well;
do not allow it to be interrupted.
I am going to travel to Mount Luofu."
He did not return for long;
after another two years, he returned to the mountain valley for over a month.
He held a grand assembly for the people of the state and preached the Dharma to them, after which he passed away beneath a great tree.
This was on the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty.
At that time, the people were in a state of unrest,
and there was no leisure to enshrine it in a stupa.
In the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Xuānzōng of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Cháng of Zhào County was transferred to serve in Shū;
he then opened the tomb and cremated [the remains], obtaining śarīras.
A stupa was erected at the site of his passing, and the report reached the imperial court.
Emperor Xuanzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Jianzhi,
and the stupa was named Jueji (Awakening Quiescence).
Later, during the reign of Emperor Daizong,
the Chancellor Fang Guan composed a preface for the stele inscription, which is extremely detailed. As recorded in the *Zhengzong ji*,
[Nanyue] Zu once composed the *Xinxin ming* (Inscription on Believing in Mind), which has circulated in the world.
The Inscription on Faith: Its text briefly states:
"The Ultimate Way is not difficult;
it only dislikes discrimination."
Simply do not harbor likes or dislikes;
then all will be transparently clear.
A deviation as slight as a hair’s breadth [will lead you astray].
Heaven and earth are vastly separated;
if you wish to attain manifestation before you,
do not harbor thoughts of compliance or resistance.
It is further said:
"Perfectly identical to the great void,
it is without deficiency and without remainder."
This is truly due to their preferences and aversions;
therefore, they are not as [successful] as [we are]. It is also said:
The two arise from the one;
even the one is not maintained.
When the single mind does not arise, [all is still].
The myriad dharmas are without fault.
It is also said:
"The True Suchness Dharmadhātu."
There is neither other nor self;
it is essential that they correspond urgently.
It is simply called non-duality.
Non-dual and entirely identical,
there is nothing it does not encompass.
The wise of the ten directions—
All enter this school.
It is further said:
"The one is all."
All is one. If you can simply be thus,
why worry that you will not reach completion?
Faith and mind are not two;
faith and mind are non-dual.
The path of words is cut off.
The full text of the *Fei qulai jin* (Neither Past, Future, nor Present) is contained in the *Shiyin ji*.

Gengyin [year]. Chen [Dynasty] Da jian 2nd year; Later Liang Tianbao 9th year; Zhou Tianhe 5th year; Northern Qi Wuping 1st year. Under the Northern Qi, the Imperial High Patriarch of the Shaoxuan Monastery, Dharma Master Tanyan.
By imperial decree, his rank was advanced to that of *Zhaoxuan Shangtong*.

*Xinmao* (the 10th day of the 10th month). The third year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty; the tenth year of the Tianbao era of the Later Liang; the sixth year of the Tianghe era of the Northern Zhou; and the second year of the Wuping era of the Northern Qi. He served as a Vinaya Master (*lǜshī*) and Head of the Clergy (*sēngzhèng*). Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty acted once again as the foster mother for the Empress Dowager Xiaotai, who was his maternal kin.
He established a sacred shrine at Taihuang Temple,
fifteen zhang in height,
in which he enshrined a relic of the Buddha’s fingernail.
It was stored in a precious casket,
and an edict was issued to the monastic officials within the realm:
those who had first received the precepts less than five years prior were [to be excluded].
All [the monks] participated in the Vinaya section.
Large lecture halls were established in the great monasteries of the capital,
and it was decreed that Master Dao-yuan should oversee and supervise them in their entirety.
He publicly announced the imperial examination;
the relevant authorities provided him with clothing and food.
Furthermore, by imperial decree, Vinaya Master Yuan was appointed as the National Head Monk (Guosengzheng), and the *Sengshi lüe* (A Brief History of the Sangha) was compiled.

Renchen (the 4th year of Dajian, the 11th year of Tianbao, the 1st year of Jiande, and the 3rd year of Wuping), September: Emperor Chen issued an edict for Xu Ling, the Vice President of the Secretariat, to compose the inscription for the Stele of the Great Master Fu of Shuanglin in Wuzhou.
The Emperor issued an edict for Zhou Hongzheng, the Vice President of the Secretariat, to compose the Stele Inscription for Upādhyāya Huìhé and the Temple Record of Chénjì Monastery.
Emperor Zhou also summoned Dhyāna Master Sēngwěi to the capital,
where he personally received his precepts and instructions.
The Emperor decreed that the empresses, consorts, dukes, and high officials should all receive the ten wholesome precepts.
He decreed that [the Master] reside at Tiānbǎo Monastery in the capital and later return to the East.
He further decreed that he be appointed as the Tripiṭaka Master of Ān Prefecture.
Emperor Zhou had long been a devout and respectful follower of the Buddha.
He constructed monasteries and erected stupas, ordained monks,
and transcribed more than a thousand volumes of Buddhist scriptures.
Suddenly, he was deluded by the Daoist Zhang Bin and first conceived the intent to destroy the Teaching.
On the seventeenth day of the fifth month of the Jiawu year, he issued an edict abolishing Buddhism.
Shortly thereafter, an imperial decree was issued to abolish Daoism as well.
The Dharma Master Jing’ai went to the palace gate to have an audience with the Emperor;
he presented his arguments at length, explaining why it was inappropriate to destroy the Daoist teachings.
When he heard the discourse on calamities and blessings, as well as karmic retribution,
Emperor Zhou changed his expression;
seeing that his own deeds were already established, he remained silent.
Once the imperial decree had been promulgated,
it could not be revoked; therefore,
he took his leave and dismissed him.
Fai withdrew to Taoyishan.
He compiled the *Sanzhaolu* (Record of the Three Jewels) in twenty fascicles, which circulated in the world as a local gazetteer.

In the year Guisi—the fifth year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty, the twelfth year of the Tianbao era of the Later Liang, the second year of the Jiande era of the Northern Zhou, and the fourth year of the Wuping era of the Northern Qi—the monk Seng’an resided at Wangwushan and lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
A female pheasant was crouching there, listening.
That year, Dao’an arrived in Yuezhou.
In one household, there was a girl whose hair was like the feathers of a pheasant.
Seeing her peaceful as if she were an old acquaintance, one knew that this daughter was indeed Zhì. *Ganying ji* (Records of Spiritual Resonance). Jia-wu:

the sixth year of Dajian, the thirteenth year of Tianbao, the third year of Jiande; the fifth year of Wuping [when Buddhism and Daoism were abolished]. Yi-wei: the seventh year of Dajian, the fourteenth year of Tianbao, the fourth year of Jiande, the sixth year of Wuping. [The reign of] Emperor Kui of the Later Liang.
In Jingzhou, the *Bianzheng lu* (Record of the Clarification of Orthodoxy) was compiled for the construction of the Tianhuang, Zhiqu, Daming, Baoguang, Siwang, and other temples.
This year, the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai arrived in Jiankang.
The Chan Master’s name was Zhiyi;
his courtesy name was De’an.
He was born into the Chen family of Huāróng in Jīngzhōu.
At the age of eighteen, he left the household life.
He first visited Master Huisi of Mount Dasu,
who immediately showed him the Bodhimanda of Samantabhadra.
He preached the Four Modes of Peaceful Practice for them.
When the Great Master was reciting the Lotus Sūtra and reached the Chapter on the Medicine King, he said:
This is true diligence;
this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata,
whereby one awakens to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
He attained the *Lü* (Lakṣa) Dhāraṇī and beheld the single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa,
solemn and as if it had not yet dispersed.
When it came time for him to take his leave and depart to travel and transform others, Sengsi said,
"You have a karmic affinity with the state of Chen."
His past endeavors were certain to bring benefit.
Upon arriving at Jiakuan Temple in Jiankang during the year of Yiwei,
he began to propagate the Dharma of Chan.
The Vice President Xu Ling, the Minister Mao Xi, and others of noble standing all received the imperial instructions.
Once, they dreamed of ascending a high mountain and seeing a monk beckoning them with his hand.
In the ninth month of that year, they arrived at Mount Tiantai.
Dīpaṃkara came out to meet him and said,
"Do you remember our invitation from yesterday?
The Great Master was struck with wonder and prostrated before him.
He then established a hermitage to practice the Way.
Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty issued an edict summoning the Master back to the capital to reside at Guangzhai Monastery.
In the ninth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, the Chen state was extinguished.
The Great Master then took up residence on Mount Lu.
In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, Prince Jin Guang was appointed to oversee the regions of Jiang and Huai;
on the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, [the Master] was at the Jincheng General Commandery in Yangzhou.
He requested the Great Master to convene an assembly of monks and confer upon him the Bodhisattva precepts,
honoring the Master with the title "Zhizhe" (The Wise One).
After a long time, he returned to Mount Lu.
King Jin requested him to leave the mountains once more to alleviate the misfortunes of Consort Xiao.
He established a seven-day fast and performed the *Guangming* Repentance.
Once his illness was cured, he returned to Mount Lu;
passing through the peaks of Mount Heng, he arrived in the Jing region and stayed at Wangquan Temple.
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, he passed away at Shicheng Temple on Mount Tai.
He was sixty-seven years of age and had forty years of monastic seniority.
The Great Master constructed thirty-six great monasteries,
commissioned the transcription of fifteen Tripitakas,
and authored more than one hundred fascicles of sutra commentaries.
He fashioned eighty thousand images made of gold, copper, earth, and wood;
he ordained fifteen thousand monks;
and those among the clergy and laity in over fifty provinces who received the Bodhisattva precepts were beyond counting.
The Great Master [Zhiyi] maintained that the Lotus Sūtra is the wondrous scripture of the One Vehicle;
it opens the provisional gate of skillful means and reveals the sublime principle of ultimate reality.
The assembly praised his minor practices and turned toward the vastness of the One Vehicle;
he subsequently produced the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

It is said that this consists of the "Explanation of Terms," the "Discernment of the Substance," the "Clarification of the Thesis," and the "Treatise on the Application" for the purpose of judging the fivefold stages of the doctrinal characteristics;
later generations followed this tradition and termed it the Tiantai Teaching.
Regarding the nine patriarchs of Tiantai:
first, Master Nanyue Huisi explored the Tripitaka and attained realization of the essential meaning of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* composed by the Great Being Nāgārjuna of the Western Heaven.
He then prostrated from afar to Nāgārjuna as his teacher,
opening the dharma-gate of the three contemplations of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle, and the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
He transmitted the essential tenets of the *Lotus Sūtra* to the Great Dhyāna Master Huisi.
Sishou transmitted it to the Great Chan Master Zhizhe;
Zhizhe transmitted it to Guanding, the Venerable Zhang’an;
and Guanding transmitted it to Weijin-yun.
Jinyun transmitted it to Dongyang Wei;
Dongyang transmitted it to Zuoxi Yuanlang;
and Yuanlang transmitted it to Zhanran, the Venerable Jingxi.
Together they constitute the nine patriarchs.
Students revere them,
calling this the Tiantai Teaching of the Fourfold Dharma, Nature, Contemplation, and Practice.
The Venerable Jingxi entered nirvana in the first year of the Xingyuan era of Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty.
Liang Su of the Hanlin Academy inscribed the following on the back of his memorial stele:
"A sage of the age, a sub-sage."

Bingshen (October): Chen Dynasty, eighth year of Dajian; Later Liang, fifteenth year of Tianbao; Zhou Dynasty, fifth year of Jiande; Northern Qi, first year of Longhua, renamed the first year of Dechang; third year of Jiande of the Zhou, tenth month.
The Lord of Zhou personally led his army to attack Qi and captured Jinzhou.
The Lord of Qi, filled with anxiety and fear, returned from Jinyang to Ye.
The generals of Jinzhou petitioned Yanzong, the Prince of Ande, saying:
The King did not become the Son of Heaven.
The people truly could not exert their utmost strength for the sake of the King.
Having no other choice, Yan Zong ascended the imperial throne.
The Zhou army surrounded Jinyang and attacked the eastern gate, capturing it.
Yanzong fought until he was exhausted and fled toward the north of the city,
where the Zhou troops captured him.
The Lord of Zhou dismounted from his horse, took him by the hand, and said,
"The Emperors of our two nations harbor no resentment or ill will;
we have come solely for the sake of the common people."
"I shall never harm you; do not fear.
He then had him restore his cap and robes and sent him on his way.
The Lord of Zhou issued a general amnesty and abolished the regulations of the Qi dynasty.
He recruited men of martial and civil virtue.
As the Zhou army advanced toward Ye,
the ruler of Qi led his high-ranking officials into the Zhuque Gate.
When asked for strategies to resist the Zhou,
everyone offered different opinions,
and the ruler of Qi did not know which course to follow.
An observer of atmospheric vapors declared that there would surely be a change of regime.
The ruler of Qi consulted with the Minister of State Affairs Gao Yuanhai and others;
they deliberated and, following the precedent of the Great Unification, abdicated the throne to the Crown Prince Heng. On the first day of the first month of the year Dingyou, the day was Yebai.
The Crown Prince of Qi, Heng, ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the era name to Chengguang and honored the former ruler of Qi as the Great Sovereign Emperor (Da Shang Huangdi).
In the year Wuchen (592), the Zhou army arrived at Ye and surrounded it.
The Qi forces went out to battle and were utterly defeated.
The Qi Sovereign fled eastward with a hundred horsemen.
The King of Qi and all those below the Emperor surrendered.
On the day Jia-wu, the Lord of Zhou entered Ye.
On the day Yi-wei, the Retired Sovereign of Qi crossed the river and entered Jizhou.
On this day, the young sovereign abdicated the throne in favor of the Grand Chancellor Ren Chengzhu Hui.
Hui issued an edict honoring the Retired Sovereign as the Unsurpassed Retired Sovereign and the young sovereign as the Heavenly King of the Song State.
In the Bingshen year, the Retired Emperor of Qi left Empress Dowager Hu at Jizhou;
he himself, along with Empress Mu, Lady Shu, the young ruler, Han Changluan, and several dozen others, fled to Qingzhou intending to enter Chen.
The Zhou forces arrived suddenly.
The Retired Emperor, the Empress-Dowager, the young Emperor, and others fled south on more than ten horsemen.
Yu Chiqin pursued them and captured them all.
Empress Dowager Hu also escorted [the relics] to Ye.
The Northern Qi dynasty, comprising five emperors for a total of twenty-eight years, was extinguished.
In the fourth month, the Lord of Zhou returned to Chang’an.
The young ruler of Northern Qi was enfeoffed as the Duke of Wen;

this was the Zhou Annals. Dingyou year: the ninth year of the Dajian era of Chen; the sixteenth year of the Tianbao era of Later Liang; the sixth year of the Jiande era of Zhou; the first year of the Chengguang era of the young ruler of Northern Qi. The state of Northern Qi was extinguished. There were six masters of scripture translation.
Fifty-two volumes of sutras and treatises were translated;
there were more than two million monks;
and over forty thousand monasteries were established, according to the local gazetteers.

Wu-xu: The tenth year of Dajian, the seventeenth year of Tianbao; the Zhou Emperor passed away, and his eldest son, Yun, ascended the throne. This was the first year of Xuazheng (578). Later, he transferred the succession to the Crown Prince and styled himself Emperor Tianyuan in the third month of the seventh year of Jiande of the Zhou dynasty.
The Turks invaded Youzhou.
Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou led his various armies to campaign against the Turks,
but in the fifth month, he fell ill.
In the sixth month, he returned to Chang’an and passed away at the age of thirty-six.
Crown Prince Yǒn then ascended the imperial throne.

Jihai (己亥): The eleventh year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty; the eighteenth year of the Tianbao era of the Later Liang. The Zhou Emperor changed his name from Chuan to Yan. The first year of the Dacheng era was renamed the first year of the Daxiang era, the first month of which [corresponds to this date].
Emperor Xuan of the Zhou, named Yun, received the court audience at the Lumen Gate.
He then began to wear Han and Wei-style robes along with his ministers,
issued a general amnesty, and changed the era name to Dacheng.
He established four assistant officials:
Da Zhuangzai Yue Wangsheng was appointed as the Grand Anticipator (Daqianyi);
the Duke of Shu, Wei Zhidong, the Regional Commander (Zongduan) of Xiangzhou, was appointed as the Grand Right Assistant (Dayoubi).
Li Mu, Duke of Zhongshan, served as Grand Left Assistant;
Yang Jian, Duke of Sui, served as Grand Rear Chancellor.
Emperor Xuan then transmitted the throne to his heir apparent, Chengchuan (Chǎn).
He changed his name to Yan and altered the year of the Dàchéng era to the first year of the Dàxiàng era.
Emperor Xuán proclaimed himself the Tiānyuán Huángdì (Celestial Origin Emperor).
In the tenth month, the images of the Buddha and the Celestial Sovereigns were restored.

In the first month of the second year of the Daxiang era, an edict was issued that all titled ladies of the inner and outer courts should carry ceremonial tablets when performing prostrations at the ancestral temple and the Imperial Altar.
All of them bowed and looked up as if they were men.
In the fifth month of the Heavenly Yuan era, the Emperor fell ill;
he summoned Liu Fang and Yan Zhiyi, dividing them into two groups, to enter his inner chambers.
He wished to entrust his final instructions,
but he became mute and could no longer speak.
When Yang Feng saw that Emperor Jing (Yan) was still a child and immature, and that his father-in-law, Yang Jian, possessed great renown, [he feared for the future].
He then conspired with the State Councilor, Duke of Pei Zheng Yi, Liu Qiu,
and others to bring Zhen into power as the regent.
On that very day, the Heavenly Sovereign passed away.
He was twenty-two years old.
His death was kept secret and not announced.
Fang interpreted the forged edict so as to consolidate the control over military affairs both within and without the capital.
Jiangu革 (Jianguo) abolished the harsh and cruel administration of Emperor Xuan and instead adopted a more lenient and magnanimous policy.
He commissioned the casting of over ten thousand Buddha statues during the Tianyuan era.

He ordered the transcription of three thousand copies of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and maintained the practice of the Eight Precepts of the Great Fast and the constant mindfulness of the Buddha, as recorded in the *Bianzheng Lu*.
In this year of the Chen dynasty, by imperial decree, Master Zhiyi was invited to move his residence to Guangzhai Monastery.
In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, [Daoxuan] served as the Governor-General of Jianghuai.
Prince Jin Guang was the future Emperor Yang.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, at the Jincheng Commandery in Yangzhou, he invited the Master to preside over a monastic assembly to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts.
The Master bestowed upon the king the Dharma-name "Dhāraṇī.
The king reverently adopted the title "Wise One" (Zhìzhě) for the Master;
it was from this point that the appellation "Great Master Zhìzhě" first began.

The Master, in his daily practice, used the system of the five periods and eight teachings to interpret the entirety of the sacred teachings that flowed eastward throughout his lifetime, leaving nothing unexhausted.
Regarding the "five periods":
the first is the period of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Second, during the period at the Deer Park, he taught the four Āgamas.
Third, during the period of the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna], he taught such sūtras as the Vimalakīrti, the Saṃdhinirmocana, the Laṅkāvatāra, the Suvarṇaprabhāsa, and the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda.
Fourth, during the period of the Prajñāpāramitā, he taught the Mahāprajñāpāramitā and the Prajñāpāramitā-ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā.
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* and the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sutras,
as well as the five [sutras] such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*,
when one speaks of the "eight teachings," it refers to these.

The four teachings of Sudden, Gradual, Esoteric, and Indeterminate, as well as the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect, correspond to the "Sudden and so forth" categories, which constitute the *huayi* (the methods of conversion).
These are like worldly medical prescriptions.
The four teachings beginning with the Tripitaka are termed *huafǎ* (the Dharma of conversion).
As in the analysis of medicinal tastes,
regarding the first, the Sudden Teaching:
the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* provides an analogy, stating that when the sun rises, it first illuminates the high mountains.
Regarding the first period:
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "For example, as milk comes from a cow,
so do the twelve divisions of the scriptures come forth from the Buddha."
The second is the gradual teaching.
The three periods and three flavors below this are collectively termed "gradual."
Initially, at the Deer Park, he taught the doctrines of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and so forth.
In terms of time, this was like the sun illuminating the deep valleys;
it was the second period.
By way of analogy, just as curd is produced from milk,
so too do the ninefold sūtras emerge from the twelvefold divisions of the canon.
Next, the Vaipulya section is clarified, including such scriptures as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*.
Criticizing the partial and refuting the small, while sighing over the great and praising the perfect—
these four teachings are all explained therein.
The *Zang* (Tripitaka) is considered the "half-character" teaching.
The *tong* (Shared), *bie* (Distinct), and *yuan* (Perfect) teachings constitute the "full letter" (*manzi*) teaching.
In terms of time, it corresponds to the "time of eating," the third period.
In terms of flavor, fresh butter is produced from curd;
likewise, the Vaipulya is produced from the ninefold canon,
followed by the Prajñāpāramitā.
In terms of time, it is the hour of *yuzhong* (the fourth period).
In terms of flavor, it is the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) extracted from the unrefined butter (*navanīta*).
This Mahāprajñāpāramitā emerged after the Vaipulya sūtras.
As for the third secret teaching,
it is because the Tathāgata’s three wheels are inconceivable.
For some individuals he teaches the sudden approach, while for others he teaches the gradual;
since they are unaware of one another's teachings yet both are able to bring about spiritual benefit, it is called "secret."
The fourth is the teaching of indeterminate meaning.
Among the aforementioned four flavors,
the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice.
Sentient beings each attain understanding according to their respective types.
Through inconceivable power, he is able to cause sentient beings to obtain sudden benefit from gradual teaching,
and gradual benefit from sudden teaching.
Because the benefits obtained differ, it is called the "teaching of non-fixity.

Next, he preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, opening up the previous sudden and gradual teachings so that they may be integrated into that which is neither sudden nor gradual; hence, it is called "opening the provisional to reveal the real."
Furthermore, it is said that provisional means are discarded to establish the ultimate reality;
it is also said that the three vehicles are unified within the One Vehicle.
As the sutra states: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Dharma of the One Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third."
He directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the unsurpassed path;
in terms of time, it is as when the sun reaches its zenith at midday.
There is nothing by which it can be compared or surpassed.
The fifth period is defined according to its flavor as the production of clarified butter (ghṛta) from matured butter (navanīta).
From this Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Lotus Sūtra emerges,
revealing, clarifying, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
and bestowing the prediction of Buddhahood upon those of the three vehicles and all sentient beings.
Next, regarding the teaching of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, there are two meanings. First,
for those who are not yet mature, the four teachings are further expounded,
fully discussing the Buddha-nature.
It causes them to be endowed with true permanence and enter great nirvana;
therefore, it is called the "Gathering" (Kun-shi) teaching.
Second, for those of dull faculties in the final age who give rise to views of annihilationism within the Buddha-dharma, thereby prematurely injuring their life of wisdom and losing the Dharma-body.
It is said that three kinds of provisional [teachings] support one perfect reality;
therefore, it is called the teaching that "supports the Vinaya and discusses the Eternal.
Regarding its timing and its flavor, it is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the four teachings of the transformative Dharma, the first is the Tripitaka Teaching (Sanzangjiao). This consists of:
first, the Sūtra Piṭaka, including the four Āgamas and other such sūtras.
Second, the Abhidharma Piṭaka, including treatises such as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*;
third, the Vinaya Piṭaka, consisting of the five divisions of the Vinaya.
These three piṭakas are names common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.
Now, taking the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna,
we speak of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and so forth; next,
we shall clarify the Shared Teaching (Pāryāptika-yāna).
Because it encompasses the preceding Tripitaka Teachings (Zangjiao) and extends into the subsequent Distinct and Perfect Teachings, it is called the "Shared Teaching" (Tongjiao).
Regarding the third, the "Distinct Teaching" (Biejiao):
it clarifies the teachings, principles, knowledge, severances, practices, stages, causes, and fruits of the Dharma for bodhisattvas alone, outside the [three] realms.
It is called "Distinct" (*bie*) because it is distinct from the three preceding teachings and distinct from the subsequent Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Regarding the fourth, the Perfect Teaching:
it is called "Perfect" because it is perfect and wondrous, complete and sufficient, and perfectly sudden; therefore, it is named the Perfect Teaching.

This refers to the perfect subduing, the perfect faith, the perfect severance, the perfect practice, the perfect stage, the perfect adornment of mastery, and the perfect establishment of sentient beings—
these are what the various Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras describe as the realm of the Buddha.
The stages not shared with the three vehicles all belong to this teaching; that is to say,
the wondrous scripture of the Lotus Sūtra dispels the attachment to the provisional teaching of the "burnt-out city."
He released the stagnant attachments of the thatched hut,
opened the provisional gateways of skillful means,
and revealed the wondrous principle of ultimate reality.
The assembly praised his minor practices and turned toward the vastness of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
He then produced the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), consisting of the "Explanation of Names," "Discernment of the Substance," and "Clarification of the Thesis."
This employs the fivefold classification of the doctrinal systems (*shōjō sō*).
As for its name, it combines both the dharma and the metaphor,
referring to the "wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle."
That is to say, the original nature of sentient beings dwells within ignorance and afflictions without being defiled by them;
it is like a lotus flower situated in the mud whose essence remains ever pure.
Therefore, this is used as its name.
This sutra reveals the provisional to manifest the real,
discards the provisional to establish the real,
and unifies the provisional so that it returns to the real.
Just as the lotus flower carries the meaning of containing, opening, and closing,
and the lotus within the flower carries the meaning of being hidden, appearing, and forming fruit,
it is also said that the trace descends from the source, and through the trace, the source is revealed.
Now, the titles of sutras do not exceed seven types: single dharmas, metaphors, persons, or combinations of these—either singly, doubly, or fully complete.
There are three single types, three double types, and one complete type that encompasses all;
the title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is precisely the first of the double types.
The Dharma and the metaphor form a pair.
The name is used to invoke the essence, and that essence is the true mark (dharmatā).
This is because all phenomenal marks are devoid of essence apart from the true mark.
As for the principle (*zong*), it is the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle;
because the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—which involves opening, showing, awakening, and entering—is worthy of veneration.
As for the function (*yong*), it is the efficacious power.
Because he possessed the power to establish the principle of reviving the abandoned assemblies,
he subsequently categorized the characteristics of the teachings according to the discourse of the Tathāgata’s single lifetime,
classifying them as the Five Periods and Eight Teachings.
Since the doctrine and principles have been clarified, there is no way to restore one's nature except through contemplative practice;
thus, one relies upon the principle of the three truths: emptiness, provisionality, and the middle.
This also involves the three types of cessation and the three types of contemplation;
in each and every contemplation of the mind,
it cannot be apprehended from moment to moment.
First emptiness, then the provisional, and finally the middle;
by departing from the two extremes, one contemplates the single mind,
like the moon beyond the clouds.
This is the practice of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
It is further said: "In destroying all delusions, nothing is more eminent than emptiness;
in establishing all phenomena, nothing is more eminent than the provisional."
In the ultimate sense, there is nothing greater than the Middle Way;
within this one Middle, all things are the Middle—there is nothing provisional, nothing empty, that is not the Middle.
It is the same for emptiness and the provisional.
This is precisely the practice-aspect of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
It is like the three eyes of Maheśvara;
they are neither vertical nor horizontal, nor are they separate from one another.
When the three contemplations are perfected,
the Dharmakāya is no longer latent; yet,
there remains concern that students may be muddled regarding the nature of cultivation or fall into partial attachments.
Furthermore, he established the doctrine of the "six levels of realization" (liu ji) to eliminate this affliction.
First, as for the Buddha in the sense of the identity with principle (li ji fo):
this refers to the beings of the ten dharma realms, down to the smallest gnat.
