Although the fundamental nature is level and even,
those who follow the stream remain unaware of it in their daily lives;
they must necessarily rely on external cultivation through verbal teachings.
Because upon hearing the name, one gives rise to faith and develops understanding.
Regarding the third point, that "the practice of contemplation is itself the Buddha":
having heard the name and attained this opening of understanding, [one realizes it].
This is because one must rely on the preceding three contemplations to return to the source.
Regarding "the fourth, the stage of semblance, is Buddhahood":
when the merit of contemplative practice becomes profound, the function of semblance [of Buddhahood] is manifested.
Regarding "the fivefold true nature is itself Buddhahood":
because the three minds are developed, one attains the functioning of True Suchness (tathatā), which increases and becomes more excellent at every stage.
Regarding "the sixth, ultimate Buddhahood":
Ignorance is forever exhausted;
because the awakened mind is perfectly consummate, one realizes that there is nothing to be realized.
Thus it is with the six aforementioned stages.
Since all are identical with the Buddha— neither deficient nor excessive—
they universally possess the three bodies of Dharma, Reward, and Transformation as the primary aspect, while residing in the four lands as their support.
As for these four lands:
First is the eternally quiescent light land of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*),
wherein the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) resides.
Second is the land of true recompense free from obstruction.
This subsumes the two types of enjoyment.
The land of self-enjoyment is where the *buddha-bhagavān* himself dwells;
the land of other-enjoyment is where bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) dwell.
Third, the land of expedient means with remainder;
fourth, the land where the pure and the defiled coexist;
both are lands of responsive transformation.
It is the dwelling place of bodhisattvas prior to the stages, of those of the two vehicles,
and of ordinary beings; in reality, it is neither body nor land,
and is devoid of superiority or inferiority.
For the sake of responding to the capacities of sentient beings, he provisionally spoke of the distinction between superior and inferior bodies and lands;
yet the Master attained the mutual fusion of body and land, such that the provisional and the ultimate were unimpeded.
Therefore, for over thirty years, day and night, he expounded [the Dharma].
It gives rise to four kinds of benefit and possesses the four *siddhāntas*.
*Siddha* means "pervasive."
*Dāna* is translated as "giving" (*śī*).
The Master’s Dharma is universally bestowed upon all sentient beings,
who each receive benefit according to their own faculties.
As it is said: "The world-siddhānta gives rise to the benefit of joy," and so forth.

Recorded by the student [Yuan] during his period of study, in the year of Yiwei (1035). The *Shizhong xinyao* (Essential Points of the Beginning and End) by the Ninth Patriarch of Tiantai, the Venerable Jingxi, states:
Now, the three truths are the inherent nature and virtue of all things.
The middle truth subsumes all phenomena;
the ultimate truth eliminates all phenomena.
Regarding conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it establishes all phenomena;
to mention one is to include the three,
for they do not exist sequentially.
That which sentient beings inherently possess cannot be obtained through artificial effort.
Alas! That the secret treasury remains unmanifested is because it is shrouded by the three delusions.
Thus, ignorance obscures the dharma-nature;
the sands of affliction obstruct transformative guidance;
and views and thoughts hinder emptiness and stillness.
However, these three delusions are but false imaginings upon the essence itself. Thereupon,
the Greatly Awakened One, the World-Honored One of Compassion,
sighed deeply and said:
Within the realm of True Suchness (tathatā), the provisional designations of sentient beings are utterly extinguished;
within the wisdom of equality, there are no forms of self or other.
It is only because sentient beings follow their own deluded thoughts that they fail to realize it for themselves and are unable to turn back from this state.
Thus, one establishes the three contemplations to shatter the three delusions,
realizes the three wisdoms, and accomplishes the three virtues.
The contemplation of emptiness shatters the delusions of views and thoughts.
Realizing all-knowledge (sarvajñā) accomplishes the virtue of prajñā;
through provisional contemplation, one destroys the delusions as numerous as motes of dust.
Realizing the knowledge of the modes of the path (mārgajñatā) accomplishes the virtue of liberation (vimukti).
The Madhyamika practitioner destroys the delusions of ignorance,
realizes the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), and accomplishes the virtues of the Dharmakāya.
Nevertheless, these three delusions, three contemplations, three wisdoms, and three virtues are not distinct from one another.
It is not that they occur at different times;
for the principle of nature inherently contains all dharmas.
Thus, the nature of these three truths is such of itself.
The three truths, when deluded, transform into the three delusions;
the destruction of these delusions relies upon the three contemplations;
and the perfection of these contemplations realizes the three wisdoms.
Wisdom is perfected through the three virtues;
from cause to fruit, it is not a gradual cultivation.
This explains the sequence of knowledge.
The principle is not sequential;
once the main framework is understood,
the details can be sought.
Gengzi (the year 560 CE): The twelfth year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty; the nineteenth year of the Tianbao era of the Later Liang; the second year of the Daxiang era of the Zhou dynasty.
In the second month, the Emperor of Zhou issued an edict, saying:
The Buddha-dharma is vast and sublime, revered by all since antiquity;
how could it be appropriate to let it remain hidden and neglected, rather than putting it into practice?
From this day forward, it should be followed by everyone from princes and dukes down to the common people.
You should all cultivate these matters and understand my intent. (From the *Zhou ji*):

On the day of Xinchou, the first month of the twentieth year of Tianbao—the thirteenth year of Dajian—was changed to the first year of Dading. In the second month, the throne was abdicated to the Sui; the Sui received the abdication from Zhou. This was the first year of Kaishuang (the first year of the Sui). It was the twelfth month of the second year of Daixiang during the reign of Emperor Jing of Zhou.
He appointed Yang Jian, the Grand Chancellor and Duke of Sui, as Chancellor of State;
he took charge of the hundred ministries and was promoted to the rank of King.
The twenty commanderies, including Anlu, were established as the Kingdom of Sui.
He was granted the privilege of being addressed by title rather than name and received the full nine insignia of investiture;
yet Fu Jian accepted only the rank of Duke of Ten Commanderies.
In the first month of the year Xinchou, Emperor Jing changed the era name to Dading.
In the second month, Yu Jicai, a Court Attendant on Special Duty and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, exhorted the Prince of Sui that he should receive the Mandate of Heaven;
Li Mu, the Grand Tutor, and Lu Ben, the Great General, likewise urged him to do so.
Thereupon, the Zhou sovereign issued an edict to abdicate the throne and retire to a separate palace.
He commanded Qi Gong Chun to present the imperial seal and sash to transfer the mandate to the Sui dynasty.
Thus, the reigns of the five Zhou emperors totaled twenty-five years before their mandate came to an end.
The Prince of Sui received the imperial regalia and entered the Guangling Hall.
He donned the *yuan* robe and *mian* crown according to the rites of the New Year’s assembly.
A general amnesty was proclaimed, and the era name was established as Kaishuang.
Excluding the six Zhou officials, he followed the old precedents of the Han and Wei dynasties by enfeoffing the Zhou Emperor as the Duke of Jie.
He passed away at the age of nine. (From the *Sui Shu*).
The Sui dynasty was founded by the Emperor surnamed Yang,
named Jian. He was a native of Huayin in Hongnong.
He was the fourteenth-generation descendant of Han Taishou Zhen.
His father, Zhong, initially served under Zhou Wen and repeatedly established military merit,
eventually attaining the rank of Taifu.
Jian inherited the title of Duke of Suiguo.
Emperor Wu of Zhou betrothed Jian’s daughter to be the consort of the Crown Prince;
the Crown Prince was Emperor Xuan.
Emperor Jing established [the Sui dynasty] with Yang Jian as regent;
he received the abdication of the Zhou and took fire as his virtue.
He resided in the capital of Chang’an.

In the third month of the first year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict was issued to establish a Buddhist monastery for the Three Jewels at the foot of each of the Five Sacred Mountains. (From the *Sanbao ji*).
The Edict of the Seventh Month states:
We humbly reflect that Emperor Taizu Wuyuan, traversing the vicissitudes of three dynasties, established the foundation of our imperial house.
In reverent admiration of Your divine wisdom, which accords with the profound stillness of the Ultimate Truth,
I have contemplated the desire to extensively honor the precious shrines and initiate the construction of a monastery,
thereby increasing the causes of merit to slightly fulfill Your profound intent.
In Xiangyang, Suijun, Jiangling, and Jinyang,
a monastery shall be established in each location and a stele erected to commemorate his virtues.
Every year, on the anniversary of the Emperor’s death, a vegetarian feast shall be held and rites performed.
The Eight Precepts Repentance is offered to support the spiritual essence.
The Imperial Edict of the Eighth Month states:
"In years past, when the Way of Zhou had declined, the various tyrants were as turbulent as boiling water."
I have dispatched my chariots and trained my soldiers to sweep away the demonic and the foul.
Among those who value integrity and righteousness, there are those who disregard life and forget death;
beneath the clash of arms, I frequently hear of their passing.
Constantly mindful of sentient beings who tread upon the suffering of blades and weapons,
he harbors the supreme Way and gives rise to the resolve for their deliverance;
he intends to establish fields of merit, that the power of the Dharma may provide secret assistance.
May the roots of goodness of those who have died in service increase;
may their rebellious companions pass from darkness into light;
and may they all investigate suffering and emptiness, thereby uprooting themselves from birth and death.
He established a monastery at the site of the battle in Xiangzhou; this is recorded in the Kaihuang Annals.
Furthermore, whenever there were those among the people who had violated the law and reached the end of their sentences, the Emperor invariably ordered the performance of vegetarian feasts for them.
That winter, the śramaṇas Zhizhou and others returned from the Western Regions,
presenting two hundred and sixty volumes of Sanskrit manuscripts.
By imperial decree, these were entrusted to the relevant authorities.
He summoned people to translate [the texts].
Emperor Sui reigned for twenty-four years and lived to the age of sixty-four;
according to the "Annals of the Emperors" in the *Sui Shu* (History of Sui).

Ren-yin (the 10th year of the sexagenary cycle): The fourteenth year of the Dajian era of Chen; the twenty-first year of the Tianbao era of the Later Liang; the second year of the Kaishuang era of Sui. In the first month [of the former year], the Emperor passed away; in the sixth month [of this year].
The Sui Emperor issued an edict stating that Longshou Mountain in Chang'an was suitable for establishing the capital;
the city was named Daxing City,
and the palace hall was named Daxing Hall.
The temple was named Daxingshan Temple.
By imperial decree, the people within the realm were permitted to leave secular life as they wished;
furthermore, they were required to contribute money based on their household population for the construction of scriptures and images.

He appointed the Dharma Master Tanyan as the Head of the Office of the Imperial Secretariat for Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuantong) and issued an imperial decree for him to assist in the translation of scriptures.
He further decreed that the Dharma Master Sengmeng should reside at Daxingshan Temple.
He was subsequently promoted to the position of Great State Preceptor of the Tripitaka for the Sui Dynasty.

Regarding the forty-five provinces through which the Emperor had passed during his former years as a prince, he established the Daxingguo Temple in each of them; this is recorded in the Kaihuang Records.
The Later Sovereign, whose personal name was Shubao,
was the eldest son of Emperor Xuan.
He ascended the throne in the first month of the year of Renyin.
In the ninth month, he established the Unobstructed Assembly (Muge-e) at the Dajeokjeon Hall.
He relinquished his person, his carriage, and his imperial regalia; these matters are recorded in the *Pyeonjeongnok*.
He occupied the throne for seven years.

The fifth year of the reign [of Emperor Wen of Sui], the fourth year of Zhide (癸卯), first year of Zhide of the Chen dynasty, twenty-second year of Tianbao of the Later Liang, third year of Kaiguang of the Sui dynasty; in the third month, he was moved to the new capital. [This corresponds to] the first month of the Sui calendar.
The Emperor issued an edict, saying:
"I venerate and honor the holy teachings and cherish the preservation of sacred shrines.
All monasteries that were abolished during the Zhou dynasty may now be restored."
An edict was further issued, stating:
"Valuing life and detesting killing is the foundation of royal governance;
the Buddha’s Way provides instruction that one may rely upon for virtuous karma."
Endowed with vital breath and possessing spiritual intelligence, life alone is of the utmost importance.
It is fitting that all under heaven be exhorted to unite their hearts in providing protection.
As for the monasteries established by the authorities within the capital and in the various provinces:
In the first, fifth, and ninth months, from the eighth day until the fifteenth, one should regularly perform circumambulation and recitation at the temple.
On these days, no living beings whatsoever—whether they be commoners or officials from near or far—shall be killed. (From the Kaihuang Records)
The Emperor further decreed that the Dharma Master Mingzhan should reside at Daxingshan Temple to translate Buddhist scriptures.
He also appointed Shi Huiyuan as the *Sha-men tong* (Patriarch) of Luozhou and the *Bianzheng lu kaihuang ji* (Director of Rectifying Orthodoxy for the Kaihuang Records).
Jiachen (the year of the Jiachen cycle): the second year of Zhide, the twenty-third year of Tianbao, and the fourth year of Kaishuang;
in the third month, Baoqiong, the Sangtong of the Chen state, entered nirvana at the age of eighty-one.
The Emperor issued an edict for the relevant authorities to provide funeral implements and to borrow the imperial ceremonial procession (*halu buo*) and insignia to adorn the burial site.
The *Shenbian zhengzhi lu* records that the Sui Emperor was born at the former site of the Boreni Temple.
The *Dianzheng lu* (Record of the Rectification of Orthodoxy) for Daxingguo Monastery was composed for Emperor Taizu Wuyuan and Empress Dowager Yuanming.

In the year Yisi, the third year of Zhide and the twenty-fourth year of Tianbao, in the fifth month, Emperor Shuikuo passed away; his son, Prince Zong, succeeded him. In the fifth year of Kaishuang, the Sui Emperor invited Master Jing to receive the Bodhisattva Precepts.
The Imperial Edict stated:
"I have long been graced with manifold blessings and reverently succeeded to the precious mandate.
I now desire to take refuge in the Perfect Enlightenment and venerate the Holy Fruits."
I now invite the Dharma Master of this sutra to receive the Bodhisattva precepts at the Great Xingshan Hall.
For the teaching of the Bodhisattva takes liberation as its priority,
and the foundation of ethical conduct begins with compassion.
Now, as the prisons are dark and gloomy, there is something stirring in my heart.
From those who have committed minor offenses downward, all may be pardoned and released.
Furthermore, he issued an edict saying:
The Buddha entrusted the True Dharma to the kings.
I, as the Honored One among men, have received this entrustment from the Buddha;
from this day forward, until the end of my own life.
Every month, they regularly invite fourteen monks (two groups of seven) to take turns in ascending and descending order to recite the sutras;
there are four masters of the sutras and three venerable elders.
In the Daxingshan Hall, the *Bianzheng lu* (Record of the Rectification of Debates) was read for all the sūtra texts.

Bingwu: the fourth year of Zhide; Hou Liang’s Gongju Gong [Zhangsun Wuji]; Guangyun’s first year; the sixth year of Kaishuang. During the Guangyun era, Prince Xiu of Shu, along with his consorts and ladies, requested that the monk Fajin confer the precepts upon them. Dingwei: the first year of Zhengming; the second year of Guangyun; the seventh year of Kaishuang; the Zhengming era of the Chen dynasty.
In the *Song Zizhi Tongjian*, the character "Xiang" (祥) was used to avoid the imperial temple name of Emperor Renzong;
here, we follow the original text.
August of the Sui dynasty.
He summoned the Prince of Liang to court.
The Prince of Liang led his ministers and set out from Jiangling.
Since the Prince of Liang was abroad, the Sui Emperor [took measures].
Cui Hongdu, Duke of Wuxiang, was dispatched with troops to garrison Jiangling.
Fearing that Hongdu would attack them, the Prince of Liang’s paternal uncle, Prince Anping Yan,
and others drove out one hundred thousand men, women, and children of the civil and military classes to flee to Chen.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor of the Sui dynasty abolished the Liang state.
He invested the former Liang ruler, Zong, as a Zhuguo (Columnar State) and conferred upon him the rank of Duke of Ju.
The three successive rulers of the Later Liang dynasty all revered and believed in the Buddha-dharma, extensively constructing stupas and monasteries.
There were one hundred and eight monasteries,
housing three thousand two hundred monks and nuns, according to the *Bianzheng lu*.
Dharma Master Chen Huibù established Qixia Temple on Mount She during the Zhìdé era in Jiānkāng.
The Emperor of the Chen dynasty and various princes all received the precepts from Huibù.
He was revered as if he were a Buddha.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of this year, he entered nirvana. This is the inscription for the stele recording his life and deeds.
Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty summoned Dharma Master Jñānagupta.
The Imperial Edict stated:
"The Emperor respectfully inquires after the Venerable Dharma Master Tanqian of Xuzhou.
We have learned that you are diligently applying yourself to the Great Teaching, bringing benefit to boundless beings."
Having received your reputation and partaken of your virtue, I truly harbor a sense of longing.
I pray that you will soon manifest your presence to satisfy my weary expectations;
may you proceed to the capital to greatly propagate the Dharma and transform the world during the Kaihuang era.

Wu-shen: Chen Dynasty, second year of Zhengming (589 CE), fifth month—Prince Yin was deposed as Crown Prince and made Duke of Wuxing; Zhang Guifei’s son Shen was established as Crown Prince. Sui Dynasty, eighth year of Kaishuang (608 CE), tenth month—a great military expedition was launched against the Chen. Li Shiqian died in the eighth year of Kaishuang.
Qian Zongyue lost his father at a young age and was renowned for his filial piety in serving his mother.
The clan elder Bozhang often sighed, saying,
"This son is our family's Yanzi."
For thirty years, he humbly distributed medicinal herbs and grain stores.
He was deeply devoted to the Buddha, and his conduct was restrained by the precepts and meditative concentration.
Some said that he was cultivating hidden virtues (*yin-de*).
Xian smiled and said, "Now,
hidden virtue is like ringing in one's own ears;
it is known only by oneself, while others have no way of knowing it."
"Now, all you virtuous ones know what I have done;
what hidden virtue (*guṇa*) could there possibly be?
Qian is most skilled in profound discourse."
There was one who harbored doubts regarding the doctrine of the Buddha’s retribution;
Sishen illustrated this for him, saying,
"Have you not heard the Classic of Changes?"
"The accumulation of good brings forth auspicious blessings, while the accumulation of evil results in calamity.
Is this not indeed a sign of fortune and misfortune?
The guest further asked about the relative superiority or inferiority of the Three Teachings.
Shiqian said,
"The Buddha is the sun;
the Way is the moon."
The Confucian [tradition] is one of the five stars.
A guest examined this in the *Beishi*. Jǐyǒu:
the third year of Zhēnmíng (591 CE), when the Northern Qi was extinguished; the ninth year of Kāihuáng (589 CE), when the world was unified under one rule, in the first month.
Emperor Chen was captured by Han Qintu, the Governor-General of Luzhou under the Sui.
The Sui Emperor issued an edict to level the cities, towns, and palaces of Jiankang, clearing them for cultivation.
He then established Jiangzhou at Shitou City and withdrew his army.
He appointed Wang Shao, the Right Vice Director of the Chancellery and Governor of Shipu, to garrison Shitou.
In the third month, the Chen ruler set out from Jiankang with his princes, dukes, and officials;
in the fourth month, they arrived at Chang’an.
The Sui Emperor bestowed great honors upon the former ruler of Chen;
he was frequently granted audiences and ranked as a third-grade official.
He passed away in the fourth year of the Renshou era.

He was posthumously granted the title of General of the Chariot and Dragoons and Duke of Changcheng County, with the posthumous name Yang. According to the *Sui Shu*, there were three translators from the Chen dynasty.
Two hundred fascicles of sutras and śāstras were translated;
one thousand two hundred and thirty-two monasteries existed;
and seventeen new monasteries were established by the state.
The number of monasteries constructed by the hundred officials was sixty-eight;
within the palace walls, there were three hundred large temples,
housing thirty-two thousand monks and nuns, according to the *Bianzheng lu*.
The above lists the five rulers, totaling thirty-three years, before their submission to the Sui.

The Sui dynasty was of the Yang clan; it claimed the virtue of Fire and was based in Chang’an. Its emperors were Gaozu Wenhuangdi, Yangdidi, Gongdi, and Prince Tong of Yue, who was the younger brother of Gongdi. [Gongdi] changed the era name to Huangtai, the first year of which was the first year of the reign of Gaozu Wenhuangdi. Gaozu Wenhuangdi’s personal name was Jian.
He succeeded Zhou in the year Xin-chou (561).
[This is seen] below the entry for the year Xin-chou. In the spring of the tenth year of Kaihuang (590), during the fourth year of Renshou (604), the Emperor visited Jinyang.
The Imperial Edict stated:
"From the tenth year of the Kaihuang era onwards,
all monks and nuns who have been privately ordained shall be permitted to remain in the monastic order."
Soon thereafter, an imperial edict was issued to establish Shengguang Temple in the capital for the Fourth Prince, Xiao, the Prince of Shu;
the Master was then summoned by decree to reside there with his assembly of disciples,
where he received the Prince’s patronage.
Chan Master Zhishun initially served Chan Master Tanyou while residing at Mount Bailu.
After ten years, he traveled north to Mount Zhanhuang.
His reputation spread far and wide.
In this year, an imperial edict was issued, stating:
"The Emperor respectfully inquires after the health of Chan Master Zhishun of Mount Hong at Changzhou."
The essence of the Way is pure and sublime, instructing the masses of living beings so that they may achieve realization at an early date;
I greatly admire this.
"I have long protected the True Dharma with diligence, day and night.
I now dispatch the Grand Master of the Palace (Kaifu), Lu Yuanshou, to personally proclaim my intentions.
I also send incense and offerings as detailed in the separate manuscript. In the eleventh year, the Emperor issued this decree:
The teachings established by the Tathāgata have their meaning rooted in equality;
the mind of the Bodhisattva is fundamentally without distinction.
Thus, they are able to serve as a bridge for all categories of beings and deliver the multitudes of living creatures.
I occupy the throne as a king among men and uphold the Three Jewels;
I constantly reflect upon the ultimate truth.
He widely expounded the Mahāyāna;
all phenomena were suddenly realized as being essentially devoid of self and other,
so how could there be "public" or "private" distinctions within meritorious deeds?
From now on, regarding all meritorious constructions,
throughout the realm they shall be undertaken collectively and established in unison according to one's inclination;
I pray that you do not give rise to discrimination.
May all dharma-gates thus converge in non-duality.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, may all together reach Bodhi. This was recorded in the Kaihuang era.
At that time, the Dharma Master Tanyan entered nirvana.
He was appointed as the Imperial Preceptor for three successive reigns.
At the time of his death, he presented a memorial to the Emperor to take leave,
entrusting him with the protection of the Dharma from without.
The Emperor mourned for him with profound grief.
The hundred officials presented white silk as a mark of mourning to accompany his funeral procession.
Xue Daoheng, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, composed the sacrificial inscription.
In brief: In the past,
when the Way was lost and the subtle guiding principles had snapped their cords,
he took refuge in secluded crags with an unshakable resolve.
High rank and generous emoluments could not turn his mind;
stern majesty and rigorous laws were insufficient to intimidate his heart.
Thus, the Sage Emperor inaugurated his auspicious reign.
The Semblance Dharma flourished once more;
Zuo stood out preeminently among those in black robes,
becoming their leader and humbling even the gravity of the North Star.
The principle of the relationship between teacher and disciple is hereby reaffirmed;
through it, the Triple Gem is propagated and protected,
and the Two Truths are proclaimed and disseminated.

His faith was sufficient to allow him to follow in the footsteps of Fotudeng and Kumārajīva, and to surpass Dao’an. *Biànzhèng lù*. In the second month of spring in the thirteenth year, an imperial edict was issued to construct the Renshǒu Palace north of Zhèng Prefecture in Fēngxiáng Commandery, Shǎnxī.
Prince Xiu, the Prince of Shu, was hunting in the wilds of Zhengzhou when his horse suddenly bolted into an ancient kiln.
The entire kiln was filled with ancient images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor issued an edict commanding all local government offices to conduct a thorough inspection and inventory of all existing images.
The [relics] were transported to the temple.
It was decreed that every commoner throughout the realm should contribute one coin, and officials were commissioned to oversee the decoration.
A memorial inscription was established, which stated:
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, Yang Jian,
the Emperor of the Sui Dynasty and disciple of the Buddha, respectfully addresses the Triple Gem of the ten directions:
Looking up with reverence, I contemplate how the Tathāgata, through his compassion, propagated the Great Way to deliver all living beings.
Severing the source of evil and opening the path of benevolence and goodness, it is that upon which all,
from the court to the countryside, rely.
During the period of disorder under the Zhou dynasty, the sacred traces were insulted and desecrated;
stupas and monasteries were destroyed and abandoned,
and the scriptures and images perished.
Thus, the ignorant have no means to guide those in delusion,
and the wise have no way to seek out the numinous sages.
Your disciple has previously relied upon the causal conditions of the Triple Gem.
Now, encountering this auspicious era, [the Emperor],
acting as the parent of the people, intends to rescue the common folk and once again manifest the sacred countenance [of the Buddha].
He once again venerated the divine transformations;
where foundations had crumbled and traces were destroyed, he restored them with renewed magnificence.
All discarded images and lost scriptures were ordered to be carved and transcribed.
I, your disciple, now before the Triple Gem, repent with a sincere heart.
I repent for all such grave offenses as the Zhou dynasty’s destruction of images, mutilation of scriptures,
disparagement of the Sangha, and demolition of monasteries.
He reverently offered one hundred and twenty thousand bolts of silk for the repair of all ruined scriptures and images.
May the Triple Gem bear witness and accept my repentance.
The Empress also offered one hundred and twenty thousand bolts of silk.
From the princes and dukes down to the officials of the various ministries and generals,
including the assistant clerks and scribes of the prefectures and counties,
as well as the monks and nuns of the monasteries and the elder residents of the capital city.
Reaching down to the common people,
he bestowed money upon each one.
On the following day, he established a vegetarian feast to celebrate the completion of the sutras and images and the commencement of the Kaihuang era.
Furthermore, an edict was issued to establish one Buddhist monastery at each of the famous mountains throughout the various provinces, and to grant them estates and fields.
In the fourteenth year, an imperial decree was issued that within all the lands under heaven, wherever there were mountain monasteries...
It was decreed that monasteries with one or more monks were permitted to receive official plaques;
those who had been privately ordained were to be registered in the local household registers.
Furthermore, an imperial edict ordered the śramaṇa Fajing and twenty other eminent masters to compile the *Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures) in seven fascicles.
This provides a general outline of the nine records and distinguishes their categories.
Dharma Master Tanchong constructed a Buddha stūpa.
It was eleven stories high.
On the thirtieth day of the tenth month, he passed away without illness.
In the tenth month, an imperial edict was issued stating that the ancestral sacrifices of the Later Qi, Later Liang, and Chen dynasties had been discontinued.
He commanded Gao Renying, Xiao Zong, and Chen Shubao to perform the seasonal sacrifices;
the necessary ritual implements were to be supplied by the relevant officials.
Chen Shubao followed the Emperor up Mount Mang at Luoyang; while attending the banquet, he composed a poem, saying:
"The sun and moon illuminate the virtue of Heaven;
the mountains and rivers fortify the imperial abode."
"In this great peace, there is no way to repay [Your Majesty's bounty].
I wish to submit a memorial for the Eastern Tour of Inspection,
along with a formal petition to request the rite of Feng and Shan."
The Emperor replied with a gracious edict. In the fifteenth year, because monks and nuns occasionally committed transgressions,
and since the internal monastic discipline established by the Buddha does not permit laypeople to observe them,
the Emperor commanded the relevant authorities to rely upon the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras.
There were prohibitions and regulations concerning the speech of śramaṇas;
he had them all transcribed and compiled into ten fascicles titled *The Ritual Standards for the Various Scriptures*.

He encouraged and guided those who left the household life, suppressed evil, and propagated goodness. In the Kaihuang era, the Emperor and Empress constructed a multi-storied stupa at the Fajie Nunnery in the capital.
Beneath it, he enshrined the Buddha’s relics.
In the seventh month, a great radiance was emitted.
The Emperor invited the Chan Master Fachun to enter the palace.
The *Sanbaoji* (Record of the Three Jewels) concerning the Empress receiving the precepts.
An imperial letter bestowed upon the śramaṇa Huize and others of Shuanglin Temple in Wuzhou,
which states in brief:
I, the Emperor, preside over the world and have caused the Teachings to flourish once more.
I desire that the Three Jewels be eternally honored and that all beings of the four modes of birth receive blessings.
I trust that you, O Masters, will propagate the Holy Way.
It was especially fitting that he should honor such virtue; in the sixteenth year [of the reign], by imperial decree, Vinaya Master Hongzun was invited to lecture on the Vinaya.
At that time, sentient beings were exclusively adhering to the *Saṃghāṭa-vinaya*, so the Master propagated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Gradually, all came to follow him as their master. In the first month of the seventeenth year, the śramaṇa Baogui presented to the Emperor the newly translated scriptures since the Kaihuang era;
the Emperor personally composed a preface for them.
Fei Changfang, a scholar-translator of the scriptures, was a native of Chengdu.
He originally served as a monk,
but when Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou abolished the Buddhist teachings, he returned to lay life.
When the Sui dynasty arose, he continued his practice as a layman (*avadātavasana*).
At that time, he participated in the translation process, receiving the oral explanations and recording the terminology and meanings with the brush.

On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month of this year, he submitted the work he had composed, titled *The Record of the Three Jewels through Successive Dynasties* (*Lidai Sanbao Ji*), consisting of one volume and fifteen fascicles.
An imperial edict was issued to implement this.
The *Ji* (Records) contains a comprehensive account of the origins and details of the translators—both monastics and laypeople—who translated the scriptures throughout successive dynasties.
In that year, all privately ordained monks and nuns throughout the empire were registered.
He also caused them to receive the precepts. In the eighteenth year, the Emperor again sent a letter to the śramaṇa Huìzé of Shuānglín Monastery in Wùzhōu, saying:
"I, the Emperor, have received the Mandate of Heaven to nurture and protect the common people."
Revering the Triple Gem with profound devotion,
they aspire that all sentient beings throughout the ten directions may receive these meritorious deeds and together attain benevolence and longevity.
"You all shall widely proclaim the holy teachings for the sake of all living beings.
Your sincere devotion and ascetic practices deeply comfort my heart.

Since the benefit [thereof] is vast and great, do not decline the labor. In the second month of the nineteenth year, Vinaya Master Zhìwén passed away. In the twentieth year, an imperial edict was issued stating that those who destroy Buddhist or Daoist images [shall be punished].

In the year of Xinyou, the first year of the Renshou era, when the Emperor was still a hidden dragon [a prince], he encountered a Buddhist monk from India. Regarding the chronicle of the Three Jewels composed by one who had committed acts of rebellion and malice:
in the first year of Renshou (601 CE), while the Emperor was yet a prince, he met a monk from India.
He was granted one bundle of the Buddha’s relics.
In the third month of that year,
an imperial edict was issued regarding thirty locations, including Qiqi, Yong, Tai, Hua, Song, and Heng states.
The *Kaishuang Lu* records that stupas for the śarīras were erected at each [site].
In the sixth month, an imperial edict stated:

"I look up with reverence to the Perfectly Awakened One’s great kindness and great compassion, which rescue and protect all sentient beings and serve as a bridge and ferry for the myriad classes of creatures."
I take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Having restored the holy teachings,
I contemplate sharing in the cultivation of meritorious deeds with all within the four seas.
May we forever create the causes for goodness so that we may together ascend to the wondrous fruit.
You should invite thirty śramaṇas who are well-versed in the characteristics of dharmas and capable of acting as guides,
each accompanied by two attendants and one subordinate official, along with one hundred and twenty catties of frankincense.
The śarīra relics were distributed along various routes and sent to thirty provinces, where stupas were erected.
In each province, there were three hundred and sixty monks.
For myself and all officials and citizens, both internal and external,
perform the Path for seven days,
concluding at the hour of the horse on the fifteenth day of the tenth month.
As below, when depositing the stone casket, he proclaimed the text of repentance:
"The Bodhisattva-disciple Emperor Jian respectfully addresses the Triple Gem."
Firmly relying on the power of the Triple Gem, I serve as the sovereign and father to all living beings.
I now distribute these relics and erect stupas,
praying that they may serve to repent for the heavy transgressions of sentient beings.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month at the hour of the horse (noon),
the Emperor took his place facing west in the Daxing Hall, holding a jade scepter.
He invited the Buddha image, three hundred and sixty śramaṇas, banners, canopies, and musical instruments.
From the time he was welcomed from Daxingshan Temple to the Hall, he burned incense and prostrated;
he then presided over the midday meal for the civil and military officials.
This concluded when the śarīra entered the stūpa.
The Emperor said,
"When the Buddha-dharma revives, there must surely be a spiritual response.
At that time, envoys from the three kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla were about to return home.
Each requested that a stūpa be erected in their own country to enshrine and venerate the śarīra;
the Emperor granted this permission by imperial decree.
On the second day of the twelfth month, thirty śarīra were dispatched by imperial edict.
It was stored in a golden casket and placed within a lapis lazuli bottle;
a stupa was erected at Daxingshan Temple in Chang’an,
where ten billion monastics and laypeople escorted it to the temple.

He established an Unrestricted Great Assembly (*amogha-mahā-pariṣad*) and performed devotional repentance and prostrations there. According to the *Kaishuang Lu*, in the first month of the second year, the Emperor again distributed the śarīra relics across fifty-three prefectures, including Qiqian, Shanxi, Hengzhou, and Hangzhou.
The construction of the stupa shall follow the same procedure as previously prescribed.
It is scheduled for the hour of noon on the eighth day of the fourth month,
at which time the stone sarcophagus shall be lowered together with the other relics.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, golden dust and precious flowers rained from the sky over Yongzhou.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, a sixteen-foot gilded bronze Buddha image was cast at Yanxing Temple in Chang’an.
Heaven rained down precious powder and silver blossoms.
That year, the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta from Western India produced the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* and other scriptures.
In total, there are thirty-nine works comprising one hundred and ninety-two fascicles.
By imperial decree, the śramaṇa Xuanzang, a scholar-translator at Xingshan Monastery,
compiled the *Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures) in five fascicles.
In total, there are five catalogs, which distinguish and categorize [the texts] according to their types. Regarding the *Shijiao lu* (Record of the Buddhist Teachings):
In the third year, because the Empress had passed away, the Emperor established Chanding Temple in the southwest of the capital.
A seven-storied pagoda was constructed.
By imperial decree, the authorities were ordered to welcome Master Xuanzhen to preside over it,
and one hundred and twenty eminent and virtuous Chan masters from throughout the realm were summoned.
Record of the Joint Residence and Practice of the Way:
Wen Zhongzi Wang Tong traveled west to Chang’an.
He had an audience at the Taiji Hall of the Emperor and presented the "Twelve Strategies for Great Peace," exalting the Way of the King and promoting his essential principles.
Examining the past and verifying it against the present,
the Emperor was greatly pleased and said,
"How late it is that you have been born!"
He presented his proposal to the high officials (gōngqīng),
but they were displeased;
they all understood that their plan would not be adopted.
Having composed songs for the eastern expedition, he returned home;
thereupon he continued the *Shi* and *Shu*, rectified the rites and music, compiled the *Yuanjing*,
