Emperor Xuanzong changed the name of Chang'an to Jingzhao Prefecture.
During the reign of Emperor Suzong, it was renamed Shangdu (the Capital).

It was subsequently ruled by Gaozu, Taizong, Gaozong, Empress Wu Zetian, Zhongzong, Ruizong, Xuanzong, Suzong, Daizong, Dezong, Shunzong, Xianzong, Muzong, Jingzong, Wenzong, Wuzong, Xuanzong, Yizong, Xizong, and Zhaozong. Then, Zhu Quanzhong established Jingzong, who was posthumously titled Aizong, and the Prince of Pu.
He was poisoned again.
He reigned for one year,
which was called the first year of the Tian-shou era.
The Basic Annals do not record the events of the first year of Emperor Pu.
Gaozu’s personal name was Yuan,
and his courtesy name was Shude.
He was a native of Chengji in Longxi.
His grandfather, Hu, along with Li Bi and seven others, assisted the Western Wei;
all eight were appointed as Shangzhuguo (Supreme Pillar of State).
Emperor Min of the Zhou dynasty received the abdication from the Western Wei and posthumously conferred upon him the title of Duke of Tang.
Fuhé gave birth to Yǎngbǐng.
Bing fathered Yuan,
both of whom inherited the title of Duke of Tang.
Yuan served under the Sui dynasty.
In the ninth year of the Daye era of Emperor Yang,
the Emperor appointed Li Yuan, the Junior Colonel of the Court of the卫尉 (Weiwu), as the Regional Inspector (Liushiou) of Honghua Commandery;
all thirteen commanderies to the west of the Pass were subject to his recruitment and mobilization.
In the first month of the twelfth year,
an edict appointed Li Yuan, Duke of Tang and General of the Right Cavalry Guards, as the Grand Guardian (Da Yuanshou) of Taiyuan.
In the eleventh month of the thirteenth year...
Li Yuan captured Chang’an and established the Gongyang Emperor.
In the third month of the year Wuyin,
the Sui Gongyang Emperor issued an edict to the Prince of Tang.
He established the offices for the Chancellor and those below him,
and was conferred the nine emoluments (*jiu xi*).
When the tragic news of Emperor Yang of Sui’s death at Jiangdu reached Chang’an...
In the fifth month, the Emperor Gōng abdicated the throne to the Tang.
Emperor Yù ascended the imperial throne.
He reigned for nine years.
He lived to the age of seventy.
In the ninth year of Wude, the year Wuyin (578), the first month of the fifth year of Wude was changed to a new era name; the commanderies were abolished and prefectures were established.
The Governor was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Cishi).
In the fifth month,
the Emperor established a Dharma assembly on the southern thoroughfare of the Zhuque Gate.
He established a Great Unrestricted Assembly (Amogha-mahā-pariṣad).
For six months, he summoned sixty-nine monks and sixty-nine Daoists;
for seven days at the Taiji Hall, they performed the ritual practice of the Way.
On the day of the dispersal [of the assembly], he established a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks, and the *Bianzheng lu* was compiled.
In the eighth month,
Xue Ju of Jincheng died.
Prince Ren'gao ascended the throne.
The Prince of Qin of the Tang dynasty, Li Shimin, surrounded him with his troops.
Ren'gao came out and surrendered.
The Xue clan was extinguished.
In the ninth month,
Li Mi surrendered to the Tang.
At first, Mi occupied the territory of Shandong and established the state of Wei.
In the twelfth month, he rebelled again and fled;
Sheng Yanshi, the General-in-Chief of the Army at Xiongzhou, ambushed and attacked him.
Zhanmi and Zhengbo were executed; Gao Kaodao of Yan occupied Yuyang;

Zheng Wangshichong, Xia Doujinde, and Li Niao of Liang in Wufeng claimed kingship; in the second year of Anji, Xiao Xian of Liang claimed the imperial title; in Qin, Xue Rengao was established; the Khan of Dingyang [was enthroned]; in the second year of Tianxing, the Liang family [ruled] Wu; in the second year, the Zhu family [ruled] Chu; on the Jimao day, the second year of Wude.

Yan and Zheng: Summer of the first year of Kaīmíng; Liang (the Tang dynasty extinguished it): second year of Wǔfèng; Tángxiàn (Táng extinguished it): third year of Dìngyáng; Wúxīng (Wú): first year of Míngzhèng; Liáng: third year; Chǔ: Gēngchén; Wǔdé: third year.

In the summer of the second year of Kaīmíng (568), the Gāoshì of Yān; in the second year of Wǔfèng (590), the Liáng Táo Xiàn of Dìngyáng, the Khagan of the Táng who destroyed him; and the Dú Fúchéng of Wú. In the first year of the Liáng dynasty, the Liáng family; in the fourth year of Yǒnglóng (681), the Zhū family of Chǔ established Língxuān Temple.
An imperial edict was issued for Li Baiyao, a庶子 (shuzi), to compose the inscription for the stele.
An imperial edict was also issued to construct the Qianchang Shengye Cizhi Zhengguo Four Great Jixian Nunnery,
where scriptures were transcribed and images were fashioned.
He donated his former residence in Jinyang to establish Xingsheng Monastery.
He also established Yixing Monastery in Bingzhou and commissioned three sandalwood statues for Emperor Taizu Yuanhuang and Empress Dowager Yuanzhen.
In the year of Xin-si, the ten great virtuous ones (da-de) were established at Cibei Temple to oversee and regulate the monks and nuns, and to distinguish and rectify the records.
In the fourth year of the Wude era, the Kaiyuan Tongbao coin was issued.
The inscription was composed and calligraphed by the Academician Ouyang Xun;
its characters are arranged in a circular pattern that can be read in every direction.
Yan and Zheng—Tang destroyed them in the summer. Tang destroyed Liang. Liu Heitai, the King of Handong. The Ruzhou Du clan. Two years. Liang and Chu. The sixth month.
Fu Yi, the Director of the Grand Historian’s Office, submitted eleven points regarding the abolition of the Buddha-dharma.
Dharma Master Falin responded to the imperial decree to debate the matter;
consequently, Fu Yi’s memorial was suppressed, and the *Bianzheng lu* (Record of the Rectification of Truth) was compiled.
Renwu (568), the fifth year of Wude:
Yanhan [established] its first year; Wu [established] its third year; Liangchu [established]. Zhang Shan’an [established] Guiwei (569), the sixth year of Wude.
Yan was extinguished by Tang; Wu was extinguished by Tang in the fourth year of the Liang dynasty; Chu was extinguished by Tang in the *jiashen* year.
In the second month of the seventh year of Wude, Yan was extinguished by Tang; Wu was extinguished by Tang in the second month of the seventh year of Wude.
The Grand Commandant (Dazongguan) was renamed the Metropolitan Commandery (Dadujufu).

In the third month, the regulations were finalized: the Grand Marshal (Taiwei), the Minister of Education (Simu), and the Minister of Works (Sikong) were established as the Three Ducal Ministers (Sanguo);

next, the Secretariat (Shangshu), Chancellery (Menxia), Secretariat-Chancellery (Zhongshu), Bureau of Historiography (Mishu), Court of Imperial Entertainments (Dianzhong), and Palace Service (Neishi) were established as the Six Ministries (Liusheng).
Next were the Censorate, followed by the Nine Ministries (si) from the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Taichang) to the Court of State Treasury (Taifu).

Next were the Four Supervisory Offices (jian), followed by the National University (Guozixue), the Office of the Supreme General of the Celestial Strategy (Tiance Shangjiangfu), and the Fourteen Armies (wei) from the Left and Right Guards (Weishi) to the Left and Right Commandant Armies (Lingweishi).
In the Eastern Palace, the Three Masters and Three Assistants, the Director of the Household (Zhen-shi), and the two Bureaus and three Monasteries were established within the Commandery (Shuai-fu).
For Princes and Dukes, administrative assistants and state officials were appointed;
for Princesses, a District Office (Yi-si) was established.
Those serving as officials in the capital are designated as civil officials (*zhishi guan*);
those serving in prefectures, counties, garrisons, and military stations are designated as external civil officials.
From the rank of *Kaifuyitongsan-si* down to *Jiangshilang*, there are twenty-eight grades constituting the civil non-active official ranks (*wensanguan*).

The thirty-one ranks from *Biaojiqu Dajiangjun* (General of the Household for the Flying Cavalry) down to *Peirong Fuwei* (Deputy Commandant of Peirong) constitute the military non-civilian offices (*wusanguan*).
The twelve grades from *Shangzhuguo* (Grand Marshal of the First Order) down to *Wuqiewei* (Cavalier of the Martial Guard) constitute the offices of merit (*xunguan*).
On the first day of the fourth month, the gengzi day, the new laws and regulations were promulgated.
Compared to the old system of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, fifty-three new articles were added.
First, the laws for the equal distribution of land and the collection of taxes, labor service, and corvée were established.
The assets and occupations of all the people were divided into nine grades.
One hundred households formed a *li* (village),
and five *li* formed a *xiang* (district).
Four households constitute a neighborhood;
four neighborhoods constitute a ward;
those located within a city or town constitute a district.
The fields constitute the village.
Families who receive stipends from the state must not compete with the common people for profit.
Artisans, merchants, and miscellaneous classes shall have no part in the ranks of the scholar-officials.
When boys and girls are first born, they are called "infants" (huáng);
at four years of age, they are called "small";
at sixteen, they are called "middle."
At twenty, one becomes a corvée laborer;
at sixty, one becomes an elder.
Each year, a census register is compiled.
The *Tang shu* states that three years after the creation of the household registers,
in the second month of the eighth year of Wude (the year of Yiyou),
the Emperor performed the ritual of offering sacrifices at the National Academy.
Three seats were arranged to represent the three schools,
and scholars from these three traditions were summoned to assemble like clouds.
Shi Hui set up a lofty net of doctrine to engage in debate.
The king and his ministers were delighted and submitted;
the entire court turned its gaze toward him.
On the day of Bingxu, the second month of the ninth year of Wude.
Fu Yi, the Director of the Grand Historian’s Office, instigated the Daoist Li Zhongqing to submit the "Treatise on the Ten Anomalies and Nine Delusions," disparaging the Buddha and the sages;
in total, he submitted seven memorials over time to denigrate the teachings.
The Chancellor Xiao Yu rebuked Fu Yi in court.
In the fourth month, the Emperor distributed Fu Yi’s memorial to all the monks.
Among them was the Dharma Master Shi Minggai.
He composed eight articles titled "Decisively Refuting Fu Yi’s Slander of the Buddha and Destruction of the Sangha.
Master Falin authored the *Ten Similes* and the *Nine Admonitions* to refute Li Zhongqing’s arguments on the "Ten Differences and Nine Delusions."
Li Shizheng, the Director of Rites under the Secretariat, authored the *Neide lun* (Treatise on Internal Virtue) in three chapters,
extolling at length the benefits of Buddhist transformation.
In the fifth month, an imperial edict was issued to purge those who were corrupt within both religions, according to the old history of the *Jiu Tang shu*.
On the fourth day of the sixth month,
Prince Qin Shimin quelled the internal rebellion with his palace guards (fu-bing).
The Emperor appointed Prince Qin as the Crown Prince.
A general amnesty was proclaimed.
The previous purge of the two teachings was suspended.
An edict was issued for the Emperor to abdicate the throne to the Crown Prince in the eighth month.
The Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne at the Xiande Hall in the Eastern Palace.
In the Basic Annals, the High Ancestor is titled the Retired Emperor (Taishang Huangdi).
Emperor Wen of Taizong: the personal name of Emperor Wen of Taizong was Shimin.
The second son of the Gaozu.
He reigned for twenty-three years.
His age was fifty-two. [Died] in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era.
In the first month of spring in the first year of the Zhenguan era (627),
the Emperor decreed that all monks and nuns within the capital must each perform seven days of ritual practice at their respective monasteries.
The necessary provisions for the fast-offering were to be supplied by the relevant officials.
On the day of the preparatory fast (*sanzai*),
all [participants] gathered at Daxingshan Temple to perform the offerings for the *Bianzheng lu*.
The Emperor said to Fu Yi:
"The Way of the Buddha is subtle and wondrous;
its sacred traces are worthy of being taken as a model."
Furthermore, retribution is manifest and has been repeatedly verified through experience;
why is it that you alone do not realize this principle?
Yi opposed the Emperor’s will,
and the Emperor detested him;
consequently, Yi was never again mentioned among the ranks of the Tang dynasty throughout his lifetime in the official histories.

He abolished animal slaughter and established monasteries. In this year, the Emperor relinquished the old palace at Taixi on Mount Zhongnan to establish Longtian Monastery for the sake of the High Ancestor;
it was later renamed Cuiwei Monastery.
The Emperor, recognizing that Shi Mingzhan was skilled in identifying the principles of governance,
issued an edict for him to enter the inner palace and partake in a vegetarian feast.
In response to the imperial summons, he extensively expounded upon the arts of governance for emperors.
The Preface and Explanatory Section takes compassion and salvation as its primary tenet.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and consequently issued an edict on the sixth day of the third month of that year, universally prohibiting slaughter.
In the third month of the second year of the Wuzi era, the Emperor,
reflecting upon the many people executed during his initial pacification of the realm, established Buddhist temples at all military encampments. (Bianzheng lu) *Wuzi* 2, 3rd month.
He then offered his imperial robes to the monks of various temples for their ritual repentance and prayers for the deceased.
The Emperor issued an edict stating:
"Since the end of the Sui dynasty, I have established my righteous intent with the heart to rescue those drowning."
In my northern expeditions and eastern campaigns, the number of those wounded and slain is beyond reckoning;
those personally executed by my hand approach one thousand.
Yet, I reflect that the holy teachings of the Tathāgata deeply esteem benevolence and compassion.
According to the precepts, the offense of killing is the most grave.
Therefore, orders were issued to the officials in charge of the various temples within the capital to perform the *zhāi* (fasting) and *xíngdào* (ritual practice) for seven days and seven nights.
Exerting one's utmost sincerity in ritual repentance,
all clothing and possessions were offered as alms,
hoping that the sufferings of the three miserable realms might thereby be liberated.
"By means of this, the sufferings of ten thousand kalpas are extensively relieved.
In the ninth month, the Emperor issued an edict stating:
"Now the hundred grains flourish and thrive."
When the myriad treasures are about to be completed,
one still fears that wind and rain may cause them to miss their season,
leaving the nurtured offspring with no place of refuge.
Daring to rely upon Your transcendent wisdom and external compassion for manifold blessings,
we pray that You will extend Your protection and grace to the billions of beings throughout the vast heavens.

In the capital city and in all monasteries and observatories throughout the empire, monks, nuns, Daoists, and others shall perform the recitation of scriptures and the practice of the Way for seven days and seven nights.
This shall be done annually in accordance with the precedent of the first and seventh months, as recorded in the Bianzheng lu.
Regarding the Vinaya Master Xuánwǎn:
In this year, the Emperor issued an edict for him to enter the palace,
where he conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the consorts, the imperial concubines, the Crown Prince, and various princes.
Wan entered nirvana in the twelfth month of the tenth year of the Zhenguan era.
Her final memorial stated:
"Sage emperors and enlightened kings revere and honor the Three Jewels."
If a śramaṇa should violate the law, he ought not to be penalized according to the same statutes as the common people.
I request that he be handed over to his own jurisdiction to be governed by the monastic code (vinaya).
I also submit the *An-yang lun* (Treatise on Peaceful Nurturing) and the *San-de lun* (Treatise on the Three Virtues).
The Emperor graciously accepted his words and issued an edict expressing deep sorrow;
he dispatched the Crown Prince to pay his respects at the funeral.
The Emperor issued an edict for the relevant authorities to provide the funeral requisites;
this was the first instance of a śramaṇa being granted a state funeral under the Tang dynasty.
Furthermore, a Buddhist stūpa was erected at the site of the burial.
In the first month of the third year of Yihou (609), the Emperor issued an edict ordering his younger son, Li Boyao, to compose the inscription for the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. Furthermore,
he decreed that the monks and nuns of the capital must perform ritual practices on the second and seventh days of every month at this monastery.

*Biànzhènglù* (Records for Discerning and Rectifying): The *Zhǎnrénwàidàyún* and other sutras were translated as a regular practice. In the third month, an imperial edict was issued for the Daixingshan Temple to begin the work of translation;
the śramaṇa Xuānmó and others served as translators.
The Vinaya Master Guṇavarman acted as the certified translator;
Falin, Huìyuè, and others took up their pens to receive his instructions;
and Huìshèng and others verified the meaning of the text.

By imperial decree, the Vice President of the Secretariat Fang Xuanling, the Palace Attendant Du Zhenglun, and the Minister of the Department of State Affairs Li Xiaogong were appointed to assist in the collation and determination [of the text].
Xiao Jing, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness and Director of the Court of Imperial Treasury, was charged with overall supervision and oversight.
*Shijiao lu* (Record of the Supply of the Hundred Officials): In the sixth month, an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Mingjing of Mízhōu to the capital to pray for rain.
*Tongjì* (Comprehensive Record): An edict was issued that Tōngyì Gōng, the former residence of the imperial family, should be established as a convent for nuns.
The *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of the Dharma) was titled *Xingsheng* (Arising Sage).

In the eleventh month, an imperial edict was issued to the abbot of Shengguang Monastery, Sengzhen, ordering him to go to the palace to welcome the embroidered images of Śākyamuni Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, the holy Sangha, and Vajrapāṇi.
He made offerings at Shengguang Temple.
In the first month of the sixth year,
he commanded forty-nine virtuous monks (da-de) from various temples to perform the ritual practice for twenty-one days.
On the day the embroidered images were distributed, he celebrated by providing a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks.
The King and high officials performed the incense offering for the *Bianzheng lu*.
In the intercalary twelfth month, he established a temple.
The Emperor, mindful that since the Sui dynasty there had been lingering spirits and obstructed souls,
issued an edict stating:
"The Sui lost the Way."
The nine regions are seething with turmoil;
I have personally led the supreme army to inflict these manifest punishments.
I fear deeply that those beneath the Nine Springs may still be submerged in cauldrons of boiling metal.
Within the eight difficulties, they are forever entangled in the conflict of ice and fire;
therefore, one should establish fields of merit to save their spirits and souls at the sites where military engagements occurred since the inception of the righteous cause.
For those righteous men and fierce warriors who have lost their lives and perished on the battlefield, temples and stupas shall be erected for each;
eminent companions shall be invited to reside there,
hoping that when the Dharma drum resounds, it will transform the blazing fires into blue lotuses.
The Pure Dharma (Qingfan) heard that the ocean of suffering was easily transformed into ambrosia;
the officials measured and determined the sites, establishing monasteries throughout,
and compiled them into detailed regulations.

In accordance with the imperial decree expressing the intent of compassion and pity upon hearing [the news], as recorded in the old annals, monasteries were established at all the fortifications the following year.
When Xue Ju was defeated at Bingzhou, Zhaoren Monastery was established there.
After defeating Wang Shichong at Luozhou, he established Zhaojue Temple;
after defeating Liu Wuzhou at Fenzhou, he established Hongji Temple;
and after defeating Song Jingang at Jinzhou, he established Ciyun Temple.
He destroyed the old fortress of Huo at Luzhou and established Puzi Temple;
he destroyed the stronghold of Dou Jiande at Zhengzhou and established Dengci Temple;
he destroyed Liu Hetu’s base at Luozhou and established Zhaofo Temple.

An imperial decree was issued for Yu Shinan, Li Boyao, Chu Suiliang, Yan Shigu, Cen Wenben, Xu Jingzong, and Zhu Zisheshan to divide the composition of the inscriptions and records for the new temple.
In the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era, the Emperor returned from his expedition against Liaodong.
For the purpose of commemorating and delivering those who perished in battle,
the *Great Canon Record* (Dianlu) for the newly established Minzhong Ge Temple in Youzhou was compiled in the Gengyin year.
The Emperor remarked that there had been no established gradations for ordinary court attire.
In the eighth month, he issued an edict stating: "From now on, those of the third rank and above shall wear purple;
those of the fourth and fifth ranks shall wear vermilion."
Those of the sixth and seventh ranks wore green;
those of the eighth rank wore blue.
Women followed the color of their husbands’ robes. (Tang Shu)
The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang departed for the Western Regions in the winter of the third year of the Zhenguan era to retrieve Buddhist scriptures not yet available in China. Upon his return,
he presented a memorial at the palace gate.
The Emperor did not grant permission.
The Master fled in secret from Yuanzhou, passed through the Yumen Pass,
and traveled to the kingdoms of Gaochang, the Yehe, and others before departing.
In the seventh year of the Zhenguan era, he reached Central India,
where he met a Mahāyāna lay practitioner and received the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
He then entered the city of Rājagṛha.
He resided at Nālandā Monastery,
where he studied the fundamental tenets of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda under the master Śīlabhadra of the Upper Hall for ten years.
Returning from Rājagṛha,
he arrived at the capital on the *bingzi* day of the first month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era.
Fang Xuanling, the Imperial Commissioner for the Defense of Chang’an, submitted a memorial to announce his arrival.
In the third month of the Renchen year, the Dharma Master was at Luoyang, which was like the Eastern Capital. On the Jihai day, he had an audience with the Emperor in the Yiluan Hall.
The Emperor said, "Why did you depart without informing me?"
He said, "When it was time to depart, I made three formal petitions, yet I did not receive a gracious permission.
I then proceeded to travel privately.
The Emperor said:
The Master was able to entrust his life to seeking the Dharma for the benefit and welfare of all living beings;
I highly commend this.
Consequently, the Master submitted a petition regarding six hundred and fifty-seven volumes of Sanskrit scriptures and treatises he had protected during his travels in the Western Regions.
He requested to go to Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song in Luoyang to perform translations for the sake of the state.
The Emperor said,
"I have recently established Hongfu Monastery for the sake of Empress Dowager Mu."
The translation may proceed there;
an imperial edict appoints the Chancellor Fang Xuanling to take exclusive charge of supervision,
and all necessary provisions shall be supplied from the Imperial Treasury.
In the sixth month of the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era,
the Emperor composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang" for the newly translated scriptures.
At that time, the Crown Prince Zhi, having beheld this Imperial Preface, subsequently composed the "Sacred Record."
The Emperor issued an edict for the Crown Prince to compose the postscript to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*.
In the eighth month, the Emperor bestowed upon the Dharma Master a hundred pieces of gold and a ground silk robe (*mò nà*), as well as a precious razor.
The Dharma Master submitted a memorial in thanks.
Briefly stated:
the robes of forbearance blend their colors with the flowing clouds of dawn;
the blade of wisdom is sharper than that which cuts jade.
I reverently wear this to subdue the demons of affliction and bear it to sever the net of worldly toil.
The third year of the Yonghui era of the High Sovereign.
When the Dharma Master was about to construct a great stupa at Ci'en Monastery to enshrine the Sanskrit manuscripts of the sutras and śāstras he had brought back from the West,
he submitted a memorial to the throne.

By imperial decree, the deceased garments and articles belonging to seven palaces, including those within the Great Interior and the Yeting of the Eastern Palace, were granted to assist the Master in his preparations.
The Dharma Master bestowed upon him the architectural systems of the Western Regions.
When the stupa was completed, it stood two hundred feet high.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of the Xianqing era, an imperial decree established Yuhua Palace as a monastery.
By imperial decree following the posthumous honors for the former Emperor, the Dharma Master was appointed to reside there.
In the following year, the Master translated the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at Yuhua Palace.
In the second month of the first year of the Linde era:
The Dharma Master instructed his disciple Dashengguang to transcribe all the sutras and śāstras he had translated, totaling seventy-five works in one thousand three hundred and thirty-five fascicles.
He further summoned his disciples to fashion images and hold a vegetarian feast, bidding them farewell before departing.
He instructed his attendants to recite the name of Maitreya Tathāgata.
On the fifth day, at midnight, he lay down on his right side and passed away.
His lifespan was sixty-five years.
The Emperor suspended court proceedings for three days.
He issued an edict that [the remains] should be enshrined in a golden inner coffin and a silver outer sarcophagus.
In the fourth month, a stupa was erected on the plains east of the Shan River.
The disciples Shen Tai, Qi Yuan, Huiyi, Huili, Mingjun, Yibao, and Dacheng Guang were all "dragon elephants" (eminent masters) of the Dharma-gate.
The Dharma Master transmitted to Kuiji the fundamental tenets of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratā-siddhi*, which he had received from the master Śīlabhadra in the Western Regions.
Chan Master Farong of Mount Niutou was a native of Yanling in Runzhou.
His secular surname was Wei.
At the age of nineteen, he mastered the Classics and Histories.
Upon subsequently reading the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtras, he attained a profound understanding of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One day, he suddenly sighed and said:
The Confucian and Daoist classics of the world are not the ultimate teaching;
Prajñā and right contemplation are the vessel for transcending the world.
He subsequently retired to Mount Maoshan.
He went to a master to shave his head.
Later, he entered the stone chamber on the northern cliff of Youqi Temple at Mount Niutou in Jiankang, where he sat in meditation contemplating the mind.
There was a marvel of hundreds of birds offering him flowers.
Tigers and wolves surrounded his dwelling.
According to the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), the Fourth Patriarch gathered and delivered him [to safety] in the fifth year of the Xinmao cycle.
The Emperor, for the sake of Empress Dowager Mu, constructed Cide Temple at Qingshanguan;
he also established Yaotai Temple at Shaoling.
He then issued an imperial decree to the Dharma Master Xuanyuan.
Within the palace gardens, at Deje Temple (De-ye-si), he had the Buddha’s Tripitaka copied for the Empress;
furthermore, he commissioned another set of the Tripitaka at Yanxing Temple (Yan-xing-si),
entrusting both projects to Won to oversee and protect.
In the sixth year of the Renchen era,
an imperial edict was issued to designate the former residence in Taiyuan as Tiangong Temple in order to offer posthumous honors to Empress Dowager Mu.
To the west of the Tai City, within Zhen'an City, he built another temple for Empress Dowager Mu;
it was also named Hongfu. According to the Bianzhenglu, in the seventh year of the Gui-si year, an imperial edict prohibited those who set up dams and enclosures to catch fish.
He also prohibited slaughter.
In the fourth month of the ninth year of the Zhenguan era, he compiled the *Bianzheng lu* (Record for Clarifying Orthodoxy) and ordained three thousand monks and nuns.
The Emperor Taishanghuang passed away.
In the eleventh month, an imperial edict was issued stating:
"The three vehicles follow a common path; the primary concern is the salvation and deliverance of beings."
The Eightfold Right Path takes refuge in compassion as its sovereign;
it flows like an ocean of wisdom to nourish all living beings,
and acts as a bridge and raft to cut down the forest of afflictions for all things.
Abiding in truth, he embodies the Way; his principles accord with supreme benevolence.
His wondrous fruits and excellent causes correspond to the accumulation of goodness.
I, the Emperor, reverently emulate the Golden Wheel and humbly receive the precious mandate.
The teachings of supreme virtue reach every corner of thought;
the regulations of the Great Sage penetrate every hidden realm.
This is intended to enable people to escape the entanglements of worldly existence and bring their families to benevolence and longevity.
Recently, due to the turmoil of war and calamity, the monastic community has diminished;
the flower pedestals and jeweled stupas have no one to look out from their doors,
and the dark-blue hair and blue lotuses are combed by the wind and bathed by the rain.
Reflecting upon this decay and ruin, I am truly filled with sorrow. It is appropriate that,
in all the provinces throughout the empire where there are monasteries,
the number of ordained monks and nuns be limited to three thousand.
Those prefectures have their large and small;
the lands have their Chinese and barbarian.
One must accord with the specific location and the extent of those to be saved.
The officials shall conduct a detailed examination and selection, ensuring that those chosen are distinguished by their virtue and practice.
This includes those who previously reduced their allowances,
returned to lay life, or were privately ordained as white-robed laypeople.
If one were to broadly include all types of karmic actions within the scope of "clinging" (*upādāna*), there would necessarily be no person who could be grasped;
thus, it is permissible to omit them from the count. I have heard that many members of the monastic community are submerged in worldly customs.
Some falsely invoke ghosts and spirits to spread baseless tales of demons;
some fraudulently claim to be physicians or shamans, pursuing profit through heterodox ways;
others burn or pierce their skin and bodies to startle the common folk and alarm the ignorant.
Or they may visit government offices to bribe officials with illicit wealth;
all such practices as these greatly undermine the holy teachings.
My heart is set upon their protection and preservation.
There shall be no leniency whatsoever.
From now on, the relevant authorities should adhere to the internal regulations and supplement them with the Golden Precepts to establish clear statutes.
(From the *Jiushi* of the *Jiu Tangshu*, Year Ten of the Zhenguan era, the third month.)
Crown Prince Chengqian asked Zhang Shiheng,
"What is the efficacy of serving the Buddha and cultivating merit?
He replied:
To serve the Buddha lies in purity, benevolence, and forbearance.
If one serves with greed, arrogance, and cruelty,
even if one exhausts their wealth in such service, it will not diminish their misfortune.
Furthermore, that good and evil must be requited is as certain as a shadow following a form;
the words of the sages are complete on this point.
To be an enlightened ruler—this is the way.
If one is loyal as a minister and filial as a son,
then blessings and prosperity will endure forever.
To act contrary to this brings disaster.
Liu Shiheng used these words to correct the mind of the Crown Prince;
yet, the Crown Prince Chengqian ultimately failed in his virtue.
In the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan era, Princess Chengqian was deposed and reduced to the status of a commoner;
Prince Jin, Zhi, was established as the Crown Prince.
*Shizhizhi*, first month of the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era.

High Minister of the Ministry of Personnel Gao Shilian, Palace Attendant Wei Ting, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites Ling Lu Ding, Fu De-phen, and Vice Director of the Secretariat Cen Wenben compiled the *Shizu Ji* (Compendium of Clan Names).
He appointed Cui Min-gan, the Gentleman Attendant for the Palace Gate, as the first; however,
the Emperor did not approve,
so he ordered a further revision and determination of the rankings.
They judged rank and status solely by the official hierarchy of the current day;
thus, the imperial clan was placed first,
followed by the maternal relatives.
The third section on the subjugation of Cui Min-gan,
totaling two hundred and ninety-three surnames and one thousand six hundred and fifty-one households,
was distributed throughout the empire. (From the *Jiu Tang Shu*).
The Venerable Dushun, whose name was Fashun,
was born into the Du clan of Yongzhou. In his youth,
Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty held him in such high esteem that he provided him with a monthly stipend for his support.
At this time, the Emperor, who had long held him in deep respect,
would frequently invite him into the palace and honor him as if he were a Buddha.
He compiled the *Huayan fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharma-realm of the Avatamsaka).
His disciple Zhiyan transmitted his teachings.
On the fifth day of the fifth month in the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he peacefully manifested parinirvāṇa (according to the Benzhuan).
On the twenty-second day of the fifth month in the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era...
The Emperor performed memorial rites for the late Empress Taimu at Hongfu Monastery.
He personally composed a prayer, stating:
"That which the sagely and wise hold in highest esteem is filial piety."
What the benevolent person loves most are their kin.
In my youth, I was blessed with the grace of being nurtured;
as I grew, I received the instruction of being raised.
When shall the longing for the *liǎo é* ever be forgotten?
This debt of infinite gratitude toward the vast heavens cannot be repaid.
As I give voice to my eternal yearning, my profound sorrow is but intensified.
In wishing to repay [your kindness], I have no other means but to rely solely upon your hidden assistance.
I respectfully offer two hundred rolls of silk as an offering to the Great Teaching of Compassion.
Should my utmost sincerity move you, [may this prayer be granted].
I hope that past transgressions may be extinguished so that there may be causes for doing good;
thus, may the blessings of future conditions be attained. (From the *Hongming ji*).
Furthermore, by imperial decree, the Buddhist Tripitaka was transcribed for Empress Dowager Mu.
An imperial edict was issued to select ten Dharma masters to perform the collation and correction [of the scriptures].
On the *guimao* day of the second month in the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan era,
the Emperor asked the Grand Master for Remonstrance (Jianyi Daifu) Chu Suiliang, saying:
"When Shun first fashioned a lacquered vessel, more than ten people remonstrated against him.
How could such a thing be worth remonstrating over?
He replied:
Extravagance is the root of peril and ruin.
If one does not stop with lacquered vessels,
one will eventually use gold and jade to make them.
"A loyal minister who loves his sovereign must guard against the gradual onset [of decline].
If calamity and disorder have already become established, there will be no further opportunity for remonstrance.
The Emperor said:
"However, when I have faults,
you should also remonstrate with me regarding them from their very inception.
The Emperor said:
A ruler possesses but a single mind,
yet those who attack it are exceedingly numerous;
some do so by means of valor and strength.
Either through eloquent speech,
or through flattery and sycophancy, or through deceit and guile,
or through the pursuit of sensual desires.
They converge upon him from all sides,
each seeking to sell their own views in order to win favor and emolument.
If the sovereign is even slightly lax and accepts one of them, ruin and extinction will follow in its wake.
This is why it is difficult [to find such a person].
In the *Di ji* (Imperial Annals), on the Lingyan Pavilion, by imperial decree, portraits of meritorious ministers were painted.
Among them was the Duke of Zhao, Changsun Wuji.
Li Xiaogong, Prince Yuan of Zhaojun;
Du Ruhui, Duke Leicheng;
and Wei Zheng, Duke Wenzheng of Zheng.
Duke Liang Fang Xuanling;
Duke Shen Gao Shilian;
and Duke E Wei Zheng (Yuchi Jingde).
Duke Wei Li Jing;
Duke Song Xiao Yu;
and Duke Baozhongzhuang Duan Zhi-xuan.
Duke Kui Liu Hongji;
Duke Zhong of Jiang Qu Tu Tong;
and Marquis Jie of Yun Yin Kaishan.
Duke Xiang of Qiao, Chai Shao;
Duke Xiang of Pi, Changsun Shunde;
and Duke Yün, Zhang Liang.
Duke Chen Junji, Marquis of Tanxiang Zhang Gongjin,
and Duke of Lu Cheng Zhijie.
Yongxing Wenyigong Yu Shinan;
Yuxianggong Liu Zhenghui;
and Jugong Tang Jian.
The Duke of Ying, Li Shiji;
and the Duke of Hu Zhuang, Qin Shubao, are recorded in the "Biographies of Loyalty and Righteousness" on the Lingyan Pavilion.
Regarding Chan Master Fenggan, Hanshan, and Shide: Master Fenggan manifested his traces at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.
He stayed in a hermitage at the northwest corner of the Scripture Hall.
While riding a tiger along a pine-lined path,
he saw a boy about ten years of age.
When he was questioned, he had no family or surname.
The Master led him back to the monastery and raised him in the kitchen,
naming him Shide (The Gleaner).
There was a poor man who came from a cold ravine;
he was called Hanshanzi (Cold Mountain Man).
The three men were in great harmony with one another.
That year, Fenggan was traveling as a wandering monk when Lü Qiu Yin happened to come to serve as the governor of Taizhou.
Shortly thereafter, he suffered from a wind ailment in his head.
Fenggan came to his residence and claimed that he was skilled at treating such an illness.
Liu Qiu saw him;
the Master took pure water and sprinkled it upon him, and he was immediately healed.
He then asked where he had come from.
He said, "There is Guoqing on Mount Tiantai.
The other asked, "Are there any worthy and enlightened men there?
Qian replied:
"Hanshan is Mañjuśrī and Shide is Samantabhadra; you should go see them.
Lüqiu went to see them and, after three days, visited the remains of Fenggan at the temple.
He went to visit the two great masters.
When Lüqiu bowed to them,
the two masters ran away, saying:
Fenggan is a loquacious Amitābha;
not knowing how to pay homage, what is he doing here?
He has retreated into a mountain cave.
The cave closed up of its own accord.
Hanshan and Shide had composed poems scattered throughout the mountains and forests;
the temple monks collected them and compiled them into a volume.
The inscription for the *Guoqing Si Ji* (Record of Guoqing Monastery) was published as a woodblock edition in the world.
Regarding the *Yijiao jing* (Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching), in the eighteenth year of the Zhenguan era,
the Emperor issued an edict stating:
When the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, he entrusts the Dharma to kings and ministers during the degenerate and frivolous final age to protect and uphold it;
however, the monastics and nuns who have left the household life must be fully equipped with the observance of the precepts.
If one indulges in sensual desires and negligence, encountering afflictions at every turn,
and involves oneself in worldly affairs such that one constantly violates the sūtras and the vinaya,
one has already lost the profound and subtle intent of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this would violate the King’s duty to receive and uphold [the teachings].
The *Śāsanānuśāsanī Sūtra* was spoken by the Buddha at the time of his parinirvāṇa;
its exhortations to the disciples are exceedingly detailed and essential.
In these degenerate times, neither the monastic nor the lay communities have shown reverence for it;
the Great Way is about to vanish, and its subtle words are nearly severed.
With eternal longing for the holy teachings, I contemplate how to propagate and elucidate them.
It is appropriate that the relevant authorities dispatch ten scribes to produce numerous copies of this scripture,
ensuring its full implementation. Furthermore,
one copy each should be presented to all officials of the capital of the fifth rank and above, as well as to the Prefectural Governors of all provinces.
If one observes that the conduct and practices of monks and nuns differ from the scriptural texts, it is appropriate to exhort them both publicly and privately to ensure they strictly follow them;
this is recorded in the *Old History of the Tang* (*Jiu Tangshu*) and the *Wenguan Cailin*.
In the second month of the nineteenth year,
the Emperor personally led an expedition against Goryeo but was unsuccessful.
In the ninth month, he returned with his army.
In the third month of the twentieth year, the imperial carriage arrived at Chang’an.
There was a monk named Shi Zhize who resided at Biancai Temple;
his dwelling was desolate and secluded, and the multitude called him a madman.
Zhi said, "Those who criticize others as mad do not realize they themselves are mad.
Having left home and departed from the secular world, they do nothing but crave food and clothing."
Whether walking or standing, obstructing or locking doors and chests,
they engage in various forms of accumulation and toil with restless unease.
If this is not madness, there is nothing else that could be called madness.
He then clapped his hands, laughed loudly, and departed abruptly; this is recorded in the *Sengzhuan*.
Fengjing Gaowang. Shi Fachong preached the Dharma in Suzhou, Hangzhou, and Jiaxing County in Western Zhejiang.
A deity named Gao Wang descended and delivered this prayer: "On my behalf,
invite Dharma Master Cong to come."
He received the Bodhisattva precepts.
After the people there had followed his words and requested the ordination,
he further bestowed a blessing, saying:
From this day forward, he completely renounced all alcohol, meat, and the five pungent roots.
Later, when seeking blessings, he invited a community of monks to the temple to perform vegetarian feasts and practice the Way.
This continued for two years.
The spirit of Haiyan County in Xiu Prefecture was Lord Poyang.
During a regular sacrifice, he descended and addressed the prayer, saying:
"On my behalf, request Dharma Master Ceng to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*."
The assembly then welcomed the Master to the lecture hall.
A deity descended again and addressed him, saying:
"In the path of the divine, there are many karmic obstacles and much suffering."
"Ever since I began listening to the Dharma, the suffering caused by tiny insects devouring me from within my scales has ceased.
I pray that you will request the Master to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* once more.
The Master then lectured on it for him again.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* records that in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era,
the Emperor returned from his expedition to Liaodong with his physical strength diminished.
He then turned his attention toward the Great Teaching.
In the eighth month, he asked Dharma Master Xuanzang,
"I wish to plant the benefits of the Dharma-gate."
"What should take precedence?
Xuanzang replied, "Sentient beings are steeped in delusion; without wisdom, they cannot be awakened."
"The sprouting of the bud of wisdom takes the planting of the Dharma as its sustenance;
the propagation of the Dharma requires people, and the ordination of monks is paramount.
The Emperor said:
He was granted a *mò* robe and precious items for Xuanzang;
Xuanzang’s letter of thanks is contained in the latter part of his previous biography.
On the *yǐmǎo* day of the ninth month, an imperial edict was issued, stating:
At the end of the Sui dynasty, the imperial rule was lost;
the empire fell into fragmentation and collapse,
and the four seas were plunged into misery and ruin.
The eight frontiers were seething like boiling cauldrons;
I, the Emperor, was personally compelled to quell the chaos and confronted the vanguard of the army,
frequently braving wind and frost while lodging upon my horse.
Recently, although I had been taking medicinal decoctions, my condition was not yet fully healed;
only in recent days have I finally recovered.
Could this not be the result of the power of merit and goodness?
In the capital and in each of the various prefectures throughout the realm, five monks were ordained at each monastery.
At that time, there were more than three thousand seven hundred monasteries in the empire;
the total number of monks ordained amounted to approximately seventeen thousand. (From the Old History of the Tang)
When Crown Prince Zhi resided in the Eastern Palace,
the weather became dark and gloomy; feeling weary in body and moved by melancholy,
he recollected his mother’s imperial dignity, which was as vast and boundless as the Great Heaven.
His compassion was boundless;
he consequently gathered materials and selected a site to establish the Great Ci’en Monastery,
in order to cultivate merit for the posthumous peace of Empress Wen-de.
By the twelfth month of that year, it was completed;
furthermore, a stupa was constructed,
and an imperial edict was issued to select fifty eminent and virtuous monks (*bhadanta*) of long-standing repute from the capital.
Each of them sent six attendants to reside at the new temple.
On the *bingchen* day of this month, the Crown Prince prepared fifty jeweled carriages to welcome the great virtuous ones,
along with several hundred decorated pavilions and jeweled canopies.
The newly acquired Sanskrit manuscripts, various sutras, auspicious images, and śarīra relics were enshrined.

By imperial decree, the nine divisions of music from the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Taichang*), as well as the musicians of Chang’an and Wannian, and those from the various temples within the capital, were to lead a procession with flowered banners into the temple.
The Emperor ascended the Anfu Gate tower, holding an incense burner to pay his respects.
Only when the scriptures and images had all passed did he cease;
the Emperor’s heart was greatly gladdened.
After Gaozong ascended the throne,
he personally composed the inscription for the Da Ci'en Monastery. According to the Tang Annals,
this was in the year Jihou (己酉), the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era.
In the fourth month of summer,
the Emperor fell ill;
in the fifth month, he passed away.
In the sixth month, the Crown Prince ascended the throne.
In the eighth month, Emperor Wen was entombed at Shaoling;
his temple name was Taizong. (From the Basic Annals.)
Gaozong (High Ancestor). His reign was known as Zhi.
His courtesy name was Weishan.
He was the ninth son of Taizong.
He was first enfeoffed as the Prince of Jin.
He reigned for thirty-four years and lived to the age of fifty-six. [His reign included the following years:

the sixth year of Yonghui, the fifth of Xianqing, the third of Longshuo, the second of Linde, the second of Qianfeng, the second of Zongzhang, the fourth of Xianheng, the second of Shangyuan, the third of Yifeng, the first of Tiulou, the first of Yonglong, the first of Kaiyao, the first of Yongchun, and the first of Hongdao.
In the first year of Yonghui, the gengxu year, and the second year, the xinhai year,
there was the Venerable Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, whose secular surname was Sima;
his family had resided in Henei for generations.
He moved his residence to Guangji County in Qizhou,
which is present-day Huaixi.
From birth, he was exceptionally extraordinary.
From childhood, he admired the various gates of liberation within the school of emptiness,
as if they were the result of past habituation;
having succeeded to the patriarchal seat, he [continued this practice].
He did not spread his mat on his side for barely sixty years.
In the seventh year of the Wude era of Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty, he resided at Mount Poutou in Qi;
this is the present-day Mount Shuangfeng.
During the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong heard of his reputation and issued three imperial edicts;
yet the Venerable One did not rise.
He was summoned once more by imperial decree.
The Emperor said to his envoy,
"If he still does not comply with my command, then bring me his head.
The envoy conveyed this intention to the road.
The Master extended his neck to await the blade.
The messenger returned and reported this to the Emperor,
who sighed in admiration and comforted him with great kindness.
By this time, the Venerable had already resided in the mountains for twenty years.
One day, he went to Huangmei County and encountered a young boy on the road.
He was about seven years old.
[The master] asked him,
"What is your surname?"
The boy said, "As for my surname, it is indeed an extraordinary one.
The Patriarch asked,
"What is this surname?"
The boy said, "This is Buddha-nature.
The Patriarch asked,
"Do you have no family name?"
The boy said, "Because my surname is K'ung (Empty), I have none.
The Patriarch silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and ordered an attendant to go to the boy's mother.
He requested permission for him to leave the household life.
Because of their past karmic connection, his mother eventually consented to let him go.
His grandfather performed the tonsure ceremony and gave him the name Hongren.
Thereafter, he issued this command:
"In the past, the Tathāgata transmitted the Eye of the True Dharma down to me.
I now entrust it to you, together with the robe and bowl."
Listen to my verse,
which says:
"The seeds of flowers possess the nature of arising."
The great condition for the continuous arising of the flowers born of the ground unites with faith;
thus, birth shall continuously become non-birth.
This occurred on the fourth day of the intercalary ninth month in the second year of the Yonghui era.
He admonished his disciples, saying:
"All dharmas are entirely liberated.
Each of you should protect and mind them, spreading their influence for the sake of the future."
Having finished speaking, he sat peacefully and passed away.
He was seventy-two years old;
his stupa was erected at his native mountain.
On the eighth day of the fourth month of the following year, the door of the stupa opened of its own accord;
his physical features were as they had been when he was alive.
During the Dali era of Emperor Daizong, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dayi.
The *Stūpa Record of the True Lineage of Ciyun* states that when the Venerable [Zongmi] once visited Niutou Mountain in Jiankang,
Chan Master She Rong categorized his lineage as a "branch line."
In the fifth year of the Yonghui era, the year Jiayin (654 CE),
by imperial decree, the śrāmaṇera Kuiji was ordained as a bhikṣu and entered the Great Ci'en Monastery.
He participated in the translation of the *Jingzhengyi*.
Ji was the younger cousin of the Duke of Zhongwu, Wei Zheng;
he resided in Chang’an.
Initially, when Dharma Master Xuánzàng requested permission from his father to leave the household life,
Ji would read the commentaries and records once and memorize them;
he also understood their meanings immediately and was proficient in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
From Master Xuanzang, he received the fundamental tenets of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda and composed approximately one hundred treatises;
he was thus titled at the time the "Master of the Hundred Treatises."
By nature he was extravagant; whenever he went out, he invariably prepared three carriages—
one for scriptures, one for books, and one for food and drink—
and people of the time called him the "Master of the Three Carriages."
He entered nirvana in the first year of the Yongchun era at the age of fifty-one;
an imperial edict was issued expressing sorrow and lamentation.
The Imperially Composed Eulogy for the Portrait.
By imperial decree, he was buried at the northern channel of Fanchuan,
near the tomb of Dharma Master Xuanzang.
Dharma Master Xuan of Zhongnan Mountain in Jingzhao was so rigorous and precise in his observance of the Vinaya that he moved the devas to provide him with celestial food offerings.
He constantly disparaged the pleasures of the Three Chariots;
consequently, Xiao Ji sought out the Dharma Master.
When midday had passed and the celestial food had not yet arrived, Daoji took his leave; only then did the deity appear.
The Vinaya Master rebuked him for arriving late.
The deity said,
"A Mahāyāna bodhisattva has just arrived here;
because his retinue is so formidable, I did not enter myself."
Upon hearing this, the Vinaya Master was greatly astonished;
consequently, those both far and near increased their reverence for him.
Master Ji (Jianzhen) stated in his *Cien Benzhuan* (The Original Biography of Ci'en): [as cited above].

The Cien Teaching: Initially, the Great Being Asaṅga of India ascended repeatedly to the Tuṣita Heaven to consult with Maitreya regarding the fundamental principles of the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) school.
When his younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, was born in the country of Puruṣapura and attained realization of the Mahāyāna,
they subsequently collaborated to compose treatises.
Throughout successive generations in India, sages and worthies have appeared to propagate its teachings.
Among them was the Master of Śāstras Śīlabhadra, a treasury of the True Dharma,
a native of Central India in the Western Heavens (India).
He was one hundred and three years of age and resided at Nālandā Monastery in the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
It happened that the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang arrived there.
Xian subsequently transmitted the fundamental tenets of the Yogācārabhūmi and the Vijñaptimātra school to Xuanzang.
Upon his return from the East,
Xuanzang transmitted them to Kuiji.
Ji then compiled the various existing theories and extensively composed commentaries and treatises.
Scholars took him as their authority,
referring to his tradition as the "Three-Wheel Dharma-Character School that Manifests Principle" (Sanche Faxiang Xianli Zong) or the "Cien Teaching" (Cien Jiao).
In the tenth month of the sixth year of Yonghui,
the year of Yi-mao, the Emperor commanded the Minister of Works Li Ji to carry the imperial seal and ribbon to enshrine Consort Wu as Empress.
Regarding the deposition of Empress Wang:
Initially, in the second year of the Zhenguan era,
Emperor Taizong summoned the daughter of Wu Shifu, the Governor of Jingzhou, into the inner palace as a Talent (cairen).
At that time, she was fourteen years old.
The Grand Astrologer submitted a memorial stating there were omens of a female ruler,
so she was sent forth to become a nun at Ganye Monastery.
In the fifth year of Yonghui, the Emperor summoned her into the palace to serve as a Consort of High Rank (Zhāoyí).
She was now enfeoffed as Empress.
On the Bingchen day, the first year of Xianqing.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict was issued stating that among the monks and nuns throughout the realm,
those who violate the laws of the state shall be punished according to the monastic code (vinaya).
He was not to be treated according to the same legal code as the common people.
In the eleventh month, the Empress gave birth to a son,
who was titled Prince of Buddhist Radiance (Foguang Wang).
This refers to Emperor Zhongzong.
On the fifth day of the twelfth month, he ordained seven monks for the sake of Prince Foguang and invited Dharma Master Xuanzang.
He shaved the head of Prince Fuguang for him to enter the monastic order (*Chūshū*).
According to the *Old History of the Tang* (*Tángshū jiùshǐ*), the Venerable Master Bǎozhǎng of a Thousand Years was a native of Central India in Western Jibin (*Xīzhú*).
He was born with his left hand clenched in a fist.
At the age of seven, he shaved his head and began his religious practice;
consequently, he was named Baozhang (Jewel-Palms).
He arrived at this land during the twenty-fourth year of the Jian’an era of Emperor Xian of the Eastern Han dynasty.
During the Wei and Jin periods,
he traveled eastward and then entered Shu in the west to pay homage to Samantabhadra.
Remaining there, he recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras daily.
There was one who sang of it, saying:
"The weary jade teeth are cold;
they seem like the rushing of a cold spring gushing forth."
Once, while sitting in meditation at midnight,
ghosts and spirits wept before the steps.
One day, he said to the assembly:
"I have a vow to remain in this world for a thousand years;
therefore, I am called 'Thousand-Year.
Next, I traveled to Mount Wutai."
He moved his residence to Huayan on Mount Zhurong, Shuangfeng in Huangmei, and Donglin on Mount Lu;
subsequently, he arrived in Jiankang just as Bodhidharma was entering the Liang dynasty.
Zhang approached him to inquire about the essential meaning and attained enlightenment.
Emperor Wu, highly admiring his years of monastic practice and spiritual realization,
invited him into the inner court.
Before long, he went to Wu,
where he composed a verse that said:
"In the city of Liang, I met the Teacher."
Having realized the mind-ground through Zen meditation,
I wandered through the two provinces of Zhejiang; there,
I fully exhausted the beauty of its mountains and waters.
Following the current downstream to the east,
he traveled from Qianqin to India;
he then went to Mount Mao and ascended Mount Taibai.
He traversed the vast expanse of Yandang, dwelling among the seventy-two monasteries of the Verdant Peaks;
he ascended Mount Chizheng, rested at Yunmen, Fahua, Zhuji, Yupu, Chifu, and Dayan.
In the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong,
he returned to Feilai Peak in Hangzhou and took up residence there;
this is the present-day Zhongtianzhi Temple.
There was a verse that went: "Traveling through all four hundred provinces of China, one wanders here especially as a man of the Way.
Later, he resided at Baoyan Monastery in Pujiang.
It was then, on the first day of the New Year in the second year of the Xianqing era, the Ding-si year, that [he passed away].
He fashioned a statue by hand, and after nine days, the image was completed.
He asked his disciple Huiyun,
"To whom does it resemble?"
Huiyun said, "He is no different from the Master.
He then bathed, sat in the lotus posture, and said to Huiyun,
"I have dwelt in this world for one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years."
I am now departing from this world.
Listen to my verse:
"In its original nature, there is neither birth nor death."
Now I likewise manifest birth and death;
having attained the mind that comes and goes at will,
I shall return here again in future lives.
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Fifty-four years later,
the Elder Sthavira Cīra came from Yunmen to the site of the stupa.
The *Liji* states:
"I hope the stupa door will open. After a short while, the stupa door indeed opened, and his bones were found linked together like gold.
