He then said to his disciple, "You shall show me where Mañjuśrī resides," and having spoken,
he suddenly vanished.
Poli then returned to his native country to retrieve the incantations,
arriving at Chang’an in the first year of the Hongdao era.
By imperial decree, Du Xingyi and the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman were commissioned to complete the translation.
Poli also took the Sanskrit manuscript and sought out the monk Shunzheng of Ximing Monastery;
Zheng reported this to the throne, and they translated it together.
This is titled the *Guhya-uttara-dhāraṇī*;
it is the third version [of this scripture] and is largely identical with, yet slightly different from, that translated by Du Ling.
Compared to other various translations, this one has been most widely disseminated.
Puli subsequently entered Mount Wutai;
his final whereabouts are not known, according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
The Fayuan zhulin (Pearl Forest of the Dharma Garden) consists of one hundred fascicles.
It was granted entry into the Tripitaka for circulation.
It was compiled by the Dharma Master Xuānhuī.
Huī, whose courtesy name was Dàoshì,
entered nirvana in the first year of the Hongdao era.
Zhètiān— whose taboo name is pronounced with the "zhē" (少反) tone— is surnamed Wǔ.
After Gaozong’s death, she gave birth to three children: Zhongzong, Ruizong, and Princess Taiping.
Upon Gaozong’s passing, Zhongzong ascended the throne.
The Empress became the Imperial Grand Dowager.
On the *wùwǔ* day of the second month in the first year of Zhōngzōng’s reign,
the Empress deposed Zhōngzōng as the Prince of Lúlíng and confined him in a separate location.
In the year Jǐwèi (719), Emperor Ruizong established Prince Yù Dàn as the Heir Apparent; however,
state affairs were decided by the Empress Dowager,
who relegated the Emperor to a separate palace.
In the fourth month of summer, the Prince of Luling was transferred to Fangzhou;
he was subsequently transferred to Junzhou.
On the jayin day of the ninth month, an amnesty was proclaimed for all under heaven.
The reign title was changed to Guangzhai.
All banners and streamers were made golden in color;
those of the eighth rank and below who previously wore blue now changed their attire to green.
The Eastern Capital, Luoyang, was renamed Shendu;
its palace was named Taichu;
and the Department of State Affairs (Shangshu Sheng) was further changed to the Wenchang Terrace (Wenchang Tai).
The Left and Right Vice Presidents (Zuoyou Puyue) served as the Left and Right Ministers (Zuoxiang).
The Six Boards were the six officials of Heaven, Earth, and the four seasons.
The Secretariat (Menxia Sheng) was the Court of the Phoenix (Luantai).
The Zhongshu Sheng (Secretariat) was renamed Fengge;
the Shizhong (Grand Councilor) was renamed Nayan;
and the Zhongshuling (Director of the Secretariat) was renamed Neishi.
The Office of the Censor-General was renamed the Left Bureau for Purifying Government;
the Right Bureau for Purifying Government was newly established.
All other titles of the ministries, courts, and agencies were likewise changed according to their semantic categories.
The Empress Dowager ruled as regent for twenty-one years. She reached the age of eighty-one.

According to the *Jiu Tang Shu*, these reign periods were: one Guangzhai; four Chigong (including one Yongchang, one Tiannou—later changed to Zaichou—and two Changshou); one Yanchai; one Tiance Wansui (later changed to Zhengsheng); one Wansui Tongtian (later changed to Wansui Dengfeng); one Shengong; two Shengli; one Jiushi; and five Chang’an.
In the first month of the year Jiashen,
the reign title of Zhongzong was changed to Sisheng.
In the second month, Prince Yu was enthroned.
The year was renamed Wenming.
On the jia-yin day of the ninth month, the year was changed to Guangzhai.
The first year of Guangzhai was the first year of Chuigong, which was the year of Yiyou.
In the second year, the Bingxu year,
white lotus flowers suddenly grew upon the mulberry trees in the garden of Huang Shougong’s residence in Quanzhou;
he consequently donated his house to establish a monastery.
The Kai-xian Temple mentioned in the *Tujing* (Illustrated Scripture) is this very place.
In the third year of the Chuigong era,
the Indian śramaṇa Divākara— translated into Chinese as Rìzhào (Sunlight)— arrived.
During the early years of the Yifeng era of Emperor Gaozong,
he arrived in Chang’an and translated the *Guhyasamāja* and other sutras.
By this time, they had together translated eighteen works comprising thirty-four fascicles in total.
The Empress Dowager personally composed the preface to her own biography.
Jichou, the first year of Yongchang; Gengchen, the first year of Tianshou.
The state name was Zhou. In the ninth month of the first year of Tianshou.
The Attendant Censor Fu Youyi led the people of Guanzhong to the palace gate to present a memorial,
requesting that the dynastic name be changed to Zhou and that the Emperor be granted the surname Wu.
The Empress Dowager approved this.
He then ascended the Zetianlou (Hall of the Empress of Heaven) and issued a general amnesty for the empire;
he changed the dynastic name from Tang to Zhou and established a new era title.
The imperial title was elevated to "Sacred and Divine Emperor.
Since the Emperor was also the heir apparent, he was granted the surname Wu.
Seven ancestral temples of the Wu clan were established in the Divine Capital.

On the first day of the eleventh month, the day being Gengchen, the sun reached its southernmost point; the Empress Dowager offered sacrifice at the Wanxiang Shengong Temple and granted a general amnesty to all under heaven.
For the first time, the Zhou calendar was adopted, designating the eleventh month of the first year of Yongchang as the first month of the first year of Caru.
The twelfth month was designated as the "Là" (臘) month;
the first month of summer was designated as the first month.
A guest from the Qin lineage then fashioned the twelve characters beginning with "Transforming Heaven and Earth" (改造天地) and presented them [to the Emperor].
In the Dinghai year, it was put into practice.
The Empress Dowager styled herself Zao;
she changed the term "zhào" (imperial edict) to "zhì" (decree).
On the *xinyou* day of the second month, the Empress Dowager administered the examination for the *gongshi* (tribute scholars) at the Hall of the Luocheng Palace.
The practice of holding palace examinations for the *gongshi* began from this point.
This continued until the tenth month of winter in the first year of the Jiushi era.
The Emperor further changed the first month to the eleventh month and the eleventh month to the first month.
This was in the second month of the first year of the Shenlong era of Zhongzong.
The national designation was restored to Tang.
The rites for the suburban sacrifices, the ancestral temples, the altars of soil and grain, the imperial mausoleums, the hundred officials, the banners and ensigns, the colors of dress,
and the written characters were all conducted according to the precedents established prior to the Yongchun era.
Furthermore, the Divine Capital was designated as the Eastern Capital,
and the Northern Capital as Bingzhou.
These were the twelve newly created characters.
"Zhào" (illumination) is written as "Zào";
"Tiān" (heaven) is written as "Qiū";
"Dì" (earth) is written as "Jiè."
The sun is represented by the character 𑖿 (jia).
The moon is represented by the character 𑖾 (jiao).
The stars are represented by the circle ○.
The ruler is represented by the character 𠁈;
the minister is represented by 𢘑;
and the carriage is represented by 𡕀.
The character for "year" (年) is written as 𠡦;
the character for "beginning" (初) is written as 𡔈;
the character for "correctly" (正) is written as 𠙺. He ordered the Chancellor to compile the *Shizhengji* (Chronicle of Current Affairs).
The *Shizheng ji* (Records of State Administration) began from this point; according to the *Jiu Tang shu*,
it was the first year of the Chángshòu era, the *rénchén* year.
In the fourth month,
an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Renjian for an audience.
The Master gazed upon the Empress Dowager.
After a long silence, he asked,
"Do you understand?
The Master replied, "I do not understand."
The Master said, "I,
an old monk, observe the precept of silence.
Having finished speaking, he departed.
The following day, Jin presented nineteen short songs (tanka).
The Empress read them and praised them,
bestowing upon him generous rewards.
Now, only one verse by Liaoyuan remains in the *Chuandeng yuying ji*.
This master was none other than Master Tengteng;
he was a successor to National Teacher Huian of Mount Song.
The National Preceptor succeeded to the fifth patriarch’s transmission of the lamp.
*Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*. The śramaṇa Dharmaruci from South India;
here translated as Fāxī (Dharma-Desire).
Previously, Emperor Gaozong had heard of his reputation.
In the first year of the Kaiyao era, he issued an imperial decree through a Western Region envoy to respectfully invite him.
He arrived in Chang'an at this time.
The Empress Dowager summoned him for an audience and changed his name to Bodhiruci,
which means "Awakening Love" (Jue'ai) in Chinese.
By imperial decree, he translated nineteen works comprising twenty-eight fascicles at Foshouji Monastery.
In the second year of the Shenlong era of Emperor Zhongzong,
his aspirations fulfilled, he returned to the capital by carriage.
By imperial decree, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* was translated at Xichongfu Monastery.
The Emperor personally received the transcription of the text.
This took place in the first year of the Jingyun era of Emperor Ruizong.
The Emperor further convened a special assembly for the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* at the White Lotus Pavilion in the Northern Garden;
he personally transcribed the text with his own hand,
while Wang Jin, He Zhizhang, and others provided literary embellishments.
Supervised by Lu Xiangxian and Wei Zhigu of the Chancellery,
the Emperor personally composed a preface which was placed at the beginning of the scripture.
This was in the first year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong.
When Kumārajīva completed his work by merging the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* he had translated with the earlier translations into a single collection of one hundred and twenty fascicles,
he no longer translated scriptures; instead,
he devoted himself exclusively to recitation and the cultivation of meditative contemplation.
He entered parinirvāṇa in the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era.
His lifespan was one hundred and fifty-six years.
On the day of his burial, he was specially granted a ceremonial procession with its full array of insignia and attendants.
His stupa was erected on the western plain of Longmen;
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial and conferred the honorary epithet "Kaiyuan Sarvajña Tripiṭaka Master."
The weight of his fame and virtue was unprecedented in antiquity.
His resolve to translate scriptures amounted to fifty-three works totaling one hundred and eighteen fascicles, as recorded in detail in the Old History of the Tang (Jiu Tang Shu).
The year of Jiawu was the first year of Yanchai;
the year of Yiwu was the first year of Tianshu Wansui.
On the day of Xinsi in the first month.
The Empress Dowager was further titled Cishi (Maitreya).
The era name was changed to Zhengsheng (Witnessing the Holy).
She was also further titled the Great Sage Emperor of the Celestial Charter and Golden Wheel.
The year was changed to Wansui Tongtian (Heavenly Pervasion of Ten Thousand Years), according to the *Jiu Tang Shu*.
The Dharma Master’s name was Yijing;
his courtesy name was Wenming.
Mangyang was from Zhuozhou; as a child with hair tied in a topknot,
he left home to become a monk,
and upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination.
In the second year of the Xianheng era of Emperor Gaozong,
at the age of thirty-seven, he traveled to the Western Regions to seek Buddhist scriptures.
He journeyed alone for twenty-five years.
Having traveled through more than thirty countries,
he returned to the region of the Yellow and Luo Rivers in the fifth month of the year Yiwei.
He obtained nearly four hundred volumes of Sanskrit texts comprising the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, totaling five hundred thousand fascicles.
One set of the true image of the Vajrāsana and three hundred grains of śarīra were personally welcomed by the Empress Dowager outside the Upper East Gate.
He was enshrined at Foshouji Temple,
where he was commanded by imperial decree to engage in translation.
Initially, he collaborated with Śikṣānanda to translate the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
In the third year of the Chang’an era, he translated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra* and other scriptures, as well as the *Ekottara-karman*.
He was supervised by Xu Guan, a Professor Extraordinary at Chengjun University.
The Empress Dowager composed the "Preface to the Newly Translated Holy Teachings.
In the first year of the Shenlong era of Emperor Zhongzong,
at the Inner Sanctuary in East Luoyang, she translated the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* and other scriptures.
The Emperor composed a preface,
titled "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka of the Great Tang’s Dragon-Rising Era.
In the second year, he accompanied the imperial entourage back to Chang’an.
An imperial decree was issued to establish a separate Translation Institute at Dajianfu Monastery to translate the *Sarvālaṃkāra-rāja-sūtra* and other scriptures.
Cui Ti, Vice Minister of the Ministry of War, and Lu Can, Palace Secretary, served as the editors of the refined prose; Zhengzi served as the scribes.
Yang Shenjiao, the Director of the Secretariat and Prince Consort, was appointed as his guardian.
In the second year of the Jinglong era of Emperor Zhongzong,
the Master was summoned to the palace to participate in the translation of scriptures.
The Sangha sat in summer retreat for ninety days.
The Emperor, mindful of how [the Master] had prayed to Bhaisajyaguru while residing in Fangzhou,
ordered the Dharma Master to translate the two-fascicle *Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhasūtra* in the Dafoguang Hall.
In the first year of the Jingyun era of Emperor Ruizong,
the Master remained at Dajianfu Monastery and translated twenty scriptures and treatises, including the *Yuxiang jing*, totaling eighty-eight fascicles.
Scholars Li Jiao and Zhang Shuo and others refined the text,
while Vice Presidents Wei Juyuan and Su Gui supervised it.
In the seventh month of the first year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong, the Dharma Master entered nirvana.
He was seventy-nine years old [in secular age] and fifty-nine years of monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa).
By imperial decree, his funeral expenses were provided.
On the high plateau north of Longmen in Ta’erjing,
the Dharma Master translated a total of fifty-six works— comprising the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras— in two hundred and thirty fascicles.
Furthermore, he separately composed nine fascicles of ritual manuals and biographies.
Although the Master had translated the entire Tripiṭaka,
he specialized in the Vinaya section and instructed his disciples; the original biography states that in this year,
by imperial decree, the śramaṇas Mingquan and others were commissioned to edit the catalogue of scriptures, producing fifteen fascicles.
According to the current edition circulating in the Great Canon,
the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* records that when the Empress Dowager heard that there was a Sanskrit manuscript of the great *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in the kingdom of Khotan,
she dispatched an envoy to seek it.
He further requested that one person well-versed in the Sanskrit language accompany the scripture.
Thereupon, the King of Khotan dispatched the Venerable Śikṣānanda—translated here as "Joy of Enlightenment"—who was exceptionally proficient in the essential principles of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
the Empress Dowager, who had responded to the imperial summons, was greatly delighted.
In the third month of this year,
he was summoned by imperial decree to enter Dàbiànkōng Monastery,
where he collaborated with Bodhiruci, Fǎlǐ, and other masters on the translation work.
Next, he moved to Fo-shou-ji Temple.
The Empress Dowager frequently visited this temple,
personally scrutinizing and revising the texts with her own hand.
He provided offerings of food and delicacies.
In the tenth month of the second year of the Shengli era, the translation of eighty fascicles of new scriptures was completed;
the Empress Dowager personally composed a preface for them.
In the fourth year of Chang’an, Śikṣānanda translated the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in seven fascicles,
which was proclaimed to the various officials at the Taiji Hall.
This is more detailed and lucid than other editions.
Nanda translated a total of nineteen sūtras and śāstras, comprising one hundred and seven fascicles.
He then returned to Khotan.
An imperial edict dispatched the Censor Huo Siguang to escort him back to his own country; this is recorded in both the *Jiu Tang Shu* and the *Xin Tang Shu*.
In the second year of the Jinglong era of Emperor Zhongzong, an edict was issued once again for Nanta to come to the capital.
The Emperor personally went to welcome him and provide hospitality, preparing all the formal rites;
he was escorted to Jianfu Temple, where he lectured on the essential meanings of the sutras.
On the tenth month of the first year of Jingyun during the reign of Emperor Ruizong, the Master entered nirvana.
At his cremation, his tongue remained unburnt.
By imperial decree, it was sent back to Khotan to erect a stupa; this is recorded in his original biography.

On the day of Jia-shen in the twelfth month of the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era (the Bing-shen year), the reign title was changed to Wansui Dengfeng. Regarding the Master Xianshou: the monk Fazang was given the title Xianshou.
His surname was Kang;
he was a native of Kangju.
His demeanor was extraordinary and upright, and his sharp intelligence was peerless.
He came to Chang’an seeking to be selected for the study of the profound teachings among renowned monks.
It happened that he was among the first to participate in the translation of scriptures by Dharma Master Xuanzang.
Later, due to differences in his understanding regarding the transcription of the text, the verification of the meaning, and the polishing of the phrasing, he departed from the translation hall.
Initially, the Dharma Master Du Shun of Dunhuang was held in profound reverence by Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
He transmitted the *Huayan fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka) to his disciple Zhiyan.
This is the Huayan (Avataṃsaka) translated during the Jin dynasty.
The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang and Fazang fully mastered its teachings;
it was now being transmitted and translated.
Xuanzang was the first to be included in their number.
When Śikṣānanda translated the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* from Khotan,
Xuanzang, along with Dharma Master Yijing and Dharma Master Fuli, were all present.
In the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era,
an imperial edict was issued for the śrāmaṇera Fazang to expound the principles of the newly translated Avataṃsaka Sūtra at Taiyuan Temple;
a white light then issued from his mouth.
An imperial decree was issued appointing ten Great Virtuous Ones (*mahāsattva*) from the capital region to bestow the full ordination according to the Tripiṭaka;
they were granted the title "Worthy Head" (*Xianshou*).
By imperial edict, they were summoned to enter Dàbiànkōng Monastery to participate in the translation work.
In the first year of the Chang’an era,
an imperial decree was issued for Xianshou to lecture on the newly translated Avataṃsaka Sūtra at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
When they reached the chapter on the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang shijie pin*), the earth shook violently.
On that very day, he was summoned for an audience at the Changsheng Hall, where he was questioned on the meaning of the ten layers of the celestial net and the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*).
Fazang’s exposition proceeded with systematic order.

Regarding these, the meaning of the celestial net consists of the ten layers of profound gates: the gate of the ocean-seal samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), the gate of the six characteristics in harmonious union, and the gate of the universal eye’s realm (*sarvacakṣuḥ-gocara*).
These various chapters of meaning constitute the comprehensive and specific web of meanings of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
The Empress Dowager was perplexed and could not reach a decision regarding them;
Fazang then pointed to the golden lion in the main hall as a metaphor.
Consequently, I have composed this "Chapter on the Golden Lion," which provides a direct and easy-to-understand path to its meaning;
it sets forth the characteristics of ten categories, both general and specific.
The Empress Dowager then attained awakening to its meaning.
Zang further established skillful means for those whose studies were not yet complete;
he took ten mirrors and arranged them in the eight directions.
There is one [image] at the top and one at the bottom, separated by a distance of more than one zhang;
they face each other on opposite sides,
with a single Buddha image installed between them.
Light one torch to illuminate it;
as their reflections intermingle and their lights cross,
the student thereby understands the meaning of the infinite interpenetration within the ocean of lands (*kṣetrasamudra*).
Zang once composed a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*,
which was esteemed by his contemporaries and circulated throughout the world.
He was also titled the National Preceptor Kangtsang.
Chengguan, the Great Universal National Preceptor Qingliang,
followed the lineage of Xianshou with the talent of a sage-like successor to the world.
He authored commentaries and treatises on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* totaling several million words.
Guifeng Zongmi succeeded him;
these two are known as the fifth patriarchs of the Huayan school.
The source of the Great Dharma flows forth abundantly, permeating the world;
it is titled *The Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Xianshou School: The Perfectly Integrated Endowment of Virtue in a Single Thought*.
National Teacher Qingliang,
whose Dharma name was Chengguan and whose secular surname was Xiahou.
He was a native of Shanyin in Yuezhou.
At the age of eleven, he left home to become a monk under Chan Master Pài of Baolin Monastery on Mount Jingshan.
He recited the Lotus Sūtra.
At the age of fourteen, he encountered an imperial favor and received ordination;
his name was registered at Baolin Monastery during the Qianyuan era of Emperor Suzong.
He studied the *Vinaya* of the Xiangbu school under Dharma Master Li of Qixia Monastery in Runzhou;
he followed Dharma Master Tan Yi in the Nanshan Vinaya tradition;
and he visited Dharma Master Xuanyi of Jinling to receive the transmission of the Three Treatises of the Guanzhong and Heshang lineages.
The flourishing of the Three Treatises in the region south of the Yangtze was due to the Master’s efforts.
During the Dali era of Emperor Daizong,
he transmitted the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Waguan Monastery.
Furthermore, at Huainan Fazang’s monastery, he received the exegesis on the *Awakening of Faith* from the Korean peninsula;
there he rehearsed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and re-examined the *Three Treatises*,
doing so for nearly twenty years.
In Suzhou, he studied the commentaries on the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, and other scriptures under Dharma Master Zhànrán.
He also visited Chan Master Zhōng of Niutou Mountain.
Chan Master Qin of Mount Jing and Chan Master Wangming of Luoyang consulted him to resolve their doubts regarding the Chan teachings of the Southern School.
Furthermore, he observed that Master Huiyun had thoroughly mastered the profound principles of the Northern School;

he had even gone so far as to study and translate the Confucian classics, histories, and minor learning texts such as the *Cangjie* and *Erya*, as well as the Indian *Siddham*, the various sectarian tenets, the four Vedas, the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), secret mantras, ritual manuals, verses, and calligraphic styles.
He thoroughly mastered all [fields of learning].
In the eleventh year of the Dali era,
he went to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
He traveled to Mount Emei to pay homage to Samantabhadra,
and upon his return, he resided at Dahuayan Temple on Mount Wutai,
where he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Vaipulya repentance ritual.
Reflecting with regret upon the old commentaries on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, I find their prose to be voluminous while their meaning remains concise;
thus, I have been filled with deep contemplation.
Moreover, Mañjuśrī presides over wisdom.
Samantabhadra presides over principle;
the two sages combined constitute Vairocana,
through whom the myriad practices are simultaneously mastered.
This is precisely the meaning of the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*.
He subsequently composed a commentary in twenty fascicles during the seventh year of the Zhenyuan era of Emperor Dezong.
Li Ziliang, the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Hedong,
requested that the Master lecture on his new commentary at Chongfu Temple.
Emperor Dezong heard of his reputation.
An imperial envoy, Li Fuguang, was sent down to proclaim an edict for him to enter the capital.
There, together with the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra, he translated the forty fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (the latter portion) presented by the kingdom of Oḍra.
In the fifth month of the following year,
the Emperor dispatched the Palace Messenger Huo Xianming to proclaim an imperial edict urging him to enter.
The Dezong Emperor treated him with great respect and retained him at the Translation Bureau to oversee the editorial corrections.
Furthermore, an imperial decree was issued to compose commentaries,
which were compiled into ten fascicles and presented for the Emperor's inspection while Shunzong was still in the position of Crown Prince.
I once received the Master’s words;

I request that you recount one volume on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and one volume on the essential points of the mind, as well as the causes and conditions for the transgression of eating meat.
The Master has composed many works that provide a detailed commentary on the essential outlines of these meanings.
There were approximately one hundred disciples who transmitted the Dharma.

This is further evidenced by the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty), compiled by the monastic head Zanning, based on the records of the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong and the third year of the Kāichéng era of Emperor Wenzong.
Chan Master Zongmi of Mount Gui on Zhongnan Mountain was a native of Xichong in Guozhou.
His secular surname was He.
His family had followed the profession of Confucian scholars for generations.
In the second year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong,
he was about to depart to take the imperial examination.
Having happened upon the Dharma seat of Chan Master Yuan of Suizhou, he tasted the flavor of his teachings and requested to shave his head and receive the precepts.
He attained full ordination within that same year.
One day, while accompanying the assembly of monks for a meal at the residence of the local official Ren Guan, he sat in the last seat.
As he was given the scripture in succession, he received the twelve chapters of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (the *Yuanjue jing*).
Before the scroll was finished, he attained profound realization.
He returned and informed Yuan, who said,
"You shall greatly propagate the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden."
"All these Buddhas have conferred this upon you.
Go now, and do not remain stagnant in a single corner.
Having thus received the command, he took his leave and departed.
He visited Chan Master Zhong of Jingnan and Chan Master Zhao of Luoyang, both of whom granted him formal predictions of his future enlightenment.
Upon reaching Xianghan, he fell ill; a monk then entrusted him with a commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra.
This was composed by the Great Master Chengguan of the Capital.
Upon reading it, he said with joy:
"In my practice of Chan, I have encountered the Southern School."
Having encountered the teaching of Perfect Enlightenment,
my mind-ground was opened and cleared by a single word;
within this single scroll, the sky of its meaning shone with brilliant clarity.
Now, having once again obtained this final manuscript,
I have sought out the capital to pay my respects to the National Teacher Qingliang.
Before long, I shall enter the hermitage on Mount Guifeng in Zhongnan once more.
During the Taihe era of Emperor Wenzong,
he was summoned to the inner palace and granted purple robes.
The Emperor repeatedly inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.
The court officials turned toward him with admiration;
only the Chancellor Pei Xiu entered deeply into the inner sanctum,
receiving his teachings and serving as his external protector.
The Master, observing that scholars of Chan and the teachings were mutually disparaging one another,
subsequently composed the *Chan Yuan Zhu Quan*.
He transcribed and recorded the various texts written by different schools that explain the fundamental principles and the words, phrases, and verses of the Chan gate.
Compiled into a single canon to bequeath to future generations on the sixth day of the first month of the first year of the Huichang era of Emperor Wuzong.
At Kōfuku-in, he admonished his disciples,
instructing them to carry his corpse away to be given to birds and beasts,
and to cremate his bones and scatter them.
Having finished speaking, he sat and passed away.
Both monastics and laypeople enshrined his entire body at Mount Guifeng.
Upon cremation, śarīra relics were obtained.
He was interred in a stone chamber.
Emperor Xuanzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dinghui,
and his stupa was named "Blue Lotus."
He lived to the age of sixty-three and succeeded Yuan of Suizhou.
He belongs to the sixth generation of the five branches below [the main line], within the Heze lineage.
An imperial edict summoned Chan Master Huian of Mount Song and Chan Master Shenxiu to the capital.
They were carried into the palace hall on a sedan chair,
where the Empress Dowager personally prostrated herself before them in worship.
He was received within the imperial palace,
where he was consulted morning and evening on matters of the Way;
he was honored and established as the National Preceptor.
At that time, from the princes and dukes down to the commoners, they heard of his reputation and came to pay their respects;
even those who merely caught sight of the dust raised by his approach would prostrate themselves.
From the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp): Chan Master Xiu of the Northern School, whose name was Shenxiu.
The successor who branched out from the Fifth Patriarch was born into the Li family of Kaifeng. In his youth,
he pursued the study of Confucianism.
Having extensively mastered a vast range of learning, he suddenly conceived the desire to leave the household life.
Upon arriving at Shuangfeng Temple in Qizhou, he met the Fifth Patriarch;
he was so filled with admiration and reverence that he entered his service.
He provided firewood and water as service in order to seek the Way,
and the Patriarch then ordained him. When the Fifth Patriarch entered nirvana, [he succeeded him].
The Master was residing at Mount Dangyang in Jiangling when the Empress Dowager heard of him and summoned him to the capital. There,
he was venerated together with National Teacher Huian at the Inner Chapel.
He was accorded exceptional honor and respect;
the Emperor ordered the establishment of Dumunsa Temple on Dangyang Mountain to commemorate his virtue.
Once King Chungjong had ascended the throne, [he further honored him].
He treated him with exceptional courtesy and respect.
Once, when the minister Zhang Yue heard the essentials of the Dharma, he observed the etiquette of a disciple.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
All Buddha-dharmas are inherently present within one's own mind;
yet, seeking them externally, he abandoned his father and fled.
On the second day of the second month in the second year of the Shenglong era of the Zhongzong reign, he entered parinirvāṇa at Tiangong Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Da Tong.
By imperial decree, he was buried at Longmen;
on the day of his interment, ceremonial insignia and a formal imperial procession were provided.
The Emperor escorted him as far as Bianqiao Bridge and issued an edict for Zhang Yue, the Director of the Secretariat, to compose the inscription for his stele.
The Master was born at the end of the Sui dynasty and lived for over one hundred years.
He reached eighty years of monastic seniority (*saṃghalava*).
At that time, Prince Qi Fan and the retired scholar Lu Hongyi both had steles erected and composed eulogies for him.
His biography is contained in the *Jiù Tángshū* (Old Book of Tang).
The practice of bestowing posthumous titles (*śrī*) upon monks began with this master.

His disciples, including Pují and Yìfú, all succeeded him in his monastic lineage. The State Preceptor of Mount Song, whose name was Huì'ān— *Note: The term "僧諡號" (sēng shì hào) refers to posthumous titles conferred upon monks;
"嗣襲師位" (sì xí shī wèi) means to succeed to the master's position in the monastic lineage; "僧傳" (sēng zhuàn) refers to the biographies of eminent monks.*
He was the son of the Wei family from Zhiyang in Jingzhou.
Having left home to become a monk in his youth,
he went into seclusion in the mountain valleys in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
During the Daye era of Emperor Yang, many laborers digging the Jiqu Canal perished from hunger;
the Master begged for food to sustain them.
When Emperor Yang heard of this, he summoned the Master.
He did not attend the assembly but entered stealthily into Mount Taihe.
He ascended Mount Heng and practiced the dhūta austerities.
During the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong, he traveled to Huangmei in Qizhou to pay his respects to the Fifth Patriarch.
He subsequently attained the essential core of the Dharma.
In the first year of the Linde era of Emperor Gaozong,
he traveled to the stone cliffs of Mount Zhongnan and settled there.
When Emperor Gaozong summoned him, he did not rise to comply and returned once more to Mount Song and Mount Shao,
declaring, "This is the place where I shall spend my final years.
Practitioners of Chan then flocked to him from all directions like spokes converging at the hub.
The Empress Dowager dispatched an envoy to summon the Master for an audience;
together with Chan Master Beixiu, he received her profound respect and honor.
The Empress Dowager enshrined the Master as National Teacher (Guoshi).
In the second year of the Shénlóng era of Emperor Zhōngzōng, he was granted a purple *kāṣāya*.
He ordained fourteen disciples and was invited into the imperial palace to receive offerings.
At that time, Emperor Zhongzong dispatched the inner attendant Xue Jian with an imperial edict summoning the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch did not respond to the summons for over three years.
Emperor Zhongzong again bestowed upon the Master a monk’s robe of coarse hemp cloth (*mò-nà*).
He took his leave to return to Mount Song.
On the third day of the third month in the third year of the Jinglong era,
he addressed his disciples, saying:
"I shall die and carry my corpse into the forest,
waiting for a wild fire to consume it.
On the eighth day, he lay down his body and passed away in tranquility.
He was one hundred twenty-eight years old.
His disciples followed his instructions,
and indeed, a wild fire spontaneously ignited for his cremation.
Eighty grains of śarīra were obtained;
five of them were large and purple in color.
These were presented and retained within the palace precincts.
In the first year of the Xiāntiān era of Emperor Ruīzōng, his disciples constructed a stūpa for him.
He is popularly known as National Master Lǎo'ān.
His dharma-heir Rénjiàn [is recorded] in the *Pòzuòduò* (The Breaking of the Hearth) and the *Sōngyuè Guīchuán Dēnglù* (The Lamp Record of the Transmission from Guī of Sōngyuè).
In the first year of Shengong (the Dingyou year), and the first year of Shenglì (the Wuxu year),
the Imperial Heir, Ruizong, earnestly petitioned to abdicate the throne in favor of the Prince of Luling.
In the ninth month, the Prince of Luling, Zhang, was established as the Crown Prince.
Furthermore, it was titled "Proclamation of a Great Pardon for the Empire. In the second year of Shengli (Jihai),
and the first year of Jiushi (Gengzi), in the tenth month of winter,
an edict was issued to once again designate the first month as the eleventh month.
The first month was the first month of the year.
*Xinchou*: the first year of Chang’an; *Renyin*: the second year; *Guimao*: the third year; *Jiachen*: the fourth year of Chang’an.
The Zhongzong: His posthumous name was Xian.
He was the seventh son of Gaozong and was established as the Crown Prince.
Initially, upon the demise of Emperor Gaozong, the Crown Prince ascended the throne.
In the first month, he honored Empress Tianhou as Empress Dowager and installed Consort Wei as Empress.
He appointed the Empress’s father, Wei Xuanzhen, as the Regional Inspector of Yuzhou.
The Emperor then appointed Xuanzhen as a Palace Attendant (Shizhong),
but Pei Yan adamantly opposed this, and the Emperor did not follow his advice.
Empress Dowager Yanbai plotted in secret;
on the wu-woo day of the second month, she deposed the Emperor and demoted him to the rank of Prince of Luling,
first transferring him to Fangzhou and subsequently to Junzhou.
Liu Xuanzhen was exiled to Qinzhou.
In the first year of the Tiānshèng Lì calendar,
he was reinstated as the Crown Prince.
In this year, the first month, on the day of Yisi, the Empress Dowager transmitted the throne to the Crown Prince.
On the day of Bingwu, the Emperor ascended the throne.
On the day of Dingwei, the Empress Dowager moved her residence to the Zhuyang Palace.
The Emperor led the hundred officials to bestow upon her the honorary title of Empress Wuzetian Dashingeng Huangdi.
On the day of Renyin in the eleventh month, she passed away.
In the second month of the first year of the Shenlong era, the national name was restored to Tang.

The banners for the suburban sacrifices, the ancestral temple, and the altars of soil and grain, as well as those for the various officials, were all conducted according to the precedents established prior to the Yongchun era.
With the divine capital at Luoyang, it was designated as the Eastern Capital;
the Northern Capital was established at Bingzhou.
The Emperor reigned for six years.
His lifespan was fifty-five years. From the second year of Shenlong to the fourth year of Jinglong—specifically, the fourth month of the first year of Shenlong, the year of Yisi.
The Emperor issued an imperial decree summoning the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi to the capital.
The text of the decree read:
"I have invited the two masters Zong and Xiu to the palace for their support."
Whenever they investigated the One Vehicle, the two masters would both defer to one another, saying,
"The Master Neng of the South secretly received the robe and dharma from Master Ren;
you should go to him and inquire."
Now, I have dispatched the Inner Attendant Xue Jian to ride with this decree to invite you.
I pray that you, Master, will look upon me with compassion and proceed swiftly to the Capital.
The Patriarch declined the invitation, citing illness as his excuse.
Jian said: "The virtuous monks of the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
It has never been the case that anyone attained liberation without relying on meditative concentration."
"I do not yet understand the Dharma taught by the Master.
The Patriarch said, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting?"
Jian said,
"When your disciple returns to court, the Sovereign will surely question me.
I pray that you, Master, will instruct me on the essentials of the mind so that I may clearly realize the Way."
The Patriarch said,
"The Way has neither light nor darkness.
Jian said, "Light is a metaphor for wisdom."
The dark condition is affliction.
If one does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter affliction, by what means can one escape from birth and death?
The Patriarch said:
If one uses wisdom to illuminate afflictions, this is the limited capacity of the two vehicles.
To distinguish it, he asked: "What is called the insight of the Mahāyāna?"
The Patriarch said:
"Luminosity and ignorance are non-dual in their nature;
this non-dual nature is itself the true nature."
The true nature does not diminish in ordinary beings,
nor does it increase in noble ones;
it remains undisturbed even while abiding amidst afflictions.
Dwelling in meditative concentration yet not being quiescent;
when nature and characteristics are both suchness (*tathatā*), this is called the Way (*mārga*).
Jian said: "Master, you speak of neither arising nor ceasing—how does this differ from the non-Buddhists?"
The Patriarch said:
"The heterodox teach the cessation of birth through birth,
and manifest cessation by means of birth."
That which is extinguished is as if not extinguished;
that which arises is said to be non-arising;
I say it is fundamentally non-arisen from the beginning.
Now there is likewise no cessation;
thus it differs from the non-Buddhists.
If you wish to know the essential point of the mind:
Simply do not deliberate upon any good or evil at all;
you will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind,
which is profoundly still and eternally abiding, with wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
After he had briefly declined the honors and returned to the palace, he submitted a memorial to his ancestors;
the Emperor praised him for a long time.
Shortly thereafter, the Emperor dispatched an envoy to bestow upon him a *mò* robe, a *kāṣāya*, an alms bowl, and five hundred rolls of silk.
The *Lengyan jing* (Śūraṃgama-sūtra), translated by the Indian śramaṇa Paramiti—
meaning "Ultimate Measure" (Prabhāmitra) in Chinese— who arrived in Guangzhou in this year and resided at Zhizhi Daochang.
It conveys the imperial intent of longing for the Dharma and transmits the Lamp of the Teachings.
In the fifth month, from within the section on Empowerment (Abhiṣeka), one chapter was recited,
titled the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
Maitreyaśrī means "Cloud Peak" in this language.
It was translated into ten fascicles,
with the Chancellor Fang Rong serving as the scribe.
At that time, Fang Rong had been demoted and exiled to Gaoyou.
Consequently, I was able to reside at the translation bureau.
The śramaṇa Huaidi served as the proofreader for the translation. Once the task of transmitting the sūtra was completed, [the preface was written].
The imperial court reprimanded him for translating privately.
Consequently, Śikṣānanda boarded a ship and returned to India with the Sanskrit manuscripts to produce a formal translation record.
In the second year of the Shénlóng era (the Bingwu year), the monk Fǎn and others were granted the fifth rank, according to the Old History of the Tang.
The Ordination through Scriptural Examinations: In the eighth month, an imperial edict was issued throughout the realm to test the scriptural exegesis of novice monks (*tonghang*).
Those who demonstrated thorough mastery without impediment were ordained as monks.
The practice of ordaining monks through scriptural examinations began from this point, according to the *Old History of the Tang*.
The śramaṇa Zhìyán was the son of the King of Khotan;
he came to the Tang at a young age.
Early on he occupied positions of honor and emolument;
he was appointed Grand General and invested as a Duke of a Commandery.
In the fifth month of that year, he requested to donate his residence to establish a monastery.
The imperial decree granted his request.
He further petitioned firmly for ordination.
On the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month, an ink-written edict stated:
In the nature of human beings, there is none who does not covet emolument and cherish their station;
yet Your Excellency’s wish is to renounce the world and leave the household life.
Having suddenly reviewed the memorial you have submitted:
With both reward and compassion in mind,
I have specially granted your prayer,
thereby fulfilling your lofty aspiration.
He was subsequently invited to reside at Zhongnanshan Zhixiang Monastery,
where he frequently participated in the translation of Buddhist scriptures and compiled the *Shijiaolu* (Records of the Translation of the Teachings).
In the first month of the third year of Jinglong (the Dingwei year), Zhang Renyuan, the Grand Commander of the Shuofang Circuit, [requested his presence].
Three Border-Surrender Cities were built along the river and belonged to Fengzhou.
The Spirit of Mount Song requested the precepts from Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song.
He was born into the Li family in Ique.
Having left home to become a monk in his youth,
he received full ordination during the Yongchun era of Emperor Gaozong’s reign and was affiliated with Xianju Monastery, where he studied the Vinaya.
Having paid his respects to National Teacher Huian, he attained sudden enlightenment into the profound essence of the teachings.
He subsequently lived in a grass hut at Pangwu on Mount Song.
One day during that year, there appeared a strange man.
Wearing a high cap and knee-length trousers with leggings, they arrived with practiced ease.
Their retinue was immense and their appearance most imposing as they went to pay their respects to the Great Master.
The Master, perceiving that they were extraordinary, addressed them, saying:
"Welcome, O worthy one! Why have you come here?
He replied, "Does the Master not recognize me?
The Master said:
"I regard the Buddha and sentient beings as equal;
I view them all with a single eye—how could I make such distinctions?
The other replied, "I am the mountain deity of this peak."
"You can bring life and death upon others;
how could you, Master, possibly look upon me with a single eye?
The Master said:
I am fundamentally unborn;
how could you cause me to die?
I regard my body as equal to space.
Regard me as being equal to you.
Can you destroy emptiness and yourself?
If you could indeed destroy both emptiness and yourself, [then you might understand].
I am neither born nor do I perish.
Since you are not yet able to be thus,
how could you possibly give birth to or cause my death?
The deity bowed his head and said,
"I am also intelligent and upright compared to other deities;
how could I have known that you, Master, possessed such vast wisdom and eloquence?"
"I pray that you grant me the true precepts so that I may cross over the world. The Teacher said:
"Since you have already requested the precepts, you are already possessed of them. Why is this?"
Outside of precepts there are no precepts;
what, then, would a precept be?
The Spirit said: "This is the principle."
"I have heard [the teachings] but remain vague and confused; I seek only the Master’s precepts.
As my disciple, I immediately prepared a seat for the Master, lit the incense burner, and set out the ritual table, saying:
"I confer upon you the five precepts.
If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can';
if you cannot, you should say 'no'."
The deity said, "I respectfully accept your instruction.
The Master asked, "Are you able to refrain from lust?
He replied, "I am also married."
The Master said, "I do not mean this; I mean the absence of desire.
[The student] said, "I can."
The Master said, "Are you able not to steal?
He replied, "What lack do I have that I would take anything by theft?
The Master said, "I do not mean this; I mean that one who enjoys offerings brings blessings to the licentious, while one who does not provide offerings brings calamity upon the virtuous."
He replied, "I can.
The Master asked,
"Are you able to refrain from killing?"
He said, "I truly hold the handle of it; I do not kill.
The Master said, "That is not what I mean. I mean that there may be excess, error, suspicion, or confusion.
He replied, "I am capable."
The Master said, "Can you avoid falsehood?
He replied, "I am upright; how could I have falsehood?"
The Master said, "I do not mean this; I mean that the sequence does not accord with the Will of Heaven.
[The student] said, "I can.
The Master said:
"Have you not been ruined by alcohol?
He replied, "I have.
The Master said, "The above constitutes the Buddha's precepts."
The Master further said:
"One should uphold with a conscious mind yet remain free from mental attachment;
one should act for the sake of others with a conscious mind yet remain free from thoughts of the self."
One who can act thus is born before heaven and earth yet does not become a vital essence;
dies after heaven and earth yet does not become old;
undergoes transformation all day long yet does not become active.
To reach ultimate stillness and silence without ceasing—
believing this, even though one marries, it is not as a wife;
even though one feasts, it is not as a taker.
Although he holds the handle, it is not power;
although he acts, it is not for a specific purpose;
although he is intoxicated, he is not deluded.
If one can be without mind regarding all things, then there is no precept;
if there is no precept, then there is no mind.
There is neither Buddha nor sentient beings.
"If there is neither you nor a self,
who is it that observes the precepts?
The spirit replied, "My supernatural powers are second only to those of the Buddha."
The Master said:
"In your ten statements regarding supernatural powers, five are possible and five are impossible.
In the Buddha's ten statements, seven are possible and three are impossible."
The deity was struck with awe; he left his seat, knelt, and asked, "May I hear it?
The Master said:
"Can you cause the Supreme Deity to travel eastward in the heavens while the seven luminaries move westward?
He replied, "I cannot.
The Master said:
"Are you able to seize the terrestrial spirits, melt the Five Peaks, and bind the Four Seas?
He replied, "I cannot.
The Master said:
These are called the five impossibilities.
The Buddha can empty all phenomena and realize the wisdom of all dharmas,
yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma.
The Buddha can know the natures of all beings and exhaustively understand events throughout billions of kalpas;
yet he cannot transform and guide those for whom he lacks the karmic affinity.
The Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot bring the realm of sentient beings to an end.
These are the three things that cannot [be avoided].
Furthermore, even fixed karma is not permanent;
even the absence of conditions constitutes a single lifetime.
The realm of sentient beings is fundamentally without increase or decrease;
it is vast and empty, with not a single person able to preside over its dharma.
That there is a dharma without a presiding master is what is called "the absence of dharma."
To be without dharma and without master is called being without mind.
As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers;
he is simply able to penetrate all dharmas through this state of no-mind.
The deity said, "I am indeed shallow and ignorant;
I have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness.
As for the precepts you have bestowed upon me, I shall faithfully practice them."
"Now I wish to repay your compassionate virtue by exerting my own abilities.
The Master said,
"I observe that this body is nothing at all."
He contemplated that all phenomena are impermanent;
being as solid as a block of wood, what further desires could he have?
The spirit said, "Master, you must command me to perform some worldly task so that I may display my minor divine powers."

Having sent forth these [teachings], there are five types of people—those who have already resolved their minds, those who have first resolved their minds, those who have not yet resolved their minds, those who do not yet believe, and those who will certainly believe—who, through my own spiritual traces, shall come to know that there is a Buddha, that there is a spirit, that there is capacity, that there is incapacity, and that there is both the spontaneous and the non-spontaneous.
The Master said,
"Non-action is non-action. Shen said,
"The Buddha also commands me, Shen, to protect the Dharma."
"Master, would you rather fall into the error of rebelling against the Buddha?
I pray that you will deign to instruct me as you wish.
Reluctantly, the Master spoke, saying:
The barrier of Dongyan Temple is vast and treeless;
while there are trees on the northern peak, its back is not shielded by them.
Can you move the trees from the north to the eastern ridge?
The deity said, "I have already received your command.
However, there will surely be clamor and commotion during the dark night;
I pray that you, Master, do not be startled."
He immediately performed a prostration and took his leave.
The master saw him off at the gate and watched him depart;
he observed that the ceremonial retinue followed in a winding procession, resembling the appearance of a sovereign.
Mists, vapors, smoke, and clouds swirled and intermingled;
banners and streamers, along with tinkling bells, vanished into the air.
That evening, indeed, there arose a violent wind and thundering peals, with rushing clouds and flashing lightning that caused the buildings to tremble and the nesting birds to clamor.
The Master said to the assembly,
"Do not fear, do not fear;
the spirit has entered into harmony with me."
At dawn the next day, the sky was clear and bright;
then all the pines and cypresses from the northern cliff had been moved to the eastern ridge,
standing there in dense, orderly rows.
The Master said to his disciples,
"After my passing, words will be unable to reach me;
if you make them a mere pretext for conversation, people will treat me as a supernatural being."
In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong,
the Master addressed his disciples, saying:
"I originally resided on the eastern ridge of this monastery."
"I shall now enter parinirvāṇa;
you may place my remains there.
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
The Master succeeded National Teacher Huian.
National Teacher [succeeded] Chan Master Wuzu Damo, according to the *Chuan Deng Lu*.
It was the year Jiyou, the third year of the Jinglong era.
In that year, Vinaya Master Dao’an was summoned to the palace to confer the precepts of refuge upon the Consort and the Princes.
An imperial eulogy for the portrait of the Precepts was composed by the Emperor at Lingguang Palace, which says:
The pearl of his precepts is bright and pure;
the stream of his wisdom is clear and serene;
his person is confined to the numinous scriptures.
The mind merges into meditative concentration;
one studies the wondrous True Doctrine and contemplates the penetrating true nature.
Maintaining the administration of justice and upholding the principles of virtuous governance,
may the Vinaya Piṭaka continue to transmit its fragrance.
Consequently, the teachings of the Image Period flourished brilliantly.
The Master entered nirvana in the fifth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong.
Emperor Ruizong’s personal name was Dan.
The eighth son of Gaozong.
He was initially enfeoffed as Prince of Yu and later as Prince of Xiang.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Jinglong era,
Emperor Zhongzong was assassinated;
Empress Wei kept the death secret and did not announce the mourning.
He established Prince Zhongmao as the Crown Prince,
issued the proclamation of mourning, and ascended the throne;
the year was named Tanglong.
Prince Li Longji, the Prince of Xiang,
quelled the internal rebellion and served as regent for the young Emperor.
Shortly thereafter, the young Emperor abdicated the throne to the Prince of Xiang.
The Prince of Xiang then ascended the imperial throne.
Having reigned for three years,
he established Longji as the Crown Prince.
In the seventh month of the second year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong, Chongmao passed away.
He was posthumously titled Emperor Shang,
having reached the age of twenty.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era,
Emperor Ruizong passed away at the age of fifty-five. This was on a gengxu day in the sixth month of the second year of Jingyun and the first year of Xiantian.
The reign title was changed to Jingyun, the first year of which fell in the eighth month.
At that time, Xue Nen, Grand General of the Left Guard, was concurrently appointed as the Military Governor (Jiedushi) and Commander-in-Chief (Du-du) of Youzhou.
The title of Jiedushi originated with Nen.
The hundred officials were granted noble ranks, and ten thousand monks and Daoists were universally ordained. (Old History of the Tang;
Renzi, the seventh month of the first year of the Xuantian era).
The Emperor transmitted the throne to the Crown Prince.
The Xuanzong’s personal name was Longji;
he was the third son of Ruizong.
He was first enfeoffed as the Prince of Chu.
He was subsequently re-enfeoffed as the Prince of Linzi.
At the beginning of the Jingyun era, he was established as the Crown Prince.
He ascended the throne in the eighth month of the first year of the Xiāntián era.
He reigned for forty-three years and reached the age of seventy-eight.
The Emperor honored his father, the Zongzong, as the Taishanghuang (Retired Sovereign). This was the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month of the Kaiyuan era and the fourteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era.
In the seventh month of autumn in the first year of Kaiyuan, the Emperor, together with Prince of Qí Fàn, Prince of Xué Yè, Guò Yuànzhen, and Wáng Máo Zhōng and Gāo Lìshì, [proceeded].
Those who plotted the deposition and enthronement of the Chancellor and committed acts of rebellion were executed:
namely, Xiao Zhizhong, Dou Huaiqing, Cen Xi, Cui Ti, Chang Yuankai, Li Ci, and others.
Meritorious officials were rewarded with ranks and titles.
The proliferation of eunuchs began from this point.
In the twelfth month, an amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and the titles of the Left and Right Secretaries of the Department of State Affairs were changed to those of the Left and Right Grand Ministers (Zhengxiang).
The Zhongshu Sheng (Secretariat) was renamed the Ziwai Sheng (Purple Microcosm Department);
the Menxia Sheng (Chancellery) was renamed the Huangmen Sheng (Yellow Gate Department);
and the Shizhong (Palace Attendant) was designated as the Jian (Supervisor).
Yongzhou was made the Jingzhao Prefecture;
Luozhou was made the Henan Prefecture;
and the Chief Administrators were appointed as Governors (Yin).
Sima served as the Junior Vice-Governor.
The Sixth Patriarch, the Venerable Great Being Huineng, was of the secular surname Lu;
his given name was Neng.
His original family register was in Fanyang, now part of Shizhou, within the region of Ji.
His father, Xing Gao, was demoted to Xinzhou during the Wude era of the Great Tang;
having been born there, he subsequently became a native of Xinxiang.
When he was only three years old, his father passed away, and his mother raised him while observing lifelong chastity.
When he grew up, the family became even more impoverished;
his grandfather would then gather firewood and sell it to provide for his mother.
One day, while passing through the marketplace, he heard a guest reciting the scripture: "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere.

In the second year of the Kaiyuan era, the Emperor issued an inquiry to Shen Guang, Dharma Master and Chief Registrar of the Left Street, asking:
"What benevolent virtues does the Buddha possess toward sentient beings?"
If you can abandon your sovereign, parents, wife, and children to serve me as your teacher,

Shenguang said:

Guang replied:
Heaven can cover but cannot support;
earth can support but cannot cover.
The sun illuminates the day but does not illuminate the night.
The moon illuminates the night but not the day;
the father can only give birth but cannot nourish,
while the mother can nourish but cannot give birth.
When the ruler possesses the Way, the ministers are loyal;

The Buddha’s grace toward sentient beings is not like this:

as a support, it sustains all those in the six realms of existence.

Thus, they universally save those in both prosperity and ruin,
and lead away both the noble and the humble.
We only pray that Your Majesty will lend your heart to this and regard it with reverence.

The *Huntian Huangdao Yi* (浑天黄道仪): This instrument models the form of the celestial sphere.
It displays the degrees of the equatorial coordinates for the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*).
Water is poured to drive the wheel, causing it to rotate automatically.
In one day and night, the movement of the heavens completes a cycle.
It is externally encircled by two wheels joined with the sun and moon, which cause them to move;
every day, the heavens travel one full circuit to the west.
The sun moves one degree per day;
the moon moves thirteen degrees per day.
A wooden box is used as the horizon plane.
Since half of the instrument's structure lies beneath the ground,
the phases of the moon— darkness, brightness, the new moon, and the full moon—
are determined with precision. Two wooden figures are erected level with the ground.
One of them has a drum placed before it,
which strikes itself when the first watch-hour (one *ke*) arrives;
