Wang Duo, the Supreme Commander of the Expeditionary Camps for all circuits, acted by imperial decree to appoint Wen as the Military Governor of Tongzhou and Huazhou.
Before long, he was granted the name Quan Zhong.

Wang Chongrong, the Acting Governor of Hedong; Yang Fuguang, the Commander of the Field Army; Wang Hui, the Commissioner for the Eastern Region; and Wang Duo, the Supreme Commander of the Field Armies of the Various Provinces, deliberated on the campaign to suppress the rebels.
Fuguang said, "Li Ke, the Vice President of the Secretariat of Yanmen, is valiant and possesses a powerful army; if he were summoned here, the rebels could be suppressed without difficulty.
At that time, Wang Duo was in Hedong.
He then issued an imperial edict in ink to summon Li Kuyong.
In the eleventh month, Kuyong led the Shatuo tribesmen—some seven thousand one hundred people who had first appeared before Emperor Yizong in the ninth year of Gantong—and marched toward Hedong.
In the third month of the third year of Zhonghe,
Kelyong advanced his army to Weiqiao and engaged the forces of Qiu Shanao at the south of the Wei River.
The rebel troops suffered a great defeat and fled in disorder.
In the fourth month, Kēyù entered the capital through the Guāngtài Gate.
Náo fought valiantly but was defeated; he set fire to the palace buildings and fled.
At that time, Kēyù was twenty-eight years old.
Having destroyed the nest [of Huang Chao] and restored Chang’an, his merit was foremost.
By imperial decree, Kěkòng was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Hedong.
In the second month of spring in the fourth year of Zhōnghé, Huang Chao fled and laid siege to Chénzhōu.
Li Kuei-yung led the armies of Pien and Hsiu to rescue him.
In the fifth month, Huai-ao led his troops northeast toward Pien-chou.
Li Kuei-yung caught up with Huai-ao at Chung-mou and launched a spirited attack, crushing his forces.
Chao Shangrang led his followers to surrender to Kegyong.
Kegyong pursued them as far as Yuanqu, the capital of Chao’s domain; when their provisions were exhausted, they returned to Bianzhou and encamped outside the city.
Zhu Quanzhong firmly requested that he enter the city and was accommodated at Shangyuan Station.
There, Zhu Quanzhong set out wine; while under the influence, Li Kelyong’s speech became somewhat insulting.
Zhu Quanzhong, feeling aggrieved, dispatched troops to surround the station and attack it.
Kegong managed to escape by descending a rope from the city walls.
In the sixth month, Li Shiyue and other generals of Wuning pursued Huang Chao to Xiaqiu and defeated him;
Chao’s forces were nearly exterminated. He fled to Langhu Valley, where his nephew Lin Yan beheaded Chao and his brothers, as well as their wives and children, and surrendered their heads.
The founding of Chao began in the second year of the Qiánfú era and ended in the seventh month of the fourth year of the Zhōnghé era, as recorded in the *Jù Táng Shū*.
Mùzhōu is the present-day Jiàn Dé Lù in the Zhèjī West Circuit. This refers to the Venerable Master Chén.
His name was Daoming.
He was a descendant of the Chen clan of Jiangnan.
Having left home to become a monk in his youth, he resided at Kaiyuan Temple in his native province.
He maintained the precepts with rigorous discipline and was thoroughly versed in the Tripitaka;
having traveled to Huangbo and attained realization of its essential meaning,
he was invited to serve as the head seat (śrāmaṇera).
The assembly requested that he reside at Guanyin Yuan,
where he remained for several decades with a constant following of over a hundred people.
Those from all quarters who sought his guidance unanimously hailed him as a venerable elder.
Later, he returned to live in the Kaiyuan Hall, where he wove *púxié* (rush shoes) to support his mother;
thus he acquired the nickname "The Rush-Shoe Man. When a celestial messenger arrived to inquire after him, the Master was there.
"Three gates are all open; through which one do you enter?
The Master called for the Minister, who responded with a "Yes.
The Master said:
He entered through the Gate of Faith.
As the Master was reading a sutra,
Minister Chen Cao asked him, "What sutra are you reading, O Monk?"
The Master said, "The Diamond Sutra.
The Shangshu asked, "Among the translations of the Six Dynasties, which one is this?
The Master held up the sutra and said:
"All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows.
In the fourth year of the Qiandfu era, he summoned his disciples and said:
"At this place, with my breath as the condition, I shall pass away.
He then sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
The people of the commandery burned his body with fragrant wood.
Relics fell like rain;
his sacred remains were collected and a statue was fashioned at the temple.
He lived to the age of ninety-eight.
Lajue (Laxi) was the sixty-sixth [patriarch].
He succeeded Chan Master Huangbo Yun;
Yun succeeded Chan Master Baizhang Hai, according to the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
Jihai, the sixth year of the Qiánfú era; Gēngzǐ, the first year of the Guǎngmíng era; Xīnchū, the first year of the Zhōnghé era.
The Chan Master Yuánnán of Lòpǔ Mountain in Lǐzhōu was named Yuán'ān.
A man from Fengxiang who roamed like a qilin,
he left home at the age of seven;
having received full ordination, he upheld the Vinaya and mastered both the sutras and the śāstras.
In this year, he attended Chan Master Linji Xuan as his attendant.
Later, he went to Jia Shan to establish a hermitage.
On the eighth month of the first year of the Guanghua era of Emperor Zhaozong, he instructed his disciples, saying:
The dharma of renunciation leaves no superfluous possessions behind;
how much less so other things!
You must keep this firmly in mind.
Time passes swiftly and the Great Way is profound and mysterious;
if one merely follows along with the flow, by what means could one realize it?
On the first day of the twelfth month, he sat peacefully and entered nirvana.
The lineage of Chan Master Hui of Jia Shan transmits the *Lamp Records*.
Jia Shan: Chan Master of Jia Shan in Li Province, named Shanhui.
He was the son of the Liao family in Guangzhou.
He left home to become a monk at a young age and received the full precepts according to his seniority.
He studied the sutras and śāstras,
thoroughly training in the three studies (śikṣā).
He resided at Helin Monastery in the region of Yangzhou, within the Jiangning Prefecture of Zhexi, during his time in Runzhou.
Following Dao-wu’s guidance,
he met Chan Master Cheng of Chuanshi at Huating and attained realization regarding the essential point of the mind.
Respectfully receiving his final testament, he withdrew from the world and forgot all worldly concerns.
During the Xiantong era of Emperor Yizong,
he resided in Fengzhou.
Disciples gathered like clouds;
following one another, they chose to settle at Jia Shan,
whereupon they eventually established a monastery.
On the seventh day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Zhonghe era, he entered nirvana.
He was buried at his native mountain and posthumously bestowed the title of Great Master Chuánmíng.
The lineage of Chan Master Cheng of Chuanshi was transmitted in the Lamp Records.
Zhonghe Year 2 (Ren-yin),
according to the Tang History, states that Zhongfeng occupied Jiangxi.
In the third year of Zhonghe, the Gui-mao year (843),
Li Kuyong recaptured the capital.
Tuoba Sigong led his troops to respond to the national crisis.

During the rebellion of Huang Chao, the imperial court appointed Si-gong as the Acting Governor of Xia-sui, granting him the surname Li; this is recorded in the first year of Baoyuan (4679 BCE) of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty.
In the Jia-chen year, the fourth year of Zhonghe (884 CE), Huang Chao was finally extinguished.
In the seventh month of autumn, Li Kuyong arrived at Jinyang and dispatched an envoy to present a memorial.
He spoke with utmost urgency, stating that Zhu Quanzhong’s envy of merit and resentment of talent would ultimately become a calamity for the state.
In total, he submitted eight memorials requesting his execution and suppression.
The Emperor, considering the current urgency of affairs,
temporarily set aside the matter of protocol and issued an edict to commend and encourage Li Kuyong, thereby resolving the situation. At that time,

due to famine and pestilence in Zhejiang, Chan Master Youzhang of the Puxian Chan Monastery in Mingzhou had collected and buried several thousand corpses of those who had died of starvation across the three prefectures of Tai, Wenzhou, and Mingzhou.
The people of the time called the Master "Bodhisattva Increasing Compassion" (*Zengbei Pusa*). According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*),
in the second month of the first year of the Guangqi era (the Yisi year),
the Emperor returned to the capital and changed the reign title.
The eunuch Tian Letong increasingly exercised his authority with unrestrained tyranny.
Wang Chongrong, the Regional Inspector of Hedong, repeatedly submitted memorials enumerating Letong’s crimes.
Wang Chongrong then petitioned Li Kuyong to lead his troops to his aid.
In the twelfth month, Li Kuyong advanced to press upon the capital.
That night, Tian Lingsi escorted the Emperor out through Kaiyuan Gate to take refuge in Fengxiang.
In the first month of the spring of the second year of Guangqi, Tian Lingsi requested that the Emperor proceed to Xingyuan.
The Emperor did not comply.
That night, Li Deyun led troops into the palace and abducted the Emperor to Xianbaoji;
the Chancellor and court officials were all unaware of it.
When he set out for Baoji to detain Yang Cheng, it was precisely at the time when the defenses of San Guan, the gateway to the Xingyuan route, were being maintained.
As soon as the imperial carriage had entered San Guan, Zhu Mei, the Military Governor of Binning, had already surrounded Baoji.
Sìxiāng Wáng Yūn was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Sùzōng.
Being ill, he could not accompany the Emperor; he remained behind at a post station along the route and was captured by Méi, who took him back to Fèngxiáng together with his captors.
In the third month, the imperial carriage arrived at Xingyuan.
Zhu Mei coerced the officials into offering the Prince of Xiang, Yingun, to temporarily oversee the affairs of the military and state.
The officials of Chang’an, including Fei Qu, Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, and others, exhorted the Prince of Xiang Yingun to ascend the throne as Emperor.
The era name was changed to Jiànzhēn.
From afar, the Emperor was honored as the Taishàng Yuánhóng Huángdì.
Yang Fugōng, the Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guard, circulated a manifesto throughout Guānzhōng, stating:
"Whoever captures the head of Zhu Mei shall be rewarded with the rank of Pacification and Difficulty (Jingnan) Regional Commander.
Zhu Mei’s general, Wang Xingyu, captured and beheaded him.
Prince Xiang fled to Hedong.
King Chongrong feigned a welcoming reception and killed Xiyun.
By imperial decree, Xingyu was appointed as the Military Governor of Jingnan Army (*Tangshu*, Basic Annals).
Master Lingyun.
His name was Zhiqin.
A native of Changxi in Fuzhou, he succeeded Changqing An;
An had succeeded Baizhang Hai.
He applied himself diligently at Mount Gui.
There, upon seeing peach blossoms, he attained enlightenment.
Later, he returned to Fuzhou and resided at Lingyun Temple, as recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu*.
In this same year, Qian Liu, the King of Wuyue, was appointed Regional Inspector of Hangzhou for his meritorious service in suppressing Dong Chang.
Yantou [Huaihai], the Chan Master of Yantou in Ezhou,
whose name was Quanhuo.
He was a member of the Ke clan from Quanzhou.
In his youth, he received the tonsure under Master Yi of Qingyuan and received the full precepts at Baoshou Temple in Chang’an.
He studied various sections of the sutras and śāstras,
and wandered leisurely within the gardens of dhyāna.
Later, he attended upon Deshan, where he attained realization of the ultimate meaning, and subsequently resided at Yantou.
Encountering Emperor Wuzong’s suppression of the teachings, he lived in seclusion as a ferryman by the lakeside.
Later, he established a hermitage on Sleeping Dragon Mountain (Wolong Shan) in Dongting,
where disciples gathered like the spokes of a wheel.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Guangqi era, he entered nirvana.
His disciples cremated his remains and obtained forty-nine śarīras,
for which they erected a stupa as an offering.
The imperial posthumous title was bestowed as Chan Master Qingyan; he succeeded Deshan Jian.
Jian succeeded Longtan Xin, as recorded in the *Fozu Tongji* (Transmission of the Lamp).
[Shishuang]: The Chan Master of Mount Shishuang in Tanzhou.
His name was Qingzhu.
He was of the Chen clan of Xinfu in Jizhou, Jiangxi.
He received the tonsure under Chan Master Shaoluan of Xishan at Hongjing.
He went to Luoyang to study the Vinaya teachings.
Upon arriving at Mount Gui, he served as the rice steward.
One day, as Guishan was picking up a grain of rice, he said to the Master:
"Do not underestimate this single grain;
hundreds of thousands of grains are born from this one grain.
The Master said:
"From this single grain, hundreds of thousands are produced.
I do not know from where this single grain itself arises.
Baizhang laughed heartily and returned to his quarters.
In the evening, he ascended the hall and said, "There are worms in the rice;
everyone, look well!
Later, he visited Chan Master Daowu Zhi.
He possessed the essential secrets of the mind.
Later, he lived in seclusion, blending with the common people at the Táo Family Ward in Liúyáng, Chāngshā;
no one recognized him.
On the occasion of the lifting of the summer retreat as requested by the Sangha, Dongshan ascended the hall and said:
"At the end of summer, when autumn begins, you brothers will go east or west;
you must go to a place ten thousand miles away where there is not a single blade of grass."
The Master said,
"Stepping out the door is already grass.
Upon hearing this, Dongshan remarked:
These were the words of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to fifteen hundred people.
Because of this reputation, the Master’s fame spread far and wide;
when the Emperor heard of the Master’s renown for the Way, he bestowed upon him purple robes.
He declined the offer.
In the third year of the Guangqi era, he entered nirvana and was buried in the northwestern corner of the monastery.
An imperial posthumous title of "Great Master Puhui" was conferred upon him.
He succeeded Dao’u’s lineage; Zhizhi succeeded Yaoshan Yan;
Yan succeeded Shitou Xiqian.
In the second month of the first year of the Wende era (5th year of the Wende era,
the Wushen year), Emperor [Xuanzong] returned to the capital from Fengxiang.
He transmitted the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) to Qingyuan Si.
In the third month, he fell ill.
On the day of Renyin, his condition became critical.
His younger brother, Prince Ji Baochang, was both virtuous and capable.
The ministers looked toward him with high expectations.

On the day of Gui-mao, Yang Fugong, the Military Commissioner for the Inspection of Troops of the Ten Armies, requested that his younger brother, Prince Jie, be established as the Imperial Heir Apparent (Huang Taidi).
That same day, the Emperor passed away.
The Last Testament:
Crown Prince Jie was renamed Min and ascended the imperial throne. Wang Jian seized control of Xichuan.
Zhaozong was the seventh son of Yizong.
He was originally enfeoffed as Prince Shou and named Jie.
His name was changed to Min.
In the first year of Longji, his name was changed again to Yue.
He reigned for sixteen years.

The total duration was thirty-eight years: one year of Longji (Dragon Era), two years of Dashun (Great Harmony), two years of Jingfu (Blessings of Fortune), four years of Qianning (Tranquility of Heaven), three years of Guanghua (Radiance of Transformation), and four years of Tianfu (Restoration of Heaven).
On the eleventh month of the first year of Longji, the Jihou year.
The Emperor changed his name to Yue.

When the Emperor was about to perform the sacrifice at the Round Altar (Yuanqiu), the Commandant of the Household and the Chief of the Imperial Secretariat both wore their robes with the lapels turned outward; this was according to established precedent for those attending from the imperial retinue.
During the reign of Emperor Xizong, [the officials] had already been equipped with sashes and tablets;
by this time, he further ordered the relevant authorities to manufacture ceremonial robes.
Kong Wei and the censors all considered this improper.
The Emperor came forth to preside over the rite and exhorted them, saying:
"What you have discussed is a matter of great importance; there are times when one must follow expedient measures.
Do not allow a minor flaw to ultimately obstruct the grand ritual."
Thereupon, eunuchs began to wear swords and jade pendants while attending sacrifices.
Gengxu, the first year of Dàshùn; Xīnhài, the second year of Dàshùn.
Yang Xingmi occupied Yangzhou.
The Chan Master of Qianqing Mountain in Hangzhou was named Chunan;
he was the son of the Zhang family of Fuzhou.
Having attained the essential meaning under Huangbo,
he first arrived at Ba’en Temple in Gusu,
where he practiced meditative concentration with great diligence for over twenty years.
He did not step beyond the threshold of his door;
he subsequently resided at Ciyun on Mount Zhihe in Qiantang.
Although he responded to conditions as they arose, he never grew weary.
He remained constantly in meditative concentration for periods of either over a month or ten days.
This was during the Guangqi era of Emperor Xizong.
The Regional Inspector Qian Liu requested that the Master descend from the mountain to receive offerings.
Upon hearing of his spiritual transformation, Emperor Xizong bestowed upon him purple robes.
In the fifth month of the first year of the Wende era of Emperor Xizong’s reign, he entered nirvana.
He lived to the age of seventy-six.
His stupa was erected in the western corner of the monastery.
The Master composed the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Destroying Heresies), which has circulated in the world.
He succeeded Chan Master Yun of Huangbo.
It was during the second year of the Dàshùn era that Sun Ru, a rebel from Xuānzhōu, plundered Qiántáng; he opened the stupa and beheld the Master.
With his hair and nails grown long all over his body, he bowed in thanks for the repair of the stupa and departed. (From the *Chuandeng lu*).
The eighth month of the first year of the Gyeongbok era, the Renzi year.
Yang Xingmi was appointed as the Regional Inspector of Huainan.
As the Xuanning calendar gradually became inaccurate,
Bian Gang, the Junior Grand Master for the Heir Apparent, completed a new calendar.
In the twelfth month, the Emperor issued an edict naming it the Jingfu Jingxuan Calendar.
In the second year, on the day Guichou, Liu Bian, the Regional Inspector of Yuzhou, was appointed as the Regional Inspector of Luzhou.
Since Liu Gongchuo, the family has for generations been held in high esteem by scholars and officials for their filial piety, fraternal duty,
and observance of ritual propriety; Liu Bi served as the Grand Minister of the Censorate.
The Emperor wished to appoint him as a high official,
but because the eunuchs detested him, he was exiled abroad for a long time.
Li Bi once admonished his descendants, saying:
In general, although one’s noble lineage and high status are formidable, they must not be relied upon.
In establishing one’s character and conducting oneself,
even a single lapse will result in a retribution heavier than that of others.
Upon death, one will have no means of appearing before one's ancestors in the underworld;
this is what makes it so fearsome.
When a gate is too high, a haughty mind easily arises.
When a clan flourishes, it becomes an object of envy for others;
when one’s virtuous conduct and genuine talent are real, people do not yet believe in them;
and even the slightest flaw is pointed out by the multitude.
This is why one cannot rely upon such things.
Therefore, those of noble birth who enjoy fine food and drink should apply themselves with even greater diligence in study and exert themselves with even greater vigor in their conduct;
they may only then hope to equal others. A jade gem has flaws, and a silken thread has knots.
The royal house occupied Fuzhou and styled themselves "Leftover Heir" (Liuhou).
Wang Rong commanded Zhending and styled himself the Prince of Zhao.
At that time, Liu Rencong served as the Military Governor of Youzhou Lulong and styled himself the Prince of Yan.
In the year Jiayin, the first year of the Qianning era,
the śramaṇa Guanhui, a native of Wuzhou, entered Shu.
He presented a poem to the Prince, saying:
With a single robe and a single bowl, he grows old;
across ten thousand waters and ten thousand mountains, he has come specifically for this.
The King of Shu treated him with extraordinary courtesy and conferred upon him an official rank.
The title "Chan Yue Da Shi" (Master Chan Moon) was also bestowed upon him by imperial decree.
He entered nirvana in the third year of the Tongguang era of Emperor Zhuangzong of the Later Tang.
The eminent monk Qi Ji was a native of Shu.
In his youth, he left the secular world to rely upon Chan Master Daoyou of Mount Mui.
At that time, Chan Master Huiji of Mount Yang was residing at the Guanyin Monastery in Yuzhang;
[Daowu] already oversaw all its administrative affairs.
There is a preface to the *zhōu* (congee) which says:
"Congee is called a 'good medicine,' as praised by the Buddha."
Its principles crown the three types of giving,
and its merit marks the ten benefits;
we pray further for the wisdom of the eminent and sagely.
May each fulfill their aspirations;
having prepared these offerings at the break of dawn,
may they forever serve as a support for pure karma.
Later, he resided at Jingu on Mount Xishan and passed away there;
his stupa remains.
Longpan was his study hall, according to the *Yunwai jitan*.
In the year Yimao, the second year of Qianning,
the following year Ma Yin took control of Hunan,
while Qian Liu concurrently governed both East and West Zhejiang.
Li Maozhen attacked the capital.
The Emperor fled to Huazhou.
Maozhen entered Chang’an.
The palace buildings and the market stalls were all consumed by fire.
On the ninth day of the first month of the third year, the Chan Master Xuanyun of Jiufeng exhorted his disciples, saying:
"Do not let your time pass in vain."
Do not let the offerings of the faithful go to waste.
Having already left the household life, you should walk only upon the Path; thus you are called a Great Man.
You say that you have already entered a state of tranquil meditative absorption.
He entered parinirvāṇa on the twentieth day of the third month.
On the day of Ding-si, the fourth year of Qianning (897), the Min Governor Wang Chang passed away, and his younger brother Shenzhi succeeded him in occupying that territory.
[There was also] Chan Master [Xuan]zhao of Zhaozhou.
His name was Congshen.
He was a native of Haoxiang in Caozhou and surnamed Hao.
As a youth, he received the tonsure under a master at Hutong Monastery in his native province.
Before receiving full ordination, he traveled to Chiyang to visit Chan Master Nanquan Yuan,
who recognized his potential.
One day he asked Quan,
"What is the Way? Quan replied, "The ordinary mind is the Way."
The Master asked,
"Can one still direct oneself toward it? Quan replied,
"To intend to direct oneself toward it is already to deviate."
The Master said,
"If you do not intend to contend, how can you know this is the Way?
Quan said, "The Way belongs neither to knowing nor to not-knowing."
To know this is false awakening;
not to know it is the indeterminate.
If one truly penetrates the Way that is free from doubt, [there is no such distinction].
"It is like the great void—vast, empty, and open.
How could one forcibly impose right and wrong?
At these words, the Master realized the principle.
He then went to Mount Song to receive the precepts at the Lapis Lazuli Altar;
subsequently, he returned to Nanquan.
After some time, the assembly invited him to reside at the Guanyin Monastery under the jurisdiction of Zhoudou in the Zhending Circuit.
First, it is said that the spiritual transformation of Dongyuan was extremely flourishing;
he composed the *Song of the Twelve Hours*,
and his verses, gāthās, and recorded sayings circulated throughout the world.
The newly arrived master asked,
"Have you ever been here before?
The monk replied, "I have never been here."
The Master said,
"Go and drink tea.
He then asked another monk:
"Have you ever been here before?
The monk said, "I have.
The Master said:
"Go and drink tea.
The head monk asked,
"Why do you say 'go and drink tea' even to one who has already been here?"
"He has never been here; go and drink tea.
The Master called for the head of the monastery.
"Yes, sir? the head responded.
The Master said,
"Go and drink tea.
At that time, Wang Rong, the regional commander of Zhending, was titled King Zhao.
Liu Ren-gong, the Regional Commander (Jiedushi) of Lu, styled himself King of Yan.
The two kings vied with one another in mutual respect and honor.
On the second day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of Qianning, he passed away while lying on his right side.
He lived to the age of one hundred and twenty.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Master Zhenji.
He succeeded Nanquan Yuan as his dharma heir.
He vowed to succeed Mazu in transmitting the lamp of the Dharma.
In the first year of the Guanghua era (888), during the Wuma year, Li Maozhen was granted amnesty.
In the eighth month, the imperial carriage returned from Huazhou to the capital.
In the second year of the Gwahwa era (847),
on the day of Jih-mi, the Chan Master Hwaeak Hyeonwi compiled the records of Chan encounters from the Zhenyuan era of Emperor Dezong onwards,
producing the *Sungju-jip* (Collection of the Holy Lineage).
Chan Master Wuzhuo of Hangzhou,
whose name was Wenxi,
was of the Zhu family from Jiaxing.
At the age of seven, he left home and received the tonsure at Changle Temple (Guoqing) in his native district.
There he studied the Vinaya and listened to the teachings.
During the reign of Emperor Wuzong, when the Buddhist teachings were suppressed and he was forced to return to lay dress, he remained in seclusion to conceal his talents.
At the beginning of Emperor Xuanzong’s reign, he visited Qi峰 Temple in Yanguan for a second time.
He then traveled to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī,
where he encountered an old man leading an ox along the road.
He invited the Master into the temple.
The old man let loose a cow and led the Master up to the hall.
The old man sat upon his couch, pointed to an embroidered cushion, and commanded him to sit.
The old man asked,
"Where have you come from recently?
The Master replied, "From the South."
The Old Man asked,
"How is the Buddha-dharma maintained in the South?
The Master replied:
"In the age of the Dharma's decay, bhikṣus rarely observe the precepts.
The old man asked,
"How large is the assembly?"
The Master said, "There were perhaps three hundred or five hundred masters.
He then asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma here?
The abbot replied:
Dragons and snakes are intermingled;
ordinary people and sages dwell together.
The Master said:
"How many people are there?
The old man replied, "Three times three before, and three times three after.
The old man then called for the boy Juntidaichá.
He further presented some butter and curd.
The old man picked up a crystal cup and asked,
"Is there such a thing as this in the South?"
The Master said, "There is none.
The old man asked,
"What do you usually use to drink your tea?"

The Master had no reply as they took their leave. The old man ordered his son to escort him back. On the way, the Master asked the boy, "What is three before and three after? The boy replied, "That is nine. The Master said, "How much is that? The boy replied, "Nine. The Master said, "How much is that? The boy replied, "Nine. The Master said, "How much is that? How could I seek further advancement without end?
The Ruler of Shu praised his ambition. The King of Zhao, Yan, and Jin:

the sixth year of Tianyou. The King of Qi: the sixth year of Tianyou. Wu, Yue, Chu, Jingnan, and Huainan: the sixth year of Tianyou. Min and Shu, Wang Jian: the second year of Wucheng. Nanping: gengwu, the fourth year of Kaiping.

*Continuation of the Baolin Zhuan* (Continued Record of the Jewel Forest), compiled by the South Peak (Nanyue) head monk Weijing. This work records the karmic encounters of the patriarchs from the Guanghua era of the Tang dynasty’s Zhaozong onwards, forming four volumes as a continuation of the *Baolin Zhuan*.
Zhao Yan, King of Jin: Tianyou Year 7. Qi Wang: Tianyou Year 7. Wu, Yue, Chu, Jingnan, and Huainan: Tianyou Year 7. Min and Shu: Wucheng Year 3. Nanping: Xinsi, the first year of Qianhua. Cian.
Zhao Wang Rong (Yan): Year 1 of Yingtian. Jin Wang: Year 8 of Tianguo. Qi Wang: Year 8 of Tianguo. Wuyue, Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu: Year 8 of Tianguo. Min, Shu, and Nanping: Liu Yan, March.
When Liu Yin, the Prince of Xiangping and Military Governor of Jinghai, passed away,
his younger brother Yan succeeded him;
he later changed his name to Gong.
Furthermore, in the eighth month of the year Gengyan, Liu Shouguang— the son of Liu Rencong, the Prince of Yan— ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the state name to Da Yan (Great Yan) and altered the era name to the first year of Yingtian.
In the second year of the Ren-shen cycle (1092), in the second month,
Chan Master Ru-ne of Mount Daochang in Huzhou established a hermitage on the mountain and traveled about riding a tiger.
Ru-ne was a native of Huzhou.
The Master succeeded to Chan Master Wuxue of Cuiwei;
Wuxue succeeded to Danxia Ran;
and Ran succeeded to Chan Master Xituan of Shitou.

In the second year of Yingtian of Zhao Yan; in the ninth year of Tianguo of Jin; in the ninth year of Tianguo of the Kings of Qi, Wuyue, Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu; and in the second year of Yongping of Min and Shu; in the second month of Nanning, the Emperor’s illness grew exceedingly severe.
Executions were carried out without constancy.
Furthermore, when discussions arose regarding military expeditions,
many of the attending officials were filled with dread and apprehension.
The Emperor’s eldest son, Prince Chen Youyu, died young.
The next was the adopted son, Prince Bo Youwen, whom the Emperor especially doted upon.
Prince Ying Yougui felt resentment in his heart.
The Emperor appointed Liu Yougui as the Regional Inspector of Lai Prefecture.
Yougui traveled incognito and entered the Left Dragon Tiger Army,
where he met the Commander-in-Chief Han Qing and informed him of his intentions.
Jing led five hundred tusker soldiers to follow Yougui;
mingling with the Controlling Crane guards, they entered to lie in ambush within the palace.
In the middle of the night, they broke through the gates and reached the inner chamber.
Wuyi’s servant Feng Ting’uo stabbed the Emperor;
he kept the death secret and did not announce the funeral,
issuing a forged edict that stated:
"My person is in peril; you should have Yu-gui temporarily preside over the affairs of the military and state.
Upon the announcement of my demise, he shall ascend the imperial throne.
In the first month of the third year of the Qiánhua era, the reign title was changed to Fènglì.
At that time, Emperor Jun’s friend Zheng was in Da Liang campaigning against Yougui.
Realizing he could not escape,
Yougui ordered Feng Ting’uo to first kill his wife, Lady Zhang, and then himself.
Ting’e also committed suicide by stabbing himself.
Emperor Jun ascended the throne at Daliang and styled the year the third year of the Qiánhua era.
Junwang Junwang was the third son of Taizu.
His original name was Youzhen,
and he was enfeoffed as Prince of Jun.
He governed Daliang,
which is Bianzhou.
In the first month of the third year of the Qiánhua era, he executed the great traitor Liu Yougui.
He then ascended the imperial throne and established his capital at Daliang.
He posthumously deposed Liu Yougui, reducing him to the status of a commoner.
In the third month, the Emperor changed his name to Huáng;
after a long time, he was further named Tiàn.
He reigned for eleven years.
His reign lasted thirty-six years.
He was posthumously titled Emperor Mo. [The eras were] Qianhua II, Zhenming VI, Longde III, and Guiyou—Qianhua Year 3.

Zhao Yan (Zhaoyan): Third year of Yingtian. Jin: Tenth year of Tianyou. Qi Wang: Tenth year of Tianyou. Wuyue Wang, Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu: Tenth year of Tianyou. Min Wang: Third year of Yongping. Nanyang Jinguangming Daochang: Chan Master Youzhang of Ruiying Monastery, Hangzhou.
He requested that the Kings of Wu and Yue establish a *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) ritual site annually at Mount Tiantai,
with a great assembly of both monastics and laypeople from all the prefectures,
which would disperse after more than a month.
The Great Assembly of Radiant Light began with the Master.
In the first month of the fourth year of the Qiánhua era (the Jiǎxū year),
after the Ruler of Jìn had conquered Yān.
Having thoroughly trained his troops and turned against Liu Ren-gong and Shi Shou-guang,
he entered Jin-yang with a song of triumph.
He presented [the captive] at the Grand Ancestral Temple and executed Shi Shou-guang.
Xie Rengong was captured and brought to Dazhou;
he was executed after performing a sacrifice at the tomb of the former king.

Zhao, Yan, and Jin destroyed [the state]. In the eleventh year of Tianyou of Jin, the Kings of Qi, Wuyue, Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu [all died] in the eleventh year of Tianyou. In the fourth year of Yongping, the Chan Master of Mount Toudi in Shuzhou of Nanping [passed away].
His name was Datong.
A native of the Liu family from Huaining in his home province,
he entered the monastic order at an early age under Chan Master Man of Baotang Temple in Luoyang.
Initially, he practiced the contemplation of *ānāpāna* (breath).
Next, he studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which illuminated the ocean of the nature (*dharmatā*).
He then visited Chan Master Xue of Cuiwei and attained sudden enlightenment into the fundamental principle.
Having thus traveled extensively with this intention,
he later retired from his native village to Mount Yintou,
where he dwelt in a thatched hut.
On the sixth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Qianhua era, he entered nirvana.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Master Ciji.
The Master succeeded Chan Master Cuibei as his dharma heir.
Binghai (10 March 915): First Year of Zhengming. Zhao, Prince of Jin:

Twelfth Year of Tianyou. Qi, Prince of Qi: Twelfth Year of Tianyou. Wuyue, King of Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu: Twelfth Year of Tianyou. Min and Shu: Fifth Year of Yongping. Nanping: Bingzi (24 February 916). Qidan, Taizu Abaoji: First Year of Shenche.

Prince of Jin, Zhao: the thirteenth year of Tianyou. Prince of Qi: the thirteenth year of Tianyou. King of Wuyue, Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu: the thirteenth year of Tianyou. King of Min: the first year of Tongzheng. Kingdom of Shu: the first year of Tongzheng. Nanping: the Khitan. The Khitan are a descendant tribe of the Xianbei who existed during the Shang dynasty.
This refers to Gaozong’s campaign against Guifang.
From the second year of the Zhengming era of Emperor Zhong of the Later Liang, Taizu Abaoji proclaimed himself emperor, established his state, and instituted an era name.
The succession comprised nine sovereigns, whose reigns lasted for a total of two hundred and fifteen years;
specifically, they occupied the throne for two hundred and nine years.
According to the *Liaozhi*, the Emperor Taizu’s name was Yifan.
His name was Abaoji;
he was the younger son of Wala.
His father, Wala, served as the Yili-jun (Vice-Commissioner).
They were like the *cishi* (provincial inspectors) of the Central Kingdom.
Previously, the Khitan tribes had been divided into eight;
each had its own great leader (*daren*), who, through mutual consultation and agreement, was elected as their king.
They raised banners and drums to issue commands to the various tribes;
every three years, they would succeed one another in turn.
When Abaoji became king, he was especially formidable.
Yong relied upon his own strength and refused to accept a replacement.
The five clans of the Xí and the seven clans of the Shìwéi all submitted to him as subjects.
He attacked the Yellow-Headed Shìwéi and returned with them; however, the seven tribes ambushed him on the border and demanded that he fulfill their agreement.
Abaoji said, "I have been king for nine years and have gained many Han people;
I request that you, Master, settle your clan in the ancient Han city."
They were maintained by Han people as a separate community.
The "Ancient Han City" permitted by the seven communities was the county of Huayan of the Tuoba Wei;
its soil was suitable for the five grains.
It possessed the advantage of salt ponds.
Subsequently, Abaoji struck down and annihilated the seven tribes, merging them into a single state.
He further launched a northern campaign against the Xiwéi and the Nǔzhēn.
He took the former territory of the Turks in the west,
attacked the Xī (Xianbei), and annihilated them;
he then reinstated a Xī king and ordered the Qīdān to oversee his troops.
The various tribes of the northeast all feared and submitted to him.
Initially, during the final years of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty Yizong, there was one named Xi'er who became king;
thus his territory began to expand.
Thereafter, Qindé became king.
Taking advantage of the many troubles in the Central Plains, his people invaded the borders.
During the final years of Emperor Liu Shouguang of Yan, the state was in decline and distress.
He dispatched his military aide Han Yanhui to seek assistance from the Khitan.
The Khitan ruler was angered that he would not prostrate himself;
after detaining him for a long time, he eventually treated him with courtesy and employed him.
Yan Hui first instructed the Khitans to establish military headquarters and government offices,
build city walls and moats,
and lay out markets and residential wards.
Because they settled Han people there,
ensuring each had a spouse to cultivate the wasteland,
the Khitans thereby became powerful and mighty.
In the second year of the Zhenming era,
Abaoji first styled himself Emperor and changed the state name to Daqidan (Great Qidan).
The year was named Shenche (Divine Establishment).
The people of the country called him the Heavenly Emperor King.
His clan name was Yelü.
He appointed his wife, Shulü, as Empress.
He established the various offices of state and ruled the country for eleven years.
He passed away at Fuyu City,
posthumously titled Taizu (Grand Ancestor).
[This was] Pudu Heshang (Bagua Monk).
His name was Qici.
He manifested his traces in Fenghua County, Mingzhou.
He constantly carried a cloth bag on a staff and brought along a tattered mat.
All implements for his personal use were stored within a bag;
when entering the market and seeing goods, he would beg for them—
whether it be fermented sauces, fish, or pickled vegetables.
As soon as he had taken it into his mouth, he placed a small portion into his bag;
at that time, he was known as Changtingzi.
On the third day of the third month in the second year of the Zhenming era, while sitting on the veranda of Yuelinsi Temple, he spoke this verse:
Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests thousands,
tens of thousands, and billions of emanations,
appearing from time to time to those of this age.
At that time, the people did not recognize him.
After he had finished his verses, he passed away peacefully.
Later, he was seen again in another province, walking along while carrying a sack on his back.
They vied with one another to paint his image and enshrine it for worship.
In the year Dingchou, the third year of Zhengming (917), the second year of the Shenche era of the Khitan,
Liu Yan of Nanping ascended the imperial throne at Fanyu.
The state name was changed to Đại Việt (Great Vietnam).
The era name was altered to Quán Hường.
In the eleventh month of the winter of the following year, he performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven.
The national name was changed to Han (Sima Tongjian). Year 14 of Tianyou, King of Qi;

Year 14 of Tianyou, Kings of Wuyue, Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu; Year 1 of Tianhan, Emperor of Min and Shu; Year 1 of Qianheng, the year of Wuyin (578), the Zhengming era; and the third year of Shenche of Abdaji, the Khitan.

Prince of Jin of Zhao: the fifteenth year of Tianyou. Prince of Qi: the fifteenth year of Tianyou. Prince of Zhao of Wu; the Kingdoms of Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu: the fifteenth year of Tianyou. Emperor of Min and Shu: the first year of Guangtai. Emperor of Han: the first year of Qianheng. The Crown Prince of Shu, Yan, ascended the throne.
In the third month, the King of Wuyue, Qiu, first established the Yuan-shuai Fu (Supreme Commander’s Headquarters) and appointed its officials.
In Huainan, he appointed Xu Zhigao as the Acting Deputy Commander of the Huainan Jiedu (Regional Military Command).
Zhikao served the Ruler of Wu with the utmost reverence.
Zhikao took Song Qichu as his chief advisor.
Longhu: Chan Master Longhu of Shaowu.
His name was Pumen;
he was the second son of Emperor Xizong of the Tang dynasty.
From childhood, he abstained from eating meat or pungent vegetables.
For a long time he had no intention of serving the world.
Emperor Xizong doted on him.
In the first year of the Zhonghe era of Emperor Xizong’s reign, the Huang Chao rebellion broke out.
The Emperor fled to Shu;
the princes of the blood and members of the imperial clan all went into hiding.
The Master cut his hair and wandered away.
A practitioner visited Chan Master Shishuang Qianzhao and asked,
"What is the separate transmission outside the teachings?
Qianzhao replied, "Wait until the mountain on my desk nods its head."
He then spoke to you directly.
The Master attained realization thereupon;
after relying on him for several years, he requested permission to travel the mountains.
The various sayings state:
"Stop as soon as you encounter Qian;
stay put as soon as you meet Chen."
He then took his leave and traveled on, passing through Shaowu and arriving at Daqian.
Gazing from afar at the mountain peak, which was lush, profound, and beautiful, he asked the elders,
"Is there anyone living there?"
The old man said, "There is one Chen Si who has long been in hiding within this place. When you,
Master, arrived, Si then shared his seat with you and lived together."
The Master lived in a thatched hut at the mouth of the Valley;
Chen then departed,
leaving only the site of the hermitage remaining.
As for the Baocheng Chan Monastery, it is the site of the master’s thatched hut.
In the third month of the first year of the Wende era of Emperor Xizong,
the master cast his iron staff upon the mountain.
He established a *maṇḍala* at the place where he had set down his staff;
monks and laypeople turned their hearts toward it, and it eventually became a great monastery.
One day, an old man came before him and said:
"I am a dragon who dwells on this mountain.
Because I have failed in my duty of bringing rain, I shall soon face divine punishment."
"I pray that you, Master, will rescue and protect me.
The Master said,
"You may come after changing your form."
Suddenly, a small snake appeared on the seat.
The Master drew it into his purification flask.
After a long while, wind and thunder accompanied the seat, and the mountain peaks shook and trembled.
The sky cleared and brightened.
The snake emerged from the jar,
and the old man came forward to thank him, saying:
If it were not for the power of the Master’s Dharma, this place would have become foul and defiled.
Seeing that the Master’s place of practice lacked water,
one should repay his virtue by providing it.
He then dug into the earth until a hole was formed;
a spring gushed forth and overflowed, eventually becoming a lake.
This is located at present-day Ban-zhang and is called Longhu (Dragon Lake).
On a certain day in the fourth year of the Zhengming era,
the Master assembled the monks and said,
"I am about to depart for another place."
He entrusted the affairs of the monastery to the two Zen practitioners, Chong and Gyo,
and then spoke this verse:
"I have fled the world's hardships to leave the household life."
The Master pointed out a place of rest.
Having resided on the mountain and led the assembly for thirty years,
he was unwilling to bestow this lightly upon others.
"Today I shall explain this clearly to you;
listen attentively as I close my eyes.
Thereupon, he mounted his tiger at dawn and arrived at Kaiyuan Temple in Xinzhou.
A monk from Longhu pursued him,
and the Master said,
"There is already Chan Master Cong in the mountains."
"I shall not return again.
Consequently, Longhu has no ancestral stupa for its founding patriarch;
there is only the site of the Kuahu (Tiger-Crossing) Hermitage.
This serves as evidence for both ancient and modern times.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Yuanjue.
The *Wudeng Huiyuan* states that the Master passed away at Longhu, which is likely incorrect.
The Master succeeded Chan Master Qingzhu of Shichuang in Tanzhou.
Zhuzi succeeded Daowu Zongzhi.
Zongzhizi succeeded Chan Master Yaoshan Weiyan.
The people of Zhijizhou were surnamed Chen. This was the year Jimao,
the fifth year of Zhenming (939 CE), the fourth year of the Shenchai era of the Khitan.

The Prince of Jin of Zhao: the sixteenth year of Tiānyòu. The King of Qí: the sixteenth year of Tiānbǎo. The Kings of Wúyuè, Chǔ, Jīnnán, Huáinán, and Wú: the first year of Wǔyì. The Kings of Míng, Shǔ, and Yǎn: the first year of Qiánhé. The King of Hàn: the first year of Qiánhēng. The fourth month of summer.
Yang of Huainan ascended the throne as King of Wu.
He changed the era name to Wuyi and established the ancestral temple and the altars of state.
The offices of state were established and the palace halls constructed;
all cultural artifacts and ceremonies were conducted according to the rites and music of the Son of Heaven.
Gengchen, the sixth year of Zhengming (the fifth year of the Shenchê era of the Khitan).

Prince of Jin, Zhao [Shouzhi]: Year 17 of Tiānyòu. King of Qí [Zhongyi]: Year 17 of Tiānyòu. King of Wúyuè [Qiān Liu]: Year 2 of Qiāndé. King of Chù [Li Jing]: Year 4 of Qiánhēng (Year of Xīn-sí). King of Míng [Wáng Shèn]: Year 1 of Lóngdé. King of Shǔ [Máng Zhōu]: Year 1 of Tiānzàn of the Khitan. King of Hàn [Liu Yán]: Year 1 of Tiānzàn of the Khitan.

Zhao Jinwang: the eighteenth year of Tianyou. Qiwang, Wuyue Wang, Chu Jingnan Wu: the first year of Shunyi. Min and Shu: the third year of Qiande. Han: the fifteenth year of Qianheng, the Ren year; the second year of Longde. Qidan: the second year of Tianzan.

In the second year of Shunyi of the Zhao, Jin, Qi, Wuyue, Chu, and Jingnan Wu [dynasties]; in the fourth year of Qiande of Min and Shu; and in the sixth year of Qianxiang of Han: Chan Master Shunde Tuo of Jingqing in Yuezhou.
He attained the Dharma under Xuefeng.
The Qian Kings of Wuyue, honoring his virtue and morality,
invited him to reside at Tiantong Temple.
Furthermore, he founded Longce Monastery to house the Master;
disciples flocked there from all directions,
whereby the study of the profound mysteries flourished in the regions of Wu and Yue.
He entered nirvana in the eighth month of the second year of the Tiānfú era of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Jìn dynasty.
He was seventy-four years old.
This was the third year of the Lóngdé era, marked by the cyclical sign *guīwèi*.
The first year of Tongguang (the third year of Tianzan of the Khitan).

The first year of Tongguang, when Zhao Tang ascended the imperial throne; the third year of Shunyi of the Qi King, the Wuyue King, Chu, and Jingnan Wu; the fifth year of Qiande of Min and Shu; and the seventh year of Qianheng of Han. In the second month of spring.
The Emperor of Liang dispatched an envoy to confer the title of King of Wuyue upon Qian Liu.
On the *jisi* day of the fourth month of summer,
Li Cunxun, the Prince of Jin, ascended the imperial throne at the southern gate of the military headquarters in Weizhou.
The state name was the Great Tang.
The reign title was changed to Tongguang.
The Tang possessed thirteen military commands (jiedu) and fifty prefectures (zhou).
He led his troops to take Liang.
The Emperor of Liang said to Huangfu Lin, "The House of Li has been our family's enemy for generations; it is unreasonable to surrender."
"My head cannot wait for that blade and saw;
I cannot take my own life.
You may sever my head."
Lín subsequently assassinated the Emperor of Liáng and then committed suicide.
In the tenth month, the Emperor of Táng entered Dàliáng.
Thus, the two rulers of the Liang dynasty combined for sixteen years before returning to the Tang.
The Tang was of the Li clan;
it ruled by the virtue of Earth.
The capital was at Ye,
which is the ancient city of Xiangzhou, now the region of Zhangde.
Later, the capital was moved to Luoyang.
Zhuangzong, Mingzong, Min Di, and Lu Wang. Zhuangzong’s personal name was Cúnxù.
He was originally a Shatuo person.
In the ninth year of the Xiántōng era of Emperor Yìzōng of the Táng dynasty, [the title] was bestowed upon his grandfather.
His surname was Li;
his name was Guochang.
His father’s name was Kegyong.
His merit in defeating Huang Chao and restoring the capital was ranked first;
he was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Hedong and successively enfeoffed as the Prince of Jin.
Upon his death, Liu Congxun succeeded him to the throne.
He extinguished the Liang dynasty and established the state called Tang,
posthumously honoring his father, Wang Kelyong, as Emperor Wuhuang.
The Emperor reigned for three years.
His life span was thirty-five years. This was the third year of the Tongguang era;
the first year of Tongguang was the Guiwei year.
In the tenth month, the Liang dynasty was extinguished and a new era name was established.
In the eleventh month, the capital was moved to Luoyang.
Jia-shen, the second year of Tongguang (925 CE); the fourth year of Tianzan of the Khitan.

The King of Zhao, Wang Maozhen, passed away in the fourth year of Shunyi of the Wuyue, Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu kingdoms; it was the sixth year of Qiandé of the Min and Han kingdoms; and the eighth year of Qianheng of the Shu kingdom, in the first month.
Li Maozhen, the Prince of Qi, dispatched his son, Li Jili, to present a memorial and tribute, declaring himself a vassal.
The Emperor treated him with great honor and changed his title to Prince of Qin.
In the fourth month, Li Maozhen, the Prince of Qin Zhongjing, passed away.
Zi-ji (子繼) succeeded [his predecessor] Ka (曮) in the temporary administration of the military government of Fengxiang.
Wei-fu (魏府) is the present-day Daming Road (大名路).
Master Xinghua (興化禪師) [was there].
His name was Cunjing.
A native of the local commandery,
he was summoned by imperial decree to enter the palace.
He attended his teacher with the etiquette of a disciple.
One day he asked,
"I have recovered the Central Plains and obtained a bright pearl."
No one had yet offered a price.
The Master said,
"Please let Your Majesty examine the pearls."
The Emperor reached out his hand to straighten the ends of the master's *fuhetou* (head-wrap).
The Master said,
"Who would dare to appraise the price of the Sovereign’s treasure?"
The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon him purple robes and a title of honor,
but the Master declined them both.
He then granted him a horse for his use.
He fell to the ground and injured one foot.
The Emperor again granted him a physician.
The Master summoned the head of the infirmary and said, "Make me a wooden leg."
The Master received him and walked around the monastery,
asking the monks,
"Do you recognize this old monk?"
The assembly said, "We are all at a loss; we do not recognize the Master.
The Master replied, "This lame-legged Dharma teacher can speak, but he cannot practice."
He went to the Dharma Hall and ordered the *vinaya-dhara* to strike the bell to assemble the community.
The Master said,
"Do you still recognize this old monk?"
The assembly was speechless.
The Master cast down his staff, sat upright, and passed away.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Guangji.
The Master succeeded Chan Master Linji Xuan in the *Chuan Deng Lu*.
The Chan Master of Nanyuan at Baoying in Ruzhou, named Huiyong, was a native of Hebei and succeeded Xinghua Jiang.
In the year of Yiyou, the third year of the Tongguang era (925 CE), the fifth year of the Tianzan era of the Khitan,
Wu Pu of Huainan established Qingliang Temple at Shitou City and formally invited Wuzong to serve as its abbot.

The Kings of Zhao, Qin, Wu, Yue, Chu, Jingnan, Huainan, and Wu; the Year 5 of Shunyi in Min; Wang Yan of Shu surrendered to the Tang and was appointed by them to [the throne] under Meng Zhi-xiang; the First Year of Bailong in Han; the Ninth Month.
The Emperor dispatched his son, Prince Wei Wang Jiyi, along with the Chief Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat Guo Chongtao, to campaign against Shu.
The ruler of Shu, Wang Yan, surrendered, carrying his coffin on a litter and offering a jade tablet in his mouth.
Meng Zhiyang, whose courtesy name was Baosheng, [was appointed to govern the region].
He was a native of Longgang in Xingzhou.
Guo Chongtao, the Grand Censor-in-Chief, had previously recommended him to Zhiyang;
as he was about to depart, he said to the Emperor:
Meng Zhixiang was trustworthy, broad-minded, and possessed strategic foresight.
On this mission to obtain Sichuan and seek a commander-in-chief,
there was no one more suitable than this man.
The Emperor approved this.
The main army then proceeded westward into San Pass, advancing at double speed to attack and subdue Shu.
Chongtao subsequently appointed Zhiyang as the Regional Inspector of Western Shu to govern Chengdu.
In the fourth year of Changxing during the Mingzong reign, he was enfeoffed as Prince of Shu.
In the first year of Qingtai during the Lüwang reign, he ascended the imperial throne and passed away.
His son, Chǎng, succeeded him.
He established the era name Jianyuan and took Mingde as the dynastic title; the state was named Shu.
It surrendered to the Song in the third year of the Qiande era of Emperor Taizu of Song.
In the forty-first year, the state was abolished.
A white dragon appeared in the Han palace,
and the Han ruler changed the era name to Bailong (White Dragon).
He changed his name to Emperor Gong (Gong Sima Tongjian).
Mingzong’s taboo name was Dan;
his original name was Siyuan.
He was a person from the Northern Di tribes whom Zhuangzong raised as his son.
He followed Zhuangzong on military expeditions and campaigns.
He repeatedly established great meritorious services.
In the first month of the year Wuxu (546),
Zhao Zaili rebelled at Ye.
Zhuangzong ordered Li Siyuan to suppress them.
In the third month, when Siyuan arrived at Ye-du,
Zhang Poba, a soldier of the Congma-zhi (Imperial Bodyguard), incited a rebellion.
The troops pressed upon the central army.
Shiyuan shouted and questioned him,
and he replied:
"Your Majesty has abandoned benevolence and relied solely on force, declaring that after the city is captured, the army of Wei Bo shall be entirely slaughtered.
We are merely afraid of death.
Now, the assembly proposes that Your Majesty ascend to the north of the Yellow River."
He ordered the Duke to rule over Hebei.
Li Siyuan wept and exhorted him,
but the assembled troops would not comply.
Shi Jingtang, the son-in-law of Shiyuan, said:
"Success in affairs arises from resolute action, while failure stems from hesitation.
Thereupon, Shiyuan ordered An Zhonghui to issue a proclamation and assemble the troops.
The military forces were in great abundance.
Li Shaorong requested that Zhuangzong travel to Guandong to pacify them.
The imperial carriage arrived at Wansheng Town.
Upon hearing that Shi Siyuan had already seized Daliang and that his various armies were deserting and rebelling,
he immediately ordered the army to turn back and return to Luoyang.
In the fourth month, Guo Congqian, a commander of the Cavalry Command,
unaware that Prince Mu Cunyi had already died,
intended to install him as the leader of a rebellion.
Leading his troops, he attacked Xingjiao Gate and entered by scaling the city walls;
the palace attendants and veteran generals cast off their armor and fled in secret.
Only Li Yanqing, He Fojin, Wang Quanbin, and some ten others fought with great resolve.
Zhuangzong was struck by an arrow;

his falconer, Shan You, supported him from the gate tower down to the eaves of the Jiangxiao Hall, where Zhuangzong extracted the arrow. Suffering from thirst and exhaustion, he passed away shortly thereafter.
Li Yanqing and the others departed in bitter lamentation,
and his attendants all dispersed.
Shanyou cremated the Emperor’s remains.
In the year Jǐchǒu, Shìyuán entered Luoyang and stayed at his private residence.
He retrieved the remains of Zhuāngzōng from the ashes and performed the funeral rites.
The officials submitted three memorials requesting that Shìyuán act as Regent, and he granted their request.
The officials deliberated on the rites for ascending the throne.
Li Shaozhen and Kong Xun argued that since the destiny of the Tang had ended, it was appropriate to establish a new national title;
however, the Regent did not agree.
Li Qi, the Minister of Personnel, said:
"If the dynastic name were changed, the late Emperor would then become a mere traveler on the road;
where could his imperial coffin be entrusted?"
"In previous dynasties, there have been many instances of succession by a collateral branch.
It would be appropriate to follow the rite of ascending the throne before the coffin of the heir apparent.
The assembly followed this advice, and the Regent then ascended the imperial throne before the coffin.
He was already sixty years of age.
He changed the era name to Tiānchéng.
Every evening in the palace, he burned incense and addressed his prayers to Heaven.
He prayed that a sage might soon be born to serve as a lord for the people.
In the first month of spring in the second year of the Tiānchéng era, he changed his name to Dàn.
He reigned for eight years.
He reached the end of his life at sixty-seven. In the fourth year of the Tiānchéng era,
the *bǐngxū* year— the sixth year of the Tiānzàn era of the Khitan—
Master Guànxiū, the "Moon of Chan" from Shu, passed away this year.

Zhao Fengxiang [reigned as] Jili (Ji-li). Year 1 of Baozheng in the Wuyue Kingdom; Year 6 of Shunyi in Chu/Jinnan; Year 1 of Tianbao in the Min Kingdom under Yanjun; Year 2 of Bailong in the Shu Jiedushi under Meng Zhiyang; and Year 2 of Bailong in Han, Wang Yanhao, the Jiedushi of Shaowu, proclaimed himself the King of the Great Min Kingdom.
He established a palace and appointed a hundred officials;
their dignified deportment and ceremonial regalia were all modeled after the system of the Son of Heaven.
He posthumously honored his father, King Shen-zhi, as King Shaowu.
In this year, it became known that Yangzi Yanbing had assassinated Yanhan;
the multitude then appointed his younger brother, Yanjun, as the Acting Regent (liuhou).
Dinghai, the second year of Tiancheng [927]: the Khitan Grand Emperor Abaoji passed away; the first year of Tiandian under Deguang [947].

Zhao Fengxiang of Wuyue: the second year of Baozheng. Chu established the state of Jingnan: the first year of Qianzhen; [Wu] ascended the imperial throne. Min: the second year of Tianbao. Shu Han: the third year of Bailong. The Khitan Taizu passed away in the seventh month of autumn in the sixth year of Tianzan.
He reigned for eleven years.
Emperor Taizong succeeded him;
his name was Deguang.
The second son of Taizu;
his mother was Shulü.
He reigned for twenty-two years.
He established the Jin dynasty and extinguished the Tang.
He changed the name of the Qidan to the Great Liao.
He once constructed Tianxiong Monastery within his primary tribal settlement to honor the Buddha.
There is a portrait of Abaoji, the Taizu of the Khitan.
In the eighth month of autumn,
Ma Yin, Prince of Chu, first established his state.
He established a palace and appointed a hundred officials, all modeled after those of the Son of Heaven;
at times he made minor changes.
He renamed the Hanlin Xueshi (Academy Scholars) as the Wenyuan Xueshi (Scholars of the Literary Garden).
The title *zhizhigao* (知制誥) means "one who knows the composition of edicts.
The Shumi Yuan (樞密院) is called the "Left and Right Offices of Essential Matters.
Your Majesty refers to it as "Dianxia" (殿下).
The imperial edict was issued as a decree.
In the eleventh month, Yang Xuanzhi, Prince of Huainan and King of Wu, ascended the throne as Emperor.
Xu Wen, the Chancellor of Wu, passed away.
The Ruler of Wu appointed his son Zhigao as Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs at Home and Abroad.
Zhigao’s original surname was Li.
This was in the second year of the Qianning era of Emperor Zhaozong of the Tang dynasty.
Yang Xingmi attacked Haozhou.
A soldier plundered him from Xuzhou;
he was eight years old at the time.
Xingmi raised him as his own son.
Xingmi’s eldest son, Wo, detested him.
Xingmi said to his general Xu Wen:
"This child’s physical appearance and discernment are quite extraordinary compared to others.
I foresee that Wang Duo will certainly not be able to tolerate him.
I now grant him to you as a son."
Wen named him Zhigao.
Zhigao served Wen with diligence and filial piety exceeding that of his other sons;
therefore, Wen loved him and appointed him to oversee the household affairs.
As he grew up, he delighted in writing and was skilled at archery;
his discernment and character were exceptionally refined. Xingmi said to Wen:
It is known that Guo Junjie’s sons were all inferior [to him].
In the second year of the Tiānfú era of Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn, he received the abdication from Wú.
*Wùzǐ* (the third year of Tiānchéng) corresponds to the second year of Tiānxiǎn of the Khitans.

In the third year of Baozheng, Zhao Fengxiang of Wuyue [reigned]; in the third year of Qianzhen, Gao Jixing of Chu-Jinnan passed away; in the third year of Qianzhen of Wu; in the first year of Dayou of the Min ruler Yanjun and the Shu Meng family; in the first year of Dayou of Han, the Min ruler Yanjun ordained twenty thousand commoners as monks.
For this reason, there are many monks in Min; see the "Genealogy of Min" in the *Old History of the Five Dynasties*.
In the twelfth month of that year, Gao Jixing, the Regional Inspector of Jingnan, passed away.
He commanded his son, Conghui, to take charge of the military administration as an acting governor.
Conghui submitted a memorial requesting internal submission,
and the Emperor issued an edict appointing Conghui as the Regional Inspector of Jingnan.
The Chan Master of Luohan Monastery in Zhangzhou was named Guichen.
He was born into the Li clan of Changshan.
He was tonsured at Wansui Temple in this prefecture by the Great Master Wuxiang.
He ascended to receive the precepts and obtained the Dharma from Chan Master Xuansha Shibei.
This master held the Great Dharma in profound secrecy and diligently concealed his realization.
The Duke Mu of Zhangzhou invited him to reside at the Shishan Dizang Monastery west of the city for over ten years;
he subsequently moved to Lohan Yuan,
where the walls were in ruins and the beds were dilapidated.
The Master remained as serene as ever.
He supported Fayen Yi,
and in the third year of the Tencho era, he entered nirvana.
He lived to the age of sixty-two.
After his cremation, his relics were enshrined in a stupa at the western corner of the monastery.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhenyi, and his name was included in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp).
Jichou (1039), the fourth year of the Tiāncheng era; the third year of the Tiānxian era of the Khitans;

the fourth year of the Bǎozheng era of Zhào Fēngxiáng and Wúyuè; the first year of the Tàihé era of Chǔ Jīnnán and Wú; the second year of the Dàyǒu era of Mǐn, Shū, and Hàn. In the ninth month, the Emperor conversed at ease with the Chancellor Fēng Dào regarding the successive bountiful harvests and the fact that all quarters were free from trouble.
Dao said, "I have often remembered that in the past,
while serving in the imperial administration under the former Emperor."
While serving as an envoy to Zhongshan, I traversed the perilous passes of the Bing and Xing Mountains.
Fearing that my horse might stumble or even collapse under the weight of the month-long journey, I held the reins with extreme care;
fortunately, no mishap occurred until we reached Zhe and Lu.
"To let go of the reins for one's own ease leads, in an instant, to ruin.
All who rule the world are just like this.
The Emperor took these words to heart.
