When the harvest is poor, the farmer dies of starvation;
when the harvest is bountiful, he is harmed by the devaluation of grain.
That farmers die of disease regardless of whether the year is good or bad is a phenomenon unique to them.
Your servant recalls the poem by the jinshi candidate Nie Yichong:
"In the second month they sell new silk;
in the fifth month they buy new grain."
"The physician has healed the sores upon his eyes,
but he has gouged out the flesh from his heart.
Although the language is vulgar, it fully captures the circumstances and sentiments of the rural folk.
"Among the four classes of people, the farmers are the most diligent and laborious;
it is essential that the ruler understand this.
The Emperor was pleased and commanded his attendants to record their poem.
He constantly recited it.
Dou Yujun of Wanping in Youzhou served as high official until he retired from the post of Grand Master of Remonstrance (Zuo Jianyi Daifu).
He fathered five sons,
all of whom attained prominent positions in government service.
Feng Dao, the Palace Attendant, presented him with a poem as a gift.
Ding Shilang of Mount Yan taught his sons with righteous principles;
the divine paulownia tree stands old and solitary.
The five branches of the immortal cassia are fragrant.
In the second year of the Xiande era of Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty,
the Grand Master, Chancellor, and Prince Wenyi of Ying, Feng Dao, passed away.
Gengyin, the first year of Changxing (the fourth year of Tianxian of the Khitan).
Zhao Fengxiang, Wuyue: the fifth year of Baozheng. Chu: King Yan died. Jingnan, Wu: the second year of Tahe. Min, Shu, Han: the third year of Dayou. In the eleventh month, King Ma Yan of Chu died.
Zi Xisheng succeeded to the position and,
following his father's final testament,
abolished the system of establishing separate states.
The former system of the regional military governors was restored.
An imperial edict appointed Xisheng as the Regional Commander of Wuan and Jingjiang.
Regarding the Yunmen School: the Chan Master Guangfeng of Mount Yunmen at Guangfeng Monastery in Shaoshan, Guangdong Province.
His name was Wenyen.
He was born in Xiushui of Western Zhejiang,
which is now Jiaxing Prefecture.
His surname was Zhang.
In his youth, he relied upon Master Zhicheng of Kongwang Temple to renounce the householder’s life.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He received his full ordination at the altar in Biling and attended under Sengcheng for several years, thoroughly investigating the Vinaya-piṭaka;
yet, he felt that his own understanding of these matters remained unclear.
He went to visit the venerable elder Muzhou.
As he pushed through the gate, Muzhou seized him and said, "Speak! Speak!"
As the Master hesitated,
Zhou pushed him out, saying,
"A 'hòulè' from the Qin dynasty has come to bore through; he has now shut the door and injured the Master's foot."
The Master followed him and attained enlightenment.
Daowu then directed him to see Chan Master Xuefeng Cui.
Having thus achieved a secret resonance with the essence of the Mind School, he was fully realized.
He then crossed the ridges and traveled extensively to pay respects at various monasteries.
Later, he arrived at Lingshu where he met Chan Master Min.
Initially, Min did not appoint him as the head seat (shouzuo).
Someone urged him to accept the position of the first seat (shouzuo),
to which Lingshu replied,
"I was born as the first seat; I left the household life as the first seat."
After a long time, he said,
"My head seat has both traveled on pilgrimage and awakened to the Way.
After another long time, he spoke again:
"My head seat has arrived.
One day, he ordered the bell to be struck to receive the head seat.
When the Master arrived, [the bell was sounded].
Min smiled and said, "I have waited for you for a very long time; why have you arrived so late?
He then immediately gave him orders.
The Master accepted the appointment without declining; this was the first year of the Changxing era, the Gengyin year.
Shortly thereafter, Liu Wang, the ruler of Guang, intended to raise an army and went to Lingshu to seek a decision on whether it should proceed.
Mingzhao understood this.
She sealed the casket with her own hand and said to her attendant,
"When the King comes, bring it out and wait for him."
Just then, a monk asked,
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Min then sat down and passed away.
When the King arrived and heard that Wenmin had already been transformed,
he was greatly astonished and marveled.
The attendant monk presented the casket to him.
The *Fazhi shu* states:
"He was the Chief Seat (*shangzuo*) in the Hall of the Eye of Humanity and Heaven.
King [Wu Zong] then invited the Master to succeed him as the presiding master of Lingshu."
He was invited to the monastery to inaugurate the Dharma;
after a long time, he moved to reside at Yunmen Mountain in Shaoyang.
In the year Wushen.
The Prince repeatedly invited him into the inner palace to inquire about the Dharma,
treating him with the etiquette due to a teacher and bestowing upon him the title Chan Master Kuangzhen.
In the seventh month, he was invited to the royal palace for offerings.
In the ninth month, he took leave of the king and returned to the mountain.
On the tenth day of the fourth month of the following year.
The Master declined the invitation of the sovereign and,
having issued admonitions to his disciples, passed away while sitting upright.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa behind the abbot’s quarters.
In the year of Bingyin,
the fourth year of Emperor Taizu of Zhao’s Qiande era,
which was also the ninth year of the Tianbao era of the Lord of Guang.
The Master showed a dream to Ruan Shaizhuang, saying,
"Give my message to the Palace Official for the Xiuhua Bureau, the Special Advance (Tejin) Li Tuo.
Tuo subsequently submitted a petition requesting that the stupa be opened.
By imperial decree, his sacred remains were invited to the inner court for veneration;
only after more than a month did they return,
whereupon the temple’s name was changed to Dajue (Great Enlightenment).
He was posthumously conferred the title of Chan Master Da Ciyun Kuangzhen Hongming.
The Master succeeded Chan Master Xuefeng Cun;
Cun succeeded Deshan Jian.
Jian succeeded Longtan Xian Chan Master.
The world revered his dharma path and designated it the Yunmen School.
Xinmao, the second year of Changxing; the fifth year of Tianxian of the Khitan.

Zhao Fengxiang of Wuyue: the sixth year of Baozheng. Chu Jingnan of Wu: the third year of Taihe. Min, Shu, and the Meng family of Han: the fourth year of Dayou. Renchen, the second year of Changxing; the sixth year of Tianxian of the Khitan.
Zhao Fengxiang of Wuyue; Yuanguan established Chu Jingnan Wu; the fourth year of Taihe; the fifth year of Dayou of Min, Shu, and Han; the second month of spring.
Initially, the Guozijian was ordered to collate and standardize the Nine Classics for carving and printing.
By the third year of the Guangshun era of the Zhou dynasty, the woodblocks were completed and the prints were circulated.
This occurred in the third month.
The King of Wuyue, Wu Su Qian Liu,
passed away at the age of eighty-one.
His middle son, Qian Fuanguan, ascended the throne.
His name was changed to Yuanguan.
In accordance with his final instructions, state protocols were dispensed with, and the rites of a regional military governor (fanzhen) were adopted.
In the seventh month of autumn.
Ma Xisheng, the Military Governor of Wujing and Anjiang, passed away.
Yuan Wei, Pan Yue, and others of the Six Armies went to Langzhou to welcome Ma Xifan, the younger brother of Xisheng, and established him as ruler.
He reigned for fifteen years and lived to the age of forty-nine. On the *guisi* day,
in the fourth year of Changxing (924), the Emperor passed away— corresponding to the seventh year of Tianxian of the Khitan.

Zhao Fengxiang was the Emperor Wenmu Yuanguan of Wuyue. [The rulers of] Chu (Jinnan), Wu, Min (Lin), and Shu (the Meng clan) were enfeoffed as kings in the fifth year of Tahe; [and] in the first month of spring in the sixth year of Dayou of the Han dynasty.
The ruler of Min, Wang Yanjun, ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the state name to Daming and designated the era year as Longqi.
His name was changed to Lin. In the second month, the Tang court appointed Meng Zhixiang as the Military Governor of the Eastern and Western Sichuan Circuits and Prince of Shu.
In the eleventh month...
The Emperor fell ill.
He issued an edict appointing his third son, Prince Song Fromhou, as his successor.
The Emperor soon passed away.
In the twelfth month, Emperor Song Wang Conghou ascended the throne; he was Emperor Min.
In the first month of the Jiawu year, the reign title was changed to Yingshun.
At that time, Lu Wang Congke, the Regional Inspector of Fengxiang and concurrently Acting Grand Councilor, was at odds with the court.
In the third month, the Prince of Lu raised the standards and drums of a great general and led his forces eastward.
When Emperor Min heard that the Prince of Lu had reached Shan,
he was struck with anxiety and alarm, not knowing what to do.
He departed through the Xuanwu Gate with fifty cavalrymen and went to Wei Prefecture,
where he relied upon the Prefectural Governor Wang Hongzhi.
Prince Lu arrived at Jiangqiao.
Feng Dao and the others all submitted memorial petitions urging him to ascend the throne.
The Lord of Lu entered to pay his respects to the Empress Dowager and the Imperial Consorts at the Western Palace;
they prostrated themselves before the coffin and wailed in grief.
The Empress Dowager issued an order deposing the Young Emperor and demoting him to the rank of Duke of E;
she then commanded the Prince of Lu to ascend the imperial throne before the imperial bier.
Wang Hongzhi transferred the Mian Emperor to the provincial office.
The Prince of Lu dispatched Luan, the son of Hongzhi and a court official (dianzhi), to administer poison to him.
Emperor Min, knowing it was poisoned, refused to drink it;
Luan then strangled him to death.
Prince of Lu: Prince of Lu’s name was Congke.
He was the adopted son of Emperor Mingzong and bore the surname Wang.
He was a native of Zhenzhou,
which is present-day Zhending Prefecture.
During the days when Emperor Mingzong was surveying the territory, [he encountered him].
He and his mother captured him and raised him as their own son.
At the age of ten, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lu and appointed as the Military Governor of Fengxiang.
When Emperor Min ascended the throne,
he dispatched Wang Congju, Prince of Yang, to go and attack him;
thus, [the latter] raised his army.
Emperor Min fled into exile.
The Prince of Lu ascended the throne by the command of the Empress Dowager.
He reigned for three years.
The year of his death was the thirtieth year [of the era].
On the fourth month of the Jiawu year, the first year of Qingtai was established. This was the eighth year of Tianxian of the Khitan.

It was the sixth year of Taihe of Zhao Fengxiang, Wuyue, Chu, Jingnan, and Wu; the second year of Longqi of Min; the first year of Mingde of Shu Cheng; and the seventh year of Dayou of Han, with an intercalary first month.
Meng Zhixiang, the Prince of Shu, ascended the imperial throne at Chengdu and changed the era name.
In the seventh month of autumn, he passed away.
The Crown Prince Renzan ascended the imperial throne and changed his name to Chang.
This was the first year of the Mingde era.
The Venerable Jìng of Guīng Monastery on Mount Tiantái first attained awakening under the words of Chan Master Xuánshā Bèi;
he resided on Mount Tiantái for over thirty years.
A questioner asked:
"My thoughts are scattered and turbulent; I do not yet understand how to subdue them.
Jing replied:
Take this fluttering mind and investigate the place where it flutters.
When you investigate and find no place, what remains of the fluttering thought?
Turn back and investigate the investigating mind itself: where, then, is the mind that performs the investigation?
Jingyin, observing the meaning of "illusion" within the teachings, composed a verse stating:
"If you say that all dharmas exist like illusions,
then committing various transgressions and evils should entail no fault."
"How is it that one does not forget the karma one has created?
It is by relying on the Buddha's compassion to provide guidance and encouragement.
A certain Elder Śānta replied to him, saying:
A phantom person creates a phantom wheel of protection;
phantom karma can summon that which is to be remedied by a phantom.
Failing to understand the phantom gives rise to all manner of phantom sufferings.
Awakening to the realization that illusions are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The traces left by the two Senior Monks (Śāntarakṣita and Padmasambhava) remain at Guoqing Temple;
this is recorded in its temple chronicles and stone inscriptions.
Yiwei, the second year of Qingtai; the ninth year of Tianxian of the Khitan.

Zhao Fengxiang [reigned] over Wuyue, Chu, Jingnan, and Wu; Tianxiang, the first year of the Min kingdom; Longqi, the third year of the Shu kingdom; Mingde, the second year of the Han kingdom; Dayou, the eighth year. Gao Conghui was the Regional Commander (Jiedushi) of Jingnan.
Xing Mingda was personally acquainted with the worthy scholar Liang Zhen, whom he entrusted with authority.
Zhen wore a crane-feather cloak and styled himself the Hermit of Jingtai.
Whenever he went to the provincial seat, he would ride a yellow ox to the hall.
Wu Jia conferred upon Xu Zhigao the titles of Senior Father, Grand Preceptor, Grand Chancellor, and Grand Marshal;
he was further enfeoffed as Prince of Qi, with the granting of exceptional ceremonial rites.
In the sixth month of the third year of the Qingtai era, he established the state of Qi, comprising ten prefectures: Jiankang, Run, Jiang, Xuan, Chi, Shi, Hui, Chang, Jiang, Rao, Xin, and Hai.
Shi Jingtang, the Regional Inspector of Hedong and Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Command,
having returned to his fief at Jinyang,
secretly devised a plan for his own preservation.
Initially, the Emperor wished to have Jingtang transfer his command to Yanzhou—
the present-day Dongping Prefecture within the region of Yanzhou—
but the Palace Attendants Li Song and Lü Qi and others all earnestly remonstrated, deeming it inadvisable.
The Emperor followed the advice of Xue Wenyu, the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
and appointed Jingtang as the Regional Inspector of Tianping; when the edict was issued,
the officials of both ranks looked at one another, their faces turning pale with alarm.
Jingtang said,
"I did not incite this rebellion;
it was initiated by the court."
"How can I simply fold my hands and die on this road?
Du Yaya Liu Zhiyuan said,
"Your Excellency occupies a strategically advantageous position."
"The troops and horses are elite and powerful;
if we were to mobilize our forces and issue a proclamation, the imperial enterprise could be achieved.
The Secretary for Records, Sang Weihan, said:
"If you, my lord, can extend your sincerity toward the Khitan, what concern could there be for failure?
Jingtang’s resolve was thus settled;
he submitted a memorial to the Emperor stating that as a foster son, he ought not to inherit the ancestral sacrifices, and requested that the succession be transferred to Prince Xu.
The Emperor, enraged, tore the memorial with his own hands and dashed it to the ground.
He issued a decree stripping Jingtang of his official rank and titles,
and appointed Zhang Jinda as the Commander-in-Chief for the Four Directions of Taiyuan.
He led his generals to campaign against him.
Li Jingtang submitted to the Khitan, declaring himself a vassal and serving them with the etiquette due to a father.
Having consented to cede territory and request an investiture,
in the ninth month, the Khitan ruler, Taizong Deguang,
arrived at Jinyang with fifty thousand cavalry— though numbering three hundred thousand— and engaged in battle.
The Tang army suffered a great defeat.
In the eleventh month, the Khitan ruler composed an imperial edict appointing Jingtang as the Emperor of the Great Jin.
An altar was constructed in the willow grove, and he ascended the throne.
A general amnesty was proclaimed, and the reign title of Changxing 7 of Emperor Mingzong was changed to Tianfu Year 1.
When Prince Lu learned that Shi Jingtang had ascended the throne as Emperor,
he took Empress Dowager Cao, Empress Liu, Prince Yong Wang Zhongmei, Song Shenqian, and others,
and carrying the Imperial Seal of State, they ascended the Wuxu Pavilion.
He burned himself to death.
The Empress piled firewood, intending to set the official residence ablaze,
but Chongmei remonstrated with her, saying:
When the new Son of Heaven arrives, he must certainly not dwell in the open air;
to do so on another day would further exhaust the people's strength.
If he dies leaving behind resentment, what use would there be in him?
Thereupon he desisted.
Later, he died together with Chongmei, the Prince of Lu.
That evening, Gaozu of Jin entered Luoyang and stayed at his former residence.
The Tang troops removed their armor and awaited their punishment;
the Emperor of Jin comforted them and released them.
He then appointed Liu Zhiyuan to oversee the capital.
Zhiyuan dispatched a Han army officer back to the camp and lodged the Khitan ruler at Tiangong Temple; within the city,
all was solemn and no one dared to violate the orders.
In the twelfth month, the Jin Emperor posthumously deposed the Prince of Lu to the rank of commoner.
Feng Dao was appointed as a Grand Coordinator (Tongpingzhangshi).
Thus, the Tang dynasty, comprising four emperors for a total of fourteen years, came to an end and was absorbed by Jin.
The Jin dynasty was of the Shi clan.
They ruled by the virtue of Metal.
The capital was moved to Bianzhou. The High Ancestor was Prince Qi; the High Ancestor’s name was Jingtang.
His surname was Shi.
He was originally a man from the Western barbarians,
possessing great physical strength and skilled in warfare.
Emperor Mingzong of the Tang dynasty loved him and gave him his daughter,
Princess Yongning, in marriage.
He was successively promoted until he attained the rank of Regional Commander (Jiedushi) of Hedong.
In the first year of the Qingtai era, he governed Taiyuan.
When he was transferred to the position of Tianping Jiedushi, he refused the command;
he subsequently raised troops and sought assistance from the Khitan.
He immediately ascended the imperial throne and entered Luoyang.
He ceded sixteen prefectures—You, Ji, Ying, Mo, Zhuo, Tan, Shun, Xin, Wei, Ru, Wu, Yun, Ying, Huan, Shuo, and Wei—to the Khitans.
He reigned for seven years. His lifespan was fifty-one years.
In the seventh year of Tianfu, the cyclical year Bingshen, the eleventh month, the first year of Tianfu was established [as the new era]. This was the tenth year of Tianxian of the Khitan.

Zhao Fengxiang: Wu-Yue, Chu, Jingnan, and Wu. Tianxiang 2nd year: Min. Tongwen 1st year: Shu. Mingde 3rd year: Han. Dàyòu 9th year: Gāolì. During the end of the Tang dynasty, the king of Gāolì was surnamed Gāo.
In the second year of the Tongguang era of Emperor Zhuangzong of the Tang dynasty,
a mission was sent from Goryeo to China;
the historical records have lost the name of its king.
In the third year of the Changxing era of Emperor Mingzong,
Wang Jian, who was acting as the regent of state affairs, dispatched an envoy.
Emperor Mingzong conferred upon Wang Jian the title of King of Goryeo.
In this year, Bingshen (56 BCE),
Goguryeo raised an army and defeated Silla and Baekje; consequently,
the various states of the Eastern Barbarians all submitted to it.
There were two capitals, six prefectures, nine regional commands, and one hundred and twenty divisions.
In the *dingyou* year, the second year of Tianfu (937), the first year of Huìtóng of the Great Liao;

Zhao Fengxiang of Wuyue re-established his state; Chu and Jingnan received the abdication [of the Later Tang]; the first year of Shēngyuán of Min; the second year of Tōngwén of Shu; the fourth year of Míndé of Hán; and the tenth year of Dàyǒu of the Great Liao, after Emperor Tàizǒng Déguāng had established the Jin dynasty.
He accepted the sixteen provinces offered to him.
In the first month of spring, he established Youzhou as the Southern Capital and changed the national designation of the Qidan state to Da Liao (Great Liao).
The years were designated by the names of the *huìtóng* (congregations).
The high ministers, the officials, and the common officers all imitated those of China,
and Chinese people were employed in their service.
In the second month,
he returned north, appointing Zhao Yanshou as the Supreme Confidential Envoy and concurrently as Grand Chancellor.
In the third month...
The Jin court deliberated on the relocation of the capital to Daliang.
In the fourth month, they arrived at Bianzhou.
King Yuanguan of Wuyue re-established his state.
It was like the story of the Light.
In the eighth month,
the Ruler of Wu issued an edict to abdicate the throne in favor of the Prince of Qi.
Xu Zhiqie ascended the imperial throne at Jiankang.
He issued a general amnesty and changed the state name to Tang—the Southern Tang.
The era name was Shengyuan.
The Honored One [Sun Quan] was titled Emperor Let;
his palaces, carriages, and regalia remained as they were before.
The ancestral temples, the calendar, the insignia, and the colors of the ceremonial robes all followed the regulations of Wu.
The following year, the Retired Emperor passed away.
The Ruler of Tang suspended court for twenty-seven days and posthumously conferred upon him the title of Emperor Rui (睿皇帝).
In the third year of the Shengyuan era of the Tang dynasty,
Zhu Jigao reverted to his surname Li and changed his name to Bian;
he first appeared during the second year of the Chengtian era of Emperor Mingzong of the Tang, the Dinghai year.
Chan Master Fengxue of Ruzhou,
whose name was Yanzhao,
was a native of Yuhang in Qiantang.
His surname was Liu; from childhood he abstained from meat.
He studied Confucianism to prepare for the jinshi examinations, but after failing the first attempt, he left the household life to become a monk.
He received the tonsure at Kaigen-ji Temple in his home province under Zhigong,
where he received full ordination and studied Tiantai *zhiguan*.
At the age of twenty-five, he went to visit Jingqing.
Chan Master Nanyuan Yong attended Chan Master Yung and attained realization of the fundamental principle.
After staying with him for six years, he took his leave.
In the second year of the Changxing era of Emperor Mingzong of the Later Tang, he arrived at the Ru River.
A thatched cottage of several rafters stood by the mountain like the home of fugitives.
When asked about it,
an elderly villager said:
In ancient times, at Xue Temple, the monks who resided there according to the Vinaya passed away, and the community abandoned the site.
The Master said,
"May I dwell here?"
The father said, "He may be my teacher," and so he remained there.
He begged for food in the villages by day and burned pine resin at night; thus he lived alone for seven years.
In the second year of the Tianfu era, when the prefectural governor, Magistrate Li, heard of the Master’s Way, he received him with the utmost courtesy and invited him to come.
On the day of Shangyuan, he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma;
he had inherited the lineage from Nanyuan Yongyong.
In the second year of the Qianguo era of Emperor Yindi of the Han dynasty, Li Junyi was appointed as the governor of Yingzhou.
The Master fled the rebels to seek refuge with him and was quartered in the prefectural study hall.
In Ruzhou, there was one Song Taishi who donated his residence to establish a Buddhist monastery named Xinsi.
He invited the Master to serve as abbot;
his dharma seat was preeminent and unsurpassed.
This was in the first year of the Guangshun era of Emperor Taizu of the Zhou dynasty.
The imperial plaque for the temple was bestowed with the name Guanghui.
The Master resided there for twenty-two years,
presiding over a community of more than a hundred followers.
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said,
"Bamboo-staff whips under the Zhangling Mountain."
On the first day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Kaibao era of Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty, he ascended the seat and spoke this verse:
"The Way lies in seizing the opportune moment; one must deliver all beings."
From afar they come with yearning, their spirits soaring;
in years to come, there will be elders whose sentiments are like his own—
day after day incense smoke, night after night lamps.
On the fourteenth day, he wrote by hand a letter bidding farewell to his various patrons;
on the fifteenth, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
He was seventy-eight years of age.
Xia was fifty-nine years old.
His master was Nanyuan Yongyong;
Yongyong succeeded Xinghua Changzhen.
The successor was enshrined by Chan Master Linji Xuan.
In the eighth month of the year Wuxu, the third year of Tianfu (928 CE), the second year of Huìtóng of the Great Liao;

the second year of Shèngyuán of the Wénmù King Yuànguàn of Zhào Fēngxiáng and Wúyuè; the second year of Shèngyuán of Chǔ Jīnnán and Táng; the third year of Tōngwén of Mǐn; the first year of Guǎngzhèng of Shǔ; and the eleventh year of Dàyǒu of Hàn.
The Emperor of Jin conferred the supreme title upon the Ruler of Great Liao and the Empress Dowager.
He appointed the Chancellor Pingchang Pindao Liu Xu as the Envoy for the Investiture Ceremony;
accompanied by a full ceremonial procession of guards, insignia, and chariots, he proceeded to the Ruler of Liao to perform the rites.
The Emperor served the Liao with great reverence;
he submitted a memorial acknowledging himself as a subject,
addressing the Liao ruler as "Father Emperor."
In the tenth month,
the Emperor established Dongjing (the Eastern Capital) at Bianzhou,
as it was a hub for boats and carriages and convenient for water transport.
Furthermore, he made Bianzhou the Prefecture of Kaifeng;
he designated Luoyang, the Eastern Capital, as the Western Capital;
and he appointed Chang’an, the Western Capital, as the Jinchang Military Commandery.
An imperial decree permitted both public and private minting of copper coins.
The inscription read: "Tianfu Yuanbao.
Jihai, the fourth year of Tianfu [939], the third year of Huìtóng of the Great Liao.

In the third year of Shengyuan of Li Sheng, the Later Tang of Jingnan; in the first year of Yonglong of the Min kingdom; in the second year of Guangzheng of the Shu kingdom; and in the twelfth year of Dayou of the Han kingdom, on the first day of the first month of spring. Zhao Fengxiang, Wu-Yue, Chu, Jingnan, and Li Sheng of the Southern Tang.
The ministers of Southern Tang repeatedly submitted memorials requesting that the Lord of Tang, Xu Zhigao, restore his surname to Li and establish the ancestral temples of the Tang dynasty.
The Lord of Tang granted their request.
He changed his name to Bian (pí biàn fǎn).
The ministers again petitioned for him to accept a supreme title,
but he would not accept it.
The Ruler of Tang did not allow members of his maternal kin to assist in governance,
nor did he permit eunuchs to involve themselves in affairs;
these were matters that other nations could not match.
In the intercalary seventh month of autumn, the ruler of Min was assassinated by Lian Zhongyu, the Commander of the Gongchen and Konghe Armies.
His uncle, Yan Yi, assumed the title of King of Min and the rank of Military Governor of Weiwu.
His name was changed to Xi,
and he was posthumously titled Lord of Min,
known as Emperor Zong of Tang.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: One night, the monk Daoyi of Shang Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou saw a brilliant light among the mountains;
going to investigate it, he discovered a tree of extraordinary fragrant wood.
He commissioned a skilled artisan to carve an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
which emitted a brilliant white light that continued day and night.
This was in the second year of the Qianguyu era of Emperor Gaozu of the Han dynasty.
There was a monk named Congxun who placed ancient Buddha relics within the *ūrṇā-kośa* (hair-treasure) of a Bodhisattva image;
at that time, the relics would occasionally appear upon the crown of its head. Furthermore, there is Mount Potalaka in the sea off Mingzhou in the Zhedong Circuit of the Qingyuan Prefecture.
This is a place where Bodhisattvas manifest themselves.
During the Dazhong era of the Tang Emperor Xuanzong,
a monk from India in the Western Regions came to the cave and burned off his finger as an offering in prayer.
He personally beheld the wondrous form of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
who bestowed upon him the essentials of the Dharma;
thus, his name and reputation first became renowned.
Later, a Japanese monk named Huie obtained a painted image of the Bodhisattva at Mount Wutai in northern Yan and left it with a local resident,
a man of the Zhang family, by the side of the mountain.
Zhang Fengzhi donated his residence to establish Guanyin Monastery.
The Gazetteer of Changguo states that the temple was first constructed in the second year of the Zhengming era of the Liang dynasty.
In the third year of the Yuanfeng era of Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty,
an envoy named Wang Shunfeng was dispatched to the Three Han;
his boat arrived at Dong Island.
A black wind suddenly arose and a tortoise carried the boat.
Shun performed sacrifices and prayers to it;
the Bodhisattva manifested his form, and the boat returned safely to the capital.
Upon hearing of this at court,
gold and silk were distributed and the temple was relocated to the southern slope of Mount Meicen.
The temple was granted the plaque "Baotu" (Precious Lotus),
which is the current monastery.
This was in the fifth year of the Tiānfú era, the Gēnzǐ year.
In the fourth year of the Huìtóng era of the Great Liao, King Xi of Min ordained eleven thousand commoners as monks (*Mín jìzǎi*).

[The reigns of] Zhào Fēngxiáng (Wùyuè), Chǔ, Jīnnán, and Táng—during the fourth year of Shēngyuán; Xi of Min—during the second year of Yǒnglóng; [the reign of] Shǔ—during the third year of Guǎngzhèng; [the reign of] Hàn—during the fourteenth year of Dàyǒu; *Xīnchōu* (the sixth year of Tiānfú); and the fifth year of Huìtóng of the Great Liao.

Zhao Fengxiang of Wuyue; his son Hongzuo ascended the throne. In the fifth year of Shengyuan of Chu Jingnan; the third year of Yonglong of Min; the fourth year of Guangzheng of Shu; and the thirteenth year of Dayou of Han, in the eighth month.
When Qian Yuan-guan, the Wénmù King of the Wúyuè state, passed away,
his son Hóngzuò ascended the throne.
Hóngzuò was mild and respectful, yet possessed clear judgment.
He was fond of books and treated scholars with courtesy, personally attending to the affairs of government.
He ruled for seven years and died at the age of twenty.
In the eleventh month, the Tang dynasty dispatched envoys to inspect the populace.
Previously, taxes had been determined based on the fertility or infertility of the land;
now, the people all praised the system for its fairness and impartiality.
On the *wùxū* day of the twelfth month of the Han year,
the Han ruler fell ill.
A Buddhist monk from India said to him, "The name 'Gōng' is not auspicious."
The Han ruler personally created the character "Lian" (龑) and named himself by it;
its meaning is derived from the phrase "the flying dragon is in the heavens," and it is pronounced like "Yan" (儼).
The ruler of Min constructed a seven-story stone pagoda on a western mound south of the city.
When the work was half-finished, three nights passed and it rose up like a canopy;
once completed, its radiance reached the heavens for another three nights.
The King comforted and favored him, bestowing upon him the name Jingguang (Pure Light), and further constructed a temple beneath it. [From] the Changle ji.
On the sixth month of the seventh year of Tianfu (the Renyin year), the Emperor passed away; this was the sixth year of Huìtóng of the Great Liao.

Zhao Fengxiang, Prince Hongzuo, Loyal and Contributing to the Wu-Yue; Chu, Jingnan, Tang—Shengyuan Year 6; Min—Yonglong Year 4; Shu—Guangzheng Year 5; Han, established by Bian—Guangtian Year 1; Nanhan, which is the same as Nanping, Guangzhou.
In the fourth month, Gaozu Liu Yan passed away.
Emperor Hongdu of Qin ascended the throne and changed his name to Bin (pinyin: bēn; Wade-Giles: p'in).
The History of the Qi Dynasty states that the Emperor was styled Chudi.
His name was Zhonggui.
He was the son of Jingru, the elder brother of Gaozu.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qi.
Of the five sons of Gaozu, all had died young;
Chongrui was still an infant.
In the sixth month of the seventh year of the Tianfu era, the High Ancestor passed away.

In the seventh month, Bingdao, the Minister of Works concurrently serving as Chief Attendant, deliberated with Jing Yanguang, the Regional Commander of Tianping and Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Bodyguard for Cavalry and Infantry.
As the state faced many hardships, it was deemed appropriate to establish an elder prince as sovereign.
Thereupon, Qi Wang Zhonggui, the Governor of Guangjin, was honored as the successor and ascended the imperial throne.
The ministers deliberated on submitting a memorial to acknowledge submission as a vassal and announce their grief to the Liao court.
Jing Yanguang requested that a letter be sent addressing the Liao emperor as "grandson" rather than "vassal.
Li Song remonstrated against this, but his advice was not followed.
Peng Dao wavered between the two positions.
The Emperor ultimately followed the counsel of Yan Guang.
The Khitan ruler was greatly incensed and dispatched an envoy to come and reprimand him.
Yanguang answered with insolence.
It was the year Bingwu, the third year of the Kaiyun era.
In the eleventh month, the Liao launched a massive campaign to destroy the Jin.
The Liao Emperor ordered Zhang Yanzé to escort the Prince of Qi to Kaifeng,
where he was not to be detained for even a moment.
The Emperor had occupied the throne for four years.
He was exiled far away to the lands of Liao.
His age at death is not recorded. It was the third year of Kaoyun, the eighth year of Tianfu, the *guimao* year;
the eighth year of Tianfu, the seventh year of Huìtóng of the Great Liao.

Zhao Fengxiang of Wuyue; Chu Jingnan of Southern Tang, year Jingsheng; Baoda Year 1 of Min; Tiande Year 1 of Shu; Guangzheng Year 6 of Han; Hongxi Year 1 of Liang; and Qianhe Year 1 of Tang. The ruler of Tang consumed elixirs from a Daoist adept, which gradually caused him to become irritable and impulsive.
Whenever the ministers presented their petitions, he would often erupt in violent rage.
He questioned the Daoist Wang Qixia, asking,
"What Way can lead to the realization of Great Peace?"
He replied,
"A king governs his mind and body before he can govern his family and state.
At present, Your Majesty has not yet been able to eliminate [these afflictions]."
To be satisfied when hungry and joyful when full—what need is there to discuss "Great Peace"?
Emperor Song praised this as the ultimate truth.
Whatever the Ruler of Tang bestowed upon him, [he accepted].
Qi Xia declined all [the honors].
In the second month, the Ruler of Tang developed carbuncles on his back.
He summoned Prince Qi Wang Jing to attend him during his illness.
He said to Jing:
"I have been ingesting metallic and mineral elixirs wishing to prolong my life,
yet they have instead harmed my vitality."
"You should take heed of this.
That evening, he passed away.
King Yeonjong (Yi Gyeong) ascended the throne.
Wang Yanzheng of the Min clan proclaimed himself emperor in Jianzhou, founding the state with the name Dayin. Initially,
after Wang Xi had established himself in the fourth year of the Tianfu era,
he became arrogant, licentious, cruel, and tyrannical, harboring suspicion toward his own kinsmen.
His younger brother, Wang Yanzheng, the Regional Inspector of Jianzhou, remonstrated with him in a letter.
Wang Xī became enraged;
consequently, the brothers harbored deep mutual suspicion and hatred, leading them into combat.
At this time, Yan Zheng proclaimed himself Emperor;
the Han Emperor Shang was arrogant and extravagant,
and did not attend to the affairs of government.
Prince Hongxi of Jin desired to plot against him;
he therefore lavishly adorned musicians and performers to entertain and please him, thereby enabling his evil intent.
Shortly thereafter, taking advantage of his drunkenness, he assassinated him.
Hongxi ascended the imperial throne;
he was Emperor Zhongzong.
He changed the era name to Qianhe.
The Fayen School: The Chan Master of Qingliang Temple in Jiankang,
named Wenyi,
was born into the Lu family of Yuhang.
At the age of seven, he received the tonsure under Chan Master Wei at Zhiting Temple in Xinding, following the new regulations.
In his youth, he received full ordination at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuezhou.
There, he thoroughly investigated the Vinaya and delved into the Confucian classics.
Shaking his mendicant’s staff, he traveled south and arrived at Fuzhou.
Finding that he had not attained great illumination under Chan Master Changqing Leng,
he intended to cross the mountain ridges and proceed to Zhangzhou.
While snow was blocking the path at Stone Mountain to the west of the city,
Chan Master Guichen of Dizang Monastery asked him,
"Venerable, you study the explanations that the triple world is mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only."
He then pointed to a stone before the steps and said,
"Is this stone inside the mind or outside the mind?
The Master replied, "It is inside the mind."
Chen said,
"What reason does a wandering monk have for doing this?
He carries a flat stone upon his heart as he travels."
The Master was at a loss for a reply;
he immediately set down his bundle beneath the seat and sought a definitive resolution for over a month.
He presented his understanding and explained the principle.
Baizhang said to him,
"The Buddha-dharma is not like that."
The Master said, "I am at a loss for words; my reasoning has reached its limit.
Zhen said:
When it was discussed that all dharmas of the Buddha-nature are already manifest,
the Master attained great enlightenment at those words;
he then remained in attendance for a long time.
This was during the second year of the Qingtai era of Emperor Li Congchao, the Prince of Lu of the Tang dynasty.
Upon arriving at Fuzhou in Jiangxi, he took his leave;
the governor of the prefecture held the Master’s Way in high esteem.
He was invited to reside at Chongshou Monastery.
During the Southern Tang dynasty,
the Ruler of Tang welcomed the Master to reside at Ba’en Chan Monastery in Jinling.
He was appointed with the title Chan Master Jinghui and transferred to Qingliang Temple,
where he extensively propagated the Dharma and transformed sentient beings.
The Ruler of Tang invited the Master to view the peony flowers and requested that he compose a poem on the spot.
The Master replied immediately:
Clad in coarse wool, I face the fragrant clusters;
from the start, our inclinations have been different.
My hair has turned white this very day.
The flowers are as red as they were last year.
Their lush beauty follows the morning dew;
their fragrant scent pursues the evening breeze.
"Why must one wait for things to wither and fall before realizing they are empty?
The Tang ruler suddenly attained awakening to the profound principle.
In the fifth year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty—
which was the first year of the Jiaotai era of the Tang—
the Master manifested illness on the seventeenth day of the seventh month.
The Ruler of Tang personally paid him honors and inquired after his well-being.
On the fifth day of the intercalary month, he took leave of the assembly and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
He was seventy-four years old.
On the fifty-fourth day of the twelfth month,
the high officials, including Li Jianxun and others,
dressed in plain white robes and escorted his whole body to be enshrined in a stupa at Danyang in Jiangning County.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dafa Yan;
his stupa was named Wuxiang.
He was later re-posthumously titled Grand Preceptor Dazhizang.
The Master had forty-three入室 (入室) disciples,
each of whom led a particular region;
those who attained awakening according to their capacities were beyond counting.
The Master succeeded Dizang Chen;
Chen succeeded Xuansha Bei;
Bei succeeded Chan Master Xuefeng Cun.
The school of the Zen tradition that is revered for its Way is called the Fayan School.
In the first year of the Kaiun era (the Jiachen year), the eighth year of the Huìtóng era of the Great Liao;

in the second year of the Bǎodà era of the Wúyuè Kingdom, Chǔ, Jīnnán, and Táng; in the seventh year of Guǎngzhèng of Mǐn under Zhū Wénjìn; and in the second year of Qiánhé of Hàn under Liù Xù, who was appointed as Minister of Works and Chancellor, the *Jiù Tángshǐ* (Old History of the Tang) was compiled.
The extraordinary traces of the Buddhas and patriarchs were all recorded [in these works],
but when Ouyang Xiu compiled the *Jiu Tangshu* (Old Book of Tang) during the Song dynasty,
he began by deleting them all.
In the first month of spring,
Zhu Wenjin, the Commander-in-Chief of Archun in Min,
and Lian Zhongyu, the Gatekeeper, assassinated the King of Min, Xi.
He summoned his officials and addressed them, saying:
"The Grand Ancestor founded the state of Min;
now his descendants have become licentious and tyrannical, and they are causing its legacy to fall."
"Heaven has grown weary of the House of Wang;
it would be fitting to select someone else of virtuous character to establish as ruler.
None among the assembly dared to speak.
Upon meeting again, Zhongyù deposed Zhū Wénjìn;
he ascended the throne wearing the *yuánmiǎn* robes and led his ministers to perform a second prostration facing north, declaring themselves his subjects.
Wénjìn styled himself the King of Mǐn.
The posthumous title of the ruler of Min, Xi, was bestowed as Emperor Jingzong.
In this year, Wenjin was killed by his subordinates;
his head was placed in a casket and sent to Yanzheng, the Prince of Jianzhou.

The following year, the Southern Tang army captured Jianzhou. Liu Yanzheng surrendered to Min; thus, after fifty years, the state was extinguished. The tolling of the bells ceased. A commoner in Shangyuan County, Jiangnan, died suddenly for three days and then revived, saying: [The bell struck me; it was like being in a great hall, where the sound was so resonant it shook my heart. My suffering was extreme. [I heard the sound of the bell striking again;

it was as if I were being dragged through a vast space. My pain was unbearable. [Suddenly, the sound of the bell ceased; my suffering vanished instantly. I opened my eyes and saw the light of day. [I realized that the sound of the bell had brought about my deliverance. I have returned to life because of the cessation of the bell’s toll. *Southern Tang, Jiangnan.* *One civilian of Shangyuan County died suddenly and revived after three days, saying:*
Upon arriving at the courtyard of a palace hall,
he suddenly saw his late father bound in extremely strict fetters.
Drawing near, he asked him:
"Why have you come here?
[He] replied, "I was misled by Song Qiqiu;
I killed more than a thousand surrendered people from Hezhou."
The prisoner’s grievance lies herein.
When you return, you may tell the successor:
whenever bells are struck in temples or monasteries, their sound must be prolonged.
Those suffering from pain find temporary relief upon hearing the bell;
it would be even more meritorious to have one cast for them.
During my reign, I once established diplomatic relations with the kingdom of Khotan.
That king sent me a jade statue of a Heavenly King (Devaputra).
I have always worn it within my topknot;
later, I concealed it in the left knee of the Buddha at Waguan Temple, where no one knew of its presence.
"You shall take this image as proof.
Once the official returned, he reported the matter in full to the Emperor of Tang,
who personally visited Waguan Temple.
He subsequently obtained a jade image from the Buddha’s knee.
Moved to tears, he cast a bell at Qingliang Temple in Jiankang,
the inscription of which read:
He offered sacrifices to the Martial Ancestor, Emperor Xiaogao.
Having been delivered from obscurity and emerged from peril,
he enshrined a jade image and erected a stupa to bury it at Mount Jiangshan (as recorded in the *Fayuan zhulin*).
The second year of Kaoyun (the *wuchen* year): the ninth year of Huìtóng of the Great Liao.

The third year of Bǎodà of Wúyuè, Chǔ, Jīngnán, and Táng; the year Mínnǎo extinguished Shǔ; the eighth year of Guǎngzhèng of Hàn; the third year of Qiánhé. The third year of Kaoyun (the *bǐwǔ* year): the tenth year of Huìtóng of the Great Liao.
Zhao Fengxiang: Wu-Yue, Chu, Jing, and Southern Tang. Baoda Year 4 (947); Shu: Guangzheng Year 9; Han: Qianhe Year 4, Dingwei; Kaiyun Year 4; Great Liao: Huìtóng Year 11.

In the fourth month of the fifth year of Baoda of the Southern Tang (the tenth year of Guangzheng of Shu and the fifth year of Qianhe of Han), Zhao Fengxiang of the Wuyue Kingdom died; Xi Guang was established as ruler of Chu; and the Taizong of Liao passed away.
He reigned for twenty-two years.
In the fifth month, Sejong ascended the throne;
his taboo name was Wǎnfan.
His name was Wuyù.
He was the son of King Tudun of Dongdan and the grandson of Taizu.
In the year Wushen, the reign title was changed to Tianlu.
In the ninth month of autumn in the fourth year of Tianlu, the year Xinhai,
he was assassinated by Yan Wang Shuya and others at Huoshendian in Xinzhou.
He reigned for five years.
In the fifth month,
King Xifan of Chu Wenzhao passed away.
The generals and aides installed his younger brother, Xi Guang.
In the sixth month, the King of Wuyue, Zhongxian Wang Hongzuo, passed away.
By his final testament, he appointed the Chancellor Hongzhong as the Regional Inspector of Zhenhai and Zhendong.
In this year, he was deposed by Hu Jinsī, the Commander-in-Chief of the Inner Guard,
who established his younger brother,
Hóngchū— the Wáng Zhòngyì— in his place.
The King was devoted to the teachings of Śākyamuni.
At the beginning of his reign,
he visited all the famous mountains and sacred sites throughout the various prefectures of the Two Zhe regions.
He bestowed gold and silk upon all to establish a monastery.
Mount Zhiti in Fuzhou is the site of the Bodhisattva Tianguan’s practice;
the King offered him the seven precious gems.
He cast one thousand images of the Buddha wearing celestial crowns and established a monastery there;
its grandeur and magnificence were preeminent throughout the Seven Min region.
In the first month of spring in the year of Dingwei,
the Liao troops arrived at Daliang.
The Jin Emperor, together with the Empress Dowager and those below them, submitted a memorial requesting surrender.
He went to meet him outside the Fengqiu Gate,
but the Liao ruler declined to see him and instead conferred upon the Jin Emperor the title of Marquis of Unrighteousness.
He was installed in Huanglongfu,
which is the city of Helong of the Murong Yan state.
The Lord of Liao changed his attire to adopt the robes and caps of China.
The hundred officials attended upon him as was the custom in former times.
He escorted the Jin Emperor, Empress Li, and Empress Ping northward,
accompanied by more than a hundred attendants from the inner palace and their retinue.
Three hundred cavalrymen from the Khitan escorted him.
In the second month, the Liao ruler returned to his capital and appointed Xiao Han as the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Daliang.
Han was the son of Empress Dowager Shulü’s elder brother;
his sister, moreover, became the empress of the Liao ruler.
Han first took "Piao" as his surname.
From this time on, the imperial clans of the Khitans all adopted the surname Xiao.
Shulü was the consort of the Great Ancestor Abaoji.
In the fourth month of summer, the Khitan ruler returned to Lincheng and fell ill.
When the illness of Luancheng became critical,
he arrived at Shahu Lin on the day of Bingzi and passed away.
The people of the country cut open his belly, filled it with several pecks of salt, and carried him northward.
The people of Jin called it "the Imperial Carcass.
Initially, Liu Zhiyuan, the Regional Inspector of Hedong,
heard that the Liao Emperor had entered Bianjing.
He divided his troops to guard the four borders to prevent incursions.
Thereupon, his generals and aides urged him to assume the title of Emperor and issue commands to the four quarters;
however, Zhiyuan did not consent.
The soldiers all said,
"Now that the Khitans have seized the Son of Heaven, the empire has no lord. Guo Wei,
the Director of Personnel for the Fan and Han regions, and Yang Bin, the Commander-in-Chief, urge him to accept the succession."
Zhiyuan followed this advice.
On the *xīnwèi* day of the second month,
he ascended the imperial throne and subsequently changed the era name to the twelfth year of Tiānfú.
The national name was changed to Han.
When Xiao Han of the Khitans heard that the Emperor of Han had arrived in the south with his army,
he intended to return north.
Fearing that China would be without a ruler,
there was at that time Li Congyi, the son of Emperor Mingzong of the Tang,
who was in Luoyang with his mother, Empress Dowager Wang Shufei.
Han welcomed him and stood by his side;
he was thus made Emperor.
He led the chieftains of the You tribes to pay him homage.
When the hundred officials came to pay their respects,
the Consort Shu wept and said,
"We, mother and son, are so lowly and weak."
"The positions held by these gentlemen will bring calamity to my family.
Han then requested that one thousand Yan troops remain to guard the various gates as an additional escort for Yisuo’s personal protection.
Han then took his leave and departed.
When the Han Emperor arrived at Luoyang,
he commanded Guo Congyi, the Defense Commissioner of Zhengzhou,
to enter Daliang first to purge the government offices and execute Li Congyi and Empress Dowager Wang Shu.
When the Han Emperor arrived at Daliang,
he further established the city of Bianzhou as the capital, Chengjing,
and took "Han" as the name of his state.
The above two rulers of the Jin dynasty combined for eleven years before being subsumed by the Han.
The Han was of the Liu clan; it ruled by the Water Virtue and had its capital at Bian. Its High Ancestor was the Hidden Emperor (Yindi). The High Ancestor’s name was Zhìyuǎn.
His name was changed to Gao.
He was a member of the Shatuo tribe,
whose ancestors had resided in Taiyuan for generations.
He served alongside the High Ancestor of Jin under Emperor Mingzong of the Tang.
When the High Ancestor of Jin ascended the throne,
he appointed Zhao Kuo-yuan as the Regional Commander of Baoyi Army.
He was transferred to the post of Regional Inspector of Hedong.
In the second year of the Kaoyun era, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Beiping.
When the Jin Emperor moved northward, [he followed].
The Emperor ascended the throne at Jinyang.
He reigned for two years.
His age was fifty-four. He styled his reign era Tianfu for two years and Qianyou for one year.
The year Wushen, the first year of Qiandao; the first year of Tiānlù of Emperor Shìzōng of the Great Liao.

In Zhàofēngxiáng (Wúyuè), Héngchū ascended the throne; in Chǔ Jīnnán, Bǎoyóng ascended the throne. It was the sixth year of Bǎodà of Táng, the eleventh year of Guǎngzhèng of Shǔ, and the sixth year of Qiánhé of Hàn. The first month.
The Emperor changed his name to Gao; on the day of Jiǎzǐ, the Old Man’s son fell ill.
On the day of Dīngchōu, he passed away in the Wànsuì Hall.
The death was kept secret and the funeral rites were not announced.
In the second month, he established his eldest son, Prince Yeong-woo, as the Crown Prince and invested him as King of Zhou.
When he ascended the imperial throne, he was eighteen years of age.
In the tenth month of winter—
Gao Conghui, Prince Wenxian of Nanping and Regional Inspector of Jingnan, passed away.
His son, Bao Rong, assumed the position of Acting Governor (Liuhou).
He governed for ten years.
He lived to the age of forty-one.
Emperor Yin (Yìndì) was named Chéngyòu;
he was the second son of the High Ancestor (Gāozǔ).
He reigned for three years.
His lifespan was twenty years. He styled his era Qianyou.
Jiyou (1009), the second year of Qianyou; the second year of Tianlu of the Great Liao.

Zhao Fengxiang was assassinated by Wu, Yue, and Chu; Xi Guang was assassinated by Jingnan Tang. In the seventh year of Baoda of Shu, and the twelfth year of Guangzheng of Han, [the Emperor] of Han was [assassinated] in the seventh year of Qianhe. National Teacher Shao’s name was Deshao.
He was the son of the Chen family of Longquan in Chuzhou.
At the age of fifteen, he left the household life;
at seventeen, he entered the monastic order under the tutelage of a teacher at Longgui Temple in his native prefecture.
He received the full precepts at Kaien-ji Temple in Shinshū in the second year of the Tongguang era of Emperor Zhuangzong of the Later Tang dynasty. Subsequently,
while traveling, he first visited Chan Master Tong of Mount Toudi.
Next, he visited Longya and Shushan.
In this manner, he traveled to study under fifty-four spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Finally, he arrived at Fuzhou in Jiangxi.
He visited Chan Master Fayan Yi.
Tired of formal inquiry, he merely followed along with the assembly.
One day, a monk asked Fayan:
"What is a single drop of water from the Cao source?
Nanquan said,
"This is a single drop of water from the Cao source."
The Master heard this by the side of his seat;
he was suddenly enlightened and reported it to Fayan.
The Eye said,
"In the future, you shall become a teacher to the king, causing the light of the ancestral Way to flourish.
He then returned to his original path.
While traveling to Mount Tiantai,
he beheld the traces left by the Chan Master Zhiyi of Zhizhe;
it was as if there were a karmic affinity from a previous life.
Initially, he stayed at White Sand.
At that time, Wang Hongchu—the Prince of Zhongyi of Wu-Yue—was serving as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Taizhou.
Having heard of the Master’s reputation, he invited him to come and inquire about the Way.
By this time, the second year of Qiandao,
the King had already succeeded to the throne of Wuyue;
he dispatched an envoy to welcome the Master and extend the rites due to a disciple.
The Venerable served as National Preceptor.
There was a śramaṇa named Yiji who transmitted the teachings of Tiantai Zhiyi;
he was none other than the Dharma Master Luoxi.
He repeatedly said to his teacher:
"The teachings of the Wise One have been distant for many years;
consequently, most have been lost and scattered."
The kingdom of Silla possesses its original texts in great abundance;
we pray that the Venerable Master, through your compassionate power, will procure them for us.
The Master then reported this to the King of Yue.
The King dispatched an envoy bearing the Master’s letter to that country;
having transcribed it in full, the envoy returned.
Thus, the complete texts of the Tiantai teachings have been preserved until the present day.
The Master possessed great power.
He had a verse that said:
"At the summit of Tongxuan Peak, it is not of this human world."
"There is no phenomenon outside the mind; the green mountains fill the eyes.
Fayan heard this and said, "This single verse alone can revive my school."
On the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month in the fifth year of the Kaibao era of Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty, he gathered his assembly to bid them farewell;
he then passed away in the lotus position atop Lotus Flower Peak at the age of eighty-two.
At sixty-five years of age,
the Master succeeded Chan Master Yiyu of Fayan.
This was the third year of Qiandu (Gengxu), the third year of Tianlu of the Great Liao.

Zhao Fengxiang: Wu, Yue, Chu, Jing, and Southern Tang. The eighth year of Baoda (Shu): Guangzheng 13. The eighth year of Qianhe (Han). Ma Xie'e, the Military Governor of Wuping, was the elder brother of Ma Xieguang.
He captured the Prince of Chu, Xi Guang, and killed him.
Xi E proclaimed himself the Military Governor of Wunan, Jingjiang, Ningyuan, and other regions, and surrendered to the Tang.
The Tang enfeoffed him as the King of Chu.
In the end, he was extinguished by the Tang dynasty.
The Ma clan was relocated to Jinling.
In the fourth month of summer.
According to the Han system, Guo Wei was appointed as the Guardian of the Capital at Ye and the Military Governor of Tianxiong,
while his position as Chief Secretary remained as before.
Guo Rong, General of the Right Gate Guard, was appointed as the Commander-in-Chief of the Inner Headquarters of Tianxiong.
Rong’s original surname was Chai; his father, Shouli, was the brother-in-law of Guo Wei.
As Wei had no son, he adopted Rong as his own.
In the fifth month, Wei received his mandate to depart and addressed the Emperor, saying:
"The Empress Dowager has served the former Emperor for a long time and has experienced many affairs of state.
Your Majesty, however, is still young in years."
There are matters for which one should receive their instructions and put them into practice:
personally welcome those who are loyal and trustworthy,
and distance oneself from the wicked and sycophantic.
Between good and evil, one must be clear and discerning.
Yang Bin, the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Right Vice President of the Council of State, and Concurrent Chancellor, shall preside over general administration.
Guo Wei, the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs and Concurrent Chief Secretary of the Palace, shall take charge of military campaigns.
Shi Hongzhao, Military Commissioner of the Gui De Commandery and Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guard, concurrently serving as Grand Secretary, was in charge of the imperial guard.
Wang Zhang, Director of the Three Departments and Acting Chancellor, oversaw the administration of finances.

Bīn and others were loyal and devoted, and the Emperor trusted and favored them; yet the Inner Guest-Attendant Yan Jìnqīng, the Imperial Secretariat’s Chief Secretary Niè Wénjìn, the Flying Dragon Attendant Hòu Kuānzàn, and the Tea and Wine Attendant of the Hanlín Academy Guō Yǔnmíng slandered the presiding officials.
As the Emperor grew older,
he grew weary of being constrained by the high ministers;
he subsequently conspired with the Grand Councillor for Confidential Affairs, Nie Wenjin, and with Zhang Yunming.
On the morning of the *bingzi* day of the eleventh month,
he had Wang Yanhong, Zhao Chongzhi, and Zhang Zhong executed beneath the eastern corridor of the Guangzheng Hall.
The Emperor dispatched the Palace Attendant Meng Ye.
Carrying a secret imperial edict, they went to Duanzhou and Ye-du to assassinate Wang Yin.

They also ordered Guo Chongwei, the Commander of Cavalry for the Ye-du Expeditionary Force, and Cao Wei, the Commander of Infantry, to kill Guo Wei and the Supervising Commissioner and Minister of Propaganda Wang Jun.
Guo Wei then gave the names Guo Chongwei and Cao Wei to the various generals and informed them of the unjust deaths of the Prince of Bin and the others, saying:
I and you gentlemen cleared away the thorns and briars to follow the late Emperor in seizing the empire,
and I was entrusted with the responsibility for his orphaned heir.
"I exerted my utmost strength to protect the state.
Now that all you gentlemen have perished,
with what heart could I live on alone?"
"You gentlemen should carry out the imperial decree and take my head to report to the Son of Heaven;
in this way, you will not be implicated.
Guo Chongwei and the others wept and said:
The Son of Heaven is still young;
this must surely be the doing of the petty sycophants around him.
I pray that you will accompany me to the court to present our grievances and sweep away these vermin to purify the imperial administration.
He could not be killed by a single messenger.
Guo Wei then left his foster son Rong to govern the capital of Ye,
and ordered Guo Chongwei to lead the cavalry as the vanguard.
He personally led a great army to follow them as far as Fengqiu.
In the eleventh month, the Emperor dispatched Murong Yanchao and others to lead troops to resist them;
Yanchao and his men were defeated in battle and fled back.
On this day, Emperor Di went out to inspect the troops.
When the army was defeated, he alone remained with several dozen palace attendants and stayed overnight at Qili Camp;
all others had fled and dispersed.
On the dawn of the day of Yiyou, the Emperor spurred his horse toward the palace and reached Xuanhua Gate.
Liu Zhu, stationed atop the gate, questioned the Emperor:
"Where are your attendants and troops?"
He shot arrows to the left and right.
The Emperor turned his chariot northwest toward Zhao Village;
by then, the pursuing troops had already arrived.
He dismounted and entered a private residence,
where he was assassinated by the rebel troops.
Guo Wei then entered through the Yongchun Gate.
On the day of Dinghai, Guo Wei led the hundred officials to the Mingde Gate to pay their respects to the Empress Dowager.
He submitted a formal petition requesting that she establish a successor to the throne for the sake of the military and state affairs.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict and decree appointing Liu Yūn—the son of Liu Chóng, the Regional Inspector of Hedong—to ascend the imperial throne as Emperor.
On the day of Gengyin, Wei led his ministers in a memorial,
stating that he had dispatched the Grand Preceptor Ping Dao to Xuzhou to welcome [the Emperor] in person.
The Emperor had been at the palace for nearly ten days when he requested that the Empress Dowager take the throne to attend to the affairs of state.
On the *renchen* day, the Empress Dowager finally ascended the throne.
Guo Wei crossed the river and took up residence in Chenzhou.
On the day of Guichou, the generals and soldiers raised a great clamor, established him as their leader, and escorted him southward.
Wei then submitted a memorial to the Empress Dowager.
I request that you attend to the ancestral temple of the Han dynasty.
With the Empress Dowager as mother,
the Military Commissioner of Wuning, Yan’yun, has already arrived at Songzhou.
Guo Wei sent a letter to Yao Yun stating that he had been pressured by various generals and was summoning Feng Dao to return first. Yun asked, "What plan do we have now?
Dao remained silent.
On the *jǐwèi* day of the twelfth month,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict deposing Emperor Yūn as the Duke of Xiāngyīn and appointing Guō Wēi,
Grand Master for Palace Attendants, to oversee the affairs of state. On the *dīngmǎo* day of the first month of spring in the *xīnhài* year:
The Han Empress Dowager issued an edict bestowing upon him the seals and insignia of the Regent,
and he ascended the throne as Emperor. The Regent Wei entered the palace through the Gaomen Gate and took his place on the throne in the Chongyuan Hall.
The Imperial Edict stated:
"I am a descendant of the House of Zhou and a scion of King Wen.
The name of my state should be Zhou."
On the day Wutyin of this month, he killed the Duke of Xiangyin at Songzhou.
Thus, the two rulers of Han together ruled for four years before returning [the mandate] to Zhou.
As for Zhou, the surname was Guo; they ruled by the virtue of Wood, with their capital at Daliang. The founders were Taizu, Shizong, and Gongdi. Taizu’s personal name was Wei.
His courtesy name was Zhongwen.
He was a native of Yao Mountain in Xingzhou.
His father, Jian, served the Jin dynasty as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Shunzhou.
Wei was orphaned at a young age and lived with the Chang family of Luzhou.
When Li Jitao, the Regional Commander (Liuhou) of Luzhou, recruited brave men for his army,
Wei, at the age of eighteen, enlisted on account of his courage and physical strength.
In the second year of the Tiānfú era of the Jìn dynasty, Fàn Yángguāng rebelled in Wèizhōu.
Wēi was then a soldier who had previously followed Yáng Guǎnyuǎn on the northern expedition.
Wei Jiu had previously been a subordinate of Liu Zhiyuan.
When he learned that Zhiyuan had requested him to remain,
people asked him the reason for this.
Wei said,
"Lord Yang possesses the talent for guile and deception,
but lacks the spirit of a hero."
"What use is it for me to obtain you?
Only Lord Liu could truly employ me.
Later, Zhizhong served as the Commandant of the Imperial Bodyguard.
When Zhao Yi ascended the imperial throne,
Wei Zan assisted him with merit and was appointed as a Participant in Governance alongside the Secretariat and Chancellery (Tongzhongshu Menxia Pingchangshi).
During the reign of Emperor Yin of the Later Han, he repeatedly established military achievements.
He served as the Leftover Guardian (Liushou) of the capital city of Ye.
In the eleventh month of the third year of the Qianguyu era of the Later Han, Emperor Yindi was assassinated,
and [the new] Emperor ascended the throne.
He reigned for three years.
His life span was fifty-two years.
In the third year of Guǎngshùn, the *xīn-hài* year, the first year of Guǎngshùn (951), Muzong ascended the throne in the ninth month of the fourth year of Tiānlù of the Great Liao.
The first year of the Yingli era: one thousand nine hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Buddha.

It was the fourth year of Qianguo of the state of Northern Zhao; the ninth year of Baoda of Fenyang, Wuyue, Jingnan, and the Tang; the fourteenth year of Guangzheng of Shu; and the ninth year of Qianhe of Han. Regarding Northern Han: at the beginning of its founding, Liu Chong served as the Regional Inspector of Hedong and concurrently as Grand Chancellor.
He was the younger brother of the late Emperor Gao’s maternal grandmother.
When the High Ancestor ascended the throne,
he appointed Chong as the Governor of Taiyuan and Acting Commissioner for the Northern Capital.
When Emperor Yin of the Han dynasty was assassinated, he intended to raise an army and march southward.
Upon hearing that his son, Yūn, had been welcomed as emperor,
he desisted, saying, "My son shall be emperor."
"What more could I seek?
When Emperor Taizu of Zhou replaced the Han dynasty and killed Liu Yūn at Songzhou,
Li Chong was filled with great rage.
On this day, he ascended the imperial throne at Jinyang.
He established the state name as Han and designated the year as the fourth year of Qianyou.
In the second month, the Liao ruler, hearing that the Northern Han had been established,
dispatched the Commander-in-Chief Pan Yulian to send a letter to his son, Liu Chengjun.
The Ruler of Han ordered Chengjun to reply, stating:
As the native dynasty had fallen into ruin,
he wished to follow the precedent of the Jin court by seeking assistance and requesting troops;
the Liao ruler was greatly pleased.
In the fourth month of summer, the Han ruler sent Zheng Gou to deliver a letter to Liao, addressing himself as a nephew and requesting the performance of the investiture rites.
The Liao Emperor ordered Prince Yan Shuyi to confer the title of Great Han Shenwu Emperor upon the Han ruler.
His name was changed to Min.
In the ninth month, the Emperor of Liao personally led an army to aid the Han,
reaching Huoshendian in Xinzhou.
Yanwang Shugui and Dainingwang Ouseng, the son of Weiwang, led troops in a rebellion and assassinated the Emperor.
Shuyi then established himself as ruler.
Shulü, the Prince of Qi and son of Taizong, fled to the Southern Mountains.
The various ministers honored him and attacked Shu Che-yu, killing him;
they then established Shu-lü as emperor along with his kinsmen and changed the era name to Ying-li.
He was buried at Mount Yiwu;
his temple name was Shizong.
He reigned for a total of five years.
Emperor Tianshun of the Liao dynasty, known as Emperor Muzong,
whose personal name was Jing and whose tribal name was Shulü.
He was later renamed Ming.
He was the eldest son of Taizong.
Initially, when Taizong was attacking Shi Jin...
Liu Di remained in attendance upon Empress Dowager Shulü.
When Emperor Taizong passed away,
the generals enthroned Shizong.
When King Sejong was assassinated,
the generals welcomed the Emperor to ascend the throne;
he proceeded from Hwasin-dae to enter the capital at Uiju.
The Emperor was young and fond of amusements, neglecting affairs of state.
Every night he drank until intoxicated,
only falling asleep at dawn.
He rose at noon;
the people of the country called him the "Sleeping King.
He reigned for eighteen years.
Yongming: The Chan Master of Yongming Temple in Hangzhou,
named Daoyan,
was a native of Hezhong Prefecture.
His surname was Wu.
Initially, he went to visit Chan Master Fayen Yi.
Fayen asked him:
The Master asked, "Aside from what you have requested to study, what sutra are you currently reading?
The Master replied, "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Nanquan said:
To which category do the six aspects—totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration—belong?
The Master replied: "The text is found within the *Daśabhūmika-parivarta*.
According to principle, however, all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, are endowed with these six aspects."
Yanjian said,
"Is emptiness itself endowed with the six characteristics or not?
The Master was bewildered and had no reply.
Yanguan said, "You asked me;
now you, Master, must ask. Thereupon, the Master asked.
"Emptiness also possesses the six characteristics; is it not so?
The Master said, "Emptiness.
Thereupon, the teacher attained enlightenment.
On another day, when some men and women arrived at the monastery,
Layman Yan asked the Master,
"The Vinaya states that if one hears the sound of hairpins and bracelets from the next room, it constitutes a violation of the precepts."
Seeing gold and silver intermingled and crimson and purple robes crowded together, he asked, "Is this breaking the precepts or not?
The Master said,
"A fine point of entry."
The Eye said,
"In the future, you shall have five hundred disciples who will be held in high esteem by kings and lords."
The Master then paid his respects and took his leave, taking up residence at an ancient temple in Quzhou where he read the Tripitaka.
Upon reaching this point, in the first year of the Guangshun era, King Hongchu, the Loyal and Magnanimous Ruler of Wuyue, invited the Master into his palace to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
He was conferred the title of Chan Master Cihua Dinghui.
He established a great monastery on the Southern Mountain called Huirì Yongmíng.
He requested that the Master reside there.
The Master then invited the Arhats from beneath the stupa to the new temple,
which fulfilled the King’s prior dream.
Thereupon, the two characters "Arhat" (Yingzhen) were further added to his title.
The Master entered nirvana in the fifth year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty. He was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Yi of Fayan;
[he was also known as] Chan Master Yongming Zhijue of Huiri Temple in Hangzhou.
His name was Yanshou.
He was of the Wang clan of Yuhang.
