wielding a blade, he assassinated the Emperor at Mount Hei.
It was the ninth month.
He was posthumously titled Emperor Tianshun,
and his temple name was Muzong.
Jingzong ascended the throne.
His taboo name was Mingji,
and he changed his name to Xian.
Sejong originally desired to have a son.
When Sejong was assassinated,
the Emperor was nine years old.
Liu Jielǐ, a member of the Imperial Kitchen and the Office of Food, bound him with felt and hid him among a pile of firewood, thereby saving his life.
Upon reaching this point, he ascended the throne;
however, afflicted by a wind-related illness, he frequently failed to attend court.
He passed away in the twelfth month of the ninth year of Ganhung, the Renwu year.
His posthumous title was Emperor Xiaocheng,
and his temple name was Jingzong.
Jisi (1969), the second year of the Kaibao era; the second year of Baoning of the Liao dynasty’s Emperor Jingzong;
the second year of Guangyun of the Northern Han’s Emperor Jiyuan; the second year of Tang of Wuyue; and the spring, sixteenth day of the second month, of the Southern Han.
On the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday,
an imperial edict was issued permitting monks from throughout the four seas to submit petitions to enter the palace courtyard for a competition in the Three Studies (Tripiṭaka).
The Kaifeng Prefecture’s Commissioner for Merit was then ordered to select ten monks to serve as examiners for the scriptural, disciplinary, and doctrinal exegesis.
Those who were fully proficient were granted purple robes and titled as "Wubiao Seng" (Monks of Universal Manifestation).
This continued until the fourth year of Taiping Xingguo during the reign of Emperor Taizong.
The Grand Secretary Gongde submitted a memorial stating that,
as the whole world is now one family, there is no need for individual petitions.

From this point forward, on the Emperor’s birthday, the Chancellor, the Princes, the Surveillance Commissioners, and the Prefects shall each recommend three monks from the Three Schools whom they know well.
Only those recommended by the Monastic Registrars of the two streets enter the palace on that day to receive a certificate from the Department of State Affairs;
this is called the "Monastic Title Conferred Before the Curtain."
He was further granted a purple robe,
known as the "Purple Robe before the Curtain.
Once the distribution was complete, he was then granted a vegetarian feast along with the others.
As for the other kings, lords, and recommenders,
they were permitted to come forth only on alternate days;
their movements were strictly regulated and their conduct was subject to inspection.
The local governors and prefects, in turn, transmitted and bestowed [the copies] upon the monks; this is recorded in the *Sengshi lüe*.
It was the Gengwu year, the third year of Kaibao (970); the third year of Baoning of the Liao; the third year of Guangyun of Northern Han;
and the years of Wuyue, Tang, and Nanhhan. [Emperor] Chao of Nanhhan surrendered; Nanhhan comprised Lingnan and Guang.
Liu Yan surrendered the entire state to the Song.
From the time Liu Yan was granted amnesty until the abolition of his state, sixty-seven years had passed.
In this year, an imperial edict was issued to renovate the ancient Fenshan Temple in the capital, renaming it Kai Bao Si.
It faces the main street in front and is bordered to the north by the Wuzhang River;
it contains several thousand rooms.

The land spanned several wards and reached the height of magnificence; according to Li Tao’s *Changbian* (Long Compilation) on the facts of the Imperial Dynasty, this was the fourth year of Kaibao (*Xinwei*), the fourth year of Baoning in the Liao dynasty.

In the fourth year of Guangyun of the Later Han, on the eleventh day of the sixth month of the Tang [calendar], an imperial edict was issued for the re-carving of one set of the Buddhist canon in golden characters at Chengdu; this is recorded in the *Song sengshi lüe* (Abridged History of Buddhist Monks of the Song) and the *Xinian lu* (Chronological Records).
Ren-shen, the fifth year of Kaibao; the fifth year of Baoning of the Liao.
The fifth year of Guangyun of Northern Han. In the Wu-Yue, the Tang Emperor personally led military campaigns to pacify the various kingdoms.
Throughout his life, he produced several collections of Buddhist scriptures inscribed in gold and silver characters.
This year, by imperial decree, one collection of Buddhist scriptures was carved for printing, totaling 130,000 woodblocks;
these are recorded in the "Section on Faith" of the *Beishan lu*.
Guiyou (10th day of the 10th month), the sixth year of Kaibao: In the first month, Emperor Gong of the Zhou and Liao dynasties passed away.

The sixth year of Baoning; the first year of Jiyuan in Northern Han; the sixth year of Guangyun in Wu and Southern Tang under the Li clan. Jiayou, the seventh year of Kaibao: The first year of Qianheng in Liao.
In the seventh year of Guangyun of the Northern Han, the Emperor of Tang of Wuyue ordered Cao Bin, Pan Mei, and Cao Han to campaign against the Southern Tang in Jiangnan.
In the eleventh month, they crossed the river with their forces.
Bīn had once received an imperial edict in person not to kill anyone.
The following winter, when they attacked and were on the verge of victory,
Bīn feigned illness and did not oversee the army.
Pan Mei led the various generals to visit him.
Yang Bin said,
"My illness cannot be cured by medicine or acupuncture."
He said, "All you gentlemen must take a public oath:
if no one kills when the city is breached, it shall naturally subside.
The generals agreed.
They burned incense together to swear an oath.
On that day, Jinling (Jiankang) was captured,
and the Li family surrendered.
Within the city, all remained in their assigned positions.
Fan Bin rose to the rank of Shixiang;
father and son were enshrined together to receive offerings in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
That his noble prosperity has endured for generations is truly the karmic retribution for not having committed murder. (From Li Tao’s *Changbian*: Original Biography of Cao Bin of Dongdu.
Year Yihai, the eighth year of Kaibao [975]; the second year of Qianheng of the Liao dynasty [981]. In the third month, he went on a diplomatic mission to Song.
The Song dynasty first established diplomatic relations with Liao during the eighth year of Guangyun of the Northern Han.

In the summer, fourth month of the Bingzi year, Li Xie of Wuyue—having previously submitted to the Southern Tang—surrendered to the Song and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Weiming; thirty-nine years after its founding, the state of the Northern Han was extinguished.
The Emperor visited the Western Capital and performed sacrifices at the Southern Suburb on the twenty-second day of the twelfth month of that year.
This was revised as the first year of the Taiping Xingguo era in *Rongzhai Xubi*.
Regarding Emperor Taizong: his taboo name was Jiǔng, and he was the younger brother of the Great Grandmother.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jin.
In the ninth year of Kaibao, Emperor Taizu passed away,
and the Emperor ascended the throne.
At the age of thirty-eight,
he laid down arms and cultivated culture,
renaming the Jangwu Hall (Hall for Military Training) as the Chongjeong Hall (Hall of Exalted Government).
In selecting worthy and virtuous individuals, one must carefully choose the Provincial Governors (Cishi).
It is said that the Cishi are those most intimately connected with the people;
if they are not the right persons, the people will suffer their calamities.
He sought out words of counsel and accepted remonstrance;
the social customs were refined and wholesome.
He occupied the throne for twenty-one years.
His age was fifty-nine.
He passed away on the seventeenth day of the tenth month.
[The following are the years of his reign: Qianming Jie (one year), Taiping Xingguo (eight years), Yongxi (four years), Duanqiong (two years), Tinghua (five years), and Zhidao (three years).
The twelfth month of the Bingzi year marks the first year of Taiping Xingguo; it is the third year of Qianheng in the Liao dynasty.

It is the ninth year of Guangyun in the Northern Han. The Dingchou year marks the second year of Taiping Xingguo; it is the fourth year of Qianheng in the Liao dynasty. It is the Ruyue [Wuyue] period.

In the tenth year of the Guangyun era of the Northern Han, the former Longxing Temple in the capital of Wuyue had been abolished by Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty and converted into the Longxing Granary. At this time,
the presiding monk struck the Dengwen Drum to petition for the restoration of the temple.
The Emperor was moved by this and issued an edict to restore it.
He bestowed upon it the name Taiping Xingguo Temple and provided funds for its reconstruction on an exceptionally grand scale.
(From the *Huangming Shiyuan*).
Wu-yin (March 23), the third year of Taiping Xingguo; the fifth year of Qianheng in the Liao dynasty;
the eleventh year of Guangyun in the Northern Han. In the third month, the ruler of Wuyue submitted a memorial to the court and surrendered his territory.
In the fourth month, Qian Chu, the Prince Zhongyi of Wuyue, submitted a memorial to return to the Song dynasty and enter the imperial court,
offering up the territories of all thirteen prefectures.
On the thirteenth day of the eighth month of autumn, Chen Hongjin submitted a memorial offering the two prefectures of Zhangzhou and Quanzhou.

On that same day, the Hanlin Scholar and Director of the Chizhao Office Li Fang, the Palace Attendant Hu Meng, the Secretariat Drafter Li Mu, Song Bai, Zheng Linji, and Xu Xuan, by imperial decree, presented the *Tàipíng guǎngjì* (Extensive Records of the Taiping Era).
The volumes were completed as five hundred fascicles.
The cataloging of the Buddha-dharma comprised thirty fascicles.
The śramaṇa Zanning accompanied the King of Wuyue to the imperial court.
The Emperor bestowed upon him the title of Great Master Tonghui and issued an edict for him to reside at Tianshou Temple in the Left Ward,
ordering him to compile the History of the Sangha.
The following year, an imperial decree ordered Ning to travel by post station to present the true-body śarīra of Śākyamuni Buddha from Ayuwang Mountain in Mingzhou;
it was then brought into the inner palace for veneration.
One *śarīra* relic was obtained.
Consequently, the ground northwest of Baosi was excavated to construct an eleven-story pagoda;
a celestial palace was fashioned at its base to enshrine it. (From the *Huángcháo Shìyuàn*).
In the tenth month of the seventh year of the Taiping Xingguo era,
an imperial edict was issued ordering Ning to compile the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*,
permitting him to return to Zhedong to take up his pen.
Initially, in the eighteenth year of the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
the śramaṇa Huìjiǎo of Jiāxiáng Monastery composed the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gāosēng zhuàn*).
It covers the period from the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Míng of the Later Han to the completion of the work during the Tianjian era, totaling fourteen fascicles.
In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty,
Vinaya Master Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery on Mount Zhongnan composed the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Spanning from the Tianjian era down to the completion of the work during the Zhenguan era, it consists of thirty fascicles.
It was begun in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty and completed in the first year of the Duan-gong era, comprising thirty fascicles.
Following the precedents and principles of the Liang and Tang dynasties, it is organized into ten categories.
First, the section on translating the scriptures;
second, the section on wisdom and understanding;
third, the section on meditative concentration.
4. The Section on Precepts and Discipline;
5. The Section on Protecting the Dharma;
and the Section on Great Resonance and Response.
7. The Section on Relinquishing the Body;
8. The Section on Recitation and Chanting;
9. The Section on Cultivating Merit.
In the *Shi zha ke sheng de* (Ten Miscellaneous Categories of Eminent Virtue),
there are five hundred and thirty-three individuals recorded in the main transmission,
and one hundred and thirty individuals recorded in supplementary entries.
In the tenth month of winter in the first year of the Duangong era,
he dispatched his disciples Xianzhong and Zhilun to the imperial court to present a memorial.
An imperial letter was bestowed upon them, along with silk, as a reward and encouragement.
An imperial edict was issued for its inclusion in the Tripitaka for circulation.
In the eleventh month, an edict commanded Ning to proceed to the capital.
In the first year of the Chunhua era, he received an imperial decree to compose the *Record of Sages and Worthies on Vulture Peak* in one hundred fascicles.
In the second year of the Chunhua era,
an imperial edict was issued appointing Ning as a compiler for the Imperial Archives to edit the *Essentials of the Dynastic Succession and Eras of Emperors*.
In the second year of the Zhizhao era, [the work was completed].
By imperial decree, Dao Ning was appointed to oversee religious affairs in the capital of Luoyang; this is recorded in the Postscript to the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*.
In the first year of the Xianping era of Emperor Zhenzong (the Wuxu year), by imperial decree, Dao Ning was promoted to the position of Right Street Supervisor of Monks (*youjie senglu*) in Bianjing.
He presided over the administrative affairs of the Buddhist community.
The following year, he was promoted to the Left Street (Zuojie).
In the second month of spring in the second year of the Xianping era, the Jihai year.
Zanning, Grand Master Tonghui, Director of the Monastic Registry for the Left Ward of Tokyo, Compiler for the Historiographic Institute, and Overseer of Religious Affairs,
passed away at the age of eighty-two.
In the third month, his entire body was interred at Tiānshòu Monastery.
In the seventh year of the Tiānshèng era of Emperor Rénzōng (the Jǐsī year),
Níng’s great-great-grandson Zōngshèng opened the stupa and performed the cremation.
He collected the remains and *śarīra* relics and returned to bury them in his ancestral home in Qiantang.
Ning was born in Lin’an County, Hangzhou.
During the Tiānchéng era of Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng, he left the household life at Xiángfú Monastery in Hángzhōu.
Upon the accession of Lù Wáng [Lì Yì] during the Qīngtài era, he traveled to Tiāntái to thoroughly investigate the Vinaya-piṭaka,
becoming widely versed in the Tripiṭaka.
Wuyue Zhongyi Wang appointed Buning as the Unified Head of the Two Monastic Quarters (Liangjie Sengtong),
bestowing upon him the title Great Master Mingyi Zongwen.
His *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha) and *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of the Sangha) both circulated throughout the world, as did his "Record of the Pagoda at Qiantang."
Ji-mao (己卯), the fourth year of Taiping Xingguo (太平興國); the sixth year of Qianheng (乾亨) of the Liao dynasty.

In the fifth month, Liu Jiyuan (劉繼元) of Taiyuan surrendered to the Song and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Pengcheng (彭城公). [The state of] Beihan (北漢) had existed for twenty-nine years before its extinction. Gengchen (庚辰), the fifth year of Taiping Xingguo; the sixth year of Qianheng of the Liao dynasty.

Regarding the translation of scriptures: the śramaṇa Fajin, who propagated the teachings of both the Exoteric and Esoteric traditions at the Prefecture of Hezhong, requested that the Tripitaka Master Dharmadeva from the Western Regions translate scriptures at Pujin.
By imperial decree, he was summoned to the capital.
At the commencement of the project of translation, an imperial decree was issued for fifty youths to study Sanskrit; this is the General Catalogue of Translated Scriptures.
Xinsi (the year 981), the sixth year of Taiping Xingguo, the eighth year of Qianheng of the Liao dynasty.
An imperial edict established [him] as the Vice Director of the Right Street of the Sangha Registry.
An imperial edict ordered the performance of a sacrificial rite for the Great Being Baozhi of Mount Zhong in Jiankang,
and a stele inscription was granted, bestowing upon him the title "Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dao-lin Zhen-jue."
Renwu, the seventh year of Taiping Xingguo (the ninth year of Qianheng in the Liao dynasty).
In the twelfth month, the Emperor passed away.
He had reigned for fifteen years.
He was posthumously titled Emperor Xiaocheng, with the temple name Jingzong.
An imperial edict established the Translation and Propagation Court at the western side of Taiping Xingguo Temple in the Eastern Capital,
following the precedents of the Tang dynasty.
The Chancellor was appointed as the Commissioner for Translating and Polishing the Scriptures,
and officials were established with their respective duties.
From the monastery of Vikramaśīla in the country of Jalandhara in Central India, the Tripiṭaka Master Dānaśīla arrived from the Western Heavens.

Together with Fatiān, Śīlagupta, and others, he translated the *Mahāyāna-alaṃkāra-rāja-sūtra*. The Emperor composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Newly Translated Tripiṭaka of the Great Song," and issued an edict permitting the tonsure of all youths throughout the empire into the monastic order.
Not restricted by the standard regulations of the officials,

from the first year to the eighth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, a total of over one hundred and seventy thousand people were ordained as monks, according to the *Sengshi lüe* (Brief History of the Sangha).
During the Great Liao, Emperor Shengzong ascended the throne.
His taboo name was Longxu.
He was the eldest son of Jingzong.
He ascended the throne at the age of twelve.
He changed the era name to Tonghe and enthroned his mother, Lady Xiao, as Empress Dowager Chengtian.
She presided over the court for a total of twenty-seven years.
He then returned the administration to the Emperor.
On the day of Guichou, he changed the era name to Kāitai (Opening Prosperity) and restored the national name to Daqieyin Qidan (Great Khitan).
On the third day of the sixth month in the tenth year of Taiping, he passed away at the Upper Capital.
His posthumous title was Emperor Tianfu.
He reigned for forty-nine years.
Guiwei, the eighth year of Taiping Xingguo (983 CE). The Liao dynasty’s Shengzong ascended the throne;
it was the first year of Tonghe.
The Emperor offered praise for the śarīra. Previously, Taizu had welcomed them from Luoyang.
During the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty,
the Buddha-tooth relic offered by Prince Jiahuang was enshrined at the Guanding Yuan of Xiangguo Si in the Eastern Capital.
The Great Śramaṇa Vinaya Master Xuanchao [was appointed its guardian].
At this point, the Emperor personally subjected it to a trial by heating it with a fierce flame.
It remained crystalline, bright, firm, and solid, its five-colored luster illuminating those around him.
The Emperor composed a eulogy, saying:
The seals are perfectly formed through the accumulation of merits over kalpas;
were it not for Master Xuanchan of the South Mountain, it would likely have been difficult to obtain this transmission.
With one's own eyes, one beholds several layers of lustrous golden radiance.
Held in hand, a single jade fragment glows with chilling brilliance;
when refined through a hundred fires, its spiritual essence penetrates through;
hidden for a thousand years, its lustrous radiance remains complete.
The cultivation of the true secret through the fruit of meditative concentration—
do not regard this with a casual mind.
He renamed the Kanjō-in (Consecration Hall) as the Hoke-in (Lotus Sutra Hall).
A multi-storied pavilion was constructed,
with Dharma Master Huizhao Huiwen presiding over the incense offerings for the Nanshan Śarīra Stele.
This was in the year Jiashen, the first year of the Yongxi era (984 CE), the second year of the Liao Tonghe era.
In the third month of spring, the Japanese monk Ryōnen entered the imperial court;
he remarked that his country had transmitted its lineage for eighty generations and had passed through three thousand two hundred years.
The Emperor said to his ministers,
"Since the late Tang and the Five Dynasties, China has been divided;
not only have its rulers risen to power one morning only to collapse the following evening."
Your subjects have likewise met with execution one after another. I,
the Emperor, am filled with trepidation as I seek to govern,
hoping that the High Heaven will look upon me with favor and provide for the long-term security of my descendants.
"You all have also preserved your hereditary rank and emoluments," as recorded in the *Shengzheng Lu* (Record of Sacred Governance) of thirteen dynasties.
An imperial edict was issued to repair the Sīguā Stūpa in Sīzhōu,
and the posthumous title "Dàshèng" (Great Sage) was added.
The temple is called Zhao Pu Benzhuan.
In the tenth month, an imperial edict summoned the recluse Chen Tuan for an audience,
and he was granted the title Master Xiyi.
He was subsequently invited to return to Mount Hua.
*Yǒngxī* Year 2 (Bǐyǒu), the third year of Liao Tǒnghé;
*Yǒngxī* Year 3 (Bǐxū), the fourth year of Liao Tǒnghé.
On the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month of autumn,
the eminent monk Wuen of Xiushui passed away while sitting upright facing west.
He had originally belonged to the Tiantai school.
Originally, from the third year of the Jianzhong era of Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty, five generations after the passing of the Venerable Jingxi,
the lineage reached Qingsong. Song had two disciples, namely Xiji.
It is said that the intent is based on the *Ji jiaokuan zhengmai* (The Correct Pulse of Silent Contemplation and Teaching), transmitted through Yitong;
Yitong transmitted it to Zhili, the Venerable Four Ming, Zunshe, and the Chan Master of Xiazhu.
The transmission was received in an unending succession;
his resolve was nurtured through the grace of personal instruction.
His fame for such kindness is recorded in the annals of the monastic history.
En transmitted it to Hong Min; Won transmitted it to Cheong;
Cheong transmitted it to Jihwon, the Dharma Master Gushan;
Qiao transmitted it to Jiqi and Xianrun.
Regarding the various masters who each held their own interpretations of the objects of contemplation (*ālambana*),
the view (*vipaśyanā*), and the stages of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*),
Zhili of Siming refuted them with eloquence. The lineage of Mount Heng subsequently denounced these as the "Mountain-Outside" (*shanwai*) school within the Tiantai teachings.
Dinghai (the 4th year of the Yongxi era; the 5th year of the Tonghe era of the Liao dynasty), the tenth month:
Dharma Master Xiji (Jingguang) of Dinghui Monastery, the sixth-generation successor of the Tiantai teacher Jingxi Zunzhe and the lineage holder of Luoxi Chuanjiao, entered nirvana.
The meaning of this is consistent with the original biography.
In Chengdu, the capital of Yizhou on the western road of Sichuan, there was the Chan Master named Chengyuan of Xianglin Monastery;
he entered nirvana in the second month.
The Master was born in Mianzhu, Hanzhou, Xichuan, into the Shangguan clan.
He succeeded Chan Master Yunmen Wenyan in the transmission of the lamp.
This was the year Wuzi (the first year of the Duan-gong era), the sixth year of the Tonghe era of the Liao dynasty.
Master Yitong transmitted the Tiantai teachings.
On the eighteenth day of the tenth month of this year, he entered nirvana at Baoyun Monastery in Mingzhou.
Tong was originally of the royal lineage of Goryeo.
At the beginning of his monastic life, he was renowned for his transmission of the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda*.
During the Tiānfú era of the Shí Jìn dynasty, he crossed the sea to visit Luóxī Xījì,
whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment and realized the profound principle of the perfect interpenetration of the ten dharma-realms.

The succession of the Dharma and its circulation have spanned more than two *ji* (twenty-four years). It is known that Zhi Li, a high disciple who followed the ritual forms, further expanded this transmission;
thus, this record of the stupa is composed.

The year Jǐchǒu (6th year of Duāngǒng), the second year of Emperor Jiànkāi, the temple was completed. The seventh year of Liao Tǒnghé, the year Gēngyīn (1st year of Chúnhuà). The eighth year of Liao Tǒnghé.
The Emperor issued an edict to Su Yijian, the Participant in State Affairs,
to compile the biographies of the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings.
Su Yijian submitted a memorial.
Zanning, the Great Master Tonghui of Tiānshòu Monastery,
and the Daoist Han Depun, an official of the Dàyǐ rank, jointly oversaw these matters. Zanning, the Great Master Tonghui,
composed the *Record of Sages and Worthies of Vulture Peak* in one hundred fascicles.
Xinmao, the second year of Chunhua (941 CE); the ninth year of Liao Tonghe.
Rencheng, the third year of Chunhua (942 CE); the tenth year of Liao Tonghe.
Guisi, the fourth year of Chunhua (943 CE); the eleventh year of Liao Tonghe.
Shoushan: Chan Master Shoushan of Ruzhou,
named Shengnian,
was the son of the Di family from Lai Prefecture.
He received his monastic training at Nanchan Temple in his native commandery.
As soon as he had completed the full ordination, he traveled extensively among the monastic assemblies,
constantly reciting the Lotus Sūtra in secret.
The multitude named him Nian Fahua.
He received the prediction and transmission from Chan Master Xuefeng Zhao and was the first patriarch at Shoushan for the opening of the Dharma.
Next, while residing at Guangjiao and Baoying Monasteries in Ye County, Ruzhou,
he ascended the hall at noon on the fourth day of the twelfth month of the third year of the Chunhua era (982) and spoke this verse:
This year I am seventy-six years old;
following conditions as they arise, I pass the days.
This year, however, I record the matters of the coming year.
"Mark this very day for next year.
On the fourth day of the twelfth month of that year, he took leave of the assembly and ascended the hall,
whereupon he spoke this verse:
The silver world and the golden body—
sentient and insentient beings are one true reality;
when light and darkness are exhausted, neither shines forth.
In the afternoon, he manifested his entire body as the sun’s orb;
having finished speaking, he passed away peacefully.
His remains were cremated, the relics were collected, and a stupa was erected.
The Master succeeded Fengxue Yanzhao;
Yanzhao succeeded Nanyuan Huiyong;
Huiyong succeeded Xinghua Cunjang.
The successors of Chan Master Linji Yixuan were twelve in total:
Fenyang Wenzhao, Yexian Guisheng,
Shending Hongyin, Guyin Yuncong, Guanghui Yuanlian, and Prime Minister Wang Sui, among others, all of whom inherited the Dharma-way of their master.
Fushan Fayuan received the transmission from Sheng;
Fayuan transmitted it to Jingyin Daozhen and others.
Their Dharma and Way flourished in later generations, as recorded in the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Monks).
Jiawu, the fifth year of Chunhua (944 CE), the twelfth year of Tonghe of the Liao dynasty.
Yiwu, the first year of Zhizhao (996 CE), the thirteenth year of Tonghe of the Liao dynasty.
Imperially composed: *Bicangquan* (Exposition of the Secret Treasury) in twenty fascicles.
He commissioned the monks of the two streets to annotate the *Yuan shi* in five fascicles and the *Xiaoyao yong* in ten fascicles.
The Great Canon was entered into the Śākya treasury and its catalog was promulgated.
In the second year of Zhìdào, the *bǐngshēn* year (the fourteenth year of the Liao Tǒnghé era),
Emperor [Zhènzōng] passed away in the third month of the third year of Zhìdào, the *dìngyōu* year (the fifteenth year of the Liao Tǒnghé era).
Shinzō was the third son of Taisō.
His posthumous name was Jō.
He ascended the throne at the age of twenty-nine.
He strove for simplicity and ease,
composing seven articles on civil and military affairs to bestow upon his ministers and officials.
He further mandated that both the transport commissioners and the prefects concurrently hold the duty of encouraging agriculture.
He performed the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tai in the east and the Si sacrifice at Fenyin in the west;
he governed with civil and literary principles for twenty-five years of great peace.
His age was fifty-four.
The second day of the twelfth month was established as the Chengtian Festival (承天節). [The reigns were: Xianping 6, Jingde 4, Taizhong 1, Xiangfu 9, Tianxi 5, and Qianxing 1.
Wu-xu, the first year of Xianping (998 CE): the sixteenth year of Liao Tonghe.
Ji-hai, the second year of Xianping (999 CE): the seventeenth year of Liao Tonghe.
Geng-zi, the third year of Xianping (1000 CE): the eighteenth year of Liao Tonghe.
In summer, there was a great drought.

Zhi Li of Tiantai in eastern Zhejiang—the Fourth Patriarch of the Lecture School—and Zun Shi of Mingzhou, the Master of Repentance at Xiaozhu, jointly practiced the Three-Week *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* Repentance for the Protection of the Nation; after three days, rain fell.

Su Wei, the Governor of Mingzhou, composed an inscription to commemorate his virtue, as well as the *Biography of the Master’s Vows and Deeds* and the *Record of the Teachings and Practices of Siming*.
Furthermore, from spring through summer, there was no rain in Western Zhejiang.
Zhang Quhua, the Palace Attendant and Governor of Hangzhou, led his subordinates in preparing banners, canopies,
and musical instruments to welcome the Great Being of Universal Pervasion from Tiantong Mountain to offer prayers at Fantian Temple.
Subsequently, seasonal rains fell throughout the four borders in abundant measure.

This was the beginning of the compassionate and miraculous response of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva appearing to meet the aspirations of the people. This is recorded as the "Account of Miraculous Responses" from Upper Zhushan.
Xinchou, the fourth year of Xianping (961); the nineteenth year of the Tonghe era of the Liao dynasty.

Dharma-xian, Tripitaka Master from India, Court Proclaiming Gentleman, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and Great Master Mingjiao, presented this newly translated scripture for the Tripitaka canon, the volume beginning with the character "Qu," accompanied by a preface composed by the Emperor.
Ren-yin, the fifth year of Xianping; the twentieth year of the Tonghe era of the Liao dynasty.

Translated by Shi Hu, the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Court Honorary Grandee, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma. *The Causes and Conditions of the Ordination of the Daughter of Anāthapiṇḍada*.
The Emperor was requested to compose the "Continuation of the Preface to the Holy Teachings" (*Jìshèngjiào xù*) for the Indic scriptural collection (*Tiānzhú jiàozàng*).
Year *Guīmǎo*, the sixth year of Xiánpíng (963 CE); the twenty-first year of the Liao dynasty’s Tǒnghé era.
The Emperor issued an edict to the Director of the Right Street Monastery to prepare ceremonial guards, musical instruments,
and ornate banners to welcome the Buddha’s tooth relic from the Great Xiangguo Temple.
He made offerings at the Pagoda of Kaibosi Temple.
The Emperor composed the following eulogy:
"In the West dwells a Sage, Śākyamuni."
Receiving all beings with compassion, you are honored by the world;

may I always aspire to advance in cultivation to increase superior fruits, so as to hope for the benefit and enrichment of the common people. [This is] the Preface to the Śarīra Praise composed during the Three Reigns.
Jiachen, the first year of the Jingde era (964 CE); the twenty-second year of the Tonghe era of the Liao dynasty.

*Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), compiled by the Song monk Daoyuan, contains the机缘 (critical dialogues and circumstances) of Śākyamuni Buddha, from the First Patriarch Kāśyapa down to the various patriarchs who transmitted the Chan lineage to the Eastern Land.
He presented the thirty-fascicle *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* for imperial inspection.
The Emperor perused it and praised it highly,
issuing an edict for Yang Yi and other scholars of the Hanlin Academy to edit and authenticate the text.
The preface was compiled and entered into the Great Canon (Tripitaka),
circulating throughout the world;
it came to the eyes of the Japanese monk Jikishō.
He brought back twenty-seven items of scriptural and commentarial topics presented by the Zen Master Enchin of his own country,
with which he had questioned the Dharma Master Zhili of Siming regarding his doubts;
these were recorded in the *Jiaoxing lu* (Record of Teaching and Practice) upon his return to his home country after receiving instruction.
The Great Dharma Master Zhili of Siming composed the *Ten Gates of Nonduality:
A Guide to the Essentials* in two fascicles, clarifying the wondrous teachings and practices of the "one mind and three contemplations" realized by [Hui]neng of Nanyue and [Zhi]yi of Tiantai.
Yisi (1007), the second year of Jingde; the twenty-third year of Tonghe of the Liao.
Bingwu (1008), the third year of Jingde; the twenty-fourth year of Tonghe of the Liao.
Dingwei, the fourth year of Jingde (967): the twenty-fifth year of the Tonghe era of the Liao.
Wushen, the first year of Dazhong Xiangfu (1008): the twenty-sixth year of the Tonghe era of the Liao.
In the tenth month of winter, the Emperor performed the Feng sacrifice at Mount Tai to worship the Supreme Deity.
On the first day of the eleventh month, he visited Qufu to offer sacrifices to Confucius and posthumously conferred upon him the title of Xuansheng Wenxuan Wang (the Dark Sage, King Wenxuan).
He posthumously conferred the title of King Shao-lie Wu-ch'eng upon Tai Gong of Ch'i,
and King Wen-hsien upon King Wen of Chou,
establishing a temple for each.
Subsequently, the name "Xuansheng" (Mysterious Sage) was changed to "Zhisheng" (Supreme Sage) to avoid the taboo name of the Imperial Ancestor.
In the second month of the Jiyou year, an imperial edict permitted the establishment of a school at the Temple of the Former Sage in Qufu; this was recorded in the imperial annals.
The Jiyou year was the second year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era [989 CE], corresponding to the twenty-seventh year of the Tonghe era of the Liao dynasty.
The Chan Master’s name was Yuxian.
He was the son of the Lin family of Changzhou in Gusu.
At the age of seven, he left home to become a monk under the Venerable Kaiyi of Yong’an in Jiaxing.
At the age of thirty, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He went to visit Chan Master Longhua Qiu,
where he realized the seal of the mind.
Upon returning to Myōkaku-in,
he devoted himself solely to drinking;
when intoxicated, he would compose songs to admonish both the clergy and the laity.
He was titled the Immortal of Wine. He sang:
"At the head of the Yangtze River, the waves are deepest."
When travelers reach this point, they all sink into silence.
When you reach the place where there are no waves at another time, [you will know].
"It is as if one were still applying effort when there are waves.
He said,
"The golden goblet is heard again to be overflowing."
The King’s Mountain has returned to report its collapse;
do not let the night-watchmen seize it.
Chase after the bright moonlight and return.
He said:
"One-six and two-six, their matters are already settled;
one-nine and two-nine, I must drink wine."
Stretching out both legs to sleep, one awakens with a sudden sound.
Rising, heaven and earth remain as they were before.
He said:
Green trees before the gate hold no singing birds;
beneath the courtyard, gray moss bears fallen flowers.
I shall briefly discuss this matter with the eastern wind.
"Whose house does this abundant spring scenery belong to?
He replied, "Autumn arrives; the mountains grow cold and the waters turn chilly."
Spring comes, willows turn green and flowers turn red;
a single movement follows ten thousand transformations.
In the riverside village, mist and rain veil all in obscurity.
There is being empty, non-empty, and neither empty nor non-empty.
With a winnowing basket, he scoops up the northwest wind and says:
Born in this Jambudvīpa world,
human sentiments are largely driven by likes and dislikes;
they simply desire to consume a little wine.
This is why they lie prostrate in the streets and on the roads;
after death, they are reborn once more in this Sahā world,
having no desire to be reborn in the Pure Land.
For what reason?
In the Western Pure Land, there is no trade in wine.
It was on the day of Shangyuan in the second year of the Xiangfu era that this occurred.
The Master sought a bath at dawn and retired to his quarters;
there, clenching his fists, raising his right hand, and opening his mouth with his left, he passed away at Dongchan Monastery in Pingjiang Prefecture.
The Master was a successor of Yanqiu of Longhua.
Qiu succeeded Changqing Leng;
Leng succeeded Chan Master Xuefeng Cun;
Cun succeeded Chan Master Deshan Jian—according to the *Wudeng Lu* (Record of the Five Lamps).
An imperial edict was issued to establish Tianqing Observatories throughout all prefectures and circuits.
Princess Shenguang was the seventh daughter of Emperor Taizong.
From birth he had abstained from pungent roots and meat;
at this time, he earnestly requested to become a monk,
and was subsequently enfeoffed as the Duke of Wu.
He was granted the name Qingliang and the title Baoji Zhengjue Dashi.
To the west of the capital city, the Chongzhen Zisheng Chan Monastery was constructed for him.
There were thirty palace ladies. By imperial decree,
the two inner courts escorted them into the temple,
where they were granted a vegetarian feast at Shen Temple.
His secular age was thirty-eight;
he entered parinirvāṇa sixteen years after his ordination as a bhikṣuṇī.

This occurred during the reign of the Imperial Court, in the *Shiyuan* (Garden of Affairs), on the year Gengxu, the third year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era [1010 CE], which corresponds to the twenty-eighth year of the Liao Tonghe era.
In the tenth month of winter,
an imperial decree was issued to rename Mingzhou Ba’en Yuan as Yanqing Yuan.
By imperial edict, the name of Daming Temple at the former residence of Lu Ji in Huating was changed to Puzhao.
By imperial decree, the name of the Chanlin Monastery in Hanting Township, Yixing County,
was changed to Shenggan Chan Temple; it was established as a monastery for the transmission of the ten directions with a rotating system of abbots.
Inscription for the Stele Recording the Temple’s Rituals for the Deities of the Mountain Sacrifices.
Xinhai, the fourth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era; the twenty-ninth year of the Liao Tonghe era.

By imperial decree, Zhao Anren, Acting State Councilor, and Yang Yi, Hanlin Academician, served as the translators and editors of the scriptures, compiling the *Da zang jing mulu* (Catalogue of the Great Canon) and the *Huangchao lei yuan* (Categorized Garden of the Imperial Dynasty).
Renzi, the fifth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era (962 CE), the thirtieth year of the Liao Tonghe era:
the Śramaṇa Juecheng, of the Kṣatriya caste from the kingdom of Kulūta in India, arrived at the capital and was lodged in the Translation Bureau.
At the age of about forty, he had mastered over forty treatises.
Ding Jingong, who was responsible for polishing the literary style of the scriptures and commentaries, praised his quick wit and intelligence;
consequently, he dispatched a translator to guide him in his studies.
Hanlin Academician Yang Yi, whose courtesy name was Mingye, prepared tea and fruit and conversed with him.
Jue declared,
"I wish to go to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī and then immediately return to my native land."
Upon entering this country, I saw pigs and sheep being slaughtered and meat hanging in the market stalls;
it was so painful that I could not bear to look.
Throughout the entire land of India to the west, no one eats meat.
On another day, the Duke of Jin asked, "Having traveled from tens of thousands of li away, what else do you intend to do?
He replied, "I also wish to pay my respects at the stupa of Vinaya Master Xuan. This is recorded in the *Huangchao leiyuan* and the *Yang Wengong tanyuan*.
Gui-chou, the sixth year of Dazhong Xiangfu (963 CE), the first year of the Kaite era of the Great Qidan [Liao Dynasty].
In the third month of spring, the Emperor bestowed his own composition, the *Fayin ji* (Collection of Dharma Sounds),
and entrusted it to the Translation Court (*Chuanyufa Yuan*) for the purpose of annotating the catalogue of the Tripitaka.
The Emperor bestowed the following "Verses on Cultivating the Mind" for the Translation Institute:
"The First Patriarch’s method of settling the mind was at Shaolin;
He did not transmit scriptures or teachings, but transmitted only the mind."

If one awakens to the nature of True Suchness from among human beings, the profound principles of the secret seal have been clearly elucidated since ancient times. This concludes the twelfth volume of the *Jiaozhengzongji* (Record of the Correct Lineage of the Teachings).
During the Great Liao, the name was again changed to the Great Qidan.
He established Youzhou as the capital, known as Xijin Fu,
and changed the reign title to Kaitai.
This continued until the second year of Xianyong, the Bingwu year.
Again, it is titled *The Great Liao*. In the year Jiayin,
the seventh year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era— the second year of the Kaite era of the Great Qidan—

the Tripitaka Master from India, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Great Master of the Transmission of the Teaching, Fatian, translated the *Vajramahāyāna-ratnarāja-sūtra*.
In the eleventh month of winter,
the Qingzhaoying Palace was completed in the capital.
Its construction had begun in the fourth month of the second year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era.
In the eleventh month of this year, the construction was completed.
In total, there were two thousand six hundred and ten sections.
Ding Jinguo was appointed as the Commissioner for the Palace Restoration.
Regarding the use of earth, wood, metal, stone, cinnabar, and lacquer, materials were sought and superior sites selected throughout the world.
Shen Cunchong’s *Bǐtán* states:
"Mount Yandang in Wenzhou is the dwelling place of the Venerable Nakula."
It was not seen by people in previous generations;
it first became revealed in this region during the timber collection for the Zhaoying Temple, as recorded in Hong Mai’s *Rongzhai Sanbi*.
The year of Yimao, the eighth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era; the third year of the Kaite era of the Great Qidan.
The Great Dharma Master Zunshe had been lecturing at Tiantai on Mount Taye for twelve years.
It was only upon reaching this point that he began his journey westward, settling at Guling Mountain Temple—now known as Lower Tiantong Temple—in Hangzhou.
Originally, the Dharma Master Huili from India resided there during the Western Jin dynasty;
it was also the site where the eminent Sui monk Zhi guan lectured on the Lotus Sūtra.
Tang Daobiao succeeded in completing it.
By the time of Emperor Xizong, it was destroyed by bandits.
On the western cliff stands the withered trunk of a cypress tree.
It remained amidst the ruins of the conflagration.
The Dharma Master sprinkled it with water and offered a prayer;
its branches and leaves flourished once more.
He diligently practiced the four kinds of samādhi and constructed a hall for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* repentance ritual,
using even a single rafter and a single brick.
He invariably recited the Great Compassion Mantra seven times.
The temple buildings were fully completed.

He subsequently received from the Imperial Court the plaque for Tianzhu Lingshan Temple and was recorded as a successor to the lineage of the Tiantai teachings and contemplation, serving as a director of repentance ceremonies.
Bingchen, the ninth year of Dazhong Xiangfu; the fourth year of Kaite of the Great Qidan.
Dingyi, the first year of Tianxi; the fifth year of Kaite of the Great Qidan.
An imperial edict was issued for the establishment of *fangsheng chi* (pools for the release of living beings) throughout the realm.
The Great Dharma Master Zhili of Mingzhou,
together with ten monks, set out from the spring of the Bingchen year.
He vowed to practice the Lotus Samādhi for three years. Upon its completion,
following the precedent of the story of Bhaiṣajyarāja, he burned his own body as an offering to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in order to be reborn in the Pure Land.
Yang Yi, the Hanlin Academician, heard of this and dispatched a long letter via postal relay,
earnestly requesting him to remain in this world;
he further entrusted the Prefectural Governor Li Yigeng with the task of providing protection.
In the fourth year of the Tianxi era,
Chancellor Kou Zhi and Yang Yi of the Hanlin Academy memorialized the Emperor regarding [his] knowledge of ritual conduct and his practice of self-sacrifice.
The Emperor said:
I merely transmit my intention, requesting that you remain in this world.
I specially bestow upon you the honorary title of Dharma-Wisdom Great Master (Fazhi Dashi) and the *Jiaoxing Lu* (Record of Teaching and Practice).
In the seventh month of autumn, the Grand Marshal, Duke Wenzheng, Wang Qie, passed away.
The Duke had served in government for eighteen years.
When his illness became critical,
he entrusted his final instructions to Yang Yi, the Hanlin Academician, saying:
I am deeply weary of the afflictions.
I vow that in future lives I shall become a bhikṣu who dwells in seclusion among the forest trees,
taking joy in contemplating the mind.
When the time came for me to change my bedding,
you shaved my beard and hair,
and I donned the three robes of dyed color.
He was cremated according to the funeral rites for fire-sacrifice.
A bone stupa (śarīra-stūpa) was erected beside his ancestral cemetery. Yi said:
A Duke is one of the Three Ducal Ministers.
To enshroud and present gifts with the *gong* robe—how could this be added to the body of a monk?
I have deliberated this with the bereaved relatives.
He merely placed his three monastic robes within the coffin, without interring any precious gems or jade;
this is recorded in Wen Ying’s *Xiangshan Lu*.
It was the year Wumu (5th year), the second year of Tianxi (1018 CE), the sixth year of Kaite of the Great Qidan (Liao Dynasty).
Jiwei (1019), the third year of Tianxi; the seventh year of Kaite of the Great Qidan.
Gengshen (1020), the fourth year of Tianxi; the eighth year of Kaite of the Great Qidan.
In the year of Xinyou, the fifth year of Tianxi (981 AD), the ninth year of the Kaite era of the Great Khitan,
an imperial edict was issued for the Palace Attendant Yu Yuanqing to travel to Yanqing Monastery in Mingzhou to perform a three-day and three-night rite of repentance on behalf of the state.
The *Xiuchan Yaoyi* (Essential Principles for Cultivating Repentance) in one fascicle, recorded in the *Jiaoxing Lu* (Record of Teaching and Practice), was composed by the Dharma Master Zhili.
In the second month of the first year of the Qiánxìng era (the Ren-xū year), the Emperor passed away; this was the first year of the Tàipíng era of the Great Qīdān (Liao).
The Emperor specially bestowed the title of Great Master Ciyun upon the Dharma Master Zunshe of Tiantzhu Monastery in Hangzhou.
Empress Dowager Liu, known as Zhangxian Mingshu, dispatched an envoy to Tiantzhu to perform repentance rituals on behalf of the state.

The Dharma Master composed one scroll of the *Huguo Jinguangming Sanmei Yi* (Ritual for the Golden Light Samādhi for Protecting the State) and submitted it with a record of his repentance in the second month of spring.
The Dharma Master Fahui of Gushan on West Lake in Hangzhou, named Zhizhuan and styled Zhongyongzi, [wrote this].
On the seventeenth day, he himself composed the funeral inscription and elegies;
on the nineteenth day, he entered parinirvāṇa.
Yuan compiled ten commentaries on the sutras.
In the capital, he lived as a neighbor to the scholar Lin Pu (Hejing);
in Tiantai, he was a friend to the Dharma Master Zunshe.
He lived to the age of forty-seven.
He was thirty-nine years old at the time of his death.
He was buried in earthenware jars.
This was in the third year of the Jingyou era of Emperor Renzong.
Due to heavy rains, a mountain collapsed and revealed its seal;
the entire body was as if alive, with nails and hair grown long,
lips red and slightly parted, and teeth like white jade or snow.
He had new clothes placed over [the remains] and interred them while scattering various famous incenses.
During the Shaoxing era of the Gaozong reign,
the Four Sages Temple was established on Mount Gu.

The *Xianju bian* (Record of Secluded Dwelling) and the *Chan zhu xingye ji* (Record of the Vows and Deeds of the Repentance Master) state that the master’s stūpa was relocated to Ma’nao Slope on North Mountain. Regarding Renzong:
he was the sixth son of Zhenzong.
At the age of thirteen, he ascended the imperial throne.
The Emperor was devoted to benevolence and generosity,
and he curbed the influence of those who sought favor through favoritism.
He entrusted the office to men of virtue and integrity,
specifically establishing six members for the Censorate,
and never grew weary of receiving remonstrances.
He established schools and founded Guanghui Monasteries to provide for the destitute;
he maintained a very frugal lifestyle himself while bestowing benefits upon the people,
such that his reign was hailed as one of extreme governance.
He established the Qianyuan Festival on the fourteenth day of the fourth month and implemented the Chongtian calendar.
He reigned for forty-one years and lived to the age of fifty-five.

[The reigns were as follows: Tiansheng nine years, Mingdao two years, Jingyou four years, Baoyuan two years, Kangding one year, Qingli eight years, Huangwu five years, Zhihe two years, and Jiayou eight years.
Guihai (the 10th day of the 10th month), the first year of Tiānshèng:
the Chōngtiān calendar was in use; the second year of Tàipíng of the Great Qīdàn.
Jiazǐ (the 1st day of the 1st month), the second year of Tiānshèng: the third year of Tàipíng of the Great Qīdàn.
The fifth generation descendant of Linji was Chan Master Shenzhao of Taiyuan Yuan at Fenyang Taizi.
His name was Shanzhao,
and he was the son of the Yu family of Taiyuan.
Having shaved his head and received full ordination,
he took up his staff and traveled to various regions.
Wherever he stayed for even a short time, he struck forth [the Dharma] according to the capacities of those who approached him.
He visited seventy-one spiritual teachers in succession before meeting Chan Master Shoushan Nian,
through whom he attained realization of the profound essence.
He traveled through the regions of Heng, Xiang, and Xiangyang,
where he was repeatedly invited by local magistrates to serve as the abbot of famous monasteries;
in total, he accepted eight such invitations.
The Master declined all such invitations.
Upon the passing of Shoushan,
the monastics and laypeople of the Western Road sent the monk Qichong to invite him to serve as abbot.
The Master was reclining in high repose with his quarters closed;
Huicong pushed open the door and entered,
admonishing him, saying:
"In the great matters of the Buddha-dharma, one should remain calm and withdraw from minor details.
Since our former teacher has departed this world, how can you wish for peaceful sleep at such a time?
The Master said:
It was not until he heard these words from someone other than a public official that he acceded to their request.
Thus, in the second year of the Tiānshèng era,
Lǐ Hòu Zhìshī, the Governor of Longdé Prefecture, invited him to reside at Chéngtiān Temple.
The price was offered three times, yet he did not rise.
When the price was offered a second time, he opened the casket.
The Master said:
The Master replied, "I am old and ill; I shall not leave the mountain.
You may go in my stead, and we shall see who arrives first. Jia said:
"It depends entirely on what the Master chooses.
The Master ordered that provisions be prepared and that they set out their gear, saying,
"I shall go on ahead."
He laid down his chopsticks and passed away.
His body was cremated, the relics were collected, and a stupa was erected.
The Master succeeded Chan Master Nian of Shoushan as his dharma heir.
There is that which is called "The Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality";
this is the Master’s own statement from his biography.
It was the year of Yichou (1035), the third year of the Tiānshèng era, the fourth year of the Tàipíng era of the Great Qīdān.
In the Bingyin year, the fourth year of the Tiānshèng era (986 CE), the fifth year of the Tàipíng era of the Great Qīdán.
An imperial edict was issued for the Tiantai teachings to be included in the Tripitaka for circulation.
Initially, the monk Sīwù of Tiānzhū Temple had requested that the teaching canon be circulated.
Having prayed to the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara since the spring of the year of Yi-chou,
his vows were finally fulfilled;
he then performed self-immolation before the temple of Ilgwan-am.
In gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness, this *Tiānzhú biéjí* (Separate Collection from India) was compiled.
In the year Dingmǎo, the fifth year of Tiānshèng (947 CE), the sixth year of Tàipíng of the Great Qīdàn (Liao Dynasty), on the ninth month, Cháo Wěi, Duke Wényuán,
Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince, composed the ten fascicles of the *Fǎzàng suìjīn* (Golden Nuggets from the Dharma-Treasury).
All these are studies for attaining realization through one's own inherent nature.
On the fifth day of the first month of spring in the sixth year of Tiānshèng (the Wùchén year), the seventh year of Tàipíng of the Great Qīdàn,
the Venerable Zhīlǐ of Fǎzhì in Míngzhōu sat cross-legged, gathered the assembly, and said:
I have established this Yanqing Daochang,
vowing to propagate the Lotus Samādhi.
You must not become those who, as the last of their kind, sever the seeds of the Buddha.
"Birth is inevitably followed by death, as surely as morning gives way to evening.
If one cultivates with focused diligence without interruption, there will be a meeting across lifetimes, generation after generation.
Having finished speaking, he suddenly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha and passed away into stillness.
After the body had been exposed in the niche for fourteen days,
his nails and hair had grown long,
yet his countenance remained as if he were alive.
During the cremation, the fire was to the north and the tongue remained unburnt.
The śarīra were of five colors and their number could not be known.

Zhao Bian, Grand Master of the Academy for the Promotion of Governance, concurrently Acting Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince, and Duke Qingxian, composed the "Epigraph on the Master’s Conduct" and the "Record of His Teachings and Deeds."
Jisi (1039), the seventh year of the Tiānshèng era; the eighth year of the Tàipíng era of the Great Qīdàn.
The Chánzōng Guǎngdēnglù (Extensive Record of the Lamp of the Chan School), compiled by Lǐ Zūnxū, Marshal of the Household, in thirty fascicles.
The Emperor composed a preface and bestowed it upon him.
The death of the Commandant is recorded in the biography of Chan Master Ciming Yuan.
*Gengwu*, the eighth year of the Tiānshèng era; the ninth year of the Tàipíng era of the Great Qīdàn.
Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra. Compiled by the Dharma Master Yichang of Changshui, whose name was Zizhu;
a native of Xiuzhou, Jiaxing.
Initially, he relied on Master Hongmin of his home province to study the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the passage, "When the two characteristics of motion and stillness are clearly seen as not arising," he attained an awakening.
He then heard of the eminent reputation of Chan Master Jue at Mount Langye in Chuzhou.
He hurried there to have an audience with him.
Upon reaching the gate, he encountered the Master ascending the seat.
He then asked:
"How can it be that from this state of pure original essence, mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Jué called out in a stern voice,
"How can it be that from this state of pure original essence, mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?"
At that very moment, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.
As he was about to announce his succession [to the Dharma], Master Jue said to him:
Your school has long been in decline;
you ought to rouse your resolve to support it in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
"I shall do as you instruct," [he replied].
Later he resided at Changshui,
where his assembly numbered nearly one thousand.
He composed the *Xianshou School’s Commentary on the Śūraṃgama Sūtra* in ten fascicles.
The Preface by Wang Sui, Imperial Censor-in-Chief, circulated in the world as the "Record of Longevity.
The Chan Master Guangzhao of Langye Mountain was named Huijiao.
He succeeded Chan Master Fenyang Shanzhao.
In the year Xinwei, the ninth year of the Tiānshèng era (the tenth year of the Tàipíng era of the Great Qīdàn), on the third day of the sixth month, the Emperor passed away.
His posthumous title was Emperor Tiānfǔ.
His temple name was Shengzong.
He reigned for forty-nine years.
In the fourth month of summer.
An imperial edict was issued to welcome the robe and alms bowl of the Sixth Patriarch, the Zen Master Dajian of Nanhua Chan Temple at Caoxi in Shaoyang Prefecture,
to be enshrined for veneration within the Qingjing Hall of the Imperial Palace on the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
An envoy was dispatched to escort him back and bestow upon the Elder of Nanhua, Pusu, the title of Great Master Zhidu and inclusion in the *Xudenglu*.
The Emperor Xingzong of the Great Qidan ascended the throne;

Having finished reading the letter from Jingchun, he descended from his seat and returned to the abbot’s quarters,
followed by the assembly in a great throng.
He sat in the full lotus posture for a long time and then passed away.

he had spent fifty-three years in the summer retreat.
The Master succeeded Chan Master Yuncong of Cizhao at Guyin Mountain in Xiangzhou.
Cong succeeded Nian of Shoushan,
and Nian succeeded Zhao of Fengxue.
The Linji school also has a *Xu deng lu* (Continued Lamp Record).
Daguan once composed the "Discourse on Nature" (*Xing bian*),
the text of which says:
When the sages and worthies of antiquity and today speak of "nature" (xing), they merely grasp its phenomenal aspect (qing).
Why is it that even if one can exhaustively investigate principles (li), one cannot fully realize nature?
It is because they do not know that the Three Powers and the myriad things are all nature itself.
The nature of heaven is above;
the nature of earth is below.
Metal is sharp, water is moist, wood is straight, fire is hot, and earth is thick.
These are the natures of the five elements.
To discuss them collectively and to examine them with precision:
The nature of the myriad things is thus clearly visible.
Among them, the most spiritual is humanity.
Humans are born from the union of yin and yang.
That which moves through transformation is emotion (*qing*).
To restrain human emotion is to restore its original purity.
That by which one may rise or fall, become worthy or foolish, is the innate disposition (*xing*); those whose disposition is superior are the noble persons (*junzi*).
External circumstances cannot delude one's nature;
though one may be mixed among petty people, they are merely like gold and jade amidst soil and stones.
As for Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang, their names have hung for ten thousand generations.
Thus, at that time, they maintained high positions and preserved the constant Way,
observing human sentiments and establishing laws according to their natures.
Yet Jie, Zhou, You, and Li were deluded by wealth and honor, thereby losing the Great Treasure.
Even if one’s own nature is led astray by emotions,
though heaven and earth are devoid of sentiment,
the winds, clouds, and the four seasons still alter their seasonal patterns.
The mountains, rivers, and myriad things disarray their forms;
only humans dwell within them.
They measure the movements of celestial time and follow the advantages of terrestrial conditions without losing their seasonal rhythm.
Therefore, humans are the heart of heaven and earth.
Sentiment, cognition, and consciousness all originate from nature (xing);
they manifest according to external objects, and thus there are merely many names for them externally.
The rest cannot be fully recounted here.
"Qing" (feeling) refers to the mind; it is drawn along by its functions.
"Yi" (intention) refers to the will; it records matters.
"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to cognition; it is the discernment of objects.
"Affection," "aversion," "joy," and "anger" are all emotions (*bhāva*).
Now, one who is a Great Sage is one whose nature (*prakṛti*) is determined.
Not being deluded by external distractions and not being led astray by emotions—
this is for the nature to restrain the emotions.
Therefore, my teaching calls this "Right Enlightenment."
The *Yijing* knows only the doctrine of exhausting principle and perfecting nature, yet it has not seen the way of emerging from antiquity and entering the present. From the *Monk Jewel Biography*:
The Chan Master Tianyi of Yuezhou was named Yihuai.
He was a son of the Chen family from Leqing, Wenzhou.
In his youth, he traveled to the capital and became a novice under the Jingde Monastery.

Renyin (6th year of Jiayou), the 8th year of Qingning of the Great Qidan; [recorded by] Chan Master Yunfeng of Xixia.
His name was Wen Yue.

Zhizhe said,

"The walls of this house are dilapidated and cold with snow.

you may prepare charcoal for the sake of the assembly.

When the Master entered the abbot’s quarters,
[Zhao]zhi said:

wherever he went, the monasteries were transformed.

Ascending the hall, he said:
If speech does not depart from its habitual molds,
how can one transcend the entanglements?
A single cloud hangs across the mouth of the valley.
How many people have been deluded by its source!

Those who rely on words perish."
"Those who cling to words are deluded.
When you all arrive here, on what basis do you speak?

If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell,
do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
[He] ascended to the hall.
The fundamental reliance of sentient beings takes the ocean of wisdom as its source;
the stream of conscious beings collectively takes the Dharmakāya as their substance.
It is only because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptualizations shift that the substance becomes differentiated.
Reaching the source, emotions are forgotten; knowing the mind, the essence is realized as unified.
Do you all Zen practitioners understand?
The ancient Buddhas and the pillar have transmitted it to one another.

if you do not understand this, it is a single-layered, double-folded intersection.

I shall drift down the Nine Rivers to enter Mount Lu,

Yuán transmitted the Way to Yuǎn;

Chan Master Yuanzhao of Hui-lin Temple in Tokyo,

was born into the Guan family of Wuxi in the western region of Zhejiang, Changzhou.

The Dharma assemblies flourished daily.
Chen Gong Xiang, the Governor of Hangzhou, ordered the Master to choose between the two monasteries of Chengtian and Xingjiao to reside in;
the people of Suzhou crowded the roads to block him and entreat him to stay.
Furthermore, out of pure compassion, he issued an official letter of invitation to inform both the clergy and the laity, saying:
"I shall borrow the Master for three years to plant the seeds of merit for this land."
I did not dare to occupy this place for long.
Upon reaching the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era,
an imperial edict was issued to expand the Xiangguo Huelin Chan Monastery, and the Master was summoned to serve as its first patriarch.
Once he had arrived at Kaifa,
the following day he was summoned for an audience at the Yanhe Hall. When the Emperor questioned him about the Way and offered him a seat,
the Master sat cross-legged.
The Emperor was pleased and presented him with tea.
The Master raised the cup and drank deeply;
he swirled it and shook it, then took his leave.
The Emperor watched him depart and said to his attendants,
"He is truly a monk of merit and wisdom."
In the seventh year of the Yuanfeng era, the Emperor visited Xiangguo Huelin Temple.

The Emperor summoned the Master to preach the Dharma at Funing Hall and bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Yuanzhao.

With the wind favorable, poles and oars are added;
the boatman sails down to Yangzhou.
In his later years, he resided at Lingyan Mountain in Pingjiang.
Those who inherited his Dharma and transmitted his teachings were beyond counting.
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Yuanfu era of Emperor Zhezong, a jiazi day, he was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
Having bathed, he lay down.
His disciples surrounded him and entreated him, saying,
"The Master's Way pervades the world."
"Today we cannot do without a verse," [the Master] said, looking at him intently.
"Foolish son, I am usually too lazy even to compose verses."
What is the purpose of making a special effort today?
Ordinarily, one lies down whenever one wishes to lie down;
one must not make a special effort to sit today.
He then sought out a brush and wrote in large characters:
"The final affairs are entrusted to Shou-rong.

His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa at Mount Lingyan.

The Master succeeded Chan Master Tianyi Huai.
Those who inherited the Dharma-way of his master were Xiu,
Yong, Sheng, Cong, Chong, Xin, Shou, and others.

and the Chan Master Cishou Huishen for Xinxin—these accounts are recorded in the *Wudeng huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps) stele inscriptions and biographies.
The Chan Master of Donglin in Jiangzhou was named Changzong.
He was born into the Shi family of Youxi in Jianzhou.

When he first arrived at Heishan in Jizhou,
he heard of Master Nanchuan’s Way;
he went to Guizong to rely upon him and remained there for twenty years.
He attained the full depth of its profound mysteries.
The Prefect of Hongzhou, Lord Rong, requested him to reside at Letan;
some even said he was Mazu returned once more.
In the third year of the Yuanfeng era,
an imperial edict was issued to convert the Donglin Monastery in Jiangzhou from a Vinaya residence into a Chan monastery.
Wang Gong Shao, a Grand Master of the Guanwen Hall, was appointed as the governor of Nanchang.
When Yu Yan wished to appoint Baojue Cixin as the abbot of Donglin,

thereupon, he submitted to the mandate.

the Master’s reputation reached the capital,

the imperial decree granted his request.

In the third year of the Yuanyou era of Emperor Zhezong, Prince Xu petitioned for the title of Chan Master Zhaojue.
The number of monastic disciples under his guidance constantly filled seven hundred.

He succeeded Huanglong Nan Chan Master in the *Xudeng Lu* (Continued Lamp Record).

Guihai (the tenth day of the tenth month), the sixth year of Yuanfeng; the nineteenth year of Xianyong of the Great Liao; the first month of the Western Xia, when several hundred thousand troops of the Xia suddenly arrived at Lanzhou—the ninth month of the Song calendar.

In the seventh year of the Yuanfeng era,
an imperial edict was issued appointing him as the first patriarch of Fayun Temple in the capital.

I bestow upon you this *mona* robe for monks.
This conveys the imperial decree that I, the Emperor, have come in person;
His Imperial Brother, the Prince of Jing, pays his respects at your seat.
In the eighth month of the fifth year of the Yuanyou era of Emperor Zhezong, he manifested illness.
An imperial decree was issued to provide medical treatment,
but the Master waved it away.
He then changed his robes and spoke a verse, saying:
"When coming, there was nothing; when departing, there is emptiness.
The affairs of south, north, east, and west are all one and the same."
"The six sense bases remain, yet they provide no benefit.

The Master said, "Take care, take care.

he passed away at the age of sixty-four.

While transporting goods up the Huai River, he arrived at Changlu to visit Xiu.

"On another day, this place shall be compared to the eastern outskirts of the city of Vārāṇasī;

For the Avataṃsaka is the supreme vehicle of sudden and perfect enlightenment, realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
To now say that it is located to the east of the city of Vārāṇasī is to rely on inference (*anumāna*)."
This is not the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
Furthermore, it mentions "another day," yet the One True Dharma-realm has neither past nor present.
Therefore it is said that throughout the ten ages of past and present, the beginning and end do not shift from the present moment of thought.
If one speaks of a different day,
how could today not be [that very same time]?
It is further said that only those who possess the Buddha-eye can know this.
Yet, the sutra states:

Thereupon, the official repented and apologized.

National Preceptor Uichon was the fourth son of King Munjong Inyo, the ruler of Goryeo.

At that time, the Grand Marshal Lü Huíqī was a youth wearing a rush-mat robe.

he once composed a commentary on the *Huayan fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharma-realm of Avataṃsaka).

While stationed on the frontier,

Suddenly, clouds and mist gathered from all sides, and a violent wind accompanied by thunder and rain shook the forest.

After a short while, something appeared.

The Grand Marshal replied:
"From early on, I have encountered obstacles and conditions that led me to meet with such an evil environment.
The youth said,
"Now they have all been extinguished."
"Official, what do you seek that you have come?
The Grand Marshal replied,
"I wish to see the Great Being."
The youth asked, "What is the purpose of wishing to see the Bodhisattva?
He replied, "I have often perused the Avataṃsaka Mahāyāna teachings; their principles are profound and their meaning is vast."

for instance, in the single chapter on the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*),

yet the Sage’s intent becomes ever more remote;
this is truly what is called "shattering the Great Way."
The Grand Marshal said,

The youth smiled and said,

Here, every blade of grass and every tree is none other than the realm of Mañjuśrī."
If, in your daily activities, you remain undeluded when encountering things,

The Grand Marshal, repenting of the error in his previous words, immediately prostrated himself with his head to the ground.

In the third year of Shao-sheng (the Bingzi year), the second year of Shouchang of the Great Liao, and the winter of the tenth month of the Western Xia, a great military expedition was launched against the Song; upon reaching Yanzhou, they withdrew because they saw that the city was well-prepared.
