Fang Zirong, the Governor of Huizhou, who had been commissioned by imperial decree to transcribe [the text], said to Zizhan:
"My wife has served the Great Sage Sengqie of Huaisi with great devotion.
Last night, he came to bid her farewell in a dream, saying:"
"Sending Su Zizhan across the South China Sea.
Now, indeed, several parts of this journey have already been determined;
what more need be feared? (From the *Song Sengshi*).
In the sixth month of the third year of the Yuánfú era, the year of Gēngchén (1090 CE),
Sūshī returned from overseas and resided in Chángzhōu;
he traveled for pleasure through Yíxīng.
Initially, while in exile in Huangzhou, he built a residence on East Slope (Dongpo),
and thus took the sobriquet "Dongpo Jushi.
On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Jianzhong Jinggu era of Emperor Huizong.
Su Shi, the Chao-feng-lang (Court Gentleman for Ceremonial Service) and Director of the Wangju Observation Post in Chengdu Prefecture, passed away in Changzhou.

Wu-yin (the 19th day of the 6th month): The first year of Yuánfú; the fourth year of Shòuchāng of the Great Liao; the first year of Yǒng’ān of the Western Xia. Ji-mao (the 2nd year of Yuánfú): The second year of Yuánfú; the fifth year of Shòuchāng of the Great Liao; the [second] year of the Western Xia. The eminent monk of Qiántáng named Dàoqián.
He gained recognition through his poetry from the eminent scholar Su Wenzhonggong Shi,
who styled him as Chanliaozi. They engaged in a continuous exchange of poems and lyrics,
singing and harmonizing with one another.
Whenever his name appeared in calligraphy,
it was invariably written as "Cānliáo. Later,
when Minister Lü Gōngzhù submitted a memorial to grant the Master the title "Miaozong," [the name remained as such].
Later, he provided a wooden tablet [for his memorial], which read: "The Venerable Master Miaozong.
There are many extant stone inscriptions concerning him throughout Jiang and Zhejiang.
Now, I briefly record it:
when the Duke departed from Qiantang,
he bid him farewell with a poem in long and short lines, saying:
Sentient beings see the wind roll the tide in from ten thousand li;
insentient things see the tide sent back to its source.
Ask those at Xixing Ferry on the banks of the Qiantang River.
How many times have the slanting rays of sunset appeared? No need for reflection.
From antiquity to the present, as we bow and look up, the men of old are no more.
Who like Old东坡 (Sōngp'o) has forgotten his artifice even in white-haired old age?
Take note of the western side of West Lake;
it is precisely where the setting mountains are most beautiful,
a misty haze of empty green.
I calculate that we poets are well-suited to one another;
such as I am and you are, we are rare indeed.
Let us agree to return together by sea to the East in years to come.
I pray that Master Xie’s noble aspirations may not be thwarted;
on the road to Xizhou, you should not turn back your head to let your robes be moistened by tears for my sake.
Master Zhongwen Ying’s eulogy says:
Alas! The petty scholars of this age must address the masters of the Way by their personal names as a sign of their contempt;
how could they know that Wen Zhong held such profound respect even for a single Buddhist monk?
How much more so for one whose virtue and character are so lofty and revered!
Master Ying succeeded Chan Master Dahui Gaofeng Puding as the Dharma heir;
he was a Dharma Master at Chongshan Temple in Chicheng, Tiantai.
His name was Youyan.
He built a hermitage beneath a *lú-mù* tree and named it Zhā'ān (The Quince Hermitage).
Longing for his native land of An-yang,
he composed four poems.
They are poignant and moving.
The first stanza says:
"The Western Land of True Purity is originally my own home;
now I recall that the journey back is a hundred thousand miles distant."
Wandering on the roads of exile, I am utterly exhausted;
solitary and bitter amidst the dust and wind, I am most worthy of pity.
Seven layers of trees tower high, offering a thousandfold joys.
The Eight Virtues Pond blooms with flowers of four colors;
do not marvel that my recent dreams of returning have become so intense—
how can one bear it when matters of honor and disgrace are boundless?
At that time, it was widely circulated and recited.
Yan had been devoted to the practice of Pure Land throughout his life;
in the fourth month of the summer in the first year of the Jianguo era of Emperor Huizong, he was nearing the end of his life.
He beheld the celestial music of the Great Lotus Pond of Jewels arranged in four rows returning to stillness.

The Master composed the *Dabù bèijiǎn* (Comprehensive Examination of the Great Sections) in four fascicles, the *Jiànnàn* (Annotations and Difficulties) in four fascicles, the *Zhùlǎn* (Aids for Reading) in four fascicles, and the *Huìduì* (Confrontations) in four fascicles, thereby circulating his exegesis on the lineage of the tradition.

Gengchen (the 17th day of the seventh month): In the third year of Yuánfú, on the first month, the Emperor passed away. In the sixth year of Shòuchāng of the Western Xia, during the autumn of the seventh month, the Liao Emperor fell gravely ill.
He admonished his grandson Yánxī, saying:
"The Southern Dynasty has maintained friendly relations for many years.
Your nature is stubborn, so do not provoke any trouble.
He further cautioned his ministers, saying:
If the successor to the throne should act recklessly,
you ministers must earnestly remonstrate and stop him.
The Emperor passed away after reigning for forty-six years.
His temple name was Daozong.
The *Liaozhi* records his posthumous title as Emperor Tianfu.
It is known from the *Song Dongzhi* that he was buried at Tailing.
He ascended the tower of Dengfeng County and requested that, using any remaining strength, the Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song be restored;
for this was the dwelling place of the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma.
From the provincial governors, prefects, and county magistrates down to the officials, commoners, artisans, and merchants, all joined in the effort without being summoned.
One morning, [the hut] was completed and named the "Wall-Facing Hermitage" (Mianbi An).
From the forest emerged twelve stalks of *zhī* fungus,
each flower a different color.
Ambrosial rain fell into the pond.
At night, light rose from all four directions and reached toward heaven,
merging into a vast array that spanned several tens of li from east to west.
The Layman Houshan Chen Shidao recorded:
Among the disciples of the Master of the Kǒng clan, Yán, Mǐn, and Rǎn all left no legacy.
After Zhònggōng, there was Xún Qīng.
After Zeng Yu came Mencius;
after Duandi Ci came Zhuang Zhou.
Yet, after Xunzi, Mencius, and Zhuang Zhou, there was no further renown.
The lineage of the Li clan was transmitted to Guan Yin;
thereafter, there is no further record of the transmission from Yin.
As for the Buddhist tradition, twenty-eight generations after Śākyamuni came to Bodhidharma.
Furthermore, six generations later came Caoxi;
from then until today, fifteen generations have passed.
That the followers of Confucius and Laozi wish to compare their origins and lineages is an error. (From the *Houshan Wenji*).
Chan Master Huītáng Bǎojiào of Mount Hóngxīng in the Yellow Dragon Mountains,
named Zǔxīn,
entered nirvana on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of winter.
The Master was born into the Wu family of Nanxiong;
he succeeded Chan Master Huanglong Nan as his dharma heir and attained the dharma-way of Baojue.
It is said: Caotang Weiqing, Sijian Wuxin, Grand Historian Huang Shanggu, and Wu Zhongli, among others, [are recorded] in the *Fodeng*.
As for Emperor Huizong, his personal name was Ji;
he was the tenth son of Emperor Shen宗.
He was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Duan.
At the age of nineteen, he ascended the imperial throne and reigned for twenty-five years.
The tenth day of the sixth month is the Tianning Festival.
At that time, having enjoyed a long period of peace,
the Suzhou and Hangzhou prefectures established manufacturing bureaus.
Zhu Mei and his son brought forth the "Flower and Stone Transport" (Huashigang) and constructed Mount Wansui at Liangyue; consequently,
every flower and stone among the common people [was seized].
It was also named after the imperial provisions;
yet he coerced [the official] into accepting bribes until his desires were fully satisfied before granting him exemption.
Cai Jing served as Grand Preceptor (Taishi).
The eunuch Tong Guan was appointed to the position of Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
He received envoys from Li Siliang, a man of Yan in the Liao state, and they returned together;
Tong Guan reported that the Liao could be conquered.
Just as the Jurchens arrived to seek an alliance,
they agreed to launch a joint attack against Liao.
Once the Jin had destroyed Liao, they proceeded to invade Song.
The Emperor then abdicated the throne to his crown prince,
who honored him as the Retired Emperor (Taishanghuang).
He was escorted northward by the goldsmiths.
He was demoted and enfeoffed as the Prince of Tianshui.

He died at Wuguo City. *Continuation of the Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government* (Xu Song Tongjian): five years of Jianzhong Jinggu, five of Chongning, four of Daguang, seven of Zhenghe, one of Zhonghe, and seven of Xuanhua.
Xinsi: The first year of Jianzhong Jinggu; the first year of the Qiandun era of the Great Liao. Tianzhu ascended the throne. In the Western Xia, Tianzhu of the Liao ascended the throne.
His name was Yanxi.
He was the grandson of Daozong and the son of the Prince of Qin, Yuanji.
He styled himself Emperor Tianzhu.
Through licentiousness and excess they lost the Way,
ultimately leading to the ruin of their state,
as recorded in the *Liaozhi*. In the year the Jurchen Grand Preceptor Yang Ge died, his son Aguda succeeded him.
*Continued Record of the Lamp*. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month of autumn, at Fayun Temple in Bianjing,
the Chan Master Foguo, named Weibai,
compiled this collection of the机缘 (kīyuan— opportune encounters) of the patriarchs of the Chan lineage.
He presented the *Xu denglu* (Continued Record of the Lamp) in thirty fascicles for imperial inspection.
The Emperor personally composed a preface and bestowed it upon him.
The text reads: [The preface would follow here.]
In the past, when Śākyamuni Tathāgata appeared in the world, he received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
he was born into the family of King Brahmāśuddha and pointed his fingers toward heaven and earth.
Yet his karmic potential has already been revealed;
as he wanders through the gates of existence, observing old age and death,
the illusory conditions suddenly fall silent.
When the Way was proclaimed at the Cock Garden (Kukkutārāma) and its fragrance spread across Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa),
the boundless realms of all lands appeared within the tip of a single hair,
and the entire scripture-scroll of the great trichiliocosm emerged from within a mote of dust.
It spread westward to the land of Zhutu and flowed eastward to Zhendan; there,
it was written by inscribing upon leaves.
Thus, although the holy teachings of a single moment were transmitted to Ānanda,
there was also the plucking of the flower and the smile.
Thus, the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was entrusted solely to Kāśyapa;
from the time of Bodhidharma’s arrival in the West, he has truly been regarded as the First Patriarch.
Its transmission passed through forty-seven and twenty-two generations until it reached Caoxi; thus,
the Way of the Twin Sala Trees shone ever more brightly,
and the flow of its single drop spread ever wider.
From Nanyue and Qingyuan downward, they branched into five schools,
each excelling in its own lineage style;
although their methods for responding to and engaging with sentient beings differed in their established doctrines.
Yet when they are brought together and traced back to their source, they are one; there is not a single instance where their arrow-tips do not meet or their whip-shadows do not coincide.
In receiving beings and benefiting sentient life, they have brought about many awakenings;
their streams and branches spread far and wide.
With its branches and leaves spreading wide and lush,
the two schools of Linji and Yunmen have flourished uniquely throughout the world. I, the Emperor,
have received the precious mandate of Heaven.
In assuming the great succession of the state,
we reverently reflect that Emperor Wenzu opened the gateway of the Way throughout the vast realm,
and Emperor Taizong elucidated the profound meaning across all under heaven.
Emperor Zhaoseng transmitted the lamp of the Dharma at Jingde,
and Emperor Yongzao widely illuminated the great lamp at Tiansheng;
both extensively propagated the true wind and assisted in divine transformation.
This was to establish a governance based on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Our august Divine Ancestor was especially inclined toward the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
In the third year of the Yuánfēng era—
By imperial decree, two great Chan monasteries were established at Daxiangguosi:
Huelin was opened in the eastern wing,
and Zhikai was built along the western corridor.
In the year of Renxu,

at the request of Princess Yueguo Dachang, along with Zhang Dunli— the Ma-duwei (Husband-to-the-Emperor) and Acting Commander-in-Chief and Inspector of Jiqing Army— he reconstructed Fayun Chan Temple in the south of the capital.
Thereupon, the patriarchal seat shone with brilliance and the monastic communities flourished in their prime;
those throughout the land who donned the square robes and aspired to the joy of Chan gathered like clouds at the capital.
Now, I respectfully recommend that the abbot of this monastery, Chan Master Weibai of Foguo, who has investigated the Supreme Vehicle and realized the First Principle, be appointed;
for he has frequently entered the inner palace and thrice ascended the high seat.
To propagate this sublime purport truly satisfies my deepest aspirations.
In the past, when the Śākyamuni Buddha preached the Lotus Sūtra,
he emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
Light illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction;
thereupon Maitreya posed his questions,
and Mañjuśrī resolved his doubts.
It was said that such were the original auspicious signs of the light of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa;
the Dharma Master Varaprabha was the one who upheld this sutra,
and the Tathāgata Samantaprabha was the one who attained its realization.
The title "Continuation of the Lamp" (Jùdēng) signifies that the meaning of lamps continuing one after another and lights merging with one another resides herein.
Alas! The ocean of perfect enlightenment fundamentally encompasses the ten directions.
Birth and extinction are like empty bubbles, leading one to sink into the three realms of existence;
because of clarity, objects are established, and as sensory dust triggers cognition,
deluded consciousness persists and wanders through the various destinies.
How truly lamentable!
If one were to turn the light inward to illuminate and cause the true to emerge and return to the source, this would indeed be such a record.
It points directly to the school of the nature (xìngzōng).
The single transmission of the mind-seal can be attained between the eyebrows and eyelashes;
it can be presented before words.
To lift up the world of Abhirati with a single hand and manifest a magnificent pavilion with a mere snap of the fingers—
such marvelous and wondrous spiritual powers are truly inconceivable.
Rejoicing among the multitude,
we have forged these excellent karmic conditions;
may we together leave behind the treacherous straits of delusion.
To accompany him upon the path of enlightenment— this is my aspiration.
This is the Dharma Master Foguo of Fayun Chan Temple in Bianjing.
His name was Weibai.
He was born into the Ran family in Jingjiang Prefecture and succeeded Chan Master Yuantong Xiu as his heir.
Xiu succeeded Tianyi Huai;
Huai succeeded Xuedou Xian Chanshi Puding.

In the *Renwu* year, the first year of the Chongning era (the second year of the Qiantong era of Emperor Tianzuo of the Great Liao, the first year of Aguda of the Jurchens), one imperial amnesty decree from the Western Xia and the Song was issued throughout the empire.
Regarding those monks of long-standing renown and virtue who have served as teachers and models for the assembly but have never been granted a posthumous title (śi),
their respective jurisdictions shall be requested to investigate and report the matter to the throne,
so that a master’s title may be conferred upon them.
An imperial edict was issued for all military prefectures and commanderies to establish Chongning Temples;
these were subsequently renamed Tianning Temples.
During the reign of Emperor Gaozong, they were further changed to Baoen Guangxiao Temples.
Posthumous honors and solemn offerings were made during the "Small Calendar" of the Southern Song’s Zhongxing era.
Guiwei (1063): the second year of Chongning; the third year of Qianlong of the Great Liao; the second year of the Jin (Jurchen); and the fourth month of Xia (Xixia) in the Song calendar.
By imperial decree, the Great Master Ciyun Zunshe of Tiantong Temple in Hangzhou was posthumously titled the Great Master Fabao;
the Dharma Master Fanzhen of Nanping was posthumously titled the Dharma Master Shixiang.
Epitaph for the Dharma Master Fahui of Nanping, posthumously titled by Imperial Decree, who did not live to see the mobilization of troops at Zhongnan Mountain.

Year Jiashen (1104), the third year of the Chongning era; the fourth year of the Qiandeng era of the Great Liao; the third year of Aguda of the Jurchens; the Spring of the second month in the Western Xia *Louzaiyuan* era; the Song dynasty.

An imperial edict was issued to establish Louzhe Gardens (Leper Fields for the Deceased) in all prefectures and counties throughout the realm to provide burial for those who died abroad and had no one to return them home. *Dongdu Dijì* (The Imperial Annals of the Eastern Capital):
On the fifth day of the fifth month of the summer in the [Song] dynasty, the Emperor personally offered praise to the Buddha’s tooth relic.
The Emperor welcomed [the relic] at the three courts; the Emperors Taizong, Zhenzong, and Renzong bestowed eulogies upon the Buddha’s tooth from the Great Xiangguo Monastery.
It was then brought into the inner palace for veneration, where the Emperor extended his utmost reverence.
Next, śarīra relics emerged from the crystal casket like falling raindrops.
The Emperor praised him with a verse, saying:
"The Great Being Śākyamuni..."
Equal to space, he reaches even a single speck of dust;
all who seek him respond to their resonance.
There is no land where he does not manifest his body.
Jade-like and translucent, with a thousand wheels present;
forged anew through a hundred refinements of diamond.
To you, I now pay respectful homage.
I universally pray that all classes of beings may be saved. This concludes the fifty-second chapter of the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Terms and Meanings).
The Chan Master of Wuzu Mountain in Qizhou was named Fayuan.
On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month in summer, he ascended the hall to bid farewell to the assembly and entered nirvana.
The Master was born in Mianzhou into the Deng family and succeeded Master Baiyun Yuan as his dharma heir.
Duansu succeeded Yangqi Hui;
Hui succeeded Chan Master Ciming Yuan.
This was the ninth generation under the Linji lineage.
Those who succeeded to the Master’s Dharma were Foguo Qin, Yuanwu, Fojian Qin, and Foyan Yuan;
these were popularly known as the "Three Buddhas."
Yuan’s successor was Huanglong Muan Zhong;
Zhong’s successor was Puan Pusa Yin Su. These are recorded in the *Fodeng Lu*.
This was composed by Chan Master Fuyan Yuan while he resided at Longmen, under the heading "Three Self-Reflections of Longmen."
First, this life is as fleeting as a horse passing through a crevice;
what leisure is there for the idle mind to engage in trivial matters?
Since you have honored the Śākya lineage, [you should not do so].
Xushao examined the teaching style of his lineage and scrutinized the fundamental principles of the ancestral school;
what was their defining character?
Second, he said:
The path of practice remains unfulfilled and the time since the Sage departed is far distant;
thus, one must truly not abandon the guidance of virtuous friends and teachers.
One should naturally exert oneself, mindful of repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Reflect only upon your own great resolve and do not let it falter.
Third, consider that conditions and karmic retributions are illusory; how can one possibly force them?
How long can human life last? It follows the abundance or scarcity of one’s household.
Whether in suffering or joy, adversity or favor, the Way is found therein.
In movement and stillness, cold and warmth, one should feel self-reproach and repentance; these are the precious instructions from the monastic groves.

Yiyou (the 15th day of the 8th month): In the fourth year of Chongning of the Great Liao (the fifth year of Qiantong), the fourth year of Aguda’s reign among the Jurchen, and the autumn of the eighth month of the Western Xia and Song, the Nine Cauldrons were cast and completed; a musical suite was composed named Dasheseng. (From the *Dongdu Shilüe*, "Emperor's Chronicle").

Bingxu: The fifth year of Chongning; the sixth year of Qiantong in the Great Liao; the fifth year of the Jurchen; the [fifth] year of Xixia. Dinghai: The first year of Daguan; the seventh year of Qiantong in the Great Liao; the sixth year of the Jurchen; the [sixth] year of Xixia. By imperial decree of the Song, the Chan Master Daokai of the Shifang Jingyin Chan Monastery in the Left Street was appointed to reside at Tianning Temple.
Li Xiaoshou, the Governor of Kaifeng, memorialized the throne requesting that Kai be granted purple robes and the title of Chan Master Dingzhao.
After Kai had finished expressing his gratitude for the imperial favor,
he submitted a memorial to decline the honor.
He did not dare to presume upon this undeserved honor and glory.
The Emperor sent Xiao Shou a second time bearing an imperial letter to convey his intent,
but Sengke remained firm and would not change his mind.
The Emperor was enraged and had Huikai arrested and handed over to Mount Tai.
An official questioned him:
"Venerable sir, do you have an illness? If you have an illness, you shall be exempt from punishment."
Kai said, "Throughout my life, I have never uttered a falsehood.
How could I dare seek advantage by feigning illness?"
He was consequently punished by being made to wear a *seungyeok* robe and sent to be registered in Zizhou.
The following year, he was released and banished;
he then established a hermitage on the banks of the Fuyong Lake.
Scholars grew increasingly close to him.
The Emperor bestowed the plaque "Huayan Chan Temple" upon his residence.
The Master was born into the Cui family of Yizhou.
He first traveled to the capital and registered his name at Shu’tai Temple.
There he sat for the examination on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
obtained ordination, and became a successor to Chan Master Qing of Touzi Mountain.
On the fourteenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Chonghe era, he entered nirvana.
Dengzhou Danxia Zichun and others succeeded him.
Zichun had two disciples.
It is said that Qingliao was Zhenxie, and Zhengjue was Hongzhi of Tiantong.
On the twentieth day of the ninth month in the twenty-seventh year of the Shaoxing era of Emperor Gaozong.
Hongzhi took his leave of the Prefectural Governor of Mingyue on the tenth day of the tenth month and returned to the monastery on the eleventh. On that same day,
he wrote by hand a letter of invitation requesting Chan Master Dahui Zonggao to serve as the *yuzhu* (administrator) to oversee the affairs following his death.
He cast aside his writing brush and passed away.
His teeth, hair, and ritual implements were filled with flowing relics.
He was buried whole in Donggok; the master was a native of Shixi, as recorded in the stele inscription.

Wuzi: The second year of Daguan (the Great View); the eighth year of Qiantong of the Great Liao; the seventh year of the Jurchen; the Western Xia and Song; Cai Jing was promoted to Grand Preceptor (Taishi).
Tong Guan was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner (Xuanchu) for the Hexi, Kangxi, and other circuits.
The Inner Attendant’s establishment of the *jié* (military rank) began from this point.
In the fifth month, Guan was promoted to the title of *Jiǎojiàn Sīkōng* (Provisional Vice President of the Department of Works) and transferred to the command of Tàiníng.
From this, Guan relied upon his merit to select and appoint his own generals and officials.
This no longer concerns the imperial court. In the prefecture of Wuxu in western Zhejiang, as recorded in the *Song Jian*, there was a man named Shao Zongyi.
He split open a clam shell, and within it appeared the image of an Arhat.
With his right shoulder bared, his head turned to look toward the left, the folds of his robes were all perfectly detailed.
The monastics and laypeople were filled with wonder and joy; they received it and brought it back to the Tiantai Jiaosi Temple at Cigan in the south of the city.
This temple overlooks the Tiao River.
During the Jianyan era, the Imperial Commissioner Yang Yingcheng passed it on to his guests for their appreciation.
Unaware, it leaped over the railing and into a stream.
Later, when the stream had dried up and the sand was exposed, it was sought out and recovered.
A pavilion was built to house it; this is recorded in the *Yunyu yangqiu*.
When the layman Hong Qingxian of Liantang, who held the official mission of the Jiangdong Commissioner, was offering alms-gold to the Sangha for a meal,
he stayed overnight at Meishan in Chizhou. There,
Chan Master Zongyiqiu of Yuchou welcomed him, and they engaged in a conversation throughout the night.
Hong asked,
"In which sutra is the practice of feeding the sangha seen, and where does its essential meaning lie?
Zong said:
The Sutra in Forty-two Sections states:
"Feeding a hundred ordinary people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person;
even feeding a thousand billion Buddhas of the three periods of time is not as good as feeding one who dwells nowhere, acts without action, and has no realization."
That which is without cultivation or realization is the solitary liberation of right mindfulness.
To be able to provide food for such a person brings merit that transcends all Buddhas.
Indeed, many predecessors have known this principle.
Hong asked, "Who was it?
Zong replied:
To cite a recent example, when Qin Shaoyou was in his place of exile in Tengzhou, he composed his own funeral elegy, which included the line:
"Who will provide the meal for the yellow-robed monks?
When Dongpo heard the news of Qin's death, he [wrote a poem].
He sent a letter with five taels of silver,
entrusting Fan Yuanzhang to provide a vegetarian feast for the monks on his behalf.
When东坡 (Sūn Dōngpō) returned north from Hainan and reached Pílíng, he passed away due to illness.
The students of the Imperial Academy collected money to provide a vegetarian feast for monks at Huilin Monastery in Dongjing;
this is recorded at the beginning of Su Dongpo’s epitaph composed by Su Huangmen.
Hong asked,
"Is there a basis for this donation of gold?
Zong replied:
Have you not seen in the Mao version of the Xiao Ya, the "Luming" (The Deer's Call), which describes the feasting of ministers and honored guests?
Having provided them with food and drink,
one further fills their purses, boxes, baskets, and caskets with gifts.
This is to convey my profound intentions.
For food and drink alone are insufficient to fully express one's reverence;
thus, I have added these gifts to manifest my earnest sincerity.
Thereupon, he recited Ding Jingu’s Memorial for Feeding Monks, which says:
"The Buddha bestowed universal wisdom;
the Way nurtures all living beings."
In all cases where one seeks to rescue those in peril and distress,
one must first manifest auspicious signs in advance. Thus,
it is said that a layman seeking official emolument has presumptuously usurped the heavy authority of the Minister of the Household.
Proclaiming grace upon the vermilion steps, I have been undeservedly favored by the profound bounty of the late Emperor;
yet, in mending the robes of Zhongshan, I have exhausted my skillful artistry,
while in blending the broth of Fu Yue, I find it difficult to satisfy all tastes.
Once, while resting in peaceful sleep, I suddenly dreamed of a pure countenance.
His wondrous instructions were clear and resonant, causing my defiled mind to awaken early;
yet his majestic deportment was profound and hidden, leaving me to regret that my ordinary vision could not perceive it.
It appears that Zhiyong’s worldly affairs were discordant and he distanced himself from harm;
yet when calamity arrived, its full scale remained unfathomable until disaster ensued.
Consequently, he was dismissed from his extraordinary office and sent to the Western Capital.
Moved by the Sage’s grace, he was granted clemency;
yet, as he was exiled to the southern frontiers, he accepted his fate with a willing heart.
His guilt was truly self-inflicted.
This calamity was not wrought by others.
Reflecting upon the scattered state of my family, I wonder where I might find refuge across ten thousand li.
Having already become a minister who has betrayed the state, what recourse remains?
The arts for governing the state were forever severed;
his journey originated from the land of Xiang,

Jǐchǒu (己丑), the third year of Dàguān (大觀) [1109], the ninth year of Qiāntǒng (乾統) of the Great Liao, the eighth year of the Jurchens, and the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the Song dynasty; the year of Xīxià (西夏).

Regarding the fourth Mingfazi (Zhaoqing): below the second generation, Dharma Master Cibian of Hangzhou followed [the lineage] from Yuanfeng through Yuanyou to Daguan, residing at Upper Zhushan for twenty-four years.
He retired to Shousheng Monastery in Chuzhou, where he entered nirvana.
He had ten dharma-heir disciples;
among them, Xizhe, Qingqing, and Qibei were the most prominent in their transmission, as recorded in the *Jiaoxinglu*.

Gengyin (the 10th day of the sixth lunar month): The fourth year of Daoguan; the tenth year of Qiantong in the Great Liao; the ninth year of the Jurchen; the [fourth] year of Xixia; and the [fifth] year of the Song.
On this day, Zhang Shangying entered the相位 (cabinet) as Chancellor.
At that time, there had been a long drought.
That evening, heavy rain fell.
The Emperor bestowed upon Shangying the two large characters "Shānglín" (The Rain for Shang), written by his own hand.

He passed away in the fourth year of the Xuanhua era.

During his days residing in Jingnan,
he maintained an air of self-importance regarding his Daoist learning and was seldom accorded the respect or approval he expected.
Yuanwu moored his boat to pay him a visit.
They engaged in an extensive discussion on the essential tenets of the Avatamsaka Sutra. Yuanwu said:
The realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the Avataṃsaka is the complete reality of both principle and phenomena; from the very beginning,
there is not a single dharma that is artificial.
Therefore, from the one comes the myriad;
understanding the myriad as the one,
the one returns to the one.
Ten thousand upon ten thousand,
vast and inexhaustible. Mind,
Buddha, and sentient beings— these three are without distinction.
Rolling out and rolling up with sovereign ease,
unimpeded and perfectly interfused—

"How rare it is to hear such an eloquent discourse!"
The eulogy for Laohu states:
"Now, Yuanwu’s harmonization of doctrine and practice was such that it caused those who had attained realization to rejoice in their hearts and submit with sincerity."

Yuanwu [Keqin], Zen Master of Zhaojue Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan.
His name was Kechin.
He was the son of the Luo family of Pengzhou;
his lineage had been devoted to Confucianism for generations.
As a child, he could compose a thousand words in a single day.
While visiting Myōjiku-ji Temple, he was moved by a Buddhist scripture and subsequently entered the monastic order.
He followed his teacher to undergo self-examination and tonsure.
From Dharma Master Wenzhao, he thoroughly studied and lectured on the sutras;
furthermore, from Minxing, he received the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Upon leaving Shu, he first visited Yuquan Hao.
He subsequently relied upon Jinluan Xin, Dayi Zhe, Huanglong Haitang Xin, and Donglin Zong,
all of whom praised him highly.
Huìtáng said, "In the future,
the lineage of Linjì shall belong to you.
Finally, he arrived at Qízhōu.
He visited Master Yan at Mount Wuzu and fully mastered his profound teachings.
It was during the Chongning era that he returned to his native village.
Guo Gong Zhizhang, the Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy and Military Governor of Chengdu,
requested that he reopen Fazuo Monastery as Zhaojue.
At the beginning of the Zhenghe era, he retired from his post and traveled south across the gorges.
At that time, the layman Wujin (Wujin Jushi), Zhang Gong Shangying, was residing in Jingnan.
The Master went to visit him and they discussed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Wujin, filled with faith and reverence, prostrated himself before the Master.
He resided at Biryam-sa and later moved to Doryun-sa.
State Censor Deng Gongzi-chang memorialized the Emperor, requesting that he be granted purple robes and a formal title.
By imperial decree, he was appointed to Mount Jiang at Jiankang;
subsequently, by edict, he was installed as the abbot of Tianning Wanshou Monastery in the capital of Bianjing.
The Emperor summoned him for an audience and bestowed upon him exceptionally generous honors and patronage.
At the beginning of the Jianyan era, he was again transferred to Mount Jinshan in Zhenjiang. Just then,
Emperor Gaozong visited Yangzhou and issued an imperial decree for him to have an audience,
bestowing upon him the title Chan Master Yuanwu.
He was transferred to Yunju in Jiangxi.
After a long time, he returned to take charge of Zhaojue.
On the day of Jiyou in the eighth month of the fifth year of the Shaoxing era (the reign title of Emperor Gaozong), he manifested a slight illness.
He sat cross-legged, wrote a verse, bid farewell to the assembly, and passed away as he set down his brush.
When cremated, his tongue and teeth remained uncorrupted,
and there were countless relics of five colors.
A stupa was erected beside Zhaojue Temple,
and he was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhengjiao.
He was the dharma heir of Chan Master Yan of Wuzu Mountain.
Yan succeeded Baiyun;
Baiyun succeeded Yangqi;
and Yangqi succeeded Chan Master Ciming Yuan.
The *Linji-pai yebu denglu* (Supplementary Lamp Record of the Linji School).

Xinmao year: the first year of the Zhenghe era; the first year of the Tianqing era of the Great Liao; the tenth year of the Jurchen Aguda; the Renchen year of the Western Xia. Zhenghe year two: the second year of the Tianqing era of the Great Liao; the eleventh year of the Jurchen Aguda; the Western Xia. Song Taishi, Duke of Chu, Cai Jing, was fond of eating quails.
He kept them confined in a cage to fatten them for slaughter.
He once dreamed that several thousand quails were petitioning him,
one of whom spoke these words:
I eat the millet from your ration to fill the meat beneath your chopsticks;
a single bowl of soup sustains hundreds of lives.
Birth and death revolve like the hub of a wheel;
observe that your life shall endure for a thousand springs.
Calamity and fortune depend upon one another, lying hidden within each other.
The Emperor was deeply apprehensive of him. In the ninth month of autumn in the Song dynasty,
the titles of the Grand Chancellor and Vice-Chancellor were changed to those of the Left and Right Attendant Censors (Zuo-you Puyue).

Gui Si (the 10th day of the tenth lunar month): In the third month of spring in the third year of Zhenghe (1113 CE), Wang Anshi was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shu. Tianqing Year 3 (1114 CE) of the Great Liao: Aghuda of the Jurchen [was proclaimed Emperor]. The twelfth year of the Western Xia: At the Miaohui Nunnery in the Eastern Capital of Song, the Abbot and Great Master Jingzhi, Huiguang.

This is why Han She-ren Zicang, in his inscription for the Guang-ta pagoda, praised him for his vast learning and skillful eloquence.
The pagoda was established at the site of Shengxiang on Mount Xi in Yuzhang; this is recorded in the *Yunwo Jitan*.
In the fourth month of the Song dynasty, the state of Jiazhou in Western Sichuan submitted a memorial.
A great tree was broken by the wind, leaving behind a withered trunk where a monk sat in meditative concentration;
his beard and hair were thick and tangled, and his fingernails and toenails grew over his body.
The Emperor ordered him to be sent to the capital.
In the eighth month of autumn, he was invited into the inner palace.
The Tripitaka Master Jin Zongchi of the Translation Institute rapped his metal gong to rouse him from his meditative absorption.
The monk said,
"I am Huichi, the younger brother of Dharma Master Huiyuan of Donglin.
I have traveled west to Mount Emei."
Because I entered meditative concentration here,
I have not known whether Master Huiyuan is free from ailment.

Master Huiyuan was a person of the Eastern Jin dynasty;

this person and that person are the body within the state of meditative absorption.
If one realizes this, one understands that Bodhi originally has no tree.
There is no need for the arduous labor of questioning Lu Neng; the *Fǎpǔdēnglù* (Record of the Universal Lamp) consists of twenty-two fascicles.
Huìchí saw [this record] in the eighth year of Yìxī of the Eastern Jìn dynasty, the Jiǎwǔ year.

In the fourth year of Zhènghé, the fourth year of Tiānqìng of the Great Liao, the thirteenth year of the Jurchen Āgū'dá, in the eighth month of autumn, he rebelled against the Liao. [This was the era of] Xiàxià and the Jurchen Jin.
Se-bon was originally a person from Silla;
his clan name was Wanyan.
"Wanyan" is equivalent to the Chinese word for "king."
For generations he served as a chieftain;
for two hundred years his clan remained subject to the Great Liao,
and they inherited the title of Regional Commander (Jiedushi) through hereditary succession.
In the fourth generation after Zhi Kangfu,
his wife Zhennü gave birth to two sons;
the elder was named Hulai.
Hu Lai gave birth to three sons.
The eldest was named He Li;
the second was named Pu La Shu.
Ji’s son was Yangge.
Yangge had three sons;
the eldest was Aguda.
The next was named Wuqima;
the youngest was named Sigai.
Sigai fathered Yanhan.
When the Jurchens reached Yangge Taishi, they first became dominant among the various tribes.
In the year Bingzi, Xiao Xie-li raised a band of followers;
the Liao state captured him.
He was subsequently reborn in the realm of the Jurchens; see the entry for the year Yihai of the Shouchang era.
The Liao court ordered Yang Ge to capture him, but Yang Ge merely executed Li.
He dispatched his eldest son, Agudata, to present the severed heads to the Liao.
From this point on, Yangge, inwardly relying on his meritorious service,
secretly harbored heterodox ambitions.
Yang Ge died.
As for Aguda’s age,
it coincided with the time when the Liao Emperor Tianzhu was addicted to plundering and exploitation.
The ruler and his subjects were both licentious and debauched.
Their ministers, Li Yan and Xiao Fengxian, were men of mediocre and trivial character, greedy and rapacious.
Aguda inherited the wealth and prosperity left by his father, Yang Ge.
With their troops strong and their horses robust, they harbored designs of a different sort.
Previously, the land of the Jurchens bordered the Five Kingdoms to the northeast;
to the east of the Five Kingdoms lay the great ocean.
Famous hawks were produced;
those that came from海东 (Haidong) were called 海東青 (Haidongqing).
Small yet agile and robust, they were capable of capturing wild geese and ducks.
Zhaowu regarded this as even more extraordinary.
The people of Liao cherished it intensely.
After Tianzuo succeeded to the throne, his demands for tribute became particularly harsh.
He coerced his own people to search for her thoroughly and present her as an offering.
It was only after the Jurchens fought five battles that they captured her;
the Jurchens suffered greatly because of this.
Furthermore, the various generals along the border were incessantly soliciting bribes and gifts every day, causing them no end of harassment.
Consequently, the various tribes became resentful and rebelled against Liao;
they secretly allied with Aguda to raise an army and plot insurrection.
In the eighth month of autumn in this gengwu year,
Aguda first rebelled,
employing Yanhan and Hushe as his chief advisors.
Eun-mok, Ge-ye, Yeol-lu, Suk-ja, Mu, and others served as generals.
With two thousand armored cavalry, they invaded Ningjiang Prefecture east of the Hontong River.
Tianzuo dispatched troops to resist them.
All were defeated, and Ningjiang Prefecture was subsequently lost.
Aguda led his troops forward in successive battles.
In the eighth month of autumn in the year of Yiwu (1135).
The Liao Emperor Tianzhu issued an edict to personally lead an expedition against the Jurchens.
As his route passed through Changchun,
the weapons and armor in the army suddenly emitted light one night.
Zhang Lin, the Chancellor of Liao, said:
"When Zhuangzong of Tang attacked Liang,
his spears and halberds emitted light at night."
Guo Chongtao said,
"Fire issuing forth and troops entering are omens of destroying the enemy.
Tianzuo was delighted and believed him.
In the eleventh month, they advanced in battle, but their forces were shattered.
Within a single day and night, Tianzhu fled five hundred li to retreat and take refuge at Changchun.
The Jurchens, taking advantage of their victory,
subsequently annexed fifty-four prefectures, including Bohai and Liaoyang; according to the *Liaozhi*,
Mount Changbai and the Tongtian River both lie within today’s Kaiyuan Road and Xianping Prefecture of Liaoyang.

Year Yiwei, the fifth year of Zhenghe (1115). In the second month, Prince Xiang was established as Crown Prince. Great Liao: the fifth year of Tianqing; Jurchen Aguda: the fourteenth year; Western Xia; Song: the fourth month.
Dharma Master Zhongli of Mingzhi at Yanqing Monastery in Mingzhou entered nirvana.
Zhongli was succeeded by Shenzhi Jianwen;
Jianwen was succeeded by Guangzhi Shangxian.
Throughout three generations, they all successively served as abbots at the ancestral monastery of Yanqing,
until its establishment reached great prosperity.
Chao Shuo-zhi composed the inscription for his stupa, titled "Stupa Inscription for the Ancestral Monastery."
The Dharma Master Yongdao of Xiangji Monastery in the Left Ward of the Song capital,
who was bestowed with the imperial title of Great Master Baojue and was a Dharma Master of the Three Baskets (Tripitaka),
transmitted [the lineage] to Chan Master Siji of Huanglong Mountain in Longfeng Prefecture.
His name was Wuxin.
He was the son of the Huang family in Shaozhou.
At birth, he had a purple fleshy protuberance on his left shoulder.
He bared his right shoulder in the manner of a *saṃghāṭī*.
At a young age, he followed the virtuous teachings at the Buddha Hall and underwent tonsure.
Upon receiving full ordination, he traveled to various regions to pay his respects to Chan Master Huìtáng Xīn.
Having mastered the essential points of the Dharma,
he succeeded him.
On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month of the year Yiwu (1095), he entered nirvana.
The relics from the cremation were five-colored;
subsequently, those who passed by that site obtained them in even greater abundance.
The *Tà* (Stūpa) is located to the north of the master’s quarters at Huìtáng;
it is the *Pǔdēng* (Universal Lamp). The Chan Master Lètán Zhàntáng of Lóngxīng Prefecture was named Wénzhǔn.
He was born into the Liang family in Xingyuan Prefecture.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled to visit various regions to pay his respects to Chan Master Zhenjing Wen,
where he served him diligently for ten years.
One day, while raising his staff to clear a water channel, droplets splashed onto his robes and he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
When Lord Li Jingzhi of Xianmu was serving as governor of Yuzhang,
he invited him to open Dharma Cloud Hermitage.
He moved to Letan.
On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the fifth year of the Zhenghe era,
he changed his robes, recited a verse, and passed away.
Upon cremation, his eyes, teeth, and prayer beads remained unburnt.
His śarīra were crystalline, spherical, and lustrous; a stupa was erected on the southern slope of the mountain.
The Minister Zhang Shangying, known as Wujin Jushi, composed the stele inscription for his life and deeds.
It was requested by Chan Master Dahuigao while he was still a fellow practitioner.
The Master succeeded Zhenjing Wen;
Wen succeeded Huanglong Nan Chan Master Puding.

Bingshen (1st day of the 9th month of autumn, the 6th year of Zhenghe; the 6th year of Tianqing of the Great Liao; the 15th year of Aguda of the Jin). On this day, the Vinaya Master Yuanzhao of Lingzhi Monastery in Hangzhou entered nirvana while seated in the full lotus posture.
He lived to the age of sixty-nine and had fifty-one years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-vassa*).
He was buried in the northwest corner of the monastery.
He was posthumously titled "Great Wisdom" (Dazhi).
Liu Tao inscribed his stupa,
and Guan Yan composed a stele commemorating his religious career.
Sun Di erected a stone inscription for him.
Zhao, whose courtesy name was Zhanyan,
was born into the Tang family of Yuhang.
The *Vinaya-mahā-śāstra* was originally established by the Buddha himself;
from Mañjuśrī downward, not a single word has been permitted to be added.
When Upāli convened the council, he did not dare to expand it by even a single character.
Throughout the human realm, the heavens, and the ten directions of the triple world,
the infinite assemblies of sages across the oceans of lands are all unified by a single discipline; this alone may be called truly majestic.
Just as in the world, rites, music, and the power of military expeditions must necessarily issue from the Son of Heaven;
the dukes, marquises, high ministers, and great officers may not presume to usurp these prerogatives.
Yet, when the Great Dharma was first transmitted to the East, [it was likewise so].
Only the Vinaya remained unclear, causing scholars to lose their way.

During the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, Daoxuan— the Great Vinaya Master of Chengzhao Monastery on Mount Zhongnan in Yongxing Commandery— composed the *Jieshu*, the *Jiemoshu*, and the *Shichao* to propagate the *Sifenlü*.
It has been transmitted for over four hundred years,
and nearly sixty schools have provided commentaries on its meaning.
Among these, the Vinaya Master Dazhaokeng of Zhongshan composed the *Huizheng ji* (Record of Rectifying the Meaning).
Only he fully exhausted the principle.
Finally, this Lingzhi Taizhi Yuanzhao,
through the *Lotus Sūtra*, revealed the perfect intent.
He composed the *Zizhi ji*.
Although his path differed from that of Master Huizheng, they reached the same goal;
he sought to elucidate the original intent of the Nanshan school.
This was further brought into accord with the Buddha’s regulations;
from this point on, the *Huizheng zizhi* (Correcting and Sustaining) also branched off as a distinct school within the Vinaya,
just as when a golden staff is broken apart, it does not lose its essential nature as gold.
*Record of Annual Entries on the Divisibility of the Fruit of the Non-Action Precept Body*.

Dingyou year, the seventh year of the Zhenghe era [1117 CE]: An imperial edict changed the title of "Jiedu Chaocha Liuhou" (Commander of the Military District and Inspector General Left Behind) to "Chengxuan Shi" (Hereditary Commandant). Tianqing year seven of the Great Liao [1151 CE]: The Jurchen Aguda was sixteen years old. Lin Lingsu of Xixia was a native of Wenzhou.
He was well-versed in esoteric arts and supplemented these with the methods of Leigong.
Initially, he traveled about, not finding favor in the regions of Xu, Hao, Huai, and Si,
where he begged for alms at various temples.
The monks treated him with contempt.
Upon reaching Chu Prefecture (present-day Huai'an Prefecture),
he engaged in a physical altercation with the monk Hui-shi and brought their dispute before the authorities.
At that time, the district magistrate Shi Zhong was delighted by his eloquence and agility;
he released him from custody and established him in a guest house,
where he questioned him regarding the arts of *tunan* (breath cultivation), alchemical refinement (*shaolian*), and ascension to flight.
It was at this point, in the first month of the seventh year of the Zhenghe era,
that Zhong took him to the capital to have an audience with the Chancellor Cai Jing,
who then introduced him to the Emperor.
Lindayan said,
"In the heavens there is the Shenxiao Wangqing Palace,
presided over by the Lord of Eternal Life."
His younger brother, the Lord of Green Flower (Qinghua Dijun), was both sons of the Jade Emperor.
Following them were the Left Minister, the Immortal Earl (Xianbo), along with the penalizing immortal officials such as Chu Hui and over eight hundred other officers.
This means that Di is the Emperor of Eternal Life (Chángshēng Dìjūn);
Cāi Jīng is the Left Minister and Immortal Lord (Xiānbó);
and Língsù is Zhǔ Huì.
The Emperor joyfully believed him and bestowed upon Lin the title "Immortal of the Golden Gate.
He constructed Tongzhengong (Palace of Penetrating Truth) to provide a dwelling for him.
The Emperor styled himself the "Imperial Teacher, Emperor Daojun.

In the second month, he issued an edict to change all the *Tianning guan* (Heavenly Peace Observatories) throughout the realm into *Shenxiao Wangqing Wanshou gong* (Shenxiao Palaces of Divine Clarity and Ten-Thousand-Year Longevity).
In locations where no observatory existed, monasteries were to be used in its stead.
Furthermore, he established images of Lord Changsheng (Changsheng Dajun) and Lord Qinghua (Qinghua Dajun),
constructed the Baolu Palace,
and instituted a curriculum for Daoist studies.
In the first year of the Xuanhua era, the Emperor received auspicious omens.
In the eleventh month of winter, he released Lin Lingsu to return to Wenzhou, where he died. (From the *Dongdu shilüe*, "Emperor's Chronicle").
The Chan Master Foshou Lingyuan of Huanglong Mountain in Longxing Prefecture.
His name was Weiqing.
Having received the Dharma within Huítáng’s quarters,
he entered nirvana on the eighteenth day of the ninth month of that autumn.
The Master succeeded Chan Master Baojue Xin of Huītáng.
His Dharma heirs—Fànhuì, Gǔdé, Fēngshǒu, and Shìzhōu—were all eminent disciples.
At that time, the layman Yichuan Xú Shīchuān, Zhū Shìyīng, and Hóng Jūfù all followed him to inquire about the Way; this is recorded in the *Pǔdēng Lù*.
Chan Master Zhikai Fojian of Bianjing was named Huiqin.
He was the son of the Wang family of Shuzhou (present-day Anqing Prefecture). At the age of seven, he became a disciple of Yuanshen at Guangjiao Monastery in his native prefecture.
He tested his mastery of what he had studied.

Every time he tasted the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* with the thought that "the Buddha’s word states that this alone is the one true reality, and all else is not real," he experienced a moment of awakening.
He then entered the quarters of Wuzu Heshang Yan.
Having deeply grasped the essential points of the Dharma, he succeeded [to his master].
When Sun Dingchen, the Governor of Shu, invited him to reside at Taiping Monastery,
the Way of the Dharma spread widely.
At the beginning of the Zhenghe era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Zhihai Monastery in Bianjing.
After five years, he requested to return home;
he received an edict permitting him to dwell at Qianshan in Jiankang.
The State Councillor Deng Gongzi had previously petitioned for the bestowal of a master’s title and purple robes.
On the eighth day of the ninth month in the seventh year of Zhenghe,
he ascended the hall and said:
The Mind-Seal of the Patriarchs is like the mechanism of an iron ox;
once it has gone, it remains firmly imprinted.

On the eighth day of the tenth month, [he spoke].

Da Jin refers to the Da Jin, that is, the Jurchen.
Agudha established a state and ascended the throne as emperor.
While the Liao Emperor Tianzhu was in the capital,

During the autumn, the women of the Jin captured more than fifty cities, including Huanglong Fu in Dongjing.
At that time, there was a man named Yang Pu.

In the eighth month of autumn,

1. The imperial title "Great Sage, Greatly Enlightened Emperor" (Dàshèng Dàmíng Huángdì); 2. The national name "Great Jin" (Dàjīn); 3. The jade-drawn ceremonial carriage; 4. The dispatch of envoys on the emperor’s birthday and the New Year; 8. An annual tribute of twenty-five hundred thousand bolts of silk and taels of silver, constituting half of the annual subsidies previously granted by the Southern Song; 9. The cession of the two circuits of Liaodong and Changchun; 10. The return of the three princes—Ahu, Chan, and Zhao—who had been born among the Jurchens. These matters were presented to the ministers for deliberation by Tianzuo.
Xiao Fengxian was greatly pleased,

Furthermore, as for the state of Donghuai, it is merely a small kingdom;

"I do not understand the text of this edict at all.

"You must be able to come before my army this coming autumn;
otherwise, I shall lead my troops to seize the capital.
Tianzuo detested hearing news of the Jurchens.

The others are called *ṛṣis* and *mahāsattvas*;

Emperor Wencheng greatly promoted [Buddhism].
Emperor Wu of Zhou, however, believed the words of Wei Yuansong and suppressed the Buddha-dharma;

Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty succeeded in reviving [the Buddhist teachings].

In our nation, the Emperor Taizu and Emperor Taizong, followed by successive sagacious rulers, translated scriptures, examined monks, and disseminated the Buddha-dharma.

Gengzi (1120): The second year of Xuanhua; the tenth year of Tianqing of the Great Liao; the third year of Tianfu of the Jin; the second year of Yuande of the Western Xia. Chen Liangbi, Grand Marshal of the Song, established a great assembly of offerings and invited various Chan and doctrinal masters.
There was a virtuous Dharma master,
a preeminent leader of the Xianshou school known as Yihǔ (Tiger of Meaning).
He sent a message to the various Chan practitioners, saying:
Our Buddha established his teachings ranging from the Small Vehicle to the Perfect and Sudden.
Having swept away both emptiness and existence to personally realize the true and eternal,
he was then adorned with the myriad virtues before being designated as a Buddha.
Yet, the Chan school transforms ordinary beings into sages with a single shout;
when examined against the various sutras and śāstras, this seems to be in contradiction.
Now, if a single shout can accord with the five teachings, it constitutes the correct teaching.
"If one cannot enter these five teachings, it constitutes a heterodox explanation.
At that time, the various Chan masters were seated in rows.
Chan Master Fazhen (Yigong) signaled with his eyes to Chan Master Cishou (Shengong).
Shen-zhou called upon Jing-in to face him.
Jing-in summoned Shan and said to him,

It is not worth troubling the great Chan masters to respond;
only the junior elder Jingyin can resolve the Dharma Master’s doubts.
As for those five teachings, the teaching of the "foolish" Hīnayāna, for instance, possesses the meaning of existence.
The Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna represents the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna represents the meaning of neither being nor non-being, nor being empty.
What is called the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna represents the meaning of being both being and emptiness simultaneously.

What is called the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle is the principle that it is empty yet not non-existent, and existent yet not empty. This single shout of mine is not only able to encompass the five teachings;
it can even penetrate all the various schools of the world, the hundred philosophers, and all arts and crafts.
He then shouted,

this is what can enter the teachings of the Hīnayāna."
He called Shan again, saying,
"Do you hear me now? Shan replied, "I do not hear."
Cheng said,
"Since you have not heard it, then that single shout just now was non-existent;
this is what can enter the Initial Teaching of the Mahayana."
When I first gave the shout,
you said there was one;
now that the shout has long since faded away, where is it?
Furthermore, you say that the Way is non-existent;
if the Way were non-existent, it would have been truly existent in the primordial beginning.
If the Way were existent, it would be truly non-existent at this very moment.
Since it is neither existent nor non-existent,
one is able to enter the Final Teaching.
At the moment I let out a shout—
Existence is not existence;
it exists because of non-existence.
At the time when there is no "non-existence," [existence does not arise].
Non-existence is not non-existence;
it is non-existence because of existence.
Thus, by realizing that existence is itself non-existence, one can enter the Sudden Teaching.
This single shout of mine does not function as a mere shout.
It transcends existence and non-existence, and both intellectual understanding and emotional attachment are forgotten.
When the Way is present, not even a hair’s breadth is established.
When the Way is non-existent, it transversely pervades empty space; thus,
this single shout enters into hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of shouts,
and those hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of shouts enter into this one shout.
"This is capable of entering the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Shansui then bowed his head in thanks.
The Master called Shansui again and said:
From a single word to a single silence, from a single movement to a single stillness,

Throughout the ten directions of empty space, the myriad phenomena stand in dense array.
The six realms of existence and the four modes of birth;

Immeasurable and wondrous meanings,

The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only.

With both marks and no-marks, a single sound and a single form,

This is still merely the gate and courtyard of transformative instruction, a provisional means adapted to capacities;

Little do you realize that within the school of our ancestral masters, mind is transmitted through mind and the Dharma is sealed by the Dharma;

He repeatedly requested to be recommended for the local examination.
In the second year of the Xining era of Emperor Shenzong,
he attained a profound realization while reading the Lotus Sūtra.
He sought to leave the household life,

He then went to Master Haiei of Baoying Temple on Longmen Mountain in Ru Prefecture to receive the tonsure and the precepts.
He was instructed to travel south in search of instruction.
First, he visited Master Qiansui of Mount Emei in Jiazhou;

He built a hermitage at Taishou Rock and sat in meditation there for twenty years.
In the seventh year of the Yuanyou era of Emperor Zhezong, he traveled to Zhejiang.
The following year, he arrived at Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou and resided there with the assembly.
The two imperial envoys, Wang and Luo, sought the Master’s essential teachings on the mind,
and disciples came to him daily.
Chan Master Tong Yuanming of Lingyin resided at the hermitage on Mount Baiyun behind the temple;
his profound transformation and teachings were widely disseminated.
He then established his own school,
naming it the Baiyun (White Cloud) School after the name of the hermitage where he resided,
and subsequently moved to Longmen Mountain in Yuhang.
The hermitage was called Fudi (Blessed Land).
He preached the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts to the dragon deities.
It was then, in the third year of the Chongning era, that [this occurred].
He went to reside at Ziyun’an (Purple Cloud Hermitage) behind Kaishua Temple at Qiantang Sixi Pagoda.
Monastics and laypeople requested that he lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Zhengji Temple;
this was a time when the Buddhist teachings were being suppressed.

He composed the *Juezheng zonglun* (Treatise on Awakening to and Adhering to the Realization of the School), the *Sanjiao bian* (Compilation on the Three Teachings), and the *Shidi ge* (Song of the Ten Stages).
In the first year of the Daguan era,
he established a hermitage at Qianjin Market in Guian County, Huzhou.
It was named Shidi (Ten Stages).
Next, he went to Jing Mountain in Wucheng, where he planted his staff and obtained a spring; he then built a hermitage and resided there.
His name was Chuchen.
His followers again requested that he return to Zhengji Temple.
Those who were jealous of him reported his debate on the *Zhengzong lun* (Treatise on Proving the School) to the authorities as being in opposition to the state administration.
In the sixth year of the Zhenghe era, he was sent for administrative detention to Sizhou in Guangnan.
In the second year of the Xuande era, his disciples Zhengbu and nine others went to the capital to submit a petition;
by imperial decree, he was released and permitted to live wherever he pleased.
On the twentieth day of the seventh month in this Xin-chou year, he expressed his gratitude.
On the third day of the eighth month, he composed a verse and presented it to the Governor, Mr.
You, indicating that they would part on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month.
When the appointed time arrived, he passed away.
His secular age was seventy-nine years;
his monastic seniority was fifty-two summer retreats.
The disciple Huineng, receiving these final instructions,
reverently enshrined the sacred remains and śarīra to be interred at Nanshan in Yuhang, Hangzhou,
in the second month of the fifth year of the Xuande era.
The stupa was named Baiyun (White Cloud),
and the monastery was named Puan (Universal Peace).
Later, his disciples changed its name to Puning (Universal Tranquility).
Among these, Chongde, Jeungsan, Songnim,
and Seonju were all places where he practiced the Way.
Also [included are] Deungcheong, Nongsan, Cheosan, Bangsan, Gwanyonsan, Gwian, and Yeomsan.
These were all sites where his *śarīra* relics were enshrined.
His school flourished in the region south of the Zhe River.

On the day of Renyin, the twelfth month of the fourth year of Xuanhua (1122), the Layman Wujin passed away. This was the second year of Baoda of the Great Liao, the fifth year of Tianfu of the Jin, and the third month of the spring of the Xia dynasty.
The Jurchens destroyed Zhongjing (the Capital of the Xi state).
Upon hearing this report while in Yanjing,
Tianzhu was greatly terrified and departed that very day through Juyong Pass.
He led five thousand cavalry westward to flee to Yunzhong Prefecture,
leaving the Chancellor Zhang Lin and Li Chuwen with Prince Chun of Yan to guard Yan.
Chun had resided in Yan for twenty years and had won the hearts of the people.
Tianzuo hurried toward Yuyang and entered Jiaoshan.
