and rectified the boundaries of the land.
Qin Hui was unable to embody the Emperor’s intent;
he stripped the generals of their authority to stifle the spirit of loyalty and righteousness,
ultimately causing the territories to remain unrecovered.
The Emperor ascended the throne at the age of twenty-one.
He reigned for thirty-six years before abdicated the throne to Xiaozong.
He styled himself the Retired Sovereign (Taishanghuang) and resided at the Deyou Palace.

He passed away at the age of eighty-two in the thirty-second year of the Shaoxing era (1162 CE), which corresponds to the fourth year of the Jianyan era in the Continued Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government (*Xu Tongjian*).

Dingwei (17th day of the intercalary month), the first year of Jianyan (1127). In the tenth month of winter, the imperial carriage went on a hunting tour to Yangzhou. Great Jin, Tianhui Year 5; Western Xia, Wushen (1st day of the intercalary month). On the first day of the first month of the second year of Jianyan (1128), an edict was issued for Kechin, the abbot of Jingshan, to enter the presence at Yangzhou, where he was granted the title Chan Master Yuanwu Puding. Great Jin, Tianhui Year 6; Western Xia, the fourth day of the tenth month of winter.
The Dharma Master Jingfan of Tiantai at Beichen Monastery in Suzhou entered nirvana.
Fan transmitted [the lineage] to Huiming;
Ming transmitted it to Yundiao.
Compiled by the Dharma Master Baoci, based on the *Lanling Ji* and the *Shengtong Sengzhuan*.

Jiyou (the year 1129), the third year of Jianyan, the seventh year of Tianhui of the Da Jin, the year of various heavenly positions in the Western Xia; the twenty-first day of the eighth month of autumn.
Dharma Master Huijue Qibei of Shang Tianzhu in Hangzhou entered nirvana;
Ye Mengde of Shilin inscribed his stupa.
Qibei authored three fascicles of a commentary on the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* and two fascicles of the *Zuyuan ji*.
His successor, Shen Huan, was as profound as a still pool; his teachings endured for a long time.

Huan once examined and discussed the ranks and positions of the various heavens, establishing the relationships of sovereign and minister, guest and host, and male and female, as well as their fundamental and manifest traces, as the primary framework.
This refers to the Honored Celestial Lord Mahābrahmā, who presides over the three realms, reigning supreme above and governing below;
all the other devas are his subjects.
Mahābrahmā is the sovereign of the three realms.
The three-eyed Maheśvara is the lord of the great trichiliocosm;
Śakra rules over the thirty-three heavens dwelling upon the earth;
and the Four Kings preside over and command the eight classes of beings.
Although the roles of ruler and subject differ,
each necessarily has its own governing principle.
It is as if great eloquence resides within the mountains and marshes.
The merit resides within the gardens of the Northern Heaven;
it is merely a guest sojourning there,
for in truth, there is no one who possesses or governs it.
Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings are male devas;
Guṇakārandavatī, Mahāprajñā, the Earth Deity, and the Tree Deity are all female devas.
One must not allow the order of male and female to be lost.
Moreover, the Mother of Ghosts has a daughter named [Goddess of] Merit,
and the Goddess of Merit has a son named [Skanda];
now Saṃjñeya’s son dwells above his mother.
This may be called a case of the mother following the son;
how could he possibly dwell above the Lord of Heaven?
Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Kings are originally Bodhisattvas dwelling on earth.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada was originally the elder brother of the Thousand Buddhas who attained Buddhahood.
How could one align their outward manifestations without first examining their fundamental basis?
Only after understanding these four meanings can one begin to speak of the celestial realm.
Huan had three disciples:
Zong’an Miaoxin, Changzhai Fabai, and Jue’an Jianyan.
Jianyan transmitted [the lineage] to Jiantang Siyi.
During the Baoqing and Shaoding eras, he resided at Upper Zhuchi;
this is recorded in the *Shengtong Sengzhuan*. In the tenth month of winter, while the Emperor was on a hunt in Taizhou, he arrived at Jin’ao Mountain Temple.
The place was profoundly still and empty, with only the vast hall filled with a pure fragrance.
There was an elderly monk with white hair who offered prayers to the various devas before the Buddha.
His words on preserving the state during times of anxiety were sincere and earnest.
The Emperor was pleased and questioned him,
to which he replied:
This is the *Huánguó Jīnguāngmíng Sānmèi Chàn* (The Repentance Ritual of the Golden Light Samādhi for Protecting the State).
Later, while the Emperor was stationed in Hangzhou,
he granted gold and silk annually to all the great monasteries within the capital.
The practice of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* repentance ritual is truly rooted in this.
Zhao Yanhui sat by the brazier in leisurely conversation.

In the second month of spring in the fourth year of Jianyan (the gengxu year), the imperial carriage was on a tour of Wenzhou and halted at Jiangxin Temple, which was subsequently renamed Longxiang. In the eighth year of Tianhui of the Jin dynasty, the Western Xia ruler Qieqie and the Jin general Yanhe spoke of the death of Zhang Bangchang.
He then petitioned the sovereign of the state to grant him the territory south of the Yellow River;
on the ninth day of the ninth month, Liu Yu, the Governor of Jinan, was enfeoffed as Emperor at Daming, with the imperial title of Da Qi (Great Qi).
The year was named Fuchang.
The Song dynasty repeatedly launched military expeditions against him,
and Yu suffered repeated defeats.
In the year Dingsi, the Jin ruler,
finding that Liu Yu was unable to establish a state, subsequently deposed him;
Qi lasted eight years before its fall.
Yu Sheng (Yusheng) was born in Jingzhou. He governed Jinan with a resolute will. Xinhai, the eighth month of autumn in the first year of Shaoxing (1131 CE):

Fan Zongyin resigned as Chancellor; Qin Hui became the Right Chancellor. Great Jin, the ninth year of Tianhui (1141 CE); Western Xia, Renzi. Gui-chou, the ninth month of autumn in the second year of Shaoxing (1132 CE): Qin Hui resigned as Chancellor; Zhu Shengfei was reinstated as the Right Chancellor. Great Jin, the tenth year of Tianhui (1142 CE); Western Xia, Ouchou. Jia-yin, the third year of Shaoxing (1133 CE): Great Jin, the eleventh year of Tianhui (1143 CE); Western Xia, Jiayin. Jiu-yu, the fourth year of Shaoxing (1134 CE): Zhao Ding served as Chancellor for the eighth time; Emperor Taizong passed away and Emperor Xizong ascended the throne. Great Jin, the twelfth year of Tianhui (1144 CE); Western Xia, Yimao. Bing-mao, the fifth year of Shaoxing (1135 CE): Great Jin, the thirteenth year of Tianhui (1145 CE); Western Xia. Dade Year 1, the ninth month of the Song dynasty (1167 CE); Bingchen.
The Emperor visited Shang Tianzhu Temple.
Because the *púsa* (bodhisattva) had been offered to him at Wansui Xiangshan,
he summoned the abbot, Yingru, to receive an audience.
In accordance with the recommendations of Bianhui,
the Emperor bestowed gold and silk, as well as monastic certificates from the Sacrificial Department, to encourage the construction.
This began in the seventh month of the third year of the Shaoxing era.
Liáng Rújiā, Grand Master of the Dragon Diagram Pavilion (Lóngtúgé Xuéshì), served as the Prefect of Lín'ān.
He memorialized that the Great Master Yùnróng should reside at Upper Zhù (Shàngzhú).
Upon this, the Emperor was pleased and recorded the excellence of Upper Zhù.
Emperor Taizong Cheng passed away in the twelfth month of the twelfth year of Tianhui.
Emperor Xizong Xiaochengdi Dan ascended the throne.
He was the legitimate grandson of Taizu and the son of Zongjun.
It is recorded that in the thirteenth year of Tianhui, the era name was changed to Tianjuan in the year Wu-wu.
In the year Xin-you, the reign title was changed to Huangtong.
On the tenth day of the twelfth month of the ninth year of Huangtong, which was the year Jisi,
he was assassinated by his younger cousin, Prince Qi Wang Liang.
Emperor Xiaocheng reigned for sixteen years.
From his youth, he was intelligent and perceptive;
he mastered the essential classics and was fond of literary composition and dignified deportment.
Emperor Taizong held him in profound esteem and respect.
During his earlier years, he was fond of killing;
in his later years, his temperament became even more violent.
The imperial clan and the high ministers were all fearful that they would not escape [punishment].
They subsequently conspired together to watch for an opportunity to assassinate him.
Once Liang had ascended the throne as Emperor, [the plot was carried out].
Dandan was posthumously deposed as King Donghun.
After Liang died, Shizong ascended the throne and conferred the posthumous title Emperor Wuling upon Dandan.
His temple name was originally Mǐnzōng;
after some time, it was changed to Emperor Xiàochéng,
and his temple name was Xīzōng according to the *Jīnzhì*.
Bingchen (the 7th year of the Xuanhe era): The 14th year of the Tianhui era of the Da Jin (Jurchen); the Chan Master of Longquan at Tiger Hill in Pingjiang, Western Xia, entered nirvana.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa in the southwest corner.
The Master was a native of Hanshan in Hezhou;
he succeeded Chan Master Yuanwu Qin,
who in turn had succeeded Wuzu Yan of the Puding lineage.

*Dingsi*: On the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the seventh year of Shaoxing (1137), an imperial edict was issued appointing Chan Master Zonggao, "Buddha-Sun," as the abbot of Nengren Chan Monastery at Mount Jing. *Wumou* of the fifteenth year of Tianhui in the Western Xia (1158); the third month of the eighth year of Shaoxing (1138), when Qin Hui was again appointed as the Right Chancellor; the first year of Tianjuan in the Jin dynasty (1149); a silk decree and ordination certificate from the Western Xia; the eighth month of autumn in the Song dynasty.
An imperial edict was issued granting silk *duodipie* (ordination certificates) to the monks and nuns throughout the realm. This is recorded in the *Shitong Xingfei Zhi Zhongxing Li*.
Jiwu—the second year of Tianjuan and the ninth year of Shaoxing—was the year when the Western Xia and Song empires sent envoys to seek peace with the Jin.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm.

In all prefectures, counties, and provinces, Baoen Guangxiao Chan Temples were established, replacing the former Chongning Wanshou Tianning Temples, to enshrine the sacrificial offerings for Emperor Huizong. This marks the restoration of the Buddhist order during the Zhongxing era, as recorded in the *Shitong Xingfei Zhi*.

Gengshen: The tenth year of Shaoxing (1140 CE), the third year of Tianquan of the Great Jin (1149 CE), the first year of Daqing of the Western Xia established by Tabo Renxiao (1146–1170 CE), the seventh day of the eleventh month of winter in the Song dynasty.
The śramaṇa named Sijing of Miaoxing Monastery at Beiguan in Hangzhou entered nirvana;
Zhang Jiucheng, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, composed an inscription for his stupa.
Jing’s kinsman, Yu of Qiantang, established Miaoxing Monastery as a reception center.
He made offerings to the Sangha totaling three million [units].
He painted an image of Amitābha Buddha that entered the realm of the sublime and miraculous;
Minister Yang Jie composed a eulogy for it, comparing it to Amitābha himself.
People followed this and praised it.
To the north of West Lake, he carved into stone the *Great Buddha Head Stūpa Inscription* and the *Monastery Record*.

In the year *Xinyou*, the eleventh year of the Shaoxing era, when Qin Hui and Zhang Jun plotted to execute the great general Yue Fei, the Jin dynasty changed its era name to *Huangtong* Year One. At that time, Zhang Jiucheng, a *Sanlang* of the Western Xia who served as the Prefect of Wenzhou under the Song, [composed this].
His courtesy name was Zishao,
and his sobriquet was Layman Wugou.
He was a native of Yanguan, Hangzhou.
In the third month of the second year of the Xiangxing era,
the Emperor held an examination for the jinshi degree,
and Liu Jiucheng ranked first.
Jiucheng said, "The achievements of the former gentry and officials surpassed those of others;
the refined and subtle attainments of the renowned Confucian scholars of the Yi and Luo regions all arose from the awakening of the mind.
It was because of this that I pursued my studies until their ultimate realization."
He first visited Chan Master Baoyin Chuming, the successor of Dadao,
and later met Chan Master Furi Gaofu at Mount Jing,
where he attained awakening to the essential point of the mind.
Having exhausted the source and fully realized his nature,
by this Xin-you year,
the Buddha-Sun further esteemed his realization.
He ascended the hall specifically for this occasion and spoke by way of citing the Shen-bi bow;
at that time, military and state affairs were pressing.
Just as they were discussing the utility of the Shenbi bow,
the Right Chancellor Qin Hui considered this a criticism of the state administration.
In the fifth month, Min Furu was exiled to Hengzhou.
He was demoted to Nan’an Commandery;
Cheng resided there in exile for fourteen years,
lodging in a monastery at Hengpu.
His discourses on the scriptures and his written works were all things unheard of by scholars.
His "Record of Mind-to-Mind Transmission" says:
The Six Classics are all sublime teachings.
However, words are but appendages to the Way;
are the Six Classics not appendages to the Way?
To be confined by the scriptures is redundant.
It is also said:
"In this world, there is nothing that is not an illusion."
People dwell within illusion and do not realize that the turmoil of ten thousand ages arises from nowhere;
they do not know from where joy, anger, love, and hatred originate.
If one considers them to be inherently existent, then phenomena would have no form.
If one considers this as fundamentally non-existent, it cannot be held accountable for anything.
As for that which is like wood or stone, even if there were something within it capable of self-awakening,
that would still be a case of mistaking illusion for awakening.
Awakening is itself illusion;
without illusion, there is no awakening.
It is because of awakening that one perceives illusion.
If one realizes that even the self is not to be attached to, how much less so the emotions of joy, anger, love, and hatred?
How much less so the dust of fame, achievement, wealth, and nobility? — From the *Luohu Ji* by Ying Zhongwen.
In the seventh month of autumn in the Song dynasty,
Dharma Master Zhizhong Liao’ran of Taizhou, who had already resided at the White Lotus Tiantai Teaching Academy for twenty-four years,
bathed and changed his robes on this occasion.
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture and preaching the Dharma.
He authored the *Nanyue Zhiguan Zongyuan Ji* in five volumes, the *Shier Buermen Shuyao* in two volumes, and the *Huxi Qianhou Ji* in eight volumes.
The various disciples who succeeded to the Dharma—
Ze-shan, Yu-hsien, Shan-t’ang, Yuan-hsing, Pai-lien, Miao-lin, Hsü-t’ang, and Pen-k’ung— are recorded in the *Shih-t’ung Seng-chuan* (Biographies of Monks of the Buddhist Tradition).

Renxu (the 12th year of Shaoxing, the 2nd year of Huangtong of the Da Jin, and the spring of the Western Xia): Empress Dowager Wei, the Consort of Emperor Hui of the Song, known as Xianren Taishou, returned from the north; she was the consort of Emperor Huizong. In the autumn, the ninth month, Qin Hui, Duke of Ji and Left Vice President of the Department of State Affairs, was enfeoffed as Grand Preceptor, Duke of Wei; according to the *Song Jian*.
Guihai (the 10th day of the tenth month): The thirteenth year of Shaoxing, the third year of Huangtong, the sixth month of the Western Xia and Jin Xia.
Prince Yingdiao was born;
an imperial edict was issued to the Great Master Haihui.
He established Dajüqing Monastery beside the palace in the capital and universally ordained all youths within the borders who were registered with the government as monks and nuns.
The Daoist masters were treated in the same manner;
in total, there were approximately one million.
In the following year, an imperial edict was issued to retain the two Chan masters Haihui and Qinghui at Dachuqing Temple.
Record of the Construction of Jijin Temple’s Jiqing Pavilion for the Reception and Offering of the Auspicious Image.
An imperial decree of the Song dynasty established Tianshen Wanshou Yuanjue Temple on the Western Hills of Lin’an Prefecture.
On the nineteenth day of the fourth month,
he ordered the temple monk Deshin, who attended the imperial residence for scripture recitation, to carry the incense and offerings.
This reached [the Emperor] on the thirteenth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Baoping era of the Lizong reign.
At the beginning, the Emperor issued an edict appointing Master Zhan as the abbot.

[He compiled] the *Fanyi mingyi* (Explanations of Terms and Meanings), a record of the stele inscription for the *Juexing yuanjue jing* (The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra) according to the teachings and contemplations of the Ten Directions Tiantai school.
It was compiled into seven fascicles by the śramaṇa Fayun of Jingde Monastery in Suzhou—present-day Pingjiang Road—in the eighth month of autumn during the Song dynasty.
Preface by the Layman Zhōu Kuí.

Jiazi year, the fourteenth year of the Shàoxīng era of the Song dynasty; the Great Jin bestowed the temple plaque upon Yánqìng Yuàn in Míngzhōu. The fourth year of Huángtǒng of the Western Xia; the first year of Yuánqìng of the Song, by imperial decree, the temple was renamed Tiānzhú Língshān Sì (Tianzhu Lingshan Temple) as a memorial for the deceased.
In the tenth month of winter in the third year of the Qingyuan era of Emperor Ningzong,
land was selected to the west of Lingyin Temple for the establishment of ancestral offerings for Empress Dowager Wu,
known posthumously as Empress Xiansheng Cili.
When it was constructed, there was a thought of dedicating it as Jianfu Temple;
however, it was subsequently returned to its original Indian name.
This occurred in the sixth month of the tenth year of the Jiading era.
Wu Yan, the Regional Commander (Jiedushi) of Qingyuan Army, requested his son to present this memorial, saying:

"I humbly request that the merit of this offering be dedicated so that the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school may be perpetually transmitted throughout the ten directions, following the precedent of the Upper and Lower Tianzhu Monasteries."
At the beginning, by imperial decree, Jingqian was appointed as the founding abbot of the Wu Temple;

his stele inscription records that in the year Yichou—the fifteenth year of the Shaoxing era and the fifth year of the Huangtong era—he, the Great Master Haihui of the Western Xia Jin Dynasty, passed away.
The Emperor, together with the Empress, personally enshrined the śarīra relics and erected stupas at five locations.
He specifically conferred upon him the posthumous title: Great Chan Master Fo-jue Youguo (Buddha-Awakening Aided-the-Nation).
In the first month of the following year, he was granted the title of State Preceptor (Guoshi) Qinghui and the posthumous name of Great Master Fuzhi Huguo.
He ascended the throne of the State Preceptor and was specially bestowed with a golden-embroidered *saṃghāṭī* robe, rare vases, incense burners, and precious vessels.

The Emperor and Empress personally attended to his feet, prostrated themselves before him, and offered him robes—an act of reverence such as had never been seen before, according to the original biography. *Pingyin*:

The sixteenth year of Shaoxing (1146 CE), the sixth year of Huangtong of the Da Jin; *Dingmao*: The seventeenth year of Shaoxing (1147 CE), the first year of Tianxing of the Western Xia, the seventh year of Huangtong of the Jin. Following the execution of Ta-la by the Jin state, the Mongol Protector Zu Yuan Huangdi [ascended] in the first year of Tianxing.
As for his son, Prince Shenghuandulaojun,
he led his father’s former retainers in rebellion and entered into an alliance with the Menggu.
Wudu, the Grand Marshal, was not yet dead;
he personally led eighty thousand arm-bowmen trained in Central China to attack him,
but could not achieve victory for several consecutive years.
In the eighth month of the sixth year of the Huangtong era,
he again dispatched Xiao Baoshounu to enter into peace negotiations with him,
ceding twenty-seven walled encampments north of the Westping River to him.
He sent annually gifts of cattle, sheep, rice, and beans,
and further appointed Aoluo Bojilie, the chieftain, as the Auxiliary Prince of Menggu;
it was only then that peace was established.
The annual gifts were exceedingly generous.
Thereupon, Aolabai Jiele proclaimed himself Emperor Zu Yuan and changed the era name to Tianxing.
The Jin used military force for years but ultimately could not subdue them;
they merely dispatched elite troops to occupy strategic points before returning.
In the winter, the Jin Generalissimo Wuzhu died, and the Jin lost its resolve.
The Tripitaka Master of the Song Dynasty was originally named Yongdao;
he was later granted the name Fadao by imperial decree.
This was in the first year of the Xuanhua era of Emperor Huizhong.
The Emperor issued an edict changing the name of the Buddha to "Great Enlightened Golden Immortal" (Dàjué Jīnxiān).
Yongdao, the Great Master Baojue of the Chongxian Xiangji Monastery in the Left Ward, submitted a memorial to remonstrate against this.
The Emperor became enraged and banished Yongdao to Daozhou.
In the seventh year of the Xuanhua era, an imperial edict was issued for Dao to return to the capital,
where he was restored to his monastic robes and appearance;
the court thereby honored him for his protection of the Dharma.
He was granted the new name Fadao.
He resided at the Zhaoxian Monastery of Zhaoqing and concurrently presided over the Xiansheng Śākyamuni Monastery of the Right Street.
In the first year of the Jianyan era of Emperor Gaozong,
the anniversary of his birth on the twenty-first day of the fifth month was designated as the Tiānshēn Festival.
Zōngzé, the Imperial Resident of Bianjing, acted in accordance with imperial decree.
He requested to reside at Tianqing Temple on Left Street.
He was appointed as a *Chujiao Lang* (Assistant Magistrate of Propagation) to serve as a military advisor for the national prayers of incense-burning.
In the third year, Dao accompanied the imperial entourage on the southern tour.
He was summoned repeatedly to the Hall of State to participate in deliberations on military and state affairs,
and it was intended to invest him with ceremonial robes and cap.
He submitted a memorial requesting this. The Emperor granted his wish,
retaining his former title of Baojue and additionally bestowing upon him the honorific title of Great Master Yuantong Faji.
In the fifth month of the fourth year, the Emperor returned his carriage to Yuezhou.
During the summer drought,
he issued an edict for Dao to pray for rain at Yuantong Jiaosi.
The rain ceased.
The Emperor was pleased.
In the second month of the second year of the Xiangxing era.
Xuandao was summoned for an audience.
After some time,
an imperial edict was issued appointing him as the abbot of Taiping Xinglong Chan Temple on Mount Lu, in Jiangzhou.
In the second month of spring in the third year,
he submitted a memorial on the road stating that the seating order for monks and Daoists should follow the established laws of the founding emperors.
In the fifth month, there was a summer drought.
The Emperor summoned Dao to enter the inner palace to pray for rain, which was highly successful.
The Emperor bestowed a golden bowl upon Dao.
From the beginning of the Xiangsheng era until this point, seventeen years had passed.
In the fourth month, he composed the *Da Song seng shi lüe* (A Brief History of the Sangha of the Great Song).
On the twenty-first day of the seventh month in autumn, sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), he said to his disciples:
"The upholding of the Dharma depends further upon you all."
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
His stupa was erected at Jiulisuong on West Lake in Hangzhou during the Jiading era of Emperor Ningzong.
The Dongyang Wu Keci composed a biography for Dao in the local gazetteer.
Wuchen (1148), the eighteenth year of the Shaoxing era, the eighth year of the Huangtong era of the Da Jin, the Western Xia, and the Song dynasty: Chan Master Fozhi.
His name was Duanyu.
He was a descendant of the Wu-Yue King, the Qian clan,
and succeeded Chan Master Qinruowen as his dharma heir.
He first resided at Danxia in Dengzhou;
he subsequently moved to Tiger Hill and then established a hermitage at Xihu on Mount Jing.
By imperial decree, he was appointed to serve as abbot at Baoning Wanshou Monastery.
After moving from Xuansha Shoushan in Min to Xichan,
he received an imperial decree to fill the vacancy at Lingyin.
That autumn, he accepted the summons to Yuwang.
The *Pudeng lu* (General Record of the Lamp) compiled by the heir-apparent, Master Shui’an of Jingci Temple, et al.

Ji-si year, the nineteenth year of the Shaoxing era. The Jin ruler was assassinated; Emperor Liang ascended the throne and changed the ninth year [of his reign] to the first year of Tiande. First year of the Tiansheng era of Western Xia. The twenty-third day of the fifth month of the Song dynasty.
An imperial edict granted the Lady Liu the title of "Court Lady" (Jieyu) and bestowed upon her a merit cloister,
with the name Baopin Chongshou (Praising Parents, Honoring Longevity).
This was in the seventeenth year of the Jiading era of Emperor Ningzong.
Initially, an imperial edict appointed Dharma Master Zhengwu Yuancui as the founding abbot to transmit the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school throughout the ten directions.
Fengshan Liu Temple is now ranked as a secondary monastery to the two [famous] temples of Zhuyuan; this is recorded in its temple history.
On the *jiazi* day of the twelfth month of the year of Metal,
Prince Liang of Qi, the Left Chancellor, ascended the imperial throne.
He posthumously honored his father as Emperor Dezong.
The era name was changed to Tiānde.
The capital was moved to Yānjīng,
and subsequently moved again to Biànjīng.
He invaded the south, reaching Yangzhou.
On the day of Yiwu in the eleventh month of the sixth year of Zhenglong,
he was assassinated by his generals at Guishan Temple in Guazhou Town.
He reigned for thirteen years.
His posthumous title was Emperor Hailing Yangwang Jinzhi.
He was the Master Monk Muga of Longxing in Jiangxi, Song China.
His name was Fazhong.
He was the son of the Yao family from Ning County in Mingzhou.
From his youth, his disposition was focused and tranquil.
He informed his relatives of his intention to leave home for the monastic life.
His parents escorted him there,
where he studied under Master Daoying of Chongjiao Monastery in the commandery.
At the age of nineteen, he underwent the scriptural examination and received ordination.
He frequented lecture halls to thoroughly investigate the teachings and principles of the Tiantai school.
He was quite conceited.
One day, while exposing his practice of meditation to others for their critique,
he became exhausted by their challenges and consequently fell into doubt.
He went to visit Chan Master Jiao at Tiantong,
who sent him south on a pilgrimage.
He subsequently traveled to the seat of Chan Master Xu at Xuefeng in Min.
Finding no resonance there,
he went to the seat of Chan Master Fuyan Yuan of Longmen in Shuzhou, Huaisi. There,
he paced freely by the water mill.
Seeing the signboard which read, "The Wheel of Dharma Constantly Turns," he attained sudden and great enlightenment.
He spoke a verse, saying:
He turns the Great Dharma Wheel;
it envelops everything before one's eyes.
What more is there to ask?
"Water pushes a stone mill.
The Buddha-eye (Buddha) nodded his head in agreement.
He took his leave and crossed the Nine Rivers to ascend Mount Lu.
Sleeping under the open sky and lodging among the grass,
with snakes and tigers as neighbors; there,
the mountains unfold and the waters flow peacefully.
He resided at Huiyi, Juzhan, Nanyue,
Shengye, Nan, Dayun, Gai, Gong’an, and Daopei— these five monasteries—
and subsequently traveled to Huanglong in Yuzhang.
In this year, the Jisi year (1069),
the Grand Marshal Duke Xing Xiaoyang donated gold to construct a stupa for the longevity of Zhongying to the east of the temple at Xiangyuan.
As soon as the work was finished,
Zhong smiled and said,
"I am about to depart."
He wrote a verse, saying:
"For sixty-six years I have wandered within a dream-like illusion;
now I sing aloud as I return, casting off my hands into the vast emptiness."
He closed his eyes and entered stillness.
He was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Fuyan Yuan;
Yuan was the heir of Wuzu Yan.
Yan succeeded Baiyun Quan; Quan succeeded Yangqi Hui;
Hui succeeded Chan Master Ciming Yuan.
This belongs to the Linji lineage.
Those who succeeded to the Dharma of Zhong were Chan Master Puan Su and others from the *Pudeng*.
Chan Master Puan Jigan Miaoji Zhenjue Zhaoxiang’s name was Yin Su.
He was born into the Yu clan of Yichun, Yuanzhou, in Jiangxi.
At the age of six, he dreamed of a strange monk who urged him to leave the household life;
his parents then sent him away.
He received instruction from Master Ken of Jūryū-in.
At the age of twenty-seven, he shaved his head;
the following year, he received full ordination.
Xian was encouraged to read the Lotus Sūtra.
The Master said,
"I have heard the fundamental purport of all Buddhas."
He realized that true understanding must be attained within one's own mind;
he then took leave of his teacher and traveled to Lake Xiang,
where he visited Chan Master Zhong of Mukan at Mount Dapui.
Question: "The myriad dharmas return to the One;
where does the One return?
Zhong held up his whisk vertically.
The Master subsequently attained realization.
Later, he returned to the academy where he had studied.
It was then, in the *kǒuyǒu* year of the Shaoxing era (1133), that there was a neighboring temple called Cihua.
The assembly requested the Master to remain.
He lived in impermanence,
using a coarse blanket for bedding, paper for clothing, and gruel for food, while remaining absorbed in meditative concentration.
One day, while reading the *Huayan jing helun* (The Combined Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra),
he spoke this verse:
"It cannot be squeezed into a ball, nor can it be pulled apart."
What need is there for Mount Nanyue or Mount Tiantai?
No one makes use of the gates of the six sense-faculties;
it only provokes the foreign monk to come here in vain.
In his leisure time, he spoke a verse, saying:
"The numinous and wondrous Suchness is no different from the great void;
it transforms the myriad things without being obstructed by spatial boundaries."
To those who came to admire the Master’s Way,
the Master expounded the Dharma according to their needs or wrote verses for them.
For those suffering from illness, he would break off grass and give it to them as medicine;
those who received it were immediately healed.
His miraculous responses were manifold.
Consequently, he renovated the Buddhist temple.
Someone asked the Master, "What practice did you cultivate to attain this?
The Master drew a single line and said: [It is like this.]
"Do you understand?
He replied, "I do not.
The Master said:
"Stop, stop; there is no need to speak.
On the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Qiandao era of Emperor Xiaozong, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Buddhas do not appear in the world."
Furthermore, there is no nirvana.
Those who enter my chamber will surely be able to achieve primordial resonance.
Guard and uphold this well; do not allow it to decline or be lost.
He requested a bath and changed his robes;
then, sitting in the full lotus posture,
he passed away at the age of fifty-five.
He had twenty-eight years of monastic seniority.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the temple,
and he repeatedly received imperial edicts conferring posthumous titles and honorary names.
The Master’s countenance was imposing and extraordinary;
his innate wisdom was divinely inspired.
He was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Huanglong Muan Zhong, as recorded in the *Fuleng*.

Gengwu: The twentieth year of Shaoxing; the second year of Tiande of the Great Jin; the eighteenth year of Xixia. Xinwei: The twenty-first year of Shaoxing; the third year of Tiande of the Great Jin; the nineteenth year of Xixia. From the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Buddha until this point, two thousand one hundred years have passed.
Chan Master Furi of Mount Jing in Hangzhou during the Song dynasty was named Zonggao.
He was born into the Xi family of Ningguo, Xuanzhou, in Jiangdong.
He succeeded to the Dharma from Chan Master Foguo Yuanwu Qin.
Initially, in the seventh year of the Xiangxing era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing;
this was in the fifth month of the eleventh year, the Xinyou year.
While lecturing on the subject of the Shenbi bow for Zhang Jicheng,
he was stripped of his clerical status by the court and exiled to Hengzhou.
Twenty-one years later, in the eleventh month, he was transferred to Meizhou.
Before long, an imperial decree was issued restoring his clerical robes.
Having received this grace, he returned north,
where those throughout the four quarters offered him vacant seats to entice his presence.
He did not accept.
On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month, an imperial decree appointed him as abbot of Guangli Chan Temple on Mount Ayuwang in Mingzhou.
In the twenty-eighth year of the Shaoxing era, he was again summoned by imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing.
On the tenth day of the eighth month in the first year of the Longxing era of Emperor Xiaozong, he entered parinirvāṇa at the Bright Moon Hall on Mount Jing.
He was seventy-five years of age;
his monastic seniority was fifty-eight summer retreats.
His entire body was interred on the mountain of the temple;
he was posthumously granted the title Pujue (Universally Awakened),
and his stupa was named Baoguang (Jewel Light).
When Emperor Xiaozong was the Prince of Puan,
he once dispatched an inner palace supervisor to Jingshan to inquire about the Way.
Furibō (Foji) presented him with this verse:
Great roots, great vessels, and great power;
they shoulder the great matter in an extraordinary way.
On the tip of a single hair, they transmit the news.
"It is luminously manifest throughout the entire realm and leaves nothing concealed.
The King praised this and subsequently invested him as a feudal prince.
He further dispatched an inner attendant to Mount Jing to provide offerings for five hundred arhats and personally inscribed the three large characters "Miaoxi An" (Amitabha Hermitage).
He composed a hymn of praise to entrust to his teacher, saying:
"Arising and ceasing are not ceasing;
eternally abiding is not abiding."
Perfect enlightenment is empty and luminous;
it manifests according to the objects before it.
At this time, Emperor Xiaozong ascended the throne.
He was conferred the honorary title of Chan Master Dahui.
He took all the imperial calligraphy he had been granted and marked them with the Imperial Seal.
The Sage’s grace was profound and generous;
his dharma heirs and disciples were exceedingly numerous.
Among them was the Right Minister Tang Situi.
Minister of State Li Bing,
Palace Secretary Wang Zao,
and Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites Zhang Jiucheng.
The Secretariat Drafter Píngjié and those among the scholar-officials who have attained the Way and achieved thorough awakening have recorded their experiences in detail,
as found in the "Extended Letters" and the "Universal Discourses."
Zhang Jun, the Grand Guardian (Shaobao), Commander of the Baoxin Army, and Duke of Wei, inscribed the stupa for him.
His recorded sayings were granted imperial permission to be included in the Buddhist canon and circulated as part of the *Pudeng lu*.
He served as the secretary within the assembly of Chan Master Qing of Lengtang Caotang during the Longxing era of the Song dynasty.
Mingxiu Yang was a native of Nanmin.
At the imperial command, Chan Master Furi Gao moved from Hengzhou to Meiyang.
While attending upon him,
the Prefect Xie Chaoyi said to his subordinates regarding the Buddhist monk Furi:
"The so-called 'Elder' appointed by the imperial court is merely a single monk."
The vacant ground to the east of the Armory Commandant’s office was used as their dwelling place.
Soon, monks arrived in numbers reaching several hundred;
they brought spades and pickaxes to level the foundations.
They transported bamboo and wood to construct thatched huts;
when they were called upon to perform tasks, none dared to be negligent.
Although the Governor had heard of their such diligent service, he [remained unaware of their specific contributions].
Furthermore, he did not yet know what kind of person the Master was.
Thereupon, he invited him for a meeting to observe his capabilities.
Having respectfully accepted the command, they conversed at leisure for an entire day, during which the Master’s discourse was brilliant and inspired.
"Appraising the past and comparing it with the present, I find that the source of truth lies on both sides.
As we maintain and re-examine these ranks, are there perhaps others who possess extraordinary talents?
He looked up and was told that there were indeed those who bore the great sūtras and śāstras upon their shoulders.
There are those who have exhausted the depths of books and histories;
there are those whose poetry and lyrics are sublime and exquisite;
and there are those whose calligraphy and ink-wash paintings are carefree and spirited.
The reason why I have not yet attained clear and thorough realization is solely due to the great matter and causal conditions of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Therefore, I did not shrink from hardships in following you here; that I may now rely upon your benevolent governance is a fortune beyond measure.

Shou was both startled and awed, realizing that his companions were all men who had forgotten their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma. From then on, he increasingly revered Master Furi Chan and dispatched his son, Chui, to seek the shortcut to the Way. Furi showed him eight pieces of dharma-talk, which are preserved in the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) section of the *Yunwo Jitan*.
Empress Dowager Wei of Song, known as Xianren, returned from the north to the Eastern Capital in the twelfth year of the Shaoxing era.

According to the *Dongdu Shilue*, on the day of Xinwei in the tenth month of the twenty-first year, a new temple was completed at Gaoting Mountain in Hangzhou and named Chongxian Xianxiao (Venerating the Ancestors and Manifesting Filial Piety). By imperial decree, Chan Master Qingliao of Dongshan’s ninth generation, Zhenxie, was summoned to serve as its founding abbot. Upon being called to the imperial presence, he pleased the Emperor, who bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered robe.
Not long after, he passed away.
His entire body was interred at the temple,
where a stele still stands today.

Zhenxie was born in Mianzhou, Shu, into the Yong clan; he succeeded Danxia Chun, who in turn succeeded Chan Master Yingrong Kai. The Empress Dowager remarked that the Four Saints of the Daoist tradition had provided extraordinary spiritual assistance.
The Gushe Temple was renamed Yanxiang Guan to serve as a place for offering incense and lamps.
The entire remains of the Venerable Master of Gushe, Dharma-Wise (Fahui) Fazhi Yuan, were interred on the Maroon Slope of the mountain, according to the *Wulin Tujì*.

Ren-shen (1132): The twenty-second year of the Shaoxing era; the Jin dynasty moved its capital from Huiningfu to Yanjing. Tiande Year 4; the Western Xia year Gui-you (1133). The twenty-third year of the Shaoxing era; the Jin dynasty changed the era name to Zhenyuan Year 1. The Song court issued an edict appointing Yuanzhi of Dongye Mountain in Taizhou as the abbot of Upper Tianzhu Monastery.
Grand Preceptor Qin Hui asked,
"Are *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* one dharma or two dharmas?
Zhi said, "They are one dharma."
To use water as an analogy: that which is still and profoundly clear is "stopping" (zhi);
that which can reflect one's beard and eyebrows is "observation" (guan).
As for the water itself, it is one and the same.
Because the minds of sentient beings suffer from the maladies of profound delusion and extreme distraction,
one employs *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as medicine to rescue and treat them.
One returns to the entire substance of the single Dharma-realm.
The quiescence of the Dharma-realm is called *śamatha* (calm abiding);
its constant illumination while in a state of quiescence is called *vipaśyanā* (insight).
How could there be two distinct essences for the clarity and stillness of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
Huìshuài joyfully contributed fifty thousand strings of cash to construct a Dharma Hall.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth month in the twenty-eighth year of the Xiangxing era, Chan Master Yuanzhi (Zhengwu) entered nirvana.
Cao Xun composed his funerary inscription.
By imperial decree, the Dharma-successor Chief Seat Ruone was appointed to succeed him as the abbot.
Peng Jie, a Palace Secretary of the Song dynasty who served as the Governor of Luzhou,
realized the Dharma of the mind under Chan Master Dahui Zonggao;
he was styled the Layman Budong.
After the Southern Song dynasty, Buddhist canons in various monasteries were fragmented and lost.
Zhi Jie printed and distributed copies to restore them, completing more than five thousand scrolls across forty-eight collections.
Furthermore, the four great divisions were likewise so;
wherever he went, he associated with worthy scholars, high officials, eminent monks, and recluses,
continuing the legacy of the Lotus Society of Mount Lu.
Every month, he established a service for mindfulness of the Pure Land.
On the third day of the tenth month of this winter, the year of Guiyou (1753),
having donned his ceremonial robes and cap and performed two prostrations facing the imperial palace, he [proceeded].
Having donned the three robes of a monk,
he ascended the high seat, sat in the full lotus posture,
and passed away while reciting a verse— thus it is recorded in the *Fǔdēng lù*.
Wherever Dharma Master Daochen (style name Yuanbian) of Wenzhou, Song, resided,
he established a Pure Land *xiannian* (recollection) ritual hall on the twenty-third day of every month.
Eminent monks from the Chan, Vinaya, and Exegetical schools all attended these assemblies, and the number of monastics and laypeople regularly exceeded ten thousand.
On the sixteenth day of the twelfth month of winter in the Guiyou year, he passed away while sitting peacefully.
His dharma-heir disciples were Falian, Huijun, and Shen Shao; Shao compiled the *Zhinan ji* (Collection of the Guiding Instructions) in two fascicles.
The *Fófǎ xìnián lù* (Record of the Buddhist Dharma Chronologically Arranged),
a treasure of the Jianghu [literati], records that in the first year of the Zhenyuan era of the Jin dynasty,
there was a subordinate official named Wang Zhongfu from Xianyang.
He propagated the discourse of the Complete Perfection (Quanzhen) school;
Ma, Qiu, Liu, and their followers joined him,
and his teaching flourished.
In the fourth year of Taihe of Emperor Zhangzong, the Yuan Xuexi composed the "Record of the Ziwai Monastery," which fully preserves the facts.

Jiaxu (1154): the twenty-fourth year of Shaoxing of the Jin Dynasty; the second year of Zhengyuan of the Western Xia. Yihai (1155): the twenty-fifth year of Shaoxing; Grand Preceptor Qin Hui, suffering from old age and illness, requested retirement for himself and his son Qi, and subsequently passed away. Zhongguang xiaoji (Small Record of Central Guang). Zhengyuan third year of the Western Xia. Bingzi (1156): the twenty-sixth year of Shaoxing; the first year of Zhenglong of the Jin Dynasty. Western Xia. During the Song Dynasty, at Yushan in Huating, there was the Chan Master Ma Ji.
His name was Fanning.
He was born into the Li family in Juxian, Mizhou, Shandong.
In his youth, he entered the monastic order under Master Miaokong at Tianning Monastery in Yizhou.
He resided at Jingju Monastery on Mount Maju in Yizhou.
At the beginning of the Shaoxing era,
he traveled by sea and arrived at Qinglong Town in Huating.
There was a high official serving as a provincial judge named Zhang Gun, whose mother, Lady Gao,
dreamed of a celestial being who said, "An ancient Buddha is coming.
The following morning, the Master arrived.
He welcomed him to the Qian family garden,
where the Master then constructed a vihāra;
while excavating the foundation, he obtained auspicious responses in the form of an iron chime, a fragmentary stele, and a Buddhist image.
Liu Yue, the Magistrate of Huating, submitted a petition to the authorities requesting that the temple he had built be granted the imperial plaque name "Jingju" (Pure Abode).
He then traveled to Mingzhou to visit Miaokong at Xuedou and established a hermitage on the Beifeng Peak of Putuo.
It is said that the present Governor of Sobaeng-gun, Mo Jang, requested [the master] to preside over Jixiang-sa.
Originally, during the Yuanfu era of Emperor Zhezong,
there was a hermitage on Mount Yu called Lingfeng.
The Ministry requested that the plaque be changed to read "Zhaoqing Chan Monastery.
Right Vice-Minister Zhu E invited the Master to serve as its founding abbot,
after which he moved to Guanghui Monastery in Mingzhou.
He returned once more to Zhaokong Temple.
On the eighth day of the first month of this Bingzi year, he entered nirvana.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the east of the abbot’s quarters.
His worldly age was seventy-six,
and his monastic seniority was fifty-nine summer retreats.
He succeeded Chan Master Ming of Xuedou as his dharma heir.
Ming succeeded Changlu He;
He succeeded Fayun Ben.
This concludes the Five Lamps Compendium of the Yunmen School.

Dingchou (1137): The 27th year of Shaoxing of the Song; the 2nd year of Zhenglong of the Jin; the 1st year of Xixia. Wuyin (1138): The 28th year of Shaoxing; the 3rd year of Zhenglong; the 2nd year of Xixia. Ji Mao (1139): The 29th year of Shaoxing; the 4th year of Zhenglong; the 3rd year of Xixia. Gengchen (1140): The 30th year of Shaoxing; the 5th year of Zhenglong; the 4th year of Xixia. In this year, the Song Emperor issued an edict bestowing a posthumous title upon the Venerable Ciyun of Tiantong Temple at Tianzhu, Hangzhou.
The presiding master of the repentance ceremony was Dharma Master Chanhui.
The inscription on the stele at the base of the Rui Guang Pagoda states:

"Xinsi, the thirty-first year of Shaoxing (1161), established by Emperor Shizong of Jin; it was rectified in the first year of Longxing (1163). It is the first year of Dading (1161) of the Western Xia-Jin Xinsi year, the seventh month of autumn."
The Jin ruler Liang moved the capital to Bianjing.
In the ninth month, Liang broke the treaty and launched an invasion of Song.
The Song Emperor issued an edict to lead a personal campaign against him.
Liang was courageous in execution and slaughter;
he raised troops and incited calamity.
At that time, heroes and elites rose up together.
The renowned Wang Youzhi and Geng Jing of Jinan raised forces;
Chen Jun of the Taihang Mountains incited and gathered a host of righteous followers;
and Yelü Woa’er, a descendant of the Khitans, rose up together with them in the desert wastes.
Thereupon, ten thousand men from one military command in Bohai rebelled against Liang and returned to Huining Prefecture.
They enthroned Liu Xiu as emperor; Xiu changed his name to Yong.
He was the grandson of Taizu.
Ji was the son of Zongfu.
On the geng day of the first month of the tenth lunar month.
Shou ascended the imperial throne and changed the era name to Dading. The Left Chancellor,
Zhang Hao, recorded Shou’s imperial amnesty decree from Bianjing and dispatched it on horseback to report to Liang.
Liang sighed and said,
"I intended to wait until the south of the Yangtze was pacified before adopting the principle of 'one campaign for great stability' to mark the beginning of a new era.
Yet this son has anticipated me."
He ordered a casket of books to be brought and showed them to him;
they were premonitory prophecies concerning the change of the reign title.

On the day of Yiwei in the eleventh month, the various generals assembled more than ten thousand troops and, with their bowstrings drawn, charged directly into the interior of Liao’s sleeping quarters.
The elite guards on both sides scattered and fled;
the generals shot at the interior of the tent,
and arrows fell like rain.
Liang then passed away.
His crown prince, Guangying, remained in Bianjing,
where he was also killed by the multitude.
Hou posthumously deposed Hualiang as Prince of Hailing and conferred upon him the posthumous title of Emperor Yang.
Lady Tudan was subsequently made the Consort of Hailing.
Xiu changed his name to Yongdu and made Yanjing his capital.
He was benevolent, generous, compassionate, and frugal.
He occupied the throne for twenty-nine years.
This is called the "Minor Yao and Shun" in the *Jin-zhi*.
Renwu (1182), the thirty-second year of the Shaoxing era of the Song, the second year of the Dading era of the Jin, the first month of the Yongyuan era of Emperor Yezhen of the Western Xia.
He entered the capital at Yan;
because his father’s name was Zongfu, his own name was changed to Zongyao.
He was posthumously honored with the title Emperor Yi.
He established Dajianqingshou Monastery to the north of the capital city of Yan and issued an imperial decree appointing Chan Master Xuanying Yi as its founding first patriarch.
The Emperor issued an edict for Prince Yan to descend with incense and grant twenty thousand strings of cash and twenty *qǐng* of irrigated fields as a record for Jīnzì Temple.
In the second month of the Song dynasty,
the Emperor returned from Jiankang to Lin’an Prefecture.
In the sixth month, by imperial decree, Jian Wang Wei, a seventh-generation descendant of Emperor Taizu,
was granted the name Jin and established as the Crown Prince.
His elder brother’s son, Zicheng, was posthumously enfeoffed as King of Xiu.
On the Bingzi day,
the Emperor abdicated the throne to the Crown Prince, who ascended to the imperial throne.
The Emperor assumed the title of Taishang Huangdi (Retired Emperor).
Residing at the Dēshòu Palace,
in the tenth month of winter,
due to incessant rain, he issued an imperial edict for the eunuch Deng Congyou to carry incense and offer prayers to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva at Upper Zhù Monastery.
That very day, the weather cleared.
The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon him three grades of royal offerings from the Inner Treasury to express his gratitude for having previously beheld the *Record of the Treasure King*.
As for Emperor Xiaozong, his posthumous name was Shaozong and his personal name was Zhen.
He enfeoffed his younger brother as king and established him as the Crown Prince.
At the age of thirty-six, he received the internal abdication and ascended the imperial throne.
He established the twenty-second day of the tenth month as the Festival of National Celebration.
With resolute intent, he sought to recover the Divine Land (Shenzhou).
When his ministers urged the Emperor to focus on internal cultivation, he replied:
Thereupon, he spread civil virtue,
sought out the grievances of the people,
and encouraged agriculture and sericulture.
He improved irrigation works,
clarified the systems of reward and punishment,
and cherished the imperial regalia.
He visited the Retired Emperor once every five days to provide the utmost service to both palaces.
He occupied the throne for twenty-seven years.
He abdicated the throne to the Crown Prince and styled himself the Retired Emperor (Taishanghuang).
He lived to the age of sixty-eight.
Record of the Patriarchs: 2nd Year of Longxing, 9th Year of Qiandao, 16th Year of Chunxi.
Guiwei (50th year of the sexagenary cycle). July, 3rd Year of Dading of the Da Jin (Great Jin), 1st Year of Longxing; Imperial Praise for Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva by the Ruler of Western Xia.
The Emperor presided over Seondeokjeon Hall and composed a eulogy for Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Great Being, Avalokiteśvara..."
By virtue of what is called the supernatural power manifested through the Universal Gate (Samantamukha),
he left his traces at Tianzhu Mountain in Hangzhou;
his arrival there dates back to ancient times.
Whenever I offer prayers,
there is a response that accords with my thoughts;
whether for rain or for sunshine, it never deviates by even a moment.
This is of assistance to the people of China.
Therefore, he composed a eulogy, saying:
"How admirable is the Great Being!"
Originally perfect and pervasive,
it manifests through speech to serve as the foundation for the world.
Brilliantly illuminating and non-dual,
they regard all equally with compassion,
responding immediately to every stimulus.
The exquisite and inconceivable stone inscription from Upper Zhuguo records that,
by imperial decree of the Song dynasty, Chan Master Liaoming of Jiangshan was appointed to reside at Jingshan.
Liaoming was born into the Lu family of Xiuzhou.
He succeeded the Chan Master Dahui Zonggao;
Prince Yang held him in profound esteem and donated his manor lands in Suzhou to him.
The annual revenue was twenty thousand *hu*. Because of this, Mount Jing was abundantly provided for, and the Stele of Master Ming’s Vocation and Practice (*Xingye Be*) was further augmented.

Jia-shen (1st year of Longxing; 4th year of Dading, Western Xia): Western Xia. Bing-you (1st year of Qiandao; 5th year of Dading, Western Xia): Western Xia. Ceng-xu (2nd year of Qiandao; 6th year of Dading, Western Xia): Western Xia. Ding-hai (3rd year of Qiandao; 7th year of Dading, Western Xia): In the second month of spring in the Song dynasty, [the Emperor] issued an edict appointing Daochang of Lingyin Monastery to reside at Jingci Monastery. Daochang was a native of Huzhou; he received his monastic training at Bukui Lukouyuan Temple. Dading 6th year, Western Xia. Dinghai 3rd year, Qiandao; 7th year, Dading, Western Xia. Spring, 2nd month of the Song dynasty.
The Emperor visited Shang Tianzhu Temple to pay his respects to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and asked the abbot, Ruone:
"Why do you perform the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* repentance ritual every year?
Nae replied,
"The Great Brahma, Honored Deva, is the lord of this Sahā world."
Śakra Devānām Indra, the Lord of Devas, governs the Heaven of the Thirty-three and oversees the lands below.
The Four Great Kings of the Quarters have sworn together to protect the Dharma and the people.
Therefore, the Buddha preached the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-samādhi* for the sake of the various devas;
this is a scripture for the golden age of an imperial reign.
It is fitting that the state maintain its ritual offerings and perform it annually.
The Emperor was pleased and promoted Nan to the rank of Right Street Monk Registrar (Youjie Senglü), granting him twenty thousand coins.
He immediately established the Hall of the Sixteen Contemplations at the site formerly occupied by the founding monk Daoyi of the Shijin period.
An imperial edict was issued for Lou Yao, a Hanlin Academician, to compose a record based on the diagrams;
it was also constructed within the Forbidden City.
On the eighth day of the fourth month of the following year, the Buddha’s birthday, [it was completed].
He invited fifty monks to enter the Inner Contemplation Hall to perform the *Rāṣṭrapāla Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-samādhi*.
After the meal, he commanded Sunul to preach the Dharma.
The Emperor was pleased and promoted him to the rank of Left Street Monk Registrar,
bestowing upon him the title of Dharma Master Huiguang.
Each of the monks was granted one roll of silk.
From that time on, it became an annual custom to bestow fifty bolts of silk on the Buddha’s birthday,
which were delivered to Upper Tianzhu Temple to be used for the performance of Buddhist rites.

In the eleventh month of the sixth year of the Qiandao era, the Emperor personally inscribed the twelve large characters "Linggan Guanyin zhi si, Linggan Guanyin baodian" (The Temple of the Responsive Avalokiteśvara,
the Precious Hall of the Responsive Avalokiteśvara) and bestowed them upon Shang Tianzhu.
On the seventh day of the first month in the ninth year of the Qiandao era,
Xuanout entered the Xuande Hall for an audience to illuminate the teachings of the Mountain Gate.
At the beginning of the fifth watch, he was summoned for an audience and granted a seat.
The Emperor said,
"Last year at the New Year, you once went to the vegetarian hall for the Bodhisattvas."
Nal replied,
"I have already received the Imperial Grace.
The Emperor said:
"How are the ritual procedures for the *Guangming* (Light) Repentance?
Nan said, "In the sutras,
there are both repentances based on principle (*li*) and repentances based on phenomena (*shi*)."
As for repentance through principle,
one sits upright and investigates the mind;
therefore it is said that karmic obstructions are like frost and dew.
All arise from deluded conceptualization;
sitting upright, one contemplates the true nature of reality.
The sun of wisdom is able to eliminate them.
There are five types of ritual repentance.
One should reverently rectify one's own mind and contemplate with sincere intent the profound meaning of emptiness in the Mahāyāna.
To follow what is good as water flows and to reform one's faults without regret is the foremost method of practicing repentance;
to serve one’s parents with filial piety precedes all other concerns.
This is the cultivation of the second repentance.
To govern the world according to the True Dharma and not oppress the people is the cultivation of the third repentance.
To refrain from killing within one's domain on the six fast days is the cultivation of the fourth repentance;
it consists of deep faith in cause and effect and maintaining the mind focused upon cause and effect.
Not forgetting the entrustment at Vulture Peak is the cultivation of the fifth repentance;
it does not require a fixed period for prostrations.
If one can practice these five,
then through the correspondence between practice and principle,
this is called the repentance of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said,
"This has truly opened my understanding.
The Emperor continued:
"What sutra do you lecture on every day?
Nang said,
"The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma."
The Emperor asked,
"In what part does the excellence of this seven-fascicle scripture lie?
Nǜ replied:
To cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
without ever disturbing the fundamental essence—
this is like turning iron into gold.

The Venerable Maudgalyāyana, fearing that it might be deficient or coarse, [intervened].
He personally employed his supernatural powers to lead thirty-two artisans up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
After observing the primary and secondary marks three times, he finally attained their true likeness; once they were completed, [he returned].
The king and his subjects revered him as if he were the true Buddha.
When the Buddha returned from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the human realm,
the king led his ministers and commoners to go together and welcome the Buddha.
This image leaped into the air and bowed its head toward the Buddha.
The Buddha stroked its head and conferred upon it this prediction:
"A thousand years after my parinirvāṇa..."
From this point, you shall extensively benefit humans and devas in the eastern land of China for one thousand two hundred and eighty-five years; in the western land [of India],
it will be sixty-eight years of the Gui-zi era.
Fourteen years in Liangzhou;

In the north, he resided at Sheng’an Temple in Yanjing for twelve years;

Xinwei (the 10th day of the second month): In the fourth year of Jiading of the Jin dynasty, the third year of Dà'ān of the Western Xia, and the first year of Guāngdìng of Emperor Shenzong, in the spring, Tàobá Xū of the Western Xia was established as the Prince of Fàn.
At first, he was attacked by a great army and sought assistance from Jin,
but Jin was unable to save him.
The people of Xia then rebelled against the Jin.
At that time, the power of the Great Dynasty grew even stronger;
it simply remained in its former territory.
A provincial administration was established in Yan-yun,
and its governance was entrusted to a high-ranking minister known as the Grand Preceptor (Taishi) and Prince (Guowang).
The ancestors of the Dàtá (Tatars) were of the same lineage as the Nǚzhēn (Jurchens);
both were descendants of the Mòhè (Mohe).
During the periods of the Northern Wei, Qi, Northern Qi, Zhou, and the Yuwén (Northern Zhou), their country was called Wùjí (Wugui).
During the Sui dynasty, they were called the Mohe.
Their territory lay six thousand li northeast of Chang’an;
to the east it bordered the sea and was divided into several dozen commanderies.
There are names such as Black Water and White Mountain;
the White Mountain was originally a subject of Koguryo,
and the Tang dynasty subsequently conquered Koguryo.
The displaced people fled into Bohai;
only Heishui remained strong and independent,
and when Bohai flourished, it brought all the Mohe tribes under its subjection.
Later, they were attacked by the Xixia and Khitan;
their tribes were dispersed.
They resided on the upper reaches of the Hunton River, at Changbai Mountain in Liaodong Kaiyuan Road, Xianping Prefecture, where the Black Water and Suli River originate.
It is said that the Hontonggang was originally called Nujin, also known as the Hontonggang;
it is the source of the Danyuan River of Goryeo.
It was, in fact, the land of the ancient Xushen, the descendants of the Heishui (Black Water) people who resided in the Yin Mountains.
They styled themselves as Tatars.
During the late Tang and the Five Dynasties periods, they frequently maintained communication with China.
At the beginning of the Song dynasty, they each once again presented tribute.
The Dàtá (Tatars) are all brave and fierce, and skilled in warfare.
Those who dwell near the lands of the Hán are called the "Mature" (Shú) Dàtá;
they are still capable of cultivating millet and broomcorn millet.
They cook and eat it in flat-bottomed earthen cauldrons.
Those who live further away are called the "Raw Tatars";
they subsist solely on hunting and gathering.
They have no armor or weapons, using only bone-tipped arrows;
this is because their land does not produce iron.
Although they maintain a market for trade with the Khitans, [they do not obtain metal].
The regulations regarding iron currency were extremely strict.
Later, when the Jurchens captured Hedong and executed Liu Yu, they abolished the iron coins.
Consequently, all iron coins from Qin and Jin fell into the hands of the Dada.
Having obtained it, he subsequently manufactured great military implements,
and the state thereby grew increasingly powerful during the height of the Jin dynasty.
The Tatars entered with tribute annually.
When the Prince of Wei, the Golden Lord, established the Tatar ruler Temüjin as Emperor Chenghiz Khan,
the two rivers of Shandong were all annexed by the Great Court.
Furthermore, there was the state of Menggu,
located to the northeast of the Jurchens;
the Tang dynasty referred to it as the Mengwu tribe.
The Jin state calls them Mengwu;
they are also called Menggu.
Their people do not cook their food over fire.
They can see in the night.
Their scales are made of the skin of the *śiśumāra* fish,
which can withstand flying arrows.
Rebellion first broke out during the Tianquan era of Emperor Xizong of the Jin Dynasty.
The Grand Marshal, Zongbi, waged war for many years but was ultimately unable to suppress it;
Zongbi is the same as Wumu, also known as the Fourth Prince. Instead of suppressing the rebels, he divided his forces to occupy strategic points and even provided them with generous bribes.
That state also styled itself the Zuyuan Emperor.
When it established its era name, it became a source of border trouble;
it captured Han Chinese men and women of the Khitan and made them its wives and concubines.
From that time on, they gradually began to consume cooked food.
Upon reaching this great era, they then styled themselves the Great Mongol State.
However, these two states resided in the eastern and western regions respectively.
They are separated by several thousand *li* when viewed from one another;
I do not know on what basis they were combined into a single name.
It was likely during the height of the Jin dynasty that the Northeastern Pacification Commission (*Dongbeizhaotaosī*) was established there.
To resist and defend against the incipient power of Goryeo,
the Southwest Pacification Commission was established to govern the northern territories occupied by the emerging state of Xixia.
In brief, when the Great Ancestor (Tàizǔ) founded the Jin dynasty, his territory comprised twenty-seven encampments; as for its northern borders,
it bordered Linhuang Prefecture to the east and neighbored the Xia Kingdom to the west.
To the south it borders Jingzhou, and to the north it reaches the country of Daren;
today, these lands are entirely possessed by the Great Court (the Chinese Empire). — *Jin zhi* (The Annals of Jin).

Ren-shen (壬申): The fifth year of Jiading; the Jin dynasty changed [the era name] to the first year of Chongqing. The Western Xia year was Gui-you (癸酉). The sixth year of Jiading; the Da-Jin dynasty changed [the era name] to the first year of Zhining. In the ninth month, it was changed to the first year of Zhenyou. In the eighth month of the Western Xia year, He-shi-lie-zhi-zhong (紇石烈執中) was appointed as Right Vice Commander-in-Chief by the Jin.
He dispatched three thousand troops skilled in martial arts to confront the enemy's main force.
On the twentieth day, they departed from Yanjing and reached Zijin Pass.
Zhi Zhong opened the pass to lure the enemy inside.
Hearing that the great army had passed through the pass and was fleeing in disarray at once,
Zhizhong returned to the capital and reported to the Emperor, saying,
"The power of the great army is formidable and difficult to withstand."
Wanyan Gang also returned in defeat.
He secretly memorialized that it was because Zhizhong had dispatched a large army into the pass.
Upon hearing this, Zhizhong feared execution.
Previously, the Left Vice Marshal Nanping Juge had distributed rewards to his troops, which the multitude resented.
Taking advantage of this public indignation and wishing to depose the ruler,
Zhizhong led his army back under the pretext of executing Nanping.
On the twenty-fourth day, the army arrived outside the Donghua Gate.
He summoned Nanping to deliberate on affairs and slew him with his own hand.
When the palace heard of the upheaval, the gates were all kept closed.
Zhizhong intended to set fire to the gate;
the gatekeeper general was about to open it when Zhizhong led his troops into the palace.
The attendants all fled in dispersal.
Zhizhong dispatched troops to seize the Emperor and his consort, imprisoning them in the former palace.
On the night of the twenty-sixth day of the month, Jia-wu, Zhizhong sent the eunuch Li Jiancheng to assassinate the sovereign at his residence.
The ruler of the country was benevolent and kind by nature;
he was the most virtuous among his brothers.
He occupied the throne for five years.
When King Seonjong ascended the throne, [he] was demoted and enfeoffed as Marquis of Donghae Commandery.
King Seonjong’s personal name was Seun;
he was the grandson of King Sejong.
Hyeonjong was the eldest son of Yun-gong.
On the *bingwu* day of the ninth month,
he ascended the throne and changed the first year of Jining to the first year of Jeongu.
He enfeoffed He-shi-lie Chih-chung as Grand Preceptor (Ta-shih), Commander-in-Chief of All Armies (Tu-yüan-shuai), Head of the Three Ministries,
and Prince of Ze. The main army reached Tsui Chin Kuan,
located two hundred li from Yanjing.
He dispatched Gao Qi, the Left Supervisor of the Army, with five thousand troops from the Jiū division to resist them.
They failed to arrive on schedule;
Zhizhong intended to execute them for this.
The King, recognizing his great merit, issued a decree commuting his death sentence.
Zhizhong was further provided with reinforcements and sent forth with the command:
"If you are victorious, you shall redeem your crime."
"If you are defeated, you shall be executed without pardon.
When they went out to battle, the army was utterly routed.
He realized that he would certainly be killed by those who had captured him.
He then led his纠察 troops (jiūjùn) to surround and seize Zhōngfǔ, storming into his bedchamber and killing him.
He withdrew to the Yìngtiān Gate to await punishment;
on the *xīnhài* day of the tenth month, the Ruler of the State, because Gāoqǐ commanded the army, did not wish to impose further punishment upon him.
He completely rounded up and executed those within the inner court who had committed regicide.
He then appointed Gao Qi as Chancellor of Military Affairs and State, concurrently serving as Grand Marshal of the Imperial Secretariat.
At that time, the main army was besieging Yanjing.
Furthermore, regarding the Song dynasty’s plan for a joint attack against the Jin:
in the *jiǎxū* year— the seventh year of Jiading (1214) of the Great Jin, the second year of Zhenyou of Western Xia,
and the third month of the Jin calendar— the capital was short of grain.
Of the soldiers and civilians, fourteen or fifteen out of ten died of starvation.
The Jin ruler dispatched an envoy to the Great Army to negotiate a peace treaty.

He demanded the Princess, ten generals who had escorted the imperial carriage, one hundred elite troops to accompany the Princess, five hundred boys and girls for each, three thousand sets of embroidered garments, three thousand imperial horses, and gold, silver, pearls, and jade.
Furthermore, he requested that the Left Chancellor, Wanyan Fuxing, be taken as a hostage;
the Jin ruler granted all these requests and provided the younger daughter of the Marquis of Donghai to fulfill them.
He further caused the King of Jin to bow from afar toward his own country;
the King did not dare refuse.
He spoke again, saying:
The Marshal had besieged Yan for a long time without ever plundering;
he desired gold and silk to reward his troops,
and the ruler likewise granted his request.
The Great Army returned north.
At that time, three *jin* of silver in the capital could not purchase three *sheng* of rice;
those who died were beyond counting.
The court deliberated on the relocation of the capital to Bianliang.
On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month, the imperial entourage set out;
on the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month, they entered the city of Bianjing.
When Da-jun returned,
he heard that Jin had moved the capital to Bian and said in anger,
"Since we have already reached peace, this relocation shows they harbor suspicions and will not let go of their resentment."
This was merely a stratagem to win me over through conciliation.
In the eighth month of the following year, they again besieged Yanjing;
they dispatched troops to seize the prefectures and commanderies of Central China and sent an envoy to Bianliang.
He requested gold, silver, and other supplies as rewards for his troops,
and the Jin Emperor granted them all.
The forces from Dongping, Daming, and Zhending who had come to assist the throne were all defeated when they encountered the main army.
From that time on, communication between the inner and outer courts was cut off.
Prince Shouxu took a secret route from Yanjing to return to Bianjing.
The palaces and imperial precincts of Yanjing were magnificent and beautiful, ranking foremost among all those of past and present.
At this point, it was burned by rebel troops. The fire did not cease for over a month.

Jin-zhi (Yi-hai): The eighth year of Jiading; the third year of Zhenyou of the Da Jin; the Bingzi year of the Western Xia. Consequently, he harbored designs to spy upon the Yangtze and Han rivers;

Wu-yin (Earth Tiger): The 11th year of Jiading; the 2nd year of Xingding; the Western Xia era. Ji-mao (Fire Rabbit): The 12th year of Jiading; the 3rd year of Xingding; the Western Xia era. Master Chijue.

In the morning, an imperial decree was issued appointing him to Huqiu to oversee the care of the elderly.

Gengchen (Metal Dragon): The 13th year of Jiading; the 4th year of Xingding of the Da Jin; the 1st year of Xinxi of the Western Xia. Empress Yang, with the support of Shì Mǐyuǎn, established Guìchéng as the Crown Prince.

This concludes the Continued Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government.
In the tenth month of the Golden Year, King Sun of the state passed away;
his temple name was Xuanzong.
He was the third son [of the previous ruler].
Shu Xu was the heir apparent and the successor to the throne; he was a follower of the Yizong school.
By nature, he was broad-minded, gentle, compassionate, and benevolent.
From his youth, he had been fond of books.
He was tall and widely learned;
his literary talent was abundant and he delighted in composing writings.
He held office for eleven years with a resolute will.
Emperor Lizong, whose personal name was Yun,
was a nephew of Emperor Ningzong.
At the age of twenty, he ascended the imperial throne.
He revered the study of the Way and honored the ranks of scholars; thus,
at the beginning of his reign, all things flourished in harmony.
In his later years, the Chancellor Jia Sidao purchased private lands to establish state-owned estates.
He suppressed military rewards and failed to distribute them;
consequently, the national prestige suffered many setbacks and declined.
He reigned for forty-one years.
He passed away at the age of sixty-one. [The reigns continued through] the Tongjian of the Song Dynasty: Baoping 3, Shaoding 6, Duanping 3, Jiaxi 4, Chunyu 12, Baoyu 6, Kaiqing 1, and Jingding 5.

*Yǐyǒu* (Year of the Earth-Sheep): The first year of Bǎoqìng (Jin); the first year of Zhèngdà (Xīxià). *Bǐngxū* (Year of the Wood-Dog): The second year of Bǎoqìng (Jin); the second year of Zhèngdà (Xīxià). thus, the Jin state fell into distress. (Jin Annals, Dinghai year).
Baokeng 3rd year (Zhengda 3rd year). Western Xia. The destruction of Western Xia began during the Tiangcheng era of Mingzong of the Later Tang dynasty of the Five Dynasties period.
While they committed acts of disorder and plunder, the prefectural cities were thrown into turmoil.
Furthermore, various garrisons in Hexi reported that Li Renfu, the Commander of the Dingnan Commandery, was secretly communicating with the Khitan.

In the third year of the Changxing era, the year of Guiwei (943), Renfu passed away.

but Renchao did not obey the imperial decree.
He dispatched his elder brother, King A-la, to guard the Qingling Pass.
He assembled the various Hu tribes within his borders, such as the Dangxu, to defend himself and treated the imperial court with contempt.
On the day of Dingchou, the second month of the second year of Emperor Qingtai’s reign.

The Regional Inspector Li Xichao submitted a memorial stating he was ill, and thus his elder brother, Xi Yin, the Military Governor (Xingjun Sima), was appointed to act as the interim governor of the military prefecture.

an imperial edict was issued appointing Liu Yīn as the Commissioner for the Southwestern Front of the Khitan to lead the punitive expedition.
On the day of Jia-yin in the first month of the second year of the Qianyou era of the Han dynasty,

On the day of Xin-wei in the second month.

Yin harbored an air of arrogance because of the many troubles in the Central Plains;
whenever a regional governor rebelled, he [would take advantage].
Chang Yin constantly assisted him in seeking heavy bribes;
the court, becoming aware of these affairs,
likewise bound him with favors and emoluments.
On the day of Gengyin in the first month of the second year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty,

he consequently blocked the roads so that the Zhou envoys could not pass.
On the day of Guiwei in the second month,

this concludes the *Tongjian* (Comprehensive Mirror) up to the tenth month of the seventh year of Taiping Xingguo during the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty.
Li Jibang came to court.

This was during the Wuyin year of the Baoyuan era of Emperor Renzong.
Zhao Yuanhao had usurped the title of Emperor;
on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month in this year, the *dinghai* year,
the great army of the Northern Court annihilated him.
A total of one hundred and ninety years. *Song Jian* (Mirror of the Song Dynasty): Wuzi: The first year of Shaoding;

the fourth year of Zhengda of the Da Jin. Jichou: The second year of Shaoding; the fifth year of Zhengda. Gengyin: The third year of Shaoding; the sixth year of Zhengda.
