In the spring of this year, the Jin dynasty changed its era name to Kaixing; in the summer, it was changed again to Tianxing. Tianxing Year 1: The Jin state was surrounded by a great army at Bianjing.
The Jurchens employed a hundred stratagems to defend the city.
As the weather turned hot in the fourth month,
the great army intended to withdraw its forces.
Furthermore, peace was negotiated and established;
the Crown Prince’s rank of Jinzi was taken as a hostage,
and the gold and silk bestowed upon him were beyond counting.
Although the enemy forces were temporarily repelled within the city,
the troops were exhausted and their strength spent;
the region south of the river was left in total disarray.
The Song army spies upon its south;
the Hong rebels disturb its east.
An imperial messenger arrives again with a command.
The Jin ruler abolished his honorary title and received the imperial decree acknowledging him as a subject.
He removed his crown and cap and shaved his head,
serving as the Guardian of the Western Capital to hand over the city to the Song.
The Jin ruler found this difficult to accept;
he personally led five thousand guardsmen to break through the encirclement and engage the main army, achieving victory.
The Left Chancellor, Wanyan Baisha, memorialized,
requesting that they cross the river to seize Weizhou and cut off their route of retreat,
proceeding northward to Weizhou where the main army would assemble in great numbers.
The Jin Emperor hurried back and was pursued by them;
the Commander-in-Chief Heduxi died for him.
Previously, once the Jin Emperor had departed, he had entrusted the affairs of the留守 (Liu-shou, Imperial Resident) to Cui Li.
After the defeat at Weizhou,
the followers of the various armies were reduced to only two thousand men.
When the capital city of Bianjing heard this, [it was alarmed].
Cui Li executed all the court officials remaining in the capital.
He then surrendered the Empress Dowager, the Empress, the Imperial Consorts, the Princesses, and the Imperial Brother, Prince Jing, to the great army.
He seized all the gold, silk, pearls, jade, and articles of luxury from the palace to present as tribute.
He styled himself King of Zheng and concurrently Chancellor.
Consequently, the main army invested him with the title of Acting Emperor of the Henan Provincial Administration.
The Jin ruler remained in Guidefu. (From the *Dajin guozhi*).

Gui-si (the 10th day of the tenth month), the sixth year of Shao-ding (1233 CE), the second year of Tian-xing of the Da-jin (Great Jin). In the second year of Tian-xing, the Jin lost its grain supplies in Gui-de.
On the wu-xu day of the sixth month, the Jin ruler moved from Hao to Cai-zhou.
In the eleventh month of the Song year, he dispatched Jiang Hai, the Grand Marshal of Xiangyang, and Meng Gong, the Commander of Xiangyang,
with a force of forty thousand troops to attack Caizhou, stationing them south of the city.
The regional commander Shi Songzhi, the nephew of [Duan] Mingyuan, transported one hundred thousand measures of grain to supply the armies of the north and south;
furthermore, he established a market at the south of the city for mutual trade.
The great army relied upon this.
On the ninth day of the twelfth month, the great army attacked the outer city and captured it.
On the sixteenth day, the great army exerted its full strength in attacking the western city but was unsuccessful.
On the eighteenth day, the great army arrived once more and breached its western wall.
On the nineteenth day, the Jin ruler distributed all his personal utensils as rewards to the soldiers.

Jia-wu, the first year of Duanping; the third year of Tianxing of the Da Jin; the Jin dynasty fell on the night of the tenth day of the first month of the Jin calendar.
Three divisions of elite troops were stationed at the Western City.

The Jin Emperor personally held the tally and seal and conferred them upon him, saying:
"The reason I entrust these to you is..."
How could I have had any choice?
Because my body is stout, I am ill-suited for horseback riding;
